Chapter 1 — SQL Fundamentals & Syntax
This is the bedrock chapter. Every SQL interview — TCS fresher pool, Infosys lateral, Razorpay phone
screen, JP Morgan GCC panel, Swiggy data role — opens with at least three or four questions from this
set, and Indian service-MNC fresher rounds lean almost entirely here. The questions are not glamorous,
but the candidates who fumble DDL-vs-DML, NULL semantics, or GROUP BY rules get cut in the first
ten minutes. Master these twenty and you'll never lose a round to a "basic" question again. Each page
below gives you the 30-second answer first, then the layered reasoning, then the one edge case the
interviewer is waiting to hear you say out loud.
Section A — Statement Categories & Schema Basics
Q1 · DDL vs DML vs DCL vs TCL — What Belongs Where
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant, Accenture · Topic: SQL Fundamentals
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can you tell me what DDL, DML, DCL and TCL stand for, and give me at least two example
statements for each category?
The 30-second answer: DDL is Data Definition Language — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE — it
changes schema. DML is Data Manipulation Language — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, (and SELECT in
many lists) — it changes rows. DCL is Data Control Language — GRANT, REVOKE — it changes
permissions. TCL is Transaction Control Language — COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT — it controls
transaction boundaries.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the one-line definition of each category — interviewers are
mentally ticking off four boxes. 2. Pair each acronym with at least two real statements; don't just expand
the acronym and stop. 3. Mention the grey areas: SELECT is technically DQL (Data Query Language) in
strict classifications but most Indian textbooks bucket it under DML, so say both and move on. 4. Be
ready for the auto-commit trap: in MySQL and Oracle, DDL statements implicitly COMMIT — so you
cannot ROLLBACK a CREATE TABLE.
Edge cases to mention: - TRUNCATE is DDL, not DML, even though it removes rows — that's why it is
faster and cannot be rolled back in MySQL. - Postgres treats DDL as transactional, so you can wrap
CREATE TABLE inside BEGIN...ROLLBACK — unique among the big engines. - GRANT and REVOKE are
sometimes called DCL and sometimes lumped under DDL by older study guides; mention both names.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 2 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 3
What NOT to say: - Do not say "DML changes the database" — DDL also changes the database; DML
specifically changes rows. - Do not forget SAVEPOINT under TCL — Indian campus panels love asking
for the third TCL statement after COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
Common follow-up: "If I run TRUNCATE inside a transaction and then ROLLBACK, what happens in
MySQL versus Postgres?" — MySQL: TRUNCATE auto-commits, ROLLBACK does nothing. Postgres:
TRUNCATE is transactional, ROLLBACK restores all rows.
-- DDL
CREATE TABLE payments (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, amount DECIMAL(12,2));
-- DML
INSERT INTO payments VALUES (1, 499.00);
-- DCL
GRANT SELECT ON payments TO analyst_role;
-- TCL
BEGIN; UPDATE payments SET amount = 599 WHERE id = 1; ROLLBACK;
Q2 · TRUNCATE vs DELETE vs DROP
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs, Cognizant · Topic: SQL
Fundamentals
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through the difference between TRUNCATE, DELETE and DROP. Which one resets the
auto-increment counter and which one is the fastest?
The 30-second answer: DELETE is DML — removes rows one at a time, fires triggers, can be rolled
back, keeps the table. TRUNCATE is DDL — deallocates pages, no per-row triggers, resets the identity
counter, much faster, usually cannot be rolled back. DROP is DDL — removes the table itself, schema
and all.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the three categories first (DML vs DDL) — that anchors every
other difference. 2. Walk through speed: DELETE writes to the WAL/redo log row by row; TRUNCATE just
marks pages as free. On a 50-million row orders table, DELETE can take an hour, TRUNCATE finishes in
seconds. 3. Mention the identity reset — TRUNCATE resets AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL and
IDENTITY in SQL Server back to the seed; DELETE does not. 4. Foreign key gotcha: TRUNCATE fails on
a table referenced by an FK with rows in the child table; DELETE works because it cascades.
Edge cases to mention: - DELETE without a WHERE clause and TRUNCATE both empty the table —
but only DELETE fires per-row triggers and audit hooks. - In Oracle and Postgres, TRUNCATE can be
made transactional; in MySQL it is implicit-commit and irreversible. - DROP can be reversed only if you
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 3 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 4
have a backup or if your engine supports flashback (Oracle) — there is no ROLLBACK after DROP in
standard SQL.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "TRUNCATE and DELETE FROM are the same with no WHERE clause"
— they are not, especially for triggers, identity counters, and FK behavior. - Do not claim DROP is
recoverable via ROLLBACK in MySQL — it is not.
Common follow-up: "You truncated the wrong table in production. What is your recovery path?" —
Restore from the latest backup plus replay binary logs / WAL up to the truncate point; there is no undo
button.
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';  -- selective, logged, slow
TRUNCATE TABLE orders;                            -- whole table, fast, no rollback (MySQL)
DROP TABLE orders;                                -- table gone, schema gone
Q3 · ALTER TABLE — Add, Modify, Drop Columns Without Killing Production
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Cred, Meesho · Topic: Schema Changes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I need to add a new gst_number column to the merchants table which has 80 million rows.
Walk me through what ALTER TABLE will do, the risks, and how you would do it safely.
The 30-second answer: ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with a nullable column and no default is usually
metadata-only in modern Postgres and MySQL 8 — instant. ADD COLUMN with a NOT NULL default
rewrites the whole table in older versions, locks it, and can take hours. The safe path: add nullable,
backfill in batches, then add the NOT NULL constraint.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the basic syntax — ADD COLUMN, MODIFY/ALTER COLUMN,
DROP COLUMN — then immediately move to the performance side. 2. Distinguish metadata-only
changes (instant) from table rewrites (slow, locking). In MySQL 8 and Postgres 11+, adding a nullable
column with no default is metadata-only. 3. Walk through the safe four-step recipe: ADD nullable column
→ backfill in chunked UPDATEs of 10k rows → add NOT NULL constraint via VALIDATE (Postgres) or
two-step (MySQL) → deploy app code. 4. Mention online DDL tools — pt-online-schema-change for
MySQL, pg_repack for Postgres — when the table is genuinely too hot for native ALTER.
Edge cases to mention: - MODIFY COLUMN to change a VARCHAR(50) to VARCHAR(100) is usually
metadata-only; shrinking it forces a full table scan to validate. - DROP COLUMN in Postgres is metadata-
only (column marked dropped, space reclaimed on next VACUUM FULL); in MySQL it rewrites the table.
- Adding an FK constraint with CHECK FULL re-scans the child table and takes a strong lock — use NOT
VALID then VALIDATE on Postgres.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 4 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 5
What NOT to say: - Do not say "ALTER TABLE is instant" — that is only true for specific cases on
specific engines and versions. - Do not propose running ALTER on an 80M-row table during peak traffic
without explaining the locking implications.
Common follow-up: "How would you backfill the gst_number column without locking the table?" —
UPDATE in batches of 5–10k rows by primary key range, with a short sleep between batches; commit
each batch; monitor replication lag.
-- Safe pattern
ALTER TABLE merchants ADD COLUMN gst_number VARCHAR(15) NULL;
-- backfill in chunks (pseudo)
-- UPDATE merchants SET gst_number = lookup(id) WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ?;
ALTER TABLE merchants MODIFY gst_number VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL;  -- MySQL
Section B — Data Types & Constraints
Q4 · Choosing Numeric Types — INT, BIGINT, DECIMAL, NUMERIC, FLOAT
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, JP Morgan, Goldman, Razorpay · Topic: Data Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I'm designing a payments table. What data type would you use for the amount in rupees, for the
order id, and why?
The 30-second answer: Amount — DECIMAL(12,2) or NUMERIC(12,2); never FLOAT for money because
binary floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly and you will see paise-level rounding errors. Order id
— BIGINT, because INT tops out at ~2.1 billion and a fast-growing Indian D2C company can hit that
ceiling within a couple of years.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the money rule: DECIMAL/NUMERIC for currency, always.
Mention 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in FLOAT — that is the canonical example. 2. For ids, default to BIGINT in any
new design — the extra 4 bytes per row is irrelevant; the cost of migrating INT to BIGINT later is
enormous. 3. INT for counts and small enums (status_code, retry_count) where ~2.1B is comfortably
more than you will ever need. 4. Mention SMALLINT and TINYINT only when storage matters at scale —
analytic warehouses, narrow lookup tables.
Edge cases to mention: - DECIMAL and NUMERIC are synonyms in the ANSI standard; in some
engines they are minutely different — call them out as effectively identical for the interview. - FLOAT and
DOUBLE store more digits but cannot represent decimal fractions exactly — fine for sensor data, deadly
for money. - BIGINT signed maxes at ~9.2 × 10^18 — effectively unlimited for an id column.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 5 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 6
What NOT to say: - Do not say "I'll use FLOAT because amounts can be fractional." That is the exact
answer that fails the question. - Do not say "INT is enough for ids, BIGINT wastes space." It is 4 bytes
per row — irrelevant against the migration cost.
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between DECIMAL(10,2) and DECIMAL(12,2)?" —
DECIMAL(10,2) holds up to 99,999,999.99 (10 total digits, 2 after the point); DECIMAL(12,2) goes up to
9,999,999,999.99 — pick based on the largest realistic amount plus headroom.
CREATE TABLE payments (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_inr DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,   -- never FLOAT for money
  status SMALLINT NOT NULL
);
Q5 · VARCHAR vs CHAR vs TEXT — When to Use Which
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Cognizant · Topic: Data Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT, and when would you use TEXT over
VARCHAR?
The 30-second answer: CHAR is fixed-length and pads with spaces; VARCHAR is variable-length up to
a defined limit; TEXT is variable-length with no practical limit but is stored off-row in most engines, which
makes it slower for filtering and indexing. Use VARCHAR for most text columns, CHAR only for genuinely
fixed-width values like country codes, TEXT for free-form blobs like product descriptions or article
bodies.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the fixed-vs-variable distinction — that is the core
difference. 2. Mention storage: CHAR(10) always uses 10 characters of storage even if you store "OK";
VARCHAR uses what you write plus 1–2 bytes of length prefix. 3. Call out TEXT's off-row storage: in
MySQL InnoDB and Postgres TOAST, large TEXT values live in a separate area and require an extra fetch
— fine if you read rarely, painful for filters. 4. Indexing limit: many engines cap the indexed length of TEXT
columns (MySQL needs a prefix length), VARCHAR is fully indexable up to its declared length.
Edge cases to mention: - VARCHAR(255) is a historical convention from MySQL where 255 was the
largest value that fit in a single byte of length prefix — not a magic number any more. - CHAR
comparisons sometimes ignore trailing spaces depending on collation — gotcha when joining CHAR to
VARCHAR. - In Postgres, VARCHAR and TEXT are essentially the same storage-wise; the length cap is
just a CHECK constraint.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 6 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 7
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always use TEXT to avoid running out of space." TEXT has real indexing
and performance costs. - Do not say "CHAR is faster because it's fixed-length" — modern engines
handle VARCHAR efficiently and CHAR wastes storage.
Common follow-up: "Why is VARCHAR(255) so common in legacy schemas?" — Historical MySQL
artefact: 255 was the largest length that fit in 1 byte of length prefix in older row formats. No longer a
constraint in modern formats.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  country_code CHAR(2) NOT NULL,         -- always 2 chars: 'IN', 'US'
  email VARCHAR(254) NOT NULL,           -- RFC max length
  bio TEXT                                -- free-form, off-row
);
Q6 · DATE vs DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP vs TIME — Which One When
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, PhonePe, JP Morgan · Topic: Data Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between DATETIME and TIMESTAMP in MySQL? Which one would you use
to store the time a payment was captured?
The 30-second answer: DATE stores just the calendar date. DATETIME stores a date + time with no
timezone awareness. TIMESTAMP also stores date + time but in MySQL is stored internally as UTC and
converted to the session timezone on read; in Postgres, TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE is the equivalent.
For a payment captured-at, use TIMESTAMP (or TIMESTAMPTZ in Postgres) so that a payment made at
3 PM IST is read correctly by your London-based reconciliation team.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the calendar-vs-instant distinction. DATE = day. DATETIME
= wall-clock time with no timezone. TIMESTAMP = a fixed instant in time. 2. For anything event-related
(paid_at, created_at, last_login) you want TIMESTAMP — multi-region teams demand timezone
correctness. 3. For birthdays and holidays, DATE is right — those are calendar concepts, not instants. 4.
Mention the MySQL TIMESTAMP 2038 problem — 4-byte signed int seconds since epoch, wraps in
January 2038. DATETIME does not have this issue and is the modern default for distant-future or distant-
past values.
Edge cases to mention: - TIMESTAMP in MySQL is automatically converted to UTC on write and back
on read; if your application sets a wrong session timezone, you get silent corruption. - Postgres has both
TIMESTAMP and TIMESTAMPTZ — always default to TIMESTAMPTZ unless you have a reason not to. -
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 7 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 8
TIME stores a duration or time-of-day without a date — rarely useful in transactional schemas,
occasionally in scheduling.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "TIMESTAMP and DATETIME are the same in MySQL." They differ in
timezone handling and storage range. - Do not store dates as VARCHAR — every junior schema has this
mistake; sorting, filtering and date arithmetic break.
Common follow-up: "How do you query all payments from yesterday in Asia/Kolkata?" — Convert the
boundary explicitly: WHERE paid_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-05-25 00:00:00+05:30' AND
paid_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-05-26 00:00:00+05:30'. Never trust implicit timezone of the
session.
CREATE TABLE payments (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  paid_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,            -- instant; UTC-stored
  refund_eligible_until DATE              -- calendar date, no time
);
Q7 · BOOLEAN, BIT, TINYINT(1) — How Engines Actually Store Truth
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Cognizant, Wipro, Accenture · Topic: Data Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Does MySQL have a real BOOLEAN type? How do you store a true/false flag like "is_verified"
portably across MySQL, Postgres and SQL Server?
The 30-second answer: MySQL does not have a true boolean — BOOLEAN and BOOL are synonyms
for TINYINT(1), and TRUE/FALSE are aliases for 1 and 0. Postgres has a real BOOLEAN type that stores
t/f. SQL Server uses BIT. The portable schema convention is to declare the column as BOOLEAN, accept
the engine-specific physical type, and never compare flags to literal integers in application code.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the MySQL gotcha — Indian campus students often think
MySQL has a real boolean and are surprised that SELECT TRUE returns 1. 2. Postgres is the cleanest
— WHERE is_verified works directly; in MySQL the same query also works because non-zero
TINYINT is truthy. 3. Mention NULL — a boolean column allows three states unless declared NOT NULL:
TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN. Design your flag columns NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE to avoid the third
state. 4. Anticipate the follow-up about indexing low-cardinality columns: a boolean alone is a poor
index; combine it with a more selective column.
Edge cases to mention: - In MySQL, you can insert 2 into a TINYINT(1) boolean column — it stores 2,
and WHERE flag = TRUE will not match because TRUE = 1 exactly. Use WHERE flag != 0 if you mean
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 8 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 9
"truthy". - In Postgres, the literals are TRUE, FALSE, 't', 'f', 'yes', 'no' — be careful when comparing
string literals. - Some ORMs (Hibernate, Sequelize) map Java/JS booleans to '1'/'0' strings — silent type
mismatch with the database column.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim MySQL's BOOLEAN is a real boolean type — it is a TINYINT(1) alias. -
Do not say "I'll use 'Y' / 'N' chars for clarity" — every linter, every analyst tool, and every JSON serializer
expects true booleans.
Common follow-up: "What's the cardinality issue with indexing a boolean column?" — Two values
means about half the rows match either way; the optimizer often prefers a full scan over the index.
Boolean columns are useful as the second column in a composite index, not as a standalone one.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  email VARCHAR(254) NOT NULL,
  is_verified BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE
);
Q8 · Column Constraints — PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT
NULL, DEFAULT
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Wells Fargo · Topic: Constraints
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
List the column-level constraints in SQL and tell me when you'd use a CHECK constraint instead
of enforcing it in application code.
The 30-second answer: Six common ones — PRIMARY KEY (uniquely identifies a row, implies NOT
NULL and UNIQUE), FOREIGN KEY (references another table's PK or unique column), UNIQUE (no
duplicates but allows NULL), CHECK (arbitrary boolean condition per row), NOT NULL (rejects NULL),
DEFAULT (assigns a value when none is supplied). Use CHECK for invariants that must hold regardless
of which application is writing — e.g., amount > 0 on a payments table.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Name all six clearly — interviewers want to hear PRIMARY KEY,
FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL, DEFAULT in one breath. 2. Distinguish PRIMARY KEY from
UNIQUE: PRIMARY KEY implies NOT NULL, UNIQUE allows one NULL (or many, depending on engine).
3. Explain CHECK with a real example: CHECK (amount > 0) on payments, CHECK (status IN
('pending','captured','failed','refunded')) on a status column. 4. Stress the database-
as-last-line-of-defence principle: app code can have bugs, multiple services may write to the same table,
CHECK constraints catch everything that slips through.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 9 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 10
Edge cases to mention: - UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs in most engines because NULL != NULL —
Postgres, MySQL, Oracle all behave this way; SQL Server allows only one NULL by default. - A
FOREIGN KEY without an index on the child column can make DELETEs on the parent very slow —
always index FK columns. - CHECK constraints were not enforced in MySQL until 8.0.16; older versions
silently parsed and ignored them.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE are the same." They differ on NULL
handling and you can have many UNIQUE columns but only one PRIMARY KEY. - Do not skip DEFAULT
— Indian campus panels often ask "name all constraints" and DEFAULT is the one most people forget.
Common follow-up: "What happens if I insert a row that violates a FOREIGN KEY constraint?" — The
INSERT is rejected with an integrity error; the transaction continues unless you have configured it to roll
back on error.
CREATE TABLE payments (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  amount_inr DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount_inr > 0),
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE
);
Q9 · Identity, Sequence, AUTO_INCREMENT, SERIAL — Auto-Generating PKs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Cognizant · Topic:
Data Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you auto-generate a primary key in MySQL, Postgres and SQL Server? What is the
difference between SERIAL and GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY?
The 30-second answer: MySQL — AUTO_INCREMENT attribute on the column. SQL Server —
IDENTITY(seed, increment). Postgres — historically SERIAL (which is sugar for a sequence + default +
ownership), but the modern ANSI-standard form is GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (or
GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for stricter control). All four ultimately use a counter; the differences
are syntax, restart behaviour, and whether the user can override the value.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Map each dialect to its keyword first — that's table stakes. 2. Walk
through SERIAL vs IDENTITY in Postgres: SERIAL is an older convenience that creates a sequence
object behind the scenes; IDENTITY is the SQL standard and gives cleaner ownership and permission
semantics. New Postgres projects should prefer IDENTITY. 3. ALWAYS vs DEFAULT — GENERATED
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 10 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 11
ALWAYS rejects user-supplied values for the column; GENERATED BY DEFAULT allows them. Use
ALWAYS for surrogate keys you never want apps to override. 4. Mention sequence holes:
AUTO_INCREMENT and sequences never reuse a number, so a rolled-back INSERT leaves a gap. Do not
promise gap-free numbering to a business stakeholder.
Edge cases to mention: - AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL is stored in memory in older versions; after a
server restart, the next value could be reset to MAX(id)+1, which can collide with rows in replication
queues — fixed in MySQL 8 with persistent counters. - IDENTITY columns in SQL Server cannot be
updated directly; you need SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON. - Sequences in Postgres are independent
objects — you can share one across multiple tables, restart it, set its value, or grant on it separately.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "AUTO_INCREMENT guarantees consecutive numbers" — it does not;
rollbacks leave gaps. - Do not say "SERIAL is the same as IDENTITY" — they are similar in effect but
differ in ownership and standards compliance.
Common follow-up: "How do you get the last inserted id?" — MySQL: LAST_INSERT_ID().
Postgres: RETURNING id on the INSERT, or currval('seq_name'). SQL Server: 
SCOPE_IDENTITY(). JDBC and most drivers also expose a getGeneratedKeys API.
-- MySQL
CREATE TABLE orders (id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, ...);
-- Postgres (modern)
CREATE TABLE orders (id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, ...);
-- SQL Server
CREATE TABLE orders (id BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, ...);
Q10 · CAST vs CONVERT — Explicit vs Implicit, When Implicit Is Dangerous
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Razorpay · Topic: Data Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between CAST and CONVERT? Give me an example where implicit type
conversion silently produced the wrong answer.
The 30-second answer: CAST is the ANSI-standard form — CAST(expr AS type) — works in
every engine. CONVERT is engine-specific: in SQL Server it takes a style code for date formatting; in
MySQL it is similar to CAST with charset support. Implicit conversion is when the engine auto-coerces —
usually fine for INT-to-BIGINT, dangerous for VARCHAR-to-NUMBER because a non-numeric string can
throw at runtime, and worst for VARCHAR-to-DATE because two engines may pick different parse
formats and silently produce different rows.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 11 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 12
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the standard answer — CAST is portable, CONVERT is
engine-specific. 2. Give the classic implicit-conversion trap: WHERE user_id = '123' where user_id
is BIGINT — works, but loses index usage in some engines because the index entries are numbers and
the comparison forces a per-row cast. 3. Date strings are the worst: WHERE order_date >
'01-02-2026' is ambiguous — is that 1 Feb or 2 Jan? Different parse settings give silently different
rows. 4. The safe rule: always cast explicitly and always use ISO 8601 date literals (YYYY-MM-DD).
Edge cases to mention: - Implicit conversion can prevent index use: comparing an indexed VARCHAR
column to an integer literal sometimes forces the engine to cast every row. - TRY_CAST (SQL Server) and
TRY_CONVERT return NULL on failure instead of throwing — useful when cleaning messy data. -
Postgres has the cast operator :: — '42'::int — which is shorter but non-standard.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "implicit conversion is harmless." It can break index use and silently
change result correctness. - Do not say "CAST and CONVERT are interchangeable" without qualifying —
they are syntactically similar but CONVERT has engine-specific extras.
Common follow-up: "How does implicit conversion break index use?" — If the engine has to cast every
indexed value to match the literal's type, it can't binary-search the index — falls back to a sequential
scan. Always cast the literal to the column's type, not the other way around.
SELECT CAST('2026-05-26' AS DATE) AS d;             -- portable
SELECT CONVERT(VARCHAR, GETDATE(), 23);              -- SQL Server: ISO date
SELECT '42'::int + 1;                                -- Postgres shorthand
Section C — NULL, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
Q11 · NULL Semantics and Three-Valued Logic
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Goldman, JP Morgan, Swiggy · Topic: NULL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does NULL mean in SQL, and why does the expression WHERE column = NULL never
return any rows?
The 30-second answer: NULL means "unknown" — not zero, not empty string, not missing. SQL uses
three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL — including NULL = NULL —
evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE only keeps rows where the predicate is TRUE. That is why WHERE
column = NULL returns nothing — you must use WHERE column IS NULL instead.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 12 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 13
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the "unknown, not missing" framing — that single mental
model fixes every NULL question. 2. Walk through three-valued logic: AND/OR/NOT have nine-row truth
tables instead of four. TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE (because
no matter what UNKNOWN turns out to be, the AND is false). 3. Give the canonical traps: NULL =
NULL is UNKNOWN; NULL <> 1 is UNKNOWN; NOT (NULL = 1) is UNKNOWN. 4. The two
correct ways to test for NULL: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. Some dialects support IS DISTINCT
FROM which treats two NULLs as equal — handy for change detection.
Edge cases to mention: - Aggregate functions skip NULLs — AVG(amount) averages only the non-
null rows, which can be surprising; COUNT(*) counts all rows, COUNT(amount) counts only non-
null amounts. - UNIQUE constraints allow multiple NULLs in most engines because NULL != NULL. -
COALESCE(col, default) is the standard way to substitute a value for NULL; NVL is the Oracle dialect;
IFNULL is MySQL.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "NULL is the same as zero" or "NULL is the same as empty string." They
are different — '' = '' is TRUE; NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN. - Do not write WHERE col =
NULL in production code and expect it to find NULL rows.
Common follow-up: "What does COUNT(DISTINCT col) do when col contains NULLs?" — It
counts only the distinct non-NULL values; NULL is excluded. To include NULL as one of the distinct
values, you have to count it separately.
SELECT * FROM users WHERE last_login_at IS NULL;        -- correct
SELECT * FROM users WHERE last_login_at = NULL;          -- always empty
SELECT COALESCE(promo_code, 'none') FROM bookings;       -- substitute
Q12 · GROUP BY — The Every-Non-Aggregated-Column Rule
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Cognizant · Topic: Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What rules govern which columns can appear in the SELECT list when you use GROUP BY? Why
does this query fail in Postgres but pass in older MySQL?
The 30-second answer: Every column in the SELECT list must either appear inside an aggregate
function (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) or appear in the GROUP BY clause. Otherwise the value would
be ambiguous — which row's value do you want? Postgres and SQL Server enforce this strictly. MySQL
before 5.7 allowed it (returning an arbitrary value) — modern MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY
enforces the rule too.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 13 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 14
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule precisely — "every non-aggregated column must
appear in GROUP BY" — that one sentence is the answer for 80% of follow-ups. 2. Explain why: a
GROUP BY collapses many rows into one; a column not in GROUP BY and not aggregated has no single
defined value to return. 3. Mention the MySQL exception: pre-5.7 it returned an arbitrary row's value from
the group, silently — a notorious source of "works on my machine" bugs. Modern MySQL with
ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode rejects it like Postgres does. 4. Functional dependency exception: if you
GROUP BY the primary key, the engine knows every other column is uniquely determined by it, and
modern Postgres allows them in SELECT — neat trick that confuses interviewers.
Edge cases to mention: - Expressions like EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) must either be in
GROUP BY exactly or wrapped in an aggregate — you cannot group by the column and select a derived
expression of it without restating it. - SELECT * with GROUP BY is almost always wrong — you are
asking for every column to be either grouped or aggregated, and * does neither. - GROUP BY with no
rows in the input returns no rows; GROUP BY () with no input still returns one row of aggregates (e.g., 
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM empty_table returns 0).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MySQL is more flexible than Postgres" as a positive — that flexibility
silently returns wrong data. - Do not put a non-aggregated, non-grouped column in SELECT and hope
the optimizer picks a sensible value.
Common follow-up: "For each merchant, show the merchant name and the total amount of orders in
May 2026." — Group by merchant id, select merchant name (functionally dependent on id), and
SUM(amount). Join merchants table for the name if it lives in another table.
SELECT merchant_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(amount_inr) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-05-01'
GROUP BY merchant_id;
Q13 · HAVING vs WHERE — Where Each One Belongs in the Pipeline
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Wells Fargo · Topic: Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When do you use HAVING and when do you use WHERE? Can you give me an example where
putting the same condition in HAVING versus WHERE produces a different answer?
The 30-second answer: WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped; HAVING filters groups
after aggregation. If you want only paid orders in your sum, that is a WHERE filter. If you want only
merchants whose total exceeds 1 lakh, that is a HAVING filter — because "total exceeds 1 lakh" can only
be evaluated after the SUM.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 14 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 15
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING
→ SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. That ordering explains every difference. 2. Give the rule: aggregates
can only appear in HAVING (and SELECT and ORDER BY); never in WHERE. 3. Show the divergent
example: WHERE amount > 1000 keeps only large individual orders before summing; HAVING
SUM(amount) > 1000 keeps merchants whose total crossed 1000. 4. Performance: filter as early as
possible — push every non-aggregate condition into WHERE so the GROUP BY processes fewer rows.
Edge cases to mention: - You can use HAVING without GROUP BY — the whole table becomes one
group, and HAVING filters that one summary row. - You cannot reference a SELECT alias inside WHERE
(in most engines), but HAVING can sometimes reference aggregated aliases. - Window functions are
evaluated after HAVING but before ORDER BY — that's why you cannot filter on a window function
result in WHERE or HAVING; you need an outer query or CTE.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "HAVING and WHERE are interchangeable." They sit at different stages
of the pipeline and produce different results. - Do not put SUM(amount) > 1000 in a WHERE clause
and expect it to work — most engines reject it; some give cryptic errors.
Common follow-up: "Show merchants whose total May revenue exceeded 1 lakh from captured
payments only." — WHERE filters payments to captured + May; GROUP BY merchant; HAVING filters to
SUM > 100000.
SELECT merchant_id, SUM(amount_inr) AS total
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'captured'
  AND paid_at >= '2026-05-01' AND paid_at < '2026-06-01'
GROUP BY merchant_id
HAVING SUM(amount_inr) > 100000;
Q14 · ORDER BY — Multiple Columns, NULL Placement, Expressions and Aliases
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro, Swiggy · Topic: Sorting
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Sort orders by date descending, then by amount descending. Where will NULLs appear by
default, and how do you control that?
The 30-second answer: ORDER BY order_date DESC, amount_inr DESC — comma-
separated, each with its own direction. NULL placement is engine-dependent: Postgres puts NULLs last
on ASC and first on DESC by default; MySQL is the opposite. Use the ANSI clause NULLS FIRST or 
NULLS LAST to control it portably (Postgres, Oracle); in MySQL emulate with ORDER BY col IS
NULL, col.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 15 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 16
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the multi-column syntax — each column gets its own ASC/
DESC. Default is ASC. 2. Walk through NULL placement defaults — Postgres ASC NULLs last, DESC
NULLs first; MySQL ASC NULLs first; Oracle ASC NULLs last; SQL Server ASC NULLs first. Memorising
the matrix is less valuable than knowing how to override it. 3. Mention that you can ORDER BY an
expression, a SELECT alias (in most engines), or a column position number — but position numbers are
brittle and discouraged in modern code. 4. ORDER BY happens after GROUP BY and HAVING — so you
can sort by an aggregate result like SUM(amount) DESC.
Edge cases to mention: - ORDER BY with LIMIT but no tie-breaker can return different rows on each
run if there are ties — always add a deterministic tie-breaker like the primary key. - ORDER BY a column
not in SELECT is legal in most engines; ORDER BY a column not visible to the query (e.g., after a
SELECT DISTINCT) may be rejected. - Sorting on a TEXT or large VARCHAR column without an index
forces a sort buffer or temporary file — can be expensive on large result sets.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume the default sort order is the same across engines — it is not for
NULLs. - Do not use ORDER BY 1, 2, 3 (position-based) in code review — it's a maintenance landmine
when the SELECT list changes.
Common follow-up: "Show the top 10 highest-value orders this month, deterministically, with NULL
amounts pushed to the bottom." — ORDER BY amount_inr DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC LIMIT
10.
SELECT id, order_date, amount_inr
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-05-01'
ORDER BY order_date DESC, amount_inr DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC
LIMIT 10;
Q15 · DISTINCT vs GROUP BY — When They Are Identical, When They Diverge
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Is SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders the same as SELECT user_id FROM
orders GROUP BY user_id? When would you choose one over the other?
The 30-second answer: For a single column with no aggregates, they are logically and (usually)
physically identical — most optimizers generate the same plan. They diverge the moment you want an
aggregate alongside the distinct values — for that, you need GROUP BY. DISTINCT is shorter and clearer
for "give me unique rows"; GROUP BY is the right choice when you want unique groups plus a metric
per group.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 16 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 17
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Begin with the equivalence claim — interviewer is checking whether
you mechanically prefer one or actually understand them. 2. Show the divergence: SELECT user_id,
COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY user_id has no DISTINCT equivalent — DISTINCT cannot
compute per-group aggregates. 3. DISTINCT applies to the entire SELECT row, not a single column — 
SELECT DISTINCT user_id, order_date gives unique (user_id, order_date) pairs, not unique
user_ids. 4. Performance: both usually trigger the same hash-aggregate or sort-distinct operator.
DISTINCT on a non-indexed wide row is just as expensive as the equivalent GROUP BY.
Edge cases to mention: - SELECT DISTINCT * is a code smell — almost always indicates a flawed
join that duplicated rows; fix the join, not the symptom. - COUNT(DISTINCT col) is its own beast —
it requires the engine to hold all distinct values in memory or spill to disk; on a wide column at scale this
can be costly. - DISTINCT does not allow ORDER BY on a column not in the SELECT list (in strict ANSI)
— sometimes a surprise.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "DISTINCT is faster than GROUP BY" or vice versa as a blanket rule —
they normally plan the same way. - Do not use DISTINCT to paper over a JOIN that's producing
duplicates — debug the JOIN.
Common follow-up: "How would you count unique users per merchant in May 2026?" — SELECT
merchant_id, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM orders WHERE order_date >=
'2026-05-01' AND order_date < '2026-06-01' GROUP BY merchant_id;.
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders;
-- equivalent
SELECT user_id FROM orders GROUP BY user_id;
-- divergent (DISTINCT cannot do this)
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY user_id;
Section D — Pagination, CASE, Type Behaviour
Q16 · LIMIT, OFFSET, FETCH, TOP — Pagination Across Dialects
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant, Razorpay · Topic: Pagination
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Page through orders 10 at a time. Show me the syntax in MySQL, Postgres and SQL Server, and
tell me the performance issue with deep OFFSETs.
The 30-second answer: MySQL and Postgres — LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 (or LIMIT 20, 10 in
MySQL's older form). SQL Server — OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY (ANSI
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 17 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 18
standard, also supported by Postgres 12+). The performance issue with deep OFFSET is that the engine
still scans and discards every row before the OFFSET — page 1000 of 10 rows means scanning 10,000
rows then throwing away 9,990. Use keyset pagination (WHERE id < last_seen_id ORDER BY id
DESC LIMIT 10) for deep paging.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Map the three dialects — that's the surface answer. 2. Always pair
LIMIT with ORDER BY — without a deterministic sort, pages can repeat or skip rows. 3. Explain the
OFFSET cost: the engine cannot skip rows for free; it must produce them and discard them. At page
5,000 on a 10-per-page list, that's 50,000 wasted rows per request. 4. Introduce keyset (a.k.a. cursor)
pagination as the production-grade alternative — uses the last row's id from the previous page as a
starting point.
Edge cases to mention: - Without ORDER BY, LIMIT picks whichever rows the engine happens to
produce first — the result is not deterministic and can change run to run. - Postgres OFFSET evaluates
the entire underlying query before discarding — index range scans can still help, but the discarded work
is real. - SQL Server before 2012 used ROW_NUMBER() OVER + a CTE to paginate — old-school but still
in legacy systems.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "OFFSET is free." Deep OFFSETs are a real performance problem and a
common Indian product company interview trap. - Do not omit ORDER BY — the page order will be non-
deterministic.
Common follow-up: "Show me a keyset pagination query for orders sorted by id descending." — 
WHERE id < :last_seen_id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10; — no OFFSET, scales to billions
of rows.
-- MySQL / Postgres
SELECT id, amount_inr FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;
-- SQL Server / Postgres (ANSI)
SELECT id, amount_inr FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;
-- Keyset (preferred for deep pages)
SELECT id, amount_inr FROM orders WHERE id < 12345 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10;
Q17 · CASE WHEN — Simple vs Searched, in SELECT vs WHERE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Accenture, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Expressions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Classify each payment as 'small' (under 500), 'medium' (500-5000) or 'large' (above 5000). Write it
as a CASE expression and explain the two forms of CASE.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 18 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 19
The 30-second answer: Searched CASE — CASE WHEN cond1 THEN x WHEN cond2 THEN y
ELSE z END — most general; conditions can be anything. Simple CASE — CASE col WHEN val1
THEN x WHEN val2 THEN y END — shorter when matching one column against constants. CASE
can sit anywhere an expression can: in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY. ELSE is optional;
without it, unmatched rows get NULL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Distinguish the two forms — that is the academic part of the answer.
2. Show the worked classification: CASE WHEN amount < 500 THEN 'small' WHEN amount <=
5000 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'large' END. 3. Mention that conditions are evaluated top-down and
the first match wins — order matters when ranges overlap. 4. CASE in WHERE is legal but often less
readable than rewriting as OR conditions; CASE in ORDER BY is a clean way to do custom sort orders
('captured' first, then 'pending', then everything else).
Edge cases to mention: - Without ELSE, an unmatched row produces NULL — easy to overlook when
downstream code assumes a non-null bucket. - Mixing data types in the THEN branches forces an
implicit cast — all branches must be type-compatible. - CASE expressions don't short-circuit boolean
evaluation in every engine — be careful with division by zero; some engines evaluate all branches before
picking one.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "CASE is only for SELECT" — it works in WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER
BY, HAVING too. - Do not say "ELSE is required" — it is optional; the default for an unmatched row is
NULL.
Common follow-up: "How would you pivot a status column into three columns showing the count of
each status per merchant?" — Use CASE inside SUM: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'captured'
THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS captured_count.
SELECT id,
       CASE
         WHEN amount_inr < 500   THEN 'small'
         WHEN amount_inr <= 5000 THEN 'medium'
         ELSE                          'large'
       END AS size_bucket
FROM payments;
Q18 · NULL in Aggregate Functions, COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT
col)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Swiggy, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic:
Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 19 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 20
What is the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column_name) and COUNT(DISTINCT
column_name)? Which one ignores NULLs?
The 30-second answer: COUNT() counts all rows including those with NULL values in any column.
COUNT(col) counts only rows where col is NOT NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-NULL
values of col. The rule across all aggregates: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT(col) all skip NULLs silently;
only COUNT() counts NULL rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the three behaviours crisply — interviewer is timing this answer.
2. Highlight the silent-skip behaviour of aggregates: AVG(amount) of a column with NULLs averages
only the non-null rows, which can give a misleadingly high average if many rows are NULL. 3. Show the
canonical use case: COUNT(*) for "how many rows", COUNT(col) for "how many had this attribute set",
COUNT(DISTINCT col) for "how many unique values". 4. Combine with conditional aggregation: 
COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'captured' THEN 1 END) — only TRUE rows contribute; the
implicit ELSE NULL is skipped by COUNT.
Edge cases to mention: - COUNT() does not look at any specific column, so the engine can sometimes
serve it from the table's row count metadata — very fast in MyISAM, slower in InnoDB and Postgres. -
COUNT(1) is identical to COUNT() in every modern engine — the old myth that COUNT(1) is faster is
false. - AVG over an all-NULL column returns NULL, not 0 — a frequent source of NaN propagation in
dashboards.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "COUNT() is slower because it counts NULLs." NULL handling is not
what makes it slow; what makes it slow is reading every row. - Do not say "COUNT(col) and COUNT() are
the same" — they differ exactly when col has NULLs.
Common follow-up: "How would you count payments per merchant, including merchants with zero
payments?" — LEFT JOIN merchants to payments, then COUNT(payments.id) (which excludes the
unmatched-row NULLs) grouped by merchant; COUNT(*) would wrongly return 1 for merchants with no
payment.
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                          AS total_rows,
  COUNT(promo_code)                 AS rows_with_promo,
  COUNT(DISTINCT promo_code)        AS unique_promos
FROM bookings;
Q19 · Implicit Conversion Pitfalls and Index Sabotage
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs · Topic:
Data Types
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 20 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 21
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
The query SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210 is slow on a 50 million
row table, even though there's an index on phone. The phone column is VARCHAR(15). Diagnose
what is happening.
The 30-second answer: Implicit type conversion is killing the index. The literal 9876543210 is a
numeric type; the column is VARCHAR. To compare them, the engine has to cast the VARCHAR column
to a number for every single row — which means the index on the original string values is useless, and
the engine falls back to a full table scan. Fix: quote the literal as a string — WHERE phone =
'9876543210'.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose the implicit conversion first — that's the headline. 2.
Explain why the index becomes useless: indexes store the column's values in their native type. A B-tree
on VARCHAR phone numbers cannot be searched by a numeric comparison, because the conversion
happens after the index would be consulted. 3. The fix is always to cast the literal, not the column. Cast
the literal to the column's type: WHERE phone = '9876543210'. Never the other way around. 4.
Add the diagnostic step: EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) reveals "type conversion" or "function on
column" notes that flag exactly this issue.
Edge cases to mention: - Functions on the indexed column (e.g., WHERE LOWER(email) =
'x@y.com') have the same effect — index unusable unless you have a functional index on 
LOWER(email). - Collation mismatches between columns being compared can trigger the same silent
cast — joining a utf8mb4 column to a latin1 column may scan instead of using the index. - Postgres is
stricter about implicit numeric-to-string conversions; MySQL is more permissive but pays the price in lost
index use.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the index is broken; rebuild it." Rebuilding does not help when the query
forces a per-row cast. - Do not propose a CAST on the column — that makes the problem worse and
explicit.
Common follow-up: "What other patterns silently kill index use?" — WHERE function(col) =
value, WHERE col + 1 = value, WHERE col LIKE '%foo%' (leading wildcard), and OR
conditions across columns without a compound index covering both. All of these defeat the index until
you rewrite the query.
-- Slow: implicit cast on every row, full scan
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210;
-- Fast: matches the indexed VARCHAR value directly
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210';
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 21 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
