Q20 · FOREIGN KEY Behaviour — ON DELETE / ON UPDATE Options
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Cognizant, Wells Fargo · Topic:
Constraints
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have an orders table with a FOREIGN KEY referencing users. The PM asks you to delete a
user. What options does the FOREIGN KEY give you, and which one is the most dangerous in
production?
The 30-second answer: Five options — RESTRICT (default in most engines, blocks the delete if any
child row exists), NO ACTION (similar but deferred until end of statement), CASCADE (deletes all child
rows along with the parent), SET NULL (sets the child FK column to NULL, requires the column to be
nullable), SET DEFAULT (sets it to the column's default value). CASCADE is the most dangerous in
production — one accidental DELETE on a parent can wipe out tens of millions of child rows silently.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Name all five options crisply — that's the breadth check. 2. Explain
RESTRICT vs NO ACTION: practically identical in most engines; technically NO ACTION is deferred to
the end of the statement so multi-row updates that resolve before commit are allowed. 3. Walk through
the CASCADE risk with a realistic example: deleting a merchant cascades to orders, payments, refunds,
audit logs — gone, irreversibly, no warning. 4. Production-grade pattern: prefer RESTRICT, do soft
deletes at the application layer (set deleted_at), and explicitly delete child rows in a controlled, audited
migration when truly needed.
Edge cases to mention: - ON UPDATE CASCADE is rarely useful because primary keys should be
immutable; if you're updating PKs, your data model has a deeper problem. - SET NULL requires the FK
column to be nullable — if you have NOT NULL on it, the engine rejects the constraint definition. - Some
engines (older MySQL with MyISAM) silently ignore FK constraints — always confirm your storage engine
actually enforces them.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "ON DELETE CASCADE is convenient." It's convenient until it isn't, and
there's no undo button. - Do not skip explaining the index on the child column — every FK should have
an index on the referencing column, otherwise parent updates and deletes do a full scan.
Common follow-up: "A user requests deletion under data-privacy obligations. How do you handle it
cleanly?" — Soft delete the user row (set deleted_at, scrub PII columns), keep the FK intact on orders for
audit and tax records, document the retention exception. CASCADE would also delete the orders, which
you usually need to retain for legal compliance.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 22 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 23
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_inr DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE RESTRICT
);
-- always index the child FK column
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
Chapter 2, Part A — Joins
Joins are the workhorse of every SQL interview round you'll ever sit in — campus drives, GCC panels,
Razorpay-Swiggy-Flipkart product loops, even the surprise screen during the manager round. If you
can't reason about joins at row-level cardinality, you don't make it past the first 20 minutes. This part of
the chapter walks through 23 join questions in the order they actually get asked — starting from the four
basic shapes, moving through self-joins, anti-joins, lateral joins and inequality joins, and finishing with the
operator-level questions (hash vs merge vs nested-loop) and large-table patterns (partition-wise joins,
star schema). Part B picks up where this ends and covers subqueries, CTEs and correlated logic — read
them together if you can.
Q21 · INNER vs LEFT vs RIGHT vs FULL OUTER — Row-Level Differences
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through what INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN return. Use
a real example and tell me which rows would be different across the four.
The 30-second answer: INNER returns only rows that match on both sides; LEFT returns every left row
plus matched right rows (NULLs where no match); RIGHT is the mirror of LEFT; FULL OUTER returns
everything from both sides padded with NULLs on unmatched cells. Pick LEFT for "all of A, plus B if
present" — that's 80% of real-world cases.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Anchor with two tables — orders (every order placed) and 
payments (only orders that triggered a payment intent). This is a realistic Indian fintech setup where
some orders never reach checkout. 2. INNER between these gives you orders that actually have a
payment row — useful for revenue reports. 3. LEFT gives you all orders, with NULLs in payment columns
for the ones that abandoned — that's how you build a funnel. 4. RIGHT gives you all payment rows,
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 23 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 24
including orphans where the order row was deleted — that's a data-integrity check. 5. FULL OUTER
returns both sets of orphans simultaneously — rare in production, useful in reconciliation. 6. Mention that
RIGHT JOIN is almost never written by hand — most engineers flip table order and use LEFT for
readability.
Edge cases to mention: - If the right side has duplicates (one order, three payment attempts), even
INNER and LEFT will multiply the left row — junior candidates miss this. - FULL OUTER is unsupported
in MySQL until 8.0.31 — you simulate with UNION of LEFT and RIGHT JOIN. - NULL never equals
NULL in a join condition — that's standard three-valued logic.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "LEFT JOIN returns all rows from both tables" — that's wrong, only the
left table is preserved. - Do not draw a Venn diagram as your only explanation; the interviewer wants
row-level reasoning.
Common follow-up: "Show me orders that were placed but never paid." — Classic anti-join: LEFT JOIN
payments and filter WHERE p.order_id IS NULL.
-- Funnel: every order, plus payment status if any
SELECT o.id, o.user_id, o.amount, p.status AS payment_status
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON o.id = p.order_id;
Q22 · Self-Join — Manager and Employee Hierarchy
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, TCS, Wells Fargo · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You've got an employees table with id, name, manager_id where manager_id is a
self-reference. Write a query that lists every employee with their manager's name. Don't drop the
CEO.
The 30-second answer: Alias the table twice — e for employee, m for manager — and write LEFT
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id. LEFT keeps the CEO row (whose manager_id
is NULL) in the result. Use COALESCE(m.name, 'No manager') for clean display.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the core idea — a self-join is just a join between two
aliases of the same table. 2. Justify LEFT over INNER: the CEO has no manager, so INNER would silently
drop the topmost row. 3. Mention that the same pattern handles "find pairs of employees sharing a
manager" — just swap the join condition to e1.manager_id = e2.manager_id AND e1.id <
e2.id. 4. Flag that multi-level hierarchy ("manager's manager's manager") is not a self-join problem —
it needs a recursive CTE, covered in Part B.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 24 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 25
Edge cases to mention: - Cycles: if A reports to B and B reports to A (data corruption), a recursive walk
loops forever — always cap depth. - Matrix orgs where one employee has two managers will produce
two rows per employee — that's the right cardinality, but be ready to explain it. - If manager_id
references a soft-deleted employee, the LEFT JOIN gives you NULL for manager name — handle with 
COALESCE.
What NOT to say: - Do not use the same alias on both sides — the query won't parse and you'll look
careless. - Do not say "self-join is a special kind of join" — it's just a regular join with the same physical
table referenced twice.
Common follow-up: "Now show me three levels — employee, manager, manager's manager." — Either
chain self-joins explicitly or, cleaner, use a recursive CTE.
SELECT e.name AS employee,
       COALESCE(m.name, 'No manager') AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
Q23 · Cross Join — Intentional vs Accidental Cardinality Blow-up
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Capgemini, HCL, Walmart Labs · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a cross join and when have you used it intentionally? And how does an accidental cross
join happen?
The 30-second answer: A cross join (Cartesian product) returns every row of A paired with every row of
B — 1000 × 1000 gives you a million rows. Intentional use: generating date spines, calendar tables, or all
combinations for a pricing matrix. Accidental: forgetting the ON clause or writing FROM a, b without a
WHERE join condition.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the operator first — explicit CROSS JOIN or the older
comma-separated FROM a, b syntax with no WHERE. 2. Give one genuinely useful example: building
a date-range × user-id grid before a LEFT JOIN to fact data, so empty days show up as zero instead of
vanishing. 3. Then the disaster case: a junior dev writes 
FROM orders, payments WHERE status = 'paid' and forgets o.id = p.order_id — the
query runs, returns 50 million rows, and OOMs the box. 4. Mention that most modern databases will fire
a warning or refuse the implicit cross join in strict mode.
Edge cases to mention: - Cross join with a tiny tally table (1 to 100) is a common trick for splitting
comma-separated values into rows. - CROSS JOIN LATERAL (covered later) is technically a cross join
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 25 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 26
with per-row context, not a flat Cartesian product. - If one side is empty, the result is empty — even if the
other side has a million rows.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "cross join is bad and never used" — that's wrong, it's deliberate for
date spines and combinatorics. - Do not say "it's the same as INNER JOIN with no condition" — true
mechanically, but interviewers want the operator name.
Common follow-up: "How do you spot an accidental cross join in a slow query?" — Look at the planner
output for "Nested Loop" with no join condition, or estimated rows that look suspiciously close to 
rows_a × rows_b.
-- Intentional: every day in May × every active merchant, for daily revenue grid
SELECT d.day, m.id AS merchant_id
FROM generate_series('2026-05-01'::date, '2026-05-31'::date, '1 day') AS d(day)
CROSS JOIN merchants m
WHERE m.status = 'active';
Q24 · Anti-Join — Three Ways to Find "Not in B", and the NOT IN Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Find users who have never placed an order. Show me three ways to write it and tell me which is
safest.
The 30-second answer: Three forms — LEFT JOIN orders ... WHERE order_id IS NULL, 
NOT EXISTS (...), and NOT IN (...). The first two are safe. NOT IN is dangerous: if the
subquery returns even one NULL, the entire result becomes empty because x != NULL evaluates to
UNKNOWN.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the three forms — interviewer wants to see you know all of
them. 2. Explain the NOT IN trap precisely: user_id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) desugars to 
user_id != 1 AND user_id != 2 AND user_id != NULL. The last conjunct is UNKNOWN, so
the whole row is UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so it's filtered out. 3. State your preference clearly — NOT
EXISTS. It handles NULLs correctly, and Postgres, SQL Server and modern MySQL all rewrite it as an
anti-join operator. 4. Mention when LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL wins: when you also need columns from the
left table and want a single pass.
Edge cases to mention: - If the joined column is declared NOT NULL, NOT IN is technically safe —
but don't trust schema you can't audit. - NOT EXISTS short-circuits on the first match per outer row
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 26 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 27
— usually faster on huge right tables. - Adding DISTINCT to fix NOT IN doesn't help — the NULL still
poisons the comparison.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "all three are equivalent" — they are not, under NULLs. - Do not say
one is always fastest — depends on cardinality and indexes on the join column.
Common follow-up: "What does the planner do with NOT EXISTS?" — Postgres and modern SQL
Server convert it to an "Anti Join" operator, which is a join that emits the left row only when no right
match exists.
SELECT u.id, u.name
FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id
);
Q25 · Semi-Join — Why EXISTS Is the Right Expression
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a semi-join? Why is EXISTS the most natural way to express it, and when would a
JOIN+DISTINCT be wrong?
The 30-second answer: A semi-join returns one row per outer match — "does at least one matching
row exist on the right?" — without multiplying rows. EXISTS expresses this directly. JOIN +
DISTINCT simulates it but is fragile: if you later add a column from the right table, the DISTINCT silently
changes meaning.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the definition — semi-join is "filter outer by existence on
inner", never duplicate outer rows. 2. Concrete example: users who have made at least one successful
payment. 
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.user_id = u.id AND p.status =
'success') returns each user exactly once. 3. Contrast with JOIN: 
JOIN payments ON ... WHERE status = 'success' returns one row per successful payment
per user — a user with 5 payments shows up 5 times. Adding DISTINCT fixes the count but loses
ordering guarantees and adds a sort. 4. Note the operator-level point: Postgres and SQL Server show
this as "Semi Join" in EXPLAIN — it's a first-class operator, not a hack.
Edge cases to mention: - Correlated EXISTS with a covering index on the right table's join column is
one of the fastest patterns in SQL. - IN (subquery) is rewritten as a semi-join by modern optimizers
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 27 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 28
— usually equivalent to EXISTS in plan. - If the inner query has aggregation, semi-join semantics still hold
— EXISTS (SELECT SUM(...) FROM ...) is always true if any row exists, because aggregates
over empty sets return one row of NULLs.
What NOT to say: - Do not use SELECT * inside EXISTS — it works but SELECT 1 reads as "I only
care that a row exists". - Do not write JOIN ... GROUP BY to dedupe when EXISTS is the intent —
it's slower and harder to read.
Common follow-up: "Why does SELECT 1 inside EXISTS not matter for performance?" — Because
the optimizer only checks for row existence, never materializes the projection.
-- Users with at least one successful payment, no duplicates
SELECT u.id, u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM payments p
  WHERE p.user_id = u.id AND p.status = 'success'
);
Q26 · LATERAL Join — Per-Row Subquery (CROSS APPLY in SQL Server)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Zerodha, Goldman · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Tell me what a LATERAL join does and give an example where you couldn't get the same result
with a plain JOIN.
The 30-second answer: LATERAL (or CROSS APPLY in SQL Server) lets the right side of a join
reference columns from the left side — effectively a correlated subquery in the FROM clause. Use it for
"top-N per group" queries — e.g., the 3 most recent orders per user — which are clumsy or impossible
with plain joins.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Anchor the syntax: FROM users u, LATERAL (SELECT ...
FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) o in
Postgres; OUTER APPLY / CROSS APPLY in SQL Server. 2. Explain why a plain join can't do this: in
a plain JOIN, you can't say LIMIT 3 per left row — you'd need a window function with 
ROW_NUMBER() ... PARTITION BY user_id and an outer filter. 3. The LATERAL form is often
clearer and sometimes faster because it leverages indexed scans on the inner table per outer row. 4. Use
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (or OUTER APPLY) to preserve outer rows that have no inner match.
Edge cases to mention: - LATERAL is in standard SQL since SQL:1999 but only became widely
supported around 2014 (Postgres 9.3, SQL Server has had APPLY since 2005). - MySQL added
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 28 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 29
LATERAL in 8.0.14 — older versions can't do this directly. - Performance depends on having an index on 
(user_id, created_at DESC) on the inner table; without it, you scan the whole table per outer
row.
What NOT to say: - Do not call it "a fancy subquery" — interviewers want the term "correlated derived
table" or "per-row join". - Do not say "you can always rewrite LATERAL as a window function" —
sometimes true, but window functions can't return arbitrary derived columns from a per-row
computation.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY in SQL
Server?" — CROSS APPLY is INNER (drops left rows with no inner match), OUTER APPLY is LEFT
(keeps them with NULLs).
-- 3 most recent orders per user, Postgres syntax
SELECT u.id, u.name, o.order_id, o.created_at
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, created_at
  FROM orders
  WHERE user_id = u.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC
  LIMIT 3
) o ON true;
Q27 · Does Multi-Table Join Order Matter?
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, Target India, AmEx · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If I write A JOIN B JOIN C, does the order I write them in matter for performance? What
does the optimizer actually do?
The 30-second answer: For INNER joins, written order does not matter — the optimizer reorders freely
based on statistics. For OUTER joins, order matters because LEFT JOIN is not commutative. Modern
optimizers consider many join shapes (left-deep, right-deep, bushy) and pick the cheapest based on
cardinality estimates.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the inner-vs-outer distinction — that's the heart of the
question. 2. For inner joins: the optimizer treats A JOIN B JOIN C as a set of join predicates and
chooses the cheapest order — often starting with the most selective filter. 3. For outer joins: (A LEFT
JOIN B) LEFT JOIN C is not the same as A LEFT JOIN (B LEFT JOIN C) because LEFT
JOIN preserves the outer table, and the inner of the second join behaves differently. 4. Mention the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 29 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 30
practical limit: Postgres explores all permutations up to join_collapse_limit (default 8); beyond
that, it follows the written order. Same idea in other engines with different knob names.
Edge cases to mention: - Bushy plans (join two pairs in parallel) are sometimes optimal but most
engines lean toward left-deep trees for simplicity. - Hints like STRAIGHT_JOIN in MySQL or 
LEADING(...) in Oracle force a specific order — last resort when stats are bad. - A missing or out-
of-date ANALYZE can lead the optimizer to pick a terrible order even when the right one is obvious.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "order always matters" — that's true only for outer joins. - Do not say
"the planner always picks the best plan" — it picks the best plan according to its cost model and stats,
which can be wrong.
Common follow-up: "How would you debug a query where you suspect the join order is wrong?" — Run
EXPLAIN ANALYZE, compare estimated vs actual rows at each join, and update stats with ANALYZE
if estimates are off by an order of magnitude.
-- Optimizer picks the cheapest order; written order is just a starting point
SELECT u.name, o.id, p.status
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE u.region = 'south' AND o.created_at > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 day';
Q28 · Join on Inequality — Range Joins and BETWEEN Joins
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you join two tables on an inequality, like BETWEEN or <? What's the performance
impact?
The 30-second answer: Inequality joins are used for range matching — slabs (income tax brackets),
effective-dated dimension lookups, "events that happened during a session". They're slower than
equality joins because hash join doesn't apply; the planner falls back to nested loop or merge join with
range scans. Indexing the range bounds helps a lot.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Anchor with a concrete example — joining a transactions table
to a gst_slabs table on txn_amount BETWEEN slab_min AND slab_max to determine the
GST rate applicable. 2. Explain the operator-level cost: hash join needs equality, so it can't be used. The
planner picks nested loop (cheap if the right table is small and indexed) or merge join with a range
condition. 3. Mention covering indexes on (slab_min, slab_max) — they help, but range overlap
is still O(N) per probe in the worst case. 4. Effective-dated joins: JOIN dim_product p ON
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 30 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 31
f.product_id = p.product_id AND f.event_date BETWEEN p.valid_from AND
p.valid_to is the standard Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 lookup pattern.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres GiST/SP-GiST indexes on range types make inequality joins
much faster than B-tree on min/max. - If ranges overlap, you can get more than one match per outer row
— verify cardinality with a quick COUNT. - Joining created_at BETWEEN start AND end without
an index is a classic O(N×M) disaster on big tables.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "inequality joins are always slow" — with the right index they can be
perfectly fine for modest sizes. - Do not say "use a subquery instead" — for range lookups, the inequality
join is the cleanest expression.
Common follow-up: "Show me an effective-dated lookup." — Standard SCD2 pattern; verify each fact
row matches exactly one dimension row.
-- Tag each transaction with the GST slab it falls into
SELECT t.id, t.amount, s.gst_rate
FROM transactions t
JOIN gst_slabs s
  ON t.amount >= s.slab_min AND t.amount < s.slab_max;
Q29 · USING vs ON — Semantic Differences
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wells Fargo · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between JOIN ... USING (col) and JOIN ... ON a.col =
b.col? When would you prefer USING?
The 30-second answer: USING is shorthand when both tables have a column with the same name — it
merges them into a single output column. ON is general — it can join on different column names or
expressions. USING is cleaner for simple equality joins on identically-named keys; ON is necessary
everywhere else.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the syntax — JOIN orders o USING (user_id) vs 
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id. 2. The big semantic difference: USING produces
one merged column in the output (you write SELECT user_id, not u.user_id); ON keeps both
columns visible. 3. With SELECT *, USING shows the joined column once; ON shows it twice (once
per table) — that's the giveaway in interview screens. 4. Mention that USING only works when column
names match exactly — different names (e.g., id vs user_id) force you to use ON.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 31 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 32
Edge cases to mention: - USING with NATURAL JOIN sounds similar but NATURAL auto-joins on all
same-name columns — covered next, and almost always a footgun. - USING is supported across
Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, SQLite — but is not supported in SQL Server (which forces you to use ON). -
You can chain USING in a multi-table join: a JOIN b USING (k) JOIN c USING (k) is valid if all
three have k.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they are identical" — output column shape differs. - Do not use USING
on a column whose semantics differ between tables (e.g., id meaning user_id in one, order_id in
another) — even if names match, the join is wrong.
Common follow-up: "In an ORM-generated query, why do you see ON everywhere and rarely USING?"
— ORMs generate explicit qualified column names because they don't assume schema symmetry —
defensive code.
-- USING merges the user_id column into one
SELECT user_id, u.name, o.id
FROM users u
JOIN orders o USING (user_id);
Q30 · NATURAL JOIN — Why You Almost Never Use It
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a NATURAL JOIN and why do most senior engineers tell you not to use it?
The 30-second answer: NATURAL JOIN auto-joins on every column with the same name across both
tables. It's a footgun because adding a new same-named column to either table (audit columns like 
created_at, updated_by) silently changes the join condition and breaks the query.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define it precisely — a NATURAL JOIN b finds all columns with
identical names in both tables and joins on equality across all of them. 2. The disaster scenario: you have
users(id, name) and orders(id, user_id, ...). A NATURAL JOIN matches on id —
but id in users is the user id, and id in orders is the order id. You get an empty result that looks
intentional. 3. Even when it works initially, a schema migration adds created_at to both tables, and
now NATURAL JOIN suddenly joins on (id, created_at) — completely silent breakage. 4.
Recommend USING or ON every time — explicit beats implicit.
Edge cases to mention: - Some engines (Oracle) used to encourage NATURAL JOIN in tutorials;
production code rarely uses it. - If you must use it, always pair with SELECT of explicit columns so you
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 32 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 33
can sanity-check the output shape. - NATURAL JOIN does not appear in any well-known production
codebase you'd respect — that itself is the answer.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "NATURAL JOIN is faster" — it isn't, it's just shorter syntax. - Do not
defend it on grounds of brevity — the silent-breakage cost is far higher than the keystroke savings.
Common follow-up: "Can you think of any case where NATURAL JOIN is genuinely useful?" — Almost
no production case. Maybe one-off REPL exploration on a tiny well-known schema.
-- The cautionary tale — DO NOT do this in production
SELECT *
FROM users
NATURAL JOIN orders;
-- Implicitly joins on every same-named column. Add an audit column later, query silently breaks.
Q31 · Self-Join with a Composite Key — Anti-Pattern Detection
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target India, Goldman, JP Morgan · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Suppose you self-join a transactions table on a composite key like (merchant_id,
txn_date) to find consecutive transactions per merchant. What's the anti-pattern here and
how do you avoid it?
The 30-second answer: Self-joining on (merchant_id, txn_date) with a t1.txn_date =
t2.txn_date - INTERVAL '1 day' style condition works but explodes if multiple transactions
exist per merchant per day. Use a window function (LAG over 
PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY txn_date) — one pass, deterministic, no cardinality
surprise.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain why people reach for self-join: they want "current row vs
previous row" and self-join feels intuitive. 2. The cardinality trap: if merchant M has 3 transactions on
May 10 and 5 transactions on May 11, the self-join produces 3×5 = 15 pair rows for that merchant-day
pair — usually not what you want. 3. The correct tool is LAG / LEAD window functions — they
compute "previous row" per partition with no row multiplication. 4. Self-join is still the right tool for "find
pairs where condition X" — e.g., finding overlapping bookings — where you genuinely need pairs.
Edge cases to mention: - If you must self-join, add an inequality like t1.txn_id < t2.txn_id to
avoid duplicate (A,B) and (B,A) pairs. - Window functions need a deterministic ORDER BY to
define "previous" — if txn_date is not unique within partition, add a tiebreaker like txn_id. - On
giant tables, LAG is usually cheaper than self-join because it's one sort, not a join.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 33 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 34
What NOT to say: - Do not say "self-join is always wrong" — it's the right tool for pair-finding problems.
- Do not skip the dedup condition on self-join pairs — duplicates will silently inflate any aggregation
downstream.
Common follow-up: "Now rewrite this as a window function and explain why it's faster." — One sort
instead of join + sort; no row multiplication.
-- Anti-pattern: self-join, risks row multiplication per merchant-date
SELECT t1.merchant_id, t1.amount AS today_amt, t2.amount AS yesterday_amt
FROM transactions t1
JOIN transactions t2
  ON t1.merchant_id = t2.merchant_id
 AND t1.txn_date = t2.txn_date + INTERVAL '1 day';
-- Correct: window function, single pass
SELECT merchant_id, txn_date, amount,
       LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY txn_date) AS prev_amount
FROM transactions;
Q32 · Joining on Functions — Index Implications
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Swiggy, Cred · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If I join two tables on UPPER(a.email) = UPPER(b.email) or 
COALESCE(a.merchant_id, b.merchant_id), what happens to my indexes?
The 30-second answer: Plain B-tree indexes on a.email are not used when the query applies a
function to the column — the index is on raw values, not on UPPER(email). Either store the canonical
form in a generated column, or create a functional/expression index on UPPER(email). COALESCE in
a join condition is even worse — it usually defeats any index entirely.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the index mechanics — B-tree indexes order rows by the
raw column value, so UPPER(email) = UPPER(?) can't binary-search them. 2. Two fixes: (a)
functional index — CREATE INDEX idx_email_upper ON users (UPPER(email)) — Postgres,
Oracle, MySQL 8 all support this; (b) generated column — email_normalized AS UPPER(email)
plus a regular index on it. 3. COALESCE in a join is harder — the optimizer can't push the predicate
through, so it usually full-scans. Restructure with UNION ALL of two joins, one per branch, often
cleaner. 4. Indian-context callout: case-insensitive email matching is the most common real reason to do
this — and the most common cause of slow login queries.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 34 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 35
Edge cases to mention: - CITEXT in Postgres is a case-insensitive text type — store emails as
CITEXT and you avoid the function entirely. - Collation-based case-insensitive matching (CI collations
in SQL Server / MySQL) avoids the function call but has its own gotchas. - Functional indexes have to
match the function exactly — UPPER(email) index won't help LOWER(email) queries.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "indexes always work" — they don't, when functions are applied. - Do
not silently apply functions in joins and assume the planner figures it out — it usually can't.
Common follow-up: "How would you handle case-insensitive joins on email at scale?" — CITEXT in
Postgres, or a stored normalized column with a regular index.
-- Slow: index on email is unused
SELECT *
FROM users u
JOIN merchants m ON UPPER(u.email) = UPPER(m.contact_email);
-- Fast: functional index makes the join sargable
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_upper ON users (UPPER(email));
CREATE INDEX idx_merchants_email_upper ON merchants (UPPER(contact_email));
Q33 · 3-Way and 4-Way Joins — Readability and Planner Behaviour
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Cognizant, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Write a 4-way join across users, orders, payments and refunds. What does the planner do, and
how do you keep this readable?
The 30-second answer: Write the joins in logical-flow order (users → orders → payments → refunds),
alias every table with a short consistent name (u, o, p, r), put filters in WHERE for clarity, and let
the optimizer reorder. For readability, one join per line with the ON condition on the same line. The
planner picks join order independently of how you wrote them (for inner joins).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the query structure — every join on its own line, short aliases.
2. Anchor on the planner: for inner joins, written order is just a hint; the optimizer reorders based on stats.
For outer joins, order is semantic — don't rely on the optimizer to rescue you. 3. Mention the readability
convention: filters that reduce a single table go in WHERE; filters that preserve outer-join semantics go in
ON. 4. Watch the cardinality — a 4-way join where any link is one-to-many can produce surprising row
counts. Sanity-check with COUNT(*) against expected.
Edge cases to mention: - If you cross join_collapse_limit in Postgres (default 8), the planner
stops exploring and uses written order — for big joins, written order suddenly matters. - 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 35 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 36
INFORMATION_SCHEMA queries that join 5+ system views can be terribly slow because stats are
missing — sometimes you have to hand-order them. - A 4-way join with SELECT * returns a wide
result — be explicit about columns to avoid surprises.
What NOT to say: - Do not write FROM a, b, c, d WHERE ... — old-style implicit joins;
reviewers will reject it. - Do not omit aliases — users.id repeated 5 times kills readability.
Common follow-up: "What if you have a filter that applies after the 3rd join — should it go in ON or
WHERE?" — In WHERE if it's an inner join; in ON if you must preserve outer-join NULLs.
SELECT u.id, u.name, o.id AS order_id, p.amount AS paid_amt, r.amount AS refund_amt
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.id
WHERE u.region = 'west'
  AND o.created_at > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 day';
Q34 · Outer Join with WHERE on the Outer Table — The Classic Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Look at this query — users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id WHERE
o.status = 'paid'. The candidate says it returns all users plus their paid orders. Are they
right?
The 30-second answer: No. Putting o.status = 'paid' in WHERE silently converts the LEFT
JOIN into an INNER JOIN, because NULL fails the equality and gets filtered out. The fix is to move the
predicate into the ON clause: ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid'. Now LEFT
semantics are preserved.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule crisply — any predicate on the outer table in WHERE
silently kills outer-join semantics. 2. Walk through what happens row by row: LEFT JOIN produces NULL 
status for users with no orders. WHERE status = 'paid' returns UNKNOWN for NULL, so
those rows are dropped. 3. The fix: move the filter to ON so it's evaluated during the join, not after. Now
unmatched rows still get NULL on the right and are preserved by LEFT semantics. 4. Mention this is the
single most common interview trap in the join section — interviewers ask it precisely because juniors fall
for it constantly.
Edge cases to mention: - WHERE o.status = 'paid' OR o.status IS NULL is another fix —
explicit, but less elegant than moving to ON. - The same trap applies to RIGHT JOIN with a predicate on
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 36 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 37
the left table. - If you genuinely want INNER semantics, leave the WHERE — don't use LEFT JOIN — be
explicit about intent.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "this is a bug in SQL" — it's standard semantics; the candidate just
doesn't know it. - Do not say "always put predicates in ON" — predicates on the outer (preserved) table
belong in WHERE; only predicates on the inner table need to be in ON.
Common follow-up: "Now show me the correct query that returns all users plus their paid orders, with
NULL for users with no paid order." — Just move the predicate to ON.
-- Wrong: silently becomes INNER JOIN
SELECT u.id, o.id, o.status
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
-- Right: filter in ON preserves LEFT semantics
SELECT u.id, o.id, o.status
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid';
Q35 · Hash Join vs Nested-Loop vs Merge Join — What and When
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan India, Target · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Tell me what hash join, nested-loop join and merge join are. When does the optimizer pick each
one?
The 30-second answer: Nested-loop scans the outer, probing the inner per row — best when outer is
small and inner has an index. Hash join builds an in-memory hash on the smaller side and probes from
the larger side — best when neither has a useful index but both fit in memory. Merge join sorts both sides
on the join key and walks them in lock-step — best when both sides are already sorted (clustered index
or pre-sorted output).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Describe each algorithm in one sentence — the operator names are
interview vocabulary. 2. Nested-loop's cost is O(N×M) without index, O(N×log M) with an index on the
inner — picked when outer is tiny or when inner has a sargable index. 3. Hash join is O(N+M) but needs
memory to hold the build side — picked for big equi-joins. Falls back to disk if memory is exhausted
(Postgres "Hash Batches > 1"). 4. Merge join needs both sides sorted — picked when the planner sees
pre-sorted input (clustered index, ORDER BY in subquery) or estimates the sort cost is cheaper than
building a hash table.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 37 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 38
Edge cases to mention: - Hash join only works for equality predicates — inequality joins fall back to
nested-loop or merge. - MySQL only added hash join in 8.0.18 — older versions used nested-loop
everywhere, which is why joins on big tables were so slow. - "Hash join with batch spill" means your
hash didn't fit in work_mem; raise it for that query or shrink the build side.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "hash join is always fastest" — for small outer with indexed inner,
nested-loop wins easily. - Do not say "merge join needs sorted input always" — it can also work on
indexed scans that produce sorted output for free.
Common follow-up: "How do you check which join the planner picked?" — EXPLAIN ANALYZE in
Postgres, EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE in MySQL 8, the graphical plan in SQL Server.
-- Inspect the chosen join algorithm
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT u.name, o.id
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.created_at > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day';
Q36 · Joining Huge Tables — Partition-Wise Joins
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target India, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have a transactions table with 5 billion rows partitioned by month and a merchants
table with 50 million rows partitioned by region. How do I make joins fast?
The 30-second answer: Use partition-wise joins — when both tables are partitioned on the join key (or a
related key), the planner joins partition-to-partition independently and in parallel, instead of building one
giant hash table. In Postgres, enable enable_partitionwise_join = on. Make sure partition
keys align and stats are fresh on every partition.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem — 5 billion × 50 million is hopeless as a single
hash join; you need to split the work. 2. Postgres declarative partitioning (since 10.x): partition both
tables on the same key (say merchant_id hash partitions) so partition i of transactions joins only
with partition i of merchants. 3. Enable enable_partitionwise_join and 
enable_partitionwise_aggregate — both are off by default in older versions. 4. With Postgres
parallel query, each partition pair can be joined by a worker in parallel — near-linear scale-out on a multi-
core box.
Edge cases to mention: - Partition pruning happens first — if your WHERE clause filters to one month,
only that partition pair joins. - Misaligned partition schemes defeat partition-wise joins — both tables
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 38 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 39
must share the partitioning strategy on the join key. - Stats are per-partition — ANALYZE the partitioned
table to refresh all child partition stats.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "just add an index" — for billions of rows, an index alone won't save you;
partitioning is the structural fix. - Do not claim partitioning is always a win — it adds complexity to
schema migrations, backups and inserts.
Common follow-up: "What if the merchants table isn't partitioned? Can we still get any benefit?" —
Postgres can still parallel-scan the transactions table and broadcast merchants to each worker — slower
than partition-wise but better than serial.
-- Postgres declarative partitioning (range on month for transactions)
CREATE TABLE transactions (id BIGINT, merchant_id INT, txn_date DATE, amount NUMERIC)
PARTITION BY RANGE (txn_date);
CREATE TABLE transactions_2026_05
  PARTITION OF transactions FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01');
-- Enable per-session
SET enable_partitionwise_join = on;
Q37 · Joining with Composite Indexes
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have a composite index on (merchant_id, txn_date). When does the planner use it for a
join, and when does it skip the index?
The 30-second answer: The composite index is used when the join condition references the leading
columns in order — merchant_id = ? alone uses it, merchant_id = ? AND txn_date
BETWEEN ... uses both. A predicate on txn_date alone, without merchant_id, can't seek the
index — most engines won't use it at all (Postgres might choose an index-only scan if it covers the
query).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the leftmost-prefix rule — composite B-tree indexes are
like a phone book sorted by (last name, first name); you can search by last name alone, but not by first
name alone. 2. Apply to joins: JOIN ... ON t.merchant_id = m.id uses the index for the seek.
Add AND t.txn_date > ... and the index narrows the range further. 3. Index-only scans (covering
index): if all columns the query needs are in the index, Postgres can skip the heap fetch — massive
speed-up for read-heavy queries. 4. Order matters: build the index with the high-selectivity column first if
your queries always filter by it.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 39 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 40
Edge cases to mention: - WHERE txn_date > ... AND merchant_id = ? is still seekable —
the engine reorders predicates. - Skip-scan (Oracle, MySQL 8.0, partial in Postgres 17) can sometimes
use the leading column even when the query doesn't filter on it — but don't rely on it. - Composite index
on (a, b) does NOT serve queries that join on b alone — that needs its own index on b.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "composite index speeds up everything that touches those columns" —
only with leftmost-prefix. - Do not over-index — every extra index slows writes, and unused indexes are
dead weight.
Common follow-up: "What order should the columns be in?" — Leftmost column should be the one
used in equality predicates by most queries; range columns later.
-- Composite index supports the join + date range
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_merchant_date ON transactions (merchant_id, txn_date);
SELECT t.id, t.amount
FROM merchants m
JOIN transactions t ON t.merchant_id = m.id
WHERE t.txn_date >= '2026-05-01';
Q38 · Joining Temporal/Range Data — Effective Dating
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, AmEx, Target · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have a fact table payments with paid_at timestamp and a dimension merchant_dim
with valid_from, valid_to (slowly-changing dimension type 2). Join them so each
payment gets the merchant attributes that were in effect at paid_at.
The 30-second answer: Join on merchant_id and the temporal range — JOIN merchant_dim m
ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.paid_at >= m.valid_from AND p.paid_at <
m.valid_to. Build an index on (merchant_id, valid_from, valid_to) and ensure dim
records are non-overlapping per merchant. This is the standard SCD2 join.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain SCD2: each row in the dimension represents one version of
merchant attributes, with valid-from / valid-to defining its window. The "current" version has valid_to
= '9999-12-31' or NULL. 2. The join uses inequality on the time bounds — falls back to nested-loop
or merge unless you have a smart range index. 3. Composite index on 
(merchant_id, valid_from, valid_to) lets the planner seek per merchant and then range-
scan the time bounds — usually fast enough. 4. Postgres-specific: use a tstzrange column with a
GiST index for genuinely large dimension tables — order-of-magnitude faster than B-tree on bounds.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 40 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 41
Edge cases to mention: - Make sure dim windows don't overlap per merchant — overlapping windows
give multiple matches and silently inflate fact rows. - Open-ended current rows with valid_to =
NULL need COALESCE(valid_to, 'infinity') in the join condition. - Use valid_to as half-
open (exclusive) to avoid boundary double-counting — that's the data warehousing convention.
What NOT to say: - Do not just join on merchant_id and assume "latest version" — you'll attribute
payments to the wrong merchant attributes when history changes. - Do not write valid_from <=
paid_at AND paid_at <= valid_to with closed bounds — boundary records will match twice.
Common follow-up: "How do you ensure dim windows don't overlap?" — Exclusion constraint in
Postgres on (merchant_id, tstzrange(valid_from, valid_to)); trigger-based check
elsewhere.
-- SCD2 join: each payment sees the merchant attributes in effect at paid_at
SELECT p.id, p.amount, m.name AS merchant_name, m.tier AS merchant_tier
FROM payments p
JOIN merchant_dim m
  ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
 AND p.paid_at >= m.valid_from
 AND p.paid_at <  COALESCE(m.valid_to, 'infinity'::timestamptz);
Q39 · Star Join Optimization — Data Warehouse Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target India, Goldman, AmEx · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In a star schema, one fact table joins to many small dimensions. How does the optimizer handle
this differently from a transactional 4-way join?
The 30-second answer: The optimizer recognises the star pattern — one big fact in the centre, many
small dimensions around it — and uses star join optimization. Each dimension is filtered first, then a
single hash join (or bitmap intersection) probes the fact table once with the combined dimension keys.
Avoids walking the giant fact multiple times.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the schema — fact_sales (billions of rows) joined to 
dim_product, dim_store, dim_date, dim_customer (each thousands or millions, small
relative to fact). 2. Naive plan: 4 sequential hash joins, each rescanning the fact in some shape. Star join
optimization: filter dimensions first to small key sets, then one bitmap-or-hash scan of the fact. 3. Oracle
has STAR_TRANSFORMATION hint; SQL Server detects star schemas heuristically; Postgres relies on
partition-wise joins and parallel scans, but no formal "star transformation". 4. Practical wins: bitmap
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 41 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 42
indexes on each fact foreign key (Oracle/Postgres BRIN), or columnar formats (DuckDB, ClickHouse,
Snowflake) where star joins are the bread and butter.
Edge cases to mention: - Snowflake (the warehouse, not the schema variant) handles star joins natively
with micro-partition pruning. - Dimension filtering selectivity matters — if no dimension reduces the fact
much, you're back to a full fact scan. - ClickHouse and DuckDB recommend denormalising small
dimensions into the fact table — sometimes faster than star join for analytical queries.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume OLTP join intuition transfers — OLAP planners optimise differently. -
Do not use star schema for OLTP — too many joins per transaction; use a normalised model.
Common follow-up: "When would you denormalize the dimensions into the fact?" — When the
dimensions are tiny and read-mostly, or when you're on a columnar store where wide tables compress
well.
-- Star-schema query — optimizer filters dims first, then probes fact once
SELECT d.day_of_week, p.category, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_key = p.product_key
JOIN dim_store s ON f.store_key = s.store_key
WHERE d.year = 2026
  AND p.category IN ('electronics', 'apparel')
  AND s.region = 'south'
GROUP BY d.day_of_week, p.category;
Q40 · Joining on NULL — Does It Match?
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, TCS, Wells Fargo · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have two tables and the join column is nullable on both sides. Will NULL on one side match
NULL on the other side?
The 30-second answer: No. In standard SQL, NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so
the join condition fails and the rows don't match. If you genuinely want NULLs to join to each other, use 
IS NOT DISTINCT FROM (Postgres) or a.col = b.col OR (a.col IS NULL AND b.col IS
NULL).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the three-valued-logic rule — NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN,
never TRUE. 2. Consequence: any row with NULL in the join column is silently dropped from INNER and
LEFT/RIGHT match sets — only kept on the preserved side of outer joins as orphans. 3. The fix when
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 42 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 43
you actually want NULLs to match: IS NOT DISTINCT FROM (Postgres, SQL standard); MySQL has 
<=> (null-safe equals); SQL Server forces you to write the OR ... IS NULL expansion. 4. Real-
world example: optional referrer_id on signups joining to a referrers dim — joining on NULL
would treat every direct-traffic user as referred by every other direct-traffic user, which is nonsense — so
plain equality is what you want, and NULL handling has to be explicit.
Edge cases to mention: - UNION deduplicates NULLs as if they were equal — inconsistent with join
semantics; another classic interview trap. - IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocks index usage in some
engines — check the plan. - Group BY treats NULLs as a single group — also inconsistent with join
equality.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "NULL matches NULL in a join" — straight wrong in standard SQL. - Do
not paper over the issue with COALESCE(col, -1) unless you're sure no real value is -1 — magic
numbers backfire.
Common follow-up: "How does Oracle differ here?" — Oracle treats empty string as NULL, which
compounds the trap; otherwise the standard rule applies.
-- Default: NULL does NOT match NULL
SELECT a.id, b.id
FROM a JOIN b ON a.key = b.key;
-- Rows with NULL in either a.key or b.key are dropped
-- Postgres: explicit NULL-safe equality
SELECT a.id, b.id
FROM a JOIN b ON a.key IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.key;
Q41 · Joining Bookings on Overlapping Time Ranges
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Ola, Razorpay · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have a bookings table with (rider_id, start_time, end_time). Find all
overlapping bookings for the same rider — these indicate a scheduling conflict.
The 30-second answer: Self-join the table on rider_id and the overlap condition a.start_time
< b.end_time AND a.end_time > b.start_time, with a.booking_id < b.booking_id to
avoid duplicate (A,B) and (B,A) pairs. Index on (rider_id, start_time) is essential; for
very large tables, use a range-typed column with a GiST index in Postgres.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the overlap condition — two intervals [a_start,
a_end] and [b_start, b_end] overlap iff a_start < b_end AND a_end > b_start.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 43 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 44
Memorise this. 2. Self-join with a.booking_id < b.booking_id so each conflicting pair appears
exactly once and a booking doesn't overlap with itself. 3. Performance: B-tree on (rider_id,
start_time) reduces it to one rider's bookings at a time; for large data, Postgres tstzrange
column with GIST (range_col) and the && overlap operator is faster. 4. Mention that this is the
same query shape used to detect double-booking in ride-hailing, hotel rooms, conference rooms,
calendar invites.
Edge cases to mention: - Decide whether touching ranges (a.end_time = b.start_time) count
as overlapping — usually no, so use strict < and >. - Open-ended bookings with end_time IS
NULL (ongoing rides) need COALESCE(end_time, 'infinity') or special handling. - For a single
rider with thousands of bookings, the self-join is O(N²) per rider — only practical with the index seek
pattern.
What NOT to say: - Do not write BETWEEN for overlap detection — it's awkward and easy to get
wrong (off-by-one on closed/open intervals). - Do not forget the < on booking_id — without it,
you'll get every pair twice and the booking matched against itself.
Common follow-up: "How would you find the maximum number of concurrent bookings per rider at any
time?" — Sweep-line algorithm: expand each booking to (start, +1) and (end, -1), sum
running totals per rider — that's a window function problem, covered in the windows chapter.
-- Overlapping bookings per rider (each pair appears once)
SELECT a.rider_id, a.booking_id AS booking_a, b.booking_id AS booking_b,
       a.start_time, a.end_time, b.start_time, b.end_time
FROM bookings a
JOIN bookings b
  ON a.rider_id = b.rider_id
 AND a.booking_id < b.booking_id
 AND a.start_time < b.end_time
 AND a.end_time   > b.start_time;
Q42 · Outer Join with Aggregation — Preserving Zeros
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Cred, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show the total order amount per user, including users who placed zero orders (they should show
as 0, not be missing).
The 30-second answer: LEFT JOIN orders to users, then COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0). Without
COALESCE, users with no orders get NULL from the SUM (SUM of zero rows is NULL, not zero), and the
report looks broken. Group by user.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 44 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 45
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the LEFT JOIN — it preserves users who have no orders,
with NULL on the order columns. 2. The aggregate trap: SUM(NULL) over an empty group is NULL. 
COUNT(*) over the LEFT JOIN counts at least 1 per user (because the user row is preserved) — use 
COUNT(o.id) instead, which doesn't count NULLs. 3. Wrap the SUM in COALESCE to surface zeros: 
COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0). 4. Same trap with AVG and other aggregates — be intentional
about NULL semantics.
Edge cases to mention: - COUNT(*) vs COUNT(o.id) is the most common bug in LEFT JOIN
aggregations — pick the right one based on whether you want to count outer rows or matched inner
rows. - Filtering on aggregate post-join: use HAVING, not WHERE — WHERE runs before grouping. - If
you also LEFT JOIN payments and aggregate both, the two LEFT JOINs can multiply each other — sub-
aggregate one in a CTE first.
What NOT to say: - Do not omit COALESCE and let NULLs leak into reports — finance teams will reject
the dashboard. - Do not switch to INNER JOIN to avoid NULLs — that drops the users you want to
preserve.
Common follow-up: "What if you also need refund totals per user from a third table?" — Don't chain
LEFT JOINs and aggregate at the end — pre-aggregate refunds in a CTE, then LEFT JOIN the two
aggregates to the user list.
-- All users, with zero for those who never ordered
SELECT u.id, u.name,
       COUNT(o.id)            AS order_count,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS total_amount
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;
Q43 · Cardinality Explosion — Two LEFT JOINs Multiplying
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Walmart Labs · Topic: Joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I LEFT JOIN orders to users, then LEFT JOIN refunds to the same query. My SUMs are suddenly
double what they should be. What's going on?
The 30-second answer: Two one-to-many LEFT JOINs from the same parent multiply each other — a
user with 3 orders and 2 refunds gives you 3 × 2 = 6 result rows, and any SUM over those rows inflates
by 2x or 3x. Fix by pre-aggregating each branch in a CTE before joining to the parent.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 45 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 46
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the multiplication geometrically — joining users to orders
gives one row per (user, order). Joining that result to refunds gives one row per (user, order, refund). If
refunds are per-user (not per-order), every order row pairs with every refund row. 2. Numerical example:
user U has 3 orders and 2 standalone refunds. The result has 3 × 2 = 6 rows. SUM(order_amount)
sums each order amount twice; SUM(refund_amount) sums each refund 3 times. 3. The fix:
aggregate each branch independently in a CTE — orders_agg and refunds_agg — then LEFT
JOIN both back to users on user_id. Each user gets exactly one row from each CTE. 4. The faster
alternative: separate aggregating subqueries with SUM(...) FILTER (WHERE ...) or scalar
correlated subqueries — depends on what reads cleaner.
Edge cases to mention: - The bug is hidden when refunds happen to be linked to orders
(refunds.order_id) — then refunds-per-user is naturally bounded by orders-per-user, and the
multiplication is less visible but still real. - COUNT(DISTINCT) is sometimes used as a band-aid — it
works for counts but not for SUMs. - Window functions can dedupe in some patterns but are usually
clumsier than CTE pre-aggregation.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use DISTINCT to dedupe" — DISTINCT runs on the whole row, not per
branch, and can't unmultiply SUMs. - Do not blame the planner — the result is mathematically correct
given the join shape; it's the query shape that's wrong.
Common follow-up: "How would you verify the bug before fixing it?" — 
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM result GROUP BY user_id for one user — if the count
exceeds the expected joined cardinality, you've caught it.
-- Bug: orders × refunds multiplication
SELECT u.id, SUM(o.amount), SUM(r.amount)
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o  ON o.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id;
-- Fix: pre-aggregate each branch
WITH orders_agg AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_orders
  FROM orders GROUP BY user_id
),
refunds_agg AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_refunds
  FROM refunds GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.id, u.name,
       COALESCE(o.total_orders,  0) AS total_orders,
       COALESCE(r.total_refunds, 0) AS total_refunds
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders_agg  o ON o.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN refunds_agg r ON r.user_id = u.id;
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 46 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q44 · Subquery in WHERE vs FROM vs SELECT vs HAVING
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You can put a subquery in WHERE, in FROM, in SELECT and in HAVING. Walk me through when
you'd pick each one with a concrete example.
The 30-second answer: WHERE for filtering rows against a list or check; FROM for treating a subquery
as a virtual table (derived table); SELECT for a per-row scalar lookup (one value); HAVING for filtering
grouped rows by a comparison against a subquery result.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the placement-equals-purpose framing — each spot
serves a different job in the query pipeline. 2. WHERE example: WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id
FROM users WHERE city = 'Mumbai') — filtering the outer row set. 3. FROM example: FROM
(SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY user_id) t — a pre-
aggregated derived table you then join or filter. 4. SELECT example: SELECT o.id, (SELECT name
FROM users WHERE id = o.user_id) AS user_name FROM orders o — a scalar lookup per
row. 5. HAVING example: 
HAVING SUM(amount) > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM order_totals) — comparing a group's
aggregate against a single value the subquery returns. 6. Be ready to say which you avoid in production:
SELECT subqueries are usually rewritten as JOINs for performance.
Edge cases to mention: - A SELECT-list subquery must return exactly one row and one column or you
get a runtime error. - HAVING runs after GROUP BY, so its subquery can reference aggregates the
WHERE clause cannot. - FROM subqueries must have an alias in standard SQL — Postgres enforces it
strictly, MySQL forgives it sometimes.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "they are all equivalent, just style" — they run at different stages and
have different cardinality rules. - Do not put a multi-row subquery in SELECT and shrug when it errors.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 47 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 48
Common follow-up: "Which one would the optimiser most likely rewrite, and why?" — A SELECT-list
correlated subquery; many planners convert it to a LEFT JOIN with aggregation when it's safe.
SELECT o.id,
       (SELECT name FROM users u WHERE u.id = o.user_id) AS user_name
FROM orders o
WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders);
Q45 · Scalar Subquery and the Multi-Row Gotcha
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Capgemini · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a scalar subquery and what's the most common runtime error you see with them?
The 30-second answer: A scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column. The classic error is
when it accidentally returns more than one row — the database throws subquery returned more
than one row in Postgres or Subquery returns more than 1 row (Error 1242) in MySQL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define scalar — one row, one column — and where it can legally
appear: anywhere an expression can. 2. The trap: a junior writes WHERE salary > (SELECT salary
FROM employees WHERE city = 'Bengaluru') thinking Bengaluru has one employee, but it has
fifty. 3. The fix is to pick an aggregate: MAX, MIN, AVG, or to add a filter that guarantees one row, or
to switch the operator to IN/ ANY/ ALL. 4. Defensive habit: wrap with LIMIT 1 only if you
genuinely don't care which row — otherwise use an aggregate.
Edge cases to mention: - A scalar subquery returning zero rows evaluates to NULL — comparisons
with NULL silently give UNKNOWN and filter out rows. - In SELECT list, a scalar subquery runs once per
outer row when correlated, once total when not — performance footgun. - Oracle has SINGLE_VALUE
operator that enforces the one-row contract at plan time.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "just add LIMIT 1" — that hides bugs and gives non-deterministic
results. - Do not confuse scalar with derived table; scalar is one value, derived is a virtual table.
Common follow-up: "What if the scalar subquery returns NULL — does the outer comparison fail?" — It
returns UNKNOWN, so the row is filtered out silently. Use COALESCE to give a safe default.
-- Safe: aggregate guarantees one row
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE city = 'Bengaluru');
