Q46 · What Makes a Subquery "Correlated"
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain what a correlated subquery is and why it can be slow.
The 30-second answer: A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, which means
it has to be evaluated once per outer row instead of once overall — that's an O(n*m) pattern that can
wreck large tables.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The defining trait: the inner query has a column reference from the
outer query in scope. 2. Contrast with a non-correlated subquery, which is independent of the outer row
and runs once. 3. Performance cost: for every outer row, the inner subquery is re-executed — unless the
optimiser rewrites it as a semi-join, which most modern planners do for EXISTS but not always for
SELECT-list subqueries. 4. When correlated subqueries are actually fine: when the outer set is small,
when the inner is index-supported, or when readability matters more than micro-optimisation.
Edge cases to mention: - A correlated subquery with EXISTS short-circuits — the inner query stops
as soon as it finds the first matching row. - A correlated subquery in SELECT list cannot use LIMIT in
some dialects (older MySQL) — workaround is a JOIN with aggregation. - Postgres's EXPLAIN ANALYZE
shows correlated subqueries as a SubPlan node — read the loops counter to spot the per-row cost.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "correlated subqueries are always slow" — modern planners often
unnest them into joins. - Do not paste a correlated subquery in an interview and say "I'd never write this"
— show you know when it reads more clearly than a join.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this correlated subquery as a JOIN." — Practice the EXISTS → semi-join
and the SELECT-list scalar → LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY rewrites.
-- Correlated: o.user_id from the outer query is used inside
SELECT u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND o.amount > 5000
);
Q47 · EXISTS vs IN — Semantic and Performance Differences
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Cred, Meesho · Topic: Subqueries
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 49 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 50
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When should I reach for EXISTS and when for IN? Are they really the same thing?
The 30-second answer: Semantically they answer the same question for non-NULL data, but EXISTS
short-circuits on first match and is the natural fit for correlated checks, while IN is cleaner with a static list
or a one-shot independent subquery. They diverge sharply when NULLs are involved.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the boolean framing — both return TRUE/FALSE per outer
row. 2. EXISTS: stops the inner scan on the first matching row, ideal when the inner table is large. 3. IN:
materialises the candidate set (logically), good when the candidate set is small and reusable. 4. NULL
behaviour: value IN (1, 2, NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN when value is not 1 or 2 — the trap
shows up with NOT IN (Q5). 5. Performance reality: modern optimisers (Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL 8)
often produce the same plan for both, so pick whichever reads better.
Edge cases to mention: - EXISTS with SELECT * vs SELECT 1 is identical in every modern
optimiser — the column list is ignored. - IN with a subquery that returns millions of rows can be heavier
than EXISTS because some planners materialise. - Oracle historically treated NOT IN poorly with NULLs
— that has improved but legacy code still has scars.
What NOT to say: - Do not say SELECT 1 is faster than SELECT * inside EXISTS — they parse
identically. - Do not claim one is always faster — measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your data.
Common follow-up: "What if I use IN (SELECT id FROM huge_table) — is the subquery
executed once or per row?" — Once, if uncorrelated; the optimiser typically builds a hash set.
-- EXISTS reads cleanly when correlated
SELECT u.id, u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
Q48 · The NOT IN NULL Trap (and the NOT EXISTS Fix)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I ran WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees) and got zero rows
even though I expected hundreds. What happened?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 50 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 51
The 30-second answer: The subquery returned at least one NULL. NOT IN with a NULL evaluates to
UNKNOWN for every outer row, which filters everything out. Fix is to add 
WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL to the subquery, or switch to NOT EXISTS, which handles
NULLs correctly.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through the logic: x NOT IN (1, NULL) becomes 
x != 1 AND x != NULL. The second condition is UNKNOWN, the AND is UNKNOWN, the row is
dropped. 2. The bug is silent — no error, just empty results — which is why it eats interview time. 3. NOT
EXISTS does not have this problem because it's a row-existence check, not a value comparison. 4.
Defensive coding habit: always filter NULLs from a NOT IN subquery, or use NOT EXISTS by default.
Edge cases to mention: - If the column inside the subquery is declared NOT NULL, NOT IN is safe —
but you cannot always rely on schema you didn't write. - LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.col IS
NULL (anti-join pattern) is also safe and often the fastest. - The same NULL trap affects <> and !=
comparisons in WHERE generally — not unique to NOT IN.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are equivalent" — they are not in the presence
of NULLs. - Do not blame the database — it is following the SQL standard's three-valued logic correctly.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite the query three ways — NOT IN with filter, NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN." —
Be able to switch between all three on the whiteboard.
-- Safe rewrite using NOT EXISTS
SELECT id, name
FROM employees e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM employees m WHERE m.manager_id = e.id
);
Q49 · ANY, SOME, ALL — What They Mean and When They Appear
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, HCL · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Have you used ANY, SOME or ALL? What do they do and can you rewrite them without those
keywords?
The 30-second answer: ANY and SOME are synonyms — x > ANY(subquery) is TRUE when x
beats at least one row, equivalent to comparing against the MIN. x > ALL(subquery) is TRUE only
when x beats every row, equivalent to comparing against the MAX. Both can be rewritten with aggregate
subqueries or with EXISTS.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 51 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 52
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the semantic mapping clearly: > ANY = > MIN, > ALL =
> MAX, < ANY = < MAX, < ALL = < MIN, = ANY = IN, <> ALL = NOT IN. 2. Why
interviewers ask: the syntax is rare in day-to-day code but shows up in legacy reports and certifications.
3. Practical example: "employees who earn more than at least one manager" → salary > ANY
(SELECT salary FROM managers). 4. The cleaner rewrite is usually aggregate-based, which is
what most teams prefer because the intent is obvious.
Edge cases to mention: - Empty subquery: > ANY () is FALSE, > ALL () is TRUE —
counterintuitive, worth memorising. - NULL in subquery: > ALL becomes UNKNOWN if any compared
row is NULL — same NULL trap as NOT IN. - MySQL supports ANY/SOME/ALL; SQLite supports them
too; some lightweight engines do not.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse = ANY with IN semantically without mentioning the NULL
caveat. - Do not say "ALL means all rows" — it means the condition holds against every returned row.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite salary > ALL (subquery) using MAX." — salary > (SELECT
MAX(salary) FROM subquery_source).
-- Equivalent forms
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM managers);
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM managers);
Q50 · Derived Table vs CTE vs Temp Table
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you use a derived table in FROM, a CTE, or a temp table? They look similar —
what's the trade-off?
The 30-second answer: Derived table is a subquery in FROM scoped to one statement. CTE
( WITH ...) is named, reusable within the same statement, and supports recursion. Temp table
persists across statements in a session, can be indexed, and is right when you reuse the same result set
several times or need stats for the planner.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Derived table: cheap, scoped to one query, no extra round trip — fine
for a one-shot aggregation. 2. CTE: same scope as derived table but named and readable; supports
recursion; in Postgres 12+ the optimiser may inline it (non-materialised) for better plans. 3. Temp table:
written to tempdb (SQL Server) or temp schema (Postgres) — survives across statements, can be
indexed, stats are collected. Worth it when you reuse the set multiple times. 4. Decision rule: one-shot =
derived or CTE; multi-statement reuse or need indexes = temp table.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 52 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 53
Edge cases to mention: - In older MySQL, derived tables were always materialised — that changed in
5.7+. - Postgres 11 and earlier always materialised CTEs (optimisation fence) — 12+ inlines by default;
use MATERIALIZED keyword to opt back in. - Temp tables in MySQL cannot be referenced more than
once in the same query — surprise gotcha.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "CTEs are always faster than subqueries" — depends on engine and
version. - Do not use a temp table for a one-shot select; that's overkill and adds I/O.
Common follow-up: "Same query — CTE or derived table — does the plan change?" — In Postgres 12+
usually no, in older Postgres yes (CTE was a fence).
WITH user_totals AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.name, ut.total FROM users u JOIN user_totals ut ON ut.user_id = u.id;
Q51 · Correlated Subquery vs JOIN Rewrite — When Each Wins
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Here's a correlated subquery — when would you rewrite it as a JOIN and when would you leave
it?
The 30-second answer: Rewrite as JOIN when you need columns from the inner table or when the
optimiser fails to unnest. Leave as correlated when it reads more clearly, when the outer set is small, or
when EXISTS gives you cheaper semi-join semantics than a JOIN-with-DISTINCT.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The correlated form is just a different surface syntax for what is often
a JOIN under the hood — modern planners frequently rewrite. 2. JOIN wins when you need columns
from both tables: SELECT u.name, o.amount FROM users u JOIN orders o ON u.id =
o.user_id. 3. Correlated EXISTS wins for "does any match exist" — cheaper than JOIN ... GROUP
BY u.id. 4. SELECT-list scalar subquery often loses to LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY when you need
multiple aggregates per outer row.
Edge cases to mention: - A JOIN where the right side has duplicates multiplies the left rows —
correlated EXISTS does not. Different cardinality, different result. - Some planners (older MySQL, older
Oracle) struggle to unnest correlated subqueries; rewriting manually helps. - EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the
truth-teller — never argue from style alone.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 53 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 54
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always rewrite correlated subqueries as JOINs" — sometimes they are
semantically different. - Do not write JOIN ... DISTINCT to dedupe and call it equivalent to EXISTS
— it does extra work.
Common follow-up: "Show me a case where the JOIN gives more rows than the correlated subquery."
— Outer user joined to orders where user has 5 orders: JOIN gives 5 rows, EXISTS gives 1.
-- Correlated form
SELECT u.name FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
-- Equivalent semi-join (deduped JOIN)
SELECT DISTINCT u.name FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
Q52 · "Subquery Returned More Than One Row" — Diagnosing the Error
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You run a query and you see "Subquery returns more than 1 row" — what does it mean and how
do you fix it?
The 30-second answer: A subquery used in a scalar context — like after =, <, > — returned
multiple rows. Fix is to either switch the operator to IN/ ANY/ ALL, or to aggregate the subquery
(MAX/MIN/AVG), or to add a filter that narrows it to one row.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Recognise the context: this error appears when the subquery is used
where a single value is expected. 2. Identify the four fixes: (a) IN if you want set membership, (b)
aggregate if you want a single derived value, (c) LIMIT 1 if you genuinely don't care which row (rare),
(d) add a stronger predicate. 3. The bug usually lives in a join-condition assumption: candidate assumed
"one product per category" but the schema allows many. 4. Defensive habit: if you write WHERE col =
(subquery), mentally check "is this guaranteed to be one row?"
Edge cases to mention: - ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 is non-deterministic without a unique tiebreaker
— add a tiebreaker like id ASC. - UPDATE/DELETE with WHERE col = (subquery) will throw
the same error. - In Postgres the message is "more than one row returned by a subquery used as an
expression" — same root cause.
What NOT to say: - Do not silently slap on LIMIT 1 without telling the interviewer it can hide the
underlying schema issue. - Do not blame the data — the query is the bug.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 54 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 55
Common follow-up: "What if the subquery returns zero rows?" — Returns NULL, comparison becomes
UNKNOWN, row is filtered out — also silent.
-- Buggy: returns many rows
SELECT name FROM products WHERE price = (SELECT price FROM products WHERE category='Phones');
-- Fixed with aggregate
SELECT name FROM products WHERE price = (SELECT MAX(price) FROM products WHERE category='Phones');
Q53 · UPDATE with a Subquery — Multi-Row Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Update every order's user_city column with the city from the users table. Show me the
Postgres and MySQL versions.
The 30-second answer: Postgres uses UPDATE ... FROM with the join in a FROM clause. MySQL
uses UPDATE table1 JOIN table2 SET ... syntax. Both achieve the same multi-row correlated
update; pure ANSI SQL would use a correlated subquery in the SET clause.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres pattern: 
UPDATE orders o SET user_city = u.city FROM users u WHERE u.id = o.user_id —
clean and readable. 2. MySQL pattern: UPDATE orders o JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
SET o.user_city = u.city — JOIN clause inside UPDATE. 3. ANSI fallback: UPDATE orders
SET user_city = (SELECT u.city FROM users u WHERE u.id = orders.user_id) —
works everywhere but slower and risks the multi-row error if the subquery is ambiguous. 4. Always wrap
in a transaction in production — and test with SELECT first using the same WHERE clause.
Edge cases to mention: - If the correlated subquery returns no match, the column is set to NULL —
guard with WHERE EXISTS or COALESCE. - Multi-row update in MySQL with a JOIN does not error
on multiple matches — it just updates with the last one matched (driver-dependent), which is dangerous.
- Postgres's UPDATE ... FROM does not handle multiple matches gracefully either — first match
wins by physical order, which is non-deterministic.
What NOT to say: - Do not run UPDATE without a SELECT preview — the number-one cause of
production incidents. - Do not assume UPDATE ... JOIN is portable — it is MySQL/MariaDB-
specific.
Common follow-up: "What if the join produces multiple matches per outer row?" — Unpredictable
behaviour. Add DISTINCT ON (Postgres) or aggregate the subquery first into a derived table.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 55 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 56
-- Postgres
UPDATE orders o SET user_city = u.city FROM users u WHERE u.id = o.user_id;
-- MySQL
UPDATE orders o JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id SET o.user_city = u.city;
Q54 · DELETE with a Subquery
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cognizant, HCL, Wipro, Capgemini · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Delete every order whose user has been inactive for more than two years. Write it three ways.
The 30-second answer: Three ways — DELETE ... WHERE user_id IN (subquery), 
DELETE ... WHERE EXISTS (correlated subquery), or vendor-specific DELETE ...
USING (Postgres) / DELETE FROM t1 USING t1 JOIN t2 ... (MySQL). EXISTS is the safest
with NULLs.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. IN form: DELETE FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT
id FROM users WHERE last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '2 years'). Watch for NULLs. 2.
EXISTS form: 
DELETE FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM users u WHERE u.id =
o.user_id AND u.last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '2 years') — NULL-safe. 3. Postgres
USING: DELETE FROM orders o USING users u WHERE u.id = o.user_id AND
u.last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '2 years' — fastest when you need columns from another
table. 4. Always start with the equivalent SELECT, run a COUNT(*), eyeball the result, then convert
SELECT to DELETE in a transaction.
Edge cases to mention: - DELETE in MySQL with a subquery on the same table needs a wrapper
derived table — MySQL forbids referencing the deleted-from table directly in the subquery. - Foreign
keys with ON DELETE CASCADE mean one DELETE can cascade across many tables — review the
schema first. - Soft delete is often the right pattern in production — flag a deleted_at instead of
removing rows.
What NOT to say: - Do not run DELETE without a LIMIT or transaction in production unless you have
a backup. - Do not assume DELETE with subquery is always slower than join-based — depends on the
planner.
Common follow-up: "How do you delete in batches to avoid lock contention?" — Loop with LIMIT
1000 per batch and commit between batches.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 56 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 57
DELETE FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM users u WHERE u.id = o.user_id AND u.last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '2 years'
);
Q55 · SELECT * with a Derived Table — Duplicate Column Name Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, TCS, Wipro · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I wrote SELECT * FROM (SELECT a.*, b.* FROM a JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id) t
and it errors. Why?
The 30-second answer: The derived table has two columns named id (one from each table) and the
database refuses to expose the duplicate when materialised. Fix is to alias each column explicitly inside
the derived table or to enumerate columns in the outer SELECT.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Derived tables enforce unique column names — once the subquery
is finalised, the outer query sees a virtual table with a fixed column list. 2. Postgres throws column
reference "id" is ambiguous (or duplicate-column error depending on context). MySQL gives 
Duplicate column name 'id'. 3. Fix one: explicit aliases inside — SELECT a.id AS a_id,
b.id AS b_id, ... FROM a JOIN b .... 4. Fix two: never use SELECT * from a JOIN inside a
derived table; enumerate columns. It's also better for index-only scans and schema evolution.
Edge cases to mention: - A plain JOIN without the derived table wrapper does allow duplicate column
names in the result set — they only break when you wrap and re-select. - Some clients (psql) will display
both columns; some ORMs blow up on duplicate column keys silently. - CTEs have the same rule — the
column list must be unique.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume SELECT * is harmless; it's the root of half the schema-evolution
bugs you'll ever see. - Do not blame the database when it's just enforcing relational closure.
Common follow-up: "What's the production lesson?" — Never SELECT * in views, CTEs, or derived
tables. Always enumerate.
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT a.id AS a_id, a.name, b.id AS b_id, b.amount
  FROM a JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id
) t;

Q56 · Semi-Join and Anti-Join via Subqueries
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Cred, Razorpay · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a semi-join and what is an anti-join? Give me the SQL surface syntax for each.
The 30-second answer: A semi-join returns left rows where at least one right match exists — expressed
in SQL as WHERE EXISTS (...) or WHERE col IN (...). An anti-join returns left rows where
no right match exists — WHERE NOT EXISTS (...) or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.col IS
NULL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the relational algebra: semi-join ⋉ keeps left rows with a
match; anti-join ▷ keeps left rows without. 2. Surface syntax for semi-join: EXISTS or IN — never
JOIN, because JOIN multiplies rows when right has duplicates. 3. Surface syntax for anti-join: NOT
EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL; avoid NOT IN because of the NULL trap. 4. Why
interviewers ask: this is the vocabulary the planner uses in EXPLAIN — when you say "semi-join hash"
the conversation accelerates.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres EXPLAIN labels these explicitly: Hash Semi Join and Hash
Anti Join. - MySQL 8 added semi-join optimisation that lets the planner unnest IN/EXISTS
subqueries into hash semi-joins. - An anti-join can be more efficient than LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
because the planner can stop scanning the right side as soon as it finds one match.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse a JOIN with semi-join — they have different cardinalities. - Do not
say "EXISTS is just IN with extra syntax" — that ignores the correlated case where EXISTS is the natural
form.
Common follow-up: "What does the planner do with NOT EXISTS in Postgres?" — Converts it to a Hash
Anti Join, which is essentially a join that emits left rows only when no right row matches.
-- Semi-join: users with at least one order
SELECT u.id, u.name FROM users u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
-- Anti-join: users with no orders
SELECT u.id, u.name FROM users u WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
Q57 · Top N Per Group — Subquery vs Window Function
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Razorpay, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 58 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 59
Give me the top three orders by amount for each customer. Show me the subquery way and the
window-function way.
The 30-second answer: Window-function way: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
ORDER BY amount DESC) then filter where the rank is ≤ 3 in a derived table. Subquery way:
correlated 
WHERE 3 > (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.user_id = o.user_id AND
o2.amount > o.amount) — works on engines without window functions but is O(n²).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Window approach is the modern default — clean, O(n log n), works
on Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL 8, Oracle. 2. Subquery approach is the legacy fallback — correlated
counter, runs once per row, expensive on large tables. 3. Tie handling: ROW_NUMBER gives a strict
order, RANK ties give "1,1,3", DENSE_RANK ties give "1,1,2" — pick based on what the interviewer
asks. 4. Engine note: pre-MySQL 8, window functions did not exist — the subquery form was the only
choice and shows up in legacy code.
Edge cases to mention: - The correlated subquery form needs a tiebreaker column or it counts ties
incorrectly — add OR (o2.amount = o.amount AND o2.id < o.id). - If the partition has fewer
than N rows, both methods return whatever exists — usually fine. - LATERAL joins (Postgres) are a third
elegant approach for top-N — worth mentioning if asked.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "window functions are always better" — on MySQL 5.7 you simply do
not have them. - Do not write the correlated form without a tiebreaker and then claim it handles ties
correctly.
Common follow-up: "What changes if you switch from ROW_NUMBER to DENSE_RANK?" — Ties get
the same rank; you may end up with more than three rows per group if ties exist.
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
) t
WHERE rn <= 3;
Q58 · Median Calculation via Subquery
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: JP Morgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 59 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 60
There is no portable MEDIAN function in standard SQL. Compute the median salary using a
subquery.
The 30-second answer: Use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) on
Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle. On MySQL where it doesn't exist, use a self-join / subquery approach: find
the value(s) where the count of smaller-or-equal equals the count of larger-or-equal, then average for
even-count cases.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the modern answer first — PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) is the
cleanest and most portable across enterprise engines. 2. The subquery approach: WHERE (SELECT
COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE salary <= s.salary) >= total/2 AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM
t WHERE salary >= s.salary) >= total/2 then AVG the result. 3. Even vs odd row counts:
even counts need the average of the two middle values; odd counts give a single value. Both fall out of
the >= total/2 condition. 4. MySQL 8 alternative: assign ROW_NUMBER(), find the middle row(s),
average.
Edge cases to mention: - Performance: the correlated COUNT(*) approach is O(n²) — fine for
thousands, painful for millions. - NULL handling: most engines ignore NULLs in PERCENTILE_CONT —
verify with your dataset. - Some engines have MEDIAN() as an extension (Snowflake, Redshift) — flag
if it's available.
What NOT to say: - Do not give only the PERCENTILE answer if asked specifically about "subquery"
approach — the interviewer wants both. - Do not forget the even-vs-odd case — that's the trap.
Common follow-up: "What's the time complexity of your subquery solution?" — O(n²) for the correlated
count, or O(n log n) with ROW_NUMBER.
-- Modern, portable
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) FROM employees;
-- Subquery fallback on MySQL 8 with ROW_NUMBER
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM (
  SELECT salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER () AS c
  FROM employees
) t WHERE rn IN ((c+1)/2, (c+2)/2);
Q59 · nth Highest Salary — Four Solutions
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant, Flipkart, Razorpay · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 60 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 61
Find the second highest salary. Then generalise to nth. Show me four different ways.
The 30-second answer: Four ways — (1) 
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM
employees) for n=2; (2) DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) then filter for 
rank = n; (3) ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1; (4) correlated WHERE n-1 =
(SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM e2 WHERE e2.salary > e.salary).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Subquery (n=2 special case): max of all salaries less than the max —
clear and easy but does not generalise to nth without nested layers. 2. DENSE_RANK: the cleanest
general solution — WHERE rnk = :n. Use DENSE_RANK not RANK so ties don't skip ranks. 3.
LIMIT/OFFSET: cleanest in MySQL/Postgres for one-shot use — ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1
OFFSET :n - 1 — but does not handle ties (treats duplicates as separate ranks). 4. Correlated
COUNT(DISTINCT): the legacy subquery approach — works on any engine, handles ties correctly via
DISTINCT, but O(n²). 5. Always ask: "do ties count as one rank or separate ranks?" That decides
DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER vs LIMIT/OFFSET.
Edge cases to mention: - If fewer than n distinct salaries exist, return NULL or empty — handle
gracefully with COALESCE. - LIMIT/OFFSET on a non-deterministic ORDER BY (with ties) is non-
portable — add a tiebreaker. - The SUBQUERY-of-MAX approach can be nested for n=3 but becomes
unreadable beyond n=2.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "all four are equivalent" — they differ in tie handling. - Do not write 
LIMIT n, 1 and call it portable — that's MySQL syntax; standard is LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1.
Common follow-up: "What if there are ties at the nth position — should you return all of them?" — Yes if
the interviewer says "every employee earning the nth highest salary"; use DENSE_RANK and return all
rows with that rank.
-- DENSE_RANK approach (cleanest general)
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM employees
) t WHERE rnk = 3;
Q60 · Subquery in SELECT (Projection) — Performance Cost
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, PhonePe, Cred · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 61 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 62
What's the performance cost of putting a subquery in the SELECT list?
The 30-second answer: If correlated, the subquery runs once per outer row — O(n*m) — which is fine
on small outer sets but devastating on large ones. Most planners try to unnest into a LEFT JOIN with
aggregation when safe, but they don't always succeed. Rewrite as a JOIN when the outer set is large or
when you have multiple correlated projections.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the cardinality: a SELECT-list correlated subquery is "for
each row in the outer, run the inner". 2. Modern planners (Postgres, SQL Server) unnest single-aggregate
correlated subqueries into LEFT JOINs — check EXPLAIN to confirm. 3. Multiple correlated subqueries in
one SELECT list multiply the per-row cost — one JOIN-with-aggregation usually beats five scalar
subqueries. 4. Non-correlated subqueries in SELECT list are evaluated once and treated as constants —
cheap and fine.
Edge cases to mention: - A non-correlated (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees) in
SELECT list runs once total — completely fine. - A correlated subquery hidden inside a CASE expression
has the same cost — count CASE branches when estimating. - Some engines cache scalar subquery
results per session — flag if the inner data is constant.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "subqueries in SELECT are always slow" — non-correlated ones are
free. - Do not assume the planner unnests every time — verify with EXPLAIN.
Common follow-up: "How would you rewrite five correlated SELECT subqueries into one query?" —
One LEFT JOIN to a pre-aggregated derived table.
-- Slow: correlated subquery per row
SELECT u.id, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id) AS order_count FROM users u;
-- Fast: aggregated derived table
SELECT u.id, COALESCE(t.cnt, 0) FROM users u
LEFT JOIN (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM orders GROUP BY user_id) t ON t.user_id = u.id;
Q61 · IN with a List vs IN with a Subquery — Planner Differences
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Is there any difference between IN (1, 2, 3) and IN (SELECT id FROM
small_table)?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 62 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 63
The 30-second answer: Yes — IN (1, 2, 3) is a constant list the planner can use to drive an
index range scan or to expand into OR-equality checks. IN (subquery) is treated as a semi-join —
the optimiser may rewrite it as a hash semi-join, a nested-loop with EXISTS-style short-circuit, or
materialise the subquery into a temp set.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Constant list: the planner sees all values at compile time, can prune
partitions, can pick an index range scan. 2. Subquery: the planner does not know cardinality at compile
time — uses estimates from stats. Plan can swing between hash semi-join (large subquery) and nested-
loop EXISTS (small subquery). 3. Common bug: an IN list with thousands of literals slows down query
parsing and can hit per-query length limits. Switch to a subquery or temp table. 4. ANALYZE / EXPLAIN
reveals what the planner actually did — never argue from intuition.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres has a limit (varies by build) on the number of IN-list parameters
before performance degrades — somewhere around a thousand items, switch to ANY(array) or a
VALUES clause. - Oracle has a hard limit of 1000 expressions in an IN list — a classic gotcha for
migrating apps. - An IN subquery with DISTINCT is redundant — the semi-join semantics already
deduplicate.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "IN (subquery) is just a syntactic sugar over IN list" — the planner
handles them differently. - Do not paste 5000 IDs in an IN list and ask why your query is slow.
Common follow-up: "What's the limit of IN list items before it becomes a bad pattern?" — A few
hundred to a thousand; beyond that use VALUES, temp table, or ANY(array).
-- Constant list
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status IN ('paid', 'refunded', 'partial_refund');
-- Subquery
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE city = 'Mumbai');
Q62 · Correlated Subquery for Running Condition Checks
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Razorpay · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
For each order, tell me whether the same user placed any earlier order on the same day. Use a
correlated subquery.
The 30-second answer: Use EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.user_id =
o.user_id AND o2.created_at < o.created_at AND DATE(o2.created_at) =
DATE(o.created_at)) — the inner query references the outer row, making it a correlated check that
returns TRUE per outer row when a same-user same-day earlier order exists.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 63 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 64
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Identify the per-row check pattern — for each outer row, run a check
against the rest of the data. 2. EXISTS is the natural shape because you just need a boolean, not a value.
3. The correlation is on two columns — user_id and the date part of created_at — both must
match. 4. Index recommendation: composite index on (user_id, created_at) makes the inner
query an index range scan and the whole pattern fast. 5. Modern alternative: LAG() window function
— but interviewers asking about correlated subqueries often want to see the EXISTS form.
Edge cases to mention: - Timezone matters when comparing dates — be explicit about session
timezone or use created_at::date consistently. - If you want a count, not just a check, replace
EXISTS with (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ...) — but be aware of the performance trade-off. -
Window function COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, DATE(created_at) ORDER BY
created_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) is a one-pass
alternative.
What NOT to say: - Do not write the correlated subquery and then claim it's O(n) — it's potentially
O(n*m) without indexes. - Do not skip the index discussion — that's what makes the difference between
200ms and 200s.
Common follow-up: "How would you rewrite this without a correlated subquery?" — Use LAG() or 
ROW_NUMBER() with a PARTITION BY user_id and date.
SELECT o.id, o.user_id, o.created_at,
       EXISTS (
         SELECT 1 FROM orders o2
         WHERE o2.user_id = o.user_id
           AND o2.created_at < o.created_at
           AND DATE(o2.created_at) = DATE(o.created_at)
       ) AS has_earlier_same_day
FROM orders o;
Q63 · Materialized vs Not Materialized CTE (Postgres 12+ Change)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What changed about CTE optimisation in Postgres 12? Should I still treat CTEs as optimisation
fences?
The 30-second answer: Before Postgres 12, every CTE was materialised — an optimisation fence the
planner could not see through, often hurting performance. From 12 onwards, simple CTEs are inlined by
default (the planner can push predicates in), unless they are recursive, side-effecting, or referenced more
than once. You can opt back into materialisation with WITH cte AS MATERIALIZED (...).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 64 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 65
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Pre-12 behaviour: CTE was materialised into a temp result, then the
outer query ran against it. Predicates from outside could not be pushed in — slow. 2. Post-12 default:
CTE is inlined like a subquery when used once and side-effect-free. Predicates push through; plans
improve dramatically. 3. Opt-out: WITH cte AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...) — explicit inline; 
WITH cte AS MATERIALIZED (...) — explicit fence (useful when the CTE is expensive and
reused). 4. Recursive CTEs are always materialised — no change there.
Edge cases to mention: - If your CTE is referenced multiple times, Postgres materialises it by default
(since 12) — re-evaluation would be worse. - A CTE with a side effect (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE inside 
WITH) is always materialised — it must run exactly once. - MySQL CTEs (8.0+) and SQL Server CTEs
are inlined by default — Postgres 12 brought it in line with the rest of the world.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "CTEs are always optimisation fences" — that's outdated for Postgres
12+ and never true for SQL Server. - Do not say "use CTEs instead of subqueries for performance" —
they are essentially identical in modern planners.
Common follow-up: "When would you explicitly use MATERIALIZED?" — When the CTE is expensive
(heavy aggregation) and referenced multiple times, or when you want to deliberately stop predicate push-
down for plan stability.
-- Explicit materialisation in Postgres 12+
WITH heavy AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) total FROM orders GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.name, h.total FROM users u JOIN heavy h ON h.user_id = u.id WHERE h.total > 10000;
Q64 · Subquery Returning Multiple Columns — Row Constructor
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Flipkart, Cred · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can a subquery return multiple columns? How would you compare two columns at once?
The 30-second answer: Yes — use a row constructor: WHERE (col_a, col_b) IN (SELECT a, b
FROM ...). The outer row matches when both columns match the same row in the subquery, not just
the columns independently.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Single-column IN is the common case; row-constructor IN is the
multi-column extension. 2. Use case: matching a composite key against a candidate set — WHERE
(city, pincode) IN (SELECT city, pincode FROM serviceable_areas). 3. The match is
tuple-wise: (Mumbai, 400001) matches only when both city and pincode appear together in the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 65 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 66
subquery, not when city matches one row and pincode matches another. 4. Supported in Postgres,
MySQL, SQL Server (with some syntax variations), Oracle.
Edge cases to mention: - Indexes on (city, pincode) make tuple-IN fast; without them, the
planner falls back to a hash semi-join. - NULL behaviour is the same trap as scalar IN — a NULL in either
side gives UNKNOWN. - Some engines optimise row-constructor IN as a join under the covers — check
EXPLAIN.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "you can't compare multiple columns in IN" — you can, with row
constructors. - Do not split into two ANDed IN clauses; that returns a different result set (cross-match).
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between (a, b) IN (subquery) and a IN
(subquery_a) AND b IN (subquery_b)?" — The first matches tuples; the second matches
independently and over-returns.
SELECT order_id FROM orders
WHERE (city, pincode) IN (SELECT city, pincode FROM serviceable_areas);
Q65 · LATERAL Subquery — Correlated Derived Tables
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Goldman · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does the LATERAL keyword do and when would you use it?
The 30-second answer: LATERAL lets a subquery in the FROM clause reference columns from
preceding FROM items — essentially a correlated derived table. Common use is "for each user, give me
the latest three orders" without resorting to window functions.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Normal derived table in FROM cannot see columns from earlier
FROM items — it's standalone. 2. LATERAL flips that: FROM users u, LATERAL (SELECT * FROM
orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) o3 — the inner
can see u.id. 3. Replaces the awkward window-function approach for top-N-per-group when you
want full row data, not just rank. 4. Available in Postgres (since 9.3), Oracle 12c+, SQL Server (via
CROSS APPLY which is the same thing). MySQL got it in 8.0.14.
Edge cases to mention: - LATERAL implicitly behaves like a JOIN — pair with LEFT JOIN LATERAL
to keep outer rows when the inner returns nothing. - SQL Server's equivalent is CROSS APPLY (inner)
and OUTER APPLY (left) — same semantics, different keyword. - Performance: LATERAL with a LIMIT
inside is often the fastest way to get top-N-per-group when the outer set is small and you have an index.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 66 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 67
What NOT to say: - Do not assume LATERAL is everywhere — MySQL added it late, SQLite still doesn't
have it. - Do not confuse LATERAL with CROSS JOIN — CROSS JOIN has no correlation.
Common follow-up: "When does LATERAL win over a window function?" — When you want a fixed limit
per group with full row data, and the outer set is small relative to the inner.
SELECT u.id, o3.*
FROM users u,
LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 3) o3;
Q66 · Subquery in HAVING — Filtering Groups Against an Aggregate
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo · Topic: Subqueries
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Find every city whose total order revenue is above the all-India average. Use a subquery in
HAVING.
The 30-second answer: Group orders by city, then in HAVING compare the group's SUM(amount)
against a subquery returning the all-India average revenue per city: 
HAVING SUM(amount) > (SELECT AVG(s) FROM (SELECT SUM(amount) s FROM orders
GROUP BY city) t).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. WHERE cannot reference aggregates — that's the job of HAVING,
which runs after GROUP BY. 2. The subquery in HAVING must return a scalar (one row, one column) —
guarantee that with an aggregate. 3. The classic pattern: city-level aggregate compared to the cross-city
average — the inner subquery first aggregates per city, then averages those aggregates. 4. Watch the
difference between "average revenue per city" (group then average) and "average revenue overall"
( AVG(amount)) — interviewer usually wants the first.
Edge cases to mention: - A correlated HAVING subquery is legal — it can reference grouped columns
from the outer query. - HAVING can reference aggregates that are not in SELECT — Postgres allows this
freely; some engines require the aggregate in SELECT. - The inner aggregation can usually be hoisted
into a CTE for readability without affecting performance.
What NOT to say: - Do not put the same filter in WHERE; aggregates are not available there. - Do not
assume HAVING runs before GROUP BY — its whole purpose is post-grouping filtering.
Common follow-up: "Could you rewrite this without HAVING using a derived table?" — Yes —
aggregate to a derived table, then filter in an outer WHERE.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 67 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 68
SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY city
HAVING SUM(amount) > (
  SELECT AVG(s) FROM (SELECT SUM(amount) s FROM orders GROUP BY city) t
);
Chapter 3, Part A — Window Functions
Window functions used to be the "advanced topic" you could skip as a fresher; that is no longer true.
Across 2024-2026 hiring cycles — TCS Digital, Infosys Power Programmer, Wipro Elite, every GCC panel
(JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs, Wells Fargo, Goldman, Target, AmEx) and every product company
(Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho, Zerodha, Flipkart, PhonePe) — window functions are baseline
expectation even for zero-experience candidates. If you cannot explain PARTITION BY versus 
GROUP BY, write a top-N-per-group query, or spot the LAST_VALUE default-frame trap, you will lose
the round. This chapter (Part A) covers Window Functions end to end across thirty questions; Part B of
the same chapter covers Common Table Expressions, both vanilla and recursive. Read both before any
interview where the JD mentions SQL.
Q67 · Window Functions Introduction — What They Do and When to Use
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a window function and how is it different from a regular aggregate? Give me an example
where you'd reach for one.
The 30-second answer: A window function computes a value across a set of rows related to the current
row — the "window" — without collapsing those rows into one. Unlike GROUP BY which reduces rows,
a window function keeps every input row and adds a new column with the computed value. Reach for
one whenever you need a per-row metric that depends on neighbouring rows: running totals, rank within
a group, previous row's value, top-N per category.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the row-preservation point — that is the single biggest
semantic difference from GROUP BY and the thing freshers miss. 2. Give the shape: function()
OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame). Every window function has this same
skeleton. 3. Give a concrete example: "rank each customer's orders by amount, keeping all order rows."
With GROUP BY customer_id you lose order-level rows; with RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY
customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) you keep them and add a rank column. 4. Mention the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 68 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 69
three families: ranking (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, 
CUME_DIST), aggregate-as-window (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX with OVER), and value
access (LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE). 5. Anticipate the follow-up:
"When would you not use one?" — when you genuinely need to collapse rows (true grouping) or when
the same result is cheaper via a self-join with an index, which is rare in 2026.
Edge cases to mention: - Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING
but before ORDER BY and LIMIT. That ordering causes the Filter-Window Trap (Q13). - You cannot
reference a window function in WHERE — wrap the query in a CTE or subquery, or use QUALIFY on
Snowflake / BigQuery / Teradata. - Window functions never reduce the row count of the input; if you
need both row-level and aggregated output in one shot, that is exactly the use case.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "window function is just a fancy GROUP BY." It is the opposite — it
preserves rows rather than collapsing them. - Do not claim window functions are slow as a blanket rule;
modern planners parallelise them and they often beat the equivalent self-join.
Common follow-up: "Show me a query that uses both GROUP BY and a window function in the same
statement." — Easy: aggregate first in a subquery, then apply the window on the aggregated rows (see
Q21).
SELECT
  order_id, customer_id, amount,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS amount_rank,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM orders;
Q68 · ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK — When Each is the Wrong
Choice
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK. Give me a scenario
where picking the wrong one quietly breaks the report.
The 30-second answer: ROW_NUMBER always gives unique sequential numbers even when sort keys
tie. RANK gives the same rank to ties but leaves gaps (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK gives the same rank
to ties without gaps (1, 2, 2, 3). Wrong choice example: using ROW_NUMBER for a leaderboard breaks
fairness because two players with identical scores get different ranks based on physical row order.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 69 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 70
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the tie behaviour — that is the entire test. 2. Walk through
one input set: scores [100, 90, 90, 80] → ROW_NUMBER gives 1,2,3,4; RANK gives 
1,2,2,4; DENSE_RANK gives 1,2,2,3. 3. Pick scenarios: leaderboards → DENSE_RANK (fair
ranks, no gaps); deduplication ("keep the latest row per user") → ROW_NUMBER with an explicit tie-
breaker; top-N where you want N positions including ties → RANK. 4. Stress that ROW_NUMBER
without a deterministic ORDER BY is non-deterministic — two runs can give different numbers, which
is a data-quality bug waiting to happen.
Edge cases to mention: - For dedup queries (SELECT ... WHERE rn = 1), always add a tie-
breaker to the ORDER BY (for example ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC) so two rows
with identical timestamps still pick the same winner each run. - RANK and DENSE_RANK are stable
across runs because tied rows share a rank; ROW_NUMBER is not. - All three require ORDER BY inside
OVER — without it the result is meaningless / not allowed.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they all do the same thing with minor differences." The tie behaviour
can silently corrupt leaderboards and dedup logic. - Do not skip the tie-breaker in dedup ROW_NUMBER
queries; reviewers in panels will hammer on that.
Common follow-up: "Write a dedup query that keeps the latest row per user_id from 
user_events." — Classic warm-up question; answer below.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC
    ) AS rn
  FROM user_events
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
Q69 · PARTITION BY Semantics vs GROUP BY
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Goldman, AmEx · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between PARTITION BY inside a window and GROUP BY in the outer
query? People mix these up — make sure I do not.
The 30-second answer: GROUP BY collapses the input into one row per group. PARTITION BY
divides the input into groups for the window function to operate over but keeps every original row. Same
grouping keys, opposite outcomes on row count.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 70 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 71
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Anchor the answer on row count — GROUP BY reduces, 
PARTITION BY preserves. 2. Give a parallel example: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount)
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id returns one row per customer. SELECT order_id,
customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) FROM orders
returns one row per order with the customer total alongside. 3. Mention scope: GROUP BY applies to
the entire query and forces every selected column to be either grouped or aggregated. PARTITION BY
is local to one OVER clause; the rest of the SELECT is unaffected. 4. Point out you can use both in
the same query — group first, then apply a window on the grouped output.
Edge cases to mention: - Without PARTITION BY, the window covers the entire result set (a single
partition) — useful for grand totals. - Multiple window functions in the same SELECT can each have
their own partition; they do not have to agree. - GROUP BY removes duplicates implicitly; PARTITION
BY does not — duplicates in the input remain in the output.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they are interchangeable in some cases" — they are not, because the
row count is different. - Do not claim PARTITION BY is slower than GROUP BY as a rule; it depends
on whether you actually need every input row.
Common follow-up: "If I write SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) without an 
ORDER BY, what frame does it use?" — Whole partition (see Q7).
-- Per-order amount alongside the customer's grand total
SELECT
  order_id, customer_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total,
  amount * 1.0 / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS share_of_customer
FROM orders;
Q70 · ORDER BY Inside OVER — When Required, When Optional
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Accenture, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Is ORDER BY inside the OVER clause always required? Walk me through when it is mandatory
and when you can leave it out.
The 30-second answer: Required for any function that depends on row order: all ranking functions
( ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST), value-access
functions (LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE), and any aggregate where
you want a running / moving result. Optional when you want an unordered aggregate over the whole
partition (for example, customer total alongside each row).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 71 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 72
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Group window functions into "needs order" versus "does not need
order" and recite the lists. 2. Give the running-total example to make the difference concrete: 
SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) gives a running
total; remove the ORDER BY and you get the customer grand total on every row. 3. Warn that ORDER
BY inside OVER is independent of the outer ORDER BY — they do different jobs. 4. Anticipate:
"What happens if I add an ORDER BY to a plain SUM() OVER ()?" — you accidentally turn it into a
running total and the numbers change. This is a common interview trap.
Edge cases to mention: - Adding ORDER BY without an explicit frame applies the default frame 
RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which is exactly what changes a
grand total into a running total (Q7). - Ranking functions require ORDER BY even if the partition has a
single row, otherwise the result is undefined / a syntax error depending on engine. - ROW_NUMBER()
OVER () without partition or order is legal on some engines but the row order is the planner's choice —
never rely on it.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "ORDER BY is always optional in OVER" — false for ranking and
value-access functions. - Do not skip the tie-breaker in ORDER BY for ranking queries that drive dedup
logic; you will get non-deterministic output.
Common follow-up: "Show me a query where adding ORDER BY inside OVER gives the wrong
number." — Running total when you meant grand total; demo below.
-- Grand total per customer (no ORDER BY)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM orders;
-- Running total per customer (with ORDER BY)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) AS running_total
FROM orders;
Q71 · Frame Clauses — ROWS BETWEEN vs RANGE BETWEEN vs GROUPS
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, Goldman, Cred · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through ROWS BETWEEN, RANGE BETWEEN and GROUPS BETWEEN. When does
each behave differently?
The 30-second answer: ROWS counts physical rows from the current row. RANGE counts logical
value distance — rows with the same ORDER BY value are treated as one peer group. GROUPS
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 72 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 73
(Postgres 11+) counts peer groups themselves. They diverge whenever the ORDER BY column has ties:
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW looks at exactly two physical rows, RANGE
includes every peer of the current row, GROUPS walks one peer-group back.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Pick a small dataset: scores [100, 90, 90, 80]. For the third
row (score 90), ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW covers rows 2 and 3 (sum =
180). RANGE BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW includes all rows whose score is
within 1 of the current 90 — both 90s are peers, so the frame is rows 2 and 3 with the same value. 
GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW covers the peer group of 100 plus the peer
group of both 90s. 2. State the practical rule: use ROWS when you mean "the last N rows" (moving
averages, lag windows). Use RANGE for time-based windows (RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7
days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW on Postgres). Use GROUPS rarely — mostly for ranking-
aware running aggregates. 3. Call out engine support: ROWS everywhere; RANGE BETWEEN value
PRECEDING on Postgres, Snowflake, BigQuery, Oracle; GROUPS on Postgres 11+ only.
Edge cases to mention: - The default frame when you specify ORDER BY but no explicit frame is 
RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, not ROWS. - RANGE with a
numeric or interval offset requires the ORDER BY to be a single numeric or date/time column; multi-
column ORDER BY fails. - For moving averages over event streams with duplicate timestamps, ROWS
and RANGE give different answers — choose deliberately.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "ROWS and RANGE are the same when there are no ties" — that is
technically true but glosses over the fact that production data always has ties. - Do not use GROUPS
without checking that the engine supports it; on MySQL and SQL Server it does not exist.
Common follow-up: "Write a 7-day moving sum using RANGE." — Below.
-- 7-day moving sum, peers included via RANGE
SELECT order_ts, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    ORDER BY order_ts
    RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS sum_last_7d
FROM orders;
Q72 · UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, CURRENT ROW, N
PRECEDING / FOLLOWING
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 73 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 74
Describe each frame boundary keyword and when you would use them.
The 30-second answer: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING = start of the partition. UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
= end of the partition. CURRENT ROW = the row being processed (or its peer group, depending on 
ROWS vs RANGE). N PRECEDING and N FOLLOWING = N rows back or forward. Combine them
around BETWEEN ... AND ... to define any window shape from "everything so far" to "the next 5
rows" to "the entire partition."
Step-by-step thought process: 1. List each keyword with a one-line meaning so the interviewer hears
coverage. 2. Map each common analytic to a frame: running total = UNBOUNDED PRECEDING TO
CURRENT ROW; reverse running total = CURRENT ROW TO UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING; centered
moving average = 2 PRECEDING TO 2 FOLLOWING; full-partition aggregate = UNBOUNDED
PRECEDING TO UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. 3. Stress the difference between CURRENT ROW under 
ROWS (the literal current row) and under RANGE (the current row plus all peers with the same ORDER
BY value). 4. Anticipate "What is the smallest frame?" — BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND CURRENT
ROW, which is one row (or its peer group).
Edge cases to mention: - BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND CURRENT ROW under RANGE is not a
single row when there are ties. - N PRECEDING / N FOLLOWING with RANGE requires the offset to
be the same data type as the ORDER BY column (numeric for numbers, interval for dates). - Frame
boundaries cannot cross: BETWEEN 5 FOLLOWING AND 2 PRECEDING is a syntax error.
What NOT to say: - Do not omit the frame when you intend a running total and assume the default does
the right thing — it does on ROWS mental model, but the default is actually RANGE (Q7). - Do not use 
UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING casually with LAST_VALUE and assume you get the partition's last value
— see Q9 for the trap.
Common follow-up: "Write a centered 5-row moving average." — AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY ts
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING).
SELECT order_ts, amount,
  AVG(amount) OVER (
    ORDER BY order_ts
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING
  ) AS centered_avg_5
FROM orders;
Q73 · The Default Frame Trap — ORDER BY Without Explicit Frame
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, PhonePe · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 74 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 75
If I write SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) with
no explicit frame, what frame does the engine use?
The 30-second answer: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. That is
the SQL standard default, applied by every major engine. So the result is a running total — but with 
RANGE semantics, meaning rows that share the same order_ts all get the same running total, not
staggered values.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the default verbatim so the interviewer knows you have read
the spec, not guessed. 2. Explain the consequence: the moment you add ORDER BY to an aggregate's
OVER, you turn a grand total into a running total. People who think ORDER BY is "just for sorting the
window" get the wrong number. 3. Highlight the RANGE vs ROWS nuance: with duplicate ORDER BY
values, RANGE lumps peers together, so two events at the same timestamp produce identical running
totals. Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW if you want strict per-row
stepping. 4. Recommend the production habit: always specify the frame explicitly when using
aggregates with ORDER BY. It is cheap insurance against this exact bug.
Edge cases to mention: - Without ORDER BY, the default frame is the entire partition — that is why 
SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) gives a grand total. - Ranking functions ignore the frame
entirely — RANK, ROW_NUMBER, DENSE_RANK use only PARTITION BY and ORDER BY. - 
LAG and LEAD also ignore the frame.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the default is the whole partition when you have ORDER BY" — that is
wrong; the default is up-to-current-row. - Do not assume RANGE and ROWS agree under the default;
they only do when the ORDER BY column has no duplicates.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this so it gives a per-row running total even when timestamps tie." — Use 
ROWS instead of the default RANGE.
-- Default frame: RANGE, so tied timestamps share a running total
SELECT order_ts, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) AS running_total
FROM orders;
-- Strict per-row stepping
SELECT order_ts, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts, order_id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total_strict
FROM orders;

Q74 · LAG and LEAD — Period-Over-Period, Default Value, Offset
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Cred, Meesho · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain LAG and LEAD. Write a query that shows each month's revenue alongside the
previous month's revenue and the month-over-month growth percentage.
The 30-second answer: LAG(col, offset, default) returns the value offset rows before
the current row in the ordered window; LEAD does the same forward. Default offset is 1; default
"default value" is NULL. For month-over-month, aggregate revenue per month in a subquery, then 
LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) to get the previous month, and divide.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the signature precisely: LAG(expression, offset,
default). Most candidates forget the default argument. 2. Explain why default matters: the
first row's LAG is NULL by default, which makes the MoM growth NULL too — sometimes you want 
default = 0 or default = expression instead. 3. Walk the query: aggregate monthly revenue
in a CTE, then in the outer query compute prev_rev = LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY month) and 
growth_pct = (rev - prev_rev) * 100.0 / NULLIF(prev_rev, 0). Always wrap the
divisor in NULLIF to avoid divide-by-zero. 4. Mention LEAD use cases: "what is the next event's
timestamp" for inter-event gaps and churn metrics.
Edge cases to mention: - LAG/ LEAD ignore the frame clause; they only need PARTITION BY and
ORDER BY. - Offset must be a non-negative integer; negative values are not allowed (use LEAD
instead). - For MoM growth across missing months, you must first generate a contiguous month series
— LAG does not skip gaps in your data.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "LAG always returns the previous row's value" — it returns the value 
offset rows back; without specifying offset you trust the default 1. - Do not divide by prev_rev
directly — divide by NULLIF(prev_rev, 0) to handle the first row and any zero-revenue months.
Common follow-up: "What if the previous month is missing entirely?" — Generate a month spine via 
generate_series (Postgres) or a calendar table, left join your data, then apply LAG on the spine.
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_ts) AS month, SUM(amount) AS rev
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, rev,
  LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_rev,
  (rev - LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY month)) * 100.0
    / NULLIF(LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
