Q75 · FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE — The Default-Frame Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Write a query to show each order alongside the first order amount and the last order amount for
that customer. Be careful with LAST_VALUE.
The 30-second answer: 
FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) works as
expected. LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts)
does not — under the default frame (RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT
ROW), LAST_VALUE returns the current row's value, not the partition's last value. Fix: extend the frame
to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the trap exactly as the interviewer would: write the naive
query, predict it returns the wrong number, explain why. 2. The "why": LAST_VALUE returns the last
value in the frame, and the default frame ends at the current row. So at row 3 of a 10-row partition, the
last value in the frame is row 3's amount. 3. The fix: add 
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to extend the frame to the
entire partition. 4. Alternative fix: use 
FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC) —
reverse the order, take the first. Often cleaner.
Edge cases to mention: - The trap does not happen with FIRST_VALUE because under the default
frame UNBOUNDED PRECEDING is the actual partition start. - NTH_VALUE(col, n) has the same
trap as LAST_VALUE — extend the frame explicitly. - Some engines (Snowflake) interpret IGNORE
NULLS modifier on these functions; check before relying on it.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "LAST_VALUE is broken in SQL" — it is following the spec exactly;
the default frame just is not what most people expect. - Do not write LAST_VALUE with just 
PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... in production code — always pin the frame, or reverse the
order and use FIRST_VALUE.
Common follow-up: "Why is this an interview favourite?" — Because it tests whether you understand
frames at all. If you do not know about default frames, you cannot read this query.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 77 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 78
-- WRONG: returns current row's amount as "last"
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) AS first_amt,
  LAST_VALUE(amount)  OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) AS last_amt_wrong
FROM orders;
-- RIGHT: extend the frame
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts) AS first_amt,
  LAST_VALUE(amount)  OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS last_amt
FROM orders;
Q76 · Running Totals — SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...) Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Flipkart · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me a running total of daily revenue for the last 30 days.
The 30-second answer: Aggregate daily revenue first, then 
SUM(daily_rev) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT
ROW). The explicit ROWS frame guarantees per-row stepping even if two rows somehow share a day.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Two layers: aggregate to one row per day, then window. Trying to do
both in one shot leads to confused queries. 2. Inside the window, specify the frame explicitly. Default 
RANGE works here because the ORDER BY column is unique per row after aggregation, but ROWS
is more defensive. 3. To restrict to "last 30 days", filter WHERE day >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL
'30 days' in the outer query — but be aware this is the Filter-Window Trap territory (Q13). For a
running total that includes the warm-up history, filter inside the CTE on a wider range. 4. Anticipate:
"What if revenue is sparse — some days have zero orders?" Either left-join a calendar / 
generate_series, or accept that gaps in the data mean gaps in the running total's day labels.
Edge cases to mention: - Without PARTITION BY, the running total is across the entire result. Add 
PARTITION BY to reset per group (per customer, per region, per month). - SUM of a NULL amount
contributes nothing — but the row still exists. To exclude entirely, filter in WHERE. - For huge tables, a
running total over the full table can be expensive — index on the ORDER BY column and consider
materialising daily aggregates first.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 78 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 79
What NOT to say: - Do not use a correlated subquery (SELECT ... WHERE day <= outer.day)
— it is the pre-2003 pattern and orders of magnitude slower. - Do not aggregate and window in one shot
without thinking about what you want to group on; usually two layers is clearer.
Common follow-up: "How would you reset the running total at the start of each month?" — 
PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', day).
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT DATE(order_ts) AS day, SUM(amount) AS daily_rev
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_ts >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '60 days'
  GROUP BY DATE(order_ts)
)
SELECT day, daily_rev,
  SUM(daily_rev) OVER (
    ORDER BY day
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total
FROM daily
WHERE day >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
ORDER BY day;
Q77 · Moving Averages
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, AmEx, Goldman · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Write a query that gives the 7-day moving average of daily revenue. What does "7-day" mean
exactly?
The 30-second answer: Two valid interpretations: a 7-row trailing average (ROWS BETWEEN 6
PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), or a 7-day calendar-time trailing average (RANGE BETWEEN
INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). They differ when days are missing — 
ROWS blindly walks 6 rows back; RANGE walks 6 days back regardless of whether intermediate days
exist in the data.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Force the interviewer to clarify "7-day": rows or calendar days? In
dashboards it almost always means calendar days, especially for sparse data. 2. Aggregate to per-day
revenue first (one row per day). 3. Apply 
AVG(daily_rev) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
for the trailing 7 rows. If days can be missing, swap to RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days'
PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (Postgres / Snowflake / BigQuery) — or left-join a calendar spine first
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 79 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 80
and stay on ROWS. 4. Be ready for "give me a centered moving average" — ROWS BETWEEN 3
PRECEDING AND 3 FOLLOWING. Centered is better for visualisations, trailing is better for live ops
dashboards.
Edge cases to mention: - For the first 6 days the trailing window has fewer than 7 rows; AVG divides
by the actual count, not by 7. If you want NULL for "not enough data yet", wrap in CASE WHEN
COUNT(*) OVER (...) < 7 THEN NULL ELSE AVG(...) END. - Centered MA leaks future data
into past rows — fine for retrospective charts, wrong for any predictive use. - On MySQL 8, RANGE with
an interval offset works only for numeric columns; for date columns convert to epoch first.
What NOT to say: - Do not call a 7-row average a "7-day average" when your data has missing days —
it is wrong by definition. - Do not use a correlated subquery for moving averages; performance is
unacceptable on real data.
Common follow-up: "How would you compute a 28-day moving average that only emits when 28 days
of data exist?" — Wrap in CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (...) = 28 THEN AVG(...) END.
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT DATE(order_ts) AS day, SUM(amount) AS daily_rev
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT day, daily_rev,
  AVG(daily_rev) OVER (
    ORDER BY day
    ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS ma_7d
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;
Q78 · NTILE — Bucketing and Unequal-Sized Buckets
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Use NTILE to split customers into 4 spend quartiles. What happens if the row count is not
divisible by 4?
The 30-second answer: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) assigns each row a
bucket number 1 through 4. When row count is not divisible, the earlier buckets get one extra row each.
With 10 rows split into 4 buckets you get sizes (3, 3, 2, 2), not (3, 3, 3, 1) and not (2, 2, 3, 3).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the bucket-size rule — that is the trick question. Most
candidates know the syntax but not the distribution. 2. Walk through the math: with N rows and B
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 80 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 81
buckets, the first N mod B buckets get ceil(N/B) rows; the rest get floor(N/B) rows. 3.
Mention the alternative: WIDTH_BUCKET (Postgres / Oracle) which splits by value range rather than row
count. Use WIDTH_BUCKET when you want equal value ranges; use NTILE when you want roughly
equal row counts. 4. For deciles, use NTILE(10). For percentiles in segmentation reports, 
NTILE(100) is standard.
Edge cases to mention: - NTILE requires ORDER BY and is sensitive to ties — tied rows can land in
different buckets depending on the tie-breaker. - For exact percentile values use PERCENTILE_CONT
or PERCENT_RANK; NTILE is for bucketing, not for the actual percentile value. - With fewer rows
than buckets (NTILE(10) on 5 rows), each row gets its own bucket and buckets 6-10 stay empty.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "buckets are always equal size" — they are not when divisibility fails. -
Do not use NTILE for marketing percentiles where the underlying values matter; you will misclassify
outliers.
Common follow-up: "Customers in the top decile of spend?" — WHERE bucket = 1 after 
NTILE(10) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC).
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spend
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, total_spend,
  NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS spend_quartile
FROM spend;
Q79 · The Filter-Window Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, Goldman, Walmart Labs, Cred · Topic:
Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I wrote SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts
DESC) AS rn FROM events WHERE event_ts >= '2026-04-01'. Why are some users
missing rows that I expected to see?
The 30-second answer: Because WHERE is evaluated before window functions. The filter throws away
every event before April 1; the window then computes ROW_NUMBER over only the surviving rows, so a
user whose latest event was in March is gone entirely. Fix: filter inside a CTE or subquery so the window
sees the full history, or use QUALIFY on Snowflake / BigQuery / Teradata to filter on the window result.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 81 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 82
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the SQL evaluation order so the interviewer knows you are not
guessing: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window functions → SELECT → 
DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Window functions sit between HAVING and SELECT. 2.
Show what that means for the query: the April filter culls the dataset; the window sees only April-onward
rows; users with only pre-April events vanish; users with both pre-April and April events get an rn = 1
that points to their first April event, not their lifetime first event. 3. Two fixes. (a) Apply the window inside a
CTE on the full table, then filter in the outer query — but only filter on plain columns, not on the window
column. (b) On Snowflake / BigQuery / Teradata, use QUALIFY which filters on the window result
without needing a subquery. 4. Anticipate the deeper version: "I want the latest event per user but only
consider April events" — that is genuinely a window-over-filtered-rows scenario and the original query
was correct for that intent. Always clarify the intent before fixing.
Edge cases to mention: - HAVING is also before window functions — you cannot reference a window
in HAVING either. - ORDER BY and LIMIT are after windows, so you can ORDER BY a window
column and LIMIT on the result. - Putting a window function in WHERE is a syntax error on every
major engine — the error message points you straight at this evaluation-order rule.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "just add a WHERE rn = 1" without restructuring — that is the
second half of the bug, see Q15. - Do not assume the user wanted lifetime-first or April-first; ask.
Different fixes for different intents.
Common follow-up: "Show me the CTE rewrite and the QUALIFY rewrite." — Both below.
-- Bug: window evaluated AFTER WHERE strips March data
SELECT user_id, event_ts,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) AS rn
FROM events
WHERE event_ts >= '2026-04-01';
-- Fix 1: CTE, then filter on the window result in the outer query
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) AS rn
  FROM events
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 AND event_ts >= '2026-04-01';
-- Fix 2: QUALIFY (Snowflake / BigQuery / Teradata)
SELECT user_id, event_ts,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) AS rn
FROM events
QUALIFY rn = 1;
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 82 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q80 · The QUALIFY Clause — Filter on Window Result
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay (data-eng panel), Walmart Labs, Meesho · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Have you used QUALIFY? Where is it supported and what does it save you?
The 30-second answer: QUALIFY is to window functions what HAVING is to aggregates — it filters
on the window result without a CTE or subquery. Supported on Snowflake, BigQuery, Teradata, and
recent Databricks. Not on Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, or Oracle.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it by analogy: WHERE → row filter; HAVING → group filter; 
QUALIFY → window filter. The mental model lands immediately. 2. Show the common dedup pattern: 
SELECT * FROM events QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY
event_ts DESC) = 1. No CTE, no subquery. 3. Call out engine support precisely so you do not look
ignorant: Snowflake, BigQuery, Teradata, Databricks. Everywhere else, fall back to a CTE wrapper. 4.
Mention you can reference the alias: QUALIFY rn = 1 works if you defined rn in the SELECT.
Cleaner than restating the whole window expression.
Edge cases to mention: - You can chain QUALIFY with WHERE and HAVING; they apply in their
normal order, QUALIFY last. - QUALIFY is evaluated after window functions, so it can reference any
window result. Do not try to use it on plain columns where WHERE belongs. - On engines without 
QUALIFY, the CTE wrapper is the idiomatic replacement — not a correlated subquery.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim QUALIFY is standard SQL — it is not; it is a vendor extension that
has spread. - Do not use QUALIFY in queries that need to run on Postgres or MySQL; you will burn a
deployment cycle.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite the dedup query for Postgres." — CTE with ROW_NUMBER, see Q2.
-- Snowflake / BigQuery / Teradata
SELECT user_id, event_ts, event_type,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) AS rn
FROM events
QUALIFY rn = 1;
Q81 · Why You Cannot Put a Window Function in WHERE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Goldman, PhonePe · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 83 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 84
I tried WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1 and got an error. Why doesn't this work,
and what's the alternative on Postgres?
The 30-second answer: Because WHERE runs before window functions are evaluated — there is
nothing to filter on yet. The alternatives are a CTE or subquery wrapping the window, then filtering on the
window column in the outer query; or QUALIFY on engines that support it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Restate the evaluation order rule from Q13 — WHERE is before
windows, so windows do not exist yet at WHERE time. 2. Give the canonical CTE rewrite for Postgres /
MySQL / SQL Server / Oracle: define rn in a CTE, filter on rn = 1 outside. 3. Mention LATERAL/
CROSS APPLY as alternative on engines that support them, useful when you want top-N per group
with extra computed columns. 4. Anticipate "Why not just nest the window?" — you literally cannot;
same error from the same rule.
Edge cases to mention: - The same rule applies in HAVING — HAVING is also before windows. -
Some engines give a clearer error message than others; Postgres says "window functions are not
allowed in WHERE". - You can reference window aliases in ORDER BY and LIMIT because those run
after windows.
What NOT to say: - Do not try to bypass with a CASE expression in WHERE — same error, same rule. -
Do not write a correlated subquery to "filter by rank" — use the CTE pattern.
Common follow-up: "Top 3 highest-paid employees per department on Postgres?" — WITH ranked
AS (SELECT ..., RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) r FROM
emp) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE r <= 3. See Q17.
-- Wrong
SELECT * FROM events
WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) = 1;
-- ERROR: window functions are not allowed in WHERE
-- Right (works on every engine)
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) AS rn
  FROM events
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
Q82 · PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, AmEx · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 84 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 85
Explain PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST. When would you use each?
The 30-second answer: PERCENT_RANK(x) = (RANK(x) - 1) / (N - 1) — relative rank in [0,
1], with the top row at 0. CUME_DIST(x) = (number of rows <= x) / N — cumulative
distribution in (0, 1]. Use PERCENT_RANK when you want "this employee is in the top 5%"; use 
CUME_DIST when you want "this employee earns more than 90% of peers."
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk the formulas with a 5-row example so the difference is
concrete. Scores [100, 90, 90, 80, 70]. RANK is [1, 2, 2, 4, 5]. PERCENT_RANK is 
[0, 0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 1]. CUME_DIST is [0.2, 0.6, 0.6, 0.8, 1]. 2. Highlight the
boundary behaviour: PERCENT_RANK includes 0 and 1; CUME_DIST excludes 0 but includes 1. 3.
Practical use: percentile-based filtering (WHERE pr <= 0.05 for top 5%) typically uses 
PERCENT_RANK; "what fraction of population is at or below me" uses CUME_DIST. 4. Both ignore
the frame clause. Both require ORDER BY inside OVER.
Edge cases to mention: - With a single-row partition, PERCENT_RANK is 0 (denominator collapses to
0 by formula but the spec says 0); CUME_DIST is 1. - Ties: both return the same value for tied rows. -
For exact percentile values (50th, 95th), use PERCENTILE_CONT / PERCENTILE_DISC (Q30), not
these ranking functions.
What NOT to say: - Do not say PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST are the same — the formulas and
the boundary inclusion differ. - Do not use these for "give me the 90th percentile value" — that is what 
PERCENTILE_CONT does.
Common follow-up: "Top 5% of customers by spend?" — WHERE pr <= 0.05 over 
PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spend DESC).
SELECT customer_id, total_spend,
  PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS pr,
  CUME_DIST()    OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS cd
FROM customer_spend;
Q83 · Top-N Per Group
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Meesho · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Top 3 highest-paid employees per department. Write it.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 85 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 86
The 30-second answer: Use ROW_NUMBER, RANK, or DENSE_RANK partitioned by department and
ordered by salary descending, wrap in a CTE, filter on the rank column outside. Choice depends on tie
behaviour: ROW_NUMBER gives exactly 3 rows per department even with ties; RANK and 
DENSE_RANK may return more than 3 if salaries tie at the boundary.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the function choice. Interviewers love asking "what if two
people are tied at salary number 3?". ROW_NUMBER picks one arbitrarily (or by tie-breaker); RANK/
DENSE_RANK keeps both — 4 rows for that department. 2. Write the CTE form (works on every
engine): WITH ranked AS (SELECT ..., DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER
BY salary DESC) r FROM emp) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE r <= 3; 3. On Snowflake /
BigQuery, use QUALIFY to skip the CTE. 4. Anticipate "What if I just need fast top-N per group without
ranking semantics?" — LATERAL join with LIMIT 3 on Postgres, or CROSS APPLY on SQL
Server. Sometimes faster than the window approach on huge tables with deep partitions.
Edge cases to mention: - Always add a tie-breaker in ORDER BY (e.g. ORDER BY salary DESC,
emp_id) to keep ROW_NUMBER deterministic. - "Top 3" with DENSE_RANK can return many more
than 3 rows if 3 distinct salary values each have multiple people. - For "top 3 by department, but only
departments with at least 5 employees", add HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 in a grouping step or filter on
a window COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) in the outer query.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "limit 3 per group is a one-liner" — it is not in standard SQL without
windows or lateral joins. - Do not use a self-join (the pre-window pattern) — quadratic in partition size
and embarrassing in 2026.
Common follow-up: "Now give me only the single top earner per department." — Same shape, WHERE
r = 1. Same dedup pattern as Q2.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT emp_id, dept, salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r
  FROM employees
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE r <= 3
ORDER BY dept, r, emp_id;
Q84 · Gaps and Islands
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 86 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 87
Given a table of daily user logins, find the longest continuous login streak per user.
The 30-second answer: Compute login_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY
user_id ORDER BY login_date) * INTERVAL '1 day' — consecutive dates produce the same
anchor, so group by (user_id, anchor) to find each streak, then take the longest per user.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the trick: if logins are consecutive, then login_date -
row_number * 1 day is constant within a streak. Different streaks get different anchors. This is the
classic "gaps and islands" technique. 2. Step 1 — assign row numbers per user ordered by date. Step 2
— compute the anchor by subtracting row_number days from the date. Step 3 — group by 
(user_id, anchor) and count rows to get streak length. Step 4 — MAX(streak_length) OVER
(PARTITION BY user_id) or ORDER BY + LIMIT 1 per user for the longest. 3. Variation: detect
islands of "active" status in time-series — same pattern with DENSE_RANK over status changes. 4.
Anticipate "what about gaps of 1 day still counting"? — adjust the granularity (subtract 2 days, etc.) or
use LAG to detect actual gap size.
Edge cases to mention: - Duplicate logins on the same date corrupt the trick; dedup first with SELECT
DISTINCT user_id, login_date. - For non-date sequences (gap = integer ID), the same idea
works: id - ROW_NUMBER() is constant within a run. - For complex islands (status changes), use the
"tabibitosan" / LAG + cumulative sum variant where you mark each row as "new island = 1" and 
SUM() OVER (...) to assign island IDs.
What NOT to say: - Do not write nested correlated subqueries — they will time out on real data. - Do not
assume dates are gap-free in the first place; check for duplicates and missing days upfront.
Common follow-up: "What if I want the current ongoing streak only?" — Filter to the island that contains
today's date.
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
    login_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date)) * INTERVAL '1 day' AS anchor
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins) d
),
streaks AS (
  SELECT user_id, anchor, COUNT(*) AS streak_len,
         MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY user_id, anchor
)
SELECT user_id, streak_start, streak_end, streak_len
FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY streak_len DESC) AS rn
  FROM streaks
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

Q85 · Sessionization — Assigning Session IDs to Event Streams
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, PhonePe, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have a user-events table. Assign session IDs where a new session starts whenever the gap
between consecutive events for a user exceeds 30 minutes.
The 30-second answer: For each event, compute 
LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) to get the previous
event. Mark a new session whenever event_ts - prev_ts > INTERVAL '30 minutes' or 
prev_ts IS NULL. Then SUM(new_session_flag) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER
BY event_ts) is the session number within the user.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Step 1 — LAG gives the previous event timestamp per user. Step 2
— flag = 1 when the gap is too big (or first event), else 0. Step 3 — running sum of the flag gives
sequential session IDs per user. Step 4 — concat with user_id if you want globally unique session
IDs. 2. Specify the frame on the running sum implicitly (ORDER BY + default RANGE UNBOUNDED
PRECEDING TO CURRENT ROW) — correct because the flag is per row and we want cumulative. 3.
Variations: 30-minute gap → product-level rule; "new session per day" → flag on date change; "new
session per visit" → combine multiple flags with OR. 4. For performance on huge event streams, partition
by user is necessary; without it the engine processes the entire table in one window.
Edge cases to mention: - Two events at the exact same timestamp produce gap = 0 — they belong to
the same session. - A user's first event always has prev_ts IS NULL, which the flag treats as a new
session — correct. - If you sessionise across user_id partitions and there are users with millions of
events, watch sort cost — index (user_id, event_ts) helps.
What NOT to say: - Do not use a window with RANGE interval frame here — LAG + cumulative-sum
is the standard pattern, more readable and engine-agnostic. - Do not forget the PARTITION BY
user_id — without it sessions bleed across users.
Common follow-up: "Now show me the duration of each session." — Group by (user_id,
session_id) and take MAX(event_ts) - MIN(event_ts).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 88 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 89
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts, event_type,
    CASE
      WHEN event_ts - LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts)
           > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
        OR LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) IS NULL
      THEN 1 ELSE 0
    END AS new_session
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_ts, event_type,
  SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS session_id
FROM flagged;
Q86 · Window Functions on Huge Tables — Sort Cost and Parallel Window
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Goldman, Razorpay · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Window functions get expensive on large tables. What drives the cost and what can you do about
it?
The 30-second answer: Cost is dominated by the sort needed to satisfy PARTITION BY ... ORDER
BY .... If a covering index matches the partition+order keys, the planner skips the sort. Otherwise,
expect an in-memory or on-disk sort proportional to N log N. Modern engines (Postgres 14+, Snowflake,
BigQuery, SQL Server) can parallelise window evaluation across partitions but not within a single
partition.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Identify the sort as the cost driver. Explain that each (PARTITION
BY, ORDER BY) combination corresponds to a sort key; the planner does one sort per distinct window
spec, sharing where possible. 2. Suggest using the same window spec across multiple expressions in
the query so the planner sorts once — that is one of the biggest wins in real-world tuning. 3. Indexing: a
btree index on (partition_keys, order_keys) can let the planner stream rows in order without
sorting. Verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. 4. Parallel: Postgres 14+ parallelises across partitions; one
giant partition gets one worker. Re-partition by adding a secondary partition key if the data is skewed.
Edge cases to mention: - Window functions cannot be pushed down past GROUP BY — if you can
pre-aggregate, do it first; aggregating then windowing is almost always cheaper than the reverse. - 
RANGE with date-interval offsets can defeat parallelisation on some engines; ROWS is friendlier. -
Materialise large window results into a temp table or CTAS if reused multiple times — windows are not
free to recompute.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 89 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 90
What NOT to say: - Do not say "indexes do not help windows" — they help when they match the sort
order. - Do not blame the window for poor performance without checking EXPLAIN first — sometimes
the cost is in the underlying scan or join.
Common follow-up: "How would you know if the planner skipped the sort?" — EXPLAIN ANALYZE
shows Sort or Index Scan above the WindowAgg node.
-- Use one window spec for two expressions; planner sorts once
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER w AS running_total,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn
FROM orders
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts);
Q87 · Combining Window with GROUP BY — Running Totals Alongside Group
Totals
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show monthly revenue for the year alongside the running year-to-date revenue, in one query.
The 30-second answer: Aggregate to monthly revenue with GROUP BY first, then apply a running 
SUM() OVER (ORDER BY month) on the aggregated rows. Window functions evaluate after GROUP
BY, so this pipeline is natural — group first, window second, all in one query.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lay out the evaluation order again: GROUP BY happens before
window functions, so the window sees one row per group. 2. Write the query as a single SELECT: 
SELECT month, SUM(amount) AS monthly_rev, SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (ORDER BY
month) AS ytd FROM ... GROUP BY month. Yes, SUM(SUM(amount)) is legal — outer SUM
is the window aggregate, inner SUM is the group aggregate. 3. If the SUM(SUM(...)) syntax bothers
reviewers, use a CTE: aggregate in CTE 1, window in the outer query. Same result, more readable. 4.
Anticipate "what if I want year-over-year too?" — add LAG(monthly_rev, 12) OVER (ORDER BY
month) for same-month-last-year.
Edge cases to mention: - The window's ORDER BY is independent of the outer ORDER BY — sort
the final output separately if needed. - For YTD across multiple years, partition by year: 
SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (PARTITION BY EXTRACT(year FROM month) ORDER BY
month). - Sparse months: if there are months with zero revenue, they will not appear unless you join a
month spine first.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 90 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 91
What NOT to say: - Do not say "you cannot mix GROUP BY and window functions" — you absolutely
can; they compose cleanly. - Do not put the window inside the GROUP BY clause — it has to be in 
SELECT.
Common follow-up: "Same query but reset YTD at the start of each year." — PARTITION BY
EXTRACT(year FROM month).
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_ts) AS month,
  SUM(amount) AS monthly_rev,
  SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (
    PARTITION BY EXTRACT(year FROM order_ts)
    ORDER BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_ts)
  ) AS ytd_rev
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1, EXTRACT(year FROM order_ts)
ORDER BY month;
Q88 · Cumulative Distinct Count
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show the cumulative count of distinct users seen by each day. There is no COUNT(DISTINCT)
OVER () — how do you do it?
The 30-second answer: Two options. (a) Find each user's first-seen date, then group by that date to get
new users per day, then SUM(new_users) OVER (ORDER BY day) gives cumulative distinct. (b) On
Postgres / Snowflake / BigQuery use approximate sketches like HLL for streaming distinct counts.
Vanilla COUNT(DISTINCT col) OVER (ORDER BY ...) is not supported.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the limitation upfront so the interviewer knows you have hit this
wall before: most engines do not allow COUNT(DISTINCT) OVER with ORDER BY (Postgres rejects
it; BigQuery has limited support; Snowflake supports it but with caveats). 2. The first-seen trick: 
MIN(event_ts) AS first_seen GROUP BY user_id, then aggregate by 
DATE(first_seen) to get new-user counts, then cumulate. This is exact, fast, and works
everywhere. 3. For approximate at scale, HLL_COUNT.MERGE_PARTIAL on BigQuery or 
APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT with HLL state on Snowflake lets you maintain running distinct estimates
with bounded error. 4. Anticipate "What about distinct per rolling window, not cumulative?" — same
approach with first-seen-within-window or HLL sketches per window.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 91 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 92
Edge cases to mention: - Snowflake supports COUNT(DISTINCT) OVER () without ORDER BY
(partition-level distinct) but not as a running count. - For "distinct active users in the last 7 days each
day", the first-seen trick does not work — you need either a self-join, a calendar+exists pattern, or HLL. -
On data warehouses the HLL approach is dominant because exact cumulative distinct does not scale.
What NOT to say: - Do not write COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) OVER (ORDER BY day) and
assume it works — Postgres throws an error, others give surprising answers. - Do not use a correlated
subquery for cumulative distinct; on a billion-row table it never returns.
Common follow-up: "What's the error class of HLL?" — Typically ~1-2% relative error, configurable on
most engines.
-- Exact cumulative distinct via first-seen trick
WITH first_seen AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(DATE(event_ts)) AS first_day
  FROM events
  GROUP BY user_id
),
daily_new AS (
  SELECT first_day, COUNT(*) AS new_users
  FROM first_seen
  GROUP BY first_day
)
SELECT first_day AS day, new_users,
  SUM(new_users) OVER (ORDER BY first_day) AS cumulative_distinct_users
FROM daily_new
ORDER BY first_day;
Q89 · Window Functions in DML — UPDATE Using Subquery With Window
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Set a is_latest = TRUE flag on the latest event per user in the events table. Use a
window function.
The 30-second answer: Window functions are not allowed directly in UPDATESET expressions —
compute them in a subquery / CTE and join back. On Postgres: UPDATE events e SET is_latest
= TRUE FROM (SELECT event_id FROM (SELECT event_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER
(PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) AS rn FROM events) t WHERE rn =
1) latest WHERE e.event_id = latest.event_id;.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 92 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 93
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule: most engines reject UPDATE ... SET col =
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) directly. Wrap in a subquery / CTE. 2. Pattern: subquery / CTE returns
the row identifiers (or values) you want to apply, the outer UPDATE joins on the primary key and applies
the change. 3. On Postgres use UPDATE ... FROM; on SQL Server use UPDATE ... FROM ...
JOIN; on MySQL 8 use UPDATE ... JOIN; on Oracle use a merge or a correlated subquery. 4.
Reset first if you are recomputing: UPDATE events SET is_latest = FALSE; then set TRUE on
the new latest, otherwise stale TRUE flags hang around.
Edge cases to mention: - Wrap in a transaction so the reset and set are atomic — otherwise concurrent
reads can see no row as latest. - For very large tables, consider an indexed boolean column and batch
updates by user; full-table updates can be a long-running write. - If multiple events tie on event_ts, 
ROW_NUMBER picks one arbitrarily — add a tie-breaker (ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id
DESC) to make this deterministic.
What NOT to say: - Do not write 
UPDATE events SET is_latest = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1 and hope — this is
rejected on every engine. - Do not skip the reset-to-FALSE step in a recompute scenario; you will end up
with multiple "latest" rows per user over time.
Common follow-up: "How would you do this on MySQL 8?" — 
UPDATE events e JOIN (subquery with row_number) latest ON e.event_id =
latest.event_id SET e.is_latest = TRUE.
-- Postgres
BEGIN;
UPDATE events SET is_latest = FALSE;
UPDATE events e
SET is_latest = TRUE
FROM (
  SELECT event_id FROM (
    SELECT event_id,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC
      ) AS rn
    FROM events
  ) ranked WHERE rn = 1
) latest
WHERE e.event_id = latest.event_id;
COMMIT;
Q90 · Multiple Windows in One Query — Named WINDOW Clause for Readability
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 93 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 94
You have three window functions in one query that all use the same partition and order. How do
you avoid repeating the OVER clause?
The 30-second answer: Use the named WINDOW clause: ... OVER w ... OVER w ... OVER
w ... FROM table WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y). Defines the window spec
once and references it by name. Supported on Postgres, MySQL 8+, SQL Server (via syntax differences),
Oracle, BigQuery, Snowflake.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the verbose version first — three 
OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) repetitions — so the interviewer sees the pain. 2.
Refactor with the WINDOW clause. The clause goes between HAVING and ORDER BY in the query.
3. Beyond readability, this can hint the planner that the three windows share a sort — though most
modern planners detect this anyway. 4. Show a variant: WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY
customer_id ORDER BY order_ts), w_unordered AS (PARTITION BY customer_id) for
two related but distinct windows.
Edge cases to mention: - The WINDOW clause name must be a simple identifier; reserved keywords
blow up. - Named windows can inherit from each other: 
WINDOW w1 AS (PARTITION BY x), w2 AS (w1 ORDER BY y) — useful for hierarchical
window specs. - On engines that do not support named windows in older versions (very old MySQL), fall
back to repeated OVER clauses.
What NOT to say: - Do not call it "the WINDOW keyword in OVER" — the WINDOW clause is its own
thing, separate from OVER. - Do not assume named windows change semantics — they are purely a
syntactic shortcut.
Common follow-up: "Can you reference the same window in OVER and override the frame?" — Yes: 
OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN ... ) inherits partition and order, overrides frame.
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER w AS running_total,
  AVG(amount) OVER w AS running_avg,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn
FROM orders
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts);
Q91 · Window vs Aggregate Within the Same Query — Conceptual Difference
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Cognizant, Accenture · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 94 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 95
Conceptually, how is SUM(amount) in SELECT ... GROUP BY different from 
SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY ...) in the same SELECT?
The 30-second answer: The first reduces the input to one row per group and emits the group sum. The
second keeps every input row and emits the group sum on each row. Same numeric answer per group,
different row count. Output cardinality is the entire difference.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Map the difference to row count, again. This is the recurring theme
for windows: rows preserved, not collapsed. 2. Show two queries side by side: 
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id (one row per
customer) versus SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER
(PARTITION BY customer_id) FROM orders (one row per order). 3. Practical hook: window
aggregates are how you compute ratios — amount * 1.0 / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY
customer_id) AS share_of_customer is one row per order with the share filled in. 4. Mention that
you can run both in one query — group at the top level for summary totals, and the window inside a
subquery for row-level metrics — but typically you choose one or the other per use case.
Edge cases to mention: - Window aggregates respect frame; group aggregates do not have a frame. - 
DISTINCT inside group aggregate (COUNT(DISTINCT x)) works; inside window aggregate it is
restricted or unsupported on most engines (Q22). - FILTER (WHERE ...) clause works on both
group and window aggregates on Postgres / SQL standard, useful for conditional sums.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they always give the same answer" — same per-group total, completely
different row count, which can mean completely different downstream behaviour. - Do not pick a window
when GROUP BY is what you need — windows on full tables when you just want a summary are
wasteful.
Common follow-up: "Customer share of total revenue across all customers?" — amount * 1.0 /
SUM(amount) OVER () (no partition = full table).
-- Group aggregate: one row per customer
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS cust_total
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Window aggregate: one row per order
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS cust_total,
  amount * 1.0 / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS share_of_customer
FROM orders;

Q92 · Median via PERCENTILE_CONT — Ordered-Set Aggregate vs Window
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, AmEx · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Compute the median order amount per customer. Then compute the running median over the last
100 orders. Walk me through both.
The 30-second answer: Median per group: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY
amount) GROUP BY customer_id — ordered-set aggregate, returns one row per customer. Running
median: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) OVER (PARTITION BY
customer_id ORDER BY order_ts ROWS BETWEEN 99 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) —
same function used as a window aggregate on engines that support it (Oracle, Snowflake, Redshift).
Postgres supports the grouped form but not the windowed form natively.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Distinguish the two forms: ordered-set aggregate (WITHIN
GROUP ... with GROUP BY) and ordered-set window aggregate (WITHIN GROUP ... with 
OVER). 2. For per-customer median, every engine supports the grouped form. Show it. 3. For running
median, vendor support diverges. Oracle, Snowflake, Redshift, SQL Server 2012+ support it as a window
function (in SQL Server, PERCENTILE_CONT is window-only — it requires OVER). Postgres has it as a
grouped aggregate only — for running median you need a CTE that windows the data then aggregates,
or a third-party extension. 4. Alternative: PERCENTILE_DISC returns an actual data value (the row
whose cumulative distribution crosses 0.5); PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates between values. For
symmetric numeric data, both are usually close.
Edge cases to mention: - Median of NULLs is undefined; PERCENTILE_CONT ignores NULLs. - On a
window with a small frame, both PERCENTILE_CONT and PERCENTILE_DISC work but the result
can swing widely with frame size — pick a frame that matches the analytic intent. - For median across a
huge table, approximate medians via APPROX_PERCENTILE are often required for latency.
What NOT to say: - Do not write MEDIAN(amount) and hope it works everywhere — only some
engines have a MEDIAN function; standard is PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5). - Do not use 
PERCENTILE_CONT as a window on Postgres in production — check support first.
Common follow-up: "What if you only have Postgres and want a running median?" — Pre-compute via
CTE per window position, or use an extension like pg_median / tdigest.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 96 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 97
-- Median per customer (Postgres, Oracle, Snowflake — NOT SQL Server, which is window-only)
SELECT customer_id,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS median_amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Running median over last 100 orders (Snowflake / Oracle / Redshift)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount)
    OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts
          ROWS BETWEEN 99 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_median_100
FROM orders;
Q93 · NTH_VALUE and the IGNORE NULLS Modifier
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Use NTH_VALUE to get each customer's third order amount. What is the IGNORE NULLS
modifier and when does it matter?
The 30-second answer: NTH_VALUE(amount, 3) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER
BY order_ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) returns
the third-ordered amount for each row in the customer's partition. The frame must span the whole
partition (same trap as LAST_VALUE). IGNORE NULLS skips NULL values when counting positions
— supported on Oracle, Snowflake, Postgres 16+, SQL Server 2022+, Redshift.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the frame caveat: NTH_VALUE shares the 
LAST_VALUE trap. Under the default frame, you may not see what you expect because the frame ends
at the current row. 2. Show the corrected query with explicit UNBOUNDED PRECEDING TO UNBOUNDED
FOLLOWING. 3. Explain IGNORE NULLS: if your amount column can be NULL, the default 
RESPECT NULLS counts NULLs in the position; IGNORE NULLS skips them. 4. Anticipate "What
about FROM LAST?" — NTH_VALUE(amount, 3) FROM LAST OVER (...) returns the third-to-
last; supported on Oracle and some others.
Edge cases to mention: - If the partition has fewer than n rows, NTH_VALUE returns NULL. - FROM
FIRST (the default) versus FROM LAST (Oracle and friends) — counts from start or from end. - 
IGNORE NULLS is also useful on LAG/ LEAD/ FIRST_VALUE/ LAST_VALUE — for filling forward,
LAG(col IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY ts) is the canonical pattern on engines that support
it.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 97 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 98
What NOT to say: - Do not use NTH_VALUE without pinning the frame; you will get NULL or the wrong
row. - Do not assume IGNORE NULLS is universal — older Postgres (pre-16) does not have it; you
need a workaround with a CTE that filters NULLs first.
Common follow-up: "Forward-fill missing values on Postgres." — Use the "last seen non-null" trick with 
COUNT(value) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS grp then 
FIRST_VALUE(value) OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY ts). Or upgrade to 16+ for 
IGNORE NULLS.
SELECT customer_id, order_ts, amount,
  NTH_VALUE(amount, 3) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS third_order_amount
FROM orders;
Q94 · Cumulative MIN / MAX — Running Extremes
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Cred, PhonePe · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show each day's revenue with the running maximum revenue seen so far that month.
The 30-second answer: MAX(daily_rev) OVER (PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', day)
ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Partition resets at
each month; the frame says "everything from the month's start up to today."
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Recognise running max / min as a direct use of MAX / MIN with
the running-total frame. 2. Pre-aggregate to one row per day if you have raw events. 3. Partition by
month to reset the running max at each month boundary; without partition the running max is across the
whole input. 4. Use explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW to be
defensive, though the default frame with ORDER BY gives the same result here.
Edge cases to mention: - The first day of the month always equals the running max for that day. - For
"running min so far this year" use PARTITION BY EXTRACT(year FROM day). - Add 
LAG(running_max) OVER (...) to detect "today is a new month high" — useful for alerting.
What NOT to say: - Do not use a self-join (WHERE other.day <= this.day) — orders of
magnitude slower than the window. - Do not forget the partition if you want monthly resets; without it you
get an all-time running max.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 98 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 99
Common follow-up: "Days where today's revenue equals the month-to-date max." — WHERE
daily_rev = running_max.
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT DATE(order_ts) AS day, SUM(amount) AS daily_rev
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT day, daily_rev,
  MAX(daily_rev) OVER (
    PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', day)
    ORDER BY day
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS month_to_date_max
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;
Q95 · Rolling Conversion Rate — Window Aggregates With Numerator and
Denominator
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Meesho · Topic: Window Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Compute the 7-day rolling conversion rate (orders / sessions) per day.
The 30-second answer: Two parallel rolling sums in one window, divided. Aggregate daily orders and
sessions first, then SUM(orders) OVER w * 1.0 / NULLIF(SUM(sessions) OVER w, 0) AS
conv_rate_7d with 
w AS (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Aggregate to daily orders and daily sessions in a CTE — one row per
day, two metric columns. 2. Apply the same window spec to both SUMs (use a named WINDOW
clause for cleanliness). 3. Divide the two rolling sums. Always wrap the denominator in NULLIF(...,
0) to avoid divide-by-zero on zero-session days. 4. Anticipate "Why not AVG(orders) /
AVG(sessions)?" — it gives the same answer only if both windows have the same row count and no
NULLs; rolling sums divided by each other are the canonical and defensive form.
Edge cases to mention: - For sparse data (missing days), join a calendar / generate_series so the
rolling window does not skip days. - 7-row rolling vs 7-day rolling matters with missing days — pick 
ROWS or RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING accordingly. - For very low session
counts, conv_rate swings wildly — apply a min-denominator filter (e.g. only emit if rolling sessions
>= 100).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 99 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 100
What NOT to say: - Do not compute conversion rate per day first and then average it — that gives the
wrong answer because each day's rate is weighted equally regardless of session count. - Do not skip 
NULLIF on the denominator; the first day of low traffic will explode.
Common follow-up: "What if I want a 28-day rolling rate that only emits when 28 days of data exist?" —
Wrap the result in CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER w = 28 THEN ... END.
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT DATE(event_ts) AS day,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'order' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'session_start' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS sessions
  FROM events GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT day, orders, sessions,
  SUM(orders)   OVER w * 1.0
    / NULLIF(SUM(sessions) OVER w, 0) AS conv_rate_7d
FROM daily
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ORDER BY day;
Q96 · Window Function Anti-Patterns to Avoid
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, AmEx · Topic: Window
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What are the common window-function anti-patterns you have seen on production review?
The 30-second answer: Five repeat offenders. (1) ROW_NUMBER for dedup without a deterministic 
ORDER BY tie-breaker. (2) LAST_VALUE without an explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame. (3)
Filtering on a window column inside WHERE — the Filter-Window Trap from Q13. (4) Repeating the
same partition+order across multiple windows instead of using the WINDOW clause. (5) Using a
correlated subquery for running totals / moving averages instead of an OVER clause.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through each anti-pattern with the symptom and the fix. This is
a great closing question because it lets you demonstrate breadth. 2. (1) Non-deterministic dedup —
symptom: results change between runs; fix: add tie-breaker. 3. (2) LAST_VALUE returning current row
— symptom: "last" matches current; fix: extend frame. 4. (3) Filter-Window Trap — symptom: missing
rows; fix: CTE or QUALIFY. 5. (4) Repeated window spec — symptom: query bloat; fix: named 
WINDOW clause. 6. (5) Correlated subquery for running totals — symptom: query times out at scale; fix:
rewrite as SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...). 7. Bonus mention: applying window after a WHERE that
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 100 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 101
strips needed history; aggregating-then-windowing when partition cardinality is huge; window over an
unindexed sort.
Edge cases to mention: - ROW_NUMBER over a stable sort key (id + timestamp) is the safest dedup
pattern; over a single ambiguous key it can return inconsistent results. - LAST_VALUE is so prone to
misuse that many style guides ban it outright in favour of FIRST_VALUE with reversed ordering. - For
audit trails, prefer windowed dedup over DISTINCT ON (Postgres-only) when you need to keep
specific columns from the winning row.
What NOT to say: - Do not pretend these are obscure edge cases; they show up on every code review
of a query with windows. - Do not say "the optimiser handles it" — the optimiser cannot rescue semantic
bugs like the LAST_VALUE trap.
Common follow-up: "Which of these would you put in a linter?" — Filter-Window Trap and 
LAST_VALUE without frame are the easiest to flag automatically; non-deterministic ORDER BY is
harder but possible.
-- Anti-pattern: running total via correlated subquery (slow)
SELECT o.order_id, o.amount,
  (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.order_ts <= o.order_ts) AS rt
FROM orders o;
-- Fix: window function
SELECT order_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    ORDER BY order_ts, order_id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS rt
FROM orders;
Chapter 3, Part B — Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
CTEs are the single biggest readability upgrade SQL has shipped in the last twenty years. The moment
your query crosses fifty lines, a well-named WITH block stops being a stylistic choice and starts being
the difference between code your future self can debug and code that becomes a black box by next
sprint. The basic form is a glorified named subquery, but the real power shows up in two places — first,
when you chain five or six CTEs to decompose a brutal analytics query into named steps that read top-
to-bottom like a recipe, and second, when you flip to WITH RECURSIVE and suddenly you can walk org
charts, traverse friend graphs, generate date dimensions on the fly and unpack comma-separated strings
without leaving SQL. This section runs thirty questions across the basic patterns, the recursive patterns,
and the planner-level gotchas that interviewers love to dig into once they realise you actually know the
syntax.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 101 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 102
Q97 · Basic WITH Clause Syntax and When It Beats a Subquery
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a CTE? Show me the syntax of a basic WITH clause and tell me when you would pick it
over an inline subquery.
The 30-second answer: A CTE is a named, temporary result set defined with WITH name AS
(SELECT ...) that the main query references like a regular table. Pick a CTE over a subquery the
moment readability suffers, when the same derived set is needed in more than one place in the query, or
when you want a self-documenting name on a derived step.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the syntax cleanly — WITH cte_name AS (SELECT ...)
SELECT ... FROM cte_name. Mention that the CTE lives only for the duration of that single
statement. 2. State the readability case: a five-level nested subquery becomes five named CTEs that
read top-to-bottom like English. 3. State the reuse case: if you need the same derived set joined twice in
your main query, a CTE writes it once; a subquery writes it twice. 4. Be honest about the trade-off: a CTE
that is referenced only once and is simple may not buy you anything over a subquery — use judgement.
Edge cases to mention: - A CTE is scoped to one statement only; the next statement cannot see it. If
you need cross-statement reuse, use a temp table. - Some optimisers (older Postgres, for example) treat
the CTE as an optimisation fence — covered in detail in a later question. - A CTE cannot be referenced in
a different session or transaction — its lifetime ends with the statement.
What NOT to say: - Do not call a CTE a "temporary table" — it is not stored anywhere on disk and has
no statistics of its own in most engines. - Do not say CTEs are always faster than subqueries; they are
usually equivalent and sometimes slower.
Common follow-up: "If a CTE is just syntactic sugar for a subquery, why does it matter?" — Because
code is read ten times more than it is written, and a named step that says monthly_revenue is worth
a hundred lines of comments on an anonymous subquery.
WITH active_users AS (
  SELECT user_id, MAX(last_login) AS last_seen
  FROM sessions
  WHERE last_login >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.name, a.last_seen
FROM users u
JOIN active_users a ON u.id = a.user_id;
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 102 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q98 · Multiple CTEs in One Statement
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Wells Fargo · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how to define two or three CTEs in the same query. What is the syntax and do I need to
repeat the WITH keyword?
The 30-second answer: You declare WITH exactly once, then separate each CTE with a comma. The
form is WITH cte1 AS (...), cte2 AS (...), cte3 AS (...) SELECT .... The final main
query then references any of them by name.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the comma rule — beginners often repeat WITH for each
block and get a parser error. 2. Each CTE has its own name and its own parenthesised SELECT. The
order of declaration matters because a later CTE can reference an earlier one, but not the other way
around. 3. Demonstrate with a two-step example: first CTE summarises orders per user, second CTE
filters that down to high-value users, main query joins them to customer details. 4. Mention the
readability win: three CTEs of ten lines each beat one subquery of thirty lines every time.
Edge cases to mention: - A CTE cannot reference a CTE declared after it — order matters in non-
recursive CTEs. - All CTEs in the WITH block share the same scope; they are all visible to the final main
statement. - Some engines (older MySQL versions before 8.0) did not support CTEs at all — always
check the version.
What NOT to say: - Do not write WITH cte1 AS (...) WITH cte2 AS (...) — that is invalid
syntax in every major dialect. - Do not assume CTEs run "in parallel" — they execute in whatever order
the planner chooses, which is usually as needed.
Common follow-up: "How many CTEs is too many?" — When you stop being able to hold the
dependency graph in your head. Five to seven is comfortable; fifteen probably means you should be
writing views or a materialised pipeline.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 103 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 104
WITH monthly_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
high_value AS (
  SELECT user_id, total
  FROM monthly_orders
  WHERE total > 50000
)
SELECT u.name, h.total
FROM users u
JOIN high_value h ON u.id = h.user_id;
Q99 · CTE Referencing Another CTE — Scoping Rules
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can one CTE reference another CTE in the same statement? Are there any ordering or scoping
rules I should know?
The 30-second answer: Yes — any CTE can reference any CTE declared before it in the same WITH
block. The scoping is strictly forward — cte2 can see cte1, but cte1 cannot see cte2 unless
we are in the recursive case, which is a special form.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Establish the forward-reference rule clearly — this is the bit that
confuses candidates who imagine CTEs as a flat namespace. 2. Walk through a three-CTE example: raw
data, aggregated, then filtered. Each step builds on the previous. 3. Mention that the main SELECT at the
end can reference any of the CTEs declared above, in any combination. 4. Contrast with recursive CTEs
(covered in later questions), where a single CTE references itself.
Edge cases to mention: - Nesting CTEs visually (one inside another) is not allowed — they must all be
declared at the same top level inside the WITH block. - A CTE can join multiple earlier CTEs — that is the
whole point of decomposition. - If two CTEs have the same name, the parser will reject the query —
names must be unique within a WITH block.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "CTEs are independent" — they are not, they form a dependency DAG. -
Do not try to forward-reference by declaring a CTE later that the earlier one needs; that throws a parser
error.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 104 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 105
Common follow-up: "Can I have a CTE that depends on two earlier CTEs?" — Absolutely, that is the
standard decomposition pattern. Each later CTE can join, union or filter against any combination of the
earlier ones.
WITH raw_orders AS (
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-04-01'
),
order_totals AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM raw_orders GROUP BY user_id
),
ranked_users AS (
  SELECT user_id, total, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS rnk
  FROM order_totals
)
SELECT * FROM ranked_users WHERE rnk <= 10;
Q100 · Recursive CTE Basics — Anchor, Recursive Member, UNION
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Flipkart · Topic: Recursive
CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the structure of a recursive CTE. What are the anchor and recursive parts, and why do we
use UNION ALL between them?
The 30-second answer: A recursive CTE has two parts joined by UNION ALL — the anchor query that
produces the seed rows, and the recursive query that references the CTE itself and runs repeatedly until
it produces no new rows. UNION ALL is used because UNION (without ALL) silently deduplicates, which
can hide rows you actually wanted and in pathological cases can also break the termination condition.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Draw the structure on a whiteboard if you can — WITH RECURSIVE
cte AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive_part) SELECT * FROM cte. 2. Explain the execution:
the anchor runs once and seeds the result. Then the recursive part runs against the latest batch of new
rows, producing more rows. This repeats until a step adds zero new rows. 3. Stress the WITH
RECURSIVE keyword — Postgres and MySQL require it explicitly. SQL Server omits the RECURSIVE
keyword but the structure is identical. 4. Hammer home why UNION ALL: UNION does an implicit
DISTINCT against the entire result so far, which can both hurt performance massively and silently change
which rows survive.
Edge cases to mention: - If your recursive part never produces zero new rows, you have an infinite loop
— engines usually cap recursion depth (Postgres has no default cap, SQL Server defaults to 100 via
MAXRECURSION). - The columns of the anchor and the recursive part must line up by position and be
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 105 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 106
type-compatible — common cause of "column type mismatch" errors. - The recursive reference can
appear only once in the recursive member (standard SQL constraint).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "UNION and UNION ALL are interchangeable here" — they are not, this
is a top-tier bug. - Do not omit the RECURSIVE keyword in Postgres or MySQL; the parser needs the
hint.
Common follow-up: "What happens if the anchor returns zero rows?" — The recursion never starts, so
the whole CTE produces zero rows. That is sometimes a real bug in your seed condition rather than a
missing UNION.
WITH RECURSIVE numbers AS (
  SELECT 1 AS n             -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1              -- recursive member
  FROM numbers
  WHERE n < 10
)
SELECT n FROM numbers;
Q101 · Recursive CTE for Organizational Hierarchy
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Given an employees table with id, name and manager_id, write a recursive CTE that
returns the full reporting chain for every employee under the CEO.
The 30-second answer: Anchor on the CEO (the row where manager_id IS NULL), then recursively
join the CTE to the employees table on e.manager_id = cte.id to walk down one level at a time.
UNION ALL between the two and you get every employee with their depth in the hierarchy.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start by identifying the seed — usually the row with 
manager_id IS NULL is the top of the tree. If multiple roots exist, the anchor returns them all. 2. The
recursive step joins the CTE (the "already visited" set, in practice just the latest layer) to the employees
table on the manager link, adding one new layer per iteration. 3. Carry a level or depth column
initialised to 1 in the anchor and incremented in the recursive step — extremely useful for indenting
output or filtering. 4. Mention the inverse: if you want a single employee's chain of bosses, flip the join
direction — anchor on the employee, recurse upward via e.id = cte.manager_id.
Edge cases to mention: - If the hierarchy contains a cycle (A reports to B, B reports to A by mistake),
the recursion never terminates without a cycle check. - An employee with no manager and not the CEO
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 106 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 107
will not appear unless the anchor is written to include them — be explicit about what "root" means in
your data. - Large hierarchies may need a recursion limit or an index on manager_id to be tolerable.
What NOT to say: - Do not use a self-join when asked specifically for a "full hierarchy" — a self-join only
goes one level deep. - Do not forget the LEFT JOIN equivalent reasoning — the recursive CTE naturally
handles all levels.
Common follow-up: "Show me how to find all direct and indirect reports of a specific manager." —
Anchor on that manager's row and recurse downward; the result is the entire subtree.
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
)
SELECT id, name, level FROM org_chart ORDER BY level, name;
Q102 · Recursive CTE for Graph Traversal — Friend of Friend
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Meesho, Flipkart, Cred, PhonePe · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Given a friendships(user_a, user_b) table, write a query that finds everyone within
three degrees of a starting user.
The 30-second answer: Anchor on the starting user, then recursively join the friendships table to the
CTE on either column to walk one edge at a time, carrying a depth counter and stopping when depth
reaches three. Use a visited-set or path column to avoid revisiting users in cycles.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Acknowledge that a friendship table is usually undirected — a pair (A,
B) implies the connection in both directions. Either store both rows or handle both directions in the join.
2. Anchor seeds with the starting user at depth zero. Recursive part joins to friendships and increments
depth. 3. Cycle prevention is essential — without it, A -> B -> A -> B loops forever. Track visited users in
an array or a string path column. 4. Cap the depth in the WHERE clause of the recursive part (WHERE
depth < 3) so you stop at the requested degree.
Edge cases to mention: - Undirected vs directed: clarify the schema before writing the join. If only one
direction is stored, you need to handle both columns. - The result may contain the same friend reached
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 107 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 108
by multiple paths — apply DISTINCT or aggregate at the end. - For very dense graphs, even three
degrees can return millions of rows — set expectations with the interviewer.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "recursive CTEs cannot do graph traversal" — they can, with
appropriate cycle handling. - Do not skip the cycle check on a graph just because hierarchies do not
need it.
Common follow-up: "How would you find the shortest path between two users?" — Track the path,
keep the minimum depth per target user, stop when the target is reached.
WITH RECURSIVE friend_network AS (
  SELECT user_a, user_b, 1 AS depth, ARRAY[user_a, user_b] AS path
  FROM friendships
  WHERE user_a = 42
  UNION ALL
  SELECT fn.user_b, f.user_b, fn.depth + 1, fn.path || f.user_b
  FROM friend_network fn
  JOIN friendships f ON f.user_a = fn.user_b
  WHERE fn.depth < 3
    AND f.user_b <> ALL(fn.path)   -- cycle check
)
SELECT DISTINCT user_b, MIN(depth) AS min_depth
FROM friend_network
GROUP BY user_b;
Q103 · Generating a Number Series with Recursive CTE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Wipro, Accenture, Walmart Labs · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Generate the numbers from 1 to 100 using a recursive CTE, without using any system functions
like generate_series or a numbers table.
The 30-second answer: Anchor with SELECT 1, recurse with 
SELECT n + 1 FROM cte WHERE n < 100, UNION ALL between them. The recursive part keeps
adding one until the WHERE clause fails.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the seed clearly — SELECT 1 AS n. 2. The recursive
member adds one and references itself, with a termination predicate that stops it at the right boundary. 3.
Mention that this is a foundational pattern — generating tally tables, date dimensions and string-splitting
all reuse the same technique. 4. In Postgres you would normally just use 
generate_series(1, 100), but the recursive form is what interviewers want to see — and what
you need on dialects without that function.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 108 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 109
Edge cases to mention: - In SQL Server, the default MAXRECURSION is 100, so generating more than
100 rows requires OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0) for unlimited. - Postgres has no default recursion
cap, so you can blow up memory if your termination condition is wrong. - MySQL recursive depth is
capped at 1000 by default via cte_max_recursion_depth.
What NOT to say: - Do not use UNION instead of UNION ALL — at depth 100, the implicit DISTINCT
cost is wasteful and unnecessary. - Do not write the termination as WHERE n <= 100 and then expect
100 rows; that gives you 101 because the row where n = 100 still satisfies the predicate.
Common follow-up: "Generate every odd number from 1 to 99." — Same pattern, but seed with 1 and
add 2 instead of 1, terminate at n < 99.
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 100
)
SELECT n FROM numbers;
Q104 · Recursive CTE for Date Dimension Generation
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Zerodha, Target · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Build a list of every date in the financial year from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 using a recursive
CTE.
The 30-second answer: Anchor with the start date, recurse by adding one day and stopping when the
date crosses the end. UNION ALL gives you 365 (or 366) one-row results, one per date in the window.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Anchor SELECT DATE '2025-04-01' AS d. 2. Recursive part 
SELECT d + INTERVAL '1 day' FROM cte WHERE d < DATE '2026-03-31' — exact date
arithmetic syntax varies by dialect. 3. Useful in BI work — you join this CTE to your fact tables with a
LEFT JOIN so days with no events still show up (instead of dropping out). 4. Mention that in production,
most teams materialise a permanent date dimension table; the recursive CTE is the on-the-fly version
when no such table exists.
Edge cases to mention: - Watch the time-zone behaviour of INTERVAL '1 day' versus + 1
integer — across DST boundaries some engines surprise you. - For a financial year you may also need
week numbers, quarter numbers and fiscal period — add them as projected columns inside the CTE. -
Generating decades of dates this way can exceed MySQL's default recursion limit; bump it or use a tally
table.

What NOT to say: - Do not say "I would just use generate_series" without acknowledging that not
