Q105 · Parsing a Comma-Separated String with Recursive CTE
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Without using STRING_SPLIT or UNNEST, write a recursive CTE that splits a comma-
separated string into one row per token.
The 30-second answer: Anchor extracts the substring before the first comma and the remaining string
after it. Recursive part keeps doing the same on the remaining string until no comma is left, at which
point the remaining string itself is the final token.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Identify the position of the next comma with POSITION or 
CHARINDEX depending on dialect. 2. Anchor projects two columns — the first token, and the rest of
the string after the first comma. 3. Recursive part takes the previous "rest" column, peels off the next
token, and shrinks the rest further. 4. Termination is implicit — once rest has no comma, the recursive
step does not produce another row.
Edge cases to mention: - Empty tokens between consecutive commas (a,,b) should still produce a
row with an empty string. - Trailing commas leave a final empty token — decide whether to keep or filter
it. - This is significantly slower than the built-in split functions; reach for the built-in when available.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim it is impossible without the built-ins; recursive CTEs are exactly the tool
for this. - Do not forget the terminator case — the final token has no comma after it and must still be
emitted.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 110 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 111
Common follow-up: "How would you keep the original ordinal position of each token?" — Carry an
integer counter starting at 1 and increment it in the recursive step.
WITH RECURSIVE split_str AS (
  SELECT
    SUBSTRING('amit,sneha,rohan,priya' FROM 1 FOR POSITION(',' IN 'amit,sneha,rohan,priya') - 1) AS token,
    SUBSTRING('amit,sneha,rohan,priya' FROM POSITION(',' IN 'amit,sneha,rohan,priya') + 1) AS rest,
    1 AS ord
  UNION ALL
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN POSITION(',' IN rest) > 0
         THEN SUBSTRING(rest FROM 1 FOR POSITION(',' IN rest) - 1)
         ELSE rest END,
    CASE WHEN POSITION(',' IN rest) > 0
         THEN SUBSTRING(rest FROM POSITION(',' IN rest) + 1)
         ELSE '' END,
    ord + 1
  FROM split_str
  WHERE rest <> ''
)
SELECT ord, token FROM split_str WHERE token <> '';
Q106 · Transitive Closure with Recursive CTE
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a transitive closure and how would you compute one with a recursive CTE?
The 30-second answer: A transitive closure of a relation R contains every pair (x, z) such that there is a
chain x -> y1 -> y2 -> ... -> z in R. The recursive CTE seeds with the original relation and joins to itself
repeatedly, accumulating new derived pairs until no new pairs appear.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define transitive closure with a concrete example: if Amit reports to
Bina and Bina reports to Chetan, then the closure says Amit transitively reports to Chetan. 2. Anchor with
the raw relation (every existing edge). 3. Recursive part joins the CTE to the original relation to extend
known reach by one hop. Carry a "from" and "to" column. 4. Avoid duplicates with DISTINCT in the final
SELECT, or use a join that filters out already-known pairs in the recursive step.
Edge cases to mention: - Without cycle prevention, a cyclic graph causes infinite recursion. - The
closure can explode in size — n nodes can produce up to n^2 pairs. - For huge graphs, an iterative
materialised approach in application code can be more memory-friendly than a single SQL recursion.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 111 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 112
What NOT to say: - Do not say "transitive closure is a graph algorithm, SQL cannot do it" — recursive
CTEs are exactly how SQL does it. - Do not assume the closure is symmetric; for a directed edge set it
usually is not.
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between transitive closure and reachability?" — Reachability
is the same idea expressed as a yes/no question between two specific nodes; closure is the full set of all
reachable pairs.
WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
  SELECT source, target FROM edges
  UNION ALL
  SELECT r.source, e.target
  FROM reach r
  JOIN edges e ON e.source = r.target
)
SELECT DISTINCT source, target FROM reach;
Q107 · Recursive CTE Termination — Preventing Infinite Loops
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What can go wrong with a recursive CTE and how do you guarantee termination?
The 30-second answer: The recursive part must eventually produce zero new rows, otherwise the query
runs forever. Guarantee termination either by including a strict inequality on a counter (like 
WHERE depth < 10), by relying on the data shape (a tree without cycles), or by adding an explicit
cycle-detection check on a path column.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Identify the three causes of non-termination: a missing or wrong
WHERE clause in the recursive part, a cycle in the underlying graph, or a recursive condition that keeps
producing the same rows. 2. The cleanest defence is a depth counter — initialise it in the anchor and
increment in the recursive step, then bound it in the WHERE clause. 3. For graph traversal, add a path
column (an array or a delimited string) and skip nodes already in the path. 4. Most engines have a
fallback hard limit — SQL Server defaults to 100 recursion levels, MySQL to 1000, Postgres to unlimited
(set statement_timeout to defend against runaway queries).
Edge cases to mention: - A poorly chosen anchor can produce the same row again in the recursive
step, looping in place — check that the join condition strictly advances state. - Using UNION instead of
UNION ALL silently dedupes — sometimes hiding the bug, sometimes preventing termination by making
the new-rows count zero too early. - Engine-level safeguards exist, but you should not rely on them; write
explicit termination conditions.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 112 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 113
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the engine will stop it automatically" — Postgres will not stop until
memory runs out. - Do not write WHERE 1=1 and hope; that is exactly how you build an infinite loop.
Common follow-up: "Show me a recursive CTE that loops forever and how to fix it." — Take any
recursive query, remove the depth check, run on a cyclic graph; fix by reintroducing the depth bound or a
cycle-detection clause.
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM nodes
  WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.id, n.parent_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM nodes n
  JOIN chain c ON n.parent_id = c.id
  WHERE c.depth < 20             -- termination guard
)
SELECT * FROM chain;
Q108 · MAXRECURSION in SQL Server and Cycle Detection
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Wells Fargo, JP Morgan, AmEx · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In SQL Server, what is MAXRECURSION and how does it differ from the cycle-detection clause in
Postgres?
The 30-second answer: MAXRECURSION in SQL Server is a query hint that caps the number of
recursive iterations — the default is 100, and setting it to 0 means unlimited. It is a safety belt, not a cycle
detector. Postgres 14 added a proper CYCLE clause to recursive CTEs that detects loops by tracking the
path and stopping when a node is revisited.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Position MAXRECURSION as a blunt instrument — it stops runaway
queries by counting iterations, but does not understand why they ran away. 2. Position the Postgres
CYCLE clause as a structural solution — it tracks a chosen column's path and marks rows that complete
a cycle so you can filter them out. 3. Mention that in dialects without CYCLE, you replicate it manually by
carrying a path column (array or string) and excluding nodes already in the path. 4. Both approaches
have a place — MAXRECURSION as a safety net, CYCLE as the precise semantic.
Edge cases to mention: - MAXRECURSION 0 is unlimited — accidentally setting that on a buggy CTE
on a cyclic graph hangs the session. - The CYCLE clause requires you to name the columns to track and
the marker column to add — it is not magic. - Other dialects (MySQL, Oracle) have their own knobs:
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 113 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 114
MySQL has cte_max_recursion_depth, Oracle has its own CONNECT BY syntax outside the CTE
family.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MAXRECURSION detects cycles" — it does not, it counts iterations. -
Do not say "every database has a CYCLE clause" — only Postgres 14+ and standard-conformant
engines do.
Common follow-up: "Show me the Postgres CYCLE clause syntax." — Covered in Q29 of this section.
-- SQL Server style: cap recursion at 50
WITH org AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, 1 AS lvl FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, o.lvl + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT * FROM org
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 50);
Q109 · WITH RECURSIVE Syntax Differences Across Dialects
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through how recursive CTE syntax differs between Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server.
The 30-second answer: Postgres and MySQL both require WITH RECURSIVE; the keyword is
mandatory. SQL Server uses plain WITH with no RECURSIVE keyword — the recursion is implied by
the self-reference. All three share the anchor + UNION ALL + recursive-member structure. SQL Server
adds the OPTION (MAXRECURSION N) hint; Postgres 14+ adds the CYCLE and SEARCH clauses.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the RECURSIVE keyword difference — that single word
trips up candidates moving between dialects. 2. Note that Oracle historically used CONNECT BY
instead of recursive CTEs, though it now supports the standard form too. 3. Highlight that the body of
the CTE — anchor, UNION ALL, recursive member — is identical across all three. The dialect differences
are only in keyword and tuning hints. 4. Be ready to explain why Postgres made RECURSIVE explicit — it
makes the parser's job easier and signals intent loudly.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL added recursive CTEs only in 8.0; pre-8.0 you simulated recursion
with stored procedures or session variables. - SQL Server's missing RECURSIVE keyword is technically
non-standard; pure ANSI SQL requires it. - Oracle accepts the standard form from 11g R2 onwards and
still supports CONNECT BY for backwards compatibility.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 114 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 115
What NOT to say: - Do not say "all SQL is the same" — even something this basic varies across
dialects. - Do not assume your Postgres CTE will run unchanged on SQL Server — at minimum, drop the
RECURSIVE keyword.
Common follow-up: "Which one would you use in a portable script?" — Standard-conformant WITH
RECURSIVE works on Postgres, MySQL, Oracle and IBM Db2; SQL Server is the odd one out, and you

-- Postgres / MySQL form
WITH RECURSIVE cte AS (...) SELECT * FROM cte;

Q110 · CTE versus Subquery — Readability and Reuse Trade-offs
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Wipro, Accenture, Razorpay · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When should you pick a CTE over an inline subquery? Are there cases where the subquery is
better?
The 30-second answer: Pick a CTE when the derived set is non-trivial, needs a meaningful name, or is
referenced more than once. Stick with a subquery when it is a one-line expression used in exactly one
place and naming it adds noise rather than clarity.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the three triggers for a CTE — complexity, naming, reuse. 2.
Acknowledge the counter-case: a subquery like (SELECT MAX(id) FROM orders) used once in a
WHERE clause is clearer inline than as a separate CTE. 3. Performance is usually equivalent on modern
engines, so the decision is almost always about readability and maintenance cost. 4. Note that in older
Postgres (pre-12) and some other engines, a CTE acts as an optimisation fence, so a subquery could be
faster — covered in detail in a later question.
Edge cases to mention: - A CTE referenced ten times in the main query is still computed once logically
(and once physically on most modern planners); a subquery copy-pasted ten times may be computed
ten times. - Correlated subqueries cannot be lifted out into a CTE without restructuring — they reference
outer columns. - Excessive CTE use can be its own anti-pattern — every step gets a name, but readers
have to bounce between definitions.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 115 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 116
What NOT to say: - Do not claim CTEs are always more performant — that has been false since
Postgres 12 made them inlineable by default. - Do not claim CTEs are always more readable — at small
sizes the subquery is fine.
Common follow-up: "Convert this nested subquery into CTEs." — A common practical exercise; aim for
one CTE per logical step.
-- Subquery form (acceptable for simple cases)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE amount > 5000);
-- CTE form (preferable when reused or complex)
WITH big_spenders AS (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE amount > 5000)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM big_spenders);
Q111 · CTE versus Temp Table — When Temp Table Wins
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A CTE and a temp table both let you name an intermediate result. When would you reach for a
temp table instead of a CTE?
The 30-second answer: Reach for a temp table when you need the intermediate result in multiple
statements, when you want to add indexes to it for repeated lookups, or when the planner is mis-
estimating row counts because the CTE is opaque. CTEs are scoped to one statement; temp tables
persist across statements within a session or transaction.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the lifetime difference — CTE lives for one statement; temp
table lives for the session or transaction. 2. State the index difference — you can create indexes on a
temp table, you cannot on a CTE. 3. State the statistics difference — temp tables can have actual row
counts gathered, leading to better plans for downstream queries. CTEs often use guesses. 4.
Acknowledge the trade-off — temp tables have setup cost (DDL, statistics, eviction) and require explicit
cleanup in some engines.
Edge cases to mention: - In SQL Server, table variables (@var) behave differently from temp tables
( #temp); table variables have very limited statistics and often misplan. - In Postgres, temp tables
vanish at end-of-session by default but can be set to vanish at end-of-transaction with ON COMMIT
DROP. - For very large intermediate sets that are joined repeatedly, a temp table with an index can be
orders of magnitude faster than a CTE.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 116 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 117
What NOT to say: - Do not say "temp tables are always faster" — small intermediate sets do not benefit
from materialisation. - Do not say "CTE is just a temp table" — they are structurally and behaviourally
different.
Common follow-up: "How would you decide in a real performance tuning session?" — Profile both, look
at the planner output, and choose based on actual numbers, not folklore.
-- Temp table allows indexing and reuse across statements
CREATE TEMP TABLE big_spenders AS
SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 50000;
CREATE INDEX idx_bs_user ON big_spenders(user_id);
SELECT u.* FROM users u JOIN big_spenders b ON u.id = b.user_id;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM big_spenders;
Q112 · CTE Materialization in Postgres — The 11 vs 12 Change
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Zerodha · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How did CTE behaviour change in Postgres 12 versus earlier versions, and why does it matter for
performance?
The 30-second answer: In Postgres 11 and earlier, every CTE was an optimisation fence — the planner
materialised it and could not push predicates into it. From Postgres 12 onward, the default is to inline a
CTE that is referenced exactly once and is side-effect-free, so the planner can optimise across the
boundary. The pre-12 behaviour is still available via the MATERIALIZED keyword.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Establish the pre-12 behaviour — every CTE acted as a fence,
sometimes producing dramatically worse plans because filters could not be pushed in. 2. Explain the
12+ default — inline single-reference, side-effect-free CTEs and treat them like subqueries for planning
purposes. 3. Note the new keyword MATERIALIZED (force the old fence behaviour) and NOT
MATERIALIZED (force the new inline behaviour even when other heuristics would not). 4. Anticipate the
question about why the change happened — to remove a footgun that punished readability with bad
plans.
Edge cases to mention: - CTEs that are referenced more than once, or are recursive, or contain side-
effect statements (data-modifying CTEs) are still materialised by default in 12+. - The MATERIALIZED hint
is the way to deliberately compute a CTE once and reuse it, which can be useful when the CTE is
expensive and used multiple times. - This change is Postgres-specific — other engines have their own
materialisation rules.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 117 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 118
What NOT to say: - Do not say "CTEs are always optimisation fences" — that is the pre-12 Postgres
view and is wrong on modern Postgres and most other engines. - Do not assume your old performance
tuning notes from Postgres 9.x still apply.
Common follow-up: "When would you force MATERIALIZED?" — Covered next in Q17.
-- Postgres 12+: this CTE is inlined by default
WITH recent_orders AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date > '2026-01-01')
SELECT * FROM recent_orders WHERE user_id = 7;
-- Force the old fence behaviour
WITH recent_orders AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date > '2026-01-01')
SELECT * FROM recent_orders WHERE user_id = 7;
Q113 · MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED Hints in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain when you would force MATERIALIZED on a Postgres CTE and when NOT MATERIALIZED
is the right call.
The 30-second answer: Use MATERIALIZED when the CTE is expensive to compute and you want it
computed once even though it is referenced multiple times — or when you want to deliberately fence the
planner because inlining produces a worse plan. Use NOT MATERIALIZED when you want inlining for
a multi-reference CTE that the planner would otherwise materialise.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the defaults: single-reference inline, multi-reference materialise,
recursive materialise, side-effect materialise. 2. MATERIALIZED is for "compute this once and reuse" or
for "I tested both plans and the materialised one is faster." 3. NOT MATERIALIZED is for "even though
this is referenced twice, inlining is fine and gives a better plan." 4. Stress that you should always confirm
with EXPLAIN ANALYZE — these hints are not folklore decisions, they are evidence-driven.
Edge cases to mention: - Data-modifying CTEs (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE inside WITH) are always
materialised — NOT MATERIALIZED cannot override that for safety reasons. - Forcing MATERIALIZED on
a cheap CTE that the planner would have happily inlined just adds overhead. - The hints exist only on
Postgres 12+; other dialects ignore the keyword or fail to parse it.
What NOT to say: - Do not sprinkle MATERIALIZED everywhere "to be safe" — you are guessing, and
you usually guess wrong. - Do not use these hints in code that has to run on non-Postgres engines
without conditional generation.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 118 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 119
Common follow-up: "How do you decide which to use?" — Run both versions with EXPLAIN
(ANALYZE, BUFFERS), compare cost and rows-removed-by-filter; pick the lower cost plan.
WITH heavy AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-04-01' AND '2026-03-31'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.name, h.total
FROM users u JOIN heavy h ON u.id = h.user_id
WHERE h.total > 100000;
Q114 · CTE in Data-Modifying Statements
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Flipkart, AmEx, JP Morgan · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can a CTE be used with INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE? Show me an example.
The 30-second answer: Yes — the WITH clause goes in front of an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE just as
it goes in front of a SELECT. The CTE produces a row set that the DML statement reads from. In
Postgres, the WITH can also contain INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements themselves, with results
piped into the final DML.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the simplest form — a CTE that computes a filter set, then 
DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM cte). 2. Walk through an update where the
CTE computes the new values per row and the UPDATE joins to it. 3. For insertion, the main statement is
INSERT INTO target SELECT * FROM cte. 4. Save the data-modifying CTE form for the next
question — it is the Postgres-specific power feature.
Edge cases to mention: - Some dialects do not allow CTEs in DML statements — older MySQL
versions, for example. - Inside transactional DML, the CTE is still a single-statement scope; its result
vanishes after the DML completes. - Carefully test that your join logic in the DML does not multiply rows
— the same junior-level bug as in SELECT joins.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "CTEs are only for SELECT" — that has been wrong since standard SQL
allowed WITH in front of any DML. - Do not assume your CTE inside an UPDATE will run only on the rows
that match — it produces the row set, then the UPDATE applies it.
Common follow-up: "Show me a CTE inside an UPDATE that uses a window function for the new
value." — A common pattern: rank rows in the CTE, then UPDATE to set status by rank.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 119 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 120
WITH inactive AS (
  SELECT user_id
  FROM sessions
  GROUP BY user_id
  HAVING MAX(last_login) < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 days'
)
UPDATE users SET status = 'dormant'
WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM inactive);
Q115 · Postgres Data-Modifying CTE with RETURNING
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In Postgres, what is a data-modifying CTE and how does the RETURNING clause make it
powerful?
The 30-second answer: Postgres lets you put INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE statements inside the WITH
block. Each DML can use a RETURNING clause to expose the affected rows as the CTE's result set,
which subsequent CTEs (or the final SELECT) can consume. This lets you express "do A, then do B
using A's outcome, then return C" in a single atomic statement.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the unique-to-Postgres part — INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
inside WITH, with RETURNING. 2. Demonstrate the classic move-rows pattern — DELETE returning
rows, INSERT those rows into an archive in one statement. 3. Stress atomicity — all the DML inside one
statement is in the same snapshot, so no race conditions between the steps. 4. Mention that other
dialects do not support this — SQL Server and MySQL require multiple statements wrapped in a
transaction.
Edge cases to mention: - The CTE referencing a data-modifying CTE sees the rows returned by
RETURNING, not the post-DML state of the table. - The order of execution of multiple data-modifying
CTEs in the same WITH is not guaranteed unless one references the other. - A data-modifying CTE is
always materialised — you cannot inline it.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres data-modifying CTEs run in a defined order" — only the data-
flow order is guaranteed. - Do not assume the rest of the statement sees the post-DML table state; it
does not, it sees the snapshot from before the statement started.
Common follow-up: "What is the atomic move-rows-to-archive pattern?" — Shown below.

  DELETE FROM orders
  WHERE order_date < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '5 years'
  RETURNING *

Q116 · Query Decomposition with CTEs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You inherit a 200-line query with five levels of nested subqueries. How would you rewrite it with
CTEs?
The 30-second answer: Identify the logical steps — usually filtering, aggregation, ranking, joining — and
lift each step into a named CTE. Order the CTEs so each one references only earlier ones. The final
SELECT becomes a short query that joins the CTEs together.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start by listing the steps the original query performs in plain English.
Each step usually maps to one CTE. 2. Name each CTE after the business concept — 
active_users, monthly_revenue, top_customers — not after technical structure. 3.
Replace the innermost subquery first, then work outward, testing after each rewrite to confirm the result
set is unchanged. 4. End with a short main SELECT that reads like a summary of the whole pipeline.
Edge cases to mention: - Sometimes the original query relied on correlated subqueries — those do not
map cleanly to CTEs and may need restructuring with window functions. - Test the rewrite carefully: a
CTE that uses different filter ordering can produce different results if the original relied on short-circuit
evaluation. - Performance can shift either way — measure the rewrite, do not assume readability is free.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "I would just leave it as-is" — long nested subqueries are exactly the
maintenance debt CTEs are designed to clear. - Do not split every micro-step into a CTE — five to seven
steps is the sweet spot.
Common follow-up: "What if the rewrite is slower?" — Investigate with EXPLAIN; consider 
MATERIALIZED hints in Postgres or temp tables for the heaviest steps.

Q117 · Performance of CTEs on Large Data — Planner Barriers
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Cred · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A colleague says CTEs always hurt performance. What is the kernel of truth in that and when is it
wrong?
The 30-second answer: The kernel of truth is that on older Postgres (pre-12) and a few other engines, a
CTE acts as an optimisation fence — filters and predicates cannot be pushed through it, so the planner
may compute a large intermediate that gets thrown away. The claim is wrong on modern Postgres 12+,
on SQL Server (which has never treated CTEs as fences), and on MySQL 8+.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Acknowledge the historical truth — anyone who learned SQL on
Postgres 9 or 10 may have war stories. 2. Walk through what changed: Postgres 12 made single-
reference, side-effect-free CTEs inlineable by default. 3. Note that other engines have always inlined
CTEs in their planners, so the "always hurts" claim was never a universal truth. 4. The right framing today
is: CTEs are a planner suggestion, and the planner is free to inline or materialise based on heuristics —
measure if in doubt.
Edge cases to mention: - Recursive CTEs are always materialised — they have to be, by the nature of
the algorithm. - Data-modifying CTEs in Postgres are always materialised — for safety. - Even with
inlining, the planner may make different choices than for a hand-written subquery — measure both.
What NOT to say: - Do not parrot "CTEs are slow" — that is a pre-2019 view. - Do not assume your
team's database is on the latest version; check first.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 122 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 123
Common follow-up: "How would you prove or disprove this on your stack?" — Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE
on the CTE form and the subquery form, compare cost and runtime.
-- On Postgres 12+, this is typically inlined and the WHERE filter is pushed in

Q118 · Recursive CTE with Multiple Anchor Members
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can a recursive CTE have more than one anchor query? Why would you want that?
The 30-second answer: Yes — the anchor portion can be a UNION ALL of multiple non-recursive
queries, all combined with the recursive member by a final UNION ALL. You would want it when the seed
of your recursion comes from multiple sources, like multiple roots of a forest of trees, or two different
starting conditions for a graph walk.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the structure — WITH RECURSIVE cte AS (anchor1
UNION ALL anchor2 UNION ALL recursive_part). 2. Demonstrate with a real case — walking a
forest of organisational hierarchies where there are multiple CEOs (one per business unit) all seeded
together. 3. Mention that some engines are strict about the placement — the recursive reference can
appear only in the final member, not in the anchors. 4. The result combines all seeds and walks them in
parallel, returning every node reachable from any seed.
Edge cases to mention: - Multiple anchors must have matching column lists with the recursive part —
same number, same types. - Different engines vary in how strictly they enforce the anchor-then-recursive
structure. - Combining anchors with UNION (without ALL) is technically allowed, but again you risk
dedupe surprises.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "a recursive CTE has exactly one anchor" — it can have several. - Do not
put the recursive reference inside an anchor — the parser will reject it.
Common follow-up: "Show me a recursive CTE that walks two separate hierarchies in one go." — That
is exactly the multiple-anchor pattern.

Q119 · Recursive CTE Returning a Hierarchy Depth Column
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wells Fargo · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Modify a recursive CTE on the employees table to return each employee's depth in the org chart.
The 30-second answer: Initialise a depth column to 1 in the anchor and increment it by one in the
recursive part. Every output row then carries the number of management levels above it, which is useful
for indenting display, capping recursion, or analysing org structure flatness.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the anchor projecting 1 AS depth. 2. The recursive part
references the CTE's current depth and adds one to it for the next layer. 3. Filter on depth in the final
SELECT to limit how deep you walk — or in the recursive WHERE to stop the recursion early. 4. Bonus
pattern — add a path column at the same time, often as an array, so you can show the full chain from
CEO to employee.
Edge cases to mention: - If your tree has multiple roots, all roots get depth 1, which may or may not be
what you want; you can offset based on a separate logic. - Depth is integer; large hierarchies could
exceed even int4 limits in theory, though never in practice. - The depth column is computed inside the
recursion, so it can be used in the WHERE for early termination.
What NOT to say: - Do not compute depth in application code after fetching; it is trivially cheap inside
the CTE. - Do not assume "level 0 is root" — choose your convention and stick with it.
Common follow-up: "Show me the max depth of the entire org." — SELECT MAX(depth) FROM
org_chart.

  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN org_chart o ON e.manager_id = o.id

Q120 · Cycle Detection with a Path Column
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how to detect and avoid cycles in a recursive CTE by tracking a path column.
The 30-second answer: Carry an array (Postgres) or a delimited string (other dialects) that accumulates
the IDs of every node already visited along the current chain. In the recursive step, only join to nodes
whose ID is not already in the path. When the path would close back on itself, that row is rejected,
breaking the cycle.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Initialise the path in the anchor with the seed ID — ARRAY[id] AS
path in Postgres. 2. In the recursive step, the new path is the old path with the new node appended. 3.
Filter the join with WHERE new_node_id <> ALL(path) — this is the cycle check. 4. The final
SELECT can either expose the path column for debugging or simply omit it for cleaner output.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres arrays are convenient; other engines use string concatenation or a
temporary support table. - The path can grow large in deep hierarchies; for narrow trees this is fine, for
wide graphs less so. - Make sure the path comparison is on a stable, unique key like the primary key.
What NOT to say: - Do not rely on engine recursion limits as your cycle defence — they fire on every
long path, cyclic or not. - Do not skip the check on the assumption that "our data has no cycles" —
production data tends to surprise.
Common follow-up: "How would you do this in a dialect without arrays?" — Concatenate IDs into a
delimited string and search for the new ID inside it before joining.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 125 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 126
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, ARRAY[id] AS path FROM nodes WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.id, n.parent_id, w.path || n.id
  FROM nodes n JOIN walk w ON n.parent_id = w.id
  WHERE n.id <> ALL(w.path)
)
SELECT * FROM walk;
Q121 · Using CTEs Inside Views
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can a view contain a CTE in its definition? Are there any restrictions?
The 30-second answer: Yes — a view's defining query can include one or more CTEs, including
recursive CTEs, in every major engine that supports both features. The restrictions are the usual view
restrictions — no parameters, no statement-level side effects, and updatability depends on whether the
view qualifies as a simple updatable view.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the simple yes — CREATE VIEW v AS WITH cte AS
(...) SELECT ... FROM cte is valid. 2. Note that the CTE inside the view runs every time the view
is queried (subject to the engine's optimisation rules). 3. Materialised views are a different story — they
can also contain CTEs but the result is precomputed. 4. Acknowledge that very complex view definitions
with deep CTE stacks can be hard to debug; sometimes a chain of simpler views is clearer.
Edge cases to mention: - A view with a recursive CTE is read-only — you cannot INSERT/UPDATE/
DELETE through it. - Some engines optimise CTE-bearing views differently from inline CTEs — measure
on your stack. - Permissions on the underlying tables are still required for the user querying the view,
unless the view is defined with elevated privileges.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "views cannot have CTEs" — they absolutely can. - Do not nest the CTE
outside the view definition — it goes inside.
Common follow-up: "Would you prefer a chain of views or one view with multiple CTEs?" — Depends
on reuse. If each intermediate is reused elsewhere, separate views. If only the final result is consumed,
one view with internal CTEs is cleaner.

Q122 · Nested Recursive CTEs
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can you have a recursive CTE that uses another recursive CTE in its definition?
The 30-second answer: You cannot literally nest one recursive CTE inside the definition of another —
the syntax does not allow it. You can, however, have multiple recursive CTEs in the same WITH block
where a later recursive CTE uses the result of an earlier recursive CTE as part of its anchor or recursive
member.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Clarify the terminology — "nested" usually means defined inside; in
WITH-block terms, all CTEs are at the same level. 2. Show that with WITH RECURSIVE a AS (...),
RECURSIVE b AS (... FROM a ...), b can reference a (including a recursive a). 3. Demonstrate a
realistic use — first recursive CTE walks the org chart, second recursive CTE walks a project dependency
tree using employees from the first. 4. Mention that the second recursive CTE still self-references for its
own recursion; a CTE cannot recurse through another CTE.
Edge cases to mention: - Performance can degrade quickly when two recursive walks compound;
profile carefully. - Some engines require the RECURSIVE keyword only once for the whole WITH block;
others allow it per CTE — check your dialect. - Cycle handling has to be done independently for each
recursive CTE.
What NOT to say: - Do not try to literally embed a WITH RECURSIVE inside another CTE body — that is
not legal SQL. - Do not assume the planner will optimise across the two recursions; usually each is
treated independently.
Common follow-up: "Show me a case where this is actually useful." — Walking both a category
hierarchy and a tag hierarchy in one statement, then joining at the leaves.

Q123 · CTE with an Inline WINDOW Clause
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, Swiggy · Topic: CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me a CTE that defines a named WINDOW clause for use inside the CTE's own SELECT.
The 30-second answer: The WINDOW clause goes inside the CTE's SELECT body, after the FROM/
WHERE/GROUP BY but before ORDER BY. You name a window once and reference it from multiple
OVER clauses in the same SELECT, which keeps long window-function lists readable.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the structure — the named window lives after WHERE and is
referenced by name in each OVER clause. 2. The advantage is DRY-ness — if three columns all use the
same PARTITION BY and ORDER BY, you write it once. 3. The named window is scoped to that single
SELECT, so it does not leak across CTEs. 4. Mention that this combines naturally with the window
functions from Part A of this chapter.
Edge cases to mention: - Named windows are part of standard SQL but support varies — older MySQL
versions do not have it. - You can layer named windows — one window inherits from another with 
INHERITS in some dialects. - The named window must be defined exactly once per SELECT; you
cannot redefine it inside.
What NOT to say: - Do not duplicate the same OVER clause across multiple columns when a named
window will do. - Do not assume the named window persists outside the SELECT — it does not.
Common follow-up: "How does this interact with PARTITION BY and ORDER BY in a window function?"
— The named window holds the partition and order specification; each OVER reference uses them as if
written inline.

WITH monthly_summary AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS mo,
    SUM(amount) AS revenue,
    RANK() OVER w AS rnk,
    SUM(amount) OVER w AS running_total
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'
  GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date))

SELECT * FROM monthly_summary;
Q124 · The UNION vs UNION ALL Bug in Recursive CTEs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Razorpay, Cred · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A recursive CTE that uses plain UNION instead of UNION ALL — what bugs can that cause?
The 30-second answer: UNION applies an implicit DISTINCT against the entire accumulated result,
which can silently drop rows you actually wanted, hide cycles instead of detecting them, and in some
cases stop the recursion early by zeroing out the new-rows count. UNION ALL is the correct default; only
use UNION if you specifically need deduplication and understand the implications.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the mechanical difference — UNION dedupes against
everything; UNION ALL just appends. 2. Walk through the silent-drop scenario — a recursive walk that
visits the same node twice along legitimately different paths loses one of them under UNION. 3. Walk
through the termination scenario — if the recursive step keeps producing rows that already exist
(because of a poorly chosen seed or join), UNION reports "zero new rows" and the recursion stops
prematurely. 4. Recommend a default — UNION ALL plus an explicit dedup step at the end if you need
uniqueness.
Edge cases to mention: - The DISTINCT cost of UNION grows with the result size — performance
suffers as the CTE accumulates more rows. - UNION's dedupe is positional — column-by-column
equality, including NULL semantics. - Some dialects warn about UNION inside recursive CTEs; others do
not.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "UNION and UNION ALL are equivalent" — they are not, particularly in
recursive contexts. - Do not use UNION "to be safe" in recursive CTEs; it is the unsafe choice.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 129 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 130
Common follow-up: "How would you dedupe the final output of a recursive CTE if you really need it?" —
Use SELECT DISTINCT in the final SELECT, or aggregate with GROUP BY — both run once, after the
recursion is complete.
-- Wrong: UNION can silently dedupe paths and stop early
WITH RECURSIVE bad AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id FROM nodes WHERE id = 1
  UNION
  SELECT n.id, n.parent_id FROM nodes n JOIN bad b ON n.parent_id = b.id
);
-- Right: UNION ALL keeps every new row; dedupe at the end if needed
WITH RECURSIVE good AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id FROM nodes WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.id, n.parent_id FROM nodes n JOIN good g ON n.parent_id = g.id
)
SELECT DISTINCT * FROM good;
Q125 · Postgres CYCLE Clause (14+)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres 14 added a CYCLE clause to recursive CTEs. Show me how it works and why it is
better than manual path tracking.
The 30-second answer: The CYCLE clause tells Postgres to track a chosen set of columns across the
recursion and add a boolean flag that becomes true when the row completes a cycle, plus a path column
for inspection. You filter on the cycle flag in the final SELECT (or the recursive WHERE) to stop loops
cleanly, without writing your own array logic.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the syntax — CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
placed after the recursive CTE's body. 2. The engine adds two new columns to the CTE: is_cycle
(boolean) and path (array of the tracked columns). 3. In the recursive part, the engine itself prevents
adding rows that would extend a cycle, or marks them as cycles depending on the variant used — check
the exact semantics in the Postgres docs. 4. The win over manual tracking is correctness and brevity —
fewer chances to mess up the cycle check, and the engine optimises the path tracking internally.
Edge cases to mention: - The CYCLE clause exists only on Postgres 14+ — earlier versions need
manual array tracking. - Other ANSI-standard databases (Oracle, Db2) have similar built-in cycle
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 130 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 131
handling; SQL Server does not currently. - For very deep paths, the array column can become memory-
heavy; you can drop it from the final SELECT to save bytes.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "CYCLE replaces UNION ALL" — it does not, it augments cycle handling
on top of the existing structure. - Do not assume this works on every database; it is Postgres 14+
specific.
Common follow-up: "What if I need to detect cycles in MySQL?" — Manual path tracking with a JSON
array or concatenated string; no built-in equivalent yet.
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id FROM nodes WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.id, n.parent_id FROM nodes n JOIN walk w ON n.parent_id = w.id
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT * FROM walk WHERE NOT is_cycle;
Q126 · Postgres SEARCH BREADTH/DEPTH FIRST Clause (14+)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: Recursive CTEs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the SEARCH BREADTH FIRST and SEARCH DEPTH FIRST clauses in Postgres recursive
CTEs and when each is useful.
The 30-second answer: The SEARCH clause tells Postgres how to order the rows of the recursion's
output — BREADTH FIRST BY col SET ord returns all rows at depth 1 before any row at depth 2,
while DEPTH FIRST BY col SET ord walks one branch all the way down before returning to
siblings. The engine adds an ordering column that you can use in the final ORDER BY.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define BFS vs DFS in plain terms — BFS visits siblings first, DFS
visits children first. 2. Show the syntax — SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET order_col
placed after the CTE body. 3. BFS is useful when you want shortest-distance-from-root output, or when
you want to process levels uniformly. DFS is useful when you want one chain at a time, like printing an
org tree with indentation. 4. The added ordering column is exposed to the outer query, so you ORDER
BY it for the desired traversal.
Edge cases to mention: - Like CYCLE, the SEARCH clause is Postgres 14+ — earlier versions emulate
the ordering manually with depth columns and array sort keys. - BFS can be more memory-intensive for
wide trees; DFS is more memory-intensive for deep ones. - Combining SEARCH with CYCLE is allowed
and frequently the right move on real graph data.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 131 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 132
What NOT to say: - Do not say "BFS and DFS are computer-science concepts, SQL does not care" —
Postgres explicitly cares as of 14. - Do not skip the ORDER BY in the outer query — without it the
SEARCH-set column is computed but ignored.
Common follow-up: "Why not just ORDER BY the depth column?" — That gives you levels, but the
SEARCH clause gives you the proper traversal sequence within each level too, matching the BFS or DFS
order exactly.
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
) SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET seq
SELECT id, name FROM org ORDER BY seq;
Chapter 4, Part A — Index Types & Design
Indexes are the single biggest performance lever in SQL — a missing index turns a 5 ms query into a 5
second one, and a wrongly designed index can silently double your write cost without helping a single
read. This section walks through the index types you'll actually use in production (B-tree, hash, GIN,
GiST, BRIN, covering, partial, expression), the rules for designing composite indexes that the planner will
actually pick, and the workload-based thinking that separates a candidate who memorised "add an index
on the WHERE column" from one who can sit with a DBA and defend their choices. Part B picks up from
here and covers query plans, EXPLAIN reading, statistics, and optimizer hints.
Q127 · B-tree Index Internals — What's Actually Stored
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, Goldman, Flipkart · Topic: Index Internals
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain how a B-tree index actually works under the hood. What does the database store, and
why is lookup O(log n)?
The 30-second answer: A B-tree index is a balanced multi-way tree where each node holds sorted key
values and pointers to child nodes; the leaves hold the actual key plus a row pointer (a heap TID in
Postgres, the clustered key in InnoDB). Lookup walks from root to leaf, doing one disk page read per
level, and because each node fans out to hundreds of children, even a billion-row table is only 4-5 levels
deep — hence the logarithmic cost.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 132 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 133
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the shape — sorted, balanced, fan-out of 100-500 per
node depending on page size and key width. 2. Explain that internal nodes are just routing — they hold
separator keys and child pointers, not row data. 3. Leaves hold either the row pointer (Postgres heap) or
the row itself if the index is the clustered index (InnoDB primary key). 4. The "log n" is base-fanout, not
base-2 — that's why a 1 billion row table needs only ~5 page reads. 5. Mention sibling pointers at the
leaf level — that's what makes range scans cheap (WHERE created_at BETWEEN ...).
Edge cases to mention: - Index page splits happen when a leaf fills up — random inserts cause more
splits than sequential ones, which is why UUID primary keys fragment InnoDB badly. - Wide keys (long
varchar) reduce fan-out and push tree height up — prefer narrow keys where you can. - Deleted entries
leave tombstones until VACUUM (Postgres) or purge (InnoDB) reclaims them — that's part of why index
bloat happens.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "indexes are sorted arrays" — they aren't, and the difference matters for
inserts. - Do not confuse B-tree with B+tree blindly — most production engines (Postgres, InnoDB, SQL
Server) use B+tree variants where only leaves hold data pointers.
Common follow-up: "Why does the planner sometimes skip the index and do a sequential scan?" —
When the estimated rows returned exceed roughly 5-10% of the table, random I/O from index lookups
costs more than a sequential scan, so the planner picks the seq scan.
-- A simple B-tree index — the workhorse
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
-- Range scans use the leaf-level sibling pointers
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-26';
Q128 · Hash Index vs B-tree — When Each Wins
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, JP Morgan, Zerodha · Topic: Index Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between a hash index and a B-tree index? When would you pick a hash
index?
The 30-second answer: Hash indexes support only equality lookups (=) and are O(1) on average,
while B-trees support equality, range, ordering and LIKE-prefix in O(log n). You pick hash when the
column is only ever filtered by exact match and you want the tiny speed edge — but in practice B-tree is
the default for almost everything.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 133 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 134
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the core trade-off — hash trades versatility for a constant-time
lookup. 2. List what hash cannot do: range scans, ORDER BY, LIKE 'prefix%', anything other than =. 3.
Mention engine support: Postgres has hash indexes (WAL-logged since 10), MySQL InnoDB has
adaptive hash indexes built on top of B-trees automatically, MySQL MEMORY engine uses hash by
default. 4. Real-world verdict: 95% of the time you should reach for B-tree first, hash only when profiling
shows a hot equality lookup on a high-cardinality column.
Edge cases to mention: - Hash collisions degrade performance — a poorly distributed key (low
cardinality) makes hash indexes worse than B-tree. - Postgres hash indexes were not crash-safe before
version 10 — older blog posts will tell you to avoid them; that advice is outdated. - InnoDB's adaptive
hash index is automatic and invisible — you cannot manually create one, but it kicks in for hot equality
lookups.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim hash indexes are "always faster" — they lose immediately on any non-
equality predicate. - Do not recommend hash indexes for primary keys — you lose ordered scans, which
kill pagination performance.
Common follow-up: "Can a hash index help with WHERE user_id IN (1, 2, 3)?" — Yes for
each individual value, but the planner has to do three separate hash lookups; a B-tree might do one
range scan if the values are clustered.
-- Postgres hash index — only for = lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_token_hash ON sessions USING hash(session_token);
-- This works
SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE session_token = 'abc123';
-- This does NOT use the hash index — falls back to seq scan
SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE session_token LIKE 'abc%';
Q129 · Composite Index Column Order — The Leftmost-Prefix Rule
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Swiggy, Meesho, Razorpay · Topic: Composite Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You create an index on (user_id, status, created_at). Which of these queries can use
the index efficiently?
The 30-second answer: The leftmost-prefix rule says a composite index on (a, b, c) can serve
queries that filter on a, on (a, b), or on (a, b, c) — but not on b alone, c alone, or (b,
c). The columns must be used in the index's left-to-right order, without skipping.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 134 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 135
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Picture the index as one long sorted key — first by a, then by b
within each a, then by c within each (a, b). 2. A query filtering only on b cannot binary-search
that structure, because rows with the same b are scattered across every value of a. 3. The skip-scan
optimisation (Oracle, MySQL 8 partially) lets the planner iterate through distinct a values and seek
within each — only viable when a has low cardinality. 4. Range predicates "stop" the index — after the
first range column, the rest of the index is useful only for ordering, not for filtering. So WHERE user_id
= 5 AND status = 'paid' AND created_at > '2026-01-01' uses all three; 
WHERE user_id = 5 AND created_at > '2026-01-01' AND status = 'paid' effectively
only uses user_id and created_at.
Edge cases to mention: - ORDER BY can use the trailing columns of the index even if you haven't
filtered on them, as long as you've equality-filtered the prefix. - A composite index on (a, b) can
serve WHERE a = 5 ORDER BY b with no separate sort step. - Column order should put the most
selective equality column first, but only if it's actually used in queries.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the index can be used in any order" — that's only true with covering
index-only scans on small tables. - Do not blindly put the highest-cardinality column first — put the
column that appears in the WHERE clause of every query first.
Common follow-up: "Why don't we just create three separate single-column indexes?" — Because
composite indexes can satisfy a multi-column WHERE in one B-tree traversal; with three single-column
indexes, the planner has to do a bitmap AND across three index scans, which is slower for selective
combined predicates.
-- Composite index — order matters
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status_date ON orders(user_id, status, created_at);
-- Uses full index
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'paid' AND created_at > '2026-05-01';
-- Cannot use index efficiently — no leftmost prefix
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at > '2026-05-01';
Q130 · Covering Index — INCLUDE Columns and Index-Only Scans
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan, AmEx · Topic: Covering
Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a covering index, and how is INCLUDE different from just adding columns to the index
key?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 135 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 136
The 30-second answer: A covering index contains every column the query needs — both for filtering
and for output — so the planner can satisfy the query from the index alone without touching the heap. 
INCLUDE (Postgres 11+, SQL Server) appends columns to the leaf entries as payload, so they're
available for SELECT but don't participate in the B-tree key ordering, sort order, or uniqueness.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the goal — eliminate the heap fetch step, which is the
expensive random I/O. 2. Explain why INCLUDE is preferred over extending the key: included columns
don't bloat the internal B-tree pages, keep fan-out high, and don't break the leftmost-prefix rule for other
queries. 3. Walk through a concrete win: a payments table with millions of rows, query SELECT
amount, currency FROM payments WHERE order_id = ?. Index on (order_id) INCLUDE
(amount, currency) lets Postgres return both columns from the index leaf directly. 4. Mention the
cost — index size grows, write amplification rises slightly because every UPDATE to an included column
must update the index too.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL doesn't have INCLUDE syntax; you get covering by extending the
composite index, accepting the key-size cost. - Postgres requires VACUUM to mark the visibility map for
index-only scans to actually skip the heap — on a heavily updated table, you may still see heap fetches
in EXPLAIN. - Don't include wide TEXT or JSON columns — they bloat the index without giving you the
speed you'd hope for.
What NOT to say: - Do not call every multi-column index a "covering index" — it's only covering for a
specific query. - Do not include columns that change frequently — every UPDATE on them triggers an
index update.
Common follow-up: "How do you verify the planner is actually doing an index-only scan?" — EXPLAIN
ANALYZE shows Index Only Scan as the node type, plus a Heap Fetches: 0 line in Postgres
if the visibility map is up to date.
-- Postgres — INCLUDE keeps key narrow, payload available
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_order_covering 
ON payments(order_id) INCLUDE (amount, currency);
-- Index-only scan
SELECT amount, currency FROM payments WHERE order_id = 12345;
Q131 · Partial Index — Indexing Only the Rows That Matter
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, PhonePe · Topic: Partial Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 136 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 137
You have a payments table with 10 million rows but only 50,000 are in 'pending' status. How
would you index the pending ones efficiently?
The 30-second answer: Create a partial index with a WHERE status = 'pending' clause —
Postgres builds the B-tree over only the matching rows, so the index is 200x smaller, fits in memory, and
is dramatically faster for queries that filter the same predicate. SQL Server calls this a filtered index;
MySQL has no native equivalent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem — most rows are dead weight for this query;
indexing them is wasteful. 2. Show the syntax: CREATE INDEX idx ON payments(created_at)
WHERE status = 'pending'. 3. Explain the matching rule — the planner uses the partial index only
when the query's WHERE clause logically implies the index's WHERE clause. So WHERE status =
'pending' AND created_at > '2026-05-01' matches; WHERE created_at >
'2026-05-01' alone does not. 4. Real-world hit list: soft-delete patterns (WHERE deleted_at IS
NULL), state machines (WHERE status IN ('pending', 'processing')), event tables (WHERE
event_type = 'payment_failed').
Edge cases to mention: - The predicate must be immutable — you cannot use 
WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days' because NOW() is volatile. - The planner
has to prove logical implication — sometimes adding a redundant filter to your query is needed to nudge
it. - Partial unique indexes are powerful: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email) WHERE
deleted_at IS NULL lets you enforce uniqueness only among active rows.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MySQL supports partial indexes via index prefix" — those are different
things; prefix indexes index the first N characters of a string column. - Do not create a partial index on a
predicate that doesn't appear in your queries — it'll never be used.
Common follow-up: "What happens when a row's status changes from 'pending' to 'paid'?" — Postgres
removes the row's entry from the partial index automatically as part of the UPDATE, similar to how it
handles any indexed column change.
-- Partial index — Postgres
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_pending_created 
ON payments(created_at) 
WHERE status = 'pending';
-- Uses the partial index
SELECT * FROM payments WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at > '2026-05-20';
Q132 · Expression Index — Indexing the Result of a Function
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Cred · Topic: Functional Indexes
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 137 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 138
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your query is WHERE LOWER(email) = ?. The index on email isn't being used. How do
you fix it?
The 30-second answer: Create an expression index on the same expression you're filtering by — 
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users(LOWER(email)). The planner can only
use an index when the query's expression matches the indexed expression exactly, so wrapping the
column in LOWER() in your WHERE clause invalidates a plain column index.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose: a function on the column kills index usage unless an index
exists on that function's output. 2. Show the fix with Postgres and Oracle syntax — both support
expression indexes natively. 3. Common cases: case-insensitive search (LOWER, UPPER), date
truncation (DATE(timestamp), DATE_TRUNC('day', ts)), JSON path extraction ((payload-
>>'user_id')), trimmed strings (TRIM(name)). 4. Mention MySQL — functional indexes were
added in 8.0.13; before that you had to add a generated column and index that.
Edge cases to mention: - The function must be IMMUTABLE in Postgres — depending on session
settings, LOWER is technically marked immutable only because Postgres assumes the locale doesn't
change at runtime; pay attention to collation-aware functions. - Inserts and updates pay the cost of
evaluating the function each time — a heavy regex or JSON parse on every write hurts. - Expression
indexes don't show up in \d table_name cleanly — they appear as (expression) rather than a
column name.
What NOT to say: - Do not rewrite the query to avoid the function if the function is semantically required
— the index is the correct fix, not contorting the SQL. - Do not create an expression index for a function
that's used in only one query — measure first.
Common follow-up: "What if I want a case-insensitive comparison without an expression index?" — Use
the citext extension in Postgres or a case-insensitive collation in MySQL/SQL Server — those keep
the column itself case-insensitive and let plain indexes work.
-- Postgres expression index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users(LOWER(email));
-- Now this uses the index
SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'rohan@example.in';
-- Date truncation index
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_date ON orders(DATE(created_at));
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-05-26';

Q133 · Unique Index vs UNIQUE Constraint
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: Constraints & Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between a unique index and a UNIQUE constraint?
The 30-second answer: Functionally they're the same — both enforce uniqueness and both are
implemented under the hood by a unique B-tree index. The difference is metadata: a UNIQUE constraint
is a logical declaration that other constraints (like foreign keys) can reference; a unique index is just an
index that happens to be unique. In Postgres and MySQL, declaring a constraint automatically creates
the index.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with "they share the implementation" — that disarms the trick
framing. 2. Explain the metadata angle: a foreign key can reference a column that has a UNIQUE
constraint, but not always a column with just a unique index (depends on engine). 3. Practical impact: a
partial unique index is possible (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), but a UNIQUE constraint cannot
have a WHERE clause — so partial uniqueness must use the index syntax. 4. Tooling — pg_dump and
ORM migrations may treat them differently when generating schema diffs.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres treats them almost identically; \d shows the unique index, and a
constraint creates one of the same name. - Composite UNIQUE constraints are common
( UNIQUE(user_id, product_id) in a cart table) — same as a composite unique index. - Adding a
UNIQUE constraint on a table with duplicate data fails — you must clean the data first.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "constraints are slower than indexes" — they aren't, because they ARE
indexes underneath. - Do not skip the partial uniqueness trick — that's the practical scenario where the
choice matters.
Common follow-up: "Can I drop the unique index that backs a UNIQUE constraint?" — No — you have
to drop the constraint first, which then drops its backing index.
-- Constraint form — declarative, FK-referenceable
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_users_email UNIQUE(email);
-- Unique index form — supports partial uniqueness
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_email_active 
ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
Q134 · Primary Key Index — Clustered vs Heap-Organised
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Storage Internals
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 139 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 140
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the difference between how MySQL InnoDB and Postgres physically store a table relative
to its primary key.
The 30-second answer: InnoDB and SQL Server use clustered indexes — the primary key IS the table;
rows live in the leaf pages of the PK B-tree, sorted by the PK. Postgres uses a heap — rows are stored in
insertion order in a separate heap file, and even the primary key is just a secondary index pointing to
heap TIDs. This explains why InnoDB primary key lookups are one I/O and secondary index lookups are
two, while Postgres treats them all equally.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the architectural contrast — clustered vs heap is the
headline. 2. Show the lookup cost: InnoDB secondary index points to the PK value, which then traverses
the PK tree (two B-tree walks). Postgres secondary index points to a heap TID directly (one B-tree walk +
one heap page read). 3. Practical implication for InnoDB — random UUID primary keys cause leaf page
splits everywhere; sequential keys (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT) keep inserts at the rightmost leaf. 4.
Implication for Postgres — CLUSTER command can physically reorder a heap to match an index, but it's
a one-time operation; new inserts go back to wherever there's free space.
Edge cases to mention: - SQL Server lets you choose — clustered index can be the PK or a different
column, and you can have a heap table with no clustered index at all. - InnoDB hides a 6-byte 
DB_ROW_ID if you don't declare a PK — but you'd be silly not to. - Postgres has TOAST tables for
large columns — those live separately from the main heap, with their own access path.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim Postgres "doesn't have clustered indexes at all" — CLUSTER
command exists and physically reorders the heap; it's just not maintained continuously. - Do not say
InnoDB secondary indexes "point to row IDs" — they point to primary key values.
Common follow-up: "Why does InnoDB recommend an integer surrogate primary key over a natural
key?" — Because every secondary index stores the full PK as the row pointer. A natural PK like email
varchar(255) makes every secondary index huge; a 4-byte INT keeps them lean.
-- InnoDB — sequential PK keeps leaf splits localised
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT,
  amount DECIMAL(10,2)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
-- Postgres CLUSTER — one-time physical reorder
CLUSTER orders USING idx_orders_created_at;

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q135 · Indexing Foreign Key Columns — The Most Forgotten Win
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: FK Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have an orders table with a foreign key to users. Do you need a separate index on the
FK column, or does the FK constraint create one automatically?
The 30-second answer: MySQL InnoDB automatically creates an index for every foreign key, but
Postgres and SQL Server do not — you must add it manually. Without that index, every join from the
parent side and every CASCADE delete on the parent triggers a full sequential scan of the child table.
This is one of the most common overlooked indexes in production.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the engine difference — interviewers love this gotcha. 2.
Explain the two pain points: joins (SELECT * FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id =
u.id) and parent-side deletes (Postgres has to scan the child table to enforce 
ON DELETE RESTRICT or to actually cascade). 3. Diagnose: a slow DELETE on the parent that's
"doing the right thing" almost always means the child's FK column isn't indexed. 4. Standard rule: index
every FK column unless you can prove the child is small and the FK is rarely joined on.
Edge cases to mention: - The FK column might be the leading column of an existing composite index
— check before adding a duplicate. - For high-write child tables, the FK index pays a write cost —
measure if the FK is genuinely needed. - If the FK is ON DELETE NO ACTION DEFERRABLE, the
locking penalty without the index is brutal during bulk deletes.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume your ORM created the index — most ORMs don't, including Django
and Rails until recently. - Do not skip the index because "we never DELETE the parent" — joins also
benefit.
Common follow-up: "How do you find unindexed FKs across your whole schema?" — Postgres has a
well-known query joining pg_constraint and pg_index; MySQL Workbench and pt-duplicate-
key-checker can flag them.
-- Postgres — must add manually
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
-- Without this index, DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 42 
-- triggers a seq scan on orders to check the FK
Q136 · Indexing Low-Cardinality Columns — When the Planner Skips
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Goldman, Razorpay · Topic: Index Selectivity
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 141 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 142
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You added an index on the status column which has only three values — and the planner still
does a sequential scan. Why, and how do you make it useful?
The 30-second answer: Low-cardinality columns produce indexes where each value matches a huge
chunk of the table — the planner correctly judges that random heap I/O across that many rows costs
more than a sequential scan. Make the index useful by combining it with a more selective column in a
composite index, by making it partial (WHERE status = 'pending'), or by accepting that you don't
need an index at all.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the planner's reasoning — when status = 'paid'
matches 80% of rows, scanning the index then jumping back to the heap 80 million times beats nothing.
2. Three real fixes: a. Composite index (status, created_at) — the leading status narrows, the
trailing column adds selectivity. b. Partial index WHERE status = 'pending' — useful when one
value is rare (the "pending" state in a state machine often is). c. BRIN or bitmap index if the table is huge
and queries scan ranges of rows. 3. Acknowledge that for a column like a boolean is_active where
99% is true, a partial index on WHERE is_active = false is often the winning pattern.
Edge cases to mention: - The 5-10% rule is rough — it depends on the row width, page fill factor, and
whether the index is covering. - Skewed distributions matter — if 'pending' is 1% and 'paid' is 99%, the
same index helps for 'pending' queries and is skipped for 'paid' queries. - ANALYZE feeds the planner's
statistics — stale stats cause wrong choices on low-cardinality columns more than anywhere else.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "low-cardinality columns should never be indexed" — partial and
composite usage break that rule routinely. - Do not force the index with hints just because you can see it
— the planner is usually right.
Common follow-up: "What's the threshold where cardinality becomes 'high enough'?" — There's no
fixed number; what matters is selectivity per query. A column with 10 values where the typical query filter
matches 100 rows out of 10 million is plenty selective.
-- Bad: indexing a low-cardinality column alone
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_status ON payments(status);  -- often skipped
-- Better: composite with a selective second column
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_status_created ON payments(status, created_at);
-- Best for skewed: partial index on the rare value
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_pending ON payments(created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 142 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
