Q137 · GIN Index — JSON, Arrays and Full-Text in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho · Topic: Postgres Index Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You're storing event payloads as JSONB and queries filter on payload->>'merchant_id'.
What index type should you use?
The 30-second answer: Use a GIN (Generalised Inverted Index) — it's designed for composite values
where you want to look up rows containing specific elements. For JSONB, GIN can index every key-
value pair (USING GIN (payload jsonb_path_ops)) so that WHERE payload @>
'{"merchant_id": "M123"}' is fast. GIN is also the right choice for array containment (WHERE
tags @> ARRAY['fraud']) and tsvector full-text search.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain GIN's structure conceptually — it's an inverted index, like a
search engine: for each indexed term, it stores the list of rows containing that term. 2. JSONB-specific
advice: default operator class indexes all keys and values (bigger index, supports more operators); 
jsonb_path_ops indexes only paths (smaller, faster, supports only @>). 3. For expression queries
( payload->>'merchant_id' = 'M123'), an expression B-tree index on that specific path is often
faster than GIN if you only care about one key. 4. GIN writes are expensive — every key in the JSONB
value becomes an index entry; the fastupdate setting batches them but trades query speed.
Edge cases to mention: - GIN on arrays supports && (overlap), @> (contains), <@ (contained by) —
pick the right operator class. - Full-text search needs to_tsvector either at query time (slow) or as a
generated/expression-indexed column. - GIN doesn't support ORDER BY — for ranked full-text, you
index with GIN and sort using ts_rank separately.
What NOT to say: - Do not use GIN for plain scalar columns — B-tree wins every time. - Do not skip the
operator class choice — jsonb_path_ops vs default is a real trade-off, not a footnote.
Common follow-up: "How do I full-text search a description column?" — CREATE INDEX
idx_products_desc_fts ON products USING GIN (to_tsvector('english',
description)) then WHERE to_tsvector('english', description) @@
to_tsquery('hindi & cotton').
-- JSONB containment with GIN
CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload_gin ON events USING GIN (payload jsonb_path_ops);
SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"merchant_id": "M123"}';
-- Array overlap
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tags_gin ON orders USING GIN (tags);
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tags && ARRAY['fraud', 'review'];
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 143 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 144
Q138 · GiST Index — Geometric and Range Types
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Flipkart, Meesho, Zomato · Topic: Postgres Index Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your delivery app needs to find all riders within 5 km of a pickup point. What index supports this?
The 30-second answer: GiST (Generalised Search Tree) — a balanced tree where each node holds a
bounding box (or analogous "key" for the data type) and supports operators like "contains," "overlaps,"
"nearest neighbour." For geospatial work you use PostGIS, which adds the geometry type and a GiST
operator class so ORDER BY location <-> point('77.5946 12.9716') returns nearest riders
in true index-sorted order.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame GiST as a generalised structure — not just for geometry; also
for range types (tstzrange, int4range) and exclusion constraints. 2. Walk through the geospatial
query — <-> is the distance operator, GiST powers k-nearest-neighbour without scanning every row.
3. Range type use case — EXCLUDE USING GIST (room WITH =, during WITH &&) enforces
that no two bookings overlap for the same room. 4. Compare with GIN — GIN is better for full
containment lookups on composite values; GiST is better for overlap, distance, and range operations.
Edge cases to mention: - GiST is lossy by default — the index gives a candidate set and the engine
rechecks each row against the real predicate. - SP-GiST is a related index type for non-balanced trees
(quadtrees, suffix trees) — niche but useful for specific data shapes. - PostGIS extension is required for
serious geospatial work; the built-in point type is limited.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "GiST is just for geometry" — range types and exclusion constraints are
huge use cases. - Do not use GiST for plain text or integer columns — you're paying a complexity cost
for no benefit.
Common follow-up: "How would you enforce 'no two events for the same room can overlap in time'?"
— ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_overlap EXCLUDE USING GIST (room_id
WITH =, during WITH &&) — exclusion constraints are GiST's killer feature.
-- PostGIS nearest-neighbour
CREATE INDEX idx_riders_location ON riders USING GIST(location);
SELECT id, name FROM riders

Q139 · BRIN Index — Append-Only Large Tables
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman · Topic: BRIN Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have a transactions log table with 5 billion rows, append-only, queries always filter on 
created_at. A B-tree index would be 100 GB. What's the alternative?
The 30-second answer: A BRIN (Block Range Index) — Postgres divides the heap into ranges (128
pages by default) and stores only the min/max of the indexed column per range. The index is
microscopic (a few MB for billions of rows) and works brilliantly when data is physically clustered by the
indexed column, which is naturally true for append-only time-series tables.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Contrast the size — B-tree stores one entry per row (~30-40 bytes
each), BRIN stores one summary per N pages. 2. Explain the trade-off: BRIN narrows the search to
candidate page ranges, then the engine scans those ranges. For created_at-correlated data, that's
a tight range; for random columns, BRIN devolves to a full scan. 3. Tunable: pages_per_range
parameter trades index size vs scan precision — smaller ranges give tighter pruning at higher index size.
4. Use cases: log tables, sensor data, financial transactions, anything that grows by appending and is
queried by the same time column.
Edge cases to mention: - Correlation matters enormously — check pg_stats.correlation for the
column; values near 1 or -1 mean BRIN will work well. - VACUUM updates BRIN summaries — long-
running transactions can leave summaries stale. - Multi-column BRIN exists but is rarely useful — the
correlation argument usually only holds for one column at a time.
What NOT to say: - Do not use BRIN on a column with random distribution — it'll be useless and you'll
blame the engine. - Do not expect BRIN to replace B-tree for OLTP point lookups — it's a range scan
tool.
Common follow-up: "How does BRIN compare to a partitioned table?" — They're complementary.
Partitioning is a coarser-grained version of the same idea (skip whole partitions). BRIN works within a
single table; partitioning is structural and helps with maintenance too.
-- BRIN on append-only timestamp column
CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_created_brin 
ON transactions USING BRIN (created_at) WITH (pages_per_range = 64);
-- Tight range query — BRIN narrows to a few page ranges
SELECT * FROM transactions 
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-05-25' AND '2026-05-26';

Q140 · Hash Index in Postgres — Old Reputation vs Modern Reality
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman, AmEx · Topic: Postgres Index
Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why did Postgres engineers historically tell people to avoid hash indexes, and is that advice still
valid?
The 30-second answer: Before Postgres 10, hash indexes were not WAL-logged — they couldn't be
replicated and weren't crash-safe; you had to REINDEX after a crash. Postgres 10 fixed this completely.
Modern hash indexes are crash-safe, replicated, and slightly smaller than B-tree for equality-only
workloads on long strings. They're still niche, but the old "never use them" advice is outdated.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the historical reason — the avoidance wasn't because hash
was inherently bad, it was because the implementation was incomplete. 2. State what changed in version
10: full WAL logging, replication support, crash recovery. 3. When to actually pick hash today: high-
cardinality columns with frequent equality lookups, where the key is long (so hash buckets save space vs
B-tree leaf entries), and where you never need range scans or ORDER BY. 4. Acknowledge the practical
truth — B-tree's versatility means most teams stick with it; hash usage in Postgres remains rare.
Edge cases to mention: - Hash indexes still don't support multicolumn indexes — only single-column. -
They don't support uniqueness enforcement — for unique constraints, you need B-tree. -
pg_stat_user_indexes shows scan counts — measure before committing to hash.
What NOT to say: - Do not parrot "hash indexes are deprecated in Postgres" — they're actively
maintained and improved. - Do not assume hash is faster than B-tree by default — modern B-trees are
extremely fast for equality lookups too.
Common follow-up: "Why doesn't hash support multi-column?" — Because the hash of (a, b)
together is unrelated to hashes of a and b separately — you'd lose the leftmost-prefix flexibility
entirely, and there's no commonly useful operator that benefits.
-- Postgres 10+ hash index — safe and replicated
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_token_hash 
ON sessions USING HASH (session_token);
-- Equality only
SELECT user_id FROM sessions WHERE session_token = 'eyJhbGc...';

Q141 · Composite vs Multiple Single-Column Indexes
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Walmart Labs, Flipkart · Topic: Index Strategy
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Should I create one index on (user_id, status) or two separate indexes on user_id
and status?
The 30-second answer: For a query that filters on both columns together, the composite index is faster
— one B-tree traversal finds the exact rows. Two single-column indexes force the planner to do a bitmap
AND across two index scans, which costs more. But two single-column indexes are more flexible — they
can serve queries that filter on either column alone. Pick composite when the queries always use both;
pick singles when each column is independently filtered.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the trade-off clearly — speed for the combined case vs
flexibility for individual cases. 2. Explain bitmap AND: each single-column index returns a bitmap of
matching row pointers, the engine ANDs them, then fetches the surviving heap pages. Two random I/O
paths instead of one. 3. The leftmost-prefix rule means the composite (user_id, status) already
serves WHERE user_id = ? alone — so you might only need the composite + one separate index on
status if status-only queries exist. 4. Write cost reminder — every additional index adds INSERT/
UPDATE cost. Three indexes is three writes.
Edge cases to mention: - For OLAP workloads with diverse predicates, bitmap-AND on single-column
indexes scales surprisingly well — that's why Postgres invests in it. - For OLTP with hot, predictable
queries, composite always wins. - If the second column is low-cardinality, the composite index isn't
much bigger than the single-column one — go composite without thinking.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "more indexes is always better" — write amplification is real. - Do not
say "always use composite" — leftmost-prefix means a composite on (a, b) doesn't help a WHERE
b = ? query at all.
Common follow-up: "How do I know what queries my app actually runs?" — Postgres 
pg_stat_statements extension, MySQL 
performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest, or query logging — never
guess, measure.
-- Composite — best for combined filter
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status);
-- Two singles — better when each is independently filtered
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);

Q142 · Index Design Decisions — Given This Workload, What Indexes?
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Index
Design Strategy
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Here's the workload for a payments table: 10 million rows, 95% reads / 5% writes, top queries
are (a) WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20, (b) WHERE
status = 'pending' AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour', (c) WHERE
order_id = ?, (d) SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = ?
AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?. The table has columns id PK, user_id, 
order_id, merchant_id, status, amount, currency, created_at. Walk me
through which indexes you'd create and why.
The 30-second answer: I'd add four indexes: a composite (user_id, created_at DESC) for
query (a) — it serves the filter and the sort with no extra step; a partial (created_at) WHERE status
= 'pending' for query (b) — tiny index since pending is rare; a single (order_id) for query (c) —
high cardinality, frequent point lookup; and a covering composite (merchant_id, created_at)
INCLUDE (amount) for query (d) so the SUM can be served from the index alone. With reads at 95%,
the write-amplification cost of four indexes is acceptable.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start by listing query patterns, not columns — you index for
queries, not for columns "that look important." 2. Query (a) — user_id + ORDER BY created_at LIMIT
20: A composite on (user_id, created_at DESC) lets the planner seek to the user, then walk the
leaf in reverse order, stopping after 20 rows. Critical for pagination performance. If I created just 
(user_id), the planner would fetch all of that user's payments and then sort them — fine for a user
with 50 payments, catastrophic for a power user with 50,000. 3. Query (b) — pending payments older
than 1 hour: Status is low-cardinality (3-4 values), but 'pending' is a tiny minority (maybe 0.1% of rows
because most payments resolve in seconds). A partial index (created_at) WHERE status =
'pending' is ~10 MB instead of 2 GB and the planner uses it whenever the WHERE clause includes 
status = 'pending'. This is the classic state-machine indexing pattern. 4. Query (c) — by
order_id: Point lookup on a high-cardinality column. Single-column B-tree index is the obvious answer.
Also doubles as the implicit FK-side index if order_id references orders.id. 5. Query (d) —
SUM aggregation by merchant + date range: This is the trickiest. Composite (merchant_id,
created_at) serves filter + range. Adding INCLUDE (amount) makes it a covering index, so
Postgres can do an index-only scan — no heap fetches for the SUM. Big win because aggregation
queries scan many rows. 6. Cardinality analysis I did mentally: - user_id: high cardinality, used in
(a) - status: low cardinality, but skewed — perfect for partial - order_id: very high cardinality,
point lookup - merchant_id: medium-high cardinality, used with date range for analytics - 
created_at: monotonic; serves ordering and range 7. Write-amplification math: 5% writes = 500k
writes/day on 10M rows. Each write updates 4 indexes (plus the heap). At ~30 µs per index update,
that's ~60 ms of write cost per second of throughput — well within capacity for any modern Postgres
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 148 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 149
instance. If writes were 50%, I'd merge (a) and (d) into a single broader composite and drop one index. 8.
What I deliberately didn't add: an index on currency (rarely filtered), an index on status alone
(covered by the partial for the only common status query), an index on amount (only used in
aggregations, never in WHERE).
Edge cases to mention: - For query (a), I used created_at DESC in the index definition — modern
Postgres supports it and the planner can use either direction, but explicit DESC avoids any chance of a
sort step on older versions. - The partial index on 'pending' becomes less useful as pending grows — for
a long-tail backlog, switch to a regular composite. - If query (d) sometimes filters by other status values
too, the covering index needs to include status in the key as well — design for the actual query
shape. - Always create new indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on production tables —
covered in detail in Q18.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "I'd just index every column" — write cost would balloon. - Do not
propose indexes without naming the query they serve — interviewers want the mapping, not a list. - Do
not skip the write-cost calculation — that's how you prove you've thought about it as a system, not just a
read optimisation.
Common follow-up: "What if the write ratio changed to 50/50?" — I'd reduce to two indexes: the
composite (user_id, created_at DESC) (most frequent query) and the partial pending index
(cheap to maintain because most rows skip it). For (c) order_id lookups I'd accept a seq scan or
denormalise the lookup into the application cache. Query (d) would move to an OLAP replica or a
materialised view refreshed hourly.
-- (a) User's recent payments — composite with sort order
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_user_created 
ON payments(user_id, created_at DESC);
-- (b) Stale pending payments — tiny partial index
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_pending_old 
ON payments(created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
-- (c) Order lookup — single column point access
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_order_id ON payments(order_id);
-- (d) Merchant aggregation — covering index for index-only scan
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_merchant_created 
ON payments(merchant_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount);
Q143 · Index-Only Scan — When the Heap Becomes Optional
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Goldman, Razorpay · Topic: Query Execution
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 149 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 150
What is an index-only scan, and what does it take for the planner to actually do one?
The 30-second answer: An index-only scan returns query results entirely from the index leaf pages
without ever reading the heap — possible only when the index contains every column the query needs. In
Postgres it additionally requires the visibility map to confirm all matching rows in the relevant heap pages
are visible to the snapshot; if not, the engine falls back to fetching the heap for those rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the win — heap fetches are the most expensive part of an
index lookup; eliminating them is often the difference between 0.1 ms and 10 ms. 2. Two requirements:
the index must cover (key columns + INCLUDE columns must include every SELECT and WHERE
column), and the engine must know the row is visible without reading it. 3. Postgres specifically — MVCC
stores visibility in the heap row, not the index entry; the visibility map is a bitmap per heap page that
marks "all rows here are visible to everyone." VACUUM updates it. 4. In InnoDB and SQL Server, index-
only scans don't need a visibility map because the clustered index has visibility built in for the PK index,
and secondary indexes track it differently — index-only is easier to achieve.
Edge cases to mention: - A high-write Postgres table will show many "Heap Fetches" in EXPLAIN even
with a covering index — schedule more frequent VACUUM or use autovacuum tuning. - A wide INCLUDE
on a heavily-updated row bloats the index for marginal gain. - ORDER BY clauses don't break index-only
scans as long as the order matches the index order.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "covering index = index-only scan" — covering is a prerequisite, not a
guarantee in Postgres. - Do not ignore the maintenance cost of frequent VACUUMs needed to keep
index-only scans hot.
Common follow-up: "What does Heap Fetches: 0 actually mean in EXPLAIN ANALYZE?" — Every
candidate row was confirmed visible via the visibility map alone — no heap I/O happened. Higher
numbers mean partial fallback.
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_user_amount 
ON payments(user_id) INCLUDE (amount, currency);
-- Postgres can satisfy entirely from the index
EXPLAIN ANALYZE 
SELECT amount, currency FROM payments WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Look for: "Index Only Scan" and "Heap Fetches: 0"
Q144 · Adding Indexes Online — Without Locking the Table
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Flipkart, PhonePe · Topic: Online DDL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 150 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 151
Your production payments table has 500 million rows and you need to add an index. A plain 
CREATE INDEX would lock the table for 20 minutes. What do you do?
The 30-second answer: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres — it takes only a brief lock
at the start and end, builds the index in the background while reads and writes continue, and takes
longer overall but doesn't block traffic. In MySQL, use pt-online-schema-change (Percona Toolkit)
or native ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE. In SQL Server, WITH (ONLINE=ON) (Enterprise
edition).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the cost of NOT going online — a long lock blocks writes;
the app's writes pile up; you cascade-fail the connection pool. 2. Walk through CREATE INDEX
CONCURRENTLY mechanics: scans the table once, builds the index, then scans again to pick up any
rows changed during the first pass — that's why it's slower wall-clock but lock-free for writes. 3. Failure
mode for Postgres concurrent index — if the build fails, you're left with an INVALID index that won't be
used by the planner; you must DROP INDEX and retry. 4. MySQL with pt-osc — creates a shadow
table, copies rows in batches, applies a trigger to capture ongoing changes, then atomically renames.
Different model, same outcome.
Edge cases to mention: - CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot be run inside a transaction in
Postgres. - For UNIQUE indexes, concurrent build is slower because it must validate uniqueness at the
end. - MySQL INSTANT ADD COLUMN (since 8.0.12) is for some DDL operations; index creation still
uses INPLACE.
What NOT to say: - Do not run plain CREATE INDEX on a high-traffic table during business hours. -
Do not assume pt-osc is risk-free — triggers add overhead and unique constraint changes are tricky.
Common follow-up: "How do you safely roll back if the concurrent build leaves an INVALID index?" — 
SELECT * FROM pg_index WHERE indisvalid = false to find them; DROP INDEX
CONCURRENTLY to remove without locking.
-- Postgres — non-blocking index build
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_payments_user_created 
ON payments(user_id, created_at DESC);
-- Check for INVALID indexes after a failed build
SELECT n.nspname, c.relname FROM pg_index i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE NOT i.indisvalid;

Q145 · Index Bloat — When and How to REINDEX
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Razorpay · Topic: Index
Maintenance
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
An index that used to be 2 GB is now 8 GB even though the table size hasn't grown. What's
happening, and how do you fix it?
The 30-second answer: That's index bloat — over time, deleted and updated rows leave dead entries in
the index pages that VACUUM marks reusable but doesn't physically reclaim. New entries can't always
fit into the gaps because of B-tree ordering, so the index grows on disk. Fix it with REINDEX INDEX
CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+) or pt-osc in MySQL — both rebuild the index without long locks.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Distinguish "table bloat" (heap) from "index bloat" — they have
different causes and fixes. 2. Explain the mechanism: when a row's indexed column is updated, the old
index entry is marked dead and a new one is inserted; VACUUM marks the dead one reusable but
cannot compact the B-tree structure. 3. Detection: Postgres pgstattuple extension reports bloat
percentage; the pg_stat_user_indexes view shows scan counts vs size. 4. Fix: REINDEX
CONCURRENTLY rebuilds in the background. For MySQL InnoDB, OPTIMIZE TABLE rebuilds the
clustered + all secondary indexes — heavy but effective.
Edge cases to mention: - HOT updates (Heap-Only Tuples) in Postgres avoid index bloat when no
indexed column changes — design schemas to favour HOT. - Long-running transactions prevent
VACUUM from cleaning up — kill that idle-in-transaction connection. - BRIN indexes don't really "bloat"
the same way because their entries are summaries, not per-row.
What NOT to say: - Do not run blocking REINDEX (without CONCURRENTLY) on a production table —
it locks reads and writes. - Do not assume autovacuum handles bloat completely — it reclaims space
within pages, not the overall index size.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL?" — VACUUM
reclaims space within existing pages (non-blocking); VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table to a new file
and reclaims to OS (blocks everything for the duration).
-- Postgres 12+ — online reindex
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_payments_user_created;
-- Or all indexes of a table
REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY payments;
-- MySQL InnoDB
ALTER TABLE payments ENGINE=InnoDB;  -- same as OPTIMIZE TABLE

Q146 · Invisible Indexes — Test-Dropping Without Risk
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, AmEx, JP Morgan · Topic: Index
Management
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You suspect an index isn't being used and want to remove it, but you're nervous a rare query
depends on it. What's the safe way to test?
The 30-second answer: Mark it invisible — MySQL 8 has ALTER TABLE ... ALTER INDEX ...
INVISIBLE and Oracle has INVISIBLE indexes. The index is still maintained on writes but the
planner pretends it doesn't exist, so any query that gets slow points to a dependency. After a confidence
period, drop it. Postgres has no native invisible index but achieves the equivalent with UPDATE
pg_index SET indisvalid = false.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the risk — dropping an index and immediately finding a
quarterly report grinds to a halt is a classic outage. 2. Show the MySQL syntax and the rollback step — 
INVISIBLE to test, VISIBLE to instantly restore. 3. Mention monitoring during the test period —
slow query log, pg_stat_statements equivalent, application timing dashboards. 4. Postgres workaround
— toggling indisvalid is hackier and not officially supported; an extension or scheduled drop-and-
restore can also work.
Edge cases to mention: - Invisible indexes still cost write amplification — you're testing read impact
only. - An index marked invisible is visible to integrity constraints — uniqueness still enforced. - Some
optimisers use index statistics even when the index is invisible; behaviour varies by version.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose dropping the index and "watching for issues" — by the time you
find out, the report has failed. - Do not skip telling the team — invisible indexes confuse the next person
to do an audit.
Common follow-up: "How do you know which indexes are unused in the first place?" — Postgres 
pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan count; MySQL sys.schema_unused_indexes view; SQL
Server sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats.
-- MySQL 8 — invisible test
ALTER TABLE payments ALTER INDEX idx_payments_status INVISIBLE;
-- Wait, monitor, confirm no queries got slow
ALTER TABLE payments DROP INDEX idx_payments_status;
-- Rollback if needed
ALTER TABLE payments ALTER INDEX idx_payments_status VISIBLE;

Q147 · Descending Indexes and ORDER BY Direction
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Swiggy, Razorpay, PhonePe · Topic: Index Sort Order
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Does ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 need a separate index, or can it use an ASC
index?
The 30-second answer: Modern Postgres can walk a B-tree in reverse, so an ASC index serves both 
ORDER BY col ASC and ORDER BY col DESC for single-column sorts. But for multi-column sorts
like ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC, you need an index whose declaration matches that exact order — 
CREATE INDEX ON t(a ASC, b DESC). MySQL didn't support DESC in index definitions before
8.0; older versions silently stored ASC and used a sort step.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the leaf-walking mechanism — B-trees have sibling pointers
in both directions in modern engines. 2. Show the multi-column trap: ORDER BY status ASC,
created_at DESC cannot be served by (status, created_at) (both ASC) in a single index
scan; the planner must sort. 3. Postgres has always supported DESC in index definitions; MySQL added
it in 8.0 (before that, the syntax was accepted but ignored). 4. Performance impact — a missing index
direction triggers a sort node, which is fine for small result sets and painful at scale.
Edge cases to mention: - NULLS FIRST vs NULLS LAST matters too — Postgres lets you specify in
both index and query; mismatches force a sort. - Composite indexes with mixed directions don't
compose well — designing one per query is sometimes inevitable. - In MySQL 8, EXPLAIN shows
whether the descending index is being used in the "key" output.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume ASC and DESC are interchangeable for composite indexes — that's
the source of many surprise sort steps. - Do not skip the NULLS positioning when designing indexes for
nullable sorted columns.
Common follow-up: "How do I check if a sort step is happening?" — Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE
shows a Sort node above the Index Scan if so; MySQL shows Using filesort in EXPLAIN.
-- Postgres — supports DESC natively, ASC walks backward
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_desc ON orders(created_at DESC);
-- Multi-column with mixed direction
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created 
ON orders(status ASC, created_at DESC);
SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE status = 'paid' 
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Q148 · Sorted Indexes for ORDER BY — Eliminating the Sort Step
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Sort Optimisation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How can an index eliminate an ORDER BY's sort step, and when can it not?
The 30-second answer: A B-tree stores data in sorted order, so if your ORDER BY columns are the
leading columns of an index (or follow equality-filtered prefix columns), the planner can return rows in
index order without an explicit sort. It cannot eliminate the sort when the ORDER BY columns aren't an
index prefix, when the directions don't match, or when the query mixes columns from multiple indexes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Restate the mechanism — the index's leaf-level traversal IS a sorted
scan; the planner just streams it out. 2. Equality-filter-then-sort case: index 
(user_id, created_at) serves WHERE user_id = 5 ORDER BY created_at with zero sort
cost. 3. Range-filter-then-sort breaks this: WHERE created_at > '...' ORDER BY user_id
cannot use the same index for both; either you sort or you create a different index. 4. ORDER BY + LIMIT
is where the index win is most dramatic — without an index, you sort millions of rows just to throw away
all but 20.
Edge cases to mention: - Adding INCLUDE columns doesn't break the sort property — only key
columns determine order. - For multi-table queries, the optimiser sometimes does a sort even if each
table contributes ordered rows — merging streams isn't always trivial. - A Memory: ... line in
Postgres EXPLAIN signals an in-memory sort; if you see disk spill, the cost is far higher.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume every ORDER BY needs an index — small result sets sort just fine in
memory. - Do not over-design composite indexes purely for sort elimination if the queries are rare.
Common follow-up: "How does ORDER BY + LIMIT 1 work with an index?" — The planner walks the
leaf, returns the first matching row, and stops — O(log n) for the seek plus one row. That's the
canonical "top-1 per group" pattern.
-- Index supports filter + sort with no sort step
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_user_created ON payments(user_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE 
SELECT * FROM payments 
WHERE user_id = 42 
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Look for: no "Sort" node, just Index Scan + Limit
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 155 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q149 · Filtered Index in SQL Server — Postgres Partial Equivalent
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: AmEx, Goldman, Wells Fargo, JP Morgan · Topic: SQL Server
Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's a filtered index in SQL Server, and how is it different from a partial index in Postgres?
The 30-second answer: Filtered indexes in SQL Server and partial indexes in Postgres are functionally
the same — you attach a WHERE clause to the index definition and only matching rows get indexed. The
syntax differs slightly (WHERE clause in both, but SQL Server has stricter predicate restrictions — no
LIKE, no BETWEEN, simple comparisons only). The performance and use cases — soft-deletes, state
machines, sparse columns — translate directly.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame as "same feature, two vendors" — interviewer wants to see
cross-engine fluency. 2. Show both syntaxes side by side. 3. Highlight SQL Server's stricter predicate
restrictions — only simple comparison operators are allowed in the filter, no functions, no LIKE. 4.
Highlight a SQL Server-specific gotcha: the connection's SET options (ANSI_NULLS,
QUOTED_IDENTIFIER, etc.) must match the index's compiled options or the planner skips the index —
common source of "why isn't my filtered index used" tickets.
Edge cases to mention: - Both engines require the query's WHERE clause to imply the index's filter for
the index to be used. - SQL Server's filtered index can have INCLUDE columns just like a regular index
— combine for covering filtered indexes. - MySQL has no native equivalent; you simulate with a
generated column + regular index, or live with the full index.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse filtered indexes with sparse columns in SQL Server — sparse
columns are a storage optimisation, unrelated to indexing. - Do not assume the index is "always cheaper
to maintain" — it only saves cost on writes that don't match the filter.
Common follow-up: "What SET options can break a filtered index?" — SET ANSI_NULLS OFF
(default OFF for ODBC connections sometimes) silently invalidates filtered indexes — keep ANSI_NULLS
ON consistently.
-- SQL Server filtered index
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX idx_orders_pending 
ON orders(created_at) 
WHERE status = 'pending';
-- Postgres partial index — same idea
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending 
ON orders(created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

Q150 · LIKE 'prefix%' vs LIKE '%suffix' — and Trigram Indexes
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Cred, Razorpay, Flipkart · Topic: Text Search Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why does an index help WHERE name LIKE 'Rohan%' but not WHERE name LIKE
'%kumar', and how do you make the second case fast?
The 30-second answer: A B-tree is sorted left-to-right, so LIKE 'Rohan%' can be served as a range
scan (name >= 'Rohan' AND name < 'Rohao'). A leading wildcard LIKE '%kumar' has no
fixed prefix to seek — every row could match — so the index is useless. The fix is pg_trgm in
Postgres: a trigram GIN/GiST index breaks every string into three-character chunks and indexes those,
so substring matches become tractable.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the alphabetical-ordering reason for B-tree prefix wins. 2.
Trigram concept — "rohan" becomes {" r", " ro", "roh", "oha", "han", "an "} indexed individually; a search
for "%kumar%" looks up trigrams of "kumar" and intersects. 3. Show the index syntax and the matching
operator — % for similarity, LIKE and ILIKE both supported via the right operator class. 4.
MySQL alternative — full-text indexes via MyISAM or InnoDB FTS for word-boundary search; no native
trigram support without third-party plugins.
Edge cases to mention: - Trigram indexes are large — three-character keys per character of input data;
budget disk accordingly. - For case-insensitive trigram search, use gin_trgm_ops with ILIKE —
Postgres normalises case for the comparison. - A leading wildcard on a B-tree expression index of 
REVERSE(name) turns '%kumar' into 'rakum%' after reversing — a classic trick when trigram
isn't available.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "LIKE always uses an index if it exists" — leading wildcards bust that
completely. - Do not propose full-text search for prefix matching — overkill; B-tree is the right tool.
Common follow-up: "Can trigram speed up fuzzy match for typos like 'Rohaan' vs 'Rohan'?" — Yes — 
pg_trgm exposes a similarity operator % and a distance operator <->; you can ORDER BY
similarity LIMIT 5 for fuzzy autocomplete.
-- B-tree handles prefix
CREATE INDEX idx_users_name ON users(name);
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'Rohan%';
-- Trigram handles substring
CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX idx_users_name_trgm ON users USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops);
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name ILIKE '%kumar%';

Q151 · Indexing for ORDER BY + LIMIT — The Pagination Killer
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy, Cred · Topic: Pagination
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your dashboard query is SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY
created_at DESC LIMIT 50 OFFSET 1000. Even with an index, it gets slow for power
users. What's happening?
The 30-second answer: The index handles the WHERE and ORDER BY efficiently, but OFFSET 1000
forces the engine to fetch and discard the first 1000 rows before returning the next 50 — so cost grows
linearly with offset, not with limit. Fix it with keyset pagination: instead of OFFSET, pass the last seen 
created_at value and add WHERE created_at < ? to skip rows via the index seek itself, in
constant time.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose the OFFSET cost — the planner can't skip rows via the
index seek; it must materialise them. 2. Demonstrate keyset pagination: WHERE user_id = ? AND
(created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50. The
composite comparison handles tie-breaking when timestamps repeat. 3. Index requirement: a composite
on (user_id, created_at, id) makes the seek O(log n) regardless of how deep in the result set
you are. 4. UX trade-off — keyset gives "next page" cleanly; jumping to page 50 directly is impossible.
Most modern apps accept this for infinite-scroll patterns.
Edge cases to mention: - If created_at isn't unique, you must include a tiebreaker (the PK is the
natural choice) — otherwise paging boundaries miss or repeat rows. - For total count display, you need a
separate COUNT(*) query — keyset doesn't give you "page X of Y" cheaply. - MySQL syntax for tuple
comparison works ((a, b) < (?, ?)); some engines need explicit AND expansion.
What NOT to say: - Do not recommend OFFSET pagination for deep pages — it does not scale, period.
- Do not skip the tiebreaker column; it's the difference between correct and silently-wrong.
Common follow-up: "How do you build a 'previous page' button with keyset?" — Reverse the sort and
invert the comparison; or keep a stack of seen cursors on the client. Most teams just disable "previous"
or fall back to OFFSET only for shallow paging.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 158 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 159
-- Slow: deep OFFSET
SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE user_id = 42 
ORDER BY created_at DESC 
LIMIT 50 OFFSET 1000;
-- Fast: keyset pagination
SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE user_id = 42 
  AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-05-25 14:00:00', 998877)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC 
LIMIT 50;
Q152 · Indexing for Filtering + Sorting in the Same Query
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Goldman, Razorpay · Topic: Composite
Index Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount > 1000 ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100. What's the optimal index?
The 30-second answer: For a query that mixes equality, range, and sort, the optimal composite index
order is equality columns first, then sort column, then range column — so (status, created_at
DESC, amount). This lets the index seek to status = 'paid', walk in created_at DESC
order for free, and apply the amount > 1000 filter as a residual check. Putting amount (range)
before created_at (sort) would force a sort step.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the canonical rule: Equality, Sort, Range (ESR) — equality
columns first because they're a clean prefix; sort column next so the index walk gives ordered output;
range column last because it breaks the leaf-walk's usefulness for further columns. 2. Walk through the
alternative (status, amount, created_at): the planner seeks to status = 'paid' AND
amount > 1000, but the rows within that range are ordered by amount, not created_at — so it
must sort. 3. Mention the trade-off — putting a range column last means the index can't filter on it as
efficiently; rows have to be loaded and checked. Acceptable if the equality + sort already narrows
enough. 4. If amount > 1000 matches only 1% of paid orders, consider a partial index WHERE
status = 'paid' AND amount > 1000 ordered by created_at — best of both worlds.
Edge cases to mention: - If the LIMIT is small, the engine streams a few rows and stops — even a
suboptimal index plan can be fast in practice. - ESR is a heuristic, not a law — verify with EXPLAIN
ANALYZE; the planner may surprise you based on statistics. - For multi-table joins, the ESR rule applies
per table, and join order interactions can complicate the picture.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 159 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 160
What NOT to say: - Do not pick column order alphabetically or by "importance" — pick by the query's
predicate shape. - Do not skip the EXPLAIN verification — index choice is a hypothesis; the plan tells you
if you were right.
Common follow-up: "What if I also need ORDER BY created_at ASC for the same data?" —
Postgres can walk a single-column index backward, but for the composite
( status ASC, created_at DESC), a query asking 
ORDER BY status ASC, created_at ASC won't get index ordering; you'd add a second index or
accept the sort.
-- Optimal: Equality, Sort, Range
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created_amount 
ON orders(status, created_at DESC, amount);
-- Bad ordering: forces a sort
-- CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_amount_created 
-- ON orders(status, amount, created_at DESC);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE 
SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount > 1000 
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100;
Q153 · When NOT to Add an Index
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Index Trade-offs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Give me three cases where adding an index is the wrong move.
The 30-second answer: First, very small tables — under a few thousand rows, a seq scan beats index
seek + heap fetch. Second, write-heavy tables where the column is rarely filtered — write amplification
will dwarf the rare read benefit. Third, low-cardinality columns where queries match a large fraction of
rows — the planner will skip the index anyway, and you've paid the maintenance cost for nothing.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the principle — every index costs write performance, disk
space, and planner time; the benefit must justify the cost. 2. Small tables: under 1000-5000 rows, a
sequential scan is one disk page read — beats any index lookup. 3. Write-heavy + rarely filtered: a
logging table writes 100k rows/min and is queried once a week by an analyst — better to do a sweep
scan once a week. 4. Low cardinality + non-skewed: a boolean is_active where 50% are true —
neither value is selective enough; the index never gets used. 5. Bonus: do not duplicate indexes. (a)
and (a, b) covers (a) already; an extra single-column index is wasted.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 160 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 161
Edge cases to mention: - "Rarely filtered" must include ORDER BY and JOIN usage too — a column
you sort or join on is being filtered effectively. - Auto-generated columns from ORMs sometimes get
unnecessary indexes — audit periodically. - Small tables today can become huge tomorrow — review
index decisions when row counts cross thresholds.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "indexes are free, just add them" — write amplification is real and
compounds across many indexes. - Do not blindly remove unused indexes without checking if they back
a UNIQUE constraint or FK.
Common follow-up: "How do I find duplicate or redundant indexes?" — Postgres has the pg_dba
toolkit; pt-duplicate-key-checker for MySQL; SQL Server has 
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats.
-- Detect unused indexes (Postgres)
SELECT schemaname, relname, indexrelname, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes 
WHERE idx_scan = 0 
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;
Q154 · Cardinality and Selectivity — What Makes a "Good" Index
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Razorpay · Topic: Index Theory
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain cardinality and selectivity. What ratio makes a column worth indexing?
The 30-second answer: Cardinality is the number of distinct values in a column; selectivity is what
fraction of rows a typical query matches. A column with high cardinality (many distinct values) and high
selectivity per query (matching <5% of rows) is the textbook ideal — those are the indexes the planner
picks every time. Low cardinality + low selectivity (each value matches a big chunk) is where indexes get
skipped.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define both terms precisely — cardinality is column-level, selectivity
is query-level. 2. Give the rough threshold: queries matching under 5-10% of rows benefit from an index;
above that, sequential scan often wins. 3. Show the math intuition — random heap I/O is roughly
30-100x slower than sequential reads, so the index has to save you that ratio's worth of work to pay off.
4. Selectivity changes per query — the same column can be selective for one filter (status =
'pending', 0.1%) and useless for another (status = 'paid', 80%) — partial indexes solve
exactly this.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 161 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 162
Edge cases to mention: - The planner uses statistics (Postgres pg_statistic, MySQL 
information_schema.statistics) to estimate selectivity — stale stats mean wrong choices; run
ANALYZE. - Multi-column statistics (CREATE STATISTICS in Postgres 10+) help when columns are
correlated. - A column's cardinality is fixed; its query selectivity depends on filter values, distribution, and
skew.
What NOT to say: - Do not conflate cardinality and selectivity — they're related but distinct. - Do not
claim "high cardinality always means good index" — selectivity per actual query is what matters.
Common follow-up: "What if my planner picks the wrong index?" — Update statistics first (ANALYZE);
if still wrong, check for missing extended statistics on correlated columns; last resort is an optimiser hint
or query rewrite.
-- Check cardinality
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT status), COUNT(*) FROM payments;
-- Postgres extended stats for correlated columns
CREATE STATISTICS stats_payments_status_currency 
ON status, currency FROM payments;
ANALYZE payments;
Q155 · How Many Indexes per Table — The Diminishing Returns Curve
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Index Strategy
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Is there a rule of thumb for the maximum number of indexes per table?
The 30-second answer: No hard rule, but the practical sweet spot for OLTP tables is roughly 4-7
indexes — enough to cover the hot read patterns without crippling write throughput. Each additional
index adds INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE cost linearly, and the planner's join-order search gets slower with
more options to consider. OLAP tables can tolerate more indexes because writes are batched.
Step-by-step thought score: 1. Open with the math — every index is one extra B-tree write per row
insert. 2. Walk through write cost: a table with 10 indexes incurs roughly 10x the index write work of a
table with one, plus the heap write. 3. Note the planner cost — more indexes = more candidate plans =
more planning time per query. Usually negligible, but for very high QPS systems it adds up. 4. Practical
advice: audit indexes quarterly; drop ones with zero scans; consolidate composite indexes that overlap.
Edge cases to mention: - Write-amplification depends on which columns change — UPDATEs that
touch only non-indexed columns are cheap (HOT updates in Postgres avoid all index work). - Partitioned
tables effectively have an index per partition for each table-level index — the count multiplies. - Hot-path
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 162 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 163
tables in a payment system should be tightly indexed; cold-path event logs can run on BRIN + partition +
nothing else.
What NOT to say: - Do not quote a specific number as gospel — "max 5 indexes" is a heuristic, not a
rule. - Do not skip the cost of UPDATEs in your calculus — they're the dominant write workload for many
tables.
Common follow-up: "What's the cost difference between adding a 5th index and a 15th?" — On
INSERT, roughly linear. On UPDATE, only indexes whose key columns changed pay the full cost; HOT
updates skip even those. So the practical curve depends on column volatility, not just count.
-- Audit query (Postgres) — find indexes by usage
SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan, 
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes 
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
ORDER BY idx_scan ASC, pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;
Q156 · Index Selectivity in Practice — Designing for Real Skew
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Index
Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have a transactions table where merchant_id distribution is heavily skewed — one
merchant has 40% of all rows, while 10,000 others have <0.01% each. How does this affect
index design?
The 30-second answer: A single B-tree index on merchant_id works perfectly for the small
merchants (highly selective) and is correctly skipped by the planner for the big one (low selectivity). The
asymmetric handling is exactly what you want. For analytic queries on the big merchant, design a
separate path: composite index (merchant_id, created_at) for time-range slicing, or partition
the table by merchant if it gets large enough.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Recognise skew is normal — payment processors, e-commerce
platforms, and ride-hailing all have power-law merchant distributions. 2. Per-query selectivity reasoning:
the planner uses histograms in pg_stats to estimate row counts per value — for the big merchant, it
expects 40% of the table and skips the index; for a small merchant, it expects 100 rows and uses the
index seek. 3. For the big merchant's queries, add the time dimension to slice: (merchant_id,
created_at) narrows by date range even within that one giant merchant. 4. If one merchant
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 163 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 164
dominates by an extreme margin (90%+), consider list partitioning by merchant — keeps the big one's
data isolated and small merchants' queries blazing fast.
Edge cases to mention: - Histogram bucket counts in Postgres default to 100 — for very skewed data,
increase default_statistics_target for that column. - A query for the big merchant + a narrow
date range may still beat seq scan — index is per-row, not per-merchant. - Skew can change over time
as new merchants grow — review every 6 months.
What NOT to say: - Do not panic about skew — it's the planner's job to handle it, and modern planners
do this well. - Do not over-partition prematurely — partitioning has operational overhead; only adopt
when scale justifies.
Common follow-up: "How do you check if Postgres has good statistics for a skewed column?" — 
SELECT most_common_vals, most_common_freqs FROM pg_stats WHERE
tablename='transactions' AND attname='merchant_id' — those show the high-frequency
values the planner is aware of.
-- Composite for big merchants with time-range slicing
CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_merchant_created 
ON transactions(merchant_id, created_at);
-- Increase histogram resolution for skewed column
ALTER TABLE transactions ALTER COLUMN merchant_id 
SET STATISTICS 500;
ANALYZE transactions;
-- For extreme skew, consider list partitioning
CREATE TABLE transactions_big_merchant 
PARTITION OF transactions FOR VALUES IN ('M0001');

Picking the right indexes (Part A) gets you halfway. The other half is being able to open a query plan,
point at the line that is killing you, and rewrite the SQL so the optimizer makes a better decision. This
section covers what EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually show, how to read a plan top-down
versus bottom-up, when the planner picks nested-loop versus hash versus merge joins, why statistics
drift and break plans, and the rewrites you will reach for again and again — subquery to JOIN, NOT IN to
NOT EXISTS, OR to UNION ALL, function-on-column to expression index. Each question is sized for a
60-to-90 second answer in an interview, with the edge case the panel is waiting to hear.

Q157 · EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE? When do you use each one in
production?
The 30-second answer: EXPLAIN shows the planner's estimated plan without running the query — it is
fast and safe. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and shows real row counts, actual timing
per node and loop counts, so you can compare estimates against reality. You use EXPLAIN to sanity-
check; you use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to debug a slow query.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the core distinction — estimation versus execution.
EXPLAIN is what the optimizer thinks will happen; EXPLAIN ANALYZE is what actually happened. 2.
Mention the cost: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query end-to-end, so on a slow query that scans a billion
rows it will be slow and may touch production data. For UPDATE or DELETE, wrap it in BEGIN and
ROLLBACK to avoid persisting changes. 3. Highlight the most useful columns: estimated rows versus
actual rows. If the estimate is 10 and the actual is 10 million, the planner has stale statistics or a
correlation it cannot see, and that is your first lead. 4. Vendor call-out: Postgres has EXPLAIN ANALYZE;
MySQL 8 has EXPLAIN ANALYZE too; SQL Server uses SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON or the actual
execution plan in SSMS; Oracle uses DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR after running with /+
GATHER_PLAN_STATISTICS /.
Edge cases to mention: - EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a destructive statement (DELETE, UPDATE) actually
performs it — always wrap in a transaction you can roll back. - The timing overhead of EXPLAIN
ANALYZE itself can inflate per-row timing on very fast nodes (microsecond hot loops). - ANALYZE in
Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE is unrelated to the standalone ANALYZE command that refreshes statistics
— same word, different operation.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "EXPLAIN runs the query" — it does not in any major engine. - Do not
skip EXPLAIN ANALYZE because "the EXPLAIN looked fine" — estimated plans lie when stats are stale.
Common follow-up: "What extra information does EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) give you?" — Buffer
hits, reads from disk, and dirty buffers per node, which lets you distinguish a CPU-bound plan from an
IO-bound one.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT order_id, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4827 AND order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';
