Q158 · Reading a Plan — Top-Down or Bottom-Up
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When you open a query plan in Postgres or SQL Server, do you read it top-down or bottom-up?
Walk me through how you actually scan it.
The 30-second answer: Execution flows bottom-up — the deepest, most indented nodes run first and
feed their parents — but you read top-down to understand the shape of the query, then dive into the
leaves to find the expensive step. The slowest single node is usually where you spend your time.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Clarify the two directions. Reading top-down tells you what the query
is trying to do; reading bottom-up traces actual execution order, because each operator pulls rows from
its children. 2. The first thing I scan is the rows column — both estimated and actual — looking for the
largest blow-up. A node that returns 50 million rows when its parent only needs 100 is the leak. 3. Next, I
look at the operator types — Seq Scan on a large table when there is a usable index is a red flag; Nested
Loop with high loop count is another. 4. Finally, I check the cost contribution of each subtree to confirm
where the time is actually going. In Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE this is "actual time" in milliseconds per
loop.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres text plans, indentation tells you parent-child — nodes at the same
indent level are siblings (typically join inputs). - SQL Server graphical plans read right-to-left, top-to-
bottom — same execution-order rule, different visual convention. - A Materialize or Memoize node hides
repeated work — its parent loop count can be misleadingly high while the child runs only once.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "I read it left-to-right" — that does not map to either rendering. - Do not
focus on the topmost cost number — that is the cumulative cost, not the cost of the root operator alone.
Common follow-up: "In a plan, what is the difference between cost and actual time?" — Cost is the
planner's unitless estimate; actual time is real milliseconds from EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The two can diverge
wildly when stats are stale.
Limit  (cost=0.00..8.27 rows=10 width=64) (actual time=0.04..0.12 rows=10 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_customer on orders  (actual rows=10 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 4827)
Q159 · Cost Units in a Plan
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Zerodha, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 166 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 167
What do the cost numbers in EXPLAIN actually represent? Is a cost of 1000 in milliseconds?
The 30-second answer: Cost is a unitless score the planner uses to compare plans — it is roughly
calibrated so 1.0 equals one sequential page fetch on the configured hardware. It is not milliseconds, not
rows, not bytes. Two costs are only comparable within the same plan on the same database; cross-
database comparisons are meaningless.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the unitless-score point. The planner only needs ordinal
correctness — plan A cheaper than plan B — and the cost reflects that. 2. In Postgres, the constants
seq_page_cost, random_page_cost, cpu_tuple_cost and cpu_operator_cost are knobs that scale the
cost. The defaults assume spinning disk; SSD shops often lower random_page_cost from 4.0 to 1.1. 3.
Cost has two parts in Postgres: startup cost (work before the first row is emitted) and total cost (work to
emit all rows). For a LIMIT 1 query, startup cost is what matters; for a full export, total cost matters. 4.
Vendor call-out: SQL Server uses subtree cost in the same flavour but tuned differently; Oracle uses CPU
cost plus IO cost. The interpretation is similar — internal score, not wall-clock time.
Edge cases to mention: - A plan with low cost can still be slow if statistics underestimated row counts.
Cost trusts stats blindly. - Adjusting random_page_cost without testing changes the planner's preference
between index scan and sequential scan across the whole database. - Cost does not account for cache
state — a cold buffer pool will make a "cheap" plan crawl.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "lower cost always means faster" — only on average and only when
stats are accurate. - Do not quote a cost as milliseconds in a status report — your senior will correct you.
Common follow-up: "Why does my Postgres plan show cost 12000 but the query runs in 50ms?" —
Probably hot cache, accurate small-row count, or planner overestimation due to default page-cost
constants on SSD hardware.
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..1934.00 rows=100000 width=64)
-- 0.00 = startup cost, 1934.00 = total cost (unitless)
Q160 · Index Scan vs Index Seek vs Sequential Scan
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Walmart Labs, Wells Fargo · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the difference between index scan, index seek and sequential scan. When does the
planner pick each?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 167 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 168
The 30-second answer: Index seek (SQL Server term) jumps directly to a specific key range using the
B-tree — cheap and bounded. Index scan reads the entire index in order — used when nearly all rows
qualify or when ordering is needed. Sequential scan reads the full table without using any index —
picked when the table is small, no usable index exists, or the filter matches a large fraction of rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the seek versus scan distinction. A seek is logarithmic on
key depth; a scan is linear on the index leaves. 2. Explain when the planner switches to sequential scan:
when the estimated fraction of matching rows is high (typically above 10 to 25 percent in Postgres),
random IO from index lookups beats sequential IO from a table scan. 3. Postgres terminology: there is no
"seek" — there are Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap Index Scan and Seq Scan. SQL Server
distinguishes Index Seek from Index Scan; MySQL EXPLAIN shows type ref, range, index, or ALL. 4. Be
ready for the trick question: a Seq Scan is sometimes correct and faster than an Index Scan — especially
on tables that fit in memory or queries that need 80 percent of rows.
Edge cases to mention: - A "Full Index Scan" (Postgres Index Scan with no Index Cond) is essentially
scanning the index instead of the heap — useful only when the index is much smaller than the table or
covers the query. - On small tables (a few hundred rows), the planner correctly ignores indexes — the
overhead of B-tree descent costs more than reading the heap. - SQL Server Index Scan with a residual
predicate looks like a seek but is actually a scan plus filter — check the Predicate property.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "sequential scan is always bad" — interviewers love correcting this. - Do
not confuse Index Only Scan with Index Scan in Postgres; they have different IO profiles.
Common follow-up: "If my query has a WHERE on an indexed column but the plan shows Seq Scan,
what do I check?" — Selectivity (too many matching rows), implicit cast on the column, function applied
to the column, stale stats, or the index is on a different column order.
-- Good: bounded lookup
Index Scan using idx_users_email on users  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1)
  Index Cond: (email = 'priya@example.in')
Q161 · Index-Only Scan — When Achievable
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, AmEx · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is an index-only scan, and how do you write a query and design an index so the planner
can use one?
The 30-second answer: An index-only scan answers a query entirely from the index, never touching the
table heap — the index must contain every column the query references (covering), and the visibility map
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 168 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 169
(Postgres) or row visibility metadata must confirm the index entries are current. You design for it by
including the projected columns in the index, either as key columns or as INCLUDE columns.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the term — the planner can satisfy SELECT and WHERE
entirely from the B-tree leaves, skipping the heap fetch. 2. Two requirements: the index must cover all
referenced columns (in WHERE, SELECT, ORDER BY, GROUP BY), and the engine must know that index
entries reflect live row state. 3. Postgres uses a visibility map per heap page — if the page is all-visible,
the index-only scan skips it. After a heavy UPDATE, you may see "Heap Fetches" in the plan; running
VACUUM updates the visibility map and reduces them. 4. SQL Server calls this a covering index; the
INCLUDE clause adds payload columns without bloating the key. Same effect: no Key Lookup needed.
Edge cases to mention: - Index-only scan on a recently updated table can degrade to many heap
fetches until VACUUM runs. - In Postgres, only B-tree and a few other AMs support index-only scan; GIN
and BRIN typically do not. - Adding INCLUDE columns bloats the index — fine for narrow payloads,
costly for wide ones.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "index-only scan never touches disk" — it touches the index pages on
disk if they are not cached. - Do not assume MySQL has a separate "index-only scan" operator —
InnoDB shows it as Using index in EXPLAIN Extra.
Common follow-up: "My index covers the columns but the plan still shows heap fetches. Why?" — The
visibility map is not marking pages all-visible yet (recent writes). Run VACUUM or wait for autovacuum.
-- Covering index for a top-N dashboard query
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date_amt
  ON orders (customer_id, order_date DESC) INCLUDE (total_amount);
Q162 · Bitmap Index Scan and Bitmap Heap Scan
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In Postgres I see Bitmap Index Scan feeding a Bitmap Heap Scan. What is happening, and why
does the planner choose this over a regular Index Scan?
The 30-second answer: The planner builds an in-memory bitmap of matching tuple IDs from one or
more indexes, ORs or ANDs the bitmaps together, then visits the heap in physical block order. It is
chosen when many rows match (random index-then-heap would thrash IO) and especially when multiple
indexes can be combined for a single query.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 169 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 170
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through the two-phase shape. Phase one: Bitmap Index Scan
collects TIDs into a bitmap. Phase two: Bitmap Heap Scan visits heap pages in physical order, recheckng
the predicate if needed. 2. Explain the win: random IO becomes sequential-ish because the heap pages
are read in block order — much friendlier to spinning disk and to OS readahead. 3. Multi-index
combination: WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND city = 'Mumbai' can use idx_status and idx_city, build
two bitmaps, AND them, and visit the heap once. A regular Index Scan can only use one index per scan
node. 4. Vendor call-out: this operator pair is distinctive to Postgres. SQL Server has Index Intersection
and Index Union in similar spirit; Oracle has bitmap conversion. MySQL InnoDB does not do bitmap
heap scans.
Edge cases to mention: - The bitmap can be "lossy" — if it overflows work_mem, it stores page-level
granularity instead of tuple-level, and the heap scan must recheck the predicate. - For very few matching
rows, a plain Index Scan is cheaper because the bitmap setup overhead is wasted. - For very many
matching rows, a Seq Scan beats the bitmap because the heap is read end-to-end anyway.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "bitmap scan is always faster than index scan" — it is a middle-ground
operator. - Do not assume the bitmap is persisted — it is rebuilt every query.
Common follow-up: "How do I encourage or discourage a bitmap scan?" — Tune work_mem,
effective_io_concurrency, and random_page_cost. SET enable_bitmapscan = off temporarily to compare
plans.
Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=...)  Recheck Cond: status = 'PENDING' AND city = 'Mumbai'
  ->  BitmapAnd
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_status
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_city
Q163 · Nested-Loop Join — When the Planner Picks It
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Join Algorithms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When does the optimizer pick a nested-loop join, and when is that a bad idea?
The 30-second answer: Nested loop is chosen when the outer side is small (or LIMIT cuts it short) and
the inner side has a usable index on the join column — for each outer row, probe the inner index. It is a
disaster when the outer side blows up to millions of rows, because that becomes millions of index
probes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Describe the algorithm: for each row in the outer table, scan or probe
the inner table for matches. Total work is outer_rows times inner_lookup_cost. 2. The planner picks it
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 170 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 171
when outer_rows is small — say, under a few thousand — and there is a B-tree index on the inner join
column so each probe is logarithmic. 3. It is the default for OLTP queries: lookup-style joins on indexed
foreign keys with selective filters. EXPLAIN shows Nested Loop with an Index Scan on the inner side. 4.
The failure mode: planner underestimates outer_rows. You see Nested Loop with loops = 4 million in
EXPLAIN ANALYZE — your query runs for hours. Fix: refresh stats, rewrite to force hash, or add a
missing index.
Edge cases to mention: - A nested loop without an inner index is a Cartesian-style scan per outer row
— O(N x M). Almost always wrong on large tables. - Postgres can wrap the inner side in a Memoize node
(since 14) to cache repeated probes — helps when the outer has duplicates on the join key. - For
correlated subqueries, the planner often materializes the outer or uses a semi-join variant.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "nested loop is the slowest join" — for small outer sides with indexed
inner, it is the fastest. - Do not blame the join algorithm without checking cardinality estimates first.
Common follow-up: "My nested loop is doing 5 million inner probes — what is the fix?" — Most often,
missing or wrong index on the inner side, or stale stats making the outer look small. Re-ANALYZE and re-
check.
Nested Loop  (cost=...)  rows=10
  ->  Index Scan on customers c  (rows=10)  Index Cond: city = 'Pune'
  ->  Index Scan on orders o     (rows=1)   Index Cond: customer_id = c.id
Q164 · Hash Join — When the Planner Picks It
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman, JP Morgan India, Target · Topic: Join Algorithms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When is a hash join the right algorithm? What does the planner need to commit to one?
The 30-second answer: Hash join is chosen when both sides are large and there is no usable index on
the join column, or when the join is non-correlated (equi-join on hashable types). The planner builds a
hash table on the smaller side in memory, then streams the larger side through it. It needs an equality
predicate and enough work_mem to hold the build side.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Describe the two phases: build (hash the smaller side into a memory
hash table) and probe (stream the larger side, hash each row, look up matches). 2. Picked when: equi-
join on a hashable column, both inputs are large, and no good index makes nested loop viable. 3.
work_mem matters — if the build side does not fit, Postgres falls back to a batched hash join that spills
to disk (multiple temp files). EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Batches > 1 and "Disk Usage" lines. 4. SQL
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 171 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 172
Server uses Grace and Recursive variants for large builds; Oracle has hash join with one-pass and multi-
pass variants. MySQL added hash join in 8.0.18 and made it the default for unindexed joins in 8.0.20.
Edge cases to mention: - Hash join requires equality — range or inequality joins (a.x < b.y) cannot hash.
- A heavily skewed build side (one key with millions of rows) causes hash collisions and pathological
probe cost. - Building on the larger side by mistake (planner picked wrong) blows memory — usually a
stats problem.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "hash join is faster than nested loop" — depends on sizes. - Do not
assume hash join works for non-equi predicates.
Common follow-up: "My hash join spills to disk — how do I know and what do I do?" — EXPLAIN
ANALYZE shows Batches > 1 or Buckets x Batches; raise work_mem for the session or add an index
that enables a different algorithm.
Hash Join  (cost=...)  Hash Cond: o.customer_id = c.id
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o
  ->  Hash  Buckets: 16384  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1024kB
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c
Q165 · Merge Join — When the Planner Picks It
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs, Wells Fargo · Topic: Join
Algorithms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When does the optimizer pick a merge join? Is it common in OLTP?
The 30-second answer: Merge join requires both inputs sorted on the join key — it is chosen when both
sides are already sorted (often via a B-tree index) or when one side is sorted and the other is cheap to
sort. It is rare in OLTP but common in analytics or when joining two large pre-indexed tables.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Describe the algorithm: two pointers, one on each sorted input,
advance together — like the merge step of mergesort. 2. The win: linear in the size of both inputs, no
hash table, no random IO. The cost is the sort, which is why the planner picks it only when sort is cheap
or unnecessary. 3. When already sorted: range scans on an index, or an ORDER BY that produces sorted
output, can feed directly into the merge. 4. SQL Server uses Merge Join for ordered indexed sources;
Oracle's Sort Merge Join is the same family. Postgres calls it Merge Join. MySQL did not have one
classically; recent versions do under specific conditions.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 172 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 173
Edge cases to mention: - If the planner has to sort one side, it adds an explicit Sort node above the
input — visible in EXPLAIN. - Merge join is sensitive to duplicates on the join key — heavy duplicates can
cause rewind logic. - For very small inputs, the constant overhead of merge loses to nested loop.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "merge join is the best for big joins" — hash join wins more often in
practice. - Do not assume merge join automatically uses indexes — it uses sortedness, which an index
can provide.
Common follow-up: "Why does merge join sometimes appear without a Sort node?" — Because the
input is already sorted by an Index Scan on the join key.
Merge Join  (cost=...)  Merge Cond: a.id = b.account_id
  ->  Index Scan using accounts_pkey on accounts a
  ->  Index Scan using idx_txn_account on transactions b
Q166 · Statistics and Why Stale Stats Break Plans
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What are statistics in a query optimizer, and why does the same query suddenly run 100x slower
one morning?
The 30-second answer: Statistics are sampled summaries of column data — row counts, distinct
values, most common values, histograms — that the optimizer uses to estimate cardinality at each step.
When stats are stale (last sampled days ago, after a bulk insert or delete), estimates diverge from reality
and the planner picks a bad plan. The fix is to ANALYZE the table.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define statistics: pg_statistic in Postgres, sys.stats in SQL Server,
all_tab_col_statistics in Oracle. Stored per column, sometimes per index. 2. Common stats: n_distinct,
null_frac, most_common_values, histogram. The planner uses these to estimate the row count of every
filter and join. 3. Stale stats scenario: an overnight bulk load multiplies the table 10x but autovacuum has
not yet sampled it. The planner thinks 100k rows, plans nested loop, hits 1 million rows, dies. 4. Fix: run
ANALYZE (Postgres), UPDATE STATISTICS (SQL Server), DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS
(Oracle). Tune autovacuum thresholds or schedule manual ANALYZE after bulk loads.
Edge cases to mention: - default_statistics_target in Postgres controls histogram resolution — raise
from 100 to 1000 for columns with skewed distributions. - Stats sample only a small fraction of rows by
default — extremely skewed columns may need higher targets or extended statistics. - After a
partitioning change or a large UPDATE that rewrites the table, manual ANALYZE is often needed even
with autovacuum on.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 173 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 174
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the database always knows the row counts" — it estimates from
samples. - Do not blame the query when the symptom is sudden — check stats freshness first.
Common follow-up: "How often should I run ANALYZE on a high-write table?" — Tune
autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor lower (default 0.1 = 10 percent change); or run nightly explicit
ANALYZE during quiet hours.
ANALYZE VERBOSE orders;
-- Or, in production after a bulk load:
ANALYZE orders (customer_id, order_date, status);
Q167 · Extended Statistics for Column Correlations
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
The planner thinks WHERE city = 'Mumbai' AND state = 'Maharashtra' will match 1000 rows but
the actual is 1 million. Why, and how do you fix it?
The 30-second answer: By default, the planner assumes column independence — selectivity of A AND
B equals selectivity(A) times selectivity(B). When columns are correlated (city implies state), this
underestimates by orders of magnitude. In Postgres, CREATE STATISTICS on the column group teaches
the planner about the dependency.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the independence assumption — it is mathematically wrong
whenever columns are functionally or partially correlated. 2. Real example: city = 'Mumbai' selects about
0.1 percent of rows; state = 'Maharashtra' selects about 9 percent; the planner multiplies and predicts
0.009 percent, but city already implies state, so the real selectivity is 0.1 percent. 3. Fix in Postgres:
CREATE STATISTICS stat_city_state (dependencies, ndistinct) ON city, state FROM orders; then
ANALYZE. The planner now models the correlation. 4. SQL Server has multi-column statistics (auto-
created with composite indexes, manually with CREATE STATISTICS); Oracle has Extended Statistics
with DBMS_STATS.CREATE_EXTENDED_STATS.
Edge cases to mention: - Three kinds of dependency stats in Postgres: ndistinct (combined distinct
values), dependencies (functional dependency strength), mcv (most common combinations). - Extended
stats are not free — they add to ANALYZE time and storage. - They do not help if the correlation is
conditional on a third column — still a known optimizer limitation.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "stats are stats, there is nothing more to add" — extended stats are a
real and underused feature. - Do not assume composite indexes give the optimizer correlation
knowledge in every engine — Postgres requires explicit CREATE STATISTICS for predicate correlation.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 174 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 175
Common follow-up: "How do I see what extended statistics exist?" — \d+ table_name in psql
shows statistics objects; query pg_statistic_ext for details.
CREATE STATISTICS stat_orders_city_state (dependencies)
  ON city, state FROM orders;
ANALYZE orders;
Q168 · MySQL 8 Histograms
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What are histograms in MySQL 8, and when does the optimizer actually use them?
The 30-second answer: MySQL 8 added column histograms (singleton or equi-height) that the optimizer
uses to estimate selectivity on non-indexed columns. They are most useful for skewed distributions
where the default uniformity assumption is wrong — for example, a status column that is 95 percent
COMPLETED.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Pre-MySQL-8, the optimizer relied on index statistics and uniformity
assumptions for non-indexed columns. Heavily skewed columns gave bad row estimates. 2. ANALYZE
TABLE orders UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON status, payment_method WITH 100 BUCKETS builds
histograms — singleton if distinct values <= buckets, equi-height otherwise. 3. The optimizer uses them
for range, equality and IN predicates on the column to estimate row counts. Visible in EXPLAIN
FORMAT=JSON in the "rows_examined_per_scan" and cost output. 4. Histograms are static — they do
not auto-refresh after DML. Re-run ANALYZE TABLE ... UPDATE HISTOGRAM after large data changes.
Edge cases to mention: - Histograms apply per column, not multi-column — for correlated predicates,
you still need an index or rewrite. - Adding an index on a column overrides the histogram in most planner
decisions because index statistics are richer. - They are stored in information_schema.column_statistics
— easy to inspect.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "histograms automatically refresh" — they do not. - Do not confuse
MySQL histograms with Postgres histograms (built into pg_statistic) — same concept, different lifecycle.
Common follow-up: "Do histograms help with skewed timestamp columns?" — Yes, especially equi-
height histograms on order_date — they let the optimizer see that the last 7 days holds 80 percent of
rows.

Q169 · Cardinality Estimation — What Goes Wrong
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is cardinality estimation, and what are the top three reasons it goes wrong in production?
The 30-second answer: Cardinality estimation is the optimizer's guess of how many rows each operator
will emit. The top three failure modes are stale statistics, correlated predicates the planner assumes
independent, and complex expressions (function calls, IN with subqueries, OR with skew) where the
estimator falls back to defaults like 10 percent or 0.5 percent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define cardinality — number of rows. Every node in a plan has an
estimate and (with EXPLAIN ANALYZE) an actual. The ratio is the most diagnostic single number in plan
reading. 2. Failure mode one: stale stats — covered in Q10. The planner is using yesterday's numbers. 3.
Failure mode two: correlated predicates — covered in Q11. Independence assumption multiplies
selectivities incorrectly. 4. Failure mode three: opaque expressions — WHERE my_udf(x) = 5 cannot be
estimated, planner uses a magic default; WHERE x IN (SELECT ...) is estimated from the subquery
output; complex OR with overlapping ranges defaults to a rough guess.
Edge cases to mention: - Skew on a single value (90 percent of orders have status = 'COMPLETED') —
without histograms, the planner uses average selectivity and underestimates "COMPLETED" or
overestimates "REFUNDED". - Filter on a computed column without an expression index — planner has
no stats for the expression. - Cross-database queries (foreign tables, dblink) — stats are usually
unavailable.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the planner always gets it right" — it is a probabilistic guess based on
samples. - Do not blame the planner without checking estimated vs actual rows first.
Common follow-up: "How do I tell the planner about a UDF's selectivity?" — In Postgres, mark it
IMMUTABLE and add a CREATE STATISTICS or use a generated stored column. In Oracle, use the
ASSOCIATE STATISTICS clause.

Q170 · Plan Regression — Same Query, New Plan
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A report that ran in 2 seconds yesterday now takes 4 minutes. The query has not changed. Walk
me through your diagnosis.
The 30-second answer: The plan changed — the SQL is identical but the optimizer is now picking a
different plan. Compare today's EXPLAIN to a known-good baseline; the usual culprits are stale or freshly
updated statistics flipping a join order, autovacuum just ran, a parameter sniffing event, or a small data
shift crossing a planner threshold.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. First, confirm it is a plan change, not a load issue. Capture EXPLAIN
today; compare to a saved plan from yesterday if you have one, or check shared cache / Query Store. 2.
Common triggers: ANALYZE just ran with a fresh sample that changed n_distinct; a new index was
added on another query and the planner picked it inappropriately here; data growth crossed an index-vs-
seqscan tipping point. 3. Verify with actual versus estimated row counts. Big mismatch on a node that
used to be tight = stats drift. 4. Mitigation: refresh stats with a higher target, add or hint the index, force
the prior plan via Query Store baseline (SQL Server), SQL Plan Baseline (Oracle), or pg_hint_plan
(Postgres).
Edge cases to mention: - Parameter sniffing in SQL Server can cause the first-execution plan to be
cached and reused for inputs it does not suit — fix with OPTION (RECOMPILE) or OPTIMIZE FOR. -
Postgres does not have per-plan baselines natively; pg_hint_plan or pg_plan_filter are extensions. -
Cron-driven nightly ANALYZE can be the unexpected cause when stats refresh changes one estimate.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the query must have changed" without checking — confirm SQL text
identity first. - Do not blame the database without comparing plans side by side.
Common follow-up: "How do you prevent this in the first place?" — Capture plans regularly
(auto_explain in Postgres, Query Store in SQL Server, AWR in Oracle); set alerts on duration regressions
per query hash.

SET auto_explain.log_min_duration = '500ms';

Q171 · Pinned Plans and Forced Plans
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your team wants to pin the plan for a critical reporting query so it never regresses. How would
you do it in SQL Server, Oracle, and Postgres?
The 30-second answer: SQL Server: Query Store forced plans — pick the known-good plan in Query
Store and force it for the query_hash. Oracle: SQL Plan Baselines
(DBMS_SPM.LOAD_PLANS_FROM_CURSOR_CACHE) — captures and pins the accepted plan.
Postgres has no native equivalent; teams use pg_hint_plan to embed hints, or maintain SQL with explicit
join order and index hints via comments the extension reads.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the use case — a high-stakes report or batch job where
occasional regression is unacceptable, more important than possible future improvements. 2. SQL
Server: enable Query Store, identify the plan by plan_id in sys.query_store_plan, call
sys.sp_query_store_force_plan. Plan is honored until you unforce. 3. Oracle: capture cursor with
DBMS_SPM.LOAD_PLANS_FROM_CURSOR_CACHE to create an accepted baseline. Optimizer will
only use baseline plans for that SQL text. 4. Postgres: install pg_hint_plan, add /+ HashJoin(a b)
IndexScan(orders idx_orders_date) / comment hints. Native plan stability is not provided.
Edge cases to mention: - Pinned plans go stale — a 1-billion-row table growth makes the forced nested
loop disastrous. Schedule periodic review. - Forcing a plan requires the underlying objects (indexes) to
still exist; dropping them invalidates the plan. - Avoid pinning as a substitute for fixing stats — it hides
the root cause.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres has native plan baselines" — it does not. - Do not pin every
query "just in case" — you lose the optimizer's improvements forever.
Common follow-up: "How do you know when to unpin?" — Periodic review: compare the pinned plan's
actual runtime against the optimizer's current best on a representative sample of inputs.
-- SQL Server: force a known-good plan in Query Store
EXEC sys.sp_query_store_force_plan @query_id = 1234, @plan_id = 5678;

Q172 · Rewrite Subquery to JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Rewrites
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Rewrite this subquery as a JOIN: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT
customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 10000).
The 30-second answer: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id =
o.customer_id WHERE o.total > 10000. The DISTINCT is needed because a customer with multiple
matching orders would otherwise appear several times. Modern optimizers usually generate identical
plans for both forms, but the JOIN version is sometimes clearer and lets you pull in columns from orders
if needed.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Identify the semantic: IN with subquery is a semi-join — one output
row per matching left row, regardless of how many right matches. 2. The JOIN equivalent multiplies rows
when the right side has duplicates — DISTINCT or GROUP BY is required to restore semi-join semantics.
3. Talk about when the rewrite is worth it: when you also want columns from orders, JOIN avoids a
second query; otherwise, EXISTS is the cleanest form because it does not need DISTINCT. 4. Be ready
for "Which plan does Postgres pick?" — usually a Hash Semi Join for both IN and EXISTS, identical plan.
Edge cases to mention: - DISTINCT in a JOIN rewrite is a real cost when the join is wide — EXISTS
avoids that. - If the subquery is uncorrelated and returns a small static list, the planner may evaluate it
once and treat it as a constant set. - The rewrite changes plan only in older optimizers (MySQL pre-5.6,
ancient SQL Server).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "JOIN is always faster than IN" — modern optimizers rewrite them to the
same shape. - Do not omit DISTINCT — duplicate rows are a real bug.
Common follow-up: "When would EXISTS beat both?" — When you only need a boolean check and the
right side has wide rows or many duplicates — EXISTS short-circuits and avoids deduplication.
SELECT DISTINCT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.total > 10000;
Q173 · NOT IN to NOT EXISTS (NULL Safety)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Rewrites
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 179 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 180
Why is NOT IN dangerous, and how does rewriting to NOT EXISTS fix it?
The 30-second answer: NOT IN against a subquery returns the empty set if the subquery yields even
one NULL — because x != NULL is UNKNOWN, the whole expression collapses to UNKNOWN, which
filters out the row. NOT EXISTS does not have this problem because it tests for existence per outer row,
treating NULLs as non-matches naturally.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through the three-valued logic: WHERE id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)
becomes id != 1 AND id != 2 AND id != NULL — the last predicate is UNKNOWN — the conjunction is
UNKNOWN — the row is excluded. 2. NOT EXISTS rewrite: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM
orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id). For each outer row, the subquery checks for a match; NULL on
either side simply does not match, so the row is correctly returned. 3. Planner behaviour: modern
optimizers transform NOT EXISTS into an anti-semi-join — efficient and correct. 4. Also mention LEFT
JOIN ... WHERE right_pk IS NULL as a third correct anti-join form, semantically equivalent to NOT
EXISTS.
Edge cases to mention: - If the column is declared NOT NULL, NOT IN is safe — but schemas evolve,
and a NOT NULL column today may become nullable tomorrow. - NOT IN with a hard-coded list (NOT IN
(1, 2, 3)) is safe because you control the list. - NULL semantics are SQL standard, not a quirk — every
compliant database behaves this way.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are interchangeable" — they are not, and this
is a classic interview trap. - Do not blame the database for "broken" NOT IN behaviour — it is standard
SQL.
Common follow-up: "How would you write the safest version once and for all?" — NOT EXISTS, every
time. It is correct, fast, and reads cleanly.
-- Unsafe: NULL in orders.customer_id makes this return zero rows
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
-- Safe: NOT EXISTS handles NULLs correctly
SELECT * FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
Q174 · OR to UNION ALL
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Walmart Labs, Cred · Topic: Rewrites
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 180 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 181
When does rewriting OR conditions as UNION ALL make a query faster?
The 30-second answer: When each side of the OR can independently use a different index, but the
combined OR predicate forces the planner into a sequential scan or a bitmap-OR scan that is
suboptimal. Splitting into two SELECTs joined by UNION ALL lets each side use its own index —
typically twice the index scans, half the runtime, much smaller IO.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose the symptom: WHERE phone = '9876543210' OR email =
'a@b.com' on a users table with separate indexes on each column. The planner may Seq Scan or do a
BitmapOr; both can be slow. 2. Rewrite: SELECT ... WHERE phone = '9876543210' UNION ALL
SELECT ... WHERE email = 'a@b.com' AND phone <> '9876543210'. Each branch uses its own index;
the AND in the second branch prevents duplicates when a row matches both. 3. If duplicates are
impossible or acceptable, UNION ALL (no dedup) is the faster choice; UNION dedups via a sort or hash.
4. Postgres often handles this via BitmapOr automatically — check the plan before rewriting.
Edge cases to mention: - UNION ALL preserves duplicates; UNION removes them — pick deliberately.
- The dedup branch (AND phone <> ...) is necessary only when the same row could match both — for
distinct columns on the same key, it is often skippable. - For three or more OR branches, the rewrite gets
verbose; consider a CTE or a temp table.
What NOT to say: - Do not blindly rewrite every OR as UNION — the planner handles many ORs well. -
Do not use UNION (with dedup) when UNION ALL would do — the sort/hash is wasted work.
Common follow-up: "What does Postgres do natively for this?" — BitmapOr: builds bitmaps for each
index, ORs them, then Bitmap Heap Scan. Often as fast as the manual UNION ALL.
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210'
UNION ALL
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = 'a@b.com' AND phone <> '9876543210';
Q175 · Function on Column — The Index Killer
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Rewrites
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why is WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' slow even with an index on email? How do you fix it?
The 30-second answer: Wrapping the column in LOWER() means the predicate is no longer on email; it
is on LOWER(email). The B-tree index on email cannot be used because the values are stored in their
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 181 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 182
original case. Two fixes: create an expression index on LOWER(email), or store emails in a normalized
lower-case column.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the principle: an index stores raw column values. A predicate
on f(column) is not a predicate the index can answer unless an index exists on f(column). 2. The fix in
Postgres: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users (LOWER(email)). The planner uses it for
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com'. 3. Vendor call-out: Postgres and Oracle support expression indexes
directly; SQL Server uses computed columns marked PERSISTED with an index on the computed
column; MySQL 8 supports functional indexes on expressions. 4. Cleaner long-term: store a normalized
column (email_lower) updated by trigger or generated column, and index that. Cheaper at query time and
clearer in joins.
Edge cases to mention: - Expression indexes require the expression to be IMMUTABLE — functions
that depend on session settings (timezone, locale) cannot be indexed. - Updating a row triggers
reindexing of the expression — slight write overhead. - Citext (case-insensitive text) in Postgres avoids
the LOWER wrap entirely.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the database should be smart enough to use the index anyway" — it
cannot, by design. - Do not skip the IMMUTABLE check — non-immutable expressions fail to index.
Common follow-up: "Same problem with DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at) — what do you do?" — Same
answer: expression index on DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at), or rewrite as created_at >= date AND
created_at < date + 1 day so the raw column index works.
-- Fix with expression index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users (LOWER(email));
-- Or rewrite to use a date range:
WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-26' AND created_at < '2026-05-27';
Q176 · Implicit Cast — The Silent Index Killer
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic:
Rewrites
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why does WHERE customer_id = '4827' (with quotes) sometimes do a sequential scan even
when customer_id is indexed?
The 30-second answer: If customer_id is an integer column and you pass a string, the database
implicitly casts one side to match the other. The cast may happen on the column side, which (like a
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 182 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 183
function) defeats the index. Pass the value with the correct type — customer_id = 4827 — and the
index is usable.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through the cast resolution. Different engines have different
rules; in some, the column gets cast to the parameter's type, turning customer_id into CAST(customer_id
AS varchar), which no integer B-tree can satisfy. 2. Classic ORM bug: parameter binding sends the value
as a string when the column is bigint; the planner casts the column. 3. Diagnose with EXPLAIN — look
for an Index Cond with a CAST around the column, or Seq Scan where you expected Index Scan. 4. Fix
at three layers: cast the parameter explicitly (CAST(? AS BIGINT)), fix the ORM type mapping, or change
the column type (rarely the right answer).
Edge cases to mention: - VARCHAR vs CHAR — implicit padding can break equality. - Numeric
precision mismatches (NUMERIC(10,2) vs DOUBLE) — cast to the higher type. - Date vs timestamp —
equality on a timestamp column with a date value can cast to timestamp at midnight, which still uses
index, but range comparisons can confuse the planner.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "implicit casts are harmless" — they are a top-three index-killer in
production code. - Do not blame the database for not magically guessing your intent.
Common follow-up: "Where do you see this most in real apps?" — Java apps passing String
parameters to a BIGINT id column; PHP apps with all-string variables. Always type your parameters
explicitly.
-- Index killed by implicit cast
WHERE customer_id = '4827'        -- column may be cast to text
-- Correct
WHERE customer_id = 4827          -- planner uses idx_customer_id
Q177 · Parameter Sniffing in SQL Server
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: AmEx, Wells Fargo, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is parameter sniffing in SQL Server, and how does it cause a query to be fast for some
inputs and terrible for others?
The 30-second answer: On first execution of a parameterised query, SQL Server uses the actual
parameter value to estimate cardinality and caches the resulting plan. If that first value was atypical —
say, a customer with 5 orders — the plan optimised for it (nested loop with bookmark lookup) is then
reused for a customer with 5 million orders, where a different plan would be far better.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 183 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 184
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain plan caching: SQL Server stores compiled plans keyed by
SQL text. Parameterised queries get one plan per text, optimised for the parameter values seen during
compilation. 2. The sniffing problem: the first set of parameter values "wins" — even if they are
unrepresentative — and every subsequent execution uses that plan. 3. Mitigations: OPTION
(RECOMPILE) recompiles every execution (CPU cost but correct plan); OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@p =
value)) hints a specific representative value; OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN) uses average density.
4. Newer: Query Store with multiple plans per query and automatic plan correction (SQL Server 2017+)
can detect regressions and revert.
Edge cases to mention: - Same problem exists in Oracle as "bind variable peeking" — solved by
adaptive cursor sharing. - Postgres has a similar effect with prepared statements: after five executions, it
switches from custom plan to generic plan; you can override with plan_cache_mode. - ORM-generated
queries are especially vulnerable because the first call wins for the lifetime of the connection pool entry.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "parameter sniffing is always bad" — it is usually correct; only the edge
case is bad. - Do not blanket-add OPTION (RECOMPILE) — it taxes CPU on hot queries.
Common follow-up: "How do you diagnose parameter sniffing?" — Look for the same query_hash in
Query Store with wildly varying durations across plan executions; compare cached_plan parameters with
actual workload distribution.
-- Force recompile for a specific call
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = @cust_id OPTION (RECOMPILE);
Q178 · Prepared Statements vs Ad-Hoc and Plan Caching
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, PhonePe · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between prepared statements and ad-hoc queries from the planner's point
of view? Why might prepared statements be slower for some queries?
The 30-second answer: Prepared statements parse and plan once, then execute many times with
different parameter values — saves CPU on planning. The risk is that the cached plan is generic (no
parameter values to use for cardinality) and may be worse than an ad-hoc plan that sees the actual
values. Postgres handles this with a 5-execution heuristic that switches between custom and generic
plans.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Two costs: parse-and-plan time versus execution time. Hot OLTP
queries amortize prepare cost; one-shot reports do not benefit. 2. Plan generality: with PREPARE foo(int)
AS SELECT ..., the planner does not know the value of $1 during planning — it uses average selectivity,
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 184 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 185
often worse than seeing the literal. 3. Postgres specifically: tracks five executions to decide if custom
plans (re-plan with each value) beat the generic plan; switches automatically. You can force with
plan_cache_mode = 'force_custom_plan' or 'force_generic_plan'. 4. Server-side prepared statements are
the default in JDBC, psycopg2 server-side cursors, and SQL Server sp_executesql — easy to forget the
optimizer caveats.
Edge cases to mention: - Massive variation in parameter selectivity (an IN list of size 1 vs 10000)
suggests custom plans. - Connection pools with prepared statement caches reuse across customers —
beware of leaking plans. - pgbouncer in transaction pooling mode breaks server-side prepared
statements unless you use protocol-level support carefully.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "prepared statements are always faster" — for one-shot queries, the
prepare overhead is wasted. - Do not assume the cached plan is the optimal plan — it may be the
average plan, not the best for any specific input.
Common follow-up: "How do you know your app is using server-side prepared statements?" — Check
the driver config; in Postgres, pg_stat_statements shows queries with $1 instead of literal values when
prepared.
PREPARE stmt(int) AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1;
EXECUTE stmt(4827);
-- Plan is decided after 5 executions in Postgres default
Q179 · Plan Cache Pollution
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is plan cache pollution, and how does an app accidentally cause it?
The 30-second answer: Plan cache pollution is when the cache fills with thousands of near-identical
plans because the application emits SQL text that differs slightly per call — typically by inlining literals
instead of using parameters. Each variant gets its own cache entry; useful plans get evicted; planning
CPU spikes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Cache keyed by exact SQL text in most engines. SELECT * FROM
orders WHERE id = 1 and SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 2 are two cache entries. 2. The cure is
parameterisation: WHERE id = ? — one cache entry for every customer id. 3. SQL Server has "forced
parameterisation" and "optimize for ad hoc workloads" to mitigate by caching only plan stubs for one-
shot SQL. 4. Postgres has pg_stat_statements that normalizes literals for monitoring, but the planner still
re-plans per text. Use server-side prepared statements via your driver.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 185 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 186
Edge cases to mention: - IN lists of varying size pollute (IN (1,2,3) vs IN (1,2,3,4)) — solve with arrays (=
ANY($1)) or temp tables. - Dynamic SQL stitched in app code is a frequent culprit. - Some ORMs
deliberately inline literals for "constants" — check the generated SQL.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the cache is unlimited" — it is bounded; eviction hurts hot queries. - Do
not blame the database; it is almost always the app.
Common follow-up: "How do you measure cache hit rate?" — In Postgres, count pg_stat_statements
rows; in SQL Server, sys.dm_exec_cached_plans and sys.dm_exec_query_stats; in Oracle,
V$LIBRARYCACHE.
-- Pollutes: each value is a separate cache entry
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 1;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 2;
-- Cache-friendly: one entry, reused
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1;
Q180 · Parallel Query
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan India, AmEx · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When does Postgres or SQL Server parallelize a query, and what makes a function "parallel
safe"?
The 30-second answer: The planner parallelises when the table is large enough (parallel_setup_cost
amortizes), the query touches enough data to benefit, and every operator and function in the plan is
parallel-safe. A parallel-safe function has no side effects, does not depend on session state, and returns
the same answer regardless of which worker executes it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres parallel triggers: max_parallel_workers_per_gather > 0,
min_parallel_table_scan_size and min_parallel_index_scan_size cleared, and a parallel-safe plan. 2.
EXPLAIN shows Gather (or Gather Merge), with parallel-aware nodes underneath (Parallel Seq Scan,
Parallel Hash Join). 3. Functions and operators are categorized: PARALLEL SAFE (default for built-ins like
+ and length), PARALLEL RESTRICTED (cannot be in parallel worker but can be in the leader),
PARALLEL UNSAFE (forces serial). User-defined functions default to UNSAFE — mark them explicitly. 4.
SQL Server has Cost Threshold for Parallelism (default 5, often raised to 50+ in OLTP) and Max Degree of
Parallelism (MAXDOP). Oracle uses PARALLEL hints and the parallel query slave pool.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 186 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 187
Edge cases to mention: - Locks held across workers — some operations (CREATE INDEX
CONCURRENTLY) cannot parallelise. - Parallel hash join scales well but bumps work_mem usage per
worker. - For OLTP, parallel query is usually disabled or limited — it steals CPU from other connections.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "more parallelism is always faster" — overhead and synchronization cost
can dominate for short queries. - Do not mark all UDFs PARALLEL SAFE without auditing for side effects.
Common follow-up: "What is parallel-restricted versus parallel-unsafe?" — Restricted runs only in the
leader; unsafe disables parallelism entirely for the query.
CREATE FUNCTION clean_phone(text) RETURNS text
  LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE
AS $$ BEGIN RETURN regexp_replace($1, '\D', '', 'g'); END $$;
Q181 · Materialized Views
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Meesho · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When is a materialized view worth the operational cost, and what refresh patterns do you use?
The 30-second answer: Worth it when the underlying query is expensive (multi-table aggregation, joins
on large tables), is read far more often than the underlying data changes, and freshness up to a known
lag is acceptable. Refresh patterns: full refresh on a schedule (cron, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW),
incremental refresh (Oracle fast refresh, manual delta merge), or trigger-driven (CDC or change tables
feeding the view).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Decision criteria: query cost > refresh cost, read-to-write ratio favors
caching, staleness window is acceptable to the business. 2. Postgres: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW;
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (locks readers) or REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY
(requires unique index, slower but non-blocking). 3. Oracle has incremental refresh via materialized view
logs that record deltas; SQL Server has indexed views with strict requirements (SCHEMABINDING,
deterministic functions). 4. Operational: track refresh duration and lag; alert if lag exceeds SLA; for very
large views, partition the underlying data and refresh only changed partitions.
Edge cases to mention: - REFRESH CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index on the view, and uses
much more IO than the non-concurrent version. - Postgres materialized views are not auto-refreshed —
you must schedule it. - For dashboards that need near-real-time data, a materialized view may not be the
right tool — consider rollup tables with incremental updates.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 187 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 188
What NOT to say: - Do not say "materialized views are just cached queries" — they are persistent
storage with their own indexes. - Do not enable concurrent refresh without considering the IO cost.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle stale results when a user is viewing the dashboard during a
refresh?" — CONCURRENTLY refresh ensures readers always see a consistent (possibly slightly stale)
view; non-concurrent locks readers.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_top_customers AS
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS lifetime_value
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
  GROUP BY customer_id;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON mv_top_customers (customer_id);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_top_customers;
Q182 · Query Hints — When Justified, When Smelly
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When is it justified to use a query hint, and when is it a code smell?
The 30-second answer: Justified when you have measured the optimizer choosing badly for a stable
workload despite correct stats, and you need a predictable plan now — typically for high-stakes batch
jobs. Smelly when used as a default tool, when stats have not been refreshed, or when the workload is
volatile and a fixed plan will eventually be wrong.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Hint vocabulary: Oracle has the richest set (/+ INDEX(t idx)
USE_HASH(a b) /); SQL Server has OPTION clauses (OPTION (HASH JOIN, LOOP JOIN)); MySQL has /+
HASH_JOIN / and ignore/use index; Postgres has none natively (use pg_hint_plan extension). 2.
Justification: regulator-mandated nightly report cannot regress; a forced join order or join method gives
predictability the optimizer cannot guarantee. 3. Smell: every other developer adds /+ INDEX / because
someone once needed it. Hints freeze the plan against future schema changes, data growth, and
optimizer improvements. 4. Always document why a hint exists. Add a comment with the date, the plan it
replaced, and the trigger for re-evaluation.
Edge cases to mention: - A hint can be silently invalid (index dropped) and the planner ignores it — no
error in some engines, just a regression. - Some hints are advisory; the optimizer can override them in
newer versions. - Forcing a join order with Oracle's LEADING hint can be brittle to query rewrites.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres has hints" without the extension caveat — it does not natively.
- Do not paste hints into queries to "speed them up" without diagnosing.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 188 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 189
Common follow-up: "What is the modern alternative to query hints?" — SQL Server Query Store forced
plans, Oracle SQL Plan Baselines, well-targeted CREATE STATISTICS. They are auditable and survive
code reviews.
-- Oracle: hint a specific index
SELECT /*+ INDEX(orders idx_orders_cust_date) */
  customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
Q183 · EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS — IO vs Compute
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In Postgres, what does EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) tell you that EXPLAIN ANALYZE alone
does not?
The 30-second answer: BUFFERS shows per-node buffer activity — shared hit (in cache), shared read
(from disk), local and temp buffer usage. It tells you whether a slow query is IO-bound (lots of shared
reads) or CPU-bound (lots of hits but still slow). It also reveals when work_mem spills cause temp file IO.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Without BUFFERS, you know wall-clock time per node; with
BUFFERS, you know the source of that time. 2. shared hit = cache hit, fast. shared read = disk read, slow
on cold cache. temp written/read = sort or hash spill — raise work_mem. 3. A node with 10ms actual
time and 100k shared hits is CPU-bound (lots of in-memory work); a node with 200ms and 5000 shared
reads is IO-bound. 4. Use this to decide whether to add indexes (reduce shared reads), raise work_mem
(eliminate temp), or restructure the query (reduce CPU).
Edge cases to mention: - track_io_timing must be enabled to see read/write times; otherwise you only
get counts. - Buffer counts include both heap and index pages; the breakdown is not separated in the
text plan. - Cold versus hot runs differ dramatically — run the query twice and look at the second run for
a steady-state picture.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "BUFFERS slows the query down" — it adds negligible overhead. - Do
not ignore temp buffer numbers; spilling is a top cause of slow analytics queries.
Common follow-up: "How do you reduce shared reads?" — Better indexes (so fewer pages are
scanned), partitioning (so unrelated partitions are skipped), or larger shared_buffers if the working set fits.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 189 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 190
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Buffers: shared hit=12345 read=678 written=0
Q184 · work_mem and Sort Spills
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan India, AmEx · Topic: Optimizer
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is work_mem in Postgres or sort_buffer_size in MySQL, and what happens when a sort
exceeds it?
The 30-second answer: work_mem is the per-operation memory budget for sorts, hash tables, and
other internal buffers. When a sort or hash exceeds it, Postgres switches to an external (on-disk) merge
sort or batched hash join — spilling to temp files. Spill IO can multiply query time tenfold or more.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define: work_mem is per-sort, per-hash, per-query — not per-
connection. A query with 5 sorts and 3 hashes can use 8 * work_mem. 2. Detect a spill: EXPLAIN
ANALYZE shows "Sort Method: external merge" or "Batches: 16" instead of "Batches: 1". With
BUFFERS, you see temp written/read. 3. Fix options: raise work_mem at the session level (SET
work_mem = '256MB') for the slow query, add an index that avoids the sort, or rewrite to reduce the data
being sorted. 4. Global work_mem is risky — each connection can use it many times; a high default plus
200 connections can OOM the host.
Edge cases to mention: - Parallel workers each get their own work_mem allocation — multiply by
max_parallel_workers_per_gather. - Some operations (DISTINCT, GROUP BY, hash aggregate) use
work_mem and spill similarly. - Spill files live in pg_default_temp_tablespace by default — moving temp
to a fast SSD can soften the pain.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "work_mem is the total memory for the query" — it is per-operation. - Do
not raise work_mem globally without considering concurrency.
Common follow-up: "When would you raise work_mem at the session level instead of globally?" — For a
one-off batch job that legitimately needs 1GB; you set it inside the transaction so other connections are
unaffected.
SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB';
SELECT customer_id, ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY order_date)
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 218MB  (no spill)

Q185 · Lateral Subquery for Top-N-Per-Group
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Walmart Labs · Topic: Rewrites
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how to get the three most recent orders per customer efficiently using LATERAL.
The 30-second answer: LATERAL lets a subquery reference columns from earlier items in the FROM list.
For top-N-per-group, you iterate over customers and laterally take the top N orders per customer — with
an index on (customer_id, order_date DESC), each lateral subquery is a cheap index scan limited to 3
rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Without LATERAL, the standard solution is ROW_NUMBER() OVER
(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) — works but sorts the entire orders table. 2.
With LATERAL and an index on (customer_id, order_date DESC), the planner does a Nested Loop: outer
customers, inner index scan with LIMIT 3 — orders of magnitude faster when there are many customers
and many orders. 3. Syntax: SELECT c.id, o.order_id, o.order_date FROM customers c, LATERAL
(SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id ORDER BY order_date DESC
LIMIT 3) o. 4. SQL Server uses CROSS APPLY (and OUTER APPLY) for the same pattern. Oracle has
LATERAL. MySQL 8.0.14+ supports LATERAL.
Edge cases to mention: - The index on (customer_id, order_date DESC) is the load-bearing part —
without it, LATERAL is no better than ROW_NUMBER. - LATERAL excludes customers with zero orders;
LEFT JOIN LATERAL keeps them. - For top-1-per-group, DISTINCT ON (Postgres) is even cleaner.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "window functions are always best for top-N" — for top-N-per-group on
indexed columns, LATERAL is often dramatically faster. - Do not omit the supporting index — the rewrite
alone does not save you.
Common follow-up: "What plan would you expect to see?" — Nested Loop with outer Seq Scan on
customers and inner Index Scan + Limit on orders.
SELECT c.id, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM customers c,
LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount
  FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 3
) o;

Q186 · MAX with Rare Filter — Index-Only Scan Opportunity
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Query Plans
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
SELECT MAX(amount) FROM payments WHERE status = 'FAILED' is slow on a 500-million-row
table. What is the right index and rewrite?
The 30-second answer: Build a partial index on (amount DESC) WHERE status = 'FAILED' — small, hot,
and a Bitmap Index Scan or Index Scan plus Limit 1 reads only the rarely-failing rows. Alternatively,
ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1 with the same index gives the planner a direct lookup. Pair with index-
only scan if no other columns are needed.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Anti-pattern: full table scan filtering for FAILED rows, then computing
MAX. On 500M rows, this is minutes even with high parallelism. 2. The right index: a partial index that
holds only the failed rows, sorted by amount. CREATE INDEX idx_payments_failed_amt ON payments
(amount DESC) WHERE status = 'FAILED'. The index is tiny (failed rows are rare), fits in cache, and
answers the query with Limit 1. 3. Rewrite to enable the optimization: SELECT amount FROM payments
WHERE status = 'FAILED' ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1. Equivalent to MAX for non-NULL amounts,
more index-friendly. 4. Confirm with EXPLAIN — you want Index Only Scan or Index Scan with Limit 1,
not a Seq Scan with Aggregate above.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres supports partial indexes natively; SQL Server has filtered indexes;
Oracle has function-based indexes; MySQL 8 supports functional indexes but lacks partial. - If amount
can be NULL, MAX ignores NULLs but ORDER BY DESC puts them first (with NULLS LAST not the
default in some engines) — use ORDER BY amount DESC NULLS LAST. - Maintenance cost of the
partial index is proportional to write rate of FAILED rows — usually very low for FAILED.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MAX needs no special handling" — at 500M rows it absolutely does. -
Do not build a full index on amount alone — large, unused for everything but this one query.
Common follow-up: "What if I need MAX(amount) per merchant_id where status = 'FAILED'?" —
Composite partial index (merchant_id, amount DESC) WHERE status = 'FAILED', then DISTINCT ON or
LATERAL with LIMIT 1 per merchant.
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_failed_amt
  ON payments (amount DESC) WHERE status = 'FAILED';
SELECT amount FROM payments
WHERE status = 'FAILED'
ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1;
