Chapter 5, Part A — ACID & Isolation Levels
Every senior backend interview in India — Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Swiggy, Zerodha, Flipkart — and
every GCC round (JP Morgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs, Target, AmEx) eventually walks into
transactions. The interviewer wants to know whether you understand what ACID actually buys you,
whether you can spot the difference between a dirty read and a non-repeatable read in a two-transaction
trace, and whether you know which isolation level your engine ships with by default. This is the chapter
where junior candidates recite textbook definitions and lose, and where the right candidate explains
trade-offs and wins. The chapter has three parts — Part A (this file) covers ACID semantics, the four
isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent; Part B covers locking, MVCC and how engines actually
implement isolation under the hood; Part C covers deadlocks, conflict resolution and production
patterns. Read them in order — the locking discussion in B only makes sense once you've internalised
the anomaly catalogue here.
Section A — ACID & Transaction Control
Q187 · What Does ACID Actually Mean
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, JP Morgan · Topic: ACID
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through ACID. Don't recite the textbook — tell me what each letter buys me in a real
payment system.
The 30-second answer: Atomicity means the transaction is all-or-nothing — either every write commits
or none do. Consistency means committed data never violates the constraints you've declared. Isolation
means concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work. Durability means once you get
a COMMIT acknowledgement, the data survives a crash.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it around a transfer of two thousand rupees from account A to
B. You debit A, credit B, write a row to the transfers ledger. ACID is what guarantees you can never
end up with A debited but B not credited. 2. Atomicity is the rollback machinery — if the credit fails for
any reason, the debit is undone. 3. Consistency is the constraint enforcement layer — primary keys,
foreign keys, CHECK constraints, NOT NULL all survive the commit. Note: "consistency" here does not
mean "users see the same data everywhere" (that is the distributed-systems definition, a different thing).
4. Isolation is the lever you tune — the cost of perfect isolation is serial execution, so engines give you
four named levels with documented trade-offs. 5. Durability is the fsync at commit time — the redo log is
flushed to disk before the engine returns OK.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 193 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 194
Edge cases to mention: - Group commit batches multiple transactions into one fsync to amortise the
disk cost — that's why throughput jumps when concurrency rises. - Durability is only as good as your
storage stack — write caches on consumer SSDs without battery backing have lost committed data in
real outages. - ACID is per-database; once you cross a service boundary the engine cannot help you,
which is why distributed transactions and the saga pattern exist.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Consistency means the data is the same everywhere" — that's the
CAP-theorem C, not the ACID C. - Do not say "ACID makes the database slow" without qualifying —
Atomicity, Consistency and Durability are cheap; Isolation is where the cost lives.
Common follow-up: "Which letter is the engine actually working hardest on?" — Isolation, by a wide
margin. The other three are essentially bookkeeping; isolation is where locks, MVCC snapshots and
conflict detection burn CPU.
-- The classic atomicity demo
BEGIN;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE id = 101;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 2000 WHERE id = 202;
  INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (101, 202, 2000);
COMMIT;
Q188 · Atomicity in Practice — Rollback and Savepoints
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Wells Fargo, Razorpay · Topic: ACID
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does atomicity really give you, and how do savepoints fit in?
The 30-second answer: Atomicity means the entire transaction commits or none of it does — there is
no in-between state visible to other sessions. Savepoints let you mark internal checkpoints inside a
transaction so you can roll back part of the work without aborting the whole thing.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the binary view — BEGIN opens a unit of work, COMMIT
publishes it, ROLLBACK throws it away. 2. The engine implements this with undo logs (or MVCC
versions) — until COMMIT, every change is reversible. 3. Savepoints add a tree of partial commits — 
SAVEPOINT s1 marks a point, ROLLBACK TO s1 undoes work after that point but keeps the rest, 
RELEASE s1 discards the savepoint marker. 4. Real use case: a bulk import where each row should
fail independently — wrap each row in a savepoint, rollback the savepoint on error, continue with the
next row, commit the batch at the end.
Edge cases to mention: - A ROLLBACK to a savepoint does not release locks acquired after the
savepoint in every engine — read your engine's docs. - If the transaction is aborted by the engine
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 194 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 195
(deadlock, serialization failure), all savepoints are gone — you must restart from BEGIN. - Nested
transactions in most engines are simulated using savepoints — there is no true nested transaction in
MySQL or Postgres.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "atomicity prevents partial failures" — it allows partial work to happen,
it just hides it from other sessions and undoes it on rollback. - Do not use savepoints inside long-running
OLTP transactions casually — they keep the transaction open longer, which hurts MVCC bloat in
Postgres.
Common follow-up: "What happens to the savepoint if the network drops mid-transaction?" — The
engine eventually times out the session and rolls back everything; the savepoints die with it.
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO payments (order_id, amount) VALUES (1001, 499);
  SAVEPOINT after_payment;
  UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'BOOK-42';
  -- inventory update failed (out of stock)
  ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_payment;
  -- payment row is preserved, inventory change is gone
COMMIT;
Q189 · Consistency — What It Really Means
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: ACID
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
The C in ACID confuses everyone. What does Consistency actually mean inside a single-node
database?
The 30-second answer: Consistency in ACID means the transaction moves the database from one valid
state to another, where "valid" is defined by the constraints you've declared — primary keys, foreign
keys, NOT NULL, CHECK, unique indexes and any triggers. If a transaction would violate any of these,
the engine aborts the COMMIT.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The trick in this question is to distinguish ACID consistency from CAP
consistency — they're unrelated concepts that share a word. 2. ACID consistency is mostly the
application's responsibility — the engine enforces the constraints you declared, but it cannot know your
business invariants (for example, "loyalty points should equal lifetime spend divided by ten") unless you
encode them as constraints. 3. The engine's job: at COMMIT, re-check deferred constraints, validate
foreign keys, run AFTER triggers. If anything fails, the COMMIT becomes a ROLLBACK. 4. The
application's job: write transactions that maintain higher-level invariants the engine cannot see — for
example, "the sum of all transfer rows for an account equals the account balance."
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 195 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 196
Edge cases to mention: - Deferrable constraints (Postgres) let you violate foreign keys mid-transaction
and only check at COMMIT — useful for circular insert orders. - A CHECK constraint with a subquery
referencing another table is not portable and is usually rejected — use a trigger instead. - Cascading
deletes happen inside the transaction's atomic unit — if any cascaded delete fails, the whole transaction
rolls back.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Consistency means readers see the latest data." That is read-your-
writes or strong consistency in distributed systems. - Do not say "the database enforces all business
rules" — it only enforces what you've declared as constraints.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between an immediate and a deferred constraint?" —
Immediate is checked after every statement; deferred is checked at COMMIT. Foreign keys are
commonly deferred for batch loads.
-- Deferred constraint pattern
BEGIN;
  SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED;
  INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id) VALUES (5001, 999);
  INSERT INTO customers (id, name) VALUES (999, 'Priya Sharma');
COMMIT;  -- FK check happens here, both rows now exist
Q190 · Isolation — The Controlled Relaxation Lever
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Flipkart, Goldman · Topic: ACID
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why is Isolation a knob with four settings instead of just being "on"?
The 30-second answer: Perfect isolation — Serializable — requires either heavy locking or expensive
conflict detection, and on a busy OLTP system that's the difference between a thousand and ten
thousand transactions per second. The four named isolation levels are graduated trade-offs: each
weaker level forbids fewer anomalies but allows more concurrency.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it as a market: the engine sells you isolation in exchange for
throughput, and you pick how much you can afford. 2. Anomalies are the unit of trade — dirty reads,
non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, lost updates, write skew. Each level outlaws a specific subset. 3.
Stronger levels need more bookkeeping: Read Committed needs only short read locks (or a per-
statement snapshot); Repeatable Read needs a snapshot for the whole transaction; Serializable needs
full conflict detection. 4. Most production systems run at Read Committed (the Postgres default) for
OLTP and step up to Repeatable Read or Serializable only for specific transactions that need it.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 196 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 197
Edge cases to mention: - The SQL standard defines four levels but leaves implementation open —
Postgres "Read Uncommitted" is silently treated as Read Committed because MVCC makes dirty reads
impossible. - MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read with gap locks, which also prevents phantoms
— stricter than the SQL standard requires. - Oracle and SQL Server (with
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT on) use snapshot isolation under the Read Committed label.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "higher isolation is always safer, use Serializable" — on a busy system
you will deadlock or hit serialization failures constantly. - Do not confuse the SQL standard isolation level
with what your engine actually delivers — read your engine's documentation.
Common follow-up: "If Serializable is correct, why is anything else allowed?" — Throughput. A bank
ledger that does ten thousand transfers per second cannot afford Serializable's conflict-detection
overhead on every read.
-- Setting isolation for a single transaction
BEGIN;
  SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;
  -- ... rest of the transaction
COMMIT;
Q191 · Durability — fsync, Redo Logs and Group Commit
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan, Zerodha · Topic: ACID
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through what actually happens between my COMMIT and the engine returning OK.
The 30-second answer: The engine writes the change to an in-memory log buffer, flushes the log to disk
with fsync (or O_DIRECT), waits for the storage acknowledgement, then returns OK to your client. The
actual data pages may not be written yet — only the redo log entry has to be durable, because crash
recovery replays the log to rebuild the pages.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with WAL — Write-Ahead Logging is the universal pattern.
Every change is first appended to a sequential log file. 2. COMMIT writes a COMMIT record to the log
and forces fsync on the log file. That's the durability boundary. 3. Data pages get written later by the
background writer or checkpointer. If the engine crashes between COMMIT and data-page flush,
recovery reads the WAL and reapplies the changes. 4. Group commit batches many concurrent
COMMITs into one fsync — instead of one fsync per transaction, you get one fsync per batch, which
dramatically improves throughput on busy systems.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 197 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 198
Edge cases to mention: - synchronous_commit = off in Postgres trades a tiny window of
durability loss for huge throughput gains — useful for analytics inserts where losing the last few seconds
is acceptable. - Consumer SSDs with write caches that ignore fsync have lost committed data in real
outages — datacentre-grade drives with power-loss protection are essential. - Replication adds a
second durability layer — synchronous replication waits for a replica to acknowledge before returning
OK, so a single-machine failure does not lose data.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "COMMIT writes to the data file" — it writes to the log; the data file is
written asynchronously. - Do not assume fsync always actually flushes — the kernel, the controller and
the drive can all lie. Test your stack.
Common follow-up: "What is the trade-off of synchronous_commit off?" — You lose up to 
wal_writer_delay worth of committed transactions on a crash. The database stays consistent, but
recent commits vanish.
-- Postgres tuning knob for durability vs throughput
SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off;  -- for this transaction only
INSERT INTO event_log (event_type, payload) VALUES ('clicked', '{}');
COMMIT;
Q192 · BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK — The Basics Done Right
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Transactions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK and tell me what happens if I forget to write
COMMIT.
The 30-second answer: BEGIN (or START TRANSACTION) opens a unit of work, COMMIT makes the
changes visible and durable, ROLLBACK throws away the changes. If you forget COMMIT and the
session closes, the engine rolls back the transaction automatically — your changes are lost.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the three-step lifecycle clearly. Most engines treat BEGIN,
START TRANSACTION and BEGIN TRANSACTION as synonyms. 2. Explain implicit vs explicit
transactions: in autocommit mode (the default for most clients), every statement is its own transaction.
BEGIN turns autocommit off until the next COMMIT or ROLLBACK. 3. Mention the connection-pool
gotcha: if a transaction is left open when the connection returns to the pool, the next user inherits it —
explicitly ROLLBACK in your finally block. 4. Be ready for the language follow-up: ANSI SQL says
START TRANSACTION; MySQL, Postgres and SQL Server all accept BEGIN as a shortcut.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 198 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 199
Edge cases to mention: - A DDL statement in MySQL (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE) implicitly
commits the current transaction — your previous DML is now durable whether you wanted it or not. -
Postgres allows DDL inside transactions and rolls it back cleanly — useful for migrations. - Some clients
(especially psql in pure interactive mode) will leave a failed transaction in an "aborted" state where every
subsequent statement errors until you ROLLBACK.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "every query is a transaction" — autocommit makes it look that way, but
explicit BEGIN changes the semantics. - Do not mix BEGIN with COMMIT WORK and SET
TRANSACTION carelessly — read your engine's docs on which combinations actually work together.
Common follow-up: "What happens if the connection drops mid-transaction?" — The engine eventually
times out the session and rolls back. Any locks held are released.
BEGIN;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
  -- error in application code here
ROLLBACK;  -- both updates undone
Q193 · Implicit vs Explicit Transactions
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Accenture, Cognizant, TCS, Wells Fargo · Topic: Transactions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between an implicit and an explicit transaction, and which one does your
JDBC driver use by default?
The 30-second answer: Implicit (autocommit) transactions wrap every single statement in its own
transaction that commits automatically when the statement succeeds. Explicit transactions are
bracketed by BEGIN and COMMIT and let you group multiple statements as one atomic unit. JDBC
defaults to autocommit on; you must call setAutoCommit(false) to use explicit transactions.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain autocommit first — it's the simpler model. Every INSERT,
UPDATE, DELETE is committed before control returns to the application. 2. The cost of autocommit:
each statement does its own fsync, so doing a thousand single-row inserts in a tight loop is hundreds of
times slower than batching them inside one explicit transaction. 3. Explicit transactions are mandatory
whenever you need atomicity across more than one statement — transfers, multi-row updates with
consistency requirements, anything with savepoints. 4. The JDBC/ORM trap: connection pools usually
reset autocommit between checkouts, but if your ORM (Hibernate, JPA, SQLAlchemy) starts a
transaction lazily, you may be inside an implicit transaction without realising it.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 199 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 200
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL's autocommit is a session variable that can be set per-connection
or globally — check SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'autocommit' if behaviour surprises you. - Postgres
has no global autocommit toggle — it's a client-side concept; psql defaults to autocommit on, JDBC the
same. - Spring's @Transactional annotation opens an explicit transaction; if you forget the
annotation, every JPA save is a separate autocommit transaction.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "autocommit is bad, always use explicit transactions" — for single-
statement OLTP work, autocommit is correct and simpler. - Do not assume your ORM has wrapped
everything in a transaction — verify.
Common follow-up: "What happens to autocommit when you call BEGIN?" — It's suspended until
COMMIT or ROLLBACK, then resumes.
-- MySQL autocommit demonstration
SET autocommit = 0;
INSERT INTO orders (id, amount) VALUES (1, 100);
INSERT INTO orders (id, amount) VALUES (2, 200);
COMMIT;  -- both inserts published together
SET autocommit = 1;
Section B — The Four Isolation Levels
Q194 · Overview of the Four Isolation Levels
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Give me the four standard isolation levels and tell me which anomaly each one prevents.
The 30-second answer: Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom
reads. Read Committed forbids dirty reads but allows non-repeatable and phantom. Repeatable Read
also forbids non-repeatable reads, allowing only phantoms. Serializable forbids all three plus write skew.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Draw the standard SQL grid mentally — four levels, three classic
anomalies, one cell per combination. 2. Read Uncommitted: no protection — a transaction can read
uncommitted changes from another. Rarely useful. 3. Read Committed: a query sees only committed
data, but two queries in the same transaction can see different snapshots — that's a non-repeatable
read. 4. Repeatable Read: every query in the transaction sees the same snapshot of existing rows, but
newly inserted rows from other transactions might appear — that's a phantom. 5. Serializable: the result
must be equivalent to some serial ordering of all concurrent transactions — no phantoms, no write skew.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 200 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 201
Edge cases to mention: - The SQL standard's grid is conservative — actual engines often deliver more
protection than required (Postgres's Repeatable Read prevents phantoms because of MVCC, MySQL
InnoDB's Repeatable Read prevents phantoms via gap locks). - Write skew is not in the SQL standard's
anomaly list — it's an additional anomaly that only Serializable prevents, recognised after the standard
was published. - The "Read Uncommitted" level in Postgres is treated as Read Committed because
MVCC has no way to expose dirty data.
What NOT to say: - Do not memorise the grid without understanding what each anomaly looks like in
concrete code — interviewers will ask you to construct one. - Do not assume the level names mean the
same thing across engines — Oracle's Serializable is actually snapshot isolation, not true serializable.
Common follow-up: "Draw me the grid on the whiteboard." — Be ready to do this from memory.
Level Dirty Read Non-Repeatable Read Phantom Read
Read Uncommitted Possible Possible Possible
Read Committed Prevented Possible Possible
Repeatable Read Prevented Prevented Possible*
Serializable Prevented Prevented Prevented
* Prevented in MySQL InnoDB and Postgres due to implementation details.
Q195 · Read Uncommitted — When (Almost Never) to Use It
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Cognizant, Accenture, Walmart Labs · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does Read Uncommitted allow, and is there any sane reason to choose it?
The 30-second answer: Read Uncommitted lets one transaction see changes made by another
transaction before that other transaction has committed — a dirty read. You almost never want this; the
only honest use case is approximate reporting on a hot table where you don't care if you read data that
will be rolled back a millisecond later.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the mechanism: at this level, the engine does no read locking
at all and ignores the visibility rules. 2. Walk through the failure mode: transaction A debits an account by
ten thousand rupees and then rolls back. Transaction B, running at Read Uncommitted, saw the debited
balance and made a decision on it — that decision is now based on data that does not exist. 3. The
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 201 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 202
almost-acceptable use case: a dashboard counting approximate row counts on a high-write table, where
being off by a few hundred rows is fine and you want to avoid any lock contention. 4. Reality check: in
Postgres this level is silently upgraded to Read Committed because MVCC cannot return uncommitted
data. In SQL Server, the WITH (NOLOCK) hint is the per-table equivalent and is widely (mis)used for
the same reason.
Edge cases to mention: - WITH (NOLOCK) in SQL Server can return rows twice, skip rows entirely, or
return rows with internally inconsistent column values during page splits — it's not a free performance
win. - Read Uncommitted does not eliminate all overhead — internal latches still apply, just not
transaction-level read locks. - In MySQL, Read Uncommitted is supported and does what you'd expect,
but the InnoDB engine still has consistency checks that may produce surprising results.
What NOT to say: - Do not call Read Uncommitted "fast" — it's marginally faster only in lock-based
engines, and in MVCC engines it's irrelevant. - Do not recommend it for any transaction that makes a
decision based on the data — you can act on data that never existed.
Common follow-up: "Why is NOLOCK so popular if it's so dangerous?" — Habit, cargo-culted advice
from old DBAs, and the fact that the failures are silent until they're not.
-- The dashboard pattern — approximate count, no lock contention
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM event_log WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour';
Q196 · Read Committed — What It Prevents and What It Doesn't
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Goldman, JP Morgan · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Read Committed is the Postgres default. What does it actually guarantee, and where does it fall
short?
The 30-second answer: Read Committed guarantees that every query sees only data that was
committed at the time the query began executing. It prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads
— two SELECT statements in the same transaction can see different values for the same row if another
transaction commits a change between them.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the visibility rule: each statement gets its own fresh snapshot.
The transaction does not have a single consistent view of the database. 2. Walk through the implication:
if you SELECT a balance, then later in the same transaction SELECT it again, you might get different
values. For reporting queries that read multiple tables, sums can be incorrect. 3. State why it's still the
default: it's cheap (no long-held locks, no per-transaction snapshot), it covers the most common failure
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 202 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 203
mode (dirty reads), and most OLTP transactions are short enough that anomalies are unlikely. 4. The fix: if
you need a consistent view across multiple statements, escalate to Repeatable Read for that transaction.
Edge cases to mention: - Even at Read Committed, an UPDATE on a row that's being modified by
another transaction will block until that transaction commits or rolls back — write locks are still
respected. - Postgres Read Committed uses a fresh MVCC snapshot per statement; SQL Server (without
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT) uses short read locks released after each statement. - A SELECT FOR
UPDATE inside Read Committed locks the rows you read — useful when you intend to update them
next.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Read Committed means I see consistent data" — between statements
within the same transaction, you do not. - Do not assume Read Committed prevents lost updates — it
does not. A read-modify-write loop at Read Committed can lose updates.
Common follow-up: "Give me a concrete example of a non-repeatable read at this level." — See Q14.
-- Read Committed: snapshot per statement
BEGIN;  -- default isolation in Postgres
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- returns 5000
  -- another transaction commits an update to balance
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- returns 4000
COMMIT;
Q197 · Repeatable Read — Snapshots and Phantom Limits
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does Repeatable Read guarantee, and what's the difference between Postgres and MySQL
InnoDB at this level?
The 30-second answer: Repeatable Read freezes a transaction-level snapshot of all rows that exist
when the transaction starts — any subsequent SELECT in the same transaction sees the same values for
those rows. The SQL standard says phantoms (newly inserted rows appearing in a re-run query) are still
allowed, but Postgres prevents them via MVCC and MySQL InnoDB prevents them via gap locks.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the snapshot mechanism: at the first read, the engine pins a
"logical clock" value, and every subsequent read filters out rows committed after that point. 2. Result:
non-repeatable reads disappear — the same SELECT always returns the same data within the
transaction. 3. The phantom hole in the standard: the standard only protects rows that already exist; new
INSERTs from other transactions can show up in a range scan re-run. Real engines often patch this. 4.
Postgres at Repeatable Read uses MVCC for everything — phantoms are naturally prevented. MySQL
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 203 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 204
InnoDB uses gap locks on index ranges to block other transactions from inserting into the scanned
range.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres Repeatable Read can fail at COMMIT with a serialization error if a
concurrent transaction modified a row you wrote — be ready to retry. - MySQL InnoDB gap locks can
cause surprising deadlocks because they lock ranges that don't contain any rows yet — a common
production issue. - Repeatable Read does not protect against write skew — that requires Serializable.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Repeatable Read is the same in every engine" — Postgres and MySQL
InnoDB behave very differently underneath. - Do not assume Repeatable Read solves all read
consistency problems — write skew is the famous exception.
Common follow-up: "Why does MySQL InnoDB default to Repeatable Read while Postgres defaults to
Read Committed?" — Historical reasons; MySQL InnoDB's gap-lock implementation makes Repeatable
Read cheap enough to be the default, while Postgres prioritises maximum concurrency at Read
Committed.
-- Repeatable Read: stable view across the whole transaction
BEGIN;
  SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- 5000
  -- another transaction commits an update
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- still 5000
COMMIT;
Q198 · Serializable — The Strongest Level and Its Implementations
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Cred, Razorpay, Zerodha · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does Serializable guarantee, and how do Postgres and MySQL InnoDB actually implement
it differently?
The 30-second answer: Serializable guarantees that the result of running concurrent transactions is
equivalent to some serial ordering of them — no anomaly is possible. Postgres uses Serializable
Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which extends snapshot isolation with conflict detection. MySQL InnoDB uses
strict two-phase locking, taking shared locks on every read and exclusive locks on writes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the guarantee in plain terms: if your transaction commits, the
database looks as if all concurrent transactions ran one after the other in some valid order. 2. Lock-based
implementation (SQL Server, MySQL InnoDB, DB2): take shared read locks and exclusive write locks,
hold them until commit. Prevents anomalies but reduces concurrency and causes deadlocks. 3. SSI
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 204 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 205
implementation (Postgres 9.1+): use snapshot isolation for reads (no locks), but track read-write
dependencies between transactions. If a dangerous cycle is detected, abort one transaction with a
serialization error. 4. Trade-off: lock-based blocks more often but completes when it doesn't deadlock;
SSI runs full speed but throws more retryable errors at COMMIT time.
Edge cases to mention: - Serializable always requires the application to be ready to retry — both lock-
based and SSI implementations can abort transactions for correctness. - Postgres SSI has lower
throughput than Repeatable Read because of the dependency tracking overhead, but higher than lock-
based Serializable on read-heavy workloads. - Oracle and MySQL marketing sometimes calls snapshot
isolation "Serializable" when it's actually weaker — read the docs.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Serializable is the safest, use it always" — the abort rate on busy
workloads will hurt; pick it transaction-by-transaction. - Do not confuse Serializable with snapshot
isolation — write skew distinguishes them.
Common follow-up: "What's the retry pattern for a Serializable transaction?" — Catch the serialization
failure error (SQLSTATE 40001), wait a short randomised time, restart the transaction from BEGIN, repeat
with a retry limit.
-- Postgres Serializable with retry-on-error in pseudocode
BEGIN;
  SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
  -- read balances, validate invariant, update
COMMIT;  -- may raise 40001 serialization_failure — retry from BEGIN
Section C — Anomalies in Detail
Q199 · Dirty Read — Concrete Two-Transaction Example
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Accenture, Cognizant · Topic: Anomalies
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me a two-transaction trace that produces a dirty read.
The 30-second answer: Transaction A updates a row but has not committed. Transaction B, running at
Read Uncommitted, reads the updated value. A then rolls back. B has now read a value that never
existed in any committed state — the dirty read.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the scene: account 101 has balance 5000. 2. Transaction A
starts and runs UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE id = 101. The
change is in A's private workspace, not yet committed. 3. Transaction B (at Read Uncommitted) runs 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 205 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 206
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101. It sees 3000 because Read Uncommitted
ignores visibility rules. 4. Transaction A hits an error and runs ROLLBACK. The balance is back to 5000.
5. Transaction B has made a decision based on a value (3000) that was never durably true. If B sent the
user an "insufficient funds" rejection or wrote a derived value to another table, the system is now in an
incorrect state.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres, dirty reads are impossible at any isolation level because MVCC
only exposes committed versions — even SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ
UNCOMMITTED gets you Read Committed semantics. - SQL Server's WITH (NOLOCK) hint is the
per-query equivalent and allows dirty reads even when the session isolation is higher. - The "phantom of
a dirty read" — reading a row that exists in a transaction's workspace but never gets committed — is the
worst kind because the decision is irreversible.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "dirty reads are fine for analytics" — even analytics can produce wrong
totals if a million-row insert rolls back. - Do not confuse dirty reads with non-repeatable reads — dirty
reads see uncommitted data, non-repeatable reads see two different committed values.
Common follow-up: "Does Postgres allow dirty reads under any setting?" — No. The architecture makes
them impossible.
-- Session A
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE id = 101;
-- (do not commit yet)
-- Session B at Read Uncommitted (e.g. MySQL or SQL Server)
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- sees 3000
-- Session A
ROLLBACK;  -- balance is back to 5000, but B already acted on 3000
Q200 · Non-Repeatable Read — Concrete Example
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Anomalies
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me a non-repeatable read at the Read Committed level.
The 30-second answer: Transaction A reads a row, transaction B updates and commits that row,
transaction A reads the same row again and sees the new value. Two reads of the same row in the same
transaction returned different values — that's the non-repeatable read.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 206 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 207
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Setup: account 101 has balance 5000. Transaction A is a reporting
transaction at Read Committed that needs to fetch the balance twice (once for display, once for
calculation). 2. A's first read: 5000. 3. Transaction B opens, updates balance to 4000, commits. 4. A's
second read: 4000. 5. A now has two inconsistent numbers in its internal state — if it was computing
"balance minus pending withdrawals" and used the first balance with the latest withdrawal list, the math
is wrong.
Edge cases to mention: - The fix is Repeatable Read — every read in A sees the same snapshot. - The
pure read case is annoying but rarely catastrophic; the dangerous case is when A reads, makes a
decision, and writes back, because that's the lost-update scenario. - An equivalent in MySQL with
autocommit and no explicit BEGIN is impossible to demonstrate — autocommit ends each statement's
transaction immediately, so each SELECT is a new transaction with its own snapshot semantics.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "non-repeatable reads are a Postgres bug" — they're explicitly allowed
at Read Committed in the SQL standard. - Do not confuse with phantom reads — non-repeatable is
about existing rows changing value; phantoms are about new rows appearing.
Common follow-up: "How do I prevent this in Postgres?" — Set the transaction to REPEATABLE READ
or SERIALIZABLE.
-- Session A at Read Committed
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- 5000
-- Session B (separate connection)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 4000 WHERE id = 101;
COMMIT;
-- Session A continues
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- 4000 — non-repeatable read
COMMIT;
Q201 · Phantom Read — Concrete Example
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Razorpay, Flipkart · Topic: Anomalies
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me a phantom read. What's the difference from a non-repeatable read?
The 30-second answer: Transaction A runs a range query like SELECT * FROM transfers WHERE
amount > 10000, transaction B inserts a new row matching that predicate and commits, transaction A
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 207 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 208
runs the same range query and sees the new row. The new row is the phantom. Non-repeatable reads
change existing rows; phantoms add or remove rows from a result set.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Setup: a treasury reconciliation transaction wants to find all transfers
above ten thousand rupees today. 2. A's first range query: returns three rows. 3. B inserts a new transfer
for fifteen thousand rupees and commits. 4. A's second range query: returns four rows. 5. The new fourth
row is a phantom — A's view of the predicate has changed because new rows materialised under it.
Edge cases to mention: - The SQL standard says Repeatable Read does not prevent phantoms; this is
the most famous gap in the standard. - Postgres Repeatable Read prevents phantoms because the
snapshot includes the entire visibility state at the start of the transaction — new rows from other
transactions are invisible. - MySQL InnoDB at Repeatable Read prevents phantoms via gap locks: when
A's range query runs, it takes locks on the gaps in the index range, blocking B's INSERT until A commits.
- Serializable always prevents phantoms by definition.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "phantoms only happen at Read Committed" — the standard allows
them at Repeatable Read as well. - Do not assume your engine follows the standard literally — test it.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between a phantom read and a lost update?" — Phantoms
are about reads seeing new rows; lost updates are about two writers overwriting each other.
-- Session A
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT * FROM transfers WHERE amount > 10000 AND created_on = CURRENT_DATE;
-- 3 rows
-- Session B inserts a new high-value transfer and commits
-- Session A in MySQL InnoDB or Postgres at Repeatable Read
SELECT * FROM transfers WHERE amount > 10000 AND created_on = CURRENT_DATE;
-- Postgres: still 3 rows. SQL-standard-only engine: 4 rows (phantom).
COMMIT;
Q202 · Lost Update — How Isolation and Locking Prevent It
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Goldman, Walmart Labs, Cred · Topic:
Anomalies
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Two transactions both want to increment a counter. Walk me through how a lost update happens
and three ways to prevent it.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 208 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 209
The 30-second answer: A reads the counter, B reads the counter, A increments and writes, B
increments and writes — B overwrites A's update with a value computed from the old read, and A's
increment is lost. Prevent it with (1) atomic updates that don't require reading first, (2) SELECT FOR
UPDATE to lock the row before reading, or (3) optimistic concurrency with a version column.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk the failure: counter starts at 100. A reads 100, B reads 100, A
writes 101, B writes 101. Final value is 101, but both transactions intended to increment, so it should be
102. 2. Fix one: replace the read-modify-write with UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1
WHERE id = X — the engine does the read and write under one lock, so concurrent updates are
serialised. 3. Fix two: SELECT value FROM counters WHERE id = X FOR UPDATE takes a row
lock that blocks the second reader until the first transaction commits. 4. Fix three: add a version
column, read (value, version), write UPDATE counters SET value = ?, version =
version + 1 WHERE id = X AND version = ?. If the row count is zero, someone else updated
first — retry.
Edge cases to mention: - At Repeatable Read in Postgres, a lost-update attempt raises a serialization
error at the second write — Postgres detects the conflict and aborts one transaction. At Read
Committed, it does not. - At Repeatable Read in MySQL InnoDB, the second UPDATE blocks until the
first commits, then proceeds — no abort, but the read value is stale. You must re-read or use SELECT
FOR UPDATE. - Optimistic concurrency works well when conflicts are rare; pessimistic locking is better
when they're common.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume that "running at Repeatable Read prevents lost updates everywhere"
— Postgres and MySQL InnoDB behave differently. - Do not solve a lost update by raising isolation level
alone in MySQL InnoDB — you also need explicit locking or retry logic.
Common follow-up: "Which approach do payment systems use?" — Atomic UPDATEs for counters;
SELECT FOR UPDATE for the account balance row during a transfer; optimistic concurrency in user-
facing screens where the row is held while the user types.
-- Atomic, no lost update possible
UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 WHERE id = 'orders_placed';
-- Pessimistic, with read-then-write pattern
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101 FOR UPDATE;
-- compute new balance in application
UPDATE accounts SET balance = ? WHERE id = 101;
COMMIT;
-- Optimistic
SELECT balance, version FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = ?, version = version + 1
  WHERE id = 101 AND version = ?;  -- rowcount = 0 means retry
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 209 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q203 · Write Skew — The Serializable-Only Anomaly
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Cred, Razorpay · Topic: Anomalies
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is write skew, and why does Snapshot Isolation allow it while Serializable does not?
The 30-second answer: Write skew is an anomaly where two transactions read overlapping data, each
makes an update based on what they read, and the combined effect violates an invariant that each
transaction individually preserved. Snapshot Isolation can't see this because each transaction's
snapshot looks correct in isolation; Serializable detects the read-write conflict across transactions and
aborts one.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Classic example: an on-call rota. Rule: at least one doctor must be
on call. Two doctors, Asha and Vikram, are both on call. Both try to mark themselves off-call
simultaneously. 2. Asha's transaction reads "two doctors on call, I can step off" and updates her row to
off-call. 3. Vikram's transaction reads "two doctors on call, I can step off" (same snapshot) and updates
his row to off-call. 4. Both commit. Now zero doctors are on call — the invariant is violated even though
each transaction's snapshot showed two doctors when it made its decision. 5. Serializable catches this
by tracking that both transactions read the row they didn't write — a read-write dependency cycle — and
aborts one.
Edge cases to mention: - Snapshot Isolation (Oracle, MySQL InnoDB at Repeatable Read with
appropriate locking, Postgres at Repeatable Read) allows write skew. - Postgres SSI at Serializable
detects write skew via dependency tracking and raises a serialization error. - The cheap fix without
Serializable: explicit locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE on the rows being checked, or a constraint that
encodes the invariant directly.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "write skew is impossible if both transactions read the same data" —
that's exactly when it happens. - Do not confuse with lost updates — lost updates overwrite the same
cell; write skew involves disjoint cells with a shared invariant.
Common follow-up: "How would you fix the doctor-on-call problem without Serializable?" — SELECT
count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call = true FOR UPDATE before the UPDATE — the lock
serialises the two transactions.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 210 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 211
-- Both transactions run at Repeatable Read
-- T1
BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call = TRUE;  -- 2
UPDATE doctors SET on_call = FALSE WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;
-- T2 (concurrent)
BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call = TRUE;  -- 2 (snapshot)
UPDATE doctors SET on_call = FALSE WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
-- Result: count = 0, invariant violated
Q204 · Read Skew — Same Family, Different Symptom
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan · Topic: Anomalies
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is read skew, and how does it differ from a non-repeatable read?
The 30-second answer: Read skew is when a single transaction reads two related rows and sees an
inconsistent state because another transaction modified one of them between the reads. It's effectively a
non-repeatable read across two different rows that should sum or balance together — the inconsistency
is in the relationship, not in any single row.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Setup: a customer has two accounts, savings and current, with
balances 5000 and 3000, total 8000. The system invariant is that the total is preserved when money is
moved between them. 2. Reporting transaction R at Read Committed reads savings: 5000. 3. Transfer
transaction T moves 2000 from savings to current and commits. 4. R reads current: 5000 (2000 plus
3000). 5. R now reports total 10000 instead of 8000 — the relationship between the two reads is wrong
even though each individual read returned a value that was committed at some point.
Edge cases to mention: - Read skew is prevented at Repeatable Read in Postgres and at Repeatable
Read in MySQL InnoDB because both reads see the same snapshot. - This is the classic argument for
running reporting and consistency-check transactions at Repeatable Read or Serializable even when the
rest of the system runs at Read Committed. - Read skew is sometimes called "inconsistent read" in older
textbooks.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse with non-repeatable read on the same row — read skew is about
two different rows whose values are related. - Do not assume reporting tools are immune — long-running
aggregations are particularly vulnerable.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 211 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 212
Common follow-up: "What's the cheapest fix for read skew in a Postgres reporting query?" — Wrap the
query in a Repeatable Read transaction; the snapshot is consistent.
-- Repeatable Read fix for read skew
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 999 AND type = 'savings';
-- another transaction commits a transfer between accounts
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 999 AND type = 'current';
-- both reads come from the same snapshot, totals are consistent
COMMIT;
Q205 · Snapshot Isolation — Vs Serializable
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Cred, PhonePe · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is Snapshot Isolation, and how is it different from Serializable?
The 30-second answer: Snapshot Isolation gives every transaction a consistent point-in-time view of
the database — reads see committed data as of the transaction's start, writes only conflict with
concurrent writes to the same rows. It prevents dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads, but it allows
write skew. Serializable also prevents write skew by tracking read-write dependencies across
transactions.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Snapshot Isolation is the implementation Postgres uses for
Repeatable Read, MySQL InnoDB uses with MVCC, Oracle uses for both Read Committed and
Serializable, and SQL Server uses when READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is on. 2. Mechanism: when a
transaction starts, the engine records the current commit sequence number. Reads filter out any row
version committed after that number. 3. Write conflicts: if your transaction tries to update a row that
another transaction has already updated since your snapshot, the engine raises a write conflict — you
abort and retry. 4. The famous gap: Snapshot Isolation does not detect read-only conflicts that lead to
write skew. Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) extends snapshot isolation with read tracking.
Edge cases to mention: - Oracle markets its Snapshot Isolation as "Serializable" — it's not the same as
true Serializable; write skew is possible. - Postgres calls its level "Repeatable Read" but it's exactly
Snapshot Isolation behaviour, stricter than the SQL standard requires. - Snapshot Isolation throughput is
close to Read Committed because reads are not blocked; the cost is the MVCC version chain
maintenance.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 212 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 213
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Snapshot Isolation is the same as Serializable" — write skew is the
counter-example. - Do not say "Oracle's Serializable is broken" — it's documented as Snapshot
Isolation; the naming is misleading but not incorrect by Oracle's definition.
Common follow-up: "When is Snapshot Isolation good enough?" — When your invariants are local to
single rows or are enforced by constraints. When you have multi-row invariants (the on-call rota, account
totals), step up to Serializable.
-- Snapshot Isolation in Postgres (called Repeatable Read)
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
-- All reads see the database as of this point
-- Writes that conflict with concurrent updates raise serialization_failure
COMMIT;
Q206 · Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) — Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Cred, Razorpay · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through how Postgres implements Serializable. Why is it called Serializable Snapshot
Isolation?
The 30-second answer: Postgres at Serializable runs every transaction at Snapshot Isolation and
additionally tracks the read and write sets of each transaction. When it detects a pattern of
dependencies that could produce a non-serializable outcome — specifically a read-write cycle — it
aborts one of the transactions with a serialization failure. The application is expected to retry.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Background: lock-based Serializable (used by SQL Server and
MySQL InnoDB at this level) takes shared read locks on every row read and holds them to commit. It
works but blocks readers behind writers. 2. SSI's idea: don't take read locks. Instead, record what each
transaction read. At commit time, check whether the read-write dependency graph contains a
"dangerous structure" — two consecutive read-write edges forming a cycle. 3. If a dangerous structure is
found, abort one of the participating transactions. The other commits successfully. 4. Trade-off: SSI does
not block readers, so throughput is much higher than lock-based Serializable on read-heavy workloads.
The cost is more retries when conflicts happen.
Edge cases to mention: - The application must catch SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure) and retry
— without retry logic, your Serializable code fails under load. - SSI has higher overhead than Repeatable
Read because of the dependency tracking; on a workload that doesn't need Serializable, prefer
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 213 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 214
Repeatable Read. - DECLARE CURSOR queries and certain index access patterns can cause more
false-positive aborts; Postgres documentation lists known cases.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "SSI is just snapshot isolation with extra steps" — the extra steps are the
difference between correct and incorrect for write-skew-prone workloads. - Do not assume SSI prevents
all retries — it can detect more false positives than lock-based Serializable because dependency analysis
is approximate.
Common follow-up: "What's the typical retry pattern?" — BEGIN; ... COMMIT; wrapped in a loop,
catching SQLSTATE 40001, exponential backoff with jitter, max five retries before surfacing the error to
the user.
-- Pseudocode for SSI retry
for attempt in 1..5:
    try:
        BEGIN;
        SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
        -- do the work
        COMMIT;
        break;
    except SerializationFailure (SQLSTATE 40001):
        ROLLBACK;
        sleep(random(0, 0.1 * 2^attempt));
Section D — Engine Defaults and Configuration
Q207 · Engine Defaults — The Cheat Sheet
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the default isolation level in Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server and Oracle?
The 30-second answer: Postgres defaults to Read Committed. MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable
Read (and prevents phantoms via gap locks). SQL Server defaults to Read Committed. Oracle defaults to
Read Committed (and offers Serializable, which is actually Snapshot Isolation).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres Read Committed: every statement sees a fresh MVCC
snapshot. Dirty reads are impossible (MVCC), but non-repeatable and phantom reads are allowed. 2.
MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read: every transaction sees a transaction-level snapshot. Phantoms are
blocked by gap locks on index ranges scanned by SELECT. 3. SQL Server Read Committed: by default
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 214 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 215
uses short read locks. With READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT = ON (recommended in modern setups), it
switches to snapshot-based reads and behaves like Postgres Read Committed. 4. Oracle Read
Committed: snapshot-based, behaves like Postgres Read Committed. Oracle's "Serializable" is actually
Snapshot Isolation.
Edge cases to mention: - Cloud-managed engines may override defaults — Amazon RDS for SQL
Server enables READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT by default; Aurora Postgres matches stock Postgres. -
Migrating from MySQL to Postgres without changing application code is a common source of surprise —
the same code runs at Repeatable Read in MySQL but Read Committed in Postgres, exposing
anomalies that were hidden. - ORMs often have a per-session or per-transaction isolation setting that
overrides the engine default — check your Hibernate or SQLAlchemy configuration.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "all major engines default to Read Committed" — MySQL InnoDB is the
exception. - Do not assume engine names mean the same behaviour — read the docs for the specific
version.
Common follow-up: "Which one is right?" — Read Committed is the better default for general OLTP
because it maximises concurrency; Repeatable Read is safer for transactions that read related rows. Pick
per-transaction, not per-engine.
-- Check your current default
-- Postgres
SHOW default_transaction_isolation;
-- MySQL
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;
-- SQL Server
DBCC USEROPTIONS;
Q208 · SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL — Syntax and Scope
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you change the isolation level, and what's the difference between session-level and
transaction-level scope?
The 30-second answer: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL <level> applies only to the next
transaction in the session. SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL <level> applies to
all future transactions in the session until the session ends. The engine default applies to all sessions that
don't override.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 215 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 216
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Three scopes: global default (engine config or SET GLOBAL in
MySQL), session-level (until the connection closes), transaction-level (just this BEGIN...COMMIT block).
2. Most production code uses transaction-level — set the level inside the BEGIN block for the specific
transaction that needs it, leave the rest at the default. 3. The MySQL syntax: SET [GLOBAL|SESSION]
TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL .... The Postgres syntax: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION
LEVEL ... (transaction scope) or SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION
ISOLATION LEVEL ... (session scope). 4. ORM gotcha: connection pools reuse connections; if you
change session-level isolation, the next user inherits it. Always set transaction-level scope in pooled
environments.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres, SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL must be the first
statement in the transaction; placing it later raises an error. - In SQL Server, SET TRANSACTION
ISOLATION LEVEL is session-scoped; to scope it per-transaction, you reset it after the COMMIT. -
JDBC's Connection.setTransactionIsolation() is session-scoped — set it explicitly per
checkout in a pool, or set it inside each transaction via SQL.
What NOT to say: - Do not change the global default to chase performance — it affects every session. -
Do not assume session-level survives a connection reset — pools may reset the session state to a clean
baseline.
Common follow-up: "How does HikariCP handle isolation level changes?" — It tracks the isolation level
set when the connection was created and resets to the configured default on return-to-pool.
-- Postgres, transaction scope
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- ... work ...
COMMIT;
-- Postgres, session scope
SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
-- MySQL, session scope
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
Q209 · Choosing Isolation Level for OLTP Workloads
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Flipkart, Cred · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you decide which isolation level to use for an OLTP system like a payments service?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 216 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 217
The 30-second answer: Start with the engine default — Read Committed in Postgres, Repeatable Read
in MySQL InnoDB — for the bulk of OLTP work. Step up to Repeatable Read for transactions that read
related rows and need a consistent view. Use Serializable only for transactions with multi-row invariants
where retry-on-failure is acceptable. Use explicit locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) where you must read-
then-write a single row safely.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. OLTP characteristics: short transactions (sub-second), high
concurrency, small number of rows per transaction, latency-sensitive. 2. Most transactions don't have
cross-row invariants — a single account debit-credit can be done atomically with UPDATE balance =
balance - X. Read Committed is fine. 3. Read-then-write patterns (read balance, validate, then
update) need either SELECT FOR UPDATE at Read Committed, or Repeatable Read with retry. 4. Multi-
row invariants (Q17's on-call rota, inventory totals) need Serializable or explicit locks across all rows in
the invariant.
Edge cases to mention: - Higher isolation increases the abort/retry rate — your application must have
retry logic for any code path that uses Repeatable Read or Serializable in Postgres. - Holding higher-
isolation transactions open for long causes MVCC bloat in Postgres (the engine cannot vacuum tuples
older than the oldest open snapshot). - For payment systems, idempotency keys are often a cheaper
way to handle retries than escalating isolation level — design the contract so duplicate submissions are
safe.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always use Serializable, it's safest" — the throughput penalty and abort
rate are real. - Do not assume one isolation level fits the whole application — pick per-transaction based
on what it does.
Common follow-up: "How does the payments team at Razorpay or Cred actually choose?" — Default to
Read Committed with SELECT FOR UPDATE on the account row during transfer; idempotency keys to
handle retries; Serializable reserved for periodic reconciliation jobs.
-- OLTP transfer pattern: Read Committed + row lock
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 202 FOR UPDATE;
-- validate, then update
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE id = 101;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 2000 WHERE id = 202;
INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (101, 202, 2000);
COMMIT;
Q210 · Choosing Isolation Level for Reporting Workloads
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan, Swiggy · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 217 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 218
A nightly reporting query needs consistent totals across many tables. How do you set up isolation
for it?
The 30-second answer: Use Repeatable Read (or Serializable Snapshot Isolation in Postgres) so the
entire report reads from one consistent snapshot. Even better, run reporting on a read replica where the
workload is isolated from OLTP traffic. If the report is read-only and very long, use Postgres's READ
ONLY DEFERRABLE mode to avoid serialization aborts.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Reporting characteristics: long-running queries, multi-table joins and
aggregates, read-only, sensitivity to read skew (inconsistent totals across related tables). 2. Read
Committed is wrong because between table reads, other transactions can commit and change the data
— totals will be inconsistent. 3. Repeatable Read pins the snapshot at the start of the report and every
subsequent read sees the same view. 4. In Postgres, 
BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY DEFERRABLE ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE waits until it
can get a safe snapshot, then runs without ever raising a serialization failure — perfect for long batch
reports.
Edge cases to mention: - Long-running Repeatable Read transactions block VACUUM in Postgres —
don't leave a reporting connection open for hours. - A reporting query on the primary OLTP database
competes for I/O with transactional work — read replicas are usually a better answer. - Replication lag
means the replica's snapshot is slightly behind the primary; for legally precise reports (audit, regulatory),
you may need a freeze point on the primary.
What NOT to say: - Do not run an hour-long reporting transaction at Read Committed and trust the
totals — they're not consistent. - Do not raise reporting isolation to Serializable expecting performance
gains — Repeatable Read on a replica is almost always better.
Common follow-up: "What if the report needs millisecond-fresh data?" — Then run it on the primary at
Repeatable Read, accept the impact on OLTP, and keep the report short.
-- Postgres long-running reporting transaction
BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY DEFERRABLE ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- multiple queries — all see the same snapshot
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM transfers WHERE created_on = CURRENT_DATE;
SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts;
-- ... more aggregations
COMMIT;
Q211 · Read Replicas and Isolation
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 218 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 219
If I send my read traffic to a Postgres read replica, what isolation guarantees do I have?
The 30-second answer: Reads on a streaming replica are always snapshot-isolated against the replica's
own state — within a transaction, you get a consistent view. But the replica is asynchronously behind the
primary by some amount of replication lag, so reads can return slightly stale data. You cannot maintain
isolation guarantees across primary and replica without explicit coordination.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Replica semantics: the replica replays the WAL from the primary, so
its state is the primary's state minus replication lag (usually milliseconds, occasionally seconds). 2. Inside
a transaction on the replica, you get the standard isolation guarantees against the replica's data — Read
Committed or Repeatable Read works as expected. 3. Cross-node consistency is the problem: write on
the primary, immediately read on the replica — you might read stale data because the replica hasn't
replayed your write yet. This breaks read-your-writes. 4. Fixes: route critical reads back to the primary,
use synchronous replication for the specific operations that need it, or use a session-pinned router that
tracks the primary's LSN and routes reads to the replica only after it has caught up.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres hot standby has a hot_standby_feedback setting that lets the
replica tell the primary about its long-running queries, preventing VACUUM from removing tuples the
replica still needs — important for long reports. - Replication lag can grow unbounded under primary
write pressure; monitor it. - Aurora and other cloud Postgres variants have very low replication lag
(single-digit milliseconds) but it's still not zero.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "read replicas have the same isolation as the primary" — they have the
same isolation but against a stale snapshot. - Do not assume read-your-writes works on a replica.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle the read-your-writes problem in practice?" — Either route the
request to the primary if it follows a write in the same user session, or stick to eventually-consistent
semantics in the UI ("your changes will appear shortly").
-- On a Postgres replica
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- consistent within the transaction
-- but might be lag-stale relative to the primary
COMMIT;
Q212 · Implicit Isolation in JDBC and ORM Connection Pools
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan, Cred · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 219 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 220
In a typical Spring + HikariCP + Hibernate setup, how is the transaction isolation level set, and
what bugs can you hit?
The 30-second answer: The isolation level can be set at the HikariCP pool level (default per connection),
in JDBC via Connection.setTransactionIsolation(), in Spring via 
@Transactional(isolation = ...), or in SQL inside the transaction. The bugs come from these
layers disagreeing — a Spring annotation that's silently ignored, a pool default that's reset between
checkouts, or an ORM that lazy-starts a transaction without inheriting your setting.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The layers, top down: application code (Spring @Transactional)
→ ORM (Hibernate session) → JDBC connection (HikariCP) → engine session. 2. Spring's 
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE) calls 
Connection.setTransactionIsolation() on the underlying JDBC connection when the
transaction starts. Without the annotation, you get the connection's default. 3. HikariCP has a 
transactionIsolation property that sets the default for every connection it hands out. If the
application changes it during a transaction and forgets to reset, the next user inherits the change. 4. The
classic bug: @Transactional on a method that's called via this.method() instead of an
injected proxy — Spring's AOP doesn't intercept, the annotation is ignored, you silently run at the
connection default.
Edge cases to mention: - HikariCP resets connection state on return-to-pool only if 
resetConnectionOnClose is enabled — read the version's docs. - Hibernate's 
FlushMode.AUTO can cause writes to happen before the transaction is explicitly committed —
surprising for code reading the database between statements. - The propagation attribute on 
@Transactional interacts with the isolation level — nested propagation creates savepoints, not new
transactions.
What NOT to say: - Do not trust that @Transactional is honoured without verifying with a test that
inspects the actual isolation level. - Do not set the pool default to Serializable and assume the app is safe
— every read query now pays the cost.
Common follow-up: "How do you verify the isolation level is actually being applied?" — Run SELECT
current_setting('transaction_isolation') (Postgres) or SELECT
@@transaction_isolation (MySQL) inside the transaction and log the result; better, write a test that
asserts the value.
// Spring + JDBC, explicit isolation
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE)
public void transferFunds(long fromId, long toId, BigDecimal amount) {
    // Inside this method, the JDBC connection runs at Serializable
    // until the method returns and Spring commits/rolls back
}

Q213 · Putting It All Together — Picking the Right Level for a Real Scenario
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Goldman, JP Morgan · Topic: Isolation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You're designing a peer-to-peer payments service in India. Walk me through the isolation level
choices for each major transaction type.
The 30-second answer: Transfer between two accounts: Read Committed with 
SELECT FOR UPDATE on both account rows. User-balance display: Read Committed, single query.
Periodic settlement reconciliation: Repeatable Read on a read replica. Promo-code redemption with
limited-quantity inventory: Serializable with retry, because the invariant is multi-row. Idempotency-key
checks: Read Committed with a unique constraint as the real guard.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. List the transaction types in the system: transfer, balance read,
statement generation, reconciliation, promo-code redemption, idempotency-key lookup. 2. For each,
identify the invariants and the read-write pattern. 3. Transfer: read two balances, validate sufficient funds,
debit, credit, log. Multi-row write but no multi-row invariant beyond conservation; SELECT FOR UPDATE
on both rows at Read Committed is enough. 4. Balance display: read one row; no isolation concern,
Read Committed. 5. Statement generation: range query over many rows; needs a consistent snapshot,
so Repeatable Read. 6. Reconciliation: hours-long aggregate over the whole ledger; Repeatable Read on
a read replica to avoid affecting OLTP, ideally Postgres's READ ONLY DEFERRABLE Serializable. 7.
Promo-code redemption: invariant "no more than N redemptions"; Serializable with retry, or a database-
side counter with atomic decrement and a CHECK constraint. 8. Idempotency-key check: insert into
idempotency_keys table with the key as a unique constraint; the constraint enforces uniqueness,
isolation level is irrelevant.
Edge cases to mention: - Indian regulatory requirements (RBI guidelines for PPI and PA-PG operators)
often dictate audit trail integrity — append-only ledger tables with strict isolation for the audit transaction.
- Idempotency keys solve duplicate-submission problems more elegantly than escalating isolation —
design the API contract to accept them. - Always benchmark — a theoretical isolation choice that
doubles your latency is the wrong choice.
What NOT to say: - Do not use one isolation level for the whole service — the levels exist to be picked
per transaction. - Do not skip the retry logic when using Repeatable Read or Serializable in Postgres —
both can raise serialization failures.
Common follow-up: "What does Razorpay or PhonePe actually do?" — They use a combination:
idempotency keys at the API layer, single-row atomic updates wherever possible (balance counters),
SELECT FOR UPDATE on the account row during transfer, and Repeatable Read for batch reconciliation.
The fanciest isolation level is rare in hot paths.

-- Transfer with SELECT FOR UPDATE at Read Committed
BEGIN;
-- lock both rows in a deterministic order to avoid deadlock
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts
  WHERE id IN (101, 202)
  ORDER BY id
  FOR UPDATE;
