Chapter 5, Part B — Locking & MVCC
This is where the rubber actually meets the road on isolation. Part A talked about what the isolation levels
promise; Part B is about how engines deliver on those promises — through lock managers, lock modes,
intent hierarchies, and the elegant trick called MVCC that lets readers and writers stop fighting each
other. The questions below come up almost exclusively in product company rounds (Razorpay, Cred,
Flipkart, PhonePe, Swiggy, Zerodha) and GCC senior rounds (Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan India,
AmEx, Wells Fargo) where the panel wants to know if you can debug a production lock-wait incident at 2
AM. Spend extra time on the MVCC, VACUUM, and SELECT FOR UPDATE blocks — those three topics
together account for roughly 60% of the lock-related follow-ups I've seen.
Q214 · Shared (S) Lock vs Exclusive (X) Lock — The Basics
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Wells Fargo · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between a shared lock and an exclusive lock, and which operations
acquire which?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 222 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 223
The 30-second answer: A shared lock (S) lets multiple transactions read the same row concurrently but
blocks anyone from writing it. An exclusive lock (X) is grabbed for writes and blocks everyone else —
readers and writers both. S is compatible with S; X is compatible with nothing.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the compatibility line — that's the actual rule. S∥S = yes,
S∥X = no, X∥X = no. 2. Map to operations: plain SELECT historically takes S (in pure 2PL engines like
SQL Server under Read Committed without snapshot, or MySQL with LOCK IN SHARE MODE). 
INSERT/ UPDATE/ DELETE always takes X on the affected rows. 3. Crucial caveat: in modern
MVCC engines (Postgres, Oracle, MySQL InnoDB with default settings), plain SELECT does not take
an S lock at all — it reads from a snapshot. S locks are only acquired with explicit FOR SHARE / LOCK
IN SHARE MODE. 4. Be ready for: "So when do S locks actually appear in Postgres?" — mainly 
SELECT FOR SHARE and DDL operations like ALTER TABLE taking lower-mode table locks.
Edge cases to mention: - SQL Server with Read Committed (default) does take short-lived S locks
during reads — that's why writers can block readers there unless you enable Read Committed Snapshot
Isolation. - The lock is on the row in row-level engines, but logically the S/X distinction also applies at
page and table grain. - A transaction holding an S lock cannot be granted an X lock on the same row
until other S holders release — this is the classic lock-upgrade deadlock that the U lock was invented to
prevent.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "SELECT always takes a shared lock." In modern MVCC engines it
usually takes none. - Do not claim X locks block only writers; they block readers too in non-MVCC
engines.
Common follow-up: "If two transactions both hold an S lock on the same row and both want to upgrade
to X, what happens?" — Classic upgrade deadlock; both wait for the other to release S. Engines either
detect it and abort one, or use a separate U lock mode to prevent it (covered in Q3).
-- Postgres: explicit shared lock
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 7001 FOR SHARE;
-- another txn can also FOR SHARE this row, but cannot UPDATE it
COMMIT;
Q215 · Update (U) Lock — Why It Exists
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: SQL Server shops, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is an Update lock and what problem does it solve that plain S and X locks do not?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 223 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 224
The 30-second answer: A U lock is an intent-to-update marker — it is compatible with existing S locks
but incompatible with other U locks and with X locks. It prevents the lock-upgrade deadlock where two
transactions both hold S, both try to upgrade to X, and deadlock waiting for each other.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the scenario first: txn A and txn B both read row R with an S
lock (legal — S∥S). Both then decide to update it. Both request X. Both wait for the other to drop S.
Deadlock. 2. Solution: when a transaction reads a row that it might later update (e.g., UPDATE ...
WHERE cursor positioning), it takes a U lock instead of S. U∥S = yes (readers still allowed), but U∥U =
no (only one would-be updater at a time). 3. When the actual write happens, U is upgraded to X cleanly
— no other U holder is in the way. 4. This is heavily a SQL Server / Sybase concept. Oracle and Postgres
avoid the problem differently via MVCC and explicit FOR UPDATE/ FOR NO KEY UPDATE modes
(Postgres takes a row-exclusive marker directly).
Edge cases to mention: - U locks appear in SQL Server query plans when you see WITH (UPDLOCK)
hints — used in read-then-write patterns inside the same transaction. - The U lock model assumes a 2PL
engine; in MVCC engines it does not strictly apply, but the analogous problem still exists and is solved by
SELECT FOR UPDATE. - The classic SQL Server pattern: SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK,
HOLDLOCK) WHERE id = ? to grab a U lock that survives until commit.
What NOT to say: - Do not say Postgres has U locks — it does not in the SQL Server sense. - Do not
call it an "upgrade lock that lets two transactions write" — only one U at a time on a row.
Common follow-up: "How does Postgres avoid this same deadlock without a U lock?" — Through 
SELECT FOR UPDATE which directly takes a row-exclusive lock at read time, and through MVCC
which avoids the S-lock-during-read situation entirely.
-- SQL Server: take U lock during read so subsequent UPDATE doesn't deadlock
BEGIN TRAN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK) WHERE id = 7001;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 7001;
COMMIT;
Q216 · Intent Locks — IS, IX, SIX and the Hierarchy
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What are intent locks (IS, IX, SIX) and why does the lock manager need them?
The 30-second answer: Intent locks are coarse-grained markers placed on a parent object (table or
page) saying "some child rows are locked in S or X mode." They let the engine check table-level
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 224 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 225
compatibility in O(1) instead of scanning every row, which is what makes lock escalation and table-level
operations like ALTER TABLE performant.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Without intent locks, when someone wants to lock the whole table in
X mode (say, an ALTER), they'd have to walk every row to confirm nobody holds a conflicting lock. That's
catastrophically slow on a billion-row table. 2. With intent locks, every row-level S sets an IS on the table;
every row-level X sets an IX. To take a table X, you check the table itself — if any IS or IX exists, you wait.
3. SIX is a compound mode: S on the table (you are reading the whole thing) plus IX (you are also writing
some specific rows). It exists so that bulk-read-mostly-with-occasional-writes scans don't need to
constantly transition between modes. 4. Compatibility matrix matters: IS∥IS = yes, IS∥IX = yes, IX∥IX =
yes (both intent only — actual row conflicts checked at row level), IS∥X = no, IX∥S = no, SIX∥SIX = no.
Edge cases to mention: - All major engines (SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL InnoDB, DB2) use intent locks;
only some expose them in monitoring views. - In Postgres these are expressed as table-level lock modes
like ROW SHARE, ROW EXCLUSIVE, SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE — same idea, different vocabulary. -
The hierarchy can be three or four levels deep: database → table → page → row. Each level needs its
own intent.
What NOT to say: - Do not say intent locks "lock the table." They do not block compatible work — they
only block conflicting coarse-grained requests. - Do not skip SIX — interviewers love testing whether you
know the compound mode exists.
Common follow-up: "Translate ROW SHARE in Postgres to SQL Server vocabulary." — That is
approximately IS — taken by SELECT FOR SHARE/ FOR UPDATE to allow row work while signalling
intent at table level.
-- Postgres: SELECT FOR UPDATE takes ROW SHARE on the table (analogous to IS/IX)
BEGIN;
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 7001 FOR UPDATE;
-- table-level ROW SHARE blocks competing ALTER TABLE but not other FOR UPDATEs on other rows
COMMIT;
Q217 · Row-level vs Page-level vs Table-level Locks
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Walmart Labs · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through row, page and table-level locks — what are the tradeoffs and which engine does
what by default?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 225 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 226
The 30-second answer: Finer granularity gives higher concurrency but higher overhead per lock
(memory, lock manager CPU); coarser granularity is cheap but blocks more transactions. Postgres,
Oracle, and MySQL InnoDB lock at the row level by default. SQL Server starts at the row level and can
escalate to page or table when row counts cross a threshold (around 5000 locks per statement).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Cost model: each lock takes around 100-200 bytes of memory in the
lock manager. A million-row UPDATE means a million locks — gigabytes of lock metadata, slow lookups.
2. Page-level (8 KB in Postgres/SQL Server, 16 KB in InnoDB): one lock covers all rows on the page.
Cheap but causes false conflicts when two transactions touch different rows that happen to live on the
same page. 3. Table-level: one lock, maximum blocking. Used for DDL and explicit LOCK TABLE. 4.
Engine defaults: Postgres only locks at row and table grain — no page locks. Oracle row only. InnoDB
row only. SQL Server row by default but escalates.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres uses a separate predicate-lock mechanism for SSI Serializable
instead of page locks — predicate locks are tracked in a special structure and can sit at index-page grain
internally. - InnoDB's row lock is logically a lock on an index record, not on a heap tuple — important
when explaining gap locks (Q12). - SQL Server's lock escalation can be tuned per table (ALTER
TABLE ... SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = DISABLE | TABLE | AUTO)).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres uses page locks by default" — it doesn't. - Do not claim row-
level is always best — there's a memory cliff at scale.
Common follow-up: "What happens when SQL Server hits the escalation threshold?" — It tries to take a
table-level X (or S, matching the work), and if that's not immediately available, it can fail with lock-
escalation deadlock errors. Usually resolved by raising threshold or batching.
-- SQL Server: disable lock escalation on a hot table
ALTER TABLE orders SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = DISABLE);
Q218 · Lock Compatibility Matrix
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Cred · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Draw the lock compatibility matrix for S, X, U, IS, IX and SIX. Which combinations are
compatible?
The 30-second answer: Anything purely intent-based (IS, IX) is compatible with anything that's also
intent-based or shared at the parent level. S conflicts with X, U, IX, SIX. X conflicts with everything
except — well, nothing. U is compatible with S only. SIX is compatible only with IS.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 226 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 227
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Memorise the principle, not the table: stronger modes block more.
The ordering roughly is IS < IX < S < SIX < U < X. 2. Two questions to ask of any pair: do they both want
to read (then mostly compatible), or does at least one want to write (then almost always conflict at the
right grain). 3. Intent locks at the table level don't conflict among themselves because the real conflict
check happens at the row level. 4. SIX is the trickiest — remember it means "I'm reading the whole thing
AND writing some rows" so it must block anyone who'd write the whole thing or read with intent to write.
Edge cases to mention: - The matrix is engine-specific in details — Oracle has additional modes like
SRX (Share Row eXclusive) that approximate SIX. - Schema locks (Sch-S, Sch-M in SQL Server) are a
separate hierarchy used for DDL — Sch-M blocks everything including reads. - Postgres has eight table-
level modes (ACCESS SHARE through ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) — same compatibility logic, different
names.
What NOT to say: - Do not recite the matrix without explaining the underlying principle — interviewers
will probe with edge pairs you haven't memorised. - Do not conflate row-grain and table-grain in the
same matrix.
Common follow-up: "If a transaction holds IX on a table and you want to take S on the table, can you?"
— No. IX means someone is writing rows; S means you want to read the whole consistent table. They
conflict.
-- Postgres: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (taken by DROP TABLE) blocks every other mode
-- BEGIN; DROP TABLE accounts; -- waits behind any open SELECT
Q219 · SELECT FOR UPDATE — What It Locks and When To Use It
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Zerodha, Flipkart · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does SELECT FOR UPDATE actually lock, and give me a real scenario where you'd use it.
The 30-second answer: It places a row-level exclusive intent on every row the query returns, blocking
other transactions from updating, deleting, or locking those rows until you commit. Use it for the classic
read-check-then-write pattern, e.g., reading a wallet balance, validating it's enough, then debiting.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Mechanics: in Postgres it takes a FOR UPDATE row lock (strongest
row-lock mode), in InnoDB it takes an X record lock plus relevant gap locks under Repeatable Read. 2.
Concrete payments scenario: wallet debit. Without FOR UPDATE, two concurrent debit requests can
both read the same balance, both pass the "enough money" check, and both write — overdrafting the
wallet. With FOR UPDATE, the second one waits. 3. Crucial: it must be inside a transaction. Outside a
transaction the lock is released immediately and you've gained nothing. 4. Be ready for FOR UPDATE
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 227 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 228
NOWAIT and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED variants — SKIP LOCKED is the killer feature for job
queues built on a SQL table.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres, FOR UPDATE also locks rows referenced by foreign keys from
the selected rows — sometimes more than you expect. Use FOR NO KEY UPDATE if you don't need
that. - It does not prevent INSERT of new rows that would also match the WHERE clause — that's the
phantom problem; gap locks (Q12) handle that in InnoDB Repeatable Read. - In auto-commit mode
(default for many drivers), each statement is its own transaction — FOR UPDATE effectively does
nothing.
What NOT to say: - Do not say it locks the table — it locks only the returned rows (plus, in InnoDB,
gaps). - Do not skip the "must be in a transaction" point.
Common follow-up: "What is FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED used for?" — Worker queue pulling. Worker
A picks row 1, locks it; worker B's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1 skips row 1
and grabs row 2. No queue server needed.
-- Wallet debit, safe against concurrent debits
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user_id = 91234 FOR UPDATE;
-- application checks balance >= 500
UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE user_id = 91234;
COMMIT;
Q220 · SELECT FOR NO KEY UPDATE and FOR KEY SHARE (Postgres)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Postgres-heavy shops · Topic: Locking ·
Dialect: Postgres
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres has four row-lock modes for SELECT — FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR
SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE. When would you pick the weaker ones?
The 30-second answer: The weaker modes exist so that you don't accidentally block foreign-key
checks. FOR KEY SHARE is the lightest — it only blocks transactions that would change the key
columns. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is the write equivalent — you're updating, but not the key, so FK
checks from other tables can still proceed.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Hierarchy from weakest to strongest: FOR KEY SHARE < FOR
SHARE < FOR NO KEY UPDATE < FOR UPDATE. 2. Postgres takes FOR KEY SHARE automatically on
rows referenced by an FK during INSERT/UPDATE of child rows. That means if you grab FOR UPDATE
on a parent row, you block child INSERTs — often unintended. 3. Use FOR NO KEY UPDATE in the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 228 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 229
common case (updating a non-key column like balance or status) — it doesn't block child-table
FK validations. 4. Use FOR KEY SHARE if you want to read a row and ensure its primary key won't
change (e.g., long-running computation referencing it) but allow updates to other columns.
Edge cases to mention: - This is largely a Postgres concern; MySQL InnoDB's analogue is the
difference between record locks and gap locks. - Forgetting to use FOR NO KEY UPDATE in high-
throughput payments where parent rows are constantly updated can cause cascading slowdowns on
child INSERTs. - The four modes were added in Postgres 9.3; pre-9.3 code that uses FOR UPDATE may
now over-lock unnecessarily — worth auditing.
What NOT to say: - Do not say all four are interchangeable. - Do not claim FOR KEY SHARE is "read-
only" — it does take a lock and is visible in pg_locks.
Common follow-up: "I have a users table referenced by orders. I do FOR UPDATE on a user row.
Why are my order INSERTs now slow?" — Because INSERT into orders takes FOR KEY SHARE on the
parent user row, which conflicts with your FOR UPDATE. Switch to FOR NO KEY UPDATE.
-- Update non-key column without blocking child FK inserts
BEGIN;
SELECT id, balance FROM users WHERE id = 91234 FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
UPDATE users SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 91234;
COMMIT;
Q221 · Lock Escalation — SQL Server and Oracle
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Locking · Dialect:
SQL Server, Oracle
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is lock escalation, when does it trigger, and why is it sometimes a problem?
The 30-second answer: Lock escalation is the engine deciding that holding too many fine-grained locks
is wasteful and converting them to one coarse lock. SQL Server does this when a single statement holds
approximately 5000 row/page locks; Oracle effectively does not escalate (it claims to keep row-level
forever). Escalation can suddenly block unrelated transactions because what was hundreds of row locks
becomes one table lock.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The motive: lock manager memory. At several gigabytes per million-
row UPDATE, escalation reclaims memory by collapsing many row locks into one table lock. 2. SQL
Server's threshold is around 5000 locks on a single object in one statement, or when total lock memory
exceeds a percentage of buffer pool. It tries to escalate; if blocked, retries periodically. 3. The risk: a
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 229 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 230
long-running UPDATE that escalates suddenly blocks all concurrent SELECTs on the same table. The
application sees a stall with no clear cause. 4. Mitigation: batch large updates into chunks of a few
hundred rows each, or ALTER TABLE ... SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = DISABLE).
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres does not escalate row locks to table locks — but it has a different
problem: it stores row locks inside the tuple header (using XID + multixact), so they're free in terms of
lock manager memory. - InnoDB also doesn't escalate — it has a fixed-size lock-table that can pressure
memory if you UPDATE a million rows in one transaction. - DB2 LUW escalates similarly to SQL Server
with a LOCKLIST parameter.
What NOT to say: - Do not say Postgres escalates — common myth. - Do not claim escalation always
helps performance — it usually hurts concurrency.
Common follow-up: "How would you safely UPDATE 10 million rows in SQL Server?" — Loop in
batches of 1000-5000 rows with explicit transactions, ideally driven by the primary key, with brief pauses
for the log to checkpoint.
-- SQL Server: batched delete to avoid escalation
WHILE 1 = 1
BEGIN
  DELETE TOP (1000) FROM audit_log WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01';
  IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 BREAK;
  WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:00.100';
END
Q222 · Lock Granularity Tradeoffs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If I asked you to design a lock manager, how would you decide whether to lock at row, page, or
table grain?
The 30-second answer: Optimise for the dominant access pattern. OLTP with single-row reads and
writes → row level. Bulk DML and DDL → table level. Anything in between either picks the smallest grain
that still gives reasonable lock-manager memory, or starts small and escalates.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Cost dimensions: lock memory (per-lock overhead), lock manager
CPU (hash-table lookups), false conflicts (two unrelated rows on same page), application latency under
contention. 2. Tradeoff curve: row level minimises false conflicts but inflates memory; table level
minimises memory but creates massive contention. 3. Mixed workloads benefit from escalation
strategies (SQL Server) or skipping page-level entirely with cheap row locks stored in tuple headers
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 230 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 231
(Postgres MVCC). 4. Design rule: pick row-level for OLTP, accept escalation or batch large jobs, use
explicit LOCK TABLE only for migrations or one-time backfills.
Edge cases to mention: - For analytics / append-only fact tables, table-level locks are often fine
because there's only one writer (the ETL). - For job-queue tables with SKIP LOCKED, row-level is
mandatory — otherwise workers serialize. - Page-level locks made sense in the 1990s when memory
was scarce; modern systems mostly avoid them.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always use the finest grain." Memory matters. - Do not say table-level
locks are always bad — they're correct for DDL.
Common follow-up: "What if you have a hot row that 10K txns/sec want to write?" — Row-level locking
won't save you; you need application-level sharding (split the counter, advisory locks, queue serialization,
or in-memory aggregation).
-- Postgres ROW EXCLUSIVE (row-level X-intent) blocks DDL but not other row writes on other rows
BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku = 'IPH-15-BLK-128';
COMMIT;
Q223 · MVCC — What It Is and Why Readers Don't Block Writers
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Postgres-heavy shops, Goldman · Topic:
MVCC
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain MVCC in your own words. Why does it mean readers don't block writers, and writers
don't block readers?
The 30-second answer: MVCC stores multiple versions of each row, tagged with the transaction IDs
that created and deleted them. A reader sees the version visible to its snapshot — it never needs to lock
anything, because the version it wants is already there. Writers create new versions without disturbing
the old ones, so readers see consistent data while writes happen in parallel.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame against the alternative: pure 2PL. There, readers grab S,
writers grab X, and they collide. That's where the famous "writers block readers" pain comes from in
legacy SQL Server or DB2. 2. MVCC's insight: keep old versions around. When txn A reads at time T, it
sees the version that was current at T. When txn B writes concurrently, it creates version T+1 without
touching version T. 3. Snapshot is the key abstraction: each reading transaction has a snapshot of which
other transactions were committed when it started. It only sees rows from those committed txns. 4. Cost:
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 231 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 232
storage (old versions must persist until no snapshot needs them) and a cleanup mechanism (VACUUM in
Postgres, undo segments in Oracle, purge thread in InnoDB).
Edge cases to mention: - "Readers don't block writers" is specifically about plain SELECT. SELECT
FOR UPDATE does take a lock. - Two writers updating the same row still block each other in MVCC —
MVCC solves the read-write conflict, not the write-write one. - Long-running readers can prevent cleanup
of versions they might still need — operational pain (Q15).
What NOT to say: - Do not say MVCC eliminates all locking — it doesn't, only read locks (mostly). - Do
not say MVCC is free — the storage and cleanup cost is real.
Common follow-up: "What happens to memory/disk when a row is updated 10 times in MVCC?" — Ten
versions exist (briefly). Old ones cleaned up by VACUUM (Postgres) or undo expiration (Oracle/InnoDB).
Bloat happens when cleanup can't keep up.
-- Postgres: long SELECT does not block concurrent UPDATEs
-- Session A: BEGIN; SELECT * FROM large_report; -- runs for 10 min
-- Session B: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE id = 7001;  -- not blocked
Q224 · MVCC Implementations — Postgres vs Oracle vs MySQL InnoDB
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman, JP Morgan, Database-platform teams · Topic:
MVCC
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do Postgres, Oracle, and MySQL InnoDB each implement MVCC differently?
The 30-second answer: Postgres stores new versions inline in the heap (every UPDATE writes a new
tuple, old becomes dead, VACUUM cleans up). Oracle stores the current version in place and pushes the
old version into undo segments (UNDO tablespace). InnoDB does the same as Oracle — current row in
place, old versions in rollback segments — with the wrinkle that secondary indexes don't carry versions,
so they trigger extra lookups.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres approach (heap-versioned): pros are simple recovery, easy
hot-standby replay; cons are heap bloat, index bloat, and the VACUUM tax. 2. Oracle approach (undo
segments): the table always has the latest committed value; older snapshots reconstruct from undo.
Pros: tables stay compact, no VACUUM. Cons: long readers can hit 
ORA-01555 snapshot too old if undo retention is too low. 3. InnoDB approach: similar to Oracle
— clustered index has latest version, rollback segments hold older. Secondary indexes are not versioned,
so to honour snapshots, InnoDB also tracks "is this row visible at my snapshot" via a back-pointer to the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 232 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 233
clustered index — extra IO for index reads. 4. SQL Server (when RCSI/Snapshot Isolation is enabled)
stores old versions in tempdb, similar in spirit to Oracle's undo but in a separate storage.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres's HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) optimisation: if the update doesn't change
any indexed column, the new version chains to the old via a pointer and the index doesn't need updating
— huge win for hot updates. - Oracle's UNDO_RETENTION parameter trades off snapshot longevity
against tablespace size. - InnoDB's history list length (visible in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS) is
the lag indicator — high values mean long readers blocking purge.
What NOT to say: - Do not say all MVCC implementations are the same — they have very different
operational profiles. - Do not claim Oracle/InnoDB never have bloat — undo can grow unbounded under
pressure.
Common follow-up: "Why does Postgres need VACUUM but Oracle doesn't?" — Because Postgres
versions live in the same heap as live rows; Oracle keeps them in a separate UNDO area that has its own
lifecycle and expires automatically.
-- Postgres: see dead tuple count
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'accounts';
Q225 · Postgres Snapshot — xmin, xmax, txid Mechanics
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Postgres-heavy shops, Cred, Razorpay, Database teams · Topic: MVCC
· Dialect: Postgres
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
At a high level, how does Postgres decide which version of a row your transaction can see? What
are xmin and xmax?
The 30-second answer: Every row carries xmin (the transaction ID that inserted it) and xmax (the
transaction ID that deleted or updated it, zero if still live). When your txn starts, it captures a snapshot —
the set of currently active transactions. A row is visible if its xmin is committed-and-before-snapshot,
and its xmax is either zero, in-the-future, or aborted.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Two hidden system columns: xmin, xmax. Plus cmin, cmax
for sub-transaction (command) ordering. 2. Snapshot at txn start: an xmin cutoff (oldest still-running
txn), an xmax cutoff (next txid to be assigned), and a list of active xids in between. 3. Visibility rules:
row is visible if its xmin is committed and not in the active list, AND its xmax is null or invisible
(uncommitted or in active list). 4. UPDATE doesn't modify a row in place — it writes a new row with new
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 233 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 234
xmin and marks the old row's xmax. The old row stays around until VACUUM determines no snapshot
can still see it.
Edge cases to mention: - Transaction ID wraparound: xids are 32-bit, so after 2 billion they wrap.
Postgres VACUUM FREEZE prevents catastrophic data loss by marking rows as visible to all current
and future txns. - Subtransactions (savepoints) use a separate xid that combines with the parent's. - 
txid_current() returns the current transaction's ID; pg_current_snapshot() returns the
snapshot for debugging.
What NOT to say: - Do not say xmin/xmax are visible columns by default — they're hidden but
accessible via SELECT xmin, xmax FROM table. - Do not confuse txid (a global counter) with the
visibility rules (which use the snapshot relative to that counter).
Common follow-up: "What happens if I never VACUUM and run out of txids?" — Wraparound failure:
Postgres halts writes to protect data. The dreaded "must be vacuumed within X transactions" warning
leads to forced shutdown if ignored.
-- Inspect MVCC metadata on rows
SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM accounts WHERE id = 7001;
Q226 · VACUUM in Postgres — Why It Exists
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Postgres shops, Razorpay, Cred, Database-platform teams · Topic:
MVCC · Dialect: Postgres
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why does Postgres need VACUUM? What exactly does it do?
The 30-second answer: VACUUM reclaims space from dead tuples (the old row versions left behind by
UPDATE/DELETE) so the heap doesn't grow forever, and it advances the "frozen xid" pointer to prevent
transaction ID wraparound. Without VACUUM, both bloat and wraparound shutdown would eventually
kill the database.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. UPDATE in Postgres = INSERT new + mark old dead. The dead tuple
still occupies its slot on the page; new inserts can't reuse it until VACUUM frees it. 2. Plain VACUUM
marks dead tuple space as reusable (visible in the free-space map) but does not return space to the OS
— the file stays the same size. New rows fill the holes. 3. VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table to
compact it and returns space to the OS, but takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — i.e., the table is
unreadable for the duration. Almost never run in production. 4. VACUUM also updates the visibility map
(helps index-only scans), advances xid horizon (FREEZE), and updates statistics if VACUUM ANALYZE.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 234 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 235
Edge cases to mention: - VACUUM cannot remove a dead tuple if any active transaction's snapshot
might still need it — long readers block cleanup (Q15). - pg_visibility extension lets you inspect
which pages are all-visible / all-frozen. - Toast tables (out-of-line storage for large columns) have their
own VACUUM cycles.
What NOT to say: - Do not say VACUUM "frees disk space" by default — it doesn't, only VACUUM
FULL does. - Do not say it's optional — autovacuum runs automatically for a reason.
Common follow-up: "Why is VACUUM FULL dangerous on a busy table?" — It takes an exclusive lock
for the entire rewrite. On a 100 GB table, that's potentially hours of blocked traffic. Use pg_repack for
online equivalent.
-- Manual vacuum with stats update
VACUUM ANALYZE orders;
-- See bloat estimate per table
SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(relid)) AS size,
       n_dead_tup, n_live_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10;
Q227 · Autovacuum — Triggers and Tuning
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy shops, Database teams · Topic: MVCC
· Dialect: Postgres
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When does autovacuum kick in, and what would you tune on a high-write table?
The 30-second answer: Autovacuum triggers on a table when dead tuples exceed 
autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor * n_live_tup
(default 50 + 0.2 × live rows). On a million-row hot table, that means waiting for ~200K dead tuples
before any cleanup — usually too lazy. Tune by lowering the scale factor or per-table threshold.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Default triggers: 20% dead-tuple fraction, plus statistics-based
analyze trigger at 10%. Both are way too high for tables with millions of rows and high churn. 2. Per-table
override: ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,
autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.01); — runs at 2% dead instead of 20%. 3.
Concurrency: by default, only a few autovacuum workers run at once (autovacuum_max_workers,
default 3). On a multi-TB DB with many hot tables, this is a bottleneck — raise it. 4. Cost-based
throttling: autovacuum sleeps based on autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit/ cost_delay to limit
IO impact. On SSDs you almost always want to raise the limit so vacuum finishes faster.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 235 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 236
Edge cases to mention: - Anti-wraparound vacuum (for prevention of wraparound) is non-
skippable — even if you've disabled autovacuum on a table, this kind runs. It's also more expensive (full
scan). - Autovacuum can be starved by long open transactions — VACUUM can't remove tuples newer
than the oldest snapshot. - Postgres 13+ added per-index vacuum parallelism
( max_parallel_maintenance_workers).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "disable autovacuum and run nightly manual VACUUM" — invites
wraparound disasters. - Do not claim defaults are fine for everyone — they're tuned for tiny conservative
installs.
Common follow-up: "How do you know autovacuum is falling behind?" — Check 
pg_stat_user_tables.last_autovacuum and n_dead_tup. Also pg_stat_activity for
active autovacuum workers and pg_stat_progress_vacuum.
-- Tighter autovacuum for a hot table
ALTER TABLE transactions SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,
  autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.01
);
Q228 · Bloat — When VACUUM Isn't Enough, pg_repack
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy shops · Topic: MVCC · Dialect:
Postgres
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is table bloat, and what do you do when VACUUM alone can't recover it?
The 30-second answer: Bloat is dead tuple space that ordinary VACUUM has marked reusable but
never returned to the OS — over time the table file grows much larger than the live data inside it. If new
writes don't reuse the space fast enough (sparse delete patterns, long-stalled writers), you need a full
table rewrite. pg_repack does it online without the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that VACUUM FULL
takes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Detect bloat: compare pg_relation_size(table) against live
row count × average row size. Or use pgstattuple / pg_repack --dry-run for a precise
estimate. 2. Why VACUUM alone fails: if you DELETE the head of a table (oldest rows) and only INSERT
to the end, the leading pages become permanently empty. VACUUM frees them but the file can only
truncate the trailing empty pages. 3. pg_repack solution: it creates a shadow table, copies live rows
in batches, replays changes via triggers, then swaps the relfilenode atomically. The lock window is
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 236 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 237
seconds, not hours. 4. Prevention: use partitioning so you can drop entire partitions instead of DELETE;
tune autovacuum aggressively on churn-heavy tables.
Edge cases to mention: - Index bloat is often worse than table bloat — every UPDATE writes a new
index entry. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+) rebuilds without locking. - pg_repack needs a
primary key or unique index; it cannot repack tables without one. - Toast tables also bloat independently
— sometimes the parent is fine but the toast is huge.
What NOT to say: - Do not recommend VACUUM FULL casually — production teams hate the lock
window. - Do not assume bloat = forgot to VACUUM — long-running readers and rare delete patterns
cause it even with perfect autovacuum.
Common follow-up: "What's the safest way to remove old data from a billion-row table?" — Partition by
date and drop partitions. DELETE doesn't truncate; partition drop does.
-- Detect bloat-prone tables (rough)
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup,
       n_dead_tup::float / NULLIF(n_live_tup, 0) AS dead_ratio
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_dead_tup > 10000
ORDER BY dead_ratio DESC NULLS LAST;
Q229 · Long-Running Transactions + Bloat — The Operational Risk
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres shops, On-call interviews · Topic: MVCC
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
One of your developers leaves a transaction open for two hours. What can go wrong in Postgres?
The 30-second answer: The long transaction holds back the global xmin horizon — VACUUM cannot
remove any dead tuple newer than that transaction's snapshot. So across every table in the database,
bloat accumulates. After enough hours, hot tables grow several times their normal size, queries slow
down, and disk fills.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Mechanism: VACUUM's correctness relies on never removing a tuple
any active snapshot might still need. The oldest snapshot in the system gates everything. 2. Symptoms:
monitoring shows n_dead_tup climbing, query latency creeping up, disk usage growing despite no
new data. pg_stat_activity shows one txn with xact_start hours ago. 3. Defense: 
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (kills sessions sitting idle inside a transaction), 
statement_timeout (kills long single queries), monitoring on now() - xact_start > '10
minutes'. 4. Same issue exists in Oracle (snapshot too old at the opposite end — the long reader fails)
and InnoDB (history list grows, purge falls behind).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 237 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 238
Edge cases to mention: - Replication slots can also pin xmin — an unconsumed logical replication slot
has the same effect as a forgotten transaction. - A 2-hour analytical SELECT on a read replica with 
hot_standby_feedback=on propagates the xmin pin back to the primary, causing primary bloat. -
Application connection-pool middleware that swallows commits can silently leave txns open.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "long transactions are only bad in Postgres." They're problematic
everywhere, just in different ways. - Do not suggest disabling autovacuum as a fix — that makes it
worse.
Common follow-up: "How would you find and kill a long-running idle transaction?" — Query 
pg_stat_activity for state = 'idle in transaction' and old state_change, then 
pg_terminate_backend(pid).
SELECT pid, usename, state, age(now(), xact_start) AS txn_age, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state IN ('idle in transaction', 'active')
  AND xact_start < now() - INTERVAL '5 minutes'
ORDER BY xact_start;
Q230 · Gap Locks (MySQL InnoDB)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: MySQL-heavy shops, Flipkart, PhonePe, Swiggy, Razorpay · Topic:
Locking · Dialect: MySQL InnoDB
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a gap lock in InnoDB, and what problem does it solve?
The 30-second answer: A gap lock locks the empty space between index records, preventing other
transactions from INSERTing rows that would land in that gap. InnoDB uses gap locks under Repeatable
Read to prevent phantom reads — without them, a re-executed range query could see new rows that
didn't exist before.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The phantom problem: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount
> 1000 returns 10 rows. Another txn INSERTs an order with amount 5000. You re-execute. Now 11
rows. That's a phantom. 2. Pure row locks don't help — you can only lock rows that exist. To prevent the
INSERT, you must lock the gap into which the new row would be inserted. 3. Gap locks are taken on
index records — InnoDB locks the gap between consecutive index entries. Under Repeatable Read,
range scans automatically take gap locks on the searched range. 4. Tradeoff: gap locks reduce
concurrency significantly. Two concurrent INSERTs into the same range can block even if they're on
totally different rows. That's why MySQL also offers Read Committed which disables gap locks.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 238 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 239
Edge cases to mention: - Gap locks only exist on unique-index range scans and non-unique index
lookups; primary-key point lookups don't take them. - SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a range under
Repeatable Read takes gap + record locks across the entire range. Heavy contention risk. - READ
COMMITTED + innodb_locks_unsafe_for_binlog (now deprecated naming) disables gap locks
but sacrifices phantom prevention.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "gap locks prevent updates" — they prevent INSERTs into the gap,
updates of existing rows are governed by row locks. - Do not claim Postgres has gap locks — Postgres
uses MVCC + predicate locks (Q19) for the same problem.
Common follow-up: "Why did my INSERT block another INSERT on a totally different value?" — Likely a
gap lock from a range SELECT FOR UPDATE in the first txn. Switch to Read Committed or narrow the
SELECT.
-- MySQL InnoDB under default Repeatable Read
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000 FOR UPDATE;
-- Other sessions cannot INSERT orders with amount in [1000, 5000] until commit
COMMIT;
Q231 · Next-Key Locks (MySQL InnoDB)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: MySQL-heavy shops, Flipkart, PhonePe, Swiggy · Topic: Locking ·
Dialect: MySQL InnoDB
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a next-key lock in InnoDB and how does it relate to gap locks?
The 30-second answer: A next-key lock is the combination of a record lock on a row plus a gap lock on
the gap immediately before it. It's the default lock mode for InnoDB index scans under Repeatable Read,
providing phantom-read prevention plus row exclusion in one unit.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Mental model: imagine the index entries as [5, 10, 20, 30]. A
next-key lock on the entry 20 covers the row 20 AND the gap (10, 20) — i.e., everything from
just after 10 up to and including 20. 2. When you SELECT ... WHERE x > 15 FOR UPDATE,
InnoDB takes next-key locks on 20 and 30 — that's row 20, gap (10,20), row 30, gap (20,30), plus
the supremum gap (30, +∞) so no INSERT > 30 either. 3. Compared to plain gap locks alone, next-key
locks let one operation atomically lock both the row and its predecessor gap, which is what you actually
need for range scans. 4. Disabled in Read Committed (no gap component, just record locks remain).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 239 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 240
Edge cases to mention: - Next-key locking on unique indexes with exact match degenerates to just the
record lock (no gap needed — uniqueness already prevents new identical row). - In replication-heavy
setups, next-key locks were once required for statement-based binlog correctness; row-based binlog
relaxes this. - Visible in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS as lock_mode X locks gap before
rec and similar.
What NOT to say: - Do not say next-key = next row lock — it specifically includes the preceding gap. -
Do not claim it's unique to MySQL — the concept exists in other engines under different names but is
most explicit in InnoDB.
Common follow-up: "Why does a SELECT FOR UPDATE on a non-existent row block other writers?" —
Even though the row doesn't exist, InnoDB takes a gap lock on where it would be, preventing concurrent
INSERT of that key. This is what makes INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE correct against
concurrent inserts.
-- InnoDB Repeatable Read; next-key locks across the range
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > 5000 FOR UPDATE;
-- Locks rows AND gaps; no new row with id > 5000 can be inserted
COMMIT;
Q232 · Predicate Locks (Postgres SSI)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Postgres shops, Razorpay, Cred, Database teams · Topic: Locking ·
Dialect: Postgres
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres claims Serializable without taking strict locks like InnoDB does. How does that work?
The 30-second answer: Postgres uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which builds on MVCC by
tracking lightweight predicate locks — records of which ranges a transaction read. At commit time, if the
system detects a dangerous read-write dependency cycle among active txns, one is aborted with a
serialization failure. No range gap locks at write time.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. MVCC alone gives Repeatable Read snapshot consistency but
allows write skew (Q from Part A). SSI adds detection. 2. Predicate locks (not real exclusive locks): for
each SELECT in a Serializable txn, Postgres records the predicate (often as page-level read marks). They
don't block anyone — they're metadata. 3. When two transactions form a "dangerous structure" — A
reads what B wrote and B reads what A wrote — SSI aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001
( serialization_failure). 4. The cost is occasional spurious aborts, which the application must
retry. The benefit is no blocking at write time — high concurrency for read-heavy Serializable workloads.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 240 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 241
Edge cases to mention: - SSI's predicate-lock memory is bounded; very long transactions can cause
Postgres to escalate to page-level or relation-level conflict tracking, increasing false aborts. - Read-only
optimisation: Postgres detects truly read-only Serializable txns and skips overhead entirely. - Not all
dialects with "Serializable" do SSI — Oracle's Serializable is closer to Snapshot Isolation, InnoDB's adds
explicit range locks.
What NOT to say: - Do not say Postgres Serializable is "lock-free" — it tracks reads via predicate-lock
structures, just not blocking ones. - Do not promise zero aborts — applications must retry on 40001.
Common follow-up: "How would my application code handle a Serializable abort?" — Catch SQLSTATE
40001, sleep briefly with jitter, and re-run the entire transaction. Idempotency at the application boundary
is critical.
-- Serializable txn; application must be ready for 40001 retry
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE status = 'pending';
INSERT INTO ledger_entries (...) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;
Q233 · Lock-Free Reads vs Locking Reads — MVCC Default
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Walmart Labs · Topic: MVCC
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In an MVCC database, when does a SELECT take a lock versus when is it lock-free?
The 30-second answer: Plain SELECT (no FOR clause) is lock-free under MVCC — it reads the
snapshot, takes no row locks, blocks no writers. Locking reads happen only when you explicitly ask: 
FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR KEY SHARE (Postgres), or LOCK IN
SHARE MODE (MySQL).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The lock-free default is the whole point of MVCC — reads never
block writes. 2. Locking reads exist for the read-check-then-write idiom where you need to make sure
the row doesn't change between SELECT and UPDATE. 3. Important caveat: at the table level, even plain
SELECT takes a weak ACCESS SHARE (Postgres) / IS (InnoDB) intent lock — it blocks DROP/ALTER
but nothing else. 4. SQL Server's situation differs by isolation: with Read Committed (legacy default)
reads take short S locks; with Read Committed Snapshot (RCSI) reads are MVCC and lock-free.
Edge cases to mention: - SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT returns immediately with an error
instead of blocking — useful for "try to lock" UX. - SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED skips
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 241 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 242
already-locked rows — ideal for worker queues. - Even lock-free reads can be slow if they have to chase
long version chains (high history-list / many dead tuples).
What NOT to say: - Do not say all SELECTs are lock-free — explicit locking modes exist. - Do not forget
the weak table-level intent.
Common follow-up: "What stops a worker from picking the same job twice in a SKIP LOCKED queue?"
— The row-level lock from the first worker is incompatible; second worker's SKIP LOCKED simply moves
past it. Atomic, no race.
-- Postgres worker queue picking one job, skipping locked ones
BEGIN;
SELECT id, payload FROM job_queue
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY priority, id
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1;
-- process the job, UPDATE status = 'done', COMMIT
Q234 · Pessimistic vs Optimistic Concurrency
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Swiggy, Goldman · Topic: Concurrency
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between pessimistic and optimistic concurrency control, and when would
you pick each?
The 30-second answer: Pessimistic locks the row up front (e.g., SELECT FOR UPDATE), assuming a
conflict is likely; optimistic doesn't lock but checks a version number at commit time, assuming conflicts
are rare. Pessimistic is safer under high contention but reduces throughput; optimistic is faster under low
contention but forces the application to handle retries.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Pessimistic pattern: open txn, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE,
perform business logic, UPDATE, commit. Lock held for the duration of business logic — bad if logic is
slow. 2. Optimistic pattern: SELECT with current version, do logic, then UPDATE ... WHERE id = ?
AND version = ? with SET version = version + 1. If row count is zero, someone else
updated — abort and retry. 3. Picking: high-contention hot rows (wallet of a celebrity) → pessimistic to
avoid retry storms. Low-contention many-row updates (user profile edits) → optimistic to avoid lock-
manager overhead. 4. Hybrid: optimistic first, fall back to pessimistic when retry rate exceeds a
threshold.
Edge cases to mention: - Optimistic doesn't prevent lost updates in the database — the WHERE clause
does. If the WHERE matches zero rows, the application must detect and retry. - Pessimistic over a slow
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 242 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 243
network is brutal — round-trip latency multiplied by lock-hold time means low throughput. - Optimistic
with a too-coarse version (whole row hash) gives false conflicts on independent column updates.
What NOT to say: - Do not say one is universally better. - Do not forget the application-level retry loop
for optimistic.
Common follow-up: "How do you implement optimistic locking in SQL?" — Version column or
last_updated timestamp; UPDATE WHERE id AND version, check affected-rows. Covered in Q22.
-- Optimistic update: only succeeds if version matches
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 500, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 7001 AND version = 12;
-- if affected_rows = 0, the row changed under us — retry
Q235 · Optimistic Locking — Version Column Pattern (OCC)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Flipkart, GCC mid · Topic: Concurrency
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Implement optimistic concurrency control with a version column. Walk me through both the
schema and the update statement.
The 30-second answer: Add an integer version column to the row. On every UPDATE, increment it
and include the old version in the WHERE. If the affected row count is zero, someone else won the race
— abort and retry the whole read-modify-write cycle.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Schema: ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN version INT
NOT NULL DEFAULT 0; 2. Read: SELECT id, balance, version FROM accounts WHERE id
= 7001; — capture version (say, 12). 3. Update: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance -
500, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7001 AND version = 12; — driver returns
affected-row count. 4. Branch on affected: 1 → success, 0 → conflict, re-read and retry up to N times
with jittered backoff.
Edge cases to mention: - Use INT BIGINT or a UUID for the version if you fear overflow over decades of
frequent updates. - A timestamp column is convenient but loses to clock skew on multi-master setups;
integer counter is safer. - Frameworks like Hibernate / JPA do this automatically with @Version — but
the application still must handle OptimisticLockException.
What NOT to say: - Do not skip the version-increment in the SET clause — without it the next conflict
can't be detected. - Do not retry infinitely — cap attempts and surface error to user.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 243 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 244
Common follow-up: "What if the user's edit and someone else's edit don't actually conflict — different
columns?" — With a single row-level version, you still get a false conflict. For finer detection, partition
fields into independent versioned groups or use per-column timestamps.
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  balance NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 500, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 7001 AND version = 12;
-- returns 1 if won, 0 if someone else updated since we read
Q236 · Pessimistic Locking — SELECT FOR UPDATE Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, TCS, Infosys · Topic: Concurrency
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me the canonical pessimistic locking pattern in SQL — a wallet debit with concurrency
safety.
The 30-second answer: Inside a transaction, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the wallet row to take a
row-exclusive lock, perform the balance check in application code, then UPDATE and commit. Other
concurrent debits wait for the lock to release.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open transaction. Outside a txn the FOR UPDATE lock is released
immediately. 2. SELECT FOR UPDATE on the wallet row. Blocks competing FOR UPDATEs on the same
row but lets unrelated rows proceed. 3. Application checks balance >= debit amount. If not, ROLLBACK
and surface insufficient-funds to user. 4. UPDATE the row, COMMIT — releases the lock for the next
waiter.
Edge cases to mention: - Always include a lock_timeout (Postgres) or 
innodb_lock_wait_timeout (MySQL) — never wait forever. - For multi-row debits in a fixed order
to avoid deadlocks (e.g., always lock lower-id wallet first when transferring). - Pair with 
SELECT FOR NO KEY UPDATE if foreign-key blocking from child tables is causing surprise stalls (Q7).
What NOT to say: - Do not forget the BEGIN — the most common bug. - Do not perform slow network
calls between SELECT FOR UPDATE and COMMIT — you'll block everyone.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 244 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 245
Common follow-up: "What if the debit logic takes 500 ms because of an external fraud-check API call?"
— Move the fraud check before the FOR UPDATE, or take the lock briefly only around the balance-and-
update, accepting a small risk window mitigated by idempotency.
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user_id = 91234 FOR UPDATE;
-- application: check balance >= 500, abort otherwise
UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE user_id = 91234;
INSERT INTO ledger (user_id, amount, type) VALUES (91234, -500, 'DEBIT');
COMMIT;
Q237 · Advisory Locks (Postgres pg_advisory_lock)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Postgres shops, Razorpay, Cred, Cron-job heavy backends · Topic:
Locking · Dialect: Postgres
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a Postgres advisory lock, and when would you use one instead of a row lock?
The 30-second answer: Advisory locks are application-defined locks identified by an arbitrary integer
key, with no row or table tied to them. Useful for mutual exclusion outside the data model — e.g., "only
one process runs the nightly billing job," "only one consumer can process this user's events," "claim
distributed leadership without an extra service."
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Two flavours: session-scoped (pg_advisory_lock(key) — held
until explicit unlock or session end) and transaction-scoped (pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) —
released at txn end). 2. Two variants per flavour: blocking (pg_advisory_lock) and try
( pg_try_advisory_lock — returns immediately with boolean). 3. Keys can be one bigint or two ints
(good for namespacing — pg_advisory_lock(MY_APP_NS, user_id)). 4. Visible in pg_locks
with locktype = 'advisory' — easy to monitor.
Edge cases to mention: - Session locks survive transaction boundaries — easy to leak. Always unlock
or rely on session end. - The key is just an integer; collisions between unrelated app features are possible
if you don't namespace. - For distributed leadership use cases, advisory locks beat Zookeeper/etcd if
Postgres is already on the critical path.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse advisory locks with row locks — they have no FK / row relationship.
- Do not use them as a substitute for FOR UPDATE on data rows.
Common follow-up: "How would you make sure a cron job runs on exactly one machine?" — Every box
tries pg_try_advisory_lock(unique_job_key). Only one succeeds, runs the job, releases.
Others retry next tick.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 245 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 246
-- Distributed mutual exclusion for a cron
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42); -- returns true on first caller
-- ... run the job ...
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42);
Q238 · LOCK TABLE — When (Almost Never) to Use Explicitly
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: GCC senior rounds, Migration-heavy teams · Topic: Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you use an explicit LOCK TABLE statement?
The 30-second answer: Almost never in OLTP. Legitimate uses are one-time migrations that need a brief
moment of exclusive access, fixing data corruption, or workflows where you genuinely need the whole
table held still (rare). For normal operations, row-level locks via FOR UPDATE are the right tool.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres syntax: LOCK TABLE accounts IN ACCESS
EXCLUSIVE MODE; — blocks every operation including SELECT. Eight modes available, picking the
weakest needed is critical. 2. MySQL: LOCK TABLES accounts WRITE; — but in InnoDB this is
usually unnecessary; row locks handle everything. 3. Use case: dual-write migration window — briefly
LOCK TABLE in EXCLUSIVE while you flip a feature flag, then release. 4. Risk: any LOCK TABLE in
production with no timeout becomes a stop-the-world incident if a previously-acquired weaker lock
holder is slow to release.
Edge cases to mention: - LOCK TABLE ... NOWAIT exists — returns error instead of waiting.
Always use it. - Postgres LOCK TABLE automatically takes the named mode plus all weaker modes —
picking ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks every read. - DDL like ALTER TABLE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
implicitly; that's the actual common case of "locking the whole table" without writing LOCK TABLE.
What NOT to say: - Do not say it's a normal performance tuning tool. - Do not skip the NOWAIT —
production stalls are how you learn this.
Common follow-up: "Why is online schema change tooling (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change,
pg_repack) a thing if we have LOCK TABLE?" — Because LOCK TABLE for an hour-long migration is
unacceptable. The tools rewrite the table in shadow form and swap atomically with a sub-second lock
window.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 246 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 247
-- Postgres: explicit lock with timeout to avoid runaway
BEGIN;
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
LOCK TABLE accounts IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE;
-- brief migration step
COMMIT;
Q239 · Waiting on Lock — lock_timeout, deadlock_timeout,
innodb_lock_wait_timeout
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: GCC senior rounds, On-call interviews, Razorpay, Cred · Topic:
Locking
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What knobs control how long a transaction waits for a lock, and what should the defaults be for
an OLTP application?
The 30-second answer: Postgres has lock_timeout (per-statement wait limit) and 
deadlock_timeout (how long to wait before running deadlock detection). MySQL InnoDB has 
innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 seconds — way too high for OLTP). SQL Server has 
LOCK_TIMEOUT (per-session, default infinite). For OLTP, set lock waits to a few seconds at most.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres lock_timeout (per-session): hard cap on how long any
one statement waits for any lock. Reasonable default for OLTP: 5-10 seconds. 2. Postgres 
deadlock_timeout (server-wide default 1s): only triggers the deadlock-detection algorithm after this
delay — the wait itself can continue indefinitely if no deadlock found. Lowering it costs CPU; raising it
delays deadlock victim selection. 3. InnoDB innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50s, way too long
for web apps): set to 5-10 seconds. Per-session override available. 4. SQL Server SET LOCK_TIMEOUT
5000; (5 seconds). Default -1 waits forever — avoid in OLTP.
Edge cases to mention: - Lock timeout returns an error to the application; the txn must decide to retry
or abort. - Statement timeout (statement_timeout in Postgres) is a stronger umbrella — kills the
whole statement regardless of cause. - Deadlock detection is automatic in every major engine — one
victim is rolled back with a specific error code. Application must retry.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "raise the timeout to fix the problem" — almost always wrong; fix the
contention instead. - Do not confuse lock timeout (waiting for lock) with statement timeout (overall
runtime cap).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 247 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 248
Common follow-up: "What error code does Postgres return on lock timeout vs deadlock?" — 55P03
(lock_not_available) for lock timeout, 40P01 (deadlock_detected) for deadlock. Catch and retry
separately.
-- Postgres: per-session lock and statement timeouts
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
SET statement_timeout = '30s';
Q240 · Diagnosing Lock Waits + Connection Pool Pitfalls
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: GCC senior rounds, On-call, Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, PhonePe · Topic:
Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A user reports the app feels stuck. You suspect lock waits. How do you investigate in Postgres,
MySQL, and SQL Server — and what connection-pool gotcha do you watch for?
The 30-second answer: Postgres: query pg_stat_activity joined with pg_locks to find the
blocking chain. MySQL: query INFORMATION_SCHEMA.INNODB_TRX and 
performance_schema.data_locks / data_lock_waits. SQL Server: sys.dm_tran_locks
joined with sys.dm_exec_requests. Connection-pool pitfall: a transaction left open by one request
because the pool returns the connection without rollback — the next request reuses it and the lock leaks
across users.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres recipe: a query joining pg_stat_activity with 
pg_locks and pg_blocking_pids gives you the blocked-blocker pairs with txn ages and SQL
text. 2. MySQL 8 recipe: performance_schema.data_lock_waits is the modern equivalent of the
old INNODB_LOCK_WAITS; join with INNODB_TRX for txn metadata. 3. SQL Server recipe: 
sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks filtered by wait_type like 'LCK%', joined to 
sys.dm_exec_requests for SQL text. Or sp_who2 for a quick look. 4. Connection-pool pitfall:
many pools (HikariCP, pgbouncer in session mode) don't automatically rollback on connection return. If
application code commits in some branches and not others, an open txn rides along to the next user.
Symptoms: unrelated users start blocking each other, locks held by sessions whose query field shows
the unrelated user's SQL.
Edge cases to mention: - pg_terminate_backend(pid) is the nuclear option — kills the session
and rolls back its txn. - pgbouncer in transaction mode is safer for leaked txns since it returns the
backend connection only between transactions, not within one. - Application frameworks often have a
"begin transaction on request, commit/rollback at end" wrapper — the bug is usually code path that
bypasses the wrapper.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 248 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 249
What NOT to say: - Do not say "just restart the database" — masks the issue and is heavyweight. - Do
not forget the pool-side defensive RESET / DISCARD ALL (Postgres) on connection return.
Common follow-up: "Write a Postgres query to show me the blocker chain right now." — Practise this.
It's a five-table join but the snippet below is close to memorisable.
-- Postgres: who is blocking whom right now
SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid,
       blocked.query AS blocked_query,
       blocking.pid AS blocking_pid,
       blocking.query AS blocking_query,
       age(now(), blocked.xact_start) AS blocked_age
FROM pg_stat_activity AS blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity AS blocking
  ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid))
WHERE blocked.wait_event_type = 'Lock';
Chapter 5, Part C — Deadlocks & Transaction Conflicts
This is the closer chapter on transactions, isolation and locking — the bit where theory meets the
production pager. Parts A and B taught you what isolation levels promise and how lock managers work;
Part C is about what breaks when two transactions want the same rows at the same time. We will walk
through deadlock formation, the wait-for graph that engines use to detect cycles, the lock-ordering
discipline that prevents most of them, and the retry-with-backoff pattern that handles the rest. Then we
will turn to real production conflict patterns I have actually debugged at Indian fintech and e-commerce
shops: the two-direction wallet transfer, the hot invoice counter, the foreign-key insert storm, MERGE
pitfalls on SQL Server, deferred constraints in Postgres, and the saga-versus-two-phase-commit choice
when one database is no longer enough. Twenty-seven questions, and the last one is the comprehensive
"talk me through deadlocks end-to-end" question that every senior backend panel eventually asks.
Q241 · What Exactly Is a Deadlock?
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Define a deadlock in your own words and draw me the classic two-resource cycle.
The 30-second answer: A deadlock is a state where two or more transactions are each waiting for a
lock that the other holds, so none can make progress — a circular wait. The simplest case is Txn A holds
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 249 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 250
row X and wants row Y, while Txn B holds row Y and wants row X. Neither will release without
committing, and neither can commit without the other releasing. The engine has to break the cycle by
killing one transaction.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the precise definition — "circular wait for resources" —
because that is the textbook phrasing the interviewer is listening for. 2. Sketch the two-transaction cycle
with concrete row IDs: Txn A locks accounts.id=1, Txn B locks accounts.id=2, then A asks for 2 and B
asks for 1. Both block forever without intervention. 3. Make the consequence explicit: a deadlock is not
slowness, it is a logical impossibility — waiting longer cannot resolve it. 4. Close with the engine's
response: detect, pick a victim (usually the cheaper rollback), throw a deadlock error to the victim's
session.
Edge cases to mention: - Deadlocks can involve three or more transactions in a longer cycle — A waits
B, B waits C, C waits A. - Not every "stuck" query is a deadlock; a long lock wait that eventually times
out is a different problem with a different fix. - Read-only transactions can still deadlock if they take share
locks (SELECT FOR SHARE) or if they touch index entries that are being modified.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the database deadlocks because it is overloaded." Load makes
deadlocks more frequent but does not cause the cycle; bad lock ordering does. - Do not call a
transaction that is simply slow a deadlock — vocabulary matters in an interview.
Common follow-up: "How is a deadlock different from livelock?" — Livelock is two transactions politely
retrying and re-conflicting forever; both are running but neither finishes. Deadlock is a frozen cycle;
livelock is a busy loop.
-- Classic two-row cycle on the accounts table
-- Session A
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;  -- holds row 1
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;  -- waits for row 2
-- Session B (interleaved)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 2;  -- holds row 2
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 1;  -- waits for row 1 -> deadlock
Q242 · How the Engine Detects a Deadlock
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through how a database actually figures out that two transactions are deadlocked.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 250 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 251
The 30-second answer: The engine maintains a wait-for graph where each node is a transaction and a
directed edge from A to B means "A is waiting for a lock held by B". A deadlock is, by definition, a cycle
in this graph. Postgres scans for cycles when a wait has lasted longer than deadlock_timeout
(default one second); MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server detect cycles immediately whenever a wait edge is
added.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the data structure — wait-for graph — because that is the
canonical algorithm and shows you understand the internals. 2. Describe the trigger differences:
Postgres is lazy (waits the timeout first to avoid wasted CPU on short waits), InnoDB and SQL Server are
eager (run the cycle check on every new wait). 3. Mention the victim choice heuristics: the engine picks
whichever transaction is "cheaper" to roll back — fewer locks held, less log written, or in SQL Server the
lowest deadlock priority. 4. Close with what the application sees: the victim's next statement (or commit)
raises a deadlock error and the transaction is automatically rolled back.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres's deadlock_timeout is a latency knob, not a correctness one
— set it lower (say 200ms) for OLTP, higher for batch. - Distributed deadlocks (across two databases or
microservices) are not detected by any single engine; you need timeouts or application-level
coordination. - Some engines log the full deadlock graph; SQL Server can emit XML deadlock graphs to
the system_health Extended Event session.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the database polls for deadlocks." Eager detection runs only on lock-
acquisition events. - Do not claim Postgres detects deadlocks instantly — the deadlock_timeout
delay is the explicit trade-off.
Common follow-up: "What is the cost of lowering Postgres's deadlock_timeout to 100ms?" — More
CPU spent running cycle checks for waits that would have resolved naturally; fine on contention-heavy
systems, wasteful on quiet ones.
-- Inspect current value in Postgres
SHOW deadlock_timeout;     -- default '1s'
-- Tune for an OLTP workload that retries fast
SET deadlock_timeout = '200ms';   -- session-level
ALTER SYSTEM SET deadlock_timeout = '200ms';  -- cluster-wide (requires reload)
Q243 · Deadlock vs Lock Wait — Different Problems
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Wipro, Flipkart, Swiggy · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 251 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 252
A query is hung for thirty seconds. How do you decide whether it is a deadlock or just a long lock
wait, and why does that matter?
The 30-second answer: A deadlock is a circular wait that the engine resolves by killing one transaction
with a specific deadlock error code. A long lock wait is a one-way wait that ends when the holder
commits, rolls back, or hits the lock-wait timeout. Look at the error message and the wait state —
different problems, different fixes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it as two distinct failure modes: cycle (deadlock) versus chain
(lock wait). The fixes have nothing in common. 2. Give the inspection commands: in Postgres, 
pg_locks plus pg_stat_activity shows who is waiting on whom; in MySQL, SHOW ENGINE
INNODB STATUS plus performance_schema.data_locks; in SQL Server, 
sys.dm_tran_locks and sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks. 3. Explain the time signature: deadlocks
resolve in roughly deadlock_timeout on Postgres (one second by default) or immediately on
InnoDB; long lock waits can stretch for minutes until the holder commits. 4. Fix-time: deadlocks need
lock ordering or retry logic; lock waits need shorter transactions, lower isolation, or a covering index that
avoids the lock altogether.
Edge cases to mention: - A long-running SELECT FOR UPDATE followed by a slow API call is the
textbook cause of lock waits — keep network I/O out of transactions. - A deadlock under serializable
isolation can appear as a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001) rather than a deadlock error (40P01) —
Postgres differentiates them. - Lock-wait timeout (MySQL: innodb_lock_wait_timeout, default
50s) trips before any deadlock check if there is no cycle.
What NOT to say: - Do not lump them together. "It's a locking issue" is junior phrasing; the senior
answer names the mode. - Do not assume retry will fix a long lock wait — if the holder never releases,
you will just retry into the same wait.
Common follow-up: "What is the SQLSTATE for a deadlock and what is it for a serialization failure?" — 
40P01 is deadlock detected, 40001 is serialization failure; both are retryable but they signal different
conditions.
-- Postgres: who is blocking whom right now?
SELECT blocked.pid     AS blocked_pid,
       blocked.query   AS blocked_query,
       blocking.pid    AS blocking_pid,
       blocking.query  AS blocking_query
FROM pg_stat_activity AS blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity AS blocking
  ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid));

Q244 · Reading a Deadlock Error Message
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Cognizant, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres has just thrown ERROR: deadlock detected at you with a multi-line DETAIL block.
What are you reading for?
The 30-second answer: You are reading for the two process IDs, the relations and rows involved, and
the statements each transaction was running when the cycle closed. That tells you exactly which two
code paths in your application interleaved badly so you can fix the lock order.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start by naming the four key fields: process IDs, lock mode, relation
(table or index), and the offending tuple or page identifier. 2. Map each PID back to your application —
log connection identifiers or application_name so you can correlate the database PID with the
request that fired it. 3. Note which transaction was chosen as the victim (Postgres logs "canceling
statement due to deadlock"); the other one survived and committed. 4. The fix is almost always
upstream: the two surviving statements show you the inconsistent lock order — sort the rows you touch
by primary key before updating them.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL's SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS LATEST DETECTED
DEADLOCK section dumps the same information but only keeps the most recent deadlock — capture it
before the next one overwrites. - SQL Server XML deadlock graphs in Extended Events give you the
wait-for cycle, lock resources, and the call stack of each session — far richer than the plain error. -
Always log the full DETAIL block; the one-line ERROR alone tells you nothing.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "deadlocks are random" — the error message has the deterministic
cause inside it. - Do not paper over the error with a blind retry without first reading the message; the
deadlock will come back.
Common follow-up: "You see the same two tables in every deadlock message for the last week. What
does that tell you?" — A consistent ordering bug between two code paths; fix the lock order once and
the recurring deadlock disappears.
-- Sample Postgres deadlock error
-- ERROR:  deadlock detected
-- DETAIL: Process 18421 waits for ShareLock on transaction 9921;
--         blocked by process 18422.
--         Process 18422 waits for ShareLock on transaction 9920;
--         blocked by process 18421.
-- HINT:  See server log for query details.
-- CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (5,3) in relation "accounts"
