Q245 · The Classic Two-Transfer Deadlock
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Zerodha · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Two users hit "send money" at the same instant — Anjali sends one thousand rupees to Rahul,
and Rahul sends one thousand to Anjali. Walk me through how this deadlocks.
The 30-second answer: Transfer one locks Anjali's row first, then asks for Rahul's. Transfer two locks
Rahul's row first, then asks for Anjali's. Each holds what the other needs — perfect cycle. The fix is to
always lock the lower-numbered account ID first regardless of the direction of the transfer.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagram the interleaving: T1 updates accounts.id=101 (Anjali), T2
updates accounts.id=247 (Rahul), then T1 wants 247 and T2 wants 101. 2. Explain why row-level locks
make this so easy to hit — both transactions hold an exclusive lock on the row they debited and need an
exclusive lock on the row they are crediting. 3. Show the fix in code: before any UPDATE, sort the two
account IDs ascending and lock them in that order with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Now both
transactions take row 101 first, the second waits, no cycle. 4. Mention the alternative — wrap the whole
transfer in a SERIALIZABLE transaction and let the engine retry — but lock ordering is cheaper and more
predictable.
Edge cases to mention: - The same problem appears in inventory transfers between warehouses,
ledger postings between general-ledger accounts, and message-passing between conversation threads.
- If you have three-leg transfers (A → B → C in one transaction), you still sort all three IDs and lock in
ascending order. - A transfer from an account to itself is a real edge case — guard with IF from_id =
to_id THEN RAISE EXCEPTION.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "we should use higher isolation level" as the first fix. SERIALIZABLE just
turns the deadlock into a serialization failure — same retry needed. - Do not claim ORM magic will save
you; Hibernate and ActiveRecord will deadlock just as cheerfully if you don't sort.
Common follow-up: "Show me the lock-order pattern in actual SQL." — Sort by primary key, SELECT
FOR UPDATE in that order, then run the debits and credits.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 254 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 255
-- Safe transfer with consistent lock order
BEGIN;
-- always lock the lower id first, regardless of direction
SELECT id FROM accounts
WHERE id IN (101, 247)
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 101;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 247;
INSERT INTO transfers(from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (101, 247, 1000);
COMMIT;
Q246 · Lock Ordering as the Universal Prevention
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If you had to give one rule to a junior engineer to stop most deadlocks, what would it be?
The 30-second answer: Always acquire locks in the same global order — usually ascending by primary
key, or alphabetical by table name when multiple tables are involved. If every transaction grabs resources
in the same direction, no two transactions can form a cycle, so deadlocks are mathematically impossible.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the principle: cycles need at least two transactions going in
different directions; force them all the same way and the cycle cannot form. 2. Concrete recipe — within
a transaction touching multiple rows of one table, sort the IDs and lock with FOR UPDATE in that order.
Across multiple tables, fix an alphabetical or dependency order (e.g. always users before orders, never
the reverse). 3. Mention the code-review checklist: any code path that updates two rows of the same
table without sorting them is a future deadlock. 4. Close with the limit: lock ordering prevents within-
database deadlocks but not distributed ones across services.
Edge cases to mention: - If you cannot sort (e.g., you don't know the second ID until midway through
the transaction), wrap in a try/retry block and accept occasional deadlocks. - For a graph of
interdependent tables, draw the dependency DAG once and write the order into a coding standard. -
Application-level lock managers (e.g., Redis Redlock) can enforce a global order across services where
the database cannot.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "increase isolation to fix deadlocks" — higher isolation usually makes
them more frequent, not less. - Do not rely on lock-free patterns alone; some operations truly need multi-
row locking and ordering is the only safe option.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 255 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 256
Common follow-up: "What if the two rows you need to lock are in different tables — how do you sort?"
— Establish a fixed table order in the team's coding standard (e.g., always lock accounts before 
transfers) and sort by primary key within each table.
-- Touching two tables: fixed order accounts -> transfers
BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id IN (:src, :dst) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
SELECT id FROM transfers WHERE id = :reversal_id FOR UPDATE;
-- now safe to mutate either table in any order
COMMIT;
Q247 · The Retry-with-Backoff Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy, Cred · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your code deadlocks one out of every thousand transactions. How do you handle it cleanly?
The 30-second answer: Wrap the whole transaction in a retry loop that catches the deadlock error
(SQLSTATE 40P01 on Postgres, 1213 on MySQL, 1205 on SQL Server), waits with exponential backoff
plus jitter, and re-runs the entire transaction. Cap retries at three to five; if it still fails, bubble the error up
as a real failure. The retried transaction must be idempotent so a partial earlier attempt doesn't corrupt
state.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the contract: deadlocks are recoverable errors, and the
engine has already rolled back the victim — your job is to start a new transaction and try again. 2. Show
the loop structure: catch the specific error code, sleep base * 2^attempt + jitter milliseconds,
retry the whole transaction (not just the failing statement). 3. Emphasise idempotency: external side
effects (emails, API calls) must not be inside the transaction, or use an outbox table so the side effect
happens only after the eventual commit. 4. Cap attempts and alert on the cap — if you retry forever, you
hide a real lock-ordering bug behind a busy loop.
Edge cases to mention: - Jitter (random 0-100ms added to each delay) prevents the two retrying
transactions from colliding again on the exact same schedule. - Some ORMs (Sequel, ActiveRecord) ship
a built-in transaction(retry_on: DeadlockError) helper — prefer the framework helper over
hand-rolled loops. - A retry loop in a long-running batch job should commit more often, not retry the
entire batch — minimise the rollback cost.
What NOT to say: - Do not retry on every error blindly — primary-key violations and check constraints
will not get better with another try. - Do not retry without backoff — two stubborn retriers can livelock
indefinitely.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 256 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 257
Common follow-up: "What is the right base delay and cap?" — A base of 25-50ms and a cap of five
retries works for OLTP; tune up if you see frequent collisions, alert if retries spike.
-- Pseudocode pattern; adapt to your language
-- for attempt in 1..5:
--   try:
--     BEGIN; ...; COMMIT; return success
--   except DeadlockDetected:
--     sleep(25ms * 2^attempt + random(0,100ms))
-- raise PermanentDeadlockError(after 5 attempts)
Q248 · Page-Level Deadlocks
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: JP Morgan, Goldman, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You insist your code locks different rows, but the deadlock log shows a conflict. What is going
on?
The 30-second answer: The engine takes locks at multiple granularities — row, page, index entry,
sometimes table. Two transactions touching different rows can still collide on the same B-tree page or
index leaf, and the deadlock surfaces as a page-level lock cycle. Look at the lock resource in the
deadlock graph; if it says page or key rather than row, you have a granularity issue, not a row-
collision bug.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the granularity hierarchy: row, page, extent, table — engines
may escalate up the hierarchy to save memory in the lock manager. 2. SQL Server is particularly known
for escalating row locks to page or table locks once a transaction touches more than five thousand rows;
that escalation is a deadlock magnet. 3. Postgres rarely takes page locks for DML but does take them on
index pages during splits; bulk loaders into the same index can collide. 4. Diagnose by reading the
deadlock graph's resource type; fix by lowering granularity (e.g., WITH (ROWLOCK) hint in SQL Server,
smaller batch sizes in Postgres) or by reordering the order rows are touched.
Edge cases to mention: - Heap tables in SQL Server escalate locks aggressively; adding a clustered
index often reduces page-level deadlocks. - MySQL InnoDB uses gap locks at REPEATABLE READ,
which lock ranges between index entries — two inserters near the same gap can deadlock. - Lock
escalation thresholds are tunable on SQL Server (ALTER TABLE ... SET (LOCK_ESCALATION =
DISABLE)) but disabling escalation can blow up memory.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 257 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 258
What NOT to say: - Do not insist "the rows are different so it cannot deadlock." Granularity changes
everything. - Do not blanket-disable lock escalation in production without understanding the memory
cost.
Common follow-up: "How would you reproduce a page-level deadlock for testing?" — Bulk-insert into
the same index leaf from two sessions with identical batch sizes; the gap-lock collision shows up reliably
under REPEATABLE READ.
-- SQL Server: read the deadlock resource type
SELECT XEvent.value('(data/value)[1]', 'varchar(max)') AS deadlock_xml
FROM (SELECT CAST(target_data AS XML) AS TargetData
      FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets st
      JOIN sys.dm_xe_sessions s ON s.address = st.event_session_address
      WHERE s.name = 'system_health' AND st.target_name = 'ring_buffer') AS Data
CROSS APPLY TargetData.nodes('//RingBufferTarget/event[@name="xml_deadlock_report"]') AS XEventData(XEvent);
Q249 · Foreign-Key Insert Deadlocks
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Goldman · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Two transactions are inserting child rows that reference different parent rows. Why do they
sometimes deadlock?
The 30-second answer: When you insert a child row, the engine takes a share-lock on the referenced
parent row to make sure it cannot be deleted mid-transaction. If two transactions each insert children
referencing two parents in opposite order — Txn A child of P1 then P2, Txn B child of P2 then P1 — the
parent share locks form the exact same cycle as a row-update deadlock.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the implicit lock: FK enforcement takes a share lock on the
parent to prevent concurrent delete; this lock is invisible in application code but very real. 2. Show the
cycle: inserts that reference multiple parents in different orders deadlock just like updates. Common in
order-line tables (each line references a product), in junction tables, and in audit-log children. 3. The fix
mirrors the transfer case: sort the parent IDs and either touch them in order or take an explicit SELECT
FOR KEY SHARE (Postgres) before the inserts. 4. Alternative fix: defer constraint checks until commit
(deferrable FKs in Postgres), which moves the lock to commit time and reduces contention.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres uses a weaker lock mode called FOR KEY SHARE for FK
enforcement since version 9.3 — older patterns assumed FOR SHARE and over-locked. - MySQL
InnoDB takes a shared lock on the parent and historically deadlocked very easily; modern versions
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 258 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 259
added the innodb_lock_wait_timeout short-circuit. - If the parent table is updated frequently
(e.g., a counter on each parent), FK checks plus those updates collide constantly.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "we should drop the foreign keys" as a deadlock fix — you trade a
deadlock for orphan rows, which is far worse in finance. - Do not assume FK locks are free; they are real
locks held until commit.
Common follow-up: "How do deferrable constraints help?" — They postpone the FK check (and the
lock) until COMMIT, so two transactions can both insert children, both check parents at commit, and only
collide if the parents are actually conflicting.
-- Postgres deferrable FK
ALTER TABLE order_lines
  ADD CONSTRAINT fk_product
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id)
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED;
BEGIN;
SET CONSTRAINTS fk_product DEFERRED;  -- already deferred, shown for clarity
INSERT INTO order_lines(order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (1, 100, 2);
INSERT INTO order_lines(order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (1, 101, 1);
COMMIT;  -- FK checked here, lock held only briefly
Q250 · Index-Level Deadlocks
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A team complains their UPDATE deadlocks even though they only touch one row. How can a
single-row update deadlock?
The 30-second answer: The row is one resource, but the indexes that point to it are separate resources.
Updating a row that participates in two indexes takes locks on both index entries, and another
transaction updating a different row that happens to live in the same index leaf can collide. The cycle
forms across indexes, not across rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Reinforce the multi-resource view: a row update is "update the heap
tuple plus every index that contains the updated columns." Each index lock is independent. 2. Walk
through a sample cycle: Txn A updates accounts(id=10, status=...) — locks heap row plus status index
entry. Txn B updates accounts(id=11, status=...) — locks heap row plus an adjacent index entry on the
same page. Page-level lock manager hands them in opposite order: cycle. 3. Symptoms in the deadlock
graph: the resource is index or key rather than row. Look for it explicitly. 4. Mitigations: drop
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 259 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 260
unused indexes, use INCLUDE columns in the index to avoid heap visits, batch updates within a single
transaction in primary-key order so index leaves are touched left-to-right.
Edge cases to mention: - Wide secondary indexes with hot-spot key prefixes (e.g., (status,
created_at) where status is mostly the same value) cluster updates onto the same leaves — high
deadlock risk. - Postgres updates rewrite the entire row even if you change one column, but HOT
updates skip index maintenance when no indexed column changed — keeps locks narrower. - Covering
indexes can reduce deadlocks by avoiding extra heap access locks under serialisable.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "you cannot deadlock a single-row update" — you absolutely can,
through indexes. - Do not blindly drop indexes to fix deadlocks; you may break the read path that
justified them.
Common follow-up: "How do you tell if a Postgres update went HOT?" — Inspect 
pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd; a high ratio of HOT to total updates means the optimiser
is avoiding index maintenance.
-- Postgres: check HOT update ratio
SELECT relname,
       n_tup_upd,
       n_tup_hot_upd,
       ROUND(100.0 * n_tup_hot_upd / NULLIF(n_tup_upd, 0), 1) AS hot_pct
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'accounts';
Q251 · Distributed Deadlocks Across Services
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have two services, each owning its own database. Can they deadlock, and who would detect
it?
The 30-second answer: Yes, they can — Service A holds a lock in DB1 while waiting for a response
from Service B, which holds a lock in DB2 waiting for Service A. Neither database can see the cross-
service wait, so the deadlock is invisible to both engines. Detection has to happen at the application level
via timeouts; resolution is to fail one side and retry.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Establish the visibility problem: each database knows only about
waits inside itself; the wait-for graph cannot cross process or network boundaries. 2. The symptom is a
request that hangs forever — both services have open transactions, both are blocked on a network call
to the other. 3. Detection must be application-level: per-call timeouts, circuit breakers, distributed-tracing
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 260 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 261
alerts when transaction duration crosses a threshold. 4. Prevention: never hold a database transaction
open across a synchronous call to another service. Use the outbox or saga pattern so each service
commits independently and reconciliation is asynchronous.
Edge cases to mention: - Even within one database, two connections that route through a service mesh
with retries can create deadlock-like patterns the engine cannot resolve cleanly. - Two-phase commit
coordinators detect distributed deadlocks at commit time but introduce their own availability problems
(see Q21). - Long-running gRPC calls inside a BEGIN ... COMMIT block are the single most common
cause of cross-service stuck transactions I have debugged.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim the database will save you — engines explicitly disclaim cross-
database deadlock detection. - Do not propose distributed locks (e.g., Zookeeper) as the default fix; they
just relocate the deadlock problem.
Common follow-up: "What's the cleanest pattern to avoid this?" — Saga: each service commits its local
transaction, publishes an event, and the next service consumes it. Compensating actions handle failures.
-- Anti-pattern: don't do this
BEGIN;
UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE user_id = 5;
-- BAD: synchronous external call inside the transaction
-- response = http_post('https://partner/transfer', amount=100)
UPDATE ledger SET ext_id = :response_id WHERE ...;
COMMIT;
Q252 · Deadlocks in Batch Jobs vs OLTP
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Wells Fargo, Target, AmEx, Walmart Labs · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your nightly settlement batch deadlocks with the live OLTP traffic every other night. How do you
reason about that?
The 30-second answer: Batch jobs lock many rows in big transactions; OLTP locks single rows in short
transactions. When they overlap, the batch's wide lock footprint conflicts with rapid-fire OLTP updates
and one side gets killed. Either run the batch in a low-traffic window, chunk it into smaller transactions, or
use a read-only snapshot for the batch and only write back the deltas.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose the asymmetry: a batch that locks 100k rows for two
minutes blocks any OLTP transaction that needs even one of those rows. Probability of collision scales
with batch size. 2. Chunking: break the batch into transactions of 1000-5000 rows each with LIMIT
and primary-key cursoring; release locks between chunks. 3. Snapshot strategy: read everything you
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 261 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 262
need from a read replica or via SET TRANSACTION SNAPSHOT (Postgres) and only the final write hits
the primary. The write itself is a single small transaction. 4. Schedule: run heavy batch at a time window
with minimal OLTP — many fintechs run reconciliation between 02:00 and 04:00 IST for this exact
reason.
Edge cases to mention: - A batch that uses SERIALIZABLE on a huge dataset is essentially a deadlock
generator; READ COMMITTED with explicit FOR UPDATE on the rows actually written is usually safer. -
Chunked batches need a stable ordering (primary key) so each chunk is deterministic and skipped rows
can be picked up on rerun. - Long batches also bloat undo logs (Postgres MVCC, MySQL undo) — a
separate problem worth mentioning if the interviewer asks.
What NOT to say: - Do not run a 4-hour batch as one transaction. Period. - Do not raise isolation to "fix"
batch deadlocks — it makes the lock footprint worse.
Common follow-up: "How do you make a chunked batch resumable?" — Track the highest processed
primary key in a checkpoint table; on rerun, start from that key.
-- Chunked nightly settlement loop (pseudo)
-- Pick rows in PK order, settle 5000 at a time, commit between chunks
DO $$
DECLARE last_id BIGINT := 0;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    WITH batch AS (
      SELECT id FROM pending_settlements
      WHERE id > last_id
      ORDER BY id
      LIMIT 5000
      FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    )
    UPDATE pending_settlements p
      SET status = 'SETTLED', settled_at = now()
      FROM batch WHERE p.id = batch.id
      RETURNING p.id INTO last_id;
    EXIT WHEN NOT FOUND;
    COMMIT;
  END LOOP;
END $$;
Q253 · High-Contention Rows and Read-Modify-Write
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, PhonePe, Swiggy · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 262 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 263
Every order increments the same invoice_counter row. Why is this slow even though each
transaction is tiny?
The 30-second answer: Because every transaction must take an exclusive lock on the same row, they
serialize one-by-one regardless of how many CPUs your database has. Throughput collapses to one
transaction per round-trip latency, and any other transaction that touches this row indirectly (e.g., through
a FK) joins the queue. Hot single rows are the most common source of production "the database is slow"
tickets.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the bottleneck: the lock manager forces strict serial execution
on the hot row. With 5ms round-trip latency and 200 writers, you get at most 200 increments per second
total — no matter the hardware. 2. The classic anti-pattern is 
SELECT counter FROM ... ; UPDATE counter SET counter = :value + 1 — two
statements, race window, deadlock-prone, and slow. 3. Atomic increment via UPDATE counter SET
counter = counter + 1 RETURNING counter collapses to one statement and one lock
acquisition — drops the window but the serial bottleneck remains. 4. Real fix: shard the counter into N
rows (counter_0..counter_31), increment a random shard, sum at read time. Throughput scales with N.
Used by Stripe, Shopify, and every fintech ledger I have audited.
Edge cases to mention: - Sharded counters work for monotonic-ish totals (revenue, click count) but not
for strict sequence numbers — you need a different pattern for gapless invoice IDs. - If you must have a
gapless sequence, accept the bottleneck and pre-allocate ranges (HiLo pattern) so each app instance
hands out 1000 IDs without touching the DB. - Postgres SEQUENCE objects use a special lock-free
mechanism — much faster than rolling your own counter row.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "we will solve it with a faster server" — vertical scaling cannot break the
serial dependency. - Do not implement counters as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; UPDATE ... —
atomic single-statement is always better.
Common follow-up: "How would you implement a sharded counter?" — N rows keyed 
(counter_name, shard_id), app hashes the increment to a random shard, read aggregates all
shards.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 263 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 264
-- Sharded counter for revenue accumulator
CREATE TABLE counters (
  name      TEXT NOT NULL,
  shard_id  INT  NOT NULL,
  value     BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (name, shard_id)
);
-- Increment a random shard
UPDATE counters
SET value = value + :amount
WHERE name = 'gross_revenue_paise'
  AND shard_id = FLOOR(RANDOM() * 32);
-- Read total
SELECT SUM(value) FROM counters WHERE name = 'gross_revenue_paise';
Q254 · The Hot Invoice Counter — A Real Production Story
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Zerodha · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your invoicing service needs gap-less invoice numbers for GST compliance. How do you
generate them without making the DB the bottleneck?
The 30-second answer: A truly gap-less invoice number forces serialisation — you cannot shard. Use a
single counter row with atomic increment, but pre-allocate ranges via the HiLo pattern: each app
instance fetches a block of, say, 100 numbers, hands them out in memory, and only revisits the DB every
100 invoices. Throughput scales with block size, and gaps appear only on app crashes (regulator usually
permits documented gaps).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Acknowledge the constraint: Indian GST law requires gap-less
sequential invoice numbers per financial year per series. Sharded counters cannot do this. 2. HiLo
pattern: a small counter table holds the next available "block start"; each app pulls a block, increments
the block-start by block_size, commits, and serves invoice numbers from local memory. 3. Risk: if
the app crashes mid-block, the unused tail is wasted — gaps. Document the policy and most regulators
accept it; otherwise reduce block size to one and accept the throughput hit. 4. Alternative for less-strict
numbering: append a per-instance suffix to a sharded counter (e.g., INV-2026-{shard}-{seq}) —
fast but no longer a single gap-less sequence.
Edge cases to mention: - The counter table must use SERIALIZABLE or SELECT FOR UPDATE to
avoid two app instances picking overlapping blocks. - A failover or rolling deploy must hand off the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 264 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 265
unused tail or accept the gap — operational discipline matters. - For financial-year-bounded series
( INV-2025-NNN), reset the counter at year boundary via a scheduled job, not lazily.
What NOT to say: - Do not pretend sharding works for gap-less sequences — the interviewer is testing
whether you understand the constraint. - Do not store invoice numbers in Redis without a write-through
to the database; a Redis flush destroys your audit trail.
Common follow-up: "What block size do you pick?" — Trade-off: larger blocks give higher throughput
but more gaps on crash. 50-100 is a common compromise for typical SaaS invoicing volumes.
-- HiLo allocator
CREATE TABLE invoice_blocks (
  series       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  next_block   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  block_size   INT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 100
);
-- Fetch a block atomically
UPDATE invoice_blocks
SET next_block = next_block + block_size
WHERE series = 'INV-2025'
RETURNING next_block - block_size AS block_start, block_size;
Q255 · Lock-Free Patterns — Append-Only and Event Sourcing
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, JP Morgan, Zerodha · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you design a write path that essentially cannot deadlock?
The 30-second answer: Make the write path append-only. Every business event becomes an immutable
INSERT into a log table, and the current state is derived by aggregating the log. INSERTs never conflict
on existing rows, so concurrent writers do not lock each other. Read paths use materialised views or
projection tables refreshed asynchronously.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the principle: row updates create lock contention; row inserts
on a table with no unique key contention create almost none. 2. Event-sourced wallet example: every
credit and debit is an INSERT into wallet_events. To compute a balance, sum the events for that
user; for performance, periodically snapshot the running balance. 3. Concurrent two-direction transfers
from Q5 stop deadlocking because both transactions just append two events each — no shared row to
lock. 4. Trade-offs: read complexity goes up, you need projection rebuilds, and unique business
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 265 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 266
invariants (e.g., "balance never goes negative") move out of the database into the application or into a
periodic check.
Edge cases to mention: - "Balance must not go negative" cannot be enforced purely append-only
without a synchronous check — either do an optimistic read-then-insert with retry, or accept eventual
reconciliation. - Event tables grow forever — partition by month and archive cold partitions. - Snapshot
tables prevent the read aggregation from getting slower as the log grows; rebuild snapshots in
background jobs.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "event sourcing eliminates all concurrency problems" — uniqueness
invariants still need handling. - Do not implement append-only as UPDATE ... last_modified =
now() — that is the opposite, you are still updating in place.
Common follow-up: "How do you enforce 'balance >= 0' in an event-sourced wallet?" — Run the debit
as INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT balance ...) >= amount with a unique constraint on
event_id; on conflict you retry with the new balance.
-- Event-sourced wallet writes
CREATE TABLE wallet_events (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     BIGINT    NOT NULL,
  amount      BIGINT    NOT NULL,  -- positive credit, negative debit
  event_type  TEXT      NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- Both transfers from Q5 become four INSERTs total, no row conflict
INSERT INTO wallet_events(user_id, amount, event_type) VALUES (101, -1000, 'transfer_out');
INSERT INTO wallet_events(user_id, amount, event_type) VALUES (247,  1000, 'transfer_in');
Q256 · The Saga Pattern for Cross-Service Workflows
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Distributed transactions across three microservices are off the table. How do you keep a multi-
step workflow consistent?
The 30-second answer: Use the saga pattern — split the workflow into a sequence of local
transactions, each in its own service and database, with a compensating action defined for each step.
On failure, you run the compensations in reverse order to roll back the parts that already succeeded. No
distributed locks, no two-phase commit.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 266 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 267
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the saga: ordered list of (forward step, compensation) pairs.
Each step commits in its own database; failures trigger compensations from the failure point backward.
2. Worked example: an order saga reserves inventory, charges the wallet, creates the shipment. If
shipment creation fails, you refund the wallet and release the inventory. 3. Orchestration vs
choreography: orchestration uses a central coordinator (state machine); choreography uses events
between services. Orchestration is easier to reason about; choreography scales better. 4. Idempotency is
non-negotiable — every step and every compensation must be safe to retry, because network failures
will redeliver messages.
Edge cases to mention: - Compensations are not always perfectly reversible (you cannot un-send a
notification email) — design "semantic" compensations like a follow-up apology email. - Long-running
sagas must persist state in a saga log so a process restart can resume. - A saga is eventually consistent,
not atomic — intermediate observers can see partial state. Document this with the business.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose two-phase commit as a casual alternative — its availability cost is
high (see Q21). - Do not skip compensations on "expected to succeed" steps — Murphy's law applies in
production.
Common follow-up: "How do you make payment charging idempotent?" — Send an idempotency key
with the charge request; the payment service stores it and returns the same result on retry.
-- Saga state log (simplified)
CREATE TABLE saga_log (
  saga_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  step        TEXT NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL,        -- pending | done | compensated | failed
  payload     JSONB,
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
Q257 · Two-Phase Commit — What and Why It's Rare
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain two-phase commit. Why do most modern systems avoid it?
The 30-second answer: 2PC is a protocol where a coordinator first asks every participant "can you
commit?" (prepare phase) and, only if all say yes, sends "commit" (commit phase). It guarantees
atomicity across multiple databases. The cost is that participants hold locks the entire time the
coordinator is reachable, and a coordinator crash between phases leaves everyone blocked — high
availability impact, very low operational tolerance.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 267 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 268
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Sketch the two phases: PREPARE asks each participant to durably
persist the transaction in a state from which it can either commit or rollback; COMMIT (or ROLLBACK) is
the final decision. 2. The atomicity guarantee is real — either all participants commit or none do. 3. The
cost: any in-doubt transaction (after PREPARE, before COMMIT) holds locks until the coordinator
recovers and resolves it. If the coordinator crashes permanently, you have manual cleanup. 4. Most
modern systems prefer eventual consistency via sagas, the outbox pattern, or distributed log streaming
— gives up strict atomicity for huge availability gains.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres supports 2PC via PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid' / COMMIT
PREPARED 'gid', but it must be explicitly enabled with max_prepared_transactions > 0. - XA
transactions in MySQL and SQL Server are 2PC variants and have a long history of bugs and operational
pain. - 2PC is still useful inside one company that controls the coordinator (e.g., a payment hub between
two internal databases) — just not across organisational boundaries.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "2PC is always wrong" — for some financial settlements it is the right
call. - Do not confuse 2PC with eventual consistency; 2PC is strict atomic commit.
Common follow-up: "What happens if the coordinator crashes after PREPARE on participant A but
before sending PREPARE to participant B?" — A is in-doubt and locked until the coordinator recovers
and resolves; B never participated and is fine. Operators must manually commit or rollback A in the
meantime.
-- Postgres 2PC syntax
BEGIN;
-- do work
PREPARE TRANSACTION 'order-42';   -- locks held, transaction in-doubt
-- coordinator decides
COMMIT PREPARED 'order-42';        -- or ROLLBACK PREPARED 'order-42';
Q258 · The Read-Modify-Write Race
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy, TCS · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your code reads a row, computes a new value in application memory, and writes it back. Why is
this dangerous under concurrency?
The 30-second answer: Between your SELECT and UPDATE another transaction can modify the same
row, and your UPDATE overwrites their change — the lost-update problem. Fix it with a single atomic
statement (UPDATE ... SET col = col + 1), an explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE lock, an
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 268 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 269
optimistic version column (WHERE version = :read_version), or by raising isolation to
SERIALIZABLE.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the race timeline: T1 reads balance=1000, T2 reads
balance=1000, T1 writes balance=900, T2 writes balance=800 (intended 1000-200). The first decrement
is lost. 2. Atomic-statement fix is simplest: let the database compute the new value. UPDATE wallet
SET balance = balance - 200 WHERE user_id = 5 cannot lose updates. 3. When you cannot
do it atomically (because the new value comes from external computation), use SELECT ... FOR
UPDATE so the second reader blocks, or an optimistic CAS: UPDATE ... WHERE version
= :read_version and retry on zero rows affected. 4. Discuss the trade-off: pessimistic (FOR
UPDATE) is simple but reduces concurrency; optimistic is high-throughput but adds retry complexity.
Edge cases to mention: - Pure ORM record.update(balance: record.balance - 200) is a
read-modify-write — almost always wrong for counters. - Optimistic locking only works if you have a
version column or a timestamp that monotonically increases; bare WHERE balance
= :read_balance is a weak version key. - Snapshot isolation (Postgres REPEATABLE READ, SQL
Server SI) raises an error on conflicting writes — built-in optimistic protection.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "the database handles concurrency" — it provides primitives; you still
have to use them. - Do not use SERIALIZABLE as a default fix; the cost of retries can exceed the cost of
getting the SQL right.
Common follow-up: "Show me an optimistic locking pattern with a version column." — 
UPDATE x SET balance = :new_value, version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND
version = :read_version — if zero rows affected, re-read and retry.
-- Optimistic locking with version column
SELECT balance, version FROM wallet WHERE user_id = 5;
-- compute new_balance in app
UPDATE wallet
SET balance = :new_balance,
    version = version + 1
WHERE user_id = 5
  AND version = :read_version;
-- if rowcount = 0, someone else updated; reread + retry
Q259 · INSERT ... ON CONFLICT — Atomic Upsert
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, Razorpay, Swiggy · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You want to insert a row if it doesn't exist and update it if it does. How do you avoid the race?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 269 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 270
The 30-second answer: Use the database's atomic upsert syntax — Postgres INSERT ... ON
CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE, MySQL INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, SQLite 
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. These execute as a single statement under a single lock
acquisition, so there is no window between "check exists" and "insert or update" for another transaction
to slip in.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose the race: the naive pattern IF EXISTS THEN UPDATE
ELSE INSERT has a TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) gap that causes either duplicate-key
errors or lost updates. 2. Show the Postgres syntax: INSERT ... VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT
(user_id) DO UPDATE SET visits = excluded.visits + 1 — clean, atomic, single round-
trip. 3. MySQL equivalent: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE visits = visits +
VALUES(visits). SQL Server uses MERGE (with caveats — see Q20). 4. Use case fit: counter
pages, session tables, idempotent webhook processing. The pattern eliminates an entire class of race
conditions.
Edge cases to mention: - ON CONFLICT requires a unique index or primary key on the conflict
columns; otherwise the conflict cannot be detected. - DO NOTHING variant is useful for idempotent
event processing — insert if new, silently skip if seen before. - Returning clause (RETURNING *) tells
you whether the row was inserted or updated by checking xmax or the version column.
What NOT to say: - Do not implement upsert as BEGIN; SELECT; IF NULL INSERT ELSE
UPDATE; COMMIT — that is exactly the race you are trying to avoid. - Do not assume MERGE is always
atomic; in some engines it is not (see Q20).
Common follow-up: "How do you tell if ON CONFLICT inserted or updated?" — Postgres: RETURNING
(xmax = 0) AS inserted; MySQL: ROW_COUNT() returns 1 for insert, 2 for update.
-- Atomic upsert for a page-view counter
INSERT INTO page_views(user_id, page_id, views, last_seen)
VALUES (5, 'p123', 1, now())
ON CONFLICT (user_id, page_id)
DO UPDATE SET views = page_views.views + 1,
              last_seen = excluded.last_seen
RETURNING views;
Q260 · MERGE INTO and Its SQL Server Deadlock Pitfalls
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 270 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 271
MERGE looks elegant. Why do experienced SQL Server engineers avoid it for high-concurrency
workloads?
The 30-second answer: SQL Server's MERGE has a well-documented set of bugs that cause it to
occasionally violate uniqueness constraints, return wrong results in concurrent execution, and deadlock
against itself under load. The MS docs themselves recommend explicit INSERT/UPDATE patterns or
upsert-by-attempt for high-throughput scenarios. Postgres MERGE (added in v15) has been better
behaved but is still newer than ON CONFLICT.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Acknowledge MERGE's appeal — single statement that handles
insert, update, delete in one go — and the disappointment that the implementation has been buggy. 2.
The classic SQL Server bug: two concurrent MERGEs targeting the same key can both pass the WHEN
NOT MATCHED check and both attempt insert, causing a primary key violation. Use HOLDLOCK hint to
serialize, but that hurts throughput. 3. SQL Server-specific deadlock: MERGE may take locks in different
orders depending on the matched/not-matched plan, leading to deadlocks under load that ON
CONFLICT/IF EXISTS patterns avoid. 4. Practical guidance: for concurrent upserts on SQL Server, prefer 
IF EXISTS UPDATE ELSE INSERT wrapped in serializable, or the "try insert, catch dup, then
update" idiom. Reserve MERGE for batch ETL where concurrency is low.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres MERGE (v15+) does not have the SQL Server bugs but still does not
have ON CONFLICT's excluded pseudo-table; use ON CONFLICT for upserts in Postgres. - Oracle
MERGE is the original and is generally considered safe but uses different syntax (no WHEN MATCHED
THEN DELETE in older versions). - BigQuery and Snowflake MERGE are designed for analytic
workloads where one-row-at-a-time concurrency is not a use case.
What NOT to say: - Do not call MERGE "the modern way to upsert" in SQL Server — it has been
controversial since 2008. - Do not blindly add HOLDLOCK without measuring the throughput impact.
Common follow-up: "Show me the safe SQL Server upsert pattern." — 
IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM target WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK) WHERE key = @k)
UPDATE ... ELSE INSERT ... inside SERIALIZABLE, or the try/catch pattern.
-- SQL Server safe upsert (no MERGE)
BEGIN TRAN;
IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK) WHERE id = @id)
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + @delta WHERE id = @id;
ELSE
    INSERT INTO accounts(id, balance) VALUES (@id, @delta);
COMMIT TRAN;

Q261 · Application-Level Locks vs Database Locks
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you reach for a Redis lock or a Zookeeper mutex instead of a database-level lock?
The 30-second answer: Use a database lock when the resource being protected lives in the database
and the lock can be held for the duration of one short transaction. Use an application-level lock (Redis,
Zookeeper, etcd) when the protected work is longer than a database transaction should be — like
running a periodic job once across a fleet of workers, or coordinating writes across multiple databases.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the choice: database locks are scoped to a transaction and
freed at commit/rollback; application locks are scoped to a TTL or a lease and freed by explicit release.
2. Database locks are correct for: row updates, FK enforcement, anything where the lock and the data
are co-located. 3. Application locks are correct for: leader election in a worker pool, ensuring a cron job
runs exactly once across N replicas, serialising writes to an external system without a database
transaction. 4. The big risk with application locks is fencing — if a process is paused (GC, network), its
lock can expire and another process can hold it, but the original may resume and act on stale
assumptions. Use a fencing token or a CAS check.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock(key)) are application-level
locks living in the database — best of both worlds: distributed coordination plus crash-detection via
session close. - Redis Redlock has well-documented edge cases under network partitions; for safety-
critical work, use Zookeeper or etcd which provide stronger guarantees. - Holding any lock — DB or app
— across a network call is asking for trouble; release before the call if possible.
What NOT to say: - Do not use a Redis lock to protect data that already lives in the database — you
have two sources of truth and they will diverge. - Do not assume Redis SETNX is a safe distributed lock
without TTL handling and fencing.
Common follow-up: "How would you ensure a nightly batch runs only once across three pods?" — Use
a Postgres advisory lock at the start of the batch; if pg_try_advisory_lock returns false, the pod
exits cleanly.
-- Postgres advisory lock to ensure single-leader batch
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(:job_id);
-- if true, this pod is the leader; do the work
-- when done or on crash, the session closing releases the lock
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(:job_id);

Q262 · Lock Timeout vs Deadlock Timeout
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, AmEx, Target · Topic: Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between lock_timeout and deadlock_timeout in Postgres?
The 30-second answer: lock_timeout is how long any one statement waits for a lock before giving
up with an error — a guard against indefinite waits. deadlock_timeout is how long the engine waits
before running a deadlock detection scan on a wait edge. They are entirely independent: 
lock_timeout caps total wait, deadlock_timeout decides when to spend CPU looking for
cycles.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define each with one sentence: lock_timeout = abort after this
much wait, deadlock_timeout = start cycle-checking after this much wait. 2. Show interaction: with 
deadlock_timeout = 1s and lock_timeout = 5s, a wait of two seconds with no cycle gets a
deadlock-check (negative result), continues waiting, and aborts at five seconds with a lock-timeout error.
3. Tuning intuition: lower deadlock_timeout for OLTP if you would rather detect deadlocks early;
raise lock_timeout for batch jobs where waiting is expected. 4. MySQL InnoDB has a different
model: innodb_lock_wait_timeout is both lock-wait abort and (since InnoDB detects deadlocks
eagerly) the only timeout you need to set.
Edge cases to mention: - statement_timeout (Postgres) is a third, even broader timer — kills any
statement exceeding the limit regardless of why it is slow. - Setting lock_timeout per-transaction is
useful for DDL: SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE ... so a stuck ALTER
does not freeze the application. - SQL Server's SET LOCK_TIMEOUT is in milliseconds and only
affects lock waits, not query execution time.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse the two — interviewers test exactly this distinction. - Do not set 
lock_timeout very high in OLTP; one stuck transaction can chain-block the whole application.
Common follow-up: "How would you run an ALTER TABLE safely on a busy Postgres database?" —
Wrap with low lock_timeout and retry on timeout: SET lock_timeout = '200ms'; ALTER
TABLE ...; RESET lock_timeout; — back off if it cannot grab the lock quickly.
-- Set per-session lock_timeout
SET lock_timeout = '500ms';
-- Or per-transaction
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '100ms';
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN kyc_status TEXT;
COMMIT;
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 273 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q263 · Deferred Constraints in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain deferrable constraints in Postgres. When does the check actually run?
The 30-second answer: A deferrable constraint can have its check postponed from "after each
statement" (the default IMMEDIATE) to "at commit time" (DEFERRED). This lets you temporarily violate
the constraint in the middle of a transaction — for example, swapping two rows that both depend on
each other — and only requires the final committed state to be consistent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the two modes: IMMEDIATE checks after every statement;
DEFERRED checks at COMMIT. A constraint declared DEFERRABLE can switch between them per
transaction via SET CONSTRAINTS. 2. The killer use case is cyclical FKs and self-referential swaps —
UPDATE A.next = B.id; UPDATE B.next = A.id would fail IMMEDIATE on the first statement but works
DEFERRED. 3. Performance angle from Q9: deferred FK checks happen at commit, so multiple insert
statements within one transaction collide less with other transactions during the body of the work. 4.
Limitation: errors at commit are harder to recover from than statement-level errors; the transaction is fully
rolled back with no chance to retry just the failing piece.
Edge cases to mention: - Only FK, UNIQUE, and EXCLUDE constraints can be DEFERRABLE in
Postgres; CHECK constraints and NOT NULL cannot. - SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED switches
every deferrable constraint in the transaction; useful for bulk loads. - MySQL does not support deferrable
constraints at all; SQL Server has limited support via WITH NOCHECK on DDL but not per-transaction.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "deferred constraints disable checking" — they only postpone it. - Do
not declare every constraint DEFERRABLE "just in case"; immediate checks catch bugs sooner.
Common follow-up: "How would you migrate data with circular FKs?" — Use DEFERRABLE INITIALLY
DEFERRED on both FKs, bulk-load both tables in any order, COMMIT, and the FK check at commit
verifies everything is consistent.
-- Cyclical FK with deferrable constraints
ALTER TABLE node
  ADD CONSTRAINT fk_parent FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES node(id)
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED;
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO node(id, parent_id) VALUES (1, 2);
INSERT INTO node(id, parent_id) VALUES (2, 1);
COMMIT;  -- both checked here, both pass

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q264 · Why Increment Counters Are a Bottleneck (Deeper)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Swiggy, Razorpay, Cred · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
We talked about the hot counter. Walk me through what actually happens inside the database
when 1000 transactions try to increment one row.
The 30-second answer: Each transaction's UPDATE waits for an exclusive row lock. The lock manager
queues them in FIFO order, and each one only runs after the previous one has committed and released
the lock. So 1000 transactions execute serially with one commit per round-trip, giving throughput of
roughly 1 / commit_latency per second — typically a few hundred per second, regardless of CPU
count.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Step into the lock manager: an exclusive row lock cannot be shared,
so the second writer blocks; the third blocks behind the second; you build a queue. 2. Each queued
writer needs the previous one's COMMIT to fully durably persist (fsync) before it can proceed, because
the new value depends on the previous transaction's outcome. 3. With 1ms commit latency, theoretical
max is 1000/sec; in practice you see lower because of network round-trips and other overheads. 4. The
fix patterns from Q13/Q14 all attack this serial dependency: shard the row, batch the increments in
memory and flush periodically, or use a sequence object.
Edge cases to mention: - Group commit (Postgres commit_delay, MySQL 
binlog_group_commit_sync_delay) can amortise fsync across multiple transactions, raising
counter throughput somewhat. - Postgres SEQUENCE uses an internal in-memory cache (CACHE n)
so allocations don't go through the WAL on every call — much faster than a counter row. - In-memory
engines (Redis INCR) hit hundreds of thousands per second by skipping disk persistence entirely — at
the cost of durability guarantees.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "we'll add an index to speed it up" — the index doesn't help a write that
is already direct lookup. - Do not blame "row lock latency" — the latency comes from waiting in the
queue, not from the lock primitive itself.
Common follow-up: "Why doesn't read concurrency help with this?" — Counters are write-only; reads
can use replicas, but the writes funnel through the primary's lock manager.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 275 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 276
-- Verify counter contention in Postgres
SELECT relname, schemaname, n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'counters'
ORDER BY n_tup_upd DESC;
-- Live blockers on the hot row
SELECT pid, wait_event_type, wait_event, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE query ILIKE '%counters%';
Q265 · The Outbox Pattern for Reliable Side Effects
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, JP Morgan, Cred · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You commit a payment in your DB and need to send a confirmation message. How do you ensure
the message is sent exactly when (and only when) the transaction commits?
The 30-second answer: Use the transactional outbox pattern. In the same transaction that records the
payment, INSERT a row into an outbox table describing the message to send. A separate background
relay polls the outbox and publishes the messages, marking them as sent. The DB transaction
guarantees both rows are present or neither; the relay guarantees at-least-once delivery; with idempotent
consumers you get effectively exactly-once.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose the naive approach: sending the message inside the
transaction means a successful send + failed commit, or successful commit + failed send. Either way,
your DB and downstream are inconsistent. 2. Outbox table is the bridge: the message lives in the
database alongside the business data, so they share atomicity. The transaction commit publishes the
intent to send. 3. The relay (a small worker) reads unsent rows, publishes to Kafka/SQS/RabbitMQ, and
marks them sent. Crashes between publish and mark mean redelivery, which is why consumers must be
idempotent. 4. Trade-offs: tiny additional latency (relay polling interval), an extra table to monitor for
backlog, but you eliminate an entire class of integration bugs.
Edge cases to mention: - Relay throughput must exceed message-generation rate; size the relay
properly or use change-data-capture (Debezium) to stream the outbox directly. - Outbox grows
unbounded — schedule a job to delete sent rows older than a retention window (e.g., 7 days). - For
ordering guarantees, partition the outbox by aggregate ID and consume per-partition serially.
What NOT to say: - Do not send messages inside BEGIN ... COMMIT blocks — that is the bug the
outbox pattern exists to fix. - Do not use the outbox for synchronous request/response; it is for fire-and-
forget events.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 276 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 277
Common follow-up: "How does this compare to two-phase commit between DB and message broker?"
— Outbox is simpler, doesn't require the broker to support 2PC, and degrades gracefully (broker outage
means messages queue up safely in the outbox).
-- Outbox table and atomic insert with business write
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate   TEXT NOT NULL,
  event_type  TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload     JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO payments(id, user_id, amount, status) VALUES (...);
INSERT INTO outbox(aggregate, event_type, payload)
  VALUES ('payment', 'payment.succeeded', '{"id":"...","amount":1000}'::jsonb);
COMMIT;
Q266 · SKIP LOCKED for Concurrent Job Queues
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Cred · Topic: Conflicts
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Five workers all want to grab the next job from a jobs table. How do they avoid stepping on
each other without serialising?
The 30-second answer: Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — each worker locks the
next available row and the others skip rows already locked by peers, so all five workers grab different
jobs in parallel without blocking. It is the canonical concurrent-queue pattern in modern Postgres,
MySQL 8+, and Oracle.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Without SKIP LOCKED, all five workers race on the same SELECT
FOR UPDATE, four block on the lock, and only one progresses at a time — the queue becomes serial. 2.
SKIP LOCKED tells the engine to ignore rows that are currently row-locked and return the next eligible
one. Five workers running this concurrently each pick different rows. 3. Pattern: SELECT id FROM
jobs WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP
LOCKED; then UPDATE jobs SET status = 'in_progress', worker = :id WHERE id
= :picked; do work; commit. 4. Failure mode: if a worker crashes mid-job, the in_progress row stays
locked until the transaction ends (connection close releases the lock); a janitor job resets stale 
in_progress rows older than a threshold back to pending.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 277 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 278
Edge cases to mention: - SKIP LOCKED is not in standard SQL; was added to Postgres 9.5, MySQL
8.0, Oracle 11g. SQL Server uses READPAST hint for similar effect. - The SKIP LOCKED scan still has
to read past locked rows, so ordering by an indexed column matters — ORDER BY priority,
created_at works only if there is a matching index. - Combine with LIMIT to bound the scan per
worker.
What NOT to say: - Do not implement queue workers by polling the same row with FOR UPDATE —
you serialise the whole pool. - Do not assume SKIP LOCKED works on all databases — it doesn't on
older MySQL or SQLite.
Common follow-up: "How do you recover from a worker that crashed mid-job?" — A scheduled task
resets in_progress rows whose picked_at timestamp is older than the job SLA back to 
pending.
-- Worker picks one job, no contention with peers
BEGIN;
SELECT id
FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
-- assume returned id = 42
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'in_progress', worker_id = :me, picked_at = now()
WHERE id = 42;
COMMIT;
-- do the actual work, then mark done
Q267 · Transactions & Deadlocks
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, JP Morgan, Goldman, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic:
Deadlocks
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Give me the complete picture: what is a deadlock, how does the engine detect it, how do you
prevent it, what do you do when you cannot prevent it, and how does behaviour differ across
Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server?
The 30-second answer: A deadlock is a circular wait between two or more transactions, each holding a
lock the other needs. Engines detect it by finding a cycle in the wait-for graph — Postgres lazily after 
deadlock_timeout (default 1s), InnoDB and SQL Server eagerly on every wait. Prevention is
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 278 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 279
consistent lock ordering (sort row IDs ascending before locking). When prevention is impossible, wrap
the transaction in a retry-with-exponential-backoff loop and make sure the work is idempotent. The
classic Indian-fintech example is two simultaneous wallet transfers between the same pair of accounts in
opposite directions — fix by always locking the lower account ID first.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define deadlock crisply: a cycle in the lock wait-for graph. Two
transactions, each holding a row the other wants, neither can release until commit, neither can commit
without the other releasing. The engine must break the cycle by aborting one transaction. 2. Walk
through detection. The wait-for graph has transactions as nodes and a directed edge from A to B
whenever A is waiting on a lock held by B. A deadlock is, by definition, a cycle. Postgres runs the cycle
scan only after a wait has lasted deadlock_timeout to avoid spending CPU on short waits — set it
to 200ms for OLTP, leave at 1s for batch. InnoDB and SQL Server check eagerly on every wait edge, so
detection is essentially instant but with continuous overhead. The victim is whichever transaction the
engine deems cheaper to roll back — SQL Server lets you bias this with DEADLOCK_PRIORITY. 3. The
classic two-transfer scenario. Anjali and Rahul both hit "send money" at the same time, in opposite
directions. Transfer one locks Anjali's row, asks for Rahul's; transfer two locks Rahul's row, asks for
Anjali's. Perfect cycle. Same shape appears in inventory transfers between warehouses, ledger postings,
and graph-walking deletes. 4. Prevention via lock ordering. Before any UPDATE, sort the row IDs
ascending and lock them in that order with SELECT FOR UPDATE. Now both transfers take Anjali first,
the second waits, no cycle ever forms. This is the single most effective deadlock prevention technique
and works across all engines. Document it as a coding standard and enforce in code review. 5. Other
prevention patterns. Atomic single-statement upserts via ON CONFLICT eliminate the read-modify-write
race window. Append-only event-sourced writes avoid row-level contention entirely. Deferrable foreign
keys in Postgres move FK checks to commit time, reducing the window for FK-induced deadlocks.
Smaller transactions reduce the lock footprint and probability of overlap. 6. The retry pattern. Even with
perfect lock ordering you will sometimes deadlock because of index-level or page-level conflicts you
cannot foresee. Wrap the transaction in a retry loop, catch the specific error code (40P01 Postgres, 
1213 MySQL, 1205 SQL Server), sleep base * 2^attempt + jitter, retry up to 3-5 times.
Bubble the error up after the cap and alert; persistent retries hide a real bug. 7. Idempotency is
mandatory. The first attempt may have triggered side effects before the deadlock killed it — emails,
external API calls. Pull all side effects out of the transaction (use the outbox pattern from Q25) and key
external operations with idempotency keys. 8. Distributed deadlocks. When the cycle crosses two
databases or two services, no single engine sees the whole graph. Use per-call timeouts, never hold a
transaction open across a synchronous network call, and prefer saga-based eventual consistency (Q16)
over distributed locks or two-phase commit (Q17).
Edge cases to mention: - Higher isolation makes deadlocks more frequent, not less. SERIALIZABLE
turns many phantom-read scenarios into serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001) that look very similar to
deadlocks (40P01) and need the same retry handling. - Hot single-row contention (Q13/Q24) is not a
deadlock but masquerades as one in slow-query reports — the fix is sharding or atomic increment, not
lock ordering. - Foreign-key insert deadlocks (Q9) happen even without explicit UPDATE because FK
enforcement takes implicit parent share locks. Deferrable FKs reduce the lock window. - Index-level
deadlocks (Q10) can occur on single-row updates because the same UPDATE touches multiple index
entries, each its own lock resource. - Lock-wait timeout (lock_timeout Postgres, 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 279 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 280
innodb_lock_wait_timeout MySQL) is unrelated to deadlock detection — it caps total wait,
independent of whether a cycle exists.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "deadlocks mean the database is overloaded" — load increases
frequency but bad lock ordering is the actual cause. - Do not retry on every error blindly. Deadlock
(40P01) and serialization failure (40001) are retryable; primary-key violation, check constraint, and FK
violation are not. Match on the specific SQLSTATE. - Do not raise isolation to fix deadlocks — usually
makes them worse and doesn't change the underlying contention pattern. - Do not propose distributed
locks (Redis, Zookeeper) as the default solution for in-database deadlocks. They are useful for cross-
service coordination, not for resources that already live in the database. - Do not hold a database
transaction open across a synchronous network call. This is the single most common production stuck-
transaction pattern.
Common follow-up: "Walk me through your last production deadlock and what you changed to fix it." —
A great answer names a specific table, the two code paths that interleaved, the lock ordering fix you
applied, and the retry pattern you added as defence in depth. Bonus marks for showing the deadlock
graph from the logs and explaining how you confirmed the fix via load testing.
-- Defensive pattern: lock ordering + retry, in the two-transfer case
-- Application pseudocode (Postgres-flavoured)
-- for attempt in 1..5:
--   try:
--     BEGIN;
--     ids := SORT([from_id, to_id]);                       -- ascending
--     SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id IN (ids) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
--     UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - amount WHERE id = from_id;
--     UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + amount WHERE id = to_id;
--     INSERT INTO transfers(from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (from_id, to_id, amount);
--     INSERT INTO outbox(event_type, payload) VALUES ('transfer.succeeded', payload);
--     COMMIT;
--     return success
--   except DeadlockDetected (SQLSTATE 40P01):
--     ROLLBACK;
--     sleep(50ms * 2^attempt + random(0,100ms))
-- raise PermanentDeadlockError
Chapter 6 — Normalization & Schema Design
Schema design is where classroom theory and production reality argue. Service MNCs love to ask the
textbook stuff by rote — recite 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF in order, draw the dependency diagram, prove the
decomposition is lossless. Product companies and GCC panels flip the script — they ask "tell me about
a time you deliberately denormalized, and what bit you six months later." Both flavours show up in the
same week of interviews, so you need to walk in carrying both vocabularies. This chapter mixes the
academic ladder with the production trade-offs — normal forms first, then star schemas, surrogate keys,
multi-tenant patterns, hierarchical data, sharding, and the hardest question of all: when to break the
rules. Read it like you're prepping for two interviews at once, because you are.
