Q268 · First Normal Form — Atomic Columns Only
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: Normal Forms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does it mean for a table to be in First Normal Form? Give me an example of a table that
violates 1NF and how you would fix it.
The 30-second answer: 1NF says every column holds a single atomic value and every row is unique —
no repeating groups, no comma-separated lists, no arrays stuffed into a varchar. Fix it by splitting the
multi-valued column into its own child table with a foreign key back to the parent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define atomic clearly — a value the database cannot meaningfully
split further for query purposes. A phone number is atomic; a comma-separated list of phone numbers is
not. 2. Give a concrete violation. A students table with a subjects column holding 
'Maths,Physics,Chemistry' breaks 1NF. You cannot index it, you cannot join on it, you cannot
count subjects without string functions. 3. Show the fix — create a student_subjects junction table
with (student_id, subject) rows. Now every cell is atomic and queries become first-class SQL.
4. Mention the modern wrinkle — JSON and array columns in Postgres or MySQL technically hold non-
atomic values, but most engineers accept them because the database can index inside them. Be ready
to defend that nuance if the interviewer pushes.
Edge cases to mention: - Repeating groups across columns (phone1, phone2, phone3) also
violate 1NF in spirit even though each cell is atomic — same fix, move to a child table. - A primary key is
required for 1NF — a table with duplicate rows and no key is not in 1NF at all. - ENUMs are atomic — a
column holding 'pending' or 'paid' is fine, only a list of statuses would be a problem.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "1NF means no NULLs" — that is a common misconception, NULLs are
perfectly allowed. - Do not claim a JSON column always violates 1NF without nuance — many
production systems intentionally use JSONB for flexible attributes.
Common follow-up: "What is the practical cost of leaving a comma-separated column in production?"
— You lose indexes, you lose joinability, you lose referential integrity, and every query needs LIKE
'%X%' which is unindexable and wrong ('Maths' matches 'Mathsy').
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 281 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 282
-- Violates 1NF
CREATE TABLE students_bad (id INT, name TEXT, subjects TEXT);
INSERT INTO students_bad VALUES (1, 'Riya', 'Maths,Physics');
-- 1NF compliant
CREATE TABLE students (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE student_subjects (
  student_id INT REFERENCES students(id),
  subject TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, subject)
);
Q269 · Second Normal Form — Killing Partial Dependencies
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, TCS, Accenture, HCL · Topic: Normal Forms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain Second Normal Form with an example. Why does 2NF only matter when you have a
composite primary key?
The 30-second answer: 2NF says no non-key column depends on only part of a composite key. It only
matters when the key is composite — if your key is a single column, you cannot have a partial
dependency, so 2NF is automatic. Fix violations by pulling the partially dependent columns into a
separate table keyed on just the relevant part.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the classic example — an order_items table with
composite key (order_id, product_id). Columns quantity and unit_price depend on
the full key, but product_name depends only on product_id. That is a partial dependency. 2.
Explain why it is bad — product_name repeats for every order line, so changing the product name
means updating thousands of rows, and the same name can drift to different spellings. 3. Show the fix —
move product_name to a products table keyed on product_id. Now order_items only
stores facts about the line, and product metadata lives in one place. 4. Hammer the single-column-key
point — if your PK is just order_id, every other column depends on the whole key by definition. 2NF
is only interesting with composite keys.
Edge cases to mention: - If you use a surrogate key like id BIGSERIAL and ignore the natural
composite, you can hide 2NF violations behind the surrogate — the underlying dependency still exists. -
2NF assumes the table is already in 1NF — if you have repeating groups, fix that first. - Reporting tables
and OLAP fact tables often violate 2NF deliberately to avoid runtime joins.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 282 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 283
What NOT to say: - Do not say "2NF means no duplicates" — that is what a primary key already
enforces, 2NF is about dependencies. - Do not skip 1NF as a prerequisite — normal forms are a ladder,
you cannot jump rungs.
Common follow-up: "How would you spot a 2NF violation in a code review?" — Look for composite
PKs where any non-key column repeats identically across rows that share part of the key — that
repetition is the smoking gun.
-- 2NF violation: product_name depends only on product_id
CREATE TABLE order_items_bad (
  order_id INT, product_id INT,
  product_name TEXT, quantity INT, unit_price NUMERIC,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
-- 2NF compliant
CREATE TABLE products (product_id INT PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id INT, product_id INT REFERENCES products,
  quantity INT, unit_price NUMERIC,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
Q270 · Third Normal Form — No Transitive Dependencies
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Cognizant, Capgemini · Topic: Normal Forms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Define Third Normal Form. What is a transitive dependency and how do you remove it?
The 30-second answer: 3NF says every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and
nothing but the key — a transitive dependency is when a non-key column depends on another non-key
column instead of the primary key. Fix it by splitting the dependent group into its own table.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Use a concrete example — an employees table with (emp_id,
name, dept_id, dept_name, dept_location). The key is emp_id, but dept_name and 
dept_location depend on dept_id, not directly on emp_id. That is transitive — emp_id
determines dept_id which determines dept_name. 2. Explain why it bites — change a
department's name and you update every employee row, with the usual drift and inconsistency risk. 3.
Show the fix — create a departments table keyed on dept_id holding dept_name and 
dept_location, and leave only dept_id in employees. 4. Make the contrast with 2NF clear —
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 283 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 284
2NF is about partial dependencies on a composite key, 3NF is about chained dependencies through any
non-key column.
Edge cases to mention: - Calculated columns like total = quantity * price look transitive but
are usually treated as denormalization for performance, not a 3NF concern — the dependency is on a
function, not another stored column. - Some 3NF violations are intentional — caching country_name
next to country_code saves a join and rarely changes. - 3NF still allows redundancy across tables —
only within a single table is the rule strict.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "3NF means foreign keys everywhere" — foreign keys are about
referential integrity, not normalization. - Do not confuse 3NF with BCNF — they overlap heavily but differ
on edge cases with overlapping candidate keys.
Common follow-up: "Is 3NF enough for production?" — For OLTP, yes, almost always. For OLAP and
reporting, 3NF is usually too join-heavy and people denormalize into star schemas.
-- 3NF violation: dept_name depends on dept_id, not emp_id
CREATE TABLE employees_bad (
  emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT,
  dept_id INT, dept_name TEXT, dept_location TEXT
);
-- 3NF compliant
CREATE TABLE departments (
  dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT, dept_location TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE employees (
  emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT,
  dept_id INT REFERENCES departments
);
Q271 · Boyce-Codd Normal Form — Stricter Than 3NF
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs · Topic:
Normal Forms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is BCNF and how is it different from 3NF? Give me an example where a table is in 3NF but
not in BCNF.
The 30-second answer: BCNF says every functional determinant must itself be a candidate key. 3NF
allows a non-prime attribute to depend on a candidate key, but BCNF closes the loophole where a prime
attribute depends on a non-key column. They differ only in rare cases with overlapping candidate keys.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 284 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 285
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Establish the rule clearly — if X → Y holds, then X must be a
superkey. No exceptions. 2. Give the canonical example — a course-instructor-room table where 
(course, day) → room and room → course. The candidate keys are (course, day) and 
(room, day). The dependency room → course has room on the left, which is not a candidate
key — that violates BCNF even though the table is in 3NF. 3. Show the fix — decompose into two tables,
one mapping room → course and another mapping (course, day) → room. The
decomposition is lossless but loses one functional dependency. 4. Acknowledge the trade-off — BCNF
decomposition can lose dependencies that 3NF preserves, which is why some teams stop at 3NF
deliberately.
Edge cases to mention: - Most 3NF tables are already in BCNF — the violating cases need overlapping
candidate keys, which are uncommon in well-designed schemas. - BCNF decomposition is always
lossless join but not always dependency-preserving — a known limitation. - For tables with a single
candidate key, 3NF and BCNF are identical — there is no way to violate one without the other.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "BCNF is just 3NF with stricter rules and you should always aim for it" —
sometimes 3NF is the right stopping point because BCNF loses dependencies. - Do not invent BCNF
violations from textbook examples without overlapping candidate keys.
Common follow-up: "When would you deliberately stay in 3NF and not go to BCNF?" — When the
BCNF decomposition would force you to lose a functional dependency that you want the database to
enforce via a single table constraint.
-- 3NF but not BCNF: room -> course, but room is not a candidate key
CREATE TABLE course_schedule (
  course TEXT, day TEXT, room TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (course, day),
  UNIQUE (room, day)
);
-- BCNF fix: two tables, lossless but loses the room->course dependency
Q272 · 4NF and 5NF — Multi-Valued and Join Dependencies
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan, Oracle India · Topic: Normal Forms
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Briefly, what do 4NF and 5NF address? Have you ever encountered a real-world violation?
The 30-second answer: 4NF removes multi-valued dependencies — when a single key implies two
independent sets of values. 5NF removes join dependencies that cannot be inferred from candidate
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 285 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 286
keys. In practice, most production schemas never explicitly worry about 4NF or 5NF because they would
be caught earlier as obvious modelling mistakes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define a multi-valued dependency — X →→ Y means X
determines a set of Y values independent of any other column. If a table holds (student,
language, hobby) where languages and hobbies are independent, you have two MVDs and a 4NF
violation. 2. Show the 4NF fix — split into (student, language) and (student, hobby).
Joining them back gives the original, but without the spurious cross-product rows. 3. Touch 5NF lightly
— it handles join dependencies that need three or more tables to reconstruct. The textbook example is 
(supplier, part, project) where you can only reconstruct the truth by joining three binary
projections. Real production almost never hits this honestly. 4. Be honest in the answer — admit these
are rare and most engineers never explicitly check for them. Interviewers asking 4NF or 5NF are usually
testing depth of knowledge, not expecting war stories.
Edge cases to mention: - A 4NF violation often hides as a single table with two independent multi-
select fields — splitting them is almost always the right call. - 5NF is more theoretical than practical —
many textbooks treat it as a curiosity. - If a 4NF or 5NF violation is profitable to keep (rare), document it
clearly.
What NOT to say: - Do not pretend you fight 5NF battles every sprint — it is intellectually dishonest and
interviewers see through it. - Do not confuse multi-valued dependencies with multi-valued columns —
the former is structural, the latter breaks 1NF.
Common follow-up: "If 4NF and 5NF are so rare, why do textbooks teach them?" — They complete the
theory and prove that 3NF and BCNF are not always enough. Knowing they exist is more important than
using them daily.
-- 4NF violation: student determines languages AND hobbies independently
-- (student, language, hobby) with cartesian product rows
-- 4NF fix: two separate tables
CREATE TABLE student_languages (student_id INT, language TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, language));
CREATE TABLE student_hobbies (student_id INT, hobby TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, hobby));
Q273 · Denormalization — When and Why
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, PhonePe, Cred · Topic: Schema Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Tell me about a time you deliberately denormalized a schema. What did you gain and what did
you give up?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 286 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 287
The 30-second answer: You denormalize when read amplification is killing you — joins, aggregates, or
cross-table lookups happen on every request and the latency budget will not stretch. You gain query
speed and simpler reads, and you give up write consistency, more storage, and the need for application-
level discipline to keep duplicated data in sync.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with a real scenario. An order listing page joins orders, users,
addresses, and payment status — at scale, the join cost crushes p95 latency, so you cache the user
name and shipping city directly on the orders row. 2. State the trade-offs explicitly — every user
name change now needs to update orders, or you accept stale data, or you run a backfill job nightly. 3.
Mention common patterns — counter columns (total_orders on users), denormalized search
columns, materialized aggregates on dashboards. 4. Show the discipline — denormalization should be a
deliberate decision logged in an ADR, not an accidental schema drift. And it usually needs invariant
checks or reconciliation jobs to catch drift.
Edge cases to mention: - For write-heavy systems, denormalization can actually hurt because every
write fans out to multiple rows. - Some denormalizations are safe because the source is immutable —
copying country_code → country_name rarely needs sync. - Denormalization is easier to add than
to remove — overcommitting is a common regret.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "denormalization is always for performance" — sometimes it is for
simplification of downstream consumers. - Do not denormalize speculatively — wait for actual evidence
of join cost, then measure the difference.
Common follow-up: "How do you keep denormalized columns in sync?" — Triggers, application-level
writes in the same transaction, async event consumers, or periodic reconciliation jobs. Each has trade-
offs; pick consciously.
-- Denormalized order table for fast listing
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT,
  user_name TEXT,        -- denormalized snapshot
  shipping_city TEXT,    -- denormalized snapshot
  total_amount NUMERIC,
  status TEXT
);
Q274 · OLTP vs OLAP — Two Different Schema Philosophies
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target India, AmEx, JP Morgan · Topic: Schema
Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 287 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 288
What is the difference in schema philosophy between OLTP and OLAP systems? Can the same
schema serve both?
The 30-second answer: OLTP is built for short, write-heavy transactions and prefers fully normalized
schemas to avoid update anomalies. OLAP is built for read-heavy analytical scans and prefers
denormalized star or snowflake schemas to avoid joins. Trying to serve both from one schema usually
compromises both — most teams replicate OLTP data into a separate analytical store.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the workload contrast — OLTP does many small queries
touching few rows each, OLAP does few queries touching millions of rows each. 2. Show how schema
follows workload — OLTP normalizes to make writes cheap and consistent, OLAP denormalizes to make
scans and aggregates cheap. 3. Explain the indexing difference — OLTP uses point-lookup B-tree
indexes, OLAP prefers columnar storage with bitmap or zone indexes. 4. Address the "can one schema
serve both" question — usually no. ETL pipelines or CDC streams ship OLTP rows into a warehouse
where the schema is reshaped into facts and dimensions.
Edge cases to mention: - HTAP systems (TiDB, SingleStore) attempt to serve both workloads from one
engine — they trade off some of each world's optimality. - Small startups often use the OLTP database
for analytics for a long time and only move once it hurts. - OLAP queries on OLTP can block writes and
trigger lock contention — a real operational risk.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "OLAP is just OLTP with more data" — the access patterns are
fundamentally different. - Do not propose running analytical workloads against your primary database in
an interview answer — interviewers wince.
Common follow-up: "How do you keep the warehouse fresh?" — Batch ETL on a schedule, CDC
streaming via tools like Debezium, or near-real-time pipelines. Pick based on freshness SLA and
engineering cost.
-- OLTP normalized
SELECT u.name, p.amount
FROM users u JOIN payments p ON u.id = p.user_id
WHERE u.id = 123;
-- OLAP denormalized fact table
SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM fct_payments
WHERE year = 2026 GROUP BY region;
Q275 · Star Schema — Fact and Dimension Tables
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target India, Flipkart, AmEx · Topic: Data
Warehousing
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 288 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 289
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through the star schema. What goes in a fact table, what goes in a dimension table, and
why is it called a star?
The 30-second answer: A star schema has one central fact table holding numeric measures and foreign
keys, surrounded by dimension tables holding descriptive attributes — drawing the relationships looks
like a star. Facts are usually narrow and very long; dimensions are wide and short.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the fact table — rows are events or transactions, columns are
quantitative measures (amount, quantity, duration) plus foreign keys into dimensions. 2. Define dimension
tables — dim_customer, dim_product, dim_date, each holding descriptive context for the
facts. 3. Explain why it scans fast — analytical queries filter on dimension attributes and aggregate fact
measures, which works well with columnar storage and bitmap indexes on the dimension keys. 4.
Mention the date dimension specifically — it is the most common dimension table because slicing by
week, quarter, fiscal year, or holiday flag is a standard analytical need.
Edge cases to mention: - A fact table can be billions of rows; dimensions are usually thousands to
millions. - Conformed dimensions (the same dim_customer shared across multiple fact tables) make
cross-domain analysis possible. - Some facts have zero measures and exist only to record an event —
these are called factless fact tables.
What NOT to say: - Do not describe star schema as just denormalized 3NF — the modelling intent is
fundamentally different. - Do not put descriptive attributes in the fact table — that bloats every row and
breaks the model.
Common follow-up: "What is grain?" — The level of detail in each fact row. One fact row per order line
is a different grain from one fact row per order. Pick the finest grain you might ever need.
CREATE TABLE fct_sales (
  sale_id BIGINT, sale_date_key INT, customer_key INT, product_key INT,
  store_key INT, quantity INT, amount NUMERIC
);
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (customer_key INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT, segment TEXT);
CREATE TABLE dim_product (product_key INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, category TEXT, brand TEXT);
Q276 · Snowflake Schema — When Normalized Dimensions Help
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Oracle India · Topic: Data Warehousing
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 289 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 290
What is a snowflake schema and when would you use it over a star schema?
The 30-second answer: A snowflake schema normalizes the dimension tables, so a dim_product
might reference dim_category which references dim_department. You snowflake when
dimensions are huge or change at different rates and storage savings or referential cleanliness outweigh
the extra join cost.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Describe the structure — dimensions decomposed into related
tables, joined in a hierarchical pattern that looks like a snowflake. 2. Explain the gain — less duplicated
text in wide dimensions, easier maintenance when a category name changes, cleaner separation when
different teams own different levels of the hierarchy. 3. Explain the cost — analytical queries now require
more joins, which hurts performance on wide aggregates and adds query authoring complexity. 4. State
the practical rule — most modern warehouses prefer star schemas because storage is cheap and BI
tools generate cleaner SQL against flat dimensions. Snowflake only when you have a strong reason.
Edge cases to mention: - Slowly changing dimensions (SCD type 2) make snowflaking harder because
history needs to be tracked across multiple normalized tables. - Some BI tools require flattened
dimensions and will materialize the joins anyway — defeats the snowflake benefit. - Columnar databases
compress repeated dimension values so well that snowflaking saves less storage than you think.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "snowflake is always better because it is more normalized" — it is a
trade-off, not an upgrade. - Do not confuse Snowflake the schema with Snowflake the data warehouse
vendor — they are unrelated.
Common follow-up: "How does this affect query performance?" — More joins, longer plans, more
memory for hash joins. On large dimensions the difference is measurable; on small ones it is negligible.
-- Snowflake variant: product references category, category references department
CREATE TABLE dim_department (department_key INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE dim_category (category_key INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, department_key INT);
CREATE TABLE dim_product (product_key INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, category_key INT);
Q277 · Slowly Changing Dimensions — Types 1, 2, 3, 6
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, AmEx, Target India, JP Morgan · Topic: Data
Warehousing
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 290 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 291
Explain the different types of slowly changing dimensions. When would you pick SCD type 2 over
type 1?
The 30-second answer: Type 1 overwrites and loses history. Type 2 inserts a new row with effective
dates so all history is preserved. Type 3 adds a column for the previous value, keeping only one step of
history. Type 6 combines all three. Pick type 2 when historical accuracy matters for analysis — type 1
when you only ever care about current state.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Use a customer dimension example. The customer moves from Pune
to Bengaluru. Type 1 overwrites the city. Type 2 inserts a new row with new effective_from / effective_to
and marks the old one expired. Type 3 adds previous_city. Type 6 keeps the type 2 history plus a
current-value column for easy filtering. 2. Justify type 2 — if you ask "how many sales came from Pune in
2024", type 1 lies because the customer now shows Bengaluru, and historical sales appear to come from
Bengaluru. Type 2 ties each sale to the dimension row that was current at the time. 3. Mention surrogate
keys — type 2 absolutely requires surrogate keys because the natural customer ID stays the same
across versions, but each version needs a distinct dimension key. 4. Discuss type 6 briefly — it satisfies
both "current state" and "historical state" queries, at the cost of redundancy.
Edge cases to mention: - Type 2 dimensions grow without bound — partitioning by year or archiving
expired rows becomes important. - Bi-temporal modelling (effective time + transaction time) extends
SCD type 2 for late-arriving data. - Some teams use append-only event tables instead of SCDs and
reconstruct state via window functions.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "type 2 is always best" — it is heavier and unnecessary for attributes
that genuinely do not need history. - Do not skip the surrogate key requirement — it is what makes type 2
work mechanically.
Common follow-up: "How do you join a fact table to a type 2 dimension correctly?" — Join on the
surrogate key that was active at the fact's event time, not the natural key. The fact captures the surrogate
at insert time.
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT,           -- natural key, repeats across versions
  name TEXT, city TEXT,
  effective_from DATE, effective_to DATE,
  is_current BOOLEAN
);
Q278 · Surrogate Key vs Natural Key
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: Keys
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 291 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 292
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you use a surrogate key over a natural key? Give me a case where the natural key
wins.
The 30-second answer: Use a surrogate key when the natural key is mutable, composite, externally
controlled, or not guaranteed unique under all future scenarios. Use the natural key when it is small,
immutable, meaningful to humans, and convenient for direct lookup — like a country code in a 
dim_country table.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define each — surrogate is a system-generated key with no business
meaning (BIGSERIAL, UUID), natural is a key that exists in the real world (PAN, GSTIN, ISBN, email). 2.
List surrogate advantages — immutable, narrow, fast to join, decoupled from business changes. If the
natural key changes (rare, but happens — like a renamed product SKU), the surrogate stays put. 3. List
natural advantages — no extra lookup needed, smaller schema, queries are self-documenting (WHERE
country_code = 'IN' reads better than WHERE country_key = 47). 4. Practical rule — most
production OLTP tables use a surrogate primary key and add a unique index on the natural key. You get
the best of both.
Edge cases to mention: - PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN feel natural but are mutable in edge cases — surrogate
is safer. - Junction tables can use the composite of the two foreign keys as the natural primary key — no
surrogate needed. - For very small reference tables (status codes, country lists), natural keys work well.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always use surrogate keys" — that is dogmatic, and natural keys are
correct in many lookup tables. - Do not use email as a primary key — emails change, and cascading
updates across foreign keys is painful.
Common follow-up: "What happens if a natural key changes after thousands of foreign key references
exist?" — Without ON UPDATE CASCADE you break referential integrity; with it, you trigger expensive
cascading writes. A surrogate avoids both.
-- Surrogate key with unique natural key index
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,    -- surrogate
  pan_number CHAR(10) UNIQUE NOT NULL,  -- natural key
  name TEXT
);
Q279 · Composite Key vs Surrogate ID
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Infosys, TCS, Razorpay, PhonePe · Topic: Keys
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 292 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 293
A junction table like order_items — do you keep the composite (order_id,
product_id) as the primary key, or add a surrogate id?
The 30-second answer: Default to the composite — it is the natural identity and self-enforces
uniqueness. Add a surrogate only when the row is referenced by other tables, when the composite is
wide and ugly to propagate, or when you anticipate the composite needing to change.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lay out the composite case — (order_id, product_id) is the
truth. It enforces that one product appears once per order without an extra constraint. 2. Lay out the
surrogate case — if another table needs to reference a specific order_item, propagating two
columns is awkward, and a single order_item_id is cleaner. 3. Mention the multiple-rows-same-
product nuance — if the business allows the same product twice in an order with different unit prices
(rare but possible for promotions), the composite no longer holds and a surrogate becomes necessary. 4.
Acknowledge framework preferences — many ORMs default to surrogate IDs everywhere, so teams
using Hibernate or Django often add a surrogate just for consistency, even on junction tables.
Edge cases to mention: - Composite keys hurt index size when wide — three or four columns of TEXT
can make a 200-byte index entry. - If the junction stores additional columns (quantity, 
unit_price), some teams call it an associative entity and lean towards a surrogate. - Wide
composite keys propagate into foreign-key tables and bloat them too — a hidden cost.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always add a surrogate to junction tables" — it adds storage and
weakens the natural uniqueness constraint. - Do not omit the unique index when you add a surrogate —
without it, you can insert the same (order_id, product_id) twice.
Common follow-up: "If you add a surrogate, where do you put the uniqueness constraint?" — A
UNIQUE index on the original composite columns — otherwise the surrogate masks duplicates.
-- Composite key as PK
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id INT, product_id INT, quantity INT, unit_price NUMERIC,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
-- Surrogate variant with uniqueness preserved
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id INT, product_id INT, quantity INT, unit_price NUMERIC,
  UNIQUE (order_id, product_id)
);

Q280 · UUID vs Auto-Increment ID
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Swiggy, PhonePe · Topic: Keys
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
UUID or auto-increment integer for primary keys? Walk me through the trade-offs.
The 30-second answer: Auto-increment is small, fast, and great for index locality, but it leaks
information (row count, growth rate) and serializes writes on the sequence. UUIDs are globally unique,
generatable client-side, and safe to expose, but they are wide, random, and destroy B-tree locality which
slows inserts on large tables.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the size and locality angle — a BIGINT is 8 bytes, a UUID is
16 bytes plus index overhead. Random UUIDs cause B-tree page splits during inserts, hurting write
throughput on large tables. 2. List integer drawbacks — sequential IDs let attackers enumerate (/
orders/1234 then /orders/1235), and a centralized sequence is a write hotspot in distributed
systems. 3. List UUID drawbacks — bigger storage, bigger indexes, random insert order, harder to read
in logs and URLs. 4. Mention the modern compromise — ULID, KSUID, UUIDv7, and Snowflake IDs are
sortable and time-prefixed, giving you UUID-like uniqueness with much better locality.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL InnoDB primary keys are physically clustered, so random UUIDs hurt
much more than they do in Postgres heap tables. - UUID v1 leaks the MAC address; UUID v4 is fully
random and safer for exposure. - Some teams use BIGINT internally and UUID externally — best of both
worlds with a translation layer.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "UUIDs are always better because they are unique" — auto-increment is
also unique within the table. - Do not ignore index size — on a billion-row table, the difference is
measured in gigabytes.
Common follow-up: "How do UUIDs affect replication?" — They let you generate IDs offline and merge
later without collisions, which is valuable in mobile-first or multi-master setups.
-- Auto-increment
CREATE TABLE orders (id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, ...);
-- UUID
CREATE TABLE orders (id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), ...);
Q281 · ULID, KSUID, Snowflake — Sortable Alternatives
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, PhonePe · Topic: Keys
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 294 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 295
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You want global uniqueness without sacrificing insert locality. What are your options beyond
UUID?
The 30-second answer: ULID, KSUID, UUIDv7, and Twitter Snowflake IDs all prefix a timestamp to the
random portion, so IDs generated later sort after IDs generated earlier. You get UUID-like uniqueness
with index locality close to auto-increment.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain why sortability matters — when IDs are inserted in order, the
B-tree grows on the right edge and page splits stay minimal, preserving insert throughput. 2. Describe
each — ULID is 26 chars base32 with 48-bit timestamp + 80-bit randomness; KSUID is 27 chars with 32-
bit timestamp; UUIDv7 is RFC standard with millisecond timestamp; Snowflake is 64-bit with timestamp
+ worker + sequence. 3. State trade-offs — ULID and KSUID need a library (no native support yet in
most DBs), UUIDv7 is becoming standard, Snowflake needs a coordinator for worker IDs. 4.
Recommend UUIDv7 for new green-field work — it is RFC standard, sortable, generatable client-side,
and is gaining first-class database support.
Edge cases to mention: - All these schemes leak the creation timestamp — if that is sensitive, stick with
random UUIDs. - Clock skew across servers can produce out-of-order IDs — use NTP and accept the
rare local reordering. - Snowflake IDs need careful worker ID assignment; collisions cause silent
duplicates.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they are all the same" — the encoding, length, and timestamp
resolution differ in ways that matter. - Do not invent your own ID scheme — pick a known one and
survive code review.
Common follow-up: "How do you generate ULIDs from your application server?" — A library generates
them client-side; the database just stores them as a CHAR(26) or BYTEA — no central coordinator
needed.
-- UUIDv7 (Postgres 18+) or use uuid_v7() extension
CREATE TABLE events (id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_v7(), payload JSONB);
Q282 · Junction Tables for Many-to-Many
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: Schema Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 295 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 296
Students and courses — a student can enrol in many courses and a course has many students.
How do you model that?
The 30-second answer: A junction table enrolments with two foreign keys, (student_id,
course_id), plus any attributes specific to the enrolment itself (grade, enrolment date). The composite
is the primary key.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule — many-to-many always needs an intermediate table.
There is no clean way to do it with just two tables. 2. Define the junction — minimal version is two FKs
forming a composite PK. Richer version adds enrolment-specific attributes that belong neither to the
student nor the course. 3. Discuss naming — call it after the relationship (enrolments, 
subscriptions) not after the two parents (student_course) when possible. Better readability
and supports future attributes. 4. Mention the natural extension — if the junction grows attributes, it
stops being a pure junction and becomes an associative entity, which often takes a surrogate PK.
Edge cases to mention: - Self-referencing many-to-many uses two FKs into the same parent table
( user_id, friend_id in a friends table). - If the same pair must repeat (a student takes the same
course twice), the composite PK fails — switch to a surrogate plus a timestamp. - Cascading deletes
need careful thought — deleting a student should usually cascade to enrolments, but a course delete
might be restricted.
What NOT to say: - Do not stuff course IDs into a comma-separated column on the student row — that
violates 1NF and breaks everything. - Do not omit the foreign key constraints — referential integrity is
free protection.
Common follow-up: "How do you efficiently query all students in a course?" — Index the junction on 
(course_id, student_id) for that direction, and on (student_id, course_id) for the
reverse — covering indexes if you need only the IDs.
CREATE TABLE enrolments (
  student_id INT REFERENCES students,
  course_id INT REFERENCES courses,
  enrolled_on DATE,
  grade CHAR(1),
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
Q283 · Polymorphic Association — The SQL Anti-Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Swiggy · Topic: Schema Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 296 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 297
A comments table has commentable_id and commentable_type so it can comment on
articles, photos, or videos. What is wrong with this design?
The 30-second answer: Polymorphic association breaks referential integrity — the database cannot
enforce a foreign key when the target table varies by row. You lose constraint protection, join
performance suffers, and queries need conditional joins or unions. Better alternatives are exclusive
foreign keys, an inheritance pattern, or a separate junction table per parent type.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose the problem — commentable_id references different
tables depending on commentable_type, so no single FK constraint can guard it. Orphan rows can
accumulate silently. 2. Describe the alternatives — option A is multiple nullable FKs with a CHECK
constraint enforcing exactly one is set; option B is a separate commentable parent table with subtype
tables; option C is dedicated article_comments, photo_comments, video_comments tables.
3. State the trade-off — polymorphic feels elegant in ORMs (Rails, Django) but the database cannot help
you, so bugs surface in production rather than at schema time. 4. Recommend option A or C for most
cases — they keep referential integrity and let the optimizer plan joins properly.
Edge cases to mention: - Some teams accept polymorphic association in low-stakes tables
(notifications, audit logs) where occasional orphans are tolerable. - Postgres now supports inheritance
and partitioning that can model polymorphic-like patterns cleanly. - Polymorphic FKs make analytics
queries painful — every report needs the type conditional.
What NOT to say: - Do not call it elegant just because the ORM hides it — that is what the framework
wants you to think. - Do not say "we can enforce it in application code" — application code drifts, the
database does not forget.
Common follow-up: "How do you migrate away from polymorphic association safely?" — Add the
proper FK columns, dual-write for a period, backfill, validate, then drop the polymorphic columns.
Standard staged migration.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 297 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 298
-- Polymorphic (anti-pattern)
CREATE TABLE comments (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  commentable_id BIGINT, commentable_type TEXT,
  body TEXT
);
-- Exclusive FK alternative
CREATE TABLE comments (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  article_id BIGINT REFERENCES articles,
  photo_id BIGINT REFERENCES photos,
  video_id BIGINT REFERENCES videos,
  body TEXT,
  CHECK (num_nonnulls(article_id, photo_id, video_id) = 1)
);
Q284 · Entity-Attribute-Value — When It Makes Sense
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Healthcare GCCs, Oracle India, Salesforce India · Topic: Schema Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When is it acceptable to use the EAV pattern, and when is it definitely the wrong call?
The 30-second answer: EAV makes sense for sparse, user-defined attribute sets where the schema
cannot be known in advance — clinical observations, custom form builders, product catalogues with
thousands of categories. It is the wrong call for any attribute set you can enumerate, because EAV
destroys type safety, query simplicity, and performance.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Describe the structure — three columns: entity ID, attribute name,
value (often stored as text and cast). You can also separate value tables by type (value_text, 
value_int, value_date). 2. Defend the rare use case — a clinical EHR where physicians record
dozens of observation types per patient, most rows sparse, new attributes added without schema
migrations. 3. List the harms — queries need self-joins per attribute, indexes are hard, types are lost,
aggregations are painful, and the optimizer has no clue what is in the data. 4. Mention the modern
alternative — JSONB columns. They preserve flexibility without abandoning the relational model and can
be indexed via GIN or expression indexes.
Edge cases to mention: - EAV combined with metadata tables (a table describing valid attributes and
their types) is the only sane way to keep some sanity. - Reporting on EAV data usually requires a
denormalized pivot — built as a materialized view. - JSONB columns have made true EAV almost
obsolete for new applications.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 298 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 299
What NOT to say: - Do not call EAV elegant or flexible without listing the costs — interviewers are
looking for nuance. - Do not use EAV when you know the attribute set — it is over-engineering for short-
term flexibility.
Common follow-up: "Why is JSONB usually a better choice today?" — Indexable, queryable with JSON
path operators, preserves types within the document, and you do not need self-joins per attribute.
-- EAV pattern
CREATE TABLE patient_observations (
  patient_id INT, attribute TEXT, value TEXT, recorded_at TIMESTAMP
);
-- Modern alternative using JSONB
CREATE TABLE patient_observations (
  patient_id INT, observations JSONB, recorded_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX ON patient_observations USING GIN (observations);
Q285 · Soft Delete — Pros, Cons, Alternatives
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: Schema Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A deleted_at column on every table — is that a good idea? What are the alternatives?
The 30-second answer: Soft delete is convenient for recovery and audit but pollutes every query with 
WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, breaks unique constraints, weakens foreign keys, and grows tables
forever. Alternatives include moving deleted rows to an archive table, append-only event sourcing, or true
hard deletes with an audit log.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lay out the convenience — undelete is a simple update, audit trail is
built in, and historical queries can include past data. 2. Lay out the friction — every read query must filter,
unique indexes need to be partial (UNIQUE (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), foreign keys
can point at soft-deleted rows leading to logical inconsistency, and table size grows without bound. 3.
Discuss alternatives — archive tables move deletes elsewhere keeping the live table clean; event
sourcing makes deletion a recorded event with state reconstruction; hard delete with separate audit
captures the deletion fact without bloating the live table. 4. Recommend a hybrid — soft delete on user-
facing entities for short-term recovery, hard delete after retention period, with audit log for forensics.
Edge cases to mention: - Compliance regulations (DPDP, RBI norms) sometimes require true deletion,
not soft delete — flag this aggressively in interviews. - Cascading soft deletes are tricky — you have to
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 299 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 300
write the cascade logic yourself; SQL does not understand deleted_at. - Soft delete fails silently
with most ORMs that do not auto-filter — every query becomes a bug waiting to happen.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose soft delete as the universal default — it has real costs. - Do not
forget about indexes — query plans degrade as the deleted fraction grows.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle unique constraints with soft delete?" — Partial unique index
that ignores deleted rows, so a deleted user can re-register the same email.
-- Soft delete with partial unique index
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, deleted_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
Q286 · Audit Log — Separate Table or Same Table With History
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Schema
Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You need to track every change to the accounts table. Do you keep history in the same table
or a separate accounts_history table?
The 30-second answer: For OLTP, keep current state in accounts and history in 
accounts_history — the live table stays small and fast, and audit queries do not slow normal
traffic. For analytical use, sometimes a single bi-temporal table with effective dates is preferable for
reconstruction queries.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Describe the separate-table approach — accounts has current
rows, accounts_history has full snapshots with valid_from, valid_to, and a 
changed_by audit field. A trigger or application logic writes to history on every update. 2. Describe
the same-table approach (SCD type 2 style) — accounts has all versions with is_current and
date columns. Current-state queries need a filter; historical queries are natural. 3. State the trade-off —
separate table keeps hot path fast and clean; same table simplifies reconstruction but bloats the working
set. 4. Mention temporal tables — some databases (SQL Server, PostgreSQL extensions, Oracle
Flashback) support system-versioned temporal tables natively.
Edge cases to mention: - High-write tables generate huge history volumes — partition the history table
by month or use compressed columnar storage. - For PII fields, audit log retention may need redaction
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 300 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 301
rules to comply with privacy laws. - Reconstructing state at an arbitrary timestamp from event logs alone
is expensive — snapshots help.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "just use triggers and forget it" — triggers can silently fail and bloat write
times. - Do not store history forever without a retention policy — that is a future operations bill.
Common follow-up: "What audit fields do you always include?" — changed_at, changed_by, 
change_type (insert/update/delete), and the full row payload (often JSONB). Minimum viable audit.
CREATE TABLE accounts (id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, balance NUMERIC, updated_at TIMESTAMP);
CREATE TABLE accounts_history (
  history_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id BIGINT, balance NUMERIC,
  valid_from TIMESTAMP, valid_to TIMESTAMP,
  changed_by TEXT, change_type TEXT
);
Q287 · Append-Only Table Design
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Schema Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When does an append-only table make sense and what changes about how you query it?
The 30-second answer: Append-only tables make sense for events, ledger entries, and audit trails
where every state change is a fact that must never be edited or deleted. Queries shift to deriving current
state via aggregation, window functions, or materialized views over the event stream.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the pattern — inserts only, no updates, no deletes. Mutations
become new rows with timestamps. The truth is the sequence, not the latest row. 2. Give examples —
bank ledger entries (every transaction is a fact), inventory movements (each stock change recorded),
payment events, user activity logs. 3. Discuss querying — current balance is SUM(amount); current
inventory is SUM(quantity_delta); current status is a window function picking the latest event per
entity. 4. Mention performance — append-only is great for write throughput (no row contention), easy to
partition by time, easy to archive cold partitions, and naturally compatible with event sourcing.
Edge cases to mention: - Snapshot rows speed up derivation — compute current balance every N
events and aggregate forward from there. - Compaction and retention policies are still needed even if
individual rows are immutable. - Append-only data is easier to replicate and audit because the order of
facts is preserved.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 301 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 302
What NOT to say: - Do not claim append-only is always slower for reads — with snapshots and
partitioning, it can be comparable to mutable schemas. - Do not forget indexes on entity_id + event_time
— most queries need that combination.
Common follow-up: "How do you correct a bad event in an append-only table?" — Insert a
compensating event that reverses the original, never modify the original. The audit trail stays clean.
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  entry_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id BIGINT, amount NUMERIC,
  event_time TIMESTAMP, event_type TEXT,
  reference_id BIGINT
);
-- Current balance via aggregation
SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) FROM ledger_entries GROUP BY account_id;
Q288 · Multi-Tenant Schema — Three Strategies
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Salesforce India, Zoho, Freshworks, Razorpay · Topic: Multi-Tenancy
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You are designing a SaaS platform serving thousands of business customers. Shared schema,
schema-per-tenant, or database-per-tenant — which do you pick and why?
The 30-second answer: Shared schema with tenant_id columns scales operationally but needs
careful row-level security and noisy-neighbour management. Schema-per-tenant offers isolation but
blows up at thousands of tenants. Database-per-tenant gives the strongest isolation and per-customer
backups but is the most expensive. Pick by tenant count, isolation needs, and per-tenant scale.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain shared schema — every table has tenant_id, every
query filters on it, indexes start with tenant_id. Cheap, dense, but a missing filter leaks data. Row-
level security (RLS) helps enforce. 2. Explain schema-per-tenant — one Postgres schema per customer.
Isolation per tenant, separate migrations risk if not automated, connection pool fragmentation, hard at
10000+ tenants. 3. Explain database-per-tenant — strongest isolation, per-tenant backup and restore,
per-tenant tuning. Most operationally expensive, only viable for small numbers of large enterprise
tenants. 4. Recommend a tiered approach — shared schema for the long tail, dedicated database for the
largest enterprise customers who need isolation guarantees.
Edge cases to mention: - Shared schema with RLS is industry standard for B2B SaaS at scale
(Salesforce, Shopify largely use shared models). - Per-tenant encryption keys force a per-tenant
database for some compliance regimes. - Migrations on shared schema apply once; on schema-per-
tenant they iterate; on database-per-tenant they orchestrate.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 302 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 303
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always isolate per customer for safety" — at scale that is operationally
infeasible. - Do not forget about cross-tenant analytics — shared schema makes it trivial, isolated models
make it painful.
Common follow-up: "How do you prevent a tenant_id filter from being forgotten?" — Row-level security
policies, or wrapping every query through a tenant-aware data access layer that injects the filter.
-- Shared schema with RLS
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC
);
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::BIGINT);
Q289 · Sharding Strategies — Range, Hash, Directory
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, Razorpay, PhonePe, Swiggy, Cred · Topic: Sharding
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through range, hash, and directory-based sharding. When does each strategy fit?
The 30-second answer: Range sharding splits by key ranges (orders by date, users by ID range) —
good for time-ordered queries but creates hotspots on the latest shard. Hash sharding spreads load
uniformly via hash(key) mod N — good for write balance but bad for range queries. Directory
sharding uses a lookup table for flexible mapping — most flexible but adds a dependency.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Range — keys map to contiguous shards. Easy to reason about,
easy to query a date range, but every new write hits the current shard (write hotspot) and resharding
requires range splits. 2. Hash — hash(user_id) mod 16 distributes uniformly. Eliminates hotspots
but range queries scatter across all shards, and resharding when N changes is painful unless you use
consistent hashing. 3. Directory — a metadata service maps each entity to a shard. Allows arbitrary
placement, easy rebalancing, but introduces a lookup hop and the directory becomes a single point of
contention. 4. State the practical pattern — hash for user-facing OLTP with even load, range for time-
series and analytical workloads, directory for systems needing per-tenant placement control.
Edge cases to mention: - Cross-shard joins and transactions are hard regardless of strategy — design
to avoid them. - Consistent hashing softens the resharding pain by minimizing keys that need to move
when N changes. - Hot keys (a celebrity user) can crush hash sharding's load balancing — sometimes
you split or replicate hot keys separately.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 303 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 304
What NOT to say: - Do not say "hash is always best because it balances load" — range queries become
impossible. - Do not introduce sharding before you have measured single-node limits — premature
sharding is a massive complexity tax.
Common follow-up: "What does a cross-shard transaction look like?" — Two-phase commit if you must,
but most teams refactor to avoid them entirely via saga patterns or per-shard data ownership.
-- Hash sharding example: pick shard via deterministic function
-- shard_id = hash(user_id) % 16
-- Range sharding example: orders by created_at quarter
Q290 · Time-Series Schema Design
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy, IoT-heavy GCCs · Topic: Schema Design
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Design a schema for storing one billion metric readings per day. What are the key choices?
The 30-second answer: Partition by time (usually daily or hourly), keep rows narrow (entity_id,
metric_name, timestamp, value), use columnar or specialised time-series storage where possible, and
aggregate into rollup tables for long-term retention. Avoid wide rows and per-metric tables.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Time partitioning is non-negotiable — partition by day for queries
that scan ranges, drop old partitions for cheap retention enforcement. 2. Schema shape — narrow 
(entity_id, metric, timestamp, value) rows scale better than wide rows with many metric
columns, because cardinality varies wildly across metrics. 3. Storage — TimescaleDB, ClickHouse,
InfluxDB, and similar specialised stores compress time-series 10x to 100x better than row-oriented OLTP.
Use them when scale justifies. 4. Rollups — keep raw data for 7 to 30 days, aggregate to 1-minute then
1-hour buckets for longer history. Storage cost drops dramatically.
Edge cases to mention: - Out-of-order writes are common in IoT — your schema and indexes must
accept them gracefully. - Cardinality explosion (millions of distinct metric labels) kills query performance
— bound your dimensions. - Compression depends on data sort order — sort by (entity_id, timestamp)
and watch ratios climb.
What NOT to say: - Do not store time-series in a vanilla normalized OLTP schema at scale — it does not
last. - Do not promise unlimited retention without rollups — that is a future operations crisis.
Common follow-up: "How do you support both real-time and historical queries from one schema?" —
Raw partition for recent data, aggregated rollup tables for older data, a unified view that picks the right
source based on the time range.

CREATE TABLE metric_readings (

CREATE TABLE metric_readings_2026_05 PARTITION OF metric_readings
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01');
Q291 · Hierarchical Data — Four Patterns
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Flipkart, Oracle India, Razorpay · Topic: Hierarchies
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Compare adjacency list, nested set, materialized path, and closure table for storing a category
tree.
The 30-second answer: Adjacency list is simple and write-friendly but slow for ancestor queries. Nested
set is fast for subtree reads but slow on writes. Materialized path is fast for both with string operations.
Closure table is the most expressive — stores every ancestor-descendant pair — at the cost of extra
storage and trigger maintenance.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Adjacency list — each row stores parent_id. Trivial to write, but
finding all descendants needs a recursive CTE on every read. 2. Nested set — each row stores left
and right numeric bounds. Reading any subtree is a single range query, but every insert or move
shifts large numeric ranges, killing write performance on busy trees. 3. Materialized path — each row
stores its full path as a string (/electronics/phones/android). Queries use LIKE 'prefix/%'
for descendants and string parsing for ancestors. Fast both ways, harder to enforce integrity. 4. Closure
table — separate table with one row per ancestor-descendant pair plus depth. Any tree query is a simple
join. Storage is O(nodes × depth) and inserts need cascade updates, but the queries are clean.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres ltree extension is a polished materialized path implementation
with operators and indexes. - For shallow trees (3-4 levels max), denormalizing level1_id, 
level2_id, level3_id is often the most pragmatic option. - Closure tables shine when subtree
queries dominate and writes are infrequent (org charts, file systems).
What NOT to say: - Do not claim one pattern is universally best — each fits different read-write ratios. -
Do not implement nested set without understanding rebalancing cost — it is the classic rookie mistake.
Common follow-up: "For a category tree on an e-commerce site, which would you choose?" —
Materialized path with ltree for most cases — fast reads, decent writes, and built-in index support.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 305 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 306
-- Adjacency list
CREATE TABLE categories (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, parent_id INT REFERENCES categories);
-- Closure table
CREATE TABLE category_closure (
  ancestor INT, descendant INT, depth INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (ancestor, descendant)
);
Q292 · Denormalizing Computed Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Cred · Topic: Denormalization
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When is it acceptable to store a computed value like order_total in the database instead of
computing it on read?
The 30-second answer: Store the computed value when the read cost is high, the recomputation is
deterministic from a fixed input set, and slight staleness is acceptable or the write path can keep it in
sync transactionally. Keep it computed on read when accuracy matters more than latency or the inputs
change frequently.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Establish the trade-off — denormalizing a computed column saves
read CPU and join cost but introduces sync risk on every input change. 2. Categorise inputs — if all
inputs come from rows you control in the same transaction, atomic updates work. If inputs come from
external sources or other services, async updates are inevitable and you accept brief staleness. 3.
Mention generated columns — most modern databases support GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...)
STORED for deterministic computations, which keeps the value in sync automatically. 4. Discuss
reconciliation — periodic jobs that recompute and detect drift catch the silent bugs that always appear
over months.
Edge cases to mention: - Aggregates like total_orders_count are notoriously hard to keep in
sync under concurrent inserts and deletes — use atomic increments or recompute on a schedule. -
Generated columns cannot reference other tables, so they only work for in-row computations. - For
dashboards, materialized views often beat ad-hoc denormalized columns — they centralize the refresh.
What NOT to say: - Do not denormalize a value that depends on a frequently-updated input — every
input change becomes a fan-out write. - Do not skip the reconciliation job — without it, drift is invisible
until a customer complains.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 306 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 307
Common follow-up: "What is the safest way to keep order_total in sync?" — Compute it in the
same transaction that inserts or updates the line items, with a server-side trigger or an explicit update in
the application's transactional write path.
-- Postgres generated column
CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  quantity INT, unit_price NUMERIC,
  line_total NUMERIC GENERATED ALWAYS AS (quantity * unit_price) STORED
);
Q293 · Materialized View vs Denormalization
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Razorpay, Flipkart, JP Morgan · Topic:
Denormalization
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between using a materialized view and adding denormalized columns to
the source table?
The 30-second answer: A materialized view is a separate object refreshed on a schedule or manually,
decoupled from the source table's writes. Denormalized columns live in the source table itself and need
to be kept in sync transactionally. Materialized views are better for analytical aggregates; denormalized
columns are better for hot read paths needing transactional consistency.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define a materialized view — a stored result set of a query,
refreshable but not auto-synced. Reads are fast; staleness is the cost. 2. Define denormalized columns
— extra columns on the source table populated on every relevant write. Real-time accuracy; write
complexity is the cost. 3. State when each fits — materialized view for dashboards, reports, and
aggregates that tolerate freshness lag. Denormalized columns for per-request lookups where freshness
must match the source. 4. Mention refresh modes — Postgres supports REFRESH MATERIALIZED
VIEW CONCURRENTLY for non-blocking refresh; some databases support incremental refresh for huge
views.
Edge cases to mention: - Materialized views can be indexed and queried like regular tables — that is
half their value. - Concurrent refresh requires a unique index on the materialized view. - If your aggregate
is per-row in the source, denormalized columns scale; if it spans rows, materialized views scale better.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "materialized views are always fresh" — they are not, refresh is on
demand. - Do not store materialized aggregates as denormalized columns when they cross many rows
— write amplification destroys throughput.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 307 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 308
Common follow-up: "How do you handle near-real-time analytics needs?" — Either schedule refreshes
every minute or use streaming aggregation (CDC + stream processor + materialized table) for true real-
time.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_daily_sales AS
SELECT DATE(sale_at) AS day, region, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM sales GROUP BY DATE(sale_at), region;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON mv_daily_sales (day, region);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_daily_sales;
Q294 · Schema Migrations — Additive vs Destructive
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Flipkart, PhonePe · Topic: Migrations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through deploying a schema change that renames a column on a busy production table.
Why is rename considered destructive?
The 30-second answer: A rename is destructive because old application code expects the old name
and breaks the moment the migration runs — you cannot deploy schema and code atomically. The safe
pattern is additive — add the new column, dual-write from the application, backfill, switch reads, then
drop the old column in a later release.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Distinguish — additive changes (new column nullable, new table,
new index concurrently) are safe to deploy any time. Destructive changes (drop, rename, type change)
break either old code or old data and require coordination. 2. Lay out the staged rename — release 1
adds the new column and dual-writes to both old and new. Release 2 backfills historical rows. Release 3
switches reads to the new column. Release 4 stops writing the old column. Release 5 drops the old
column. 3. Mention online tools — pt-online-schema-change, gh-ost, pg_repack for non-blocking
schema changes on huge tables. 4. Note the rollback consideration at every step — if release 3 fails, you
must be able to flip back to the old column, which means it must still hold valid data.
Edge cases to mention: - Adding a NOT NULL column with no default is destructive in many engines
because it requires a full table rewrite — add nullable, backfill, then add the constraint. - Index creation
should always be CONCURRENTLY in Postgres or ONLINE in MySQL on busy tables. - ENUMs are
notoriously painful to migrate — many teams prefer lookup tables for that reason.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN in a single deploy on a live
system — it is a recipe for outage. - Do not skip the backfill step — partial data in the new column will
silently corrupt downstream consumers.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 308 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 309
Common follow-up: "What happens if you drop the old column too early?" — Any rolled-back
deployment or surviving old process will throw column-not-found errors and the rollback path is broken.
Always give a generous deprecation window.
-- Staged rename: phone_no -> contact_number
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN contact_number TEXT;
UPDATE customers SET contact_number = phone_no WHERE contact_number IS NULL;
-- Then in later releases: switch reads, stop writes to old, drop old.
Q295 · When to Break Normalization Rules
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: Schema
Philosophy
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Give me a real production scenario where you knowingly broke normal form. What was the
justification and what was the cost?
The 30-second answer: A common case is snapshotting prices on the order_lines row at
purchase time — strictly a 3NF violation because the price already exists in the products table, but
historical orders must reflect the price the customer actually paid, not the current price. The cost is
duplicated data; the benefit is correctness over time.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the snapshot example — orders must immortalize the deal
as it was. If you store only product_id and look up the current price at read time, every price change
retroactively changes order history. That is wrong. 2. Generalize the principle — normalize to eliminate
redundancy of facts that are timeless, denormalize to capture facts that are bound to a point in time. 3.
Add a second example — caching user_country on orders for analytics speed even though it
could be joined. The join is cheap; the denormalization is for predictable query plans on a billion-row
analytical table. 4. State the discipline — every deliberate denormalization should be documented in the
migration, motivated by a measured need, and accompanied by a sync strategy (or a clear "this is a
snapshot, do not sync" note).
Edge cases to mention: - Snapshotting includes more than price — product name, tax rate, currency,
applied discounts. Anything the customer agreed to at that moment. - Counter caches
( comment_count on posts) are a frequent 3NF violation; they need atomic increments or periodic
recompute. - Reporting columns added to OLTP tables for product-team convenience are a slippery
slope — push these into a warehouse instead.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim normalization is always best — interviewers want pragmatic
judgement. - Do not claim denormalization is free — every duplicated value is a future bug surface.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Common follow-up: "How do you know when denormalization has gone too far?" — When you can no
longer answer "what is the source of truth for this field" with one sentence, you have a problem.
CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id BIGINT, product_id BIGINT,
