Q296 · Database-First vs Code-First Schema Design
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Microsoft IDC, Oracle India, Salesforce India, TCS · Topic: Schema
Workflow
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Database-first or code-first schema design — which do you prefer and why?
The 30-second answer: Database-first models the schema in DDL or a dedicated tool, then generates
or hand-writes code to match. Code-first defines entities in application code and generates the schema
from them. Database-first respects the database as the source of truth and is preferred for shared, long-
lived systems; code-first is faster for solo or small-team apps where the schema closely mirrors the
domain model.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define each clearly — database-first starts with DDL scripts, ER
diagrams, or tools like Liquibase. Code-first starts with classes in Hibernate, Entity Framework, Django
ORM, or SQLAlchemy, and the framework generates migrations. 2. List database-first advantages — full
control over constraints, indexes, partitioning, sequences, RLS policies, and edge SQL features.
Migrations are explicit and reviewable. 3. List code-first advantages — domain model stays close to
code, DTOs map cleanly, less context switching, refactoring tools work end-to-end. 4. State the
recommendation — code-first for monoliths owned by one team and one application; database-first
when multiple services share the schema or DBAs need a seat at the table.
Edge cases to mention: - Code-first generated migrations are notoriously bad at non-trivial changes
(rename, type change, index conditions) — review every generated migration before applying. -
Database-first plays better with multi-language ecosystems — one schema, many service clients. -
Hybrid approaches are common — code-first for the bulk, with hand-written SQL migrations for the
tricky bits.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 310 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 311
What NOT to say: - Do not say "ORMs solve everything" — they hide important schema details that bite
at scale. - Do not write off code-first as amateur — top product companies ship serious systems with it.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle conflicts between ORM-generated migrations and DBA-
managed schemas?" — Treat the database as the source of truth, regenerate the ORM model from the
schema, and disable ORM auto-migrations in production environments.
-- Database-first migration (Liquibase changelog style)
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  invoice_number TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, invoice_number)
);
CREATE INDEX ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC);
Chapter 7 — Aggregations & Grouping
Every reporting query you will ever write lives in this chapter — sales by month, top customers by GMV,
refund rate by city, distinct payers per campaign — and almost every panel I have sat in spends at least
one full question stress-testing whether you understand the rules properly. The mechanics look
deceptively simple — SUM here, GROUP BY there — but interviewers know the gotchas: the ANSI rule
about every non-aggregated column appearing in GROUP BY, MySQL's old loose mode versus
ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY in 5.7+, the difference between WHERE and HAVING, how COUNT(*) and
COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col) each behave differently with NULLs, conditional aggregation via
SUM(CASE WHEN ...) versus the cleaner FILTER clause, GROUPING SETS and ROLLUP and CUBE for
multi-level totals, the GROUPING() function to tell a rollup NULL apart from a data NULL, ordered-set
aggregates like PERCENTILE_CONT for median, ARRAY_AGG and STRING_AGG and LISTAGG for
collapsing groups into a single value, pivoting via CASE versus a native PIVOT operator, approximate
count distinct via HyperLogLog, and how the planner uses (or refuses to use) an index when you GROUP
BY an expression. This chapter walks through all of it in the same Q&A shape as Chapters 1–6 so you
can drill straight into interview prep.
Q297 · GROUP BY Basics — What Can Appear in SELECT
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Accenture, Wipro · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 311 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 312
Explain GROUP BY in your own words. What columns are allowed in the SELECT list of a
grouped query, and what happens if you put one that is not allowed?
The 30-second answer: GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same values in the grouping columns
into a single output row per group. The SELECT list may only contain the grouping columns themselves,
aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, MAX), constants, or expressions built purely from these
— any other column raises an error under ANSI SQL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the collapsing metaphor — one output row per distinct
combination of GROUP BY columns. That sentence alone tells the interviewer you understand the
semantics. 2. State the rule precisely: every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in the
GROUP BY clause. This is the rule the interviewer wants to hear word-for-word. 3. Give a concrete
example: SELECT city, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY city — legal. 
SELECT city, customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY city — illegal
because customer_id is neither grouped nor aggregated. 4. Mention that some engines (older
MySQL, SQLite) silently pick an arbitrary value for the ungrouped column, which is dangerous — covered
properly in Q2 and Q3.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres allows you to skip listing a column in GROUP BY if it is functionally
dependent on the primary key — e.g. you can SELECT customer_id, customer_name,
COUNT(*) and group only by customer_id if customer_id is the PK of customers. - Aliases
from the SELECT list cannot be referenced in GROUP BY in most dialects (Postgres allows it; SQL
Server does not). - Constants like SELECT 'India' AS country, SUM(amount) FROM orders
GROUP BY ... are always fine.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim GROUP BY "sorts" the result — it groups, and ordering is only a
historical side-effect of certain plans. - Do not say "you can put any column in SELECT" — that is the
MySQL trap from 5.6 days.
Common follow-up: "Why does ANSI require every non-aggregated column in GROUP BY?" —
Because otherwise the value for that column is ambiguous when the group contains more than one
distinct value, and the engine has no principled way to choose.
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
Q298 · Every-Non-Aggregated-Column Rule — ANSI vs MySQL Traditional
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro, TCS · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 312 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 313
If I run SELECT city, customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY city,
what should happen? What actually happens in different databases?
The 30-second answer: Under ANSI SQL the query is invalid and should throw an error because 
customer_id is neither in GROUP BY nor wrapped in an aggregate. Postgres and SQL Server reject
it. Old MySQL (and SQLite) accept it and return an arbitrary customer_id value picked from one of
the rows in each group — useful for nothing and dangerous in production.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Quote the ANSI rule first: every non-aggregated column must be
listed in GROUP BY. Interviewers test for this exact phrasing. 2. Walk through what each engine does:
Postgres throws column "customer_id" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be
used in an aggregate function. SQL Server throws a similar error. MySQL in the old default
mode silently returned a random representative. 3. Explain why MySQL's behaviour was bad: the chosen
value depended on storage order, indexes used and even the plan — so the same query could return
different numbers on different days. 4. State that MySQL 5.7 changed the default to
ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, aligning it with ANSI — covered in Q3.
Edge cases to mention: - Functional dependency: if customer_id is functionally determined by the
grouping column (e.g. you group by email and email is unique per customer), Postgres recognises
this and allows it. - ANY_VALUE(customer_id) is the standard escape hatch to say "I really do want
an arbitrary value, don't yell at me" — supported in MySQL 5.7+ and BigQuery. - This rule applies to
expressions too: SELECT city, customer_id + 1 ... still violates it.
What NOT to say: - Do not call the MySQL behaviour "a feature." It is a historical wart that MySQL itself
fixed. - Do not say the engine "picks the first row" — there is no first row in a relational set.
Common follow-up: "How do you fix the query if you want the largest customer_id per city?" —
Use MAX(customer_id), or a window function with ROW_NUMBER and a filter.
-- Correct: aggregate or group
SELECT city, MAX(customer_id) AS top_customer_id, SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
Q299 · ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY Mode in MySQL 5.7+
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Cred · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 313 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 314
What is ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY in MySQL and why was it added?
The 30-second answer: ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is an SQL mode flag that makes MySQL reject
GROUP BY queries which violate the ANSI rule (every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in
GROUP BY or be functionally dependent on it). It became the default in MySQL 5.7 to bring MySQL in
line with Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle and the SQL standard.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the mode: when ON, MySQL behaves like every other ANSI-
compliant database. When OFF (legacy mode), it returns the random-representative-value behaviour that
bit so many teams. 2. Explain why it matters in practice: when teams upgrade from MySQL 5.6 to 5.7 or
8.0, queries that "worked" suddenly throw errors. Senior engineers know to grep the codebase for
grouped queries before the upgrade. 3. Mention how to inspect: SELECT @@sql_mode; shows
current modes. To turn it off temporarily, you can SET sql_mode = (SELECT
REPLACE(@@sql_mode, 'ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY', '')) — though you should fix the queries
instead. 4. Bring up ANY_VALUE() as the right escape hatch when you genuinely want an arbitrary
representative.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL's functional-dependency detection is weaker than Postgres — it
covers primary keys but not all unique-constraint cases. - AWS RDS and Aurora MySQL ship with
ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY on by default; turning it off cluster-wide requires a parameter group change. -
The mode applies per session, so libraries can set it differently from your interactive shell — leading to
"works locally, breaks in CI" surprises.
What NOT to say: - Do not advise "just turn it off." That hides bugs and breaks portability. - Do not say it
affects only SELECT — it also affects views and stored procedures that contain grouped queries.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite a query that fails ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY without changing the data
returned." — Wrap the offending column in MAX() or ANY_VALUE(), or add it to the GROUP BY.
-- Works under ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY
SELECT city, ANY_VALUE(customer_id) AS sample_cust, SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
Q300 · GROUP BY with HAVING vs WHERE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wells Fargo, JP Morgan · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 314 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 315
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? Can you always replace one with the
other?
The 30-second answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after the aggregate
is computed. They are not interchangeable — you cannot reference an aggregate in WHERE, and you
should not push row-level predicates into HAVING because that prevents index usage.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING →
SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE happens before GROUP BY, HAVING after. 2. Give a clean
example: WHERE status = 'paid' filters orders before grouping (uses index on status); HAVING
SUM(amount) > 100000 filters groups whose total exceeds a lakh. 3. Show the common mistake: 
HAVING status = 'paid' works in some dialects but is semantically wrong — push it to WHERE
for performance. 4. Mention that HAVING can reference both aggregate functions and the grouping
columns themselves.
Edge cases to mention: - HAVING without GROUP BY treats the whole table as one group — SELECT
COUNT(*) FROM orders HAVING COUNT(*) > 0 is legal. - You cannot reference SELECT aliases
in HAVING in SQL Server (must repeat the aggregate expression); Postgres and MySQL allow it. -
Filtering on grouping columns in HAVING vs WHERE is logically equivalent but the planner usually
pushes them to WHERE anyway — don't rely on this, write it correctly.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "HAVING is just WHERE for grouped queries." That is a common but
wrong simplification. - Do not put WHERE SUM(amount) > 100000 — it is illegal because the
aggregate has not been computed yet.
Common follow-up: "Why does pushing predicates into WHERE matter for performance?" — WHERE
can use indexes and reduce rows before sorting/hashing for GROUP BY; HAVING runs after, so the
database may have already done a lot of unnecessary work.
SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY city
HAVING SUM(amount) > 100000;
Q301 · COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT col)
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Accenture, Cognizant, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 315 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 316
Tell me the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column). When
would you reach for each?
The 30-second answer: COUNT(*) counts every row including NULLs. COUNT(col) counts non-NULL
values of col. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts the number of distinct non-NULL values. They give
different numbers whenever NULLs or duplicates exist in col.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with NULL handling — that is the differentiator. COUNT(*)
includes a row even if every column is NULL; COUNT(col) skips rows where col is NULL. 2. Give a
tiny worked example: 10 orders, 3 with coupon_code NULL. COUNT(*) = 10, 
COUNT(coupon_code) = 7. If 4 of those 7 use the same coupon and 3 use distinct ones, 
COUNT(DISTINCT coupon_code) = 4. 3. State the common interview use-case: 
SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) is functionally the same as COUNT(*)
FILTER (WHERE status='paid') or COUNT(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 END). 4.
Mention performance: COUNT(DISTINCT) is the slowest because the engine must build a hash or sort to
dedupe — covered in Q10.
Edge cases to mention: - COUNT(1) and COUNT(*) are identical in every modern engine — no,
COUNT(1) is not faster; that is a myth from 1990s Oracle. - In Postgres, COUNT(*) OVER () gives
total row count alongside other columns without a separate query. - COUNT over an empty set returns 0
(not NULL) — unlike SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX which return NULL.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim COUNT(1) is faster than COUNT() — modern planners treat them
identically. - Do not say COUNT(col) and COUNT() "always return the same" — only true if the column is
NOT NULL.
Common follow-up: "In a left-joined query, why do COUNT() and COUNT(right_table.id) differ?" —
Because LEFT JOIN creates NULL rows on the right when no match exists; COUNT() counts them,
COUNT(right.id) does not.
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                     AS total_orders,
  COUNT(coupon_code)           AS orders_with_coupon,
  COUNT(DISTINCT coupon_code)  AS unique_coupons_used
FROM orders;
Q302 · Performance of COUNT(*) on Large Tables — Fast Counts
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 316 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 317
SELECT COUNT(*) on a fifty-crore-row orders table takes forty seconds. How do you make it
instant?
The 30-second answer: Exact COUNT(*) requires scanning the whole table or a covering index, which is
unavoidable. For approximate counts, read from the system catalogs — pg_class.reltuples in
Postgres, INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES.TABLE_ROWS in MySQL — which return the planner's
estimate in microseconds. For dashboards that need a near-real-time number, maintain a counter table
updated by triggers or async aggregation jobs.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose first: explain why COUNT(*) is slow — Postgres has MVCC,
so each tuple visibility must be checked; MySQL InnoDB has no internal row count, so it must scan. 2.
Offer the catalog trick: SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE relname =
'orders'; returns an estimate that is usually accurate to within a percent if ANALYZE has run recently.
3. For accurate-enough counts in MySQL: SELECT TABLE_ROWS FROM
INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES WHERE TABLE_NAME='orders'; — also an estimate. 4. Final
layer: precomputed counters. A counts table with one row per entity, updated by triggers or batch
jobs, gives O(1) reads at the cost of write overhead.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres VACUUM or autovacuum keeps reltuples fresh — if stats are
stale, the estimate drifts. - A partial index covering the predicate (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) can
make SELECT COUNT(*) faster because the index is smaller than the heap. - BigQuery, Snowflake
and other columnar engines maintain exact row counts in metadata and COUNT(*) is already instant.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "add an index on a column" — COUNT(*) does not use a column-level
index unless it is a covering one. - Do not propose SELECT COUNT(1) — same speed.
Common follow-up: "How accurate is pg_class.reltuples?" — Within a few percent for tables
that get autovacuumed regularly; can drift further on insert-heavy tables until the next ANALYZE.
-- Postgres fast estimate
SELECT reltuples::bigint AS estimated_rows
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname = 'orders';
Q303 · SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX — NULL Handling
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Infosys, Cognizant · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 317 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 318
What happens when SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX encounter NULLs in the column? What if every
row is NULL?
The 30-second answer: All four aggregates skip NULLs silently. AVG divides by the count of non-NULL
values, not the total row count. If every input value is NULL — or if the grouped set is empty for that
group — they return NULL, not zero (except COUNT, which returns 0).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule: aggregates ignore NULLs. This is consistent across
every dialect. 2. Walk through AVG carefully: AVG(refund_amount) over 10 rows where 6 are NULL
averages just the 4 non-NULL values. If you wanted to treat NULL as zero, use 
AVG(COALESCE(refund_amount, 0)). 3. Mention MIN and MAX: order-sensitive operations skip
NULLs, so MIN(birth_date) returns the earliest non-NULL date. 4. Final point: when every value is
NULL, the result is NULL — wrap in COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) for a numeric default.
Edge cases to mention: - SUM over an empty set returns NULL, not 0 — surprising the first time you hit
it in a report. - AVG(salary) and SUM(salary)/COUNT(*) give different answers when some
salaries are NULL. - Boolean aggregation: in Postgres, bool_and and bool_or ignore NULLs; in
MySQL you use MIN(flag::int) and MAX(flag::int) style tricks.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "NULLs are treated as zero." They are not — they are skipped entirely. -
Do not say AVG always returns a decimal — in some engines it returns the integer division if the input is
integer (SQL Server is one).
Common follow-up: "Why is SUM(x)/COUNT(*) sometimes different from AVG(x)?" — Because
COUNT(*) counts all rows including those where x is NULL, while AVG divides by the count of non-NULL
x values.
SELECT
  customer_id,
  SUM(amount)                  AS total_paid,
  AVG(amount)                  AS avg_order_value,
  COALESCE(SUM(refund_amount), 0) AS total_refunded
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
Q304 · Conditional Aggregation — SUM(CASE WHEN …)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 318 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 319
Without using FILTER or multiple subqueries, how do you compute the count of paid orders and
the count of refunded orders in a single grouped query?
The 30-second answer: Use conditional aggregation — wrap a CASE expression inside SUM or
COUNT. SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) gives the paid count; 
SUM(CASE WHEN status='refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) the refunded count. Both run in a
single pass over the data.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem: you want multiple counts/sums conditioned on
different predicates in one query. The naive approach is multiple subqueries; the elegant approach is
conditional aggregation. 2. Show the pattern: SUM(CASE WHEN <predicate> THEN <value> ELSE
0 END) works in every dialect. 3. Note the COUNT trick: 
COUNT(CASE WHEN <predicate> THEN 1 END) — the ELSE branch defaults to NULL, which
COUNT skips. This is shorter than the SUM-CASE form. 4. State the performance win: one scan over the
table instead of N scans for N subqueries — verified by EXPLAIN showing a single Seq Scan with
multiple Aggregate nodes feeding off it.
Edge cases to mention: - For averages with conditions, use AVG(CASE WHEN ... THEN x END)
— the NULL ELSE keeps the denominator honest. - The FILTER clause (Q9) is a cleaner, ANSI-standard
alternative in Postgres and SQLite. - Be careful with ELSE 0 vs ELSE NULL — for COUNT they
differ, for SUM they don't.
What NOT to say: - Do not write five separate subqueries and JOIN them — interviewer is testing
exactly this anti-pattern. - Do not say "use IF()" — it works in MySQL but is non-portable.
Common follow-up: "What if I want the percentage of paid orders per city?" — 100.0 * SUM(CASE
WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) — the 100.0 forces float division.
SELECT
  city,
  COUNT(*)                                                AS total_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid'     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS paid,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS refunded,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid'     THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS paid_gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
Q305 · FILTER Clause (Postgres / SQL Standard) — Cleaner Conditional
Aggregation
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 319 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 320
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me the same paid-vs-refunded breakdown using the FILTER clause. Which databases
support it?
The 30-second answer: The SQL:2003 FILTER clause attaches a WHERE-style predicate to an
aggregate: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='paid'). It is supported in Postgres, SQLite
3.30+ and HSQLDB. SQL Server, MySQL and Oracle do not yet implement it, so you fall back to
SUM(CASE WHEN ...).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Introduce FILTER as the ANSI-standard alternative to SUM-CASE. It
reads as natural English: "count all orders filtered by status equals paid." 2. Write the example: 
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='paid') AS paid — half the characters of the SUM-CASE
equivalent. 3. Note dialect support: Postgres since 9.4, SQLite 3.30, plus standard mandates it. SQL
Server / MySQL / Oracle still require the CASE workaround. 4. Mention that FILTER works with any
aggregate — SUM, AVG, ARRAY_AGG, PERCENTILE_CONT — not just COUNT.
Edge cases to mention: - FILTER and window functions compose: SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE
status='paid') OVER (PARTITION BY city) is valid in Postgres. - The FILTER predicate is
evaluated per row before aggregation — same semantics as CASE inside the aggregate. - For ORDER
BY within the aggregate (e.g. ARRAY_AGG), FILTER and ORDER BY can coexist: ARRAY_AGG(id
ORDER BY id) FILTER (WHERE status='paid').
What NOT to say: - Do not claim it is faster than SUM-CASE — Postgres compiles both to the same
plan in most cases. - Do not assume MySQL supports it — junior candidates often confuse Postgres
extensions with universal SQL.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite the FILTER query for SQL Server." — Replace each 
FILTER (WHERE p) with CASE WHEN p THEN x END inside the aggregate.
-- Postgres / SQLite / standard SQL
SELECT
  city,
  COUNT(*)                                  AS total,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='paid')     AS paid,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='refunded') AS refunded,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status='paid')  AS paid_gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;

Q306 · COUNT(DISTINCT) — Common Performance Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Swiggy, Flipkart · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why is COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) slow on a billion-row events table, and what would you do to
speed it up?
The 30-second answer: COUNT(DISTINCT) must dedupe every value, which forces either a hash table
sized to the cardinality or a sort over the entire grouped subset — both of which spill to disk on large
data. Speed it up by using approximate count distinct (HyperLogLog, BigQuery's
APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, Snowflake's APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, Postgres's hll extension)
when an exact number is not required.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the mechanics: deduplication needs memory proportional to
the cardinality of the distinct values. With a billion unique users you cannot fit them in RAM. 2. Show the
trap: COUNT(DISTINCT) in a query with multiple grouping columns multiplies the work — the planner
must dedupe per group. 3. Offer the approximate alternative: HyperLogLog gives 99% accuracy with
constant memory (~12 KB per sketch). BigQuery exposes it as APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT; Snowflake
the same; Redshift has APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT; Postgres needs the hll extension. 4. Mention
pre-aggregated daily tables as the production solution: materialise distinct user counts per day, then sum
or merge sketches.
Edge cases to mention: - Multiple COUNT(DISTINCT) in one query is even worse — each needs its own
dedup pipeline. Postgres handles them by sorting; some engines parallelise. - For exact counts, a
covering index on the distinct column lets the engine do an Index Only Skip Scan (Postgres 13+, MySQL
8 with loose index scan). - HyperLogLog sketches are mergeable — you can store one sketch per day
and combine them later for weekly/monthly distincts without re-scanning raw events.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "add an index" without specifying it must cover the distinct column. - Do
not promise exact results from APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT — it is approximate by design.
Common follow-up: "How accurate is HyperLogLog?" — Standard error around 1.04 / sqrt(m) where m
is the number of registers; with the default 2^14 registers you get ~0.81% error.
-- BigQuery / Snowflake / Redshift
SELECT
  DATE(event_ts) AS day,
  APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(user_id) AS daily_users
FROM events
GROUP BY day;

Q307 · Approximate Count Distinct — HyperLogLog Mechanics
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Swiggy, PhonePe, Goldman · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain at a high level how HyperLogLog estimates cardinality without storing the actual values.
The 30-second answer: HyperLogLog hashes each input value, splits the hash into a bucket index and
a remainder, and tracks the maximum number of leading zeros seen in the remainder per bucket. The
cardinality estimate is derived from the harmonic mean of those max-leading-zero counts scaled by the
number of buckets. Memory is constant (kilobytes) regardless of input size, and accuracy is around 1%.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the intuition: if you hash values uniformly, observing a hash
with k leading zeros is roughly a 1-in-2^k event, suggesting you have seen on the order of 2^k distinct
items. 2. Walk through the algorithm: take a uniform hash, use the first b bits to pick a bucket (m = 2^b
buckets), use the remaining bits to count leading zeros, and store only the max per bucket. 3. Cardinality
estimate: n ≈ α_m · m^2 / (sum over buckets of 2^(-max_zeros)) — you do not need
the formula in the interview, just the harmonic-mean intuition. 4. Mention sketch mergeability — two
HLLs covering disjoint sets can be merged by taking bucket-wise max, giving the HLL of the union. This
is why APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT scales horizontally.
Edge cases to mention: - Small cardinalities have higher error — HyperLogLog++ from Google switches
to LinearCounting below a threshold. - Hash quality matters — a bad hash function degrades accuracy.
Production engines use MurmurHash3 or xxHash. - BigQuery exposes the sketches as bytes
( HLL_COUNT.INIT, HLL_COUNT.MERGE, HLL_COUNT.EXTRACT), so you can pre-compute and
merge later.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "it samples the data" — HyperLogLog observes every value, it just
stores almost nothing. - Do not claim it works for joins or sums — it is strictly a cardinality estimator.
Common follow-up: "How would you estimate distinct users over a sliding 7-day window cheaply?" —
Keep one HLL sketch per day, merge the last 7 sketches at query time, extract the cardinality. O(7)
merges.
-- BigQuery: precompute daily sketches, merge for weekly distinct users
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT DATE(event_ts) AS day, HLL_COUNT.INIT(user_id) AS sketch
  FROM events GROUP BY day
)
SELECT HLL_COUNT.MERGE(sketch) AS weekly_users
FROM daily
WHERE day BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 6 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE();
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 322 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q308 · ARRAY_AGG / STRING_AGG / GROUP_CONCAT — Dialect Comparison
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want to collapse all product names a customer has ever ordered into a single comma-separated
string per customer. Show me how in Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server.
The 30-second answer: Use the dialect's collection aggregate — STRING_AGG(product_name,
',') in Postgres and SQL Server 2017+, GROUP_CONCAT(product_name SEPARATOR ',') in
MySQL, and LISTAGG(product_name, ',') in Oracle. ARRAY_AGG returns an array instead of a
string in Postgres and BigQuery if you want to keep typed elements.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Compare the three function names side by side — interviewers love
this matrix. 2. Show the Postgres / SQL Server form: STRING_AGG(product_name, ',') WITHIN
GROUP (ORDER BY product_name) — note the WITHIN GROUP form for ordered aggregation. 3.
Show the MySQL form: 
GROUP_CONCAT(product_name ORDER BY product_name SEPARATOR ', '). Default
separator is comma. 4. Mention size limits — MySQL's group_concat_max_len defaults to 1024
bytes and truncates silently. Production teams raise it to several MB.
Edge cases to mention: - NULL values are skipped by all of these — wrap in COALESCE if you want a
placeholder. - ARRAY_AGG in Postgres returns NULL when the group is empty (from a left join with no
matches); use COALESCE(ARRAY_AGG(x), '{}'). - LISTAGG in Oracle 12.2+ supports ON
OVERFLOW TRUNCATE to avoid the dreaded ORA-01489 when the concatenated string exceeds 4000
bytes.
What NOT to say: - Do not call them "the same function in different databases" — they have subtle
ordering and NULL differences. - Do not forget the separator in GROUP_CONCAT — the default is
comma in MySQL but engines vary.
Common follow-up: "What if I need the result deduplicated?" — GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT
product_name) in MySQL; STRING_AGG(DISTINCT product_name, ',') in Postgres; 
LISTAGG(DISTINCT ...) in Oracle 19c+.
-- Postgres
SELECT customer_id,
       STRING_AGG(product_name, ', ' ORDER BY product_name) AS products
FROM order_items
GROUP BY customer_id;

Q309 · ARRAY_AGG ORDER BY — Controlling Element Order
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Swiggy · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When you collapse values into an array with ARRAY_AGG, the order looks random. How do you
guarantee a specific order?
The 30-second answer: Use the ORDER BY clause inside the aggregate: 
ARRAY_AGG(product_name ORDER BY ordered_at). Without that clause, the order is whatever
the planner decides — usually but not always heap order, and never something you should rely on.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Establish the rule: aggregates can take an ORDER BY inside the
parentheses, separate from the query's outer ORDER BY. This is ANSI standard. 2. Write the example: 
ARRAY_AGG(product_name ORDER BY ordered_at DESC) AS recent_first — gives the
customer's products in reverse chronological order. 3. Mention that this matters for downstream
consumers who treat the first element as "most recent" or "primary." 4. Bring up FIRST_VALUE/
LAST_VALUE window functions as the alternative when you want just one element, not the whole
sequence.
Edge cases to mention: - The ORDER BY can reference columns not in the GROUP BY — they apply
per group during aggregation. - MySQL's GROUP_CONCAT, Postgres's STRING_AGG and Oracle's
LISTAGG all support the same internal ORDER BY. - Combined with FILTER: 
ARRAY_AGG(id ORDER BY id) FILTER (WHERE status='paid') — keeps both ordering and
predicate.
What NOT to say: - Do not put ORDER BY at the end of the SELECT and expect it to sort within each
group — it sorts the outer result. - Do not say "the order is always insertion order" — it depends on the
plan.
Common follow-up: "How do you get the top three recent orders per customer as an array?" — 
ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY ordered_at DESC)[1:3] in Postgres, or a subquery with
ROW_NUMBER and a filter.
SELECT customer_id,
       ARRAY_AGG(product_name ORDER BY ordered_at DESC) AS purchase_history
FROM order_items
GROUP BY customer_id;

Q310 · LISTAGG (Oracle, SQL:2016)
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You are working in Oracle. How do you collapse the city names for each state into a comma-
separated string?
The 30-second answer: Use LISTAGG(city, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY city)
grouped by state. LISTAGG was added in Oracle 11g Release 2 and standardised in SQL:2016. It returns
VARCHAR2 up to 4000 bytes by default — use ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE from 12.2 onwards to avoid
the overflow error.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the syntax: LISTAGG(expr, delimiter) WITHIN GROUP
(ORDER BY ...) — the WITHIN GROUP is mandatory because LISTAGG is an ordered-set aggregate.
2. Walk through the example: SELECT state, LISTAGG(city, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER
BY city) FROM cities GROUP BY state. 3. Mention the 4000-byte VARCHAR2 limit in older
Oracle versions and the ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE WITH COUNT extension that returns a truncated
string with a count of omitted elements. 4. Compare quickly: LISTAGG is to Oracle what STRING_AGG is
to Postgres / SQL Server and GROUP_CONCAT is to MySQL — same job, different name and minor
syntax.
Edge cases to mention: - DISTINCT support was added only in Oracle 19c — LISTAGG(DISTINCT
city, ', '). - Without ORDER BY in WITHIN GROUP, Oracle treats it as unordered and the result is
non-deterministic. - NULLs are skipped silently — wrap in NVL if you need a placeholder.
What NOT to say: - Do not omit the WITHIN GROUP clause — Oracle raises a syntax error. - Do not
assume CLOB output — it is VARCHAR2 by default; use LISTAGG(...) WITHIN GROUP (...) ON
OVERFLOW TRUNCATE for long lists.
Common follow-up: "How do you do this in Oracle 11g Release 1 (no LISTAGG)?" — Use WM_CONCAT
(undocumented) or hierarchical query with CONNECT_BY_ROOT and SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH.
Modern code avoids both.
-- Oracle 12.2+
SELECT state,
       LISTAGG(city, ', ' ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE WITH COUNT)
         WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY city) AS cities
FROM cities
GROUP BY state;

Q311 · GROUPING SETS — Multiple Groupings in One Query
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Goldman, AmEx · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want total sales by city, by state and overall — all in a single query. How?
The 30-second answer: Use GROUPING SETS — a single query block that lets you specify multiple
grouping combinations. GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((city), (state), ()) returns three
logical result sets stacked together: per city, per state and the grand total (empty grouping).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem: without GROUPING SETS you would UNION
ALL three separate GROUP BY queries — same data scanned three times, ugly to maintain. 2. Show the
syntax: GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((city), (state), ()). The empty parentheses denote
the grand-total row. 3. Explain the result shape: every row has both city and state columns, but
for state-level rows city is NULL and vice versa; for the grand-total row both are NULL. 4. Bring in the
GROUPING() function (Q18) as the tool to tell rollup NULLs apart from data NULLs.
Edge cases to mention: - Supported in Postgres 9.5+, SQL Server, Oracle, BigQuery, Snowflake.
MySQL 8.0 only added ROLLUP; GROUPING SETS proper is not yet in MySQL. - The set of grouping
columns must still cover everything in SELECT that is not aggregated. - Performance: a smart planner
scans the table once and computes all grouping levels in one pass — much faster than UNION ALL of
three queries.
What NOT to say: - Do not write three subqueries and UNION ALL them — that's the anti-pattern the
interviewer is looking for you to replace. - Do not say () means "no GROUP BY" — it means an
explicit empty grouping, which produces one grand-total row.
Common follow-up: "Can I combine GROUPING SETS with a regular GROUP BY column?" — Yes: 
GROUP BY country, GROUPING SETS ((city), (state), ()) produces those three
groupings per country.
SELECT country, state, city,
       SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((country, state, city), (country, state), (country), ());
Q312 · ROLLUP — Hierarchical Totals
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Wells Fargo, Goldman, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 326 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 327
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want sales by country, then sub-totalled per country, then a grand total — all in one query.
Which feature do I use?
The 30-second answer: ROLLUP. GROUP BY ROLLUP(country, state, city) produces sub-
totals at each level of the hierarchy plus a grand total at the end — equivalent to GROUPING SETS of 
(country, state, city), (country, state), (country) and ().
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define ROLLUP as a shorthand for hierarchical GROUPING SETS —
it generates n+1 grouping levels for n columns, removing one column from the right each time. 2.
Walk through the rows: full detail rows have all three columns populated; the state-aggregate row has
city as NULL; the country-aggregate row has both state and city NULL; the final grand-total row has all
three NULL. 3. Mention MySQL's WITH ROLLUP syntax — GROUP BY country, state, city
WITH ROLLUP — slightly different from the ANSI form but does the same job. 4. Tie back to
GROUPING() to distinguish rollup NULLs from real NULLs in the data.
Edge cases to mention: - Order of columns in ROLLUP matters — ROLLUP(country, state)
produces country sub-totals, while ROLLUP(state, country) would produce state sub-totals. -
MySQL WITH ROLLUP does not allow ORDER BY in the same query block; you must wrap the result in
a subquery. - BigQuery, Snowflake, Postgres and SQL Server all support the standard ROLLUP syntax.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse ROLLUP with CUBE — ROLLUP is hierarchical (n+1 groupings),
CUBE is combinatorial (2^n groupings). - Do not put ROLLUP inside the SELECT list — it belongs in the
GROUP BY clause only.
Common follow-up: "How does ROLLUP differ from CUBE?" — ROLLUP gives only the hierarchical
prefixes; CUBE gives every possible subset of grouping columns. For 3 columns, ROLLUP makes 4
levels and CUBE makes 8.
SELECT country, state, city, SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP(country, state, city)
ORDER BY country NULLS LAST, state NULLS LAST, city NULLS LAST;
Q313 · CUBE — All Combinations
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 327 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 328
When would you use CUBE instead of ROLLUP?
The 30-second answer: Use CUBE when you need totals across every possible combination of
grouping columns, not just the hierarchical ones. CUBE(a, b, c) produces 2^3 = 8 grouping sets — 
(a,b,c), (a,b), (a,c), (b,c), (a), (b), (c) and ().
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Contrast with ROLLUP: ROLLUP gives prefixes only (hierarchical),
CUBE gives the full power set. 2. Sketch the use case: a finance dashboard that needs gross margin
sliced by every combination of product category, region and channel — CUBE gives the full cross-tab in
one query. 3. Mention complexity: CUBE on 5 columns is 32 grouping sets — be deliberate, do not use it
casually because the row count explodes. 4. Bring in the GROUPING() function (Q18) to label each
output row with which dimensions are rollup totals vs raw values.
Edge cases to mention: - Supported in Postgres 9.5+, SQL Server, Oracle, BigQuery, Snowflake. Not
yet in MySQL (only WITH ROLLUP). - Combining with regular GROUP BY: GROUP BY year,
CUBE(category, region) cubes within each year. - Memory: a smart planner computes all 2^n
groupings in a single pass using a multi-level hash aggregate — but on huge data it can spill.
What NOT to say: - Do not use CUBE as a "give me all combinations just in case" — pick the specific
groupings you need with GROUPING SETS. - Do not say "CUBE is faster than ROLLUP" — it does
strictly more work.
Common follow-up: "What's the output row count for CUBE on 3 columns over a 1000-row table?" —
Up to 1000 detail rows plus aggregate rows for each of the 8 grouping sets — depends on how many
distinct values each column has.
SELECT category, region, channel, SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM sales
GROUP BY CUBE(category, region, channel);
Q314 · GROUPING() Function — Distinguishing NULLs
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, AmEx, Wells Fargo · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In a ROLLUP query, how do you tell a NULL that means "grand total" apart from a NULL that
means "no data"?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 328 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 329
The 30-second answer: Use the GROUPING() function: GROUPING(city) returns 1 if the row's city
column is a rollup-generated NULL (i.e. city is not part of the current grouping set), and 0 otherwise. You
wrap it in a CASE to display 'Grand Total' instead of NULL, or to filter to a specific grouping level.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the problem cleanly: ROLLUP and CUBE introduce NULLs in
the grouping columns for sub-total and grand-total rows. Without GROUPING() you cannot distinguish
those from data NULLs. 2. Show the basic use: CASE WHEN GROUPING(city) = 1 THEN 'All
Cities' ELSE city END AS city_label. 3. Mention GROUPING_ID — a bitmask combining the
GROUPING() output for multiple columns, useful for filtering to a specific grouping set: WHERE
GROUPING_ID(country, state, city) = 0 keeps only the most detailed level. 4. Tie back to
reports: GROUPING() is what makes pivot-style summary reports clean.
Edge cases to mention: - GROUPING() works in Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, BigQuery, Snowflake.
MySQL has GROUPING() since 8.0 for use with WITH ROLLUP. - The function takes the column as
argument — GROUPING(city), not GROUPING('city') — and the column must appear in the
GROUP BY clause. - Combined with HAVING: HAVING GROUPING(city) = 0 filters out summary
rows entirely.
What NOT to say: - Do not use IS NULL to detect rollup NULLs — that hits both data NULLs and
rollup NULLs. - Do not call it GROUPING() without a column argument — it is not a count.
Common follow-up: "How do you keep only the grand-total row?" — HAVING GROUPING(country)
= 1 AND GROUPING(state) = 1 AND GROUPING(city) = 1 or HAVING
GROUPING_ID(country, state, city) = 7.
SELECT
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(country) = 1 THEN 'All Countries' ELSE country END AS country,
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(state)   = 1 THEN 'All States'    ELSE state   END AS state,
  SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP(country, state);
Q315 · Cumulative Aggregation — Window vs Subquery
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, PhonePe · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want a running total of daily sales — each row showing the cumulative sum up to that day. Show
me the window-function way and the subquery way.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 329 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 330
The 30-second answer: Use a window function: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS
BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). The subquery alternative — 
SELECT day, (SELECT SUM(x.amount) FROM daily x WHERE x.day <= d.day) FROM
daily d — works but is O(n^2) and dramatically slower on anything beyond a few thousand rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Introduce window functions as the canonical answer — supported in
every modern database (Postgres 8.4+, MySQL 8, SQL Server 2012+, Oracle, BigQuery, Snowflake). 2.
Write the window: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) — default frame is RANGE BETWEEN
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which gives the running total. 3. Compare performance:
window is a single pass over the sorted rows; correlated subquery rescans the relation for each row —
quadratic. 4. Mention partitioning: OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY day) gives
running totals per customer in the same query.
Edge cases to mention: - Default frame for ordered window aggregates is RANGE not ROWS — this
matters when multiple rows tie on day; ROWS gives a strict cumulative count, RANGE bunches ties. -
MySQL 8 added window functions; older MySQL versions need the subquery or session-variable hack. -
BigQuery and Snowflake support window aggregates with the same standard syntax.
What NOT to say: - Do not use a self-join with LEFT JOIN ... ON x.day <= d.day — that is the
same quadratic problem in disguise. - Do not claim the correlated subquery is "more readable" — it is
slower and harder to extend.
Common follow-up: "How do you get a moving 7-day window instead of cumulative?" — 
SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
SELECT day,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_gmv
FROM daily_sales
ORDER BY day;
Q316 · Pivoting via CASE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Accenture, Wells Fargo · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have a long-format table with (customer_id, month, amount) and I want a wide report
with one row per customer and one column per month for the last six months. Write the SQL.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 330 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 331
The 30-second answer: Use conditional aggregation with one CASE expression per output column: 
SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-01' THEN amount END) AS jan_2026, SUM(CASE WHEN
month = '2026-02' THEN amount END) AS feb_2026, .... Group by customer_id. This is the
portable pivot pattern that works in every database.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define pivoting: turning row labels into column headers. Useful for
reports the business wants in wide format. 2. Write the pattern: one SUM(CASE WHEN month='YYYY-
MM' THEN amount END) per desired output column. Use SUM not just plain CASE to collapse
multiple rows per (customer, month). 3. Explain why you should not use ELSE 0 here — leaving it as
NULL means SUM ignores it; ELSE 0 distorts AVG if you ever change the aggregate. 4. Bring in PIVOT
(Q21) as the SQL-Server / Oracle specific syntax that is cleaner but non-portable.
Edge cases to mention: - The output columns are fixed at query write time — you cannot pivot on a
dynamic set of months without procedural code or dynamic SQL. - For percentage breakdowns (CASE
WHEN ... THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END), AVG gives the share directly. - Postgres has the crosstab
function in the tablefunc extension as an alternative.
What NOT to say: - Do not write twelve subqueries and join them — that's the anti-pattern. - Do not say
"use a pivot table" without showing SQL — interviewers want the query.
Common follow-up: "What if I want only the months that have any data?" — That's dynamic pivoting;
you need to generate the SQL string at runtime in the app layer, or use a server-side procedure.
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2025-12' THEN amount END) AS dec_2025,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-01' THEN amount END) AS jan_2026,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-02' THEN amount END) AS feb_2026,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-03' THEN amount END) AS mar_2026,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-04' THEN amount END) AS apr_2026,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-05' THEN amount END) AS may_2026
FROM monthly_sales
GROUP BY customer_id;
Q317 · Pivoting via PIVOT (SQL Server / Oracle)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Wells Fargo, JP Morgan, Goldman, TCS · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Do you know the native PIVOT operator? Write the same monthly report using PIVOT in SQL
Server.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 331 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 332
The 30-second answer: SQL Server and Oracle have a native PIVOT (aggregate FOR
pivot_column IN (value1, value2, ...)) clause. It is syntactic sugar over the CASE pattern
— readable when the column list is short, awkward when it is long, and not supported in Postgres or
MySQL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the SQL Server syntax: SELECT * FROM (subquery with
the three columns) AS src PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR month IN ([2026-01],
[2026-02], ...)) AS p. 2. Highlight what the PIVOT clause does: chooses an aggregate, a column
whose values become headers, and a fixed list of those values. Everything else in the source becomes a
grouping key implicitly. 3. Mention Oracle's slightly different syntax — PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR
month IN ('2026-01' AS jan, '2026-02' AS feb, ...)) — and the column aliasing. 4.
State the limitation: the IN list must be a constant set. For dynamic columns you need dynamic SQL.
Edge cases to mention: - Implicit grouping is by every column not in the PIVOT clause and not in the
FOR list — pre-project your source to avoid surprises. - Postgres has no PIVOT operator; use 
tablefunc.crosstab() or the manual CASE pattern. - BigQuery added PIVOT in 2021 — same
idea, slightly different syntax for the IN list.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume PIVOT is portable — it is not. Always check the dialect. - Do not skip
the source subquery; PIVOT requires a clean projection, otherwise the implicit grouping picks up
unwanted columns.
Common follow-up: "How would you do this with dynamic months?" — Build the SQL string in your
application or use SQL Server's dynamic SQL via sp_executesql.
-- SQL Server
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, [month], amount FROM monthly_sales
) src
PIVOT (
  SUM(amount) FOR [month] IN ([2025-12],[2026-01],[2026-02],[2026-03],[2026-04],[2026-05])
) AS pvt;
Q318 · Unpivot Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cognizant, Wipro, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
The opposite problem now — I have a wide table with one column per month, and I want to
convert it back to long format. How?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 332 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 333
The 30-second answer: Use the UNPIVOT operator in SQL Server / Oracle, the unnest plus VALUES
trick in Postgres, or a UNION ALL of selects (one per column) in any dialect. Each option turns one wide
row into N long rows where N is the number of unpivoted columns.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the universal solution: UNION ALL one SELECT per
column. Verbose but works everywhere. 2. Show SQL Server's UNPIVOT:
... UNPIVOT (amount FOR month IN (jan, feb, mar)) AS u — clean and readable. 3.
Postgres uses lateral with VALUES: SELECT customer_id, m.month, m.amount FROM
monthly_wide w, LATERAL (VALUES ('jan', w.jan), ('feb', w.feb), ('mar',
w.mar)) AS m(month, amount). 4. Mention BigQuery's UNPIVOT (added 2021) and Snowflake's
UNPIVOT operator.
Edge cases to mention: - UNPIVOT in SQL Server skips NULL values silently by default; if you want to
keep them you have to convert to non-NULL placeholders first. - The UNION ALL approach is portable
but does N scans of the table — fine for small tables, bad for large ones. - Postgres's jsonb_each is
a neat alternative when the wide row is already JSON: it unpivots key-value pairs natively.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "unpivot is just pivot in reverse" — they are operators on the same data
shape, but the semantics around NULL handling and column lists differ. - Do not write CROSS APPLY
when LATERAL is the modern term in Postgres.
Common follow-up: "Why would you store data in wide form if it's painful to query?" — Sometimes you
don't choose — legacy systems, CSV imports, spreadsheet exports. Knowing how to unpivot is what
gets you back to a queryable shape.
-- Portable union approach
SELECT customer_id, '2026-01' AS month, jan_2026 AS amount FROM monthly_wide
UNION ALL
SELECT customer_id, '2026-02', feb_2026 FROM monthly_wide
UNION ALL
SELECT customer_id, '2026-03', mar_2026 FROM monthly_wide;
Q319 · Conditional COUNT — Buckets in One Query
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want the count of orders in three buckets — below ₹500, ₹500 to ₹2000, and above ₹2000 — in
a single query.
The 30-second answer: Conditional COUNT with CASE expressions: COUNT(CASE WHEN amount <
500 THEN 1 END), COUNT(CASE WHEN amount BETWEEN 500 AND 2000 THEN 1 END),
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 333 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 334
COUNT(CASE WHEN amount > 2000 THEN 1 END). The ELSE branch is implicit NULL, which
COUNT skips. One pass over the data.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Restate the requirement: bucket the rows and count each bucket —
a histogram with three bins. 2. Choose the pattern: COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END) is cleaner than
SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) because there is no need for ELSE 0 — COUNT ignores
NULL. 3. Suggest extending to dollars: replace THEN 1 with THEN amount and COUNT with 
SUM to get total GMV per bucket. 4. Mention width_bucket (Q28) for many-bin histograms where
writing each CASE manually becomes painful.
Edge cases to mention: - Boundary conditions: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends; if you have rows
exactly at the boundary they go in one bin only. - Add a sanity check: the three bucket counts should
sum to COUNT() — if not, you missed a range. - For percentage shares, divide each conditional count by
COUNT() over the same query (no need for a subquery).
What NOT to say: - Do not write three separate queries and union them — interviewer is testing whether
you know conditional aggregation. - Do not forget the boundary rounding — < 500 vs <= 500
changes the answer.
Common follow-up: "What if buckets are dynamic — defined in another table?" — Cross join your data
with the bucket table, JOIN ON amount BETWEEN bucket_low AND bucket_high, then GROUP
BY bucket.
SELECT
  COUNT(CASE WHEN amount < 500                    THEN 1 END) AS low,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN amount BETWEEN 500 AND 2000     THEN 1 END) AS mid,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN amount > 2000                   THEN 1 END) AS high,
  COUNT(*)                                                    AS total
FROM orders;
Q320 · Median Calculation — PERCENTILE_CONT vs Workarounds
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Cred · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Compute the median order amount. Use the modern approach, then show me how you'd do it
without PERCENTILE_CONT.
The 30-second answer: Modern: SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY
amount) FROM orders — ANSI SQL ordered-set aggregate, supported as a standalone aggregate in
Postgres, Oracle, BigQuery, Snowflake. SQL Server implements PERCENTILE_CONT only as a window
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 334 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 335
function (requires OVER). Older / MySQL: use ROW_NUMBER and a self-aware filter — pick the middle
row(s) of the sorted set and average them if the count is even.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with PERCENTILE_CONT — interviewers want to know you
know the modern function. Mention that 0.5 = median, 0.95 = 95th percentile. 2. Differentiate from
PERCENTILE_DISC, which returns an actual value from the data set; PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates
between rows when the percentile rank is non-integer. 3. Show the MySQL workaround: SELECT
AVG(amount) FROM (SELECT amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS rn,
COUNT(*) OVER () AS n FROM orders) t WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((n+1)/2), CEIL((n+1)/
2)) — handles both odd and even counts. 4. Mention 
PERCENTILE_CONT() WITHIN GROUP (...) OVER (PARTITION BY ...) for median per
group.
Edge cases to mention: - NULLs are ignored by PERCENTILE_CONT — same as other aggregates. -
For per-group median, use a window-style invocation in Postgres / Oracle: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5)
WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) OVER (PARTITION BY city). - MySQL 8 added
PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST but still not PERCENTILE_CONT — the workaround remains.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "median is just AVG of MIN and MAX" — that's the range midpoint, not
the median. - Do not write a stored procedure when a single query suffices.
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between PERCENTILE_CONT and PERCENTILE_DISC?" —
CONT interpolates between two adjacent values when the rank lands between rows; DISC picks the
value at the lower of those two rows. CONT can return a value that does not appear in the data; DISC
cannot.
-- Postgres / Oracle (SQL Server uses IDENTITY(1,1) instead) / BigQuery
SELECT city,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS median_amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
Q321 · Mode — Most Frequent Value
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, AmEx, Wells Fargo · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Find the most common payment method per city. What's the cleanest way?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 335 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 336
The 30-second answer: Postgres has a native MODE() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY
payment_method) ordered-set aggregate. Elsewhere, use ROW_NUMBER over COUNT(*) per 
(city, payment_method) and pick the top row per city, or use a correlated subquery / lateral join.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the Postgres / Oracle native: MODE() WITHIN GROUP
(ORDER BY payment_method) — returns the single most frequent value (alphabetically first on ties
for Postgres). 2. Walk through the portable approach: aggregate to (city, method, cnt), then use
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY cnt DESC, method) and filter to rn =
1. 3. Mention tie-breaking: MODE() with no second tiebreaker is non-deterministic on ties; the
ROW_NUMBER approach lets you specify which method wins on a tie. 4. Note this is the same pattern
as top-N per group from Chapter 8 — mode is just top-1 by count.
Edge cases to mention: - For multiple modes when there is a tie, you need RANK() OVER
(PARTITION BY city ORDER BY cnt DESC) and filter to rk = 1 — returns all tied modes. - Empty
group: MODE returns NULL; the ROW_NUMBER approach returns no row. - NULLs in the data: MODE
skips NULLs in the input the same way other aggregates do.
What NOT to say: - Do not call mode "the average of the most common values" — that is not what
mode means. - Do not write a subquery per city — terrible at scale.
Common follow-up: "How would you compute mode without a window function?" — Self-join the
aggregated counts on city, max(cnt) per city, then pick the matching method. Possible but
ugly.
-- Postgres native
SELECT city,
       MODE() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY payment_method) AS top_method
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
-- Portable
SELECT city, payment_method, cnt
FROM (
  SELECT city, payment_method, COUNT(*) AS cnt,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY city, payment_method
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
Q322 · Standard Deviation — STDDEV vs STDDEV_POP vs STDDEV_SAMP
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, AmEx, Wells Fargo · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 336 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 337
What is the difference between STDDEV_POP and STDDEV_SAMP, and which does plain
STDDEV map to?
The 30-second answer: STDDEV_POP divides by N (the full population size); STDDEV_SAMP divides by
N - 1 (sample variance, Bessel's correction). Plain STDDEV is dialect-dependent — Postgres treats it as
STDDEV_SAMP, Oracle treats it as STDDEV_SAMP, SQL Server's STDEV is also sample-based. Be
explicit when it matters.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain when each applies: STDDEV_POP if you have the whole
population (e.g. every order ever placed); STDDEV_SAMP if your data is a sample of a larger population
(most empirical statistics). 2. The N-1 correction matters for small samples; for large samples the two are
nearly identical. 3. State the dialect mapping: Postgres / Oracle / MySQL / SQL Server all default to
sample variance for plain STDDEV or STDEV — but write the explicit name to remove doubt. 4.
Mention VAR_POP and VAR_SAMP — same pattern for variance, and the square root relationship:
STDDEV_SAMP = SQRT(VAR_SAMP).
Edge cases to mention: - STDDEV_SAMP on a single row returns NULL (cannot divide by N-1 = 0);
STDDEV_POP returns 0. - Both ignore NULLs and treat the remaining values as the dataset. - BigQuery
uses STDDEV (sample) and STDDEV_POP; Snowflake uses STDDEV and STDDEV_POP (where STDDEV
is sample by default).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they are the same on large data" — they converge but they are not
identical. - Do not use plain STDDEV in financial reports without checking the dialect's default.
Common follow-up: "How do you compute the coefficient of variation per city?" — 
STDDEV_SAMP(amount) / NULLIF(AVG(amount), 0) — guards against division by zero.
SELECT city,
       AVG(amount)         AS mean_amount,
       STDDEV_SAMP(amount) AS sample_sd,
       STDDEV_POP(amount)  AS population_sd
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;
Q323 · Histogram via width_bucket or CASE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Swiggy, Target, PhonePe · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 337 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 338
Build a 10-bucket histogram of order amounts between ₹0 and ₹10,000.
The 30-second answer: Use Postgres's width_bucket(amount, 0, 10000, 10) which returns
the bucket number 1 to 10 (plus 0 for values below the low bound and 11 for values above). Group by
the bucket number and count. For other dialects, derive the bucket with FLOOR(amount / 1000) +
1 and clamp.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the function: width_bucket(value, low, high,
bucket_count) is ANSI standard, supported in Postgres and Oracle, returning equal-width bucket
numbers. 2. Build the query: SELECT width_bucket(amount, 0, 10000, 10) AS bucket,
COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY bucket ORDER BY bucket. 3. For dialects without
width_bucket (MySQL, SQL Server), use LEAST(GREATEST(FLOOR(amount/1000), 0), 9) + 1
AS bucket — same effect. 4. Mention that for non-uniform bins (e.g. log scale), you need CASE
expressions or width_bucket with an array of breakpoints (Postgres extension).
Edge cases to mention: - width_bucket returns 0 for values below low and bucket_count + 1 for
values at or above high — handle these explicitly if you do not want them. - For very skewed data,
equal-width bins are uninformative — quantile-based bins via NTILE are usually better. - For visualisation,
add a bucket_low and bucket_high label per row using the same arithmetic.
What NOT to say: - Do not write ten CASE WHENs by hand if width_bucket is available — it's exactly
what the function is for. - Do not say it works on logarithmic bins by default — it does not; you'd take
LOG of the input first.
Common follow-up: "How would you make the bins logarithmic instead?" — 
width_bucket(LOG(amount), LOG(1), LOG(10000), 10) — assumes positive values.
-- Postgres
SELECT width_bucket(amount, 0, 10000, 10) AS bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       MIN(amount) AS bucket_low,
       MAX(amount) AS bucket_high
FROM orders
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY bucket;
Q324 · TOP-N With Ties — RANK vs FETCH FIRST WITH TIES
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 338 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 339
Give me the top 5 customers by GMV. What if there's a tie at the boundary — should the 6th row
be included?
The 30-second answer: If you must include all ties at the boundary, use 
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS WITH TIES (SQL:2008) — supported in Postgres 13+, SQL Server, Oracle
12c+. Or use RANK() OVER (ORDER BY gmv DESC) in a CTE and filter WHERE rk <= 5. Plain 
LIMIT 5 truncates arbitrarily and breaks ties non-deterministically.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the tie problem: with LIMIT 5 and three customers tied for
4th place, you arbitrarily keep one and drop two — different runs may return different customers. 2.
Introduce FETCH FIRST N ROWS WITH TIES — ANSI standard since SQL:2008. Requires ORDER
BY to determine ties. 3. Compare with the RANK approach: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY gmv DESC)
AS rk WHERE rk <= 5 — same idea, more portable across older databases (works in MySQL 8 too).
4. Mention DENSE_RANK if you want "top 5 distinct GMV values regardless of how many customers
share them."
Edge cases to mention: - LIMIT in Postgres / MySQL has no WITH TIES variant — you must use FETCH
FIRST or the RANK CTE. - ROW_NUMBER ties are broken arbitrarily by the planner — use RANK or
DENSE_RANK if you care about ties. - Combined with grouping: top 5 customers per city via RANK()
OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY gmv DESC).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the database will sort and pick consistently" — it won't, plans change. -
Do not claim LIMIT 5 is identical to FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY in terms of tie handling — they
are the same, but neither handles ties.
Common follow-up: "What if I want the top 5% of customers by GMV?" — 
NTILE(20) OVER (ORDER BY gmv DESC) and filter to tile = 1.
-- Postgres 13+ / SQL Server / Oracle 12c+
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS gmv
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY gmv DESC
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS WITH TIES;
Q325 · GROUP BY on Expression — When Planner Uses an Index
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman, Walmart Labs, Flipkart · Topic: Aggregations &
Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 339 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 340
GROUP BY DATE(created_at) is slow on a hundred-million-row table. Why, and how do you
make it fast?
The 30-second answer: A regular B-tree on created_at cannot be used to group by 
DATE(created_at) because the function changes the value the engine would compare. Create a
functional index on DATE(created_at) — Postgres, MySQL 8+, Oracle and SQL Server all support
computed-column or expression indexes. Alternatively, store the truncated date as a generated column
and index it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain why the index does not help: the planner compares the
indexed value (a timestamp) to the grouping expression (a date). It cannot prove they correspond without
trying every row. 2. Introduce expression indexes: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders
(DATE(created_at)) — Postgres, MySQL 8+. The planner can then group via index range scan. 3.
Show the alternative — a virtual / generated column created_date GENERATED ALWAYS AS
(DATE(created_at)) STORED indexed normally. 4. Mention BRIN indexes for naturally ordered data
(time series) — small and effective for date-grouped scans on huge tables.
Edge cases to mention: - The expression in GROUP BY must exactly match the indexed expression — 
DATE(created_at) and DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at) are not the same to the planner. -
Functional indexes are immutable — the function must be deterministic. - BigQuery / Snowflake do not
have user-defined indexes; you partition the table by date instead — same outcome, different
mechanism.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "just add an index on created_at" — that does not help here. - Do not
blame "the database" without diagnosing — run EXPLAIN, look for Seq Scan vs Index Scan.
Common follow-up: "What if the GROUP BY is on a CASE expression that depends on multiple
columns?" — Same trick: index the expression directly, as long as it is deterministic.
-- Postgres functional index
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_day ON orders (DATE(created_at));
-- Query that can now use it
SELECT DATE(created_at) AS day, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE(created_at);
Q326 · Aggregating JSON and Arrays
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Swiggy · Topic: Aggregations & Grouping
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 340 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 341
The events table stores a JSONB column payload with {"category": "...",
"amount": ...}. Give me total amount per category in Postgres.
The 30-second answer: Extract the JSON fields with the ->> operator and cast appropriately, then
aggregate: SELECT payload->>'category' AS category, SUM((payload-
>>'amount')::numeric) FROM events GROUP BY payload->>'category'. For better
performance on large JSON tables, create an expression index on the category key.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the JSON extraction operators: -> returns JSON; ->>
returns text; #> and #>> for nested paths. 2. Group by the extracted key and aggregate the numeric
value cast from text. 3. Index hint: CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload->>'category')) — a
Postgres functional index on the key makes the GROUP BY use an index scan. 4. Mention 
jsonb_each_text and jsonb_array_elements for cases where you need to expand the JSON
into rows first.
Edge cases to mention: - Casting (payload->>'amount')::numeric throws if any value is non-
numeric — wrap in a CASE or use nullif to skip. - MySQL has equivalent JSON functions
( JSON_EXTRACT, ->>); SQL Server uses JSON_VALUE; BigQuery uses dot notation on STRUCT. -
For arrays inside JSON, unnest first: LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(payload->'items') AS
item gives one row per item.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "JSON queries are always slow" — with the right expression index they
are competitive with normal columns. - Do not use -> when you want text — ->'category'
returns JSON, including the surrounding quotes; ->>'category' returns the bare text.
Common follow-up: "How do you aggregate values inside a JSON array per row?" — Use 
jsonb_array_elements to unnest into a derived table, then aggregate normally.
-- Postgres
SELECT payload->>'category' AS category,
       SUM((payload->>'amount')::numeric) AS total_amount,
       COUNT(*) AS events
FROM events
GROUP BY payload->>'category'
ORDER BY total_amount DESC;
