Q327 · UNION vs UNION ALL — Semantic and Performance Difference
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wells Fargo · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL? Which one should I default to and why?
The 30-second answer: UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result; UNION ALL keeps
every row from every input. UNION ALL is faster because it skips the sort/hash deduplication step —
default to it unless you genuinely need distinct rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the semantic difference — UNION is a set union
(duplicates removed), UNION ALL is a multiset union (everything kept). 2. Explain the cost: UNION needs
to sort or hash every row across both inputs to detect duplicates, which is O(N log N) work plus memory.
UNION ALL is a simple streaming concatenation. 3. Make the recommendation concrete: if you know the
two inputs cannot overlap (e.g. last-month orders + this-month orders), UNION ALL is correct and cheap.
If you are combining customers from two regions and the same email might appear in both, UNION is
what you want. 4. Be ready for the follow-up: "How would you dedupe more efficiently than UNION?" —
sometimes a GROUP BY on the natural key after UNION ALL is faster, especially if you also want
aggregation.
Edge cases to mention: - UNION treats NULLs as equal for deduplication purposes — (1, NULL)
and (1, NULL) collapse to one row, even though NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN in WHERE. -
UNION DISTINCT is the SQL standard name; most engines accept it as a synonym. - If you have an
index that already produces sorted, unique output, UNION may be nearly free — but you cannot rely on
this; check the plan.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "UNION is always slower" — when the planner sees a unique index
covering the union key, the dedup is essentially free. - Do not claim UNION ALL gives wrong results in
production — it gives the result the query asked for; the bug is in choosing the wrong operator.
Common follow-up: "You have ten partition tables you want to combine before aggregating. UNION or
UNION ALL?" — UNION ALL, every time. The aggregation will dedupe naturally, and you avoid an
unnecessary sort.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 342 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 343
-- Fast: known non-overlapping months
SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders_apr
UNION ALL
SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders_may;
Q328 · INTERSECT — What It Does and When to Reach for It
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Accenture, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain INTERSECT with an example. When would you use it instead of a JOIN?
The 30-second answer: INTERSECT returns rows that appear in both result sets, deduplicated. Reach
for it when you want the conceptually-clean answer to "which keys appear in both these queries",
without writing a self-join or an IN subquery.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Concrete example: users who placed orders in both March and April.
Two SELECTs returning user_id, with INTERSECT between them. 2. Compare to alternatives: 
INNER JOIN on user_id works but multiplies rows if either side has duplicates; IN with two
subqueries is verbose. INTERSECT is the cleanest expression of "set membership in both." 3. Mention
column compatibility: both inputs must have the same number of columns and compatible data types in
order. The result column names come from the first SELECT. 4. Anticipate: "Is it standard SQL?" Yes —
supported by Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite and MySQL 8.0.31+.
Edge cases to mention: - INTERSECT removes duplicates by default; INTERSECT ALL (Postgres,
Oracle) preserves multiplicity — useful when counts matter. - NULLs in matching positions are treated as
equal, same as UNION's deduplication. - Performance is typically a sort-merge or hash; large inputs
benefit hugely from indexes on the join columns.
What NOT to say: - Do not call INTERSECT a JOIN — it is a set operation that works on entire rows, not
column matches. - Do not assume MySQL has always supported it; older versions need EXISTS
workarounds.
Common follow-up: "Find products bought by every customer in your premium tier." — Classic
"relational division" problem; INTERSECT chained across per-customer queries is one approach, but a 
GROUP BY product_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM
premium_customers) is usually cleaner.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 343 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 344
-- Users active in both March and April
SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE order_month = '2026-03'
INTERSECT
SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE order_month = '2026-04';
Q329 · EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle) — Set Subtraction
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Wipro, TCS, Walmart Labs, AmEx · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does EXCEPT do? And what's the Oracle equivalent? Show me a use case from a real
reconciliation job.
The 30-second answer: EXCEPT returns rows from the first query that do not appear in the second,
deduplicated. Oracle calls the same operator MINUS. It's the natural way to express "in source, not in
target" — the bread-and-butter of reconciliation between systems.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the standard-vs-Oracle naming so the interviewer knows
you've worked across both. 2. Concrete reconciliation scenario: nightly job loads orders_staging
from upstream; you run SELECT order_id FROM orders_staging EXCEPT SELECT order_id
FROM orders to find rows that the staging table has but production hasn't ingested. The output is your
missing-rows backlog. 3. Mention column compatibility: same number of columns, compatible types,
deduplication of NULLs as equal. 4. Be ready for: "Why not just do a LEFT JOIN with IS NULL?" — Both
work; EXCEPT is more declarative and dedupes for free, but LEFT JOIN lets you pull additional columns
from the source without subquerying.
Edge cases to mention: - EXCEPT ALL (Postgres, Oracle 21+) preserves multiplicity — if the left has
three copies and the right has one, you get two. - MySQL added EXCEPT in 8.0.31; for older versions,
use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL. - Performance is typically hash-based; an index
on the comparison columns matters a lot on large tables.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse EXCEPT with NOT IN — NOT IN blows up on NULL in the
inner set; EXCEPT does not. - Do not assert that MINUS works in Postgres — it doesn't; you'll have to
switch keywords.
Common follow-up: "What if I want both 'in source not in target' AND 'in target not in source' in one
query?" — Run (A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (B EXCEPT A) — covered in Q8 as the symmetric-
difference / diff pattern.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 344 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 345
-- Orders in staging that haven't been ingested into production
SELECT order_id FROM orders_staging
EXCEPT
SELECT order_id FROM orders;  -- Oracle: MINUS
Q330 · Column Compatibility in Set Operations
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Cognizant, Infosys, Wells Fargo, Target · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What are the rules for column compatibility across UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT? Where do
people get tripped up?
The 30-second answer: Every branch must have the same number of columns, and the corresponding
columns must be of compatible types (the engine will coerce numeric and string families). Column names
come from the first branch — the names in subsequent branches are ignored.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the three rules: same column count, position-based
matching, type compatibility. 2. Explain the "type compatibility" nuance — INT and BIGINT will merge;
INT and TEXT will not (Postgres throws, MySQL silently coerces — bug magnet). 3. Common trip-up:
people assume column names match by name, not position. If branch 1 is SELECT user_id, name
and branch 2 is SELECT name, user_id, the result is nonsense but executes. 4. Anticipate: "What if
one branch has a NULL column and the other has a typed column?" — NULL is typeless until paired; the
engine takes the type from the non-null side.
Edge cases to mention: - DATE and TIMESTAMP unify to TIMESTAMP in Postgres; the precision of the
looser type wins. - VARCHAR(50) and VARCHAR(100) unify to the wider; CHAR-padded strings can
introduce trailing-space surprises. - ENUM types do not unify cleanly in MySQL — cast both sides to a
common string type first.
What NOT to say: - Do not insist that column names matter for matching — they do not, and you will
look junior. - Do not assume implicit conversion is always safe — in MySQL, '1' vs 1 unify silently
but with weird collation effects.
Common follow-up: "How would you align two SELECTs with different column sets for a UNION?" —
Add NULL AS missing_col (with an explicit CAST if needed) to the side that lacks the column, in
the right position. Be explicit about types when NULLs appear.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 345 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 346
-- Pad the missing column with NULL of the correct type
SELECT id, name, email FROM users_v1
UNION ALL
SELECT id, name, CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR(255)) FROM users_v2;
Q331 · ORDER BY with UNION — Only at the End
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Accenture, Razorpay · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Where does ORDER BY go when you use UNION? What happens if you put it on each branch?
The 30-second answer: ORDER BY applies to the final combined result, so it goes once at the end of
the last SELECT. Per-branch ORDER BY is either rejected (Postgres, SQL Server) or silently ignored
(some MySQL setups) because the union must reshuffle anyway.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the rule: one ORDER BY, at the very end, after the last
branch. 2. Explain why: UNION is conceptually a single result-set producer; the engine is free to
interleave or sort the combined output however it likes during deduplication. A per-branch ORDER BY
would be meaningless. 3. Note the syntax workaround if you really need per-branch ordering — wrap
each branch in a derived table with (SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT N) and union the
wrappers. This is useful for "top 5 from each region" patterns. 4. Mention column reference: ORDER BY
at the end references the first branch's column names (or positional ORDER BY 1, 2).
Edge cases to mention: - LIMIT and OFFSET also belong only at the end of the union, unless wrapped
per-branch. - Postgres lets you write ORDER BY against any column expression from the first branch;
SQL Server is stricter about needing the column to appear in the SELECT list. - For very large unions,
sorting at the end can spill to disk — sometimes pre-sorting each branch with an index helps the engine
do a merge-sort.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "ORDER BY each branch for performance" — it is at best ignored, at
worst rejected. - Do not assume the union preserves the order of the branches — it does not; rows may
interleave.
Common follow-up: "Give me the top 3 sellers from North and top 3 from South in one result, ordered
by region then rank." — Wrap each as a derived table with its own ORDER BY + LIMIT, UNION ALL them,
then ORDER BY at the outer level.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 346 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 347
(SELECT 'North' AS region, seller_id, sales FROM north_sales ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 3)
UNION ALL
(SELECT 'South' AS region, seller_id, sales FROM south_sales ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 3)
ORDER BY region, sales DESC;
Q332 · Set Operations vs JOIN — When Each Is the Right Tool
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Swiggy, Cred, JP Morgan · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you reach for a set operation versus a JOIN? They feel similar — when does the
distinction actually matter?
The 30-second answer: JOIN combines columns from two tables row-by-row using a match condition;
set operations combine entire rows of compatible result sets. Use JOIN when you need columns from
both sides; use set operations when you are asking a yes/no question about row membership across
queries.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the distinction: JOIN is horizontal (widening rows with more
columns); UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT are vertical (stacking or filtering whole rows). 2. Give a concrete
contrast: "Customers who appear in both the iOS and Android user tables" — INTERSECT on 
user_id. "Customers with their iOS device model and their Android device model side by side" —
INNER JOIN. 3. Mention the duplication subtlety: a JOIN can multiply rows when the match isn't one-to-
one; set operations dedupe (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT) or preserve (UNION ALL). 4. Performance
angle: set operations often need full materialisation and sort/hash for dedupe; JOIN with good indexes
can stream. Choose by intent first, then optimise if needed.
Edge cases to mention: - Anti-join (A LEFT JOIN B ... WHERE B.id IS NULL) and EXCEPT
solve overlapping problems; benchmark on your data. - Semi-join (WHERE EXISTS) and INTERSECT-
on-key both express "in both" but EXISTS lets you keep extra columns from A without losing them to the
set dedup. - Some optimizers rewrite EXCEPT as anti-join internally — check EXPLAIN.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim JOIN can always replace set operations — UNION across
heterogeneous sources (e.g. multiple shards) has no JOIN equivalent. - Do not assume INTERSECT is
always faster than a JOIN with DISTINCT — depends on the planner and your indexes.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this EXCEPT as a LEFT JOIN." — Practice both directions; interviewers
love checking that you can move between formulations.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 347 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 348
-- EXCEPT vs LEFT JOIN equivalence
SELECT order_id FROM staging EXCEPT SELECT order_id FROM live;
-- Equivalent
SELECT s.order_id FROM staging s
LEFT JOIN live l ON s.order_id = l.order_id
WHERE l.order_id IS NULL;
Q333 · Preserving Duplicates with UNION ALL — Why It Matters
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Cognizant, Goldman, Target · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why would I deliberately want to keep duplicates across a UNION? Give me a realistic scenario.
The 30-second answer: You want duplicates whenever each row represents an independent fact — a
payment, a click, a sensor reading — and aggregating across branches must count each one. Stripping
duplicates with UNION would silently undercount whenever two branches genuinely contain identical
rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Concrete fact-table scenario: hourly clickstream from two regions.
Same (user_id, page, hour) could legitimately appear in both. UNION ALL preserves both rows
so a downstream COUNT(*) reflects total clicks. 2. Performance bonus: UNION ALL skips the dedup
pass entirely — for partitioned tables stitched together, it is essentially free compared to UNION. 3.
Highlight the safety angle: if you know your branches cannot overlap (different time periods, different
shards), UNION ALL is both correct and faster. UNION there is just slower with no upside. 4. Mention the
analytical pattern: pre-aggregate per branch, UNION ALL the aggregates, then aggregate again at the
top level — classic for combining multi-region telemetry.
Edge cases to mention: - UNION ALL is stable in the sense that row count equals sum of branch row
counts; downstream sanity checks rely on this. - Some optimisers turn SELECT DISTINCT ... FROM
(UNION ALL ...) into a fused operator that is faster than UNION directly. - Beware of accidentally
creating duplicates when migrating from UNION to UNION ALL — re-check downstream consumers.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume "duplicates are always bad" — fact tables are full of legitimate
repeats. - Do not switch UNION to UNION ALL just for speed without checking whether the original logic
relied on deduplication.
Common follow-up: "You changed UNION to UNION ALL and your numbers doubled. What happened?"
— Your branches overlap; either filter one side or revert to UNION; or pre-aggregate to a granularity
where overlap is impossible.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 348 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 349
-- Sum clicks across two regions where overlap is meaningful
SELECT page, COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM (
  SELECT page FROM clicks_north
  UNION ALL
  SELECT page FROM clicks_south
) t
GROUP BY page;
Q334 · Diff Between Two Tables — EXCEPT + UNION Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, JP Morgan, AmEx · Topic: Set Operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Give me a single query that returns rows present in only one of two tables — the symmetric
difference. How do you make it tell you which side each row came from?
The 30-second answer: (A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (B EXCEPT A) is the symmetric difference.
To label the side, add a string literal column in each branch: 
SELECT 'only_in_A' AS source, ... FROM (A EXCEPT B) and the equivalent for B.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Write the symmetric-difference pattern first — interviewers want to
see the EXCEPT-UNION ALL combo recognised on sight. 2. Add the source label so the diff is
actionable: when you hand the result to ops, they need to know which side is missing the row. 3. Mention
the inverse — rows present in both — is INTERSECT; the three pieces (only A, only B, both)
make a full Venn breakdown. 4. Performance note: each EXCEPT does its own sort/hash dedup. For
huge tables, a single FULL OUTER JOIN with a CASE expression is often faster and shows both sides
plus matched rows in one pass.
Edge cases to mention: - Both inputs must have identical column projections; if schemas differ, project
a common subset first. - NULLs collapse as equal in EXCEPT, just like UNION — useful for tables with
nullable comparison columns. - For row-level diff including column-level differences (not just key
presence), FULL OUTER JOIN with CASE WHEN a.col IS DISTINCT FROM b.col is the better
tool.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose two separate queries and tell the user to eyeball them — give one
labelled result. - Do not use OR to mix EXCEPT branches; UNION ALL is the only safe combiner.
Common follow-up: "Now show me rows where the key exists in both but a column value differs." —
That's a FULL OUTER JOIN with a WHERE a.col IS DISTINCT FROM b.col filter; covered in
JOIN chapter but worth knowing here.

Q335 · UPSERT in Postgres — INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Zerodha · Topic: MERGE / UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you do an UPSERT in Postgres? Walk me through the syntax and what EXCLUDED
refers to.
The 30-second answer: Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key_cols) DO UPDATE SET col =
EXCLUDED.col. The ON CONFLICT clause needs a unique or primary-key constraint on the named
columns; EXCLUDED is a virtual row containing the values that the failed insert was trying to set.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the canonical form first — most candidates know "ON
CONFLICT" but stumble on EXCLUDED. 2. Explain EXCLUDED: when a row conflicts, Postgres binds
the proposed insert values to a virtual table named EXCLUDED, so SET amount =
EXCLUDED.amount means "use the new amount we tried to insert." 3. Mention the existing-row
reference: inside the DO UPDATE, the conflicting row's current values are accessible by the table name
(or alias), so SET amount = orders.amount + EXCLUDED.amount does an additive upsert. 4.
Note the conflict target options: by column list (user_id, day), by constraint name ON
CONSTRAINT uq_orders_user_day, or DO NOTHING if you just want to skip.
Edge cases to mention: - The conflict target must be an actual unique constraint or unique index; a
regular index will not do. - Partial unique indexes work as conflict targets, but you must include their 
WHERE clause in the conflict spec for the planner to use them. - Triggers fire as expected: INSERT
triggers on the insert path, UPDATE triggers on the conflict path.
What NOT to say: - Do not call this "MERGE" — Postgres also has a MERGE statement (added in 15),
but ON CONFLICT is the idiomatic upsert and has different concurrency semantics. - Do not assume DO
UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.* is valid — you must list each column.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 350 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 351
Common follow-up: "What's the locking story?" — ON CONFLICT acquires a row lock on the conflicting
row; it is safe under concurrent inserts without needing SERIALIZABLE isolation, which is why it's the
recommended upsert path in Postgres.
INSERT INTO daily_totals (user_id, day, amount)
VALUES (42, '2026-05-26', 199)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, day)
DO UPDATE SET amount = daily_totals.amount + EXCLUDED.amount;
Q336 · INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — When and Why
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy · Topic: MERGE / UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why would you use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING? Isn't that just swallowing errors?
The 30-second answer: DO NOTHING gives you an idempotent insert — if the row already exists, the
insert silently no-ops instead of raising a unique-violation error. It's perfect for at-least-once event
ingestion where retries are expected and re-processing is harmless.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it as idempotency, not error-swallowing — that reframe
matters in the interview. 2. Use the canonical scenario: a webhook handler receives 
payment_confirmed events, sometimes duplicated by the provider. The handler does INSERT ...
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING and returns 200, knowing duplicates are absorbed cleanly.
3. Mention the RETURNING gotcha: with DO NOTHING, RETURNING gives you nothing for the
conflicted rows, so you cannot tell from the result whether the row was actually inserted or skipped. Use 
xmax = 0 trick or do an explicit lookup if you need that signal. 4. Contrast with DO UPDATE: DO
NOTHING is the right choice when the existing row is authoritative; DO UPDATE is right when the new
payload should win or merge.
Edge cases to mention: - DO NOTHING also suppresses other constraint violations targeted by the
conflict spec — but unrelated constraint failures (e.g. CHECK) still raise. - Concurrent inserts with DO
NOTHING are safe; Postgres serialises on the unique index. - Without specifying a conflict target, ON
CONFLICT DO NOTHING suppresses any unique-violation — useful sometimes, dangerous mostly.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "it ignores all errors" — only unique-key conflicts on the targeted
columns are absorbed. - Do not use it without a conflict target unless you genuinely want to suppress
every unique violation in the table.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 351 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 352
Common follow-up: "How do you tell whether a particular insert was actually inserted versus skipped?"
— Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET id = EXCLUDED.id RETURNING *,
(xmax = 0) AS was_inserted — the xmax trick is the well-known Postgres idiom.
INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id, payload)
VALUES ('evt_123', '{"amount":499}')
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING;
Q337 · MySQL UPSERT — INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Flipkart · Topic: MERGE / UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's MySQL's equivalent of Postgres ON CONFLICT? Are there any traps?
The 30-second answer: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE col = VALUES(col) (or 
col = NEW.col in MySQL 8.0.20+). It triggers on any unique-key violation, not just a named one —
and that breadth is the main trap.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the syntax; note VALUES(col) references the would-be
insert value (legacy syntax), and the newer alias-based AS new ... SET col = new.col is the
preferred modern form. 2. Spell out the trap: ON DUPLICATE KEY reacts to a violation of any unique
key on the table, not a specific one. If you have two unique indexes and a conflict happens on the
"wrong" one, the UPDATE still runs against the existing matching row — which may not be the row you
expected. 3. Mention auto-increment behaviour: a conflicting insert still increments the auto-increment
counter on InnoDB by default, leading to gaps. Set innodb_autoinc_lock_mode=0 if gaps are
unacceptable (rarely worth the contention cost). 4. Contrast with REPLACE INTO — covered in Q28; ON
DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE is almost always the safer choice.
Edge cases to mention: - The affected-rows count is 1 for insert, 2 for update (a MySQL quirk) — your
client library may or may not expose that. - If the row exists but the UPDATE makes no actual change,
MySQL reports 0 affected rows. - Multi-row INSERT with ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE is supported and
atomic per row but not transactional unless wrapped explicitly.
What NOT to say: - Do not call it "MERGE" — MySQL has no MERGE statement; this is the only native
upsert path. - Do not use the legacy VALUES() function in MySQL 8.0.20+ — it emits a deprecation
warning.
Common follow-up: "How do you upsert multiple rows in one statement?" — Provide a multi-row
VALUES list; ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE applies per row independently. Useful for batch ingestion.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 352 / 521

INSERT INTO daily_totals (user_id, day, amount) VALUES
  (42, '2026-05-26', 199),
  (43, '2026-05-26', 299) AS new
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE amount = daily_totals.amount + new.amount;
Q338 · SQL Server MERGE — Syntax and Concurrency Bugs
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: MERGE /
UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How does SQL Server's MERGE work? And why do some senior engineers recommend never
using it for upsert?
The 30-second answer: MERGE takes a source and target, declares match conditions, and branches
into WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED actions. It is powerful but has a long history of known
concurrency bugs and edge cases — Microsoft MVPs widely recommend using INSERT ... WHERE
NOT EXISTS + UPDATE under serialisable isolation instead for high-concurrency upserts.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk the syntax: MERGE INTO target USING source ON
match_condition WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
INSERT .... 2. Acknowledge the power: in a single statement you can insert new rows, update
existing ones and even delete unmatched-by-source rows — useful for slowly-changing-dimension Type
2 loads. 3. Surface the concurrency story: under concurrent execution, MERGE has been the source of
duplicate-key violations and deadlocks because the read of source/target and the write are not protected
as a single locked unit by default. Microsoft has fixed several of the worst issues but the community
advice (Aaron Bertrand's blog, Paul White posts) remains cautious. 4. Recommend the practical
workaround for concurrent upsert: explicit transaction at HOLDLOCK/SERIALIZABLE, attempt UPDATE,
then INSERT WHERE NOT EXISTS, all within BEGIN TRY/CATCH.
Edge cases to mention: - MERGE requires a semicolon terminator in SQL Server — a notorious source
of confusing parse errors. - Source duplicates against a single target row cause MERGE to fail with "the
MERGE statement attempted to UPDATE or DELETE the same row more than once" — pre-aggregate
the source. - Triggers and OUTPUT clauses interact with MERGE in non-obvious ways; test thoroughly.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim MERGE is the standard upsert — it's optional in the ISO spec, and
dialects implement it differently or not at all. - Do not assume MERGE is atomic for concurrency without
explicit isolation control — that's the bug.
Common follow-up: "What's your concrete recommendation for upsert in SQL Server today?" — For
high-concurrency workloads, an explicit transaction with UPDATE WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK)
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 353 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 354
followed by INSERT WHERE NOT EXISTS is the safe pattern; MERGE is acceptable for batch loads
where you control the source.
MERGE INTO daily_totals AS t
USING (VALUES (42, '2026-05-26', 199)) AS s(user_id, day, amount)
ON t.user_id = s.user_id AND t.day = s.day
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET amount = t.amount + s.amount
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (user_id, day, amount) VALUES (s.user_id, s.day, s.amount);
Q339 · MERGE WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED Patterns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan, Target · Topic: MERGE /
UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the various WHEN clauses in MERGE. Can you have multiple WHEN MATCHED
branches?
The 30-second answer: MERGE supports WHEN MATCHED [AND extra_condition] THEN
UPDATE/DELETE, WHEN NOT MATCHED [BY TARGET] THEN INSERT, and WHEN NOT MATCHED
BY SOURCE THEN UPDATE/DELETE. Yes, multiple WHEN MATCHED branches are allowed if each has
a distinguishing predicate.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lay out the three families: matched, not matched (new row in
source), not matched by source (row vanished from source — used for soft deletes or SCD). 2. Show the
conditional branching: WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_active = 0 THEN DELETE plus WHEN
MATCHED AND s.is_active = 1 THEN UPDATE SET ... lets you encode a state machine in one
statement. 3. Mention the "not matched by source" clause as the rarely-known third option — invaluable
for full-refresh dimension tables. 4. Anticipate the dialect spread: SQL Server has all three; Postgres 15
MERGE supports MATCHED and NOT MATCHED but the "NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE" wording
landed in Postgres 17.
Edge cases to mention: - Branches are evaluated in order; the first matching one wins. Put more
specific predicates first. - Mixing INSERT and DELETE across branches is allowed; the engine plans both
paths. - An OUTPUT (SQL Server) or RETURNING (Postgres) clause emits one row per affected row, with
an $action column indicating INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE — invaluable for audit.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume Postgres MERGE has full SQL Server parity — they share the
surface but not every clause is available pre-17. - Do not stack WHEN MATCHED branches without 
AND predicates — without distinguishing conditions, only the first ever fires.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 354 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 355
Common follow-up: "How would you use MERGE for a Type 2 SCD load?" — Use WHEN MATCHED
AND s.hash <> t.hash to expire the old row (UPDATE valid_to = NOW()), then a separate
INSERT step (often outside MERGE) for the new version — pure-MERGE SCD2 is tricky because one
source row needs both an UPDATE and an INSERT, which MERGE cannot do natively.
MERGE INTO products t
USING staging_products s ON t.sku = s.sku
WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_active = 0 THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_active = 1 AND s.price <> t.price THEN UPDATE SET price = s.price
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (sku, price, is_active) VALUES (s.sku, s.price, 1);
Q340 · Postgres 17 MERGE with RETURNING Clause
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: MERGE / UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres 17 added a RETURNING clause to MERGE. What does it give you and why is 
merge_action() useful?
The 30-second answer: RETURNING on MERGE emits one row per affected row, just like RETURNING
on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. The new merge_action() function tells you which branch fired — 
'INSERT', 'UPDATE' or 'DELETE' — so a single round trip both performs the upsert and tells
the caller what actually happened per row.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the value: before Postgres 17, you had to choose between
MERGE (powerful but no RETURNING) and ON CONFLICT (RETURNING but only one action). Now
MERGE gives you both. 2. Show merge_action() in RETURNING — combined with the row's
columns, your application learns exactly which keys were created vs updated vs removed without a
second query. 3. Mention the use case: audit logging, downstream change-stream emission,
idempotency tracking — any pipeline that needs "what changed" feedback per row. 4. Be ready for:
"Can you filter RETURNING?" Yes — wrap the MERGE in a CTE and filter the CTE output, just as you
would with INSERT/UPDATE.
Edge cases to mention: - The RETURNING list can reference target columns (post-write state) and
source columns; for DELETEs, source columns reflect the matched source row. - Available only in
Postgres 17 and later — for earlier versions, an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... RETURNING handles the
upsert case but not three-way actions. - Combining RETURNING with WITH cte AS (MERGE ...)
lets you chain — e.g. log to an audit table in the same statement.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 355 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 356
What NOT to say: - Do not assume MySQL's INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY supports RETURNING —
it does not, even in 8.x. - Do not promise this feature in older Postgres — it really is 17+; mistake = lost
credibility.
Common follow-up: "How would you log every change to an audit table in one statement?" — Use 
WITH changed AS (MERGE ... RETURNING merge_action() AS action, id, ...) INSERT
INTO audit_log SELECT NOW(), action, id, ... FROM changed.
-- Postgres 17+
WITH changed AS (
  MERGE INTO daily_totals t
  USING incoming s ON t.user_id = s.user_id AND t.day = s.day
  WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET amount = t.amount + s.amount
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (user_id, day, amount) VALUES (s.user_id, s.day, s.amount)
  RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.user_id, t.day, t.amount
)
SELECT * FROM changed;
Q341 · Bulk INSERT — COPY, LOAD DATA INFILE, BULK INSERT
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Cred, Target · Topic: Bulk Load
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the fastest way to load a million rows into Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server respectively?
The 30-second answer: Postgres: COPY ... FROM STDIN (or \copy from psql). MySQL: LOAD
DATA INFILE (or LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE for client-side files). SQL Server: BULK INSERT or
bcp. All three bypass per-row overhead and stream rows in chunks.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the three commands so the interviewer knows you've used
each. 2. Explain why row-by-row INSERT is slow: per-statement parsing, per-row WAL/redo, per-row
constraint checks, per-row index updates. Bulk loaders batch these. 3. Production tips: drop or disable
secondary indexes during bulk load and rebuild after; widen work_mem or bulk_logged recovery
model temporarily; load into an unlogged or staging table first if you can tolerate the durability tradeoff. 4.
Mention transactional behaviour: COPY runs in a single transaction in Postgres (atomic — all or nothing);
LOAD DATA INFILE is transactional in InnoDB; BULK INSERT defaults to minimal logging in 
BULK_LOGGED recovery model.
Edge cases to mention: - LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE is often disabled by default for security (--
local-infile=1 flag required client and server side). - COPY in Postgres expects either text (tab-
separated) or CSV format with carefully configured escape characters; mis-quoting is the leading cause
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 356 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 357
of corrupt loads. - BULK INSERT requires the file to be visible from the SQL Server service account, not
from your client machine — a frequent first-time stumble.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose row-by-row INSERTs in a loop for a million-row load — that's an
instant downgrade signal. - Do not assume bulk loaders skip constraints — they enforce PK/UNIQUE/FK
by default; you must explicitly disable if you want speed (and accept the risk).
Common follow-up: "How do you load a file that doesn't quite match the table schema?" — COPY
supports column lists and CSV header skipping; LOAD DATA INFILE supports (@col1, @col2) SET
col_actual = TRIM(@col1) for inline transformation.
-- Postgres COPY
COPY orders (id, user_id, amount) FROM '/data/orders.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true);
-- MySQL
LOAD DATA INFILE '/data/orders.csv' INTO TABLE orders
  FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' IGNORE 1 LINES (id, user_id, amount);
-- SQL Server
BULK INSERT orders FROM 'C:\data\orders.csv' WITH (FORMAT='CSV', FIRSTROW=2);
Q342 · INSERT INTO ... SELECT — Copy with Transformation
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Bulk Load
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how to copy data from one table to another with transformation. What are the gotchas?
The 30-second answer: INSERT INTO target (cols) SELECT expr_list FROM source
WHERE .... The SELECT can transform, filter, aggregate, JOIN — anything. Gotchas: column order
matters, types must align, and the whole thing runs as a single transaction unless you batch.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the canonical form with explicit column lists on both sides —
never rely on positional matching of unnamed INSERT INTO target SELECT * FROM source
because schema drift breaks it silently. 2. Highlight the transformation power: rename, recast, compute,
aggregate during the copy. Common use: snapshotting a normalised live table into a denormalised
reporting table. 3. Transaction gotcha: a million-row INSERT INTO ... SELECT generates a million WAL
records and locks. For huge migrations, chunk it (INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... WHERE id
BETWEEN x AND y LIMIT N) in a loop with commits between. 4. Mention CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS
SELECT) as the close cousin when the target doesn't yet exist — faster because the new table starts
empty and can skip WAL via CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE in Postgres.
Edge cases to mention: - DEFAULT values on the target apply only to columns omitted from the column
list; if you include the column in your list and pass NULL, the default does not fire. - IDENTITY / SERIAL
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 357 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 358
columns: in Postgres, omit them from the insert column list to let the sequence assign; in SQL Server,
use SET IDENTITY_INSERT target ON if you want to preserve source values. - Locking: INSERT
INTO ... SELECT takes a row-share lock on the source; large copies can interact with concurrent writers
— schedule off-peak.
What NOT to say: - Do not use SELECT * in production copy queries — schema drift will silently
misalign columns. - Do not assume the INSERT honours the SELECT's ORDER BY for storage order
(only matters in clustered-index databases like SQL Server with WITH (TABLOCK)).
Common follow-up: "How would you copy 100M rows without taking the system down?" — Batch by
primary-key ranges, commit per batch, throttle with pg_sleep or sleep equivalents, and monitor
replication lag.
INSERT INTO orders_archive (id, user_id, amount, archived_at)
SELECT id, user_id, amount, NOW()
FROM orders
WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 year';
Q343 · PIVOT — Turning Rows into Columns (SQL Server / Oracle)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: PIVOT / UNPIVOT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how PIVOT works. Turn monthly sales rows into one row per region with twelve month
columns.
The 30-second answer: PIVOT (aggregate(value_col) FOR pivot_col IN (lit1,
lit2, ...)) rotates rows into columns. SQL Server and Oracle have a dedicated PIVOT operator; in
Postgres and MySQL, you emulate it with conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Jan'
THEN amount END) AS jan).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the SQL Server PIVOT skeleton: a subquery projecting just the
three relevant columns (region, month, amount), then PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR month IN
([Jan], [Feb], ...)) AS p. 2. Stress that the pivot value list (Jan, Feb, ...) must be hard-
coded — PIVOT cannot expand a list dynamically. For dynamic pivots, you build the statement string at
the application layer or use dynamic SQL. 3. Show the equivalent conditional aggregation pattern that
works in every dialect: SELECT region, SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Jan' THEN amount END)
AS jan, ... GROUP BY region. 4. Mention that PIVOT is syntactic sugar over conditional
aggregation under the hood — same plan, different ergonomics.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 358 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 359
Edge cases to mention: - PIVOT requires the input subquery to project exactly the columns involved;
extra columns become part of the implicit GROUP BY and may explode row counts unexpectedly. -
NULL handling: if no source row matches a pivot value for a group, the cell is NULL — coalesce to 0 in
the outer SELECT if you need a numeric grid. - Oracle PIVOT supports multiple aggregates 
(SUM(amount) sum, COUNT(*) cnt FOR ...) producing columns like Jan_sum, Jan_cnt.
What NOT to say: - Do not promise PIVOT in MySQL or Postgres — there is no native operator; emulate
it. - Do not write a PIVOT and forget to wrap the source in an explicit subquery — extra columns in the
base table will silently change the grouping.
Common follow-up: "What if I don't know the month list at write time?" — Build the SQL as a string at
the app layer, or in T-SQL use STRING_AGG to construct the pivot column list and EXEC
sp_executesql to run the assembled statement.
-- SQL Server
SELECT region, [Jan], [Feb], [Mar]
FROM (SELECT region, month, amount FROM sales) src
PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR month IN ([Jan], [Feb], [Mar])) AS p;
Q344 · UNPIVOT — Turning Columns into Rows
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Target · Topic: PIVOT /
UNPIVOT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Now go the other way. I have one row per region with twelve month columns; give me three
columns: region, month, amount.
The 30-second answer: UNPIVOT (amount FOR month IN ([Jan], [Feb], ...)) flips
columns into rows. In dialects without UNPIVOT (Postgres pre-15, MySQL), simulate with CROSS JOIN
LATERAL (VALUES ('Jan', jan), ('Feb', feb), ...) AS u(month, amount) or a UNION
ALL across single-column SELECTs.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk the SQL Server UNPIVOT first: source has region, jan,
feb, mar; output is one row per (region, month, amount). 2. Show the portable LATERAL VALUES trick
— works in Postgres and any dialect with VALUES-in-FROM support, and is often more readable than
UNPIVOT. 3. Highlight the NULL behaviour: UNPIVOT drops rows where the source column is NULL. If
you need to keep them, the LATERAL VALUES form preserves NULLs naturally. 4. Anticipate: "Why
would I want a wide table unpivoted?" — Almost any analytics workflow prefers long-format data
because GROUP BY and pivot tools (Tableau, Looker) operate on long format more flexibly.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 359 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 360
Edge cases to mention: - All unpivoted columns must share a compatible data type — you cannot
UNPIVOT an INT and a DATE into the same output column. - UNPIVOT in SQL Server uses dataset-style
names; quoting with square brackets handles reserved words and unusual identifiers. - For very wide
tables (200+ columns), code-generate the LATERAL VALUES list from 
information_schema.columns.
What NOT to say: - Do not implement UNPIVOT by writing 12 separate UNION ALL queries when
LATERAL VALUES does it in one block — the former is verbose and brittle. - Do not claim UNPIVOT
preserves NULLs — by default it drops them; explicitly say "with INCLUDE NULLS" or use the LATERAL
pattern.
Common follow-up: "Unpivot a wide table with 50 numeric columns." — Generate the VALUES tuple list
from information_schema.columns in a templating step; keeps the SQL maintainable as new
columns are added.
-- Portable LATERAL form (Postgres)
SELECT region, month, amount
FROM sales_wide s,
LATERAL (VALUES ('Jan', jan), ('Feb', feb), ('Mar', mar)) AS u(month, amount);
Q345 · PIVOT via Conditional Aggregation (Postgres / MySQL)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: PIVOT / UNPIVOT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres and MySQL don't have a PIVOT keyword. How do you pivot anyway?
The 30-second answer: Conditional aggregation — wrap each pivoted value in a CASE inside an
aggregate and GROUP BY the surviving dimension. SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN
amount END) AS paid_amount, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN amount END)
AS failed_amount, ... with GROUP BY user_id.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the pattern: pick the dimension that becomes the row key
(GROUP BY column), the dimension that becomes the new column headers (CASE branches), and the
value (the aggregate target). 2. Explain why this is universal: every SQL engine since 1992 has supported 
CASE inside aggregates, so this works without dialect features. 3. Talk about which aggregate to pick:
SUM for additive, MAX for boolean (one-hot style), COUNT for counts, BOOL_OR for presence in
Postgres. 4. Anticipate the dynamic-columns question: if the set of column headers is unknown at write
time, you must build the SQL string in the app layer — there is no truly dynamic pivot in pure SQL.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 360 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 361
Edge cases to mention: - NULLs in the CASE ELSE branch are skipped by aggregates like SUM and
AVG (giving you the intended "no-value" cell); be explicit if you want 0 instead with 
COALESCE(SUM(...), 0). - FILTER clause (SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status =
'paid')) is cleaner Postgres/standard syntax than CASE inside SUM, and the planner handles it
identically. - For high-cardinality pivots (hundreds of columns), conditional aggregation becomes
unwieldy — consider keeping the data long and pivoting at the BI layer.
What NOT to say: - Do not pretend Postgres has PIVOT — it does not (the tablefunc extension's 
crosstab() is the closest thing, covered in Q20). - Do not write CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0
END summed for a presence flag when MAX(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END) or BOOL_OR is what
you mean — they have different semantics for counts.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this with FILTER syntax." — 
SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid — same plan, cleaner read, ISO
SQL standard.
SELECT
  user_id,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')   AS paid,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refund') AS refund
FROM payments
GROUP BY user_id;
Q346 · crosstab() in Postgres tablefunc Extension
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: PIVOT / UNPIVOT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does Postgres's crosstab function do? When is it worth using over conditional aggregation?
The 30-second answer: crosstab() is a function from the tablefunc extension that takes a
SQL string of (row_key, category, value) triples and returns a wider record with one column
per category. It shines when you have many pivot columns and want server-side pivoting without writing
out one CASE per column.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the extension prereq: CREATE EXTENSION
tablefunc; — not in core Postgres; some managed services need this enabled by the admin. 2.
Show the two-argument form: first arg is the source query producing (row_key, category,
value) ordered by row_key, second arg names the pivot categories so the returned record has
predictable column types. 3. Stress the output-typing oddity: you must declare the column list in the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 361 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 362
calling query (AS ct(region TEXT, jan NUMERIC, feb NUMERIC, ...)) because the function
returns a generic record. 4. Compare to conditional aggregation: for 3-5 categories, CASE/FILTER is
clearer. For 20-50 categories, crosstab() reduces boilerplate dramatically.
Edge cases to mention: - The source query must be ordered by row_key (and category, if multi-row) —
otherwise crosstab silently emits wrong results because it relies on grouping consecutive rows. - Missing
(row, category) combinations produce NULL cells; the result has no row for a row_key that had zero
categories. - Performance: crosstab is essentially syntactic sugar over the same conditional-aggregation
plan, plus the overhead of crossing a function boundary.
What NOT to say: - Do not use crosstab without ordering the input — the silent-wrong-answer trap. - Do
not assume RDS/Aurora has tablefunc enabled by default — check before deploying.
Common follow-up: "What happens if I forget the ORDER BY?" — Grouping breaks; rows from different
keys leak into each other's output rows. Always include ORDER BY 1, 2 in the source query.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS tablefunc;
SELECT * FROM crosstab(
  $$SELECT region, month, amount FROM sales ORDER BY 1, 2$$,
  $$VALUES ('Jan'),('Feb'),('Mar')$$
) AS ct(region TEXT, jan NUMERIC, feb NUMERIC, mar NUMERIC);
Q347 · TABLESAMPLE — Random Sample of a Large Table
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Cred, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Advanced Single-
Query
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I need a random 1% sample of a 500M-row table for an ad-hoc analysis. What's the fastest way?
The 30-second answer: Use TABLESAMPLE — SELECT * FROM orders TABLESAMPLE
BERNOULLI (1) (1%) or TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1). BERNOULLI samples row-by-row (accurate
fraction, slower); SYSTEM samples whole blocks (faster, less uniform). For most ad-hoc analyses,
SYSTEM is the right speed/accuracy tradeoff.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Compare the two methods: BERNOULLI scans every row and
includes each with probability p; SYSTEM picks random blocks (8 KB pages in Postgres) and includes all
rows on those blocks. 2. Explain why ORDER BY RANDOM() LIMIT N is terrible at scale — it sorts the
entire table by a random column. TABLESAMPLE is orders of magnitude faster. 3. Mention 
REPEATABLE (seed) for reproducible samples — handy when collaborating on a sampled dataset
across sessions. 4. Cover dialect notes: SQL Server has TABLESAMPLE (block-based only); MySQL has
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 362 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 363
no TABLESAMPLE — use WHERE RAND() < 0.01 (still scans every row, but much cheaper than
ORDER BY RAND()).
Edge cases to mention: - SYSTEM sampling correlates with physical layout; if data is clustered by date,
your "random" sample may have skewed date distribution. - For very small percentages, BERNOULLI
may return fewer rows than expected due to variance; sample slightly larger and LIMIT. - Postgres can
combine TABLESAMPLE with WHERE filters, but the sample applies first so total result rows shrink
twice.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose ORDER BY RANDOM() LIMIT 100 for a large table — it's a
junior-grade answer. - Do not assume TABLESAMPLE gives a statistically perfect SRS — block-based
SYSTEM has cluster bias.
Common follow-up: "How do I get a repeatable sample for two teams to share?" — TABLESAMPLE
BERNOULLI (1) REPEATABLE (42) — the seed makes the random choice deterministic across
runs.
-- Postgres: ~1% by block
SELECT * FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1) REPEATABLE (42);
-- ~1% by row (more uniform)
SELECT * FROM orders TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1);
Q348 · WITH ORDINALITY — Row Numbers from Set-Returning Functions
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Advanced Single-Query
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does WITH ORDINALITY do in Postgres? Give me a use case where it saves the day.
The 30-second answer: WITH ORDINALITY attaches an auto-incrementing position column to the
output of a set-returning function, starting at 1. Without it, the function returns just the values; with it, you
get (value, ordinality) pairs so you can join back to original positions.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk the canonical example: SELECT
unnest(ARRAY['a','b','c']) WITH ORDINALITY AS u(element, position). You get 
('a', 1), ('b', 2), ('c', 3) — perfect for preserving order through an unnest. 2. Show the
killer use case: JSON arrays. SELECT j.value, j.ordinality FROM
jsonb_array_elements(payload) WITH ORDINALITY AS j(value, ordinality) — you
can correlate each array element back to its position for stable updates or joins. 3. Combine with
LATERAL to unnest per row while preserving the source row's identity AND the position within its array.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 363 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 364
4. Mention that this is standard SQL (since SQL:2003) but rarely implemented — Postgres has it; many
others do not.
Edge cases to mention: - Ordinality starts at 1 and increments by 1; there is no syntax for 0-based or
custom-step. - Ordering of the set-returning function's output is preserved only within a single call;
multiple invocations in the same SELECT may interleave unpredictably. - Works with any set-returning
function: unnest, jsonb_array_elements, generate_series, string_to_table, even
user-defined.
What NOT to say: - Do not use row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ...) to fake ordinality on an
unnested array — the inner ordering is not preserved; WITH ORDINALITY is the only correct path. - Do
not assume this works in MySQL or SQL Server — it does not; emulate with window functions over a
derived numbering column.
Common follow-up: "Update the third element of a JSONB array in place." — Use 
WITH ORDINALITY to find it, then jsonb_set with the path; the ordinality value gives you the
index for the path.
SELECT element, position
FROM unnest(ARRAY['onboarding','payment','done']) WITH ORDINALITY AS u(element, position);
-- (onboarding,1), (payment,2), (done,3)
Q349 · LATERAL with Set-Returning Functions
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, JP Morgan · Topic: Advanced Single-Query
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain LATERAL with an example involving a set-returning function. Why is it different from a
regular subquery in FROM?
The 30-second answer: LATERAL lets a derived table or function call in the FROM clause reference
columns from earlier items in the same FROM clause. Without LATERAL, a subquery in FROM is
evaluated once independently; with LATERAL, it's evaluated per left-side row, like a correlated subquery
you can use as a table source.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the difference with a concrete example: you have orders
and a function get_top_lines(order_id) RETURNS TABLE. Without LATERAL, you cannot pass 
o.id into the function from the FROM clause; with LATERAL you can. 2. Combine LATERAL with set-
returning functions: SELECT o.id, l.sku, l.qty FROM orders o, LATERAL
get_top_lines(o.id, 3) l — you get up to 3 line rows per order, all in one fluent expression. 3.
Highlight that LATERAL is the "for each row in the left, evaluate the right" pattern — formally a CROSS
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 364 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 365
APPLY in SQL Server. 4. Mention practical patterns: top-N-per-group via LATERAL on a subquery,
JSON array exploding per row, computing per-row scalars that you also reuse later in the SELECT.
Edge cases to mention: - LEFT JOIN LATERAL preserves the outer row even when the function returns
zero rows — pair with ON true to make it explicit. - LATERAL implies an implicit comma-join order;
the LATERAL side cannot be referenced from items to its left. - Postgres, Oracle and SQL Server (as
CROSS/OUTER APPLY) all support this; MySQL added LATERAL in 8.0.14.
What NOT to say: - Do not call LATERAL "just a subquery" — the lateral reference is what makes it
powerful; a regular FROM subquery cannot see other FROM items. - Do not assume CROSS APPLY
and LATERAL are syntactically identical — semantically equivalent, syntactically different.
Common follow-up: "Get the 3 most recent orders per user in one query." — SELECT u.id,
recent.* FROM users u, LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) recent — the prototypical LATERAL top-N pattern.
-- Top 3 most expensive line items per order
SELECT o.id, l.sku, l.amount
FROM orders o,
LATERAL (
  SELECT sku, amount FROM order_lines
  WHERE order_id = o.id
  ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3
) l;
Q350 · generate_series() and Sequence Generation Patterns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Flipkart · Topic: Advanced Single-Query
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you generate a series of dates for a calendar dimension, or fill in gaps in a time series,
without a calendar table?
The 30-second answer: Postgres has generate_series(start, stop, step) for integers,
dates and timestamps — perfect for producing every day in a range. In MySQL/SQL Server (where there
is no native equivalent), use a recursive CTE bounded by date math or a numbers table.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the Postgres date version: SELECT d::date FROM
generate_series('2026-01-01'::date, '2026-12-31'::date, '1 day') d — instant
calendar. 2. Use case for gap-filling: LEFT JOIN your daily-aggregated metric against the generated
series so dates with zero events still appear (with COUNT 0 / SUM 0 after coalescing). 3. Show the
MySQL recursive CTE equivalent: 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 365 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 366
WITH RECURSIVE cal AS (SELECT DATE '2026-01-01' AS d UNION ALL SELECT d + 1
FROM cal WHERE d < '2026-12-31') SELECT * FROM cal. 4. SQL Server can do the same
recursive CTE with OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0) to override the default 100-step limit.
Edge cases to mention: - generate_series with timestamps is timezone-aware in Postgres — pass
timestamptz inputs if you care about DST. - For very long ranges (decades), recursive CTEs in MySQL
may hit cte_max_recursion_depth (default 1000); increase the session variable. - A persistent
calendar table is often a better long-term choice than generating series on the fly — it can hold attributes
like is_holiday, fiscal_quarter, etc.
What NOT to say: - Do not use a recursive CTE in Postgres for date series when generate_series exists
— it's slower and more verbose. - Do not generate huge series unbounded; always bound by an end
date or LIMIT to prevent runaway plans.
Common follow-up: "Fill in zero-revenue days in the past 90 days for each user." — Cross-join
generate_series of dates with the user list, LEFT JOIN actual sales, COALESCE the amount to 0.
Standard gap-fill pattern.
-- Postgres: every day in May 2026
SELECT d::date AS day
FROM generate_series('2026-05-01'::date, '2026-05-31'::date, '1 day') d;
Q351 · DELETE with USING / DELETE with JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you delete from one table based on a condition that requires JOINing to another table?
Each dialect does it slightly differently.
The 30-second answer: Postgres: DELETE FROM target USING other WHERE join_cond AND
filter. MySQL: DELETE t FROM target t JOIN other o ON ... WHERE .... SQL Server:
DELETE FROM target FROM target JOIN other ON ... WHERE .... All three say "delete
rows from target that match a condition you can only express by referencing another table."
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show all three dialect forms — interviewers love when you can write
the same logical operation in each major engine. 2. Stress that the table being deleted from is the one
named immediately after DELETE (or in the FROM list); the joined table contributes filter logic only. 3.
Concrete use case: delete payments whose orders have been soft-deleted. DELETE FROM payments
USING orders WHERE payments.order_id = orders.id AND orders.deleted_at IS NOT
NULL. 4. Anticipate: "Why not DELETE with a subquery?" — Subquery works too (DELETE FROM
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 366 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 367
payments WHERE order_id IN (SELECT id FROM orders WHERE deleted_at IS NOT
NULL)) and is more portable; JOIN-style is more readable when you need columns from multiple joined
tables for filtering.
Edge cases to mention: - ON DELETE CASCADE on a FK will delete child rows automatically —
sometimes a JOIN-DELETE is reinventing what the schema already does. - DELETE with JOIN can be
slow on huge tables; batch with WHERE id BETWEEN x AND y LIMIT N to avoid long-running
transactions and replication lag. - Some dialects allow deleting from multiple tables in one statement
(MySQL: DELETE t1, t2 FROM ...); rarely a good idea — explicit is clearer.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume Postgres allows DELETE FROM target JOIN other — it does
not; use USING instead. - Do not run a large unbatched JOIN-DELETE in production without
monitoring replication and lock waits.
Common follow-up: "How would you safely delete 10M rows without blocking the table?" — Loop in
batches of 10K-50K with explicit transactions and short sleeps, optionally with a covering index on the
filter column for fast row identification.
-- Postgres
DELETE FROM payments USING orders
WHERE payments.order_id = orders.id AND orders.deleted_at IS NOT NULL;
-- MySQL
DELETE p FROM payments p JOIN orders o ON p.order_id = o.id WHERE o.deleted_at IS NOT NULL;
Q352 · UPDATE with FROM / JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Same setup for UPDATE — how do you update one table using values from another?
The 30-second answer: Postgres: UPDATE target SET col = other.col FROM other WHERE
join_cond. MySQL: UPDATE target t JOIN other o ON ... SET t.col = o.col. SQL
Server: UPDATE target SET col = o.col FROM target t JOIN other o ON .... The
semantics are identical — pull values from the joined table into the target.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show each dialect; mention that the Postgres form is closest to SQL
standard with the explicit FROM clause. 2. Concrete example: update orders.payment_status
from a staging table after a reconciliation run. UPDATE orders o SET payment_status =
s.new_status FROM payment_recon s WHERE o.id = s.order_id. 3. Stress the cardinality
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 367 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 368
trap: if the join condition matches multiple right-side rows for one left row, the behaviour is dialect-
specific — Postgres picks an arbitrary one (and logs a warning in stricter modes); MySQL also picks
arbitrarily. Pre-aggregate or use DISTINCT ON to avoid this. 4. Anticipate: "Why not a correlated
subquery in SET?" — Works too (SET col = (SELECT s.col FROM staging s WHERE s.id =
orders.id)) but it's harder for the planner to optimise as a join.
Edge cases to mention: - Updating the join column itself (e.g. SET id = ...) is risky; the row may
move in the index and confuse the in-flight scan — separate the rename into its own statement. - WHEN
multiple update candidates exist, you can rank with DISTINCT ON or window functions in a derived
table, then JOIN to that. - Always confirm the affected-row count after a JOIN-UPDATE — if it's wildly
higher than expected, you may have an accidental cartesian.
What NOT to say: - Do not put the join condition in the SET clause's subquery and then forget the outer
WHERE — you'll update every row in the target with NULL where the subquery doesn't match. - Do not
use UPDATE-JOIN to do bulk insert-or-update; that's what MERGE / ON CONFLICT is for.
Common follow-up: "What if multiple staging rows match the same target row?" — Pre-aggregate the
staging side to one row per target key, or use DISTINCT ON (target_id) ... ORDER BY
priority in Postgres to deterministically pick the winner.
-- Postgres
UPDATE orders o
SET payment_status = s.new_status
FROM payment_recon s
WHERE o.id = s.order_id;
Q353 · TRUNCATE vs DELETE — Performance and Transactional Differences
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What's the difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE? Why is TRUNCATE faster, and what
does it cost you?
The 30-second answer: DELETE removes rows one-by-one (logged, fires triggers, can be ROLLBACK-
ed), respecting WHERE clauses. TRUNCATE drops and recreates the table's data pages — instant,
minimally-logged, but no WHERE, no per-row triggers, may reset identity counters, and can't be
ROLLBACK-ed in some dialects.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Tabulate the differences: row-by-row vs page-drop; logged vs
minimally logged; triggers vs no triggers; ROLLBACK-able everywhere in Postgres but auto-commits in
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 368 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 369
MySQL (DDL behaviour); identity reset in SQL Server (with RESEED) and Oracle (with REUSE
STORAGE), depends on Postgres options. 2. Use case for TRUNCATE: staging tables that are wiped
before each batch load — instant clear, no per-row WAL. 3. Use case for DELETE: anywhere you need a
WHERE clause, want triggers to fire, or want to ROLLBACK if subsequent steps fail. 4. Mention foreign-
key gotchas: TRUNCATE refuses (Postgres without CASCADE) when other tables reference the truncated
rows; CASCADE truncates them too, which is rarely what you want.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres TRUNCATE is transactional and can ROLLBACK; MySQL
TRUNCATE on InnoDB is technically a DDL statement and implicitly commits before and after. -
TRUNCATE in SQL Server requires ALTER permission, not just DELETE — privilege model differs. -
DELETE leaves dead row versions (Postgres) requiring VACUUM; TRUNCATE reclaims space
immediately.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume TRUNCATE always resets the auto-increment — in Postgres it
depends on RESTART IDENTITY; default is CONTINUE IDENTITY. - Do not use TRUNCATE inside
a routine app transaction in MySQL expecting ROLLBACK to undo it — it commits.
Common follow-up: "You truncate a table that has FKs from another table. What happens?" — Postgres
refuses unless you TRUNCATE ... CASCADE (which truncates the referencing table too); MySQL/
InnoDB also refuses. Generally a sign you should DELETE with conditions instead.
-- Postgres: instant wipe of staging
TRUNCATE TABLE staging_orders RESTART IDENTITY;
-- DELETE with condition (the only option when you need WHERE)
DELETE FROM staging_orders WHERE batch_id = 42;
Q354 · REPLACE INTO (MySQL) — Why It's Not an UPSERT
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Flipkart · Topic: MERGE / UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
MySQL has REPLACE INTO. Isn't that an upsert? Why do experts warn against using it?
The 30-second answer: REPLACE INTO is DELETE + INSERT under the hood when a unique-key
conflict is detected — not a true UPDATE. That means triggers fire as deletes-and-inserts, auto-
increment values change, foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE wipe out child rows, and replication
can record extra events. ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE is the correct upsert.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the mechanism — DELETE + INSERT — because it
explains every gotcha. 2. Walk the consequences one by one: trigger semantics differ (BEFORE/AFTER
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 369 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 370
DELETE then BEFORE/AFTER INSERT instead of BEFORE/AFTER UPDATE); identity columns advance;
ON DELETE CASCADE wipes children silently; row-based replication records two events instead of one.
3. Give the scenario: a users table with REPLACE INTO and addresses(user_id) REFERENCES
users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. Every REPLACE INTO on users deletes all addresses. Real
production outages have been caused exactly by this. 4. State the recommendation clearly: use 
INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE for upsert semantics; reserve REPLACE INTO for the
rare case where DELETE+INSERT is genuinely what you want.
Edge cases to mention: - REPLACE INTO requires the same INSERT privilege plus DELETE privilege —
different from ON DUPLICATE KEY's required INSERT + UPDATE. - For tables with multiple unique keys,
REPLACE may delete multiple existing rows in a single REPLACE — silently — to clear the way for the
new one. - Auto-increment value of the new row is fresh, not the deleted row's value — FK references to
that ID become invalid.
What NOT to say: - Do not call REPLACE INTO "an upsert" without immediately flagging the DELETE
semantics — that's the trap. - Do not assume application code dependent on the same primary-key
value after a REPLACE will keep working — it may not, if the AI counter advances.
Common follow-up: "Why does REPLACE INTO still exist if it's dangerous?" — Historical and there are
niche cases (e.g. wanting trigger semantics of DELETE+INSERT, or full row replacement when partial
UPDATE is wrong). Mostly: legacy; for new code, prefer INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
-- DANGEROUS if children depend on this row via ON DELETE CASCADE
REPLACE INTO users (id, name, email) VALUES (42, 'Asha', 'asha@example.com');
-- SAFE upsert
INSERT INTO users (id, name, email) VALUES (42, 'Asha', 'asha@example.com')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE name = VALUES(name), email = VALUES(email);
Q355 · RETURNING Clause — Single-Round-Trip Writes in Postgres / Oracle
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, JP Morgan · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does the RETURNING clause do? Show me how it saves a round trip in an INSERT, an
UPDATE and a DELETE.
The 30-second answer: RETURNING (Postgres and Oracle) appends a SELECT-style projection to
INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, emitting one row per affected row right back from the DML. You avoid the
classic INSERT-then-SELECT-currval or UPDATE-then-SELECT pattern — one statement, one round trip,
no race.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 370 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 371
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show INSERT RETURNING: INSERT INTO orders (user_id,
amount) VALUES (42, 199) RETURNING id, created_at — the server-assigned ID and
timestamp come back without a second query. 2. UPDATE RETURNING: useful for state-machine
transitions where you want to know which rows actually changed and their new state. UPDATE orders
SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 1 AND status = 'pending' RETURNING id, status.
3. DELETE RETURNING: archive-then-delete pattern. DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at
< NOW() RETURNING * — capture the deleted rows for an audit log in the same statement. 4.
Combine with CTEs: WITH d AS (DELETE FROM sessions WHERE ... RETURNING *) INSERT
INTO sessions_archive SELECT * FROM d — atomic move in one statement.
Edge cases to mention: - RETURNING can reference any column of the affected row, including
computed columns and generated identities. - For multi-row INSERT, RETURNING emits one row per
inserted row; useful for bulk inserts with server-side ID assignment. - Oracle uses RETURNING ...
INTO for PL/SQL variables; the pure-SQL form (RETURNING ... FROM style emitting a result set) is
mostly Postgres territory.
What NOT to say: - Do not insist RETURNING is in every dialect — MySQL has nothing equivalent; SQL
Server's analogue is OUTPUT (Q30). - Do not skip RETURNING * when you actually need just one
column — be explicit; * is wasteful in wire-traffic terms.
Common follow-up: "How do you do this in MySQL?" — Insert and call LAST_INSERT_ID() for the
new ID; for updates and deletes, there is no native equivalent — you must SELECT before or after,
accepting a race window.
-- INSERT RETURNING
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, amount) VALUES (42, 199)
RETURNING id, created_at;
-- Archive-then-delete in one shot
WITH gone AS (
  DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < NOW() RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO sessions_archive SELECT * FROM gone;
Q356 · OUTPUT Clause (SQL Server) — Equivalent of RETURNING
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
SQL Server has OUTPUT instead of RETURNING. How does it compare? What can it do that
RETURNING can't?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 371 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 372
The 30-second answer: OUTPUT emits one row per affected row from INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/
MERGE, with access to two virtual tables — inserted (post-image) and deleted (pre-image). For
UPDATE, you can return both the old and the new value in the same row — something RETURNING
does not natively support.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show INSERT OUTPUT: INSERT INTO orders (user_id,
amount) OUTPUT inserted.id, inserted.created_at VALUES (42, 199). Note that 
inserted is the only useful pseudo-table for INSERT. 2. Show UPDATE OUTPUT: UPDATE orders
SET status = 'paid' OUTPUT deleted.status AS old_status, inserted.status AS
new_status WHERE id = 1. Captures the change delta atomically. 3. Show DELETE OUTPUT: 
DELETE FROM sessions OUTPUT deleted.* WHERE expires_at < GETDATE() — archive
the deleted rows in one round trip. 4. Mention OUTPUT INTO: pipe the OUTPUT into another table
directly: OUTPUT inserted.id, inserted.created_at INTO audit_log(order_id,
created_at) — single-statement audit trail.
Edge cases to mention: - OUTPUT works on MERGE too, with an $action column ('INSERT' /
'UPDATE' / 'DELETE') — invaluable for tracking what each branch did. - Triggers and OUTPUT both fire
on the same DML; if you have an AFTER trigger that modifies the row further, OUTPUT sees the pre-
trigger state for that statement. - Some constraints on OUTPUT clauses with constraints or computed
columns — rare in practice but worth checking docs for complex cases.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume inserted is available for DELETE or deleted for INSERT —
each DML exposes only the relevant pseudo-tables. - Do not conflate OUTPUT with triggers — they
coexist and have different lifecycles.
Common follow-up: "How do you log a before-and-after diff for every UPDATE?" — OUTPUT
deleted.col_a AS old_a, inserted.col_a AS new_a, ... INTO audit_log — emits the
diff into your audit table directly from the UPDATE statement.
-- Capture before/after on update
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'paid'
OUTPUT deleted.status AS old_status, inserted.status AS new_status
WHERE id = 1;
-- Archive deletes inline
DELETE FROM sessions
OUTPUT deleted.* INTO sessions_archive
WHERE expires_at < GETDATE();
