2008 — procedural SQL is not optional. You will be asked to write a stored procedure in PL/pgSQL, T-
SQL or PL/SQL, defend why you'd choose a function over a procedure, debug a misbehaving trigger,
and explain whether business logic belongs in the database at all. Modern stacks (Razorpay, Cred,
Swiggy, anything Postgres-on-RDS with a Go or Node service in front) lean lighter on procs and heavier
on application code — but even those teams ask "when would you reach for a stored procedure?" and
they expect a thoughtful answer, not a reflex. This chapter walks through the thirty questions that come
up most often, with the dialect call-outs you absolutely need because procedural SQL is the most
vendor-divergent corner of the language.
Q357 · Stored Procedure vs Function — The Semantic Difference
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant, Wells Fargo · Topic: Procedures vs
Functions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between a stored procedure and a function in SQL? Where would you use
one over the other?
The 30-second answer: A function is meant to compute and return a value (scalar or table) and is
callable from inside a SELECT or WHERE clause; a procedure is meant to perform an action (DML,
multiple statements, transaction control) and is invoked with CALL or EXEC. Functions typically
cannot have side effects on data; procedures usually can. Procedures can manage transactions;
functions usually run inside the caller's transaction.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the returning-a-value vs performing-an-action framing —
that is what the interviewer is testing. 2. Mention callability: functions can sit in a SELECT list (SELECT
calc_gst(amount) FROM invoices); procedures cannot. 3. Talk about side effects. In Postgres a
function can technically do DML, but the convention is "function = pure-ish, procedure = side-effects." In
Oracle, functions historically were not allowed to modify data inside a query. 4. Mention transactions —
only procedures can run COMMIT and ROLLBACK inside the body (Postgres 11+, SQL Server T-SQL,
Oracle PL/SQL).
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL has both FUNCTION and PROCEDURE, and functions are
restricted by log_bin_trust_function_creators for replication safety. - SQL Server scalar UDFs
are notorious for forcing row-by-row execution before the 2019 inlining work — covered in a later
question. - Postgres blurs the line — a FUNCTION can do DML, and pre-11 there was no 
PROCEDURE at all; people wrote everything as functions.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "functions cannot modify data" as an absolute — that depends on the
dialect and the volatility tag. - Do not say "procedures are always faster" — that is folklore, not
architecture.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 373 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 374
Common follow-up: "Then why does Postgres even have procedures if functions can do everything?" —
Because procedures can issue COMMIT/ ROLLBACK mid-body, which functions cannot. That is the
real reason CREATE PROCEDURE was added in Postgres 11.
-- Postgres: function returns a value, callable in SELECT
CREATE FUNCTION calc_gst(amount NUMERIC) RETURNS NUMERIC
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT amount * 0.18 $$;
-- Postgres: procedure performs an action, called with CALL
CREATE PROCEDURE settle_invoice(p_invoice_id BIGINT)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE invoices SET status = 'SETTLED' WHERE id = p_invoice_id;
  COMMIT;
END $$;
CALL settle_invoice(101);
Q358 · When Procedural SQL Is the Right Call (Modern Trade-offs)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic:
Architecture
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Modern teams say "keep logic in the application." When would you still write a stored procedure
in 2026?
The 30-second answer: When you need to minimise network round-trips for a chatty, multi-statement
workflow; when you need a single transactional boundary that the application cannot easily provide;
when multiple consumer apps must share the exact same logic and you cannot host a shared service; or
when row-level performance matters and shipping the data to the app is the bottleneck.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Acknowledge the modern bias — Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred-style
stacks push logic into Go/Node/Java services because procs are hard to test, hard to version, and hard
to scale horizontally. 2. List the legitimate use cases: complex bulk-update jobs
( SETTLE_PAYOUTS_FOR_DAY), reconciliation, end-of-day batch, outbox writers, audit trails, anything
where shipping 5 lakh rows to the app and back is wasteful. 3. Mention the GCC reality: banks at JP
Morgan India, Wells Fargo, Goldman often have decades-old Oracle PL/SQL packages — you will be
asked to extend them, not replace them. 4. Be ready to defend "I'd put this in the app, not in a proc" —
interviewers respect a reasoned no.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 374 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 375
Edge cases to mention: - Procedures defeat horizontal scaling — the DB becomes the bottleneck. A Go
service can scale to 50 pods; the proc cannot. - ORM frameworks (JPA, Entity Framework, GORM) can
call procs but cannot easily diff/version them — drift is a real risk. - Cloud-managed Postgres on RDS or
Aurora has limits on LANGUAGE plperlu, plpython3u etc — you may not get the extension you
want.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always use procs because they are faster" — that is 2005 thinking. - Do
not say "never use procs" — that disqualifies you from any bank or GCC role.
Common follow-up: "Have you ever moved logic out of a stored procedure into application code?
Why?" — Be ready with a real story: testability, observability, deploy independence, or freeing the DB
CPU.
-- Reasonable proc use: bulk settlement that touches 1M rows per night
CREATE PROCEDURE settle_eod_payouts(p_run_date DATE)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE payouts SET status='SETTLED', settled_at=now()
  WHERE status='PENDING' AND run_date = p_run_date;
END $$;
Q359 · PL/pgSQL Basics — Block Structure
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Cred, Zerodha · Topic: PL/pgSQL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Write a basic PL/pgSQL function that takes a customer id and returns their total order amount.
Walk me through the block structure.
The 30-second answer: PL/pgSQL functions live inside $$ ... $$ dollar-quoted blocks. The body
has an optional DECLARE for local variables, a mandatory BEGIN ... END for the executable
section, and an optional EXCEPTION block for error handling. You write RETURN <value> to send a
scalar back.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the skeleton — CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS ...
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE ... BEGIN ... END $$; 2. Explain the use of 
SELECT ... INTO for assigning query results to variables — this is PL/pgSQL-specific syntax. 3.
Mention RAISE NOTICE for debug output and RAISE EXCEPTION for errors. 4. Call out that 
LANGUAGE sql is a different beast — no DECLARE, no procedural control flow, just a single SQL
expression.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 375 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 376
Edge cases to mention: - SELECT INTO STRICT raises an exception if zero or more than one row is
returned — useful for invariants. - Variables shadowing column names is a classic bug. Prefix locals with 
v_ or _ by convention. - Postgres re-parses the body on every fresh session for the first call — be
aware on connection-poolers.
What NOT to say: - Do not call dollar-quoting "string escaping" — it is a literal delimiter that avoids
quote-escaping headaches. - Do not assume PL/pgSQL is the only language available — Postgres
supports plpython3u, plperl, pltcl too (often disabled on RDS).
Common follow-up: "What happens if the customer does not exist?" — Without STRICT, the variable
becomes NULL and the function returns NULL. With STRICT, you get a NO_DATA_FOUND exception
you can trap.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION customer_total(p_customer_id BIGINT)
RETURNS NUMERIC
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  v_total NUMERIC;
BEGIN
  SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) INTO v_total
  FROM orders WHERE customer_id = p_customer_id;
  RETURN v_total;
END $$;
Q360 · T-SQL Basics — Stored Procedure on SQL Server
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Accenture, Wells Fargo · Topic: T-SQL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Write a T-SQL stored procedure that takes an order id, returns the order header and the line items
as two result sets.
The 30-second answer: Use CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE, declare parameters with @ prefix,
write each SELECT as a separate statement — SQL Server happily returns multiple result sets to the
client. Use SET NOCOUNT ON at the top to suppress row-count chatter.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the skeleton: CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE
dbo.get_order @order_id INT AS BEGIN ... END. 2. Mention SET NOCOUNT ON — without
it, the (1 row affected) messages are sent to the client and can confuse ORMs like Entity
Framework and Dapper. 3. Two SELECTs return two result sets — drivers like ADO.NET's 
SqlDataReader.NextResult() walk them. 4. Talk about parameter direction — defaulting to IN;
OUTPUT params are declared @name INT OUTPUT.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 376 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 377
Edge cases to mention: - CREATE OR ALTER requires SQL Server 2016 SP1 or newer; older
versions force a DROP IF EXISTS + CREATE pattern. - SET XACT_ABORT ON is critical when
you want a runtime error to roll back the whole transaction — by default, T-SQL is lenient. - Returning
more than one result set breaks some ORMs that map to a single entity — coordinate with the
application team.
What NOT to say: - Do not use CREATE PROCEDURE without OR ALTER on modern SQL Server —
you'll annoy reviewers. - Do not forget SET NOCOUNT ON — that is a giveaway you have not written T-
SQL in production.
Common follow-up: "How does the .NET application read both result sets?" — using var rdr =
cmd.ExecuteReader(); rdr.Read(); ...; rdr.NextResult(); rdr.Read(); ...
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE dbo.get_order
  @order_id INT
AS
BEGIN
  SET NOCOUNT ON;
  SELECT id, customer_id, total_amount, status FROM dbo.orders WHERE id = @order_id;
  SELECT id, order_id, sku, qty, unit_price FROM dbo.order_lines WHERE order_id = @order_id;
END
Q361 · PL/SQL Basics — Oracle Package Structure (Light Touch)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo · Topic: PL/SQL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If you walked into an Oracle shop tomorrow, what is the first thing you'd notice about how procs
and functions are organised compared to Postgres or SQL Server?
The 30-second answer: Oracle organises related procedures and functions into PACKAGE (the spec)
and PACKAGE BODY (the implementation) — a namespace plus a public/private boundary in one.
Postgres and SQL Server have no such concept; you get loose functions and procedures with at best a
schema as the only grouping.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the package concept — it is what an Oracle dev cares
about most. 2. The spec declares what is callable from outside; the body holds the implementation plus
private helpers. 3. Mention that compiling the spec invalidates dependants, but compiling only the body
does not — this matters for deploys. 4. Acknowledge you only need a light touch unless the role is
explicitly Oracle PL/SQL — but knowing packages exist is enough to pass a screening round.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 377 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 378
Edge cases to mention: - PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION lets a sub-procedure commit
independently of the caller — useful for audit logs that must persist even on rollback. - Package-level
variables persist for the duration of the session — a footgun if you forget. - Oracle's compilation model is
strict — a broken body marks the package INVALID and callers fail until it is recompiled.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim Postgres has packages — schemas are not the same thing. - Do not
over-claim PL/SQL experience if you have only read about it. GCC interviewers spot this fast.
Common follow-up: "What is PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION and when have you used it?" —
Audit logging that must survive a parent rollback, or rate-limit counters that must commit immediately.
-- Oracle package spec
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE pkg_orders AS
  FUNCTION get_total(p_order_id NUMBER) RETURN NUMBER;
  PROCEDURE cancel_order(p_order_id NUMBER);
END pkg_orders;
/
-- Oracle package body
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pkg_orders AS
  FUNCTION get_total(p_order_id NUMBER) RETURN NUMBER IS
    v_total NUMBER;
  BEGIN
    SELECT total_amount INTO v_total FROM orders WHERE id = p_order_id;
    RETURN v_total;
  END;
  PROCEDURE cancel_order(p_order_id NUMBER) IS
  BEGIN
    UPDATE orders SET status='CANCELLED' WHERE id = p_order_id;
  END;
END pkg_orders;
/
Q362 · MySQL Stored Procedure Syntax and DELIMITER
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Meesho, Zerodha · Topic: MySQL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Why do MySQL stored procedure scripts almost always start with DELIMITER //? What does
that actually do?
The 30-second answer: The MySQL client uses ; to separate statements. A procedure body contains
semicolons inside it, which would otherwise be interpreted as end-of-statement and break the parser. 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 378 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 379
DELIMITER // tells the client "use // as the statement terminator instead," so the entire CREATE
PROCEDURE ... END is treated as one statement. Reset it to ; afterwards.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it as a client-side parsing issue, not a server-side language
feature. 2. Show the canonical pattern: DELIMITER // ... CREATE PROCEDURE foo() BEGIN ...
END // ... DELIMITER ;. 3. Mention that some clients (MySQL Workbench, DBeaver) abstract this
away; the CLI mysql and most CI pipelines do not. 4. Be ready for the question about parameter
directions — MySQL supports IN, OUT, INOUT.
Edge cases to mention: - The delimiter is a per-client convention; the server has no idea what // is. It
just sees a single string. - If you forget to reset to ;, every subsequent statement in the script confuses
the client. - Migration tools like Liquibase or Flyway handle this for you with delimiter::END
markers — read their docs.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "DELIMITER is part of the SQL standard" — it is a MySQL CLI
convention. - Do not paste a multi-line procedure into the mysql shell without delimiter handling — it
will fail in spectacular ways.
Common follow-up: "What's the equivalent in Postgres?" — Dollar-quoting ($$) plays the same role; it
lets you put semicolons inside the body without confusing the parser.
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE refund_order(IN p_order_id INT, OUT p_refund_amount DECIMAL(10,2))
BEGIN
  SELECT total_amount INTO p_refund_amount FROM orders WHERE id = p_order_id;
  UPDATE orders SET status='REFUNDED' WHERE id = p_order_id;
END //
DELIMITER ;
Q363 · IN, OUT and INOUT Parameters
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, AmEx · Topic: Parameters
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain IN, OUT and INOUT parameters with a real example. Which databases support each?
The 30-second answer: IN is the default — caller passes a value, callee reads it. OUT — callee
writes a value, caller reads it after the call. INOUT — both directions. PL/SQL, MySQL and PL/pgSQL
(in procedures since 14) all support the three modes; SQL Server uses OUTPUT keyword instead of 
OUT/ INOUT and a single parameter declared OUTPUT can be read on both sides.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 379 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 380
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the three modes plainly — interviewers test vocabulary first. 2.
Give an example: a settlement procedure that takes the order id as IN and returns the refund amount
as OUT. 3. Mention that returning data via OUT params is older school; returning a result set (a SELECT
inside the procedure) is more modern and ORM-friendly. 4. Be ready for "Why not just RETURN it like a
function?" — procedures may need to return multiple values plus a result set; OUT params let you do
both.
Edge cases to mention: - In SQL Server T-SQL, the caller must include OUTPUT in the EXEC call
too: EXEC dbo.foo @x OUTPUT;. - In Postgres functions (not procedures) before 14, OUT
parameters were essentially a way to define a composite return type. - Java JDBC 
CallableStatement requires you to registerOutParameter before executing — easy to
forget.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "OUT params are faster than returning a result set" — they are different
tools, not a perf shootout. - Do not confuse INOUT with a global variable — it is still scoped to the call.
Common follow-up: "How does a JDBC client read an OUT parameter?" — 
cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.NUMERIC); cs.execute(); BigDecimal x =
cs.getBigDecimal(2);.
-- Postgres procedure with INOUT
CREATE PROCEDURE adjust_balance(INOUT p_balance NUMERIC, p_delta NUMERIC)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  p_balance := p_balance + p_delta;
END $$;
DO $$ DECLARE v_bal NUMERIC := 1000;
BEGIN
  CALL adjust_balance(v_bal, 250);
  RAISE NOTICE 'New balance: %', v_bal;  -- 1250
END $$;
Q364 · Returning a Result Set vs a Scalar Value
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Return Types
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you have a stored procedure return a single scalar versus a full result set? How does
the application read each?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 380 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 381
The 30-second answer: Return a scalar (via RETURN in a function, or via OUT/RETURN code in a proc)
when the caller needs a single computed value — a count, a status, a derived id. Return a result set
when the caller needs rows — a list of orders, a paginated query, a dashboard panel. Result sets are read
with cursors on the client (ResultSet/ SqlDataReader/ pg_cursor); scalars are read directly.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Pose it as an API design question, not just a syntax question. 2.
Scalars are simpler and cache-friendly — ORMs map them cleanly to a single field. 3. Result sets are the
natural shape when the procedure is essentially a SELECT with parameters — common in report and
dashboard scenarios. 4. Mention that some teams prefer to wrap everything in procs (banking, fintech
back-office) for an audit boundary; others prefer plain SELECT calls from the app.
Edge cases to mention: - SQL Server procs returning multiple result sets confuse strict ORMs — you
may need a multi-mapping layer or move to a function/TVF. - Postgres RETURNS TABLE is essentially
"function returns a result set" — it streams rows back, the caller iterates. - Oracle uses 
SYS_REFCURSOR as the canonical way for a procedure to return a result set to a client.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "you cannot return a result set from a stored procedure" — every major
dialect supports it, just differently. - Do not return a giant result set when only a scalar is needed — that
is a wasted round-trip.
Common follow-up: "Show me how Oracle returns a result set from a procedure." — OUT p_cur
SYS_REFCURSOR + OPEN p_cur FOR SELECT ....
-- SQL Server: returns one row
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE dbo.get_order_count
  @customer_id INT, @cnt INT OUTPUT
AS BEGIN
  SET NOCOUNT ON;
  SELECT @cnt = COUNT(*) FROM dbo.orders WHERE customer_id = @customer_id;
END
Q365 · Table-Valued Functions — Inline vs Multi-Statement (SQL Server)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, JP Morgan · Topic: T-SQL TVF
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the difference between an inline table-valued function and a multi-statement table-valued
function in SQL Server. Which performs better and why?
The 30-second answer: An inline TVF is essentially a parameterised view — its body is a single SELECT,
and the optimizer can inline (merge) it into the calling query for accurate cardinality estimates. A multi-
statement TVF declares a return table variable and INSERTs into it, then returns it; the optimizer treats
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 381 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 382
it as a black box with a hard-coded row estimate (1 row, or 100, depending on version), so plans degrade
badly.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the cardinality estimate point — that is the real
performance reason. 2. Inline TVF: RETURNS TABLE AS RETURN (SELECT ...) — no DECLARE,
no BEGIN/END. 3. Multi-statement TVF: RETURNS @t TABLE(...) AS BEGIN INSERT INTO
@t ... RETURN END. 4. Recommend the inline form whenever the logic fits a single SELECT —
almost always faster.
Edge cases to mention: - SQL Server 2017 introduced interleaved execution that helps multi-statement
TVF estimates somewhat, but it does not fully close the gap. - 2019's scalar-UDF inlining is a separate
feature from TVF inlining — do not conflate them. - Inline TVFs cannot have control flow (IF/CASE outside
SELECT, loops) — if you need that, you are stuck with multi-statement or a refactor.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "both perform the same" — multi-statement TVFs are a well-known
performance trap. - Do not use a multi-statement TVF when an inline one would do — that is a code-
smell.
Common follow-up: "What is the row estimate for a multi-statement TVF in older SQL Server versions?"
— 1 row before 2014; 100 rows from 2014 onwards (cardinality estimator change).
-- Inline TVF — parameterised view
CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.orders_by_customer(@cust_id INT)
RETURNS TABLE AS RETURN (
  SELECT id, total_amount, created_at FROM dbo.orders WHERE customer_id = @cust_id
);
-- Usage
SELECT * FROM dbo.orders_by_customer(101);
Q366 · Set-Returning Functions in Postgres — RETURNS TABLE / SETOF
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho · Topic: PL/pgSQL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Write a Postgres function that returns a list of orders for a given customer. What is the difference
between RETURNS SETOF and RETURNS TABLE?
The 30-second answer: RETURNS SETOF orders returns a set of rows of the existing orders
table type. RETURNS TABLE (id BIGINT, amount NUMERIC, ...) defines an ad-hoc row type
inline. Functionally equivalent; the TABLE form is preferred when you want to project specific columns or
compose them from multiple tables.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 382 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 383
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show both signatures side by side — interviewers want to see you
have used both. 2. Use RETURN QUERY inside the body to stream rows back from a SELECT. 3.
Mention that the function is then callable like a table: SELECT * FROM
orders_for_customer(101); — that is the SRF idiom. 4. Note that LANGUAGE sql is often a
better choice than LANGUAGE plpgsql for these (covered next).
Edge cases to mention: - RETURN QUERY does not actually return at that point — execution
continues; RETURN (no QUERY) ends the function. - If you forget RETURN QUERY and just write a
SELECT, the rows are discarded silently. - The output column names from RETURNS TABLE(...) are
visible inside the function body as if they were local variables — collisions cause bugs.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim Postgres has TVFs in the SQL Server sense — Postgres calls them
SRFs (set-returning functions), and the semantics are slightly different. - Do not return a giant result set
when a streaming cursor would be better.
Common follow-up: "What if the function needs to compute totals, not just return rows?" — Use 
RETURN QUERY SELECT ..., SUM(...) OVER (...) FROM ... — window functions inside the
SRF.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION orders_for_customer(p_cust_id BIGINT)
RETURNS TABLE (id BIGINT, amount NUMERIC, status TEXT)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY
  SELECT o.id, o.total_amount, o.status
  FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = p_cust_id
  ORDER BY o.created_at DESC;
END $$;
SELECT * FROM orders_for_customer(101);
Q367 · LANGUAGE sql vs LANGUAGE plpgsql in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Goldman · Topic: PL/pgSQL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In Postgres, when would you use LANGUAGE sql and when would you use LANGUAGE
plpgsql? Is there a performance difference?
The 30-second answer: Use LANGUAGE sql when the function body is a single SQL expression or
query — it is simpler, the planner can inline it into the calling query, and there is no PL/pgSQL interpreter
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 383 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 384
overhead. Use LANGUAGE plpgsql when you need procedural control flow — variables, IF, LOOP,
EXCEPTION handlers. SQL functions are typically faster for simple cases because of inlining.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it as "SQL = declarative single expression, PL/pgSQL =
procedural block with control flow." 2. Talk about inlining: a simple LANGUAGE sql function used in a
WHERE clause can be replaced by its body during planning, so the planner can use indexes correctly.
PL/pgSQL functions are usually treated as opaque. 3. Mention that PL/pgSQL has higher first-call
overhead because it parses and plans the body lazily and caches it per session. 4. Be ready for: "If they
are otherwise equivalent, default to SQL" — that is the conventional wisdom.
Edge cases to mention: - LANGUAGE sql cannot use RAISE, IF/THEN, or EXCEPTION — once
you need any of those, you must move to PL/pgSQL. - Inlining requires the function to be marked
appropriately (volatility, strictness) — see the next question. - Postgres 14+ supports SQL-standard 
BEGIN ATOMIC for SQL functions, which improves dependency tracking — older versions used the
string-body form.
What NOT to say: - Do not default to PL/pgSQL for everything — you lose inlining and add overhead. -
Do not claim SQL functions are always faster — for complex bodies with lots of control flow, PL/pgSQL
is the only option.
Common follow-up: "Can a SQL function call another function?" — Yes, just like any SELECT can. And
the inner one can also be inlined if it qualifies.
-- SQL function — inlinable
CREATE FUNCTION gst_amount(amount NUMERIC) RETURNS NUMERIC
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT amount * 0.18 $$;
-- PL/pgSQL function — has control flow
CREATE FUNCTION grade_score(s INT) RETURNS TEXT
LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$
BEGIN
  IF s >= 90 THEN RETURN 'A';
  ELSIF s >= 75 THEN RETURN 'B';
  ELSE RETURN 'C';
  END IF;
END $$;
Q368 · IMMUTABLE, STABLE, VOLATILE — Postgres Function Volatility Tags
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: PL/pgSQL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 384 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 385
What do IMMUTABLE, STABLE and VOLATILE mean on a Postgres function? Why does it matter
for indexing?
The 30-second answer: IMMUTABLE means the function always returns the same output for the same
input and reads no database state — the planner can evaluate it once, cache results, and use it in
expression indexes. STABLE means it returns the same value within a single statement but may
depend on database state; usable in indexes for the duration of a scan. VOLATILE (default) means
anything goes — the planner cannot optimise around it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define each tag clearly — order matters: IMMUTABLE → STABLE →
VOLATILE, weakest constraints last. 2. Give examples: lower(text) is IMMUTABLE; now() is
STABLE; random() is VOLATILE. 3. The killer use case: only IMMUTABLE functions can appear in
expression indexes (CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))). 4. Mention that mis-tagging a
function as IMMUTABLE when it actually reads tables causes silent wrong results when indexed.
Edge cases to mention: - A function marked IMMUTABLE that does a SELECT from a table is a foot-
gun: the planner may use cached results that no longer reflect the table. - STABLE is enough for
partial-index predicates and for functions used in WHERE that the planner needs to push down. -
Default is VOLATILE — be explicit; reviewers notice.
What NOT to say: - Do not mark a function IMMUTABLE just to "make it faster" — correctness first. - Do
not confuse the SQL standard DETERMINISTIC (MySQL) with Postgres IMMUTABLE — the spirit is
similar but the rules differ.
Common follow-up: "What happens if you index on a STABLE function?" — Postgres refuses;
expression indexes require IMMUTABLE.
-- IMMUTABLE — eligible for expression indexes
CREATE FUNCTION normalise_email(t TEXT) RETURNS TEXT
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT lower(trim(t)) $$;
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_norm ON users (normalise_email(email));
Q369 · Functions in WHERE Clause — Index Implications
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Razorpay, Cred · Topic: Indexes
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 385 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 386
Why does wrapping a column in a function inside a WHERE clause often kill the index? What can
you do about it?
The 30-second answer: The planner needs to compare the indexed column directly. Wrapping it in a
function (WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com') means the index on email no longer matches
the predicate. The fix is to create a matching expression index (CREATE INDEX ON t
(lower(email))) or rewrite the query so the column is bare on the left side.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule: "function on column = no index seek." 2. Give the
classic example — WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-05-26' — and the fix 
WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-26' AND created_at < '2026-05-27'. 3. The other fix:
expression index on date_trunc('day', created_at). The function must be IMMUTABLE (or at
least STABLE for some uses). 4. Mention SARGable predicates as the underlying concept — even if the
interviewer does not use the term, you should.
Edge cases to mention: - Implicit conversion is the same trap: WHERE numeric_col = '123' may
cast every row. - SQL Server is stricter than Postgres about needing the type to match exactly to use an
index. - In Oracle, function-based indexes are the equivalent — same idea, same syntax around 
CREATE INDEX ... ON t (func(col)).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the index just is not used, no big deal" — full table scans on a 10-crore-
row table are a big deal. - Do not claim the database "decides" not to use it for fun — the predicate
genuinely is not seekable.
Common follow-up: "How do you spot this in an EXPLAIN plan?" — Look for Seq Scan (Postgres) or
Table Scan / Index Scan with filter (SQL Server) on the table where you expected an 
Index Seek.
-- Bad: function on column kills the index
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com';
-- Fix A: expression index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email));
-- Fix B: store normalised value at write time and index it
Q370 · Function Inlining — Postgres SQL and SQL Server Scalar UDF (2019+)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, JP Morgan · Topic: Optimization
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 386 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 387
Explain function inlining in Postgres and the scalar UDF inlining work in SQL Server 2019. Why
does it matter?
The 30-second answer: Inlining means the planner replaces a function call with its body inside the
calling query, so it can be optimised as one unit — accurate cardinality, index use, parallelism. Postgres
has done this for simple LANGUAGE sql functions for years (a feature called "SQL function inlining").
SQL Server 2019 introduced "Scalar UDF Inlining" (project Froid) that does the same for scalar T-SQL
UDFs that were historically a perf disaster.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the perf story — un-inlined scalar UDFs forced row-by-row
execution in SQL Server and crippled queries. 2. Postgres inlining conditions: LANGUAGE sql, single
SELECT body, no DML, volatility compatible with the call site. 3. SQL Server 2019 conditions: scalar
UDF, no time-dependent intrinsic, no aggregate, set compatibility level 150+. 4. Mention that inlining can
be disabled per-query (OPTION (USE HINT('DISABLE_TSQL_SCALAR_UDF_INLINING'))) if a
plan regresses.
Edge cases to mention: - SQL Server 2022 expanded the conditions further — fewer cases blocked. -
Postgres SQL inlining is invisible in EXPLAIN: the body is folded in before planning, so the function
name disappears. - Disabling inlining via OPTION (RECOMPILE) or hints is a real release-time tool
when plans regress on upgrade.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "stored procedures are inlined" — they are not. Only functions, and only
under specific conditions. - Do not assume your perf problem is solved by upgrading SQL Server — test
the specific function.
Common follow-up: "What did Microsoft call the SQL Server 2019 inlining project?" — Project Froid.
Bonus points for naming it.
-- SQL Server 2019+: scalar UDF that may be inlined
CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.gst_amount(@amount DECIMAL(10,2))
RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)
WITH INLINE = ON  -- explicit opt-in/out
AS BEGIN RETURN @amount * 0.18 END
Q371 · Error Handling — TRY/CATCH, EXCEPTION, DECLARE HANDLER
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Error Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 387 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 388
Walk me through error handling inside a stored procedure in SQL Server, Postgres and MySQL.
What is the equivalent in each?
The 30-second answer: SQL Server uses BEGIN TRY ... END TRY BEGIN CATCH ... END
CATCH with ERROR_MESSAGE()/ ERROR_NUMBER() inside the CATCH. Postgres uses BEGIN ...
EXCEPTION WHEN <condition> THEN ... END inside a PL/pgSQL block. MySQL uses 
DECLARE ... HANDLER FOR <condition> <statement> declared at the top of the block.
Oracle is similar to Postgres with EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN ....
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the three syntaxes side by side — that is the recall test. 2.
Mention RAISERROR/ THROW (SQL Server), RAISE EXCEPTION (Postgres), SIGNAL SQLSTATE
(MySQL) for raising your own errors. 3. Always combine TRY/CATCH with transaction control — log the
error, then ROLLBACK and rethrow. 4. Be ready for "What happens if you do not handle an error?" — the
transaction state in SQL Server is determined by XACT_ABORT; in Postgres the whole transaction
aborts and subsequent commands fail until ROLLBACK.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres, an unhandled exception inside a PL/pgSQL block aborts only the
current sub-transaction (savepoint); the outer transaction can be salvaged with EXCEPTION WHEN
OTHERS. - SQL Server's TRY/CATCH does not catch compile-time errors — only runtime. - MySQL
handlers come in CONTINUE, EXIT and UNDO flavours; most production code uses EXIT.
What NOT to say: - Do not swallow errors with an empty CATCH/EXCEPTION block — that hides bugs.
- Do not use RAISERROR (with E) in new SQL Server code — use THROW.
Common follow-up: "In Postgres, what is the difference between RAISE NOTICE and RAISE
EXCEPTION?" — NOTICE writes a message and continues; EXCEPTION aborts the block and
propagates.
-- SQL Server
BEGIN TRY
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
  THROW;
END CATCH;
-- Postgres
BEGIN
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
EXCEPTION WHEN check_violation THEN
  RAISE NOTICE 'check failed: %', SQLERRM;
  ROLLBACK;
END;

Q372 · Transaction Management Inside Procedures
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo · Topic:
Transactions
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can a stored procedure manage its own transactions? What about a function?
The 30-second answer: Procedures can manage transactions in T-SQL (BEGIN TRAN/COMMIT/
ROLLBACK), in PL/SQL (COMMIT/ ROLLBACK directly), in MySQL (with the usual caveats), and in
Postgres 11+ procedures. Functions in most dialects cannot — they run inside the caller's transaction
and cannot issue COMMIT/ROLLBACK. That is the single biggest reason Postgres added procedures in
version 11.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the rule: procedures yes, functions usually no. 2. Discuss
the autonomous transaction pattern — when a sub-operation must commit even if the caller rolls back.
Oracle has PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION; Postgres uses dblink or background workers;
SQL Server uses linked-server tricks. None are pretty. 3. Mention SAVEPOINTs — most dialects support
them for nested partial rollback within a single transaction. 4. Be ready for "How do you implement an
audit log that survives rollback?" — separate connection, autonomous transaction, or queue-based
pattern.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres procedures, you can only COMMIT if there is no open cursor and
no transaction-bound state — otherwise you get an error. - SQL Server has @@TRANCOUNT — nested 
BEGIN TRAN increments, but only the outermost COMMIT actually commits. - MySQL DDL inside a
procedure implicitly commits — a common surprise.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume BEGIN TRAN in a procedure starts a fresh transaction if one
already exists — it nests. - Do not assume ROLLBACK inside a procedure rolls back only the
procedure's work — it rolls back to the outermost savepoint by default.
Common follow-up: "What is @@TRANCOUNT and why do batch jobs check it before COMMIT?" —
Defensive coding: do not COMMIT if you are nested inside a larger caller transaction.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 389 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 390
-- Postgres 11+ procedure with explicit transaction control
CREATE PROCEDURE settle_batch(p_run_date DATE)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE r RECORD;
BEGIN
  FOR r IN SELECT id FROM payouts WHERE run_date = p_run_date AND status = 'PENDING'
  LOOP
    UPDATE payouts SET status='SETTLED' WHERE id = r.id;
    IF mod(r.id, 1000) = 0 THEN COMMIT; END IF;
  END LOOP;
  COMMIT;
END $$;
Q373 · Cursors — How, When, Why Mostly Avoid
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, AmEx, JP Morgan · Topic: Cursors
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain cursors. When would you use one and why are they generally discouraged?
The 30-second answer: A cursor lets you walk through a result set row by row inside a stored
procedure — DECLARE cur CURSOR FOR ..., OPEN, FETCH NEXT, CLOSE, DEALLOCATE.
They are discouraged because they force row-at-a-time processing which is dramatically slower than a
single set-based UPDATE or INSERT…SELECT. Use them only when the logic genuinely cannot be
expressed as a single statement — typically when each row depends on a side effect of the previous
one.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the canonical SQL Server cursor: DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH
NEXT INTO, WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0. 2. The killer point: a single UPDATE ... FROM is usually
10-100x faster than a cursor doing the same work. 3. Legitimate cursor uses: complex per-row side
effects (calling external systems, generating non-deterministic ids, audit trails with branching), or batched
processing where you commit every N rows. 4. Mention that Postgres has FOR ... IN ... LOOP
which is essentially a hidden cursor — same performance trade-off applies.
Edge cases to mention: - SQL Server cursors have many options (FORWARD_ONLY, STATIC, 
DYNAMIC, LOCAL/ GLOBAL) — LOCAL FAST_FORWARD is the cheapest. - Forgetting CLOSE
and DEALLOCATE leaks resources for the session. - Postgres REFCURSOR is a different thing — it is
a way to pass a query handle back to a client, not a row-walker.
What NOT to say: - Do not write a cursor when a single set-based statement does the job — that is the
most common interview red flag. - Do not claim cursors are "always bad" — there are real cases.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 390 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 391
Common follow-up: "Show me how you would rewrite this cursor as a single UPDATE." — Practice this;
it is a 2-minute litmus test for whether you actually think in sets.
-- SQL Server cursor (avoid when set-based works)
DECLARE @id INT, @amt DECIMAL(10,2);
DECLARE cur CURSOR LOCAL FAST_FORWARD FOR
  SELECT id, amount FROM payouts WHERE status='PENDING';
OPEN cur;
FETCH NEXT FROM cur INTO @id, @amt;
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN
  EXEC dbo.notify_external_system @id, @amt;  -- legitimate side effect
  FETCH NEXT FROM cur INTO @id, @amt;
END
CLOSE cur; DEALLOCATE cur;
Q374 · Trigger Basics — BEFORE vs AFTER, ROW vs STATEMENT
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Accenture, Wells Fargo · Topic: Triggers
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain BEFORE vs AFTER triggers, and FOR EACH ROW vs FOR EACH STATEMENT triggers.
The 30-second answer: A BEFORE trigger fires before the row is written and can modify the row being
inserted/updated (NEW.col := ...). An AFTER trigger fires after the write and is used for side
effects (audit, derived inserts). FOR EACH ROW fires once per affected row and exposes NEW/ OLD; 
FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once per statement regardless of row count and is cheaper for bulk
operations.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the four-quadrant model: {BEFORE, AFTER} × {ROW,
STATEMENT}. 2. BEFORE ROW is where you mutate NEW to enforce derived columns. AFTER ROW is
where you log to an audit table. 3. STATEMENT triggers are best when you only need to react to
"something changed" rather than per-row data — e.g., refresh a materialised view, invalidate a cache. 4.
Note that SQL Server does not have BEFORE/AFTER in the standard sense — it has INSTEAD OF and
AFTER (FOR/AFTER). Postgres and Oracle have BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres AFTER ... STATEMENT triggers can use transition tables
( REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS ...) to see the full delta in one place — efficient for bulk audit. -
BEFORE ROW triggers run for every row even on bulk inserts — expensive on large COPY/INSERT-
SELECT. - Order of multiple triggers on the same table is alphabetical by name in Postgres — easy to
forget.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 391 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 392
What NOT to say: - Do not say "BEFORE triggers prevent inserts" without nuance — they prevent only
by raising an exception or returning NULL. - Do not assume statement-level triggers do not see the data
— they can, via transition tables.
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between OLD and NEW in a trigger?" — OLD is the row
before the change (NULL on INSERT); NEW is after (NULL on DELETE).
-- Postgres: BEFORE ROW trigger that auto-fills a derived column
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION set_full_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.full_name := NEW.first_name || ' ' || NEW.last_name;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER trg_set_full_name
BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON users
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_full_name();
Q375 · Trigger Use Cases — Audit Logs, Derived Columns, Validation
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro, Wells Fargo · Topic: Triggers
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Give me three legitimate, defensible use cases for triggers.
The 30-second answer: Audit logs — capture who changed what and when into a history table; derived
columns — keep a denormalised field in sync (full name from first/last, search vectors, computed totals);
validation — enforce business invariants that cannot be expressed as a CHECK constraint or foreign key
alone.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Name the three and give an example for each. 2. Audit: AFTER
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE writing to customers_audit(operation, old_row, new_row,
changed_by, changed_at). Use current_user/ SESSION_USER to capture the actor. 3.
Derived: BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE setting NEW.total = NEW.qty * NEW.price — but flag the
alternative, GENERATED columns, in the next question. 4. Validation: BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE that
raises an exception if a cross-table invariant is violated (e.g., "a discount may not exceed the customer's
tier max").
Edge cases to mention: - For audit, an AFTER STATEMENT trigger with transition tables is the
modern, efficient pattern. - For derived columns, prefer generated/computed columns where the DB
supports them — fewer moving parts. - For validation, prefer constraints (CHECK, FK, UNIQUE) where
possible; triggers only when the rule spans tables.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 392 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 393
What NOT to say: - Do not list "complex business logic" as a use case — that is exactly the anti-pattern,
covered next. - Do not say "anything you can do in the app" — most teams want app logic in the app.
Common follow-up: "How do you capture the application user, not just the DB user, for audit?" — Pass
an app-set session variable (SET LOCAL app.user_id = '12345') and read it inside the trigger.
-- Postgres audit trigger
CREATE TABLE customers_audit (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, op TEXT, old_row JSONB, new_row JSONB,
  changed_by TEXT DEFAULT current_user, changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION audit_customers() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO customers_audit(op, old_row, new_row)
  VALUES (TG_OP, to_jsonb(OLD), to_jsonb(NEW));
  RETURN NULL;
END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER trg_customers_audit
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON customers
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_customers();
Q376 · Trigger Anti-Patterns — Business Logic and Cascading Triggers
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Triggers
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What are the classic anti-patterns with triggers? Why do senior engineers usually want them
removed?
The 30-second answer: Business logic in triggers — it becomes invisible side effects that the
application is unaware of, making debugging nightmarish. Cascading triggers — a trigger fires another
trigger which fires another, forming chains nobody can trace. Performance traps — per-row triggers on
bulk operations multiply cost. Hidden coupling — schema changes break trigger code in surprising ways.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the observability point: a developer reads the app code,
sees an INSERT, and has no idea that three triggers, two audit inserts and a derived update also
happened. 2. Cascading example: INSERT on orders fires a trigger that updates 
customer_summary, which fires a trigger that recomputes analytics_daily. Now an EXPLAIN
of a simple INSERT is incomprehensible. 3. Performance: a 1-lakh-row bulk INSERT with a row trigger
that does even a single index lookup becomes a multi-minute job. 4. The cultural reason: triggers cannot
be code-reviewed, traced, or version-controlled with the application code easily — they drift.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 393 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 394
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres triggers can be RECURSIVE — easy to write an infinite loop
accidentally if the trigger updates the same table. - SQL Server has a server-level setting nested
triggers and recursive triggers — defaults differ. - Some teams adopt a rule: triggers may
only write to audit tables, nothing else. Worth stating in interview.
What NOT to say: - Do not defend complex business triggers as "encapsulation" — that is folklore from
the 1990s. - Do not say "we have always done it this way" — interviewers want reflection, not defence.
Common follow-up: "Tell me about a bug you debugged where a trigger was the root cause." — Have a
real story or a believable hypothetical: e.g., a row count was higher than expected because an audit
trigger double-inserted.
-- Anti-pattern: business logic in a trigger
CREATE TRIGGER trg_send_email AFTER INSERT ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION send_order_confirmation();  -- DON'T
-- Better: write to an outbox table, app processes it
Q377 · Trigger Performance Impact
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Razorpay, Goldman · Topic: Triggers
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do triggers affect performance? How would you measure their cost?
The 30-second answer: Row-level triggers add per-row CPU and any I/O the trigger body does — on
bulk inserts this multiplies the cost dramatically. Statement-level triggers add a fixed overhead per
statement, regardless of row count, so they are cheaper. Measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE in Postgres
(trigger times appear at the bottom of the plan) or with SET STATISTICS TIME ON in SQL Server.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the row-vs-statement cost model. 2. EXPLAIN ANALYZE in
Postgres shows a "Trigger ..." line per trigger with time= and calls= — read that. 3. SQL Server's
actual execution plan shows trigger execution as a sub-plan; statistics time gives the per-trigger CPU. 4.
The other hidden cost: triggers prevent some bulk operations from being minimally logged (SQL Server)
and from using COPY fast-path (Postgres in some cases).
Edge cases to mention: - A trigger that does its own SELECT can lock-escalate or hold locks longer
than expected. - Triggers can prevent partition-wise operations and parallel plans in some optimisers. -
In Postgres, FOR EACH STATEMENT with transition tables is the preferred pattern for audit on bulk
inserts.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 394 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 395
What NOT to say: - Do not say "triggers are free" — they never are. - Do not optimise prematurely —
measure before you remove or rewrite.
Common follow-up: "How would you migrate from a per-row audit trigger to a statement-level one
without losing data?" — Use transition tables (Postgres 10+, SQL Server) — the statement trigger sees
the full delta.
-- Postgres: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows trigger cost
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
INSERT INTO orders(customer_id, total_amount) VALUES (1, 100);
-- Trigger trg_set_full_name: time=0.123 calls=1
Q378 · INSTEAD OF Triggers — When You Need Them
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo · Topic: Triggers
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is an INSTEAD OF trigger? When would you use one?
The 30-second answer: An INSTEAD OF trigger replaces the original DML — when the trigger fires,
the original INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE does not happen automatically; the trigger body decides what to
do. The killer use case is making views updatable when they otherwise would not be (joins, aggregates,
computed columns) — the trigger translates the view-level DML into the appropriate base-table writes.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define INSTEAD OF clearly — it is a replacement, not an addition. 2.
Use case 1: updatable views. The view has a JOIN, so a direct UPDATE is ambiguous. INSTEAD OF
UPDATE picks which base table(s) to update. 3. Use case 2: routing inserts to a partition or sharded child
table. 4. Postgres and SQL Server both support INSTEAD OF; MySQL has very limited support (only on
views with restrictions).
Edge cases to mention: - The trigger body must do the actual work — easy to forget and accidentally
make a no-op. - INSTEAD OF triggers fire even for bulk DML, but they can be set as STATEMENT-level in
some dialects to amortise cost. - Conflicting INSTEAD OF and AFTER triggers can create non-obvious
ordering bugs.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse INSTEAD OF with BEFORE — BEFORE happens, then the DML
happens; INSTEAD OF replaces the DML. - Do not put INSTEAD OF triggers on base tables unless you
really mean it — that hides the DML semantics.
Common follow-up: "What is an alternative to INSTEAD OF for updatable views in Postgres?" — Simple
views (single table, no aggregates) are updatable automatically; the updatable_views extension and
PostgreSQL 9.3+ auto-updatable views cover many cases.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 395 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 396
-- Postgres: INSTEAD OF trigger on a view
CREATE VIEW order_summary AS
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer_name, o.total_amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION update_order_total() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE orders SET total_amount = NEW.total_amount WHERE id = NEW.id;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER trg_view_update INSTEAD OF UPDATE ON order_summary
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION update_order_total();
Q379 · Disabling Triggers Temporarily
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Triggers
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You are running a one-off bulk data load. The triggers on the target table would multiply the cost.
How do you disable them temporarily and safely?
The 30-second answer: Postgres: ALTER TABLE t DISABLE TRIGGER trg_name (or ALL);
SQL Server: DISABLE TRIGGER trg_name ON t; MySQL has no per-trigger disable — you DROP
and re-CREATE. Always wrap in a transaction or maintenance window, re-enable in the same script, and
verify post-load that the derived data is consistent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the syntax per dialect. 2. Warn about the risk: while triggers are
disabled, audit logs and derived columns will be wrong; plan a back-fill. 3. The defensive pattern: disable
→ load → re-enable → run a back-fill SELECT-INTO to populate audit and derived columns. 4. Note
Postgres has DISABLE TRIGGER USER (skip user-defined triggers but keep system triggers like FK)
— useful nuance.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres, DISABLE TRIGGER ALL also disables internal triggers used
by foreign keys — usually a bad idea. Use DISABLE TRIGGER USER instead. - SQL Server's 
DISABLE TRIGGER ... ON ALL SERVER is a server-level scope — make sure you scope to a
single table. - After re-enabling, the trigger does not fire retroactively — affected rows during the disable
window are skipped permanently.
What NOT to say: - Do not disable FK enforcement triggers in production without a maintenance
window — referential integrity gaps are painful to fix. - Do not forget to re-enable. Add it to a FINALLY
style block (BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE
TRIGGER ...).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 396 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 397
Common follow-up: "Is there a way to skip a trigger only for a single statement?" — Postgres has 
session_replication_role = 'replica' for the session, which skips most user triggers. Use
with extreme care.
-- Postgres
ALTER TABLE orders DISABLE TRIGGER trg_audit;
-- bulk load happens here
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE TRIGGER trg_audit;
INSERT INTO orders_audit(op, new_row) SELECT 'INSERT', to_jsonb(o) FROM orders o WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 hour';
Q380 · Sequence vs SERIAL vs IDENTITY — Generating IDs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Razorpay, Cred · Topic: ID Generation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between a sequence, SERIAL and IDENTITY? Which is the modern
preferred choice?
The 30-second answer: A SEQUENCE is a standalone database object that hands out monotonically
increasing numbers — nextval('seq'). SERIAL is a Postgres legacy shortcut that creates a
sequence and wires it as the default on a column. IDENTITY is the SQL-standard form, supported by
Postgres 10+, SQL Server (always), and Oracle 12c+. Modern preference: GENERATED ALWAYS AS
IDENTITY — explicit, portable, and free of the ownership/permissions quirks of SERIAL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define each: sequence (object), SERIAL (Postgres macro), IDENTITY
(standard column property). 2. Show the syntax: id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
PRIMARY KEY vs id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY. 3. Mention the quirks of SERIAL — the underlying
sequence is owned by the column but inserts can overflow if the app manually inserts an id (gaps in the
sequence). 4. Note MySQL uses AUTO_INCREMENT which is column-bound; it is similar in spirit to
IDENTITY.
Edge cases to mention: - Sequences are not transactional — nextval increments even if the
transaction rolls back, so you can have gaps. This is intentional for concurrency. - GENERATED ALWAYS
AS IDENTITY rejects manual inserts; GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY allows them. - SQL
Server IDENTITY_INSERT ON lets you manually insert into an IDENTITY column for one statement.
What NOT to say: - Do not promise "gapless ids" from any of these — sequences and identities all have
gaps under load. - Do not say SERIAL is deprecated — it still works in Postgres; it is just not
recommended in new code.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 397 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 398
Common follow-up: "How would you guarantee gapless invoice numbers?" — You cannot with a
sequence; use a separate counter table with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and accept the lock
contention as the cost.
-- Modern Postgres preferred form
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  amount NUMERIC NOT NULL
);
-- SQL Server
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  amount DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
);
Q381 · AFTER INSERT Trigger for Outbox Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Topic: Triggers
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through implementing the transactional outbox pattern using an AFTER INSERT trigger.
Why is this safer than the application publishing directly to Kafka?
The 30-second answer: On every INSERT into the business table, an AFTER INSERT trigger writes a
row into an outbox table inside the same transaction. A separate poller process (or Debezium-style
CDC) reads outbox and publishes to Kafka. Because the business write and the outbox write share
one transaction, the message is published if and only if the business state changed — no dual-write
inconsistency.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the problem: dual-write — write to DB then publish to Kafka
— can leave one side committed and the other not. 2. Show the trigger that inserts a JSON payload into 
outbox(id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, payload, status, created_at). 3. The
poller selects WHERE status='PENDING' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes, marks 'SENT'. 4.
Mention Debezium / CDC as an alternative: read the transaction log directly, no outbox table needed —
but more infrastructure.
Edge cases to mention: - Outbox can grow large — archive or partition it. - SKIP LOCKED is critical to
allow multiple poller workers without contention (Postgres 9.5+, MySQL 8+, SQL Server with
READPAST). - Ordering: if you care about order per aggregate, the poller must group by aggregate_id
and process sequentially.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 398 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 399
What NOT to say: - Do not claim Kafka transactions solve this — Kafka transactions are between Kafka
topics, not between Kafka and a database. - Do not put the Kafka publish inside the trigger — that
breaks the transactional boundary and re-introduces dual-write.
Common follow-up: "What is Change Data Capture and how does it compare to the outbox table?" —
CDC reads the WAL/redo log directly (Debezium), so no trigger needed; less app-side code but more
infrastructure to run.
-- Postgres outbox trigger
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_type TEXT, aggregate_id BIGINT,
  payload JSONB, status TEXT DEFAULT 'PENDING',
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION outbox_order_created() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO outbox(aggregate_type, aggregate_id, payload)
  VALUES ('order', NEW.id, jsonb_build_object('event','order.created','order_id',NEW.id,'amount',NEW.total_amount));
  RETURN NULL;
END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER trg_outbox_order AFTER INSERT ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION outbox_order_created();
Q382 · Generated/Computed Columns — Alternative to Triggers
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Meesho · Topic: Schema
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When can you use generated columns instead of a trigger to maintain a derived field?
The 30-second answer: Whenever the derived value is a deterministic expression of other columns in
the same row, prefer a generated column — GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * price) STORED.
The DB maintains it, you cannot accidentally write to it, and the optimiser knows it is deterministic.
Triggers should only be used when the derived value depends on other tables or on non-row-local state.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the rule: same-row deterministic → generated column;
cross-row or cross-table → trigger. 2. Show Postgres syntax: GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...)
STORED. MySQL has STORED and VIRTUAL. SQL Server has AS (expr) PERSISTED. 3.
Generated columns can be indexed (STORED) — that is the killer feature for search and sort scenarios.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 399 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 400
4. Note Postgres only supports STORED, not VIRTUAL — important when comparing with MySQL
features.
Edge cases to mention: - The generation expression must be IMMUTABLE in Postgres — you cannot
reference now() or another table. - Adding a STORED generated column rewrites the whole table —
expensive on large tables. - MySQL VIRTUAL generated columns are computed on read — index them
with a functional index if needed.
What NOT to say: - Do not use a trigger to maintain full_name = first || ' ' || last when
a generated column does it cleaner. - Do not assume generated columns work across joins — they do
not; same-row only.
Common follow-up: "How would you store a tsvector for full-text search?" — tsv tsvector
GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || body)) STORED, then
GIN index on tsv.
CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  qty INT, unit_price NUMERIC(10,2),
  line_total NUMERIC(12,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * unit_price) STORED
);
Q383 · Security — SECURITY DEFINER vs SECURITY INVOKER
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: Security
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the difference between SECURITY DEFINER and SECURITY INVOKER on a stored
procedure or function? What are the security risks?
The 30-second answer: SECURITY INVOKER (default) runs the body with the caller's privileges —
they need direct grants on every object touched. SECURITY DEFINER runs it with the privileges of the
function owner — useful when you want to give controlled access to data without granting it directly. The
risk is privilege escalation: a poorly written SECURITY DEFINER function with dynamic SQL is an SQL-
injection-into-superuser vector.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define both with examples. 2. The legit pattern: a function owned by 
app_admin that allows app_user to update one specific row in a sensitive table — the user has no
direct grant. 3. The risk: search_path attacks in Postgres (caller manipulates schema search path so the
function executes a different table). Always SET search_path = pg_catalog, public inside
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 400 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 401
DEFINER functions. 4. Mention SQL Server's EXECUTE AS OWNER / EXECUTE AS USER clauses —
same concept.
Edge cases to mention: - Dynamic SQL inside DEFINER functions is the classic exploit —
concatenated user input runs with elevated privileges. - Postgres has SECURITY DEFINER ... SET
search_path = ... to lock the path at function definition time. - Granting EXECUTE on a DEFINER
function silently grants access to the underlying tables — audit carefully.
What NOT to say: - Do not default to SECURITY DEFINER — that is a privilege-escalation magnet. - Do
not use dynamic SQL in DEFINER functions without parameterising every input.
Common follow-up: "What is the search_path attack in Postgres?" — Attacker creates a table in their
own schema with the same name, sets search_path, and the DEFINER function operates on the
attacker's table. Always set search_path explicitly.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION refund_order(p_order_id BIGINT)
RETURNS VOID
LANGUAGE plpgsql
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = pg_catalog, public
AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE orders SET status='REFUNDED' WHERE id = p_order_id;
END $$;
Q384 · Stored Procedure and ORM Interaction
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: ORMs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your Spring Boot or .NET application uses JPA / Hibernate / Entity Framework. How do you call a
stored procedure from it? What goes wrong?
The 30-second answer: JPA has @NamedStoredProcedureQuery and 
EntityManager.createStoredProcedureQuery. Entity Framework Core has FromSqlRaw / 
ExecuteSqlRaw and explicit DbCommand for procs. The friction: ORMs map rows to entities and
procs may return shapes that do not match, may have multiple result sets, may return refcursors (Oracle),
or may need OUT parameter registration. Mapping conventions also differ — JPA column naming, EF's
keyless entities.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the canonical Spring Data / JPA pattern with @Procedure
annotation. 2. Mention the EF Core approach with FromSqlRaw for result-set-returning procs. 3. The
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 401 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 402
pain points: OUT parameter registration, refcursors in Oracle (need OracleTypes.CURSOR), and
Postgres procedures vs functions (procedures need CallableStatement.execute(), not 
executeQuery). 4. Note that many teams adopt the rule: ORMs for CRUD, raw JDBC/Dapper for
procs — fewer surprises.
Edge cases to mention: - Hibernate's named procedure mapping does not support all dialect quirks —
fall back to plain JDBC for edge cases. - Postgres procedures (since 11) cannot be called inside a JDBC 
executeQuery — must use CallableStatement.execute(). - EF Core 7+ has improved
stored procedure support but TVPs (table-valued parameters) still need raw SQL.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim ORMs handle procs transparently — they all have rough edges. - Do
not embed business logic in procs just because the ORM is annoying — fix the integration, not the
architecture.
Common follow-up: "How would you map a refcursor returned by an Oracle proc to a list of entities?" —
Use CallableStatement.registerOutParameter(2, OracleTypes.CURSOR), then 
ResultSet rs = (ResultSet) cs.getObject(2); and walk it manually.
// Spring Data JPA
@Procedure(procedureName = "settle_invoice")
void settleInvoice(@Param("p_invoice_id") Long invoiceId);
// JDBC for trickier cases
try (CallableStatement cs = conn.prepareCall("{ call get_order_count(?, ?) }")) {
  cs.setInt(1, customerId);
  cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.INTEGER);
  cs.execute();
  int count = cs.getInt(2);
}
Q385 · Versioning Stored Procedures — Migration Patterns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Razorpay, Cred · Topic: Migrations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you version stored procedures so the team can deploy changes safely?
The 30-second answer: Keep the proc source in the same repo as the application, in a db/
migrations/ folder, with one timestamped file per change. Use a migration tool — Flyway, Liquibase,
Sqitch, or EF Migrations — that tracks applied versions in a schema_version table. Always use 
CREATE OR REPLACE (Postgres, Oracle) or CREATE OR ALTER (SQL Server 2016+) so re-running
the migration is idempotent.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 402 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 403
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The principle: procs are code; they belong in version control with the
app. 2. Flyway pattern: V001__create_settle_proc.sql, V002__update_settle_proc.sql
— incremental, immutable history. 3. For breaking changes, deploy the new proc under a versioned
name (settle_invoice_v2), switch callers gradually, drop the old one in a follow-up release. 4.
Mention idempotent re-runs: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ... in Postgres, 
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE ... in SQL Server 2016+, DROP IF EXISTS; CREATE for older
versions.
Edge cases to mention: - Long-running deploys: a proc replace acquires a lock; on busy systems
schedule during low traffic. - Some dialects mark dependants invalid on proc replace (Oracle); recompile
them as part of the migration. - Rollback: keep a rollback SQL alongside each forward migration, or rely
on a separate down-migration file (Liquibase).
What NOT to say: - Do not edit procs directly in production via SSMS or pgAdmin — that leaves no
audit trail and breaks reproducibility. - Do not commit procs to a "stored_procedures" repo separate from
the app — drift is guaranteed.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle a proc that has a breaking signature change while old app
pods are still running?" — Side-by-side versions: deploy v2 alongside v1, migrate callers, drop v1 next
release.
-- V015__update_settle_invoice.sql (Flyway)
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE settle_invoice(p_invoice_id BIGINT, p_settled_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now())
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE invoices SET status='SETTLED', settled_at = p_settled_at WHERE id = p_invoice_id;
END $$;
Q386 · Testing Stored Procedures
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Testing
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you write tests for stored procedures? What makes them harder to test than application
code?
The 30-second answer: Three layers: unit tests with a framework like pgTAP (Postgres), tSQLt (SQL
Server), or utPLSQL (Oracle) — these run inside the DB and assert on outputs and side effects.
Integration tests from the app side — spin up a real DB in Docker, run migrations, invoke the proc,
assert. Avoid mocking the DB entirely. The difficulty: procs depend on schema state, are slow to set up
and tear down, and require careful fixture management.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 403 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 404
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show pgTAP / tSQLt as the in-DB option — they let you write 
BEGIN; ... ; ROLLBACK; style tests with proper assertions. 2. From the app: Testcontainers (JVM)
or Docker Compose to spin up a real DB; run migrations against it; call the procs through the same client
the app uses. 3. Fixtures: every test seeds its own data and rolls back at the end; isolated transactions
per test. 4. Talk about CI integration — these tests are slower than pure unit tests, so they typically run
on a separate CI stage.
Edge cases to mention: - Schema drift between dev/test/prod is the biggest practical risk — always
migrate the test DB with the same tool as prod. - Some procs do non-transactional work (DDL, COMMIT
inside body) — those need separate test cleanup logic. - For triggers, test by inserting/updating and
asserting on the side effects (audit rows, derived columns).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "we test in QA manually" — that fails any quality bar above startup-level.
- Do not mock the DB and pretend that covers the proc — you would only be testing your mock.
Common follow-up: "How would you set up a Testcontainers-based integration test for a Postgres
procedure in Java?" — @Testcontainers class, PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new
PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16"), run Flyway against pg.getJdbcUrl(), then
connect via DataSource and call the proc.
-- pgTAP example
BEGIN;
SELECT plan(2);
INSERT INTO invoices(id, amount, status) VALUES (1, 100, 'PENDING');
CALL settle_invoice(1);
SELECT is((SELECT status FROM invoices WHERE id = 1), 'SETTLED', 'invoice is settled');
SELECT isnt((SELECT settled_at FROM invoices WHERE id = 1), NULL, 'settled_at populated');
SELECT * FROM finish();
ROLLBACK;
Chapter 10, Part A — JSON in SQL
JSON columns went from "nice to have" to expected in product company rounds across 2024-2026 —
every Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho, PhonePe and Flipkart panel I've sat in front of now asks at least
one JSON question, and GCC rounds at Walmart Labs, JP Morgan and Target are catching up fast. The
trouble is that JSON is the most divergent area across engines — Postgres has jsonb and SQL/JSON
path, MySQL has its own JSON type with JSON_TABLE, SQL Server has OPENJSON and 
JSON_VALUE, and the SQL:2016 standard added syntax that very few vendors actually implement.
This section covers Postgres jsonb deeply because that's what most Indian product teams run on,
plus MySQL JSON, SQL Server JSON and the standard functions you should call out when the
interviewer asks "is this portable?". Read it once for breadth, then drill the four or five Qs that map to
whatever stack the company you're interviewing at actually uses.

Q387 · JSON vs JSONB in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres has two JSON types — json and jsonb. What's the difference and which one
would you pick for a user_preferences column?
The 30-second answer: json stores the raw text exactly as you sent it; jsonb parses it into a
binary decomposed form. jsonb is slower to insert and slightly larger on disk but much faster to
query, supports GIN indexes, and dedupes keys — pick jsonb for user_preferences and
basically every other production case.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the storage difference: json is just text with a validity
check; jsonb is parsed once and stored as a tree of keys and values. 2. State the consequences: 
jsonb strips whitespace, removes duplicate keys (keeping the last one), and does not preserve key
order — json preserves all three. 3. Push the performance angle: every ->, ->>, @> operator on
json has to re-parse the text; jsonb walks the binary tree directly. Over millions of rows the gap is
enormous. 4. Close with indexing — only jsonb supports GIN indexes and the path-based operators,
which is the reason almost every Indian product team I've seen defaults to jsonb.
Edge cases to mention: - If you need to preserve the exact incoming bytes for audit or signature
verification, json is the right choice — jsonb will reorder keys. - jsonb insert is roughly 5-15%
slower than json because of the parse step; for write-heavy logs people sometimes pick json. - 
jsonb has a soft limit around 268 MB per value but practical performance degrades long before that.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they're basically the same." The query performance gap is one to two
orders of magnitude on indexed lookups. - Do not claim json supports GIN indexes — it does not.
Common follow-up: "If I already have a json column in production, how would you migrate to 
jsonb?" — ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN col TYPE jsonb USING col::jsonb — but
it rewrites the whole table, so do it during a maintenance window or use a shadow column with a backfill.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL,
  preferences JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb
);
Q388 · When to Use a JSON Column vs Separate Relational Schema
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: JSON
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 405 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 406
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A product manager says "let's just dump everything into a JSON column, it's flexible." When is
that the right call and when is it a trap?
The 30-second answer: Use JSON for sparse, schema-light, rarely-queried payloads — feature flags,
user preferences, third-party API responses. Use a relational schema for anything you filter, join, or
aggregate on regularly. The trap is querying inside JSON on the hot path — that's slow and hard to index
well.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the decision rule: how often do you need to filter or join on
the fields inside? If the answer is "every read", use columns; if it's "almost never", use JSON. 2. Give the
canonical good case: user_preferences with notification settings, theme, language — read on
login, almost never queried by content, varies per user. 3. Give the canonical bad case: 
order_status shoved inside a JSON blob — you'll filter on it in every list query, and now every read
pays the JSON parse cost. 4. Mention the middle ground — generated columns from a JSON field,
which gets you JSON storage flexibility plus a real indexed column.
Edge cases to mention: - For high-cardinality nested arrays you read together (an order's line items),
JSON can actually be faster than a separate child table because you avoid the join. - If multiple services
own different slices of the document, JSON conflicts on write — relational columns with explicit
ownership are cleaner. - Analytics teams hate JSON columns because BI tools can rarely shred them —
if data goes to a warehouse, prefer columns.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "always normalise" — that's dogma. Modern teams happily mix. - Do
not say "JSON is always faster because no joins" — querying inside JSON is slow.
Common follow-up: "Show me a hybrid design for an orders table." — Core columns id,
user_id, total, status, created_at; JSON column for metadata (UTM, device, A/B
bucket) that you rarely filter on.
-- Good: hot fields as columns, cold metadata as JSONB
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  total_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL,
  metadata JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
