Q389 · JSON Column Anti-Patterns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Meesho, PhonePe, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through the worst JSON column design you've seen in production and why it was bad.
The 30-second answer: The classic one is putting hot filter fields inside JSON — WHERE
preferences->>'plan' = 'pro' on a hundred-million-row table with no expression index. Every
read parses JSON, every query does a full scan. Fix by either promoting the field to a real column or
adding a generated column with a btree index on it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the most common anti-pattern: storing fields you filter on
inside JSON without an expression or generated-column index — your EXPLAIN plan will show a seq
scan on every query. 2. Anti-pattern two: deeply nested arrays you have to unnest on every read. Each
unnest is per-row work; over time it becomes the slowest query in your system. 3. Anti-pattern three:
schema drift — three services writing different shapes into the same JSON column with no validation, so
reads have to handle five variants. 4. Anti-pattern four: storing very large blobs (images base64-encoded,
full third-party responses) — the column gets TOASTed and every read becomes an out-of-line fetch.
Edge cases to mention: - A small JSON column you only read together with the row is fine even without
indexes — the problem is filtering and aggregating. - If you must filter on a JSON field, expression
indexes (CREATE INDEX ON t ((col->>'field'))) save you, but only for exact matches. -
ORMs often default to JSON for any unstructured field — review migrations before they hit production.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "JSON columns are always bad." They are great for the right use case. -
Do not blame the database; the schema decision is on the developer.
Common follow-up: "How would you migrate a hot field out of JSON without downtime?" — Add a real
column, dual-write for a release, backfill in batches, swap reads, then drop the JSON path.
-- Anti-pattern: hot filter inside JSON with no index
SELECT id FROM users WHERE preferences->>'plan' = 'pro';
-- Plan: Seq Scan on users (cost=0.00..1820000.00 rows=...)
Q390 · Postgres -> vs ->> Operators
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Zerodha · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 407 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 408
What is the difference between the -> and ->> operators in Postgres? Give me a query that
uses both.
The 30-second answer: -> returns a JSON (or JSONB) value — keeps the JSON type. ->> returns
the same field cast to text. You use -> when you want to chain further JSON access, ->> when you
want a string you can filter on or display.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the return-type rule: arrow keeps JSON, double-arrow
gives text — that's the whole distinction. 2. Show a chaining example: preferences-
>'notifications'->>'email' walks two keys with -> and pulls the leaf as text with ->>. 3.
Warn about a common bug — using -> in a WHERE clause and comparing to a string literal returns
false because you're comparing JSON to text. Use ->> for filters. 4. Mention numeric indices: tags-
>0 for the first element of a JSON array, tags->>0 for the same element as text.
Edge cases to mention: - If the key doesn't exist, both operators return SQL NULL — they do not
throw. Helpful for missing fields. - If the value is JSON null, -> returns the JSON null value,
while ->> returns SQL NULL. Subtle but bites you. - #> and #>> are the path versions — 
preferences #>> '{notifications,email}' does the same as the chain above with a single
operator.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they're interchangeable" — they return different types. - Do not write 
WHERE preferences->'plan' = 'pro' — that comparison will silently never match.
Common follow-up: "How would you cast a JSON number to an integer?" — (col-
>>'count')::int — go through text, then cast.
SELECT id,
       preferences -> 'notifications'        AS notif_json,
       preferences ->> 'language'            AS lang_text,
       preferences #>> '{notifications,email}' AS notif_email
FROM users
WHERE preferences ->> 'plan' = 'pro';
Q391 · SQL/JSON Path — @?, @@, jsonb_path_query
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Goldman, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 408 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 409
Postgres 12+ added SQL/JSON path support. Explain jsonb_path_query, @? and @@,
and when you'd reach for them over the -> operators.
The 30-second answer: SQL/JSON path is a mini-language for navigating and filtering JSON in one
expression. jsonb_path_query(col, '$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 1)') returns matching
values, @? tests whether a path expression matches any value, and @@ tests whether a path
predicate evaluates true. Use them when you want to express a multi-step filter — especially inside
nested arrays — that would be ugly with chained -> calls.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start by framing path syntax: $ is the document root, .key
walks objects, [*] walks arrays, ? (@.field > 5) filters. 2. Explain each operator: @? returns
boolean — "does any value match this path?". @@ evaluates a path predicate (one that returns
boolean) and returns its result. jsonb_path_query actually returns the matching JSON values as a
set. 3. Show the canonical use case — finding orders that contain a high-value line item: payload @?
'$.items[*] ? (@.amount > 10000)'. 4. Mention indexing — GIN with the jsonb_path_ops
opclass accelerates @? and @@ significantly.
Edge cases to mention: - Path expressions use a different quoting style than JSON itself — double
quotes inside the path string conflict with SQL; use the standard $.key form for safety. - 
jsonb_path_query returns a set; if you only want the first match, use 
jsonb_path_query_first to avoid scalar-vs-set bugs. - Lax mode (default) silently coerces
missing keys; strict mode raises errors — pick strict when you want loud failures during testing.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim path syntax is "the same as JSONPath you saw on the internet" —
Postgres SQL/JSON path is similar but not identical. - Do not use path query in a tight inner loop without
a GIN index — it can be slower than a flat ->>.
Common follow-up: "How does this compare to MySQL?" — MySQL implements JSON_TABLE and 
JSON_EXTRACT with a JSONPath-like syntax but lacks @? and @@; the path semantics are similar
but not identical.
-- Orders with a line item over Rs 10,000
SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE payload @? '$.items[*] ? (@.amount_paise > 1000000)';
Q392 · jsonb_set and jsonb_insert — Updating JSON
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Meesho, Cred, Razorpay · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 409 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 410
A user updates one notification preference. Write the query to update only that key in the 
preferences JSONB column without overwriting the whole document.
The 30-second answer: Use jsonb_set(preferences, '{notifications,email}',
'"false"'::jsonb, true) — the path is an array of keys, the new value must be JSONB, and the
fourth argument true creates the key if it does not exist.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start by warning what people get wrong: a naive UPDATE users
SET preferences = '{...}'::jsonb blows away every other field; partial update is mandatory. 2.
Show jsonb_set signature: target, path array, new value (as jsonb), create-if-missing flag. 3.
Differentiate jsonb_insert — it inserts at a position without overwriting; useful for adding into
arrays. jsonb_set overwrites. 4. Mention concurrency — even with jsonb_set, two simultaneous
updates to different keys in the same document are last-writer-wins on the whole row; use row-level
locks or merge in app code if that matters.
Edge cases to mention: - The new value argument must be JSONB — string literals need 
'"false"'::jsonb (note the inner quotes for a JSON string). - For deeply nested paths the array
form gets long; use || (concat) when you're replacing a whole subtree. - Postgres 16 added 
jsonb_set_lax which gives you control over what happens when the new value is SQL NULL —
useful for upsert-style merges.
What NOT to say: - Do not use string concatenation to "patch" JSON — quoting nightmares plus
injection risk. - Do not forget the cast — passing a raw text value to jsonb_set raises a type error.
Common follow-up: "How would you remove a key?" — Use the - operator: preferences -
'old_key'. For nested removal, use #- with a path: preferences #-
'{notifications,sms}'.
UPDATE users
SET preferences = jsonb_set(
  preferences,
  '{notifications,email}',
  'false'::jsonb,
  true
)
WHERE id = 1042;
Q393 · jsonb_path_exists — Testing Without Returning
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Walmart Labs · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 410 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 411
What does jsonb_path_exists do, and how is it different from jsonb_path_query?
The 30-second answer: jsonb_path_exists(col, '$.items[*] ? (@.gst_invoice ==
true)') returns a boolean — true if at least one value matches the path expression. 
jsonb_path_query returns the matching values themselves as a set. Use exists in WHERE
clauses, use query when you actually need the values.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the return-type difference: boolean vs set of values. 2.
Explain why you'd reach for jsonb_path_exists over @? — both do the same thing semantically,
but jsonb_path_exists takes named parameters via the vars argument, so you can bind safely
without string-formatting paths. 3. Show the parameter binding: jsonb_path_exists(col,
'$.items[*] ? (@.amount > $threshold)', '{"threshold": 10000}'::jsonb) — the
third argument injects values without SQL string concatenation. 4. Mention that silent => true
suppresses errors from path syntax issues — handy for messy data.
Edge cases to mention: - Like @?, jsonb_path_exists benefits from a GIN index with 
jsonb_path_ops. - The function returns SQL NULL if the input column is NULL — not false. Wrap
with COALESCE in filter logic. - Parameter binding via the vars argument is the cleanest way to build
dynamic JSON queries from application code.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "jsonb_path_exists is faster than @?" — they compile to roughly
the same plan. - Do not pass user input into a path string without parameter binding — same injection
risk as string-built SQL.
Common follow-up: "Show me the same query using @?." — WHERE col @? '$.items[*] ?
(@.amount > 10000)' — the operator form is shorter; the function form gives you parameter
binding.
SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE jsonb_path_exists(
  payload,
  '$.items[*] ? (@.gst_invoice == true)'
);
Q394 · GIN Indexes on JSONB — When and How
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 411 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 412
You have a hundred-million-row events table with a payload JSONB column. Queries that
filter by keys inside payload are slow. How do you index it?
The 30-second answer: Add a GIN index on payload — CREATE INDEX ON events USING GIN
(payload jsonb_path_ops). That accelerates @>, @? and @@ operators. If you only query
specific keys, an expression index on (payload->>'key') is smaller and faster for that one access
pattern.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the two flavours of GIN: the default opclass
( jsonb_ops) indexes every key and value, supports more operators but is larger; jsonb_path_ops
indexes only paths, is smaller and faster but only accelerates @>, @?, @@. 2. State the decision: if
you do many ? and ?| key-existence queries, default opclass. If you do containment queries (@>), 
jsonb_path_ops is roughly 30% smaller and faster. 3. Talk about size — GIN on a 100M row JSONB
column can easily be 20-50 GB; budget accordingly. 4. Show the alternative — an expression index on
the specific path: CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload->>'event_type')) is tiny and
lightning fast for that one filter.
Edge cases to mention: - GIN indexes are slow to write — every insert updates the index for every key
in the document. On write-heavy tables, batch loads suffer. - fastupdate=on (default) accumulates
updates in a pending list; queries scan the pending list, so right after a bulk insert the first query is slow.
Run VACUUM to merge. - For containment with @>, GIN is essential; without it Postgres scans every
row.
What NOT to say: - Do not add a GIN index "just in case" — they're expensive on writes and disk. - Do
not say "expression indexes work for all queries" — they only help for the exact expression you indexed.
Common follow-up: "How do you check if the GIN index is actually being used?" — EXPLAIN
(ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and look for Bitmap Index Scan on <index_name>. If you see Seq
Scan, the planner thinks the index isn't helpful — possibly bad statistics.
CREATE INDEX events_payload_path_idx
  ON events USING GIN (payload jsonb_path_ops);
-- Now this uses the index
SELECT id FROM events
WHERE payload @> '{"event_type": "checkout_started"}';
Q395 · Expression Index on a Specific JSON Path
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 412 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 413
You only ever filter by one JSON key — say payload->>'event_type'. Do you really need a
GIN index?
The 30-second answer: No — a btree expression index on ((payload->>'event_type')) is
smaller, faster on writes, and gives equality plus range performance for that one path. GIN is overkill
when you index a single known field.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the size comparison — a btree expression index on one
text field is a small fraction of a GIN index over the whole document. 2. Explain why writes are faster:
btree updates one entry per row per insert; GIN updates one entry per key per row. 3. Show the index
and emphasise that the query must use exactly the same expression — payload->>'event_type'
not payload->'event_type'. 4. Mention the partial index trick: if you mostly filter WHERE
payload->>'status' = 'pending', a partial index WHERE (payload->>'status') =
'pending' is even smaller.
Edge cases to mention: - Expression must be IMMUTABLE — Postgres won't let you index a function
that varies. Most JSON operators are immutable. - If you cast inside the index — ((payload-
>>'amount')::int) — your query must also cast or the planner won't match. - Stats are collected
for the expression value, so the planner has decent cardinality estimates after ANALYZE.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "GIN is always the answer for JSONB" — it's the wrong default for
known single-key queries. - Do not assume the planner finds the index if your query expression is even
slightly different.
Common follow-up: "Can you do a composite expression index?" — Yes: 
CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload->>'event_type'), created_at DESC) for filter-
then-sort access patterns.
CREATE INDEX events_type_idx
  ON events ((payload->>'event_type'));
-- Uses the index for equality and range
SELECT id, created_at
FROM events
WHERE payload->>'event_type' = 'checkout_started';
Q396 · MySQL JSON_EXTRACT and -> Shortcut
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 413 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 414
How do you read a value out of a JSON column in MySQL? Show me both the function and the
shortcut.
The 30-second answer: JSON_EXTRACT(preferences, '$.language') returns the JSON value;
the -> operator is shorthand for the same thing. To get the unquoted text use 
JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(...)) or the ->> shortcut.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the canonical function: JSON_EXTRACT(col,
'$.path') — the path uses JSONPath syntax with $ as root. 2. Introduce the -> shorthand — 
col->'$.path' is the same as JSON_EXTRACT(col, '$.path'). 3. Explain the quoting issue: 
JSON_EXTRACT returns JSON, so a string comes back wrapped in double quotes. JSON_UNQUOTE
strips them; ->> does extract-and-unquote in one step. 4. Warn about a common Postgres-vs-MySQL
trip-up: MySQL needs $.field, Postgres uses bare keys with ->>. Different dialect, same idea.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL has a single JSON type — no json vs jsonb split. Internally
it's a binary representation similar to Postgres jsonb. - Filtering inside JSON in MySQL needs either a
generated column with an index or a multi-valued index (8.0.17+) — direct path filters won't use indexes.
- MySQL's JSON type sorts using its own internal order, which is not the same as text comparison —
never rely on raw JSON comparisons for ordering.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MySQL JSON works the same as Postgres jsonb" — operator names
and indexing are different. - Do not put '$.field' paths inline in user input — quote them safely.
Common follow-up: "How would you index this for fast filtering?" — Add a stored generated column on 
JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(col, '$.field')) and index that column.
-- MySQL
SELECT id,
       preferences->'$.language'   AS lang_json,
       preferences->>'$.language'  AS lang_text
FROM users
WHERE preferences->>'$.plan' = 'pro';
Q397 · MySQL JSON_TABLE — Shredding to Relational
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 414 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 415
An orders row has a line_items JSON array. Write a MySQL query that returns one row
per line item with the order id and item SKU.
The 30-second answer: Use JSON_TABLE — it turns a JSON array into a derived table you can join.
Define the column mapping with COLUMNS (sku VARCHAR(64) PATH '$.sku', qty INT PATH
'$.qty') and Cross Join it to the parent rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the goal: shredding a JSON array into row-per-element so the
rest of SQL works normally. 2. Show the syntax: 
JSON_TABLE(line_items, '$[*]' COLUMNS (sku VARCHAR(64) PATH '$.sku', qty INT
PATH '$.qty')) AS items. 3. Explain $[*] — iterate every element of the array. COLUMNS
extracts each leaf using its own path. 4. Mention NESTED PATH for inner arrays — JSON_TABLE can
flatten two levels of array in a single call.
Edge cases to mention: - JSON_TABLE is MySQL 8.0+ only; older versions had no clean way to
shred arrays. - If a path is missing, the column is NULL by default; ERROR ON ERROR makes it fail
loudly instead. - Performance: every query re-shreds the JSON. For high-traffic reads, persist the rows
into a child table.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "you can do this with JSON_EXTRACT in a loop" — that's application-
side, not SQL. - Do not skip the CROSS JOIN — without it JSON_TABLE returns the array elements
without parent context.
Common follow-up: "What's the Postgres equivalent?" — jsonb_array_elements(line_items)
in a LATERAL subquery, which is the same shredding pattern.
-- MySQL
SELECT o.id AS order_id, items.sku, items.qty
FROM orders o,
JSON_TABLE(
  o.line_items, '$[*]'
  COLUMNS (
    sku VARCHAR(64) PATH '$.sku',
    qty INT PATH '$.qty'
  )
) AS items;
Q398 · SQL Server JSON_VALUE and JSON_QUERY
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Wells Fargo, JP Morgan, Goldman, AmEx · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 415 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 416
SQL Server stores JSON as text. How do you read scalar values versus nested objects from a
JSON column?
The 30-second answer: JSON_VALUE(col, '$.path') returns a scalar (text or number) — fails for
objects/arrays. JSON_QUERY(col, '$.path') returns a JSON fragment — fails for scalars. Pick the
function that matches the expected return type.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start by stating SQL Server has no native JSON type — it's 
NVARCHAR(MAX) with helper functions and ISJSON for validation. 2. Show both functions side by
side: JSON_VALUE for leaf strings/numbers, JSON_QUERY for nested structures. 3. Warn about the
type mismatch trap — calling JSON_VALUE on an object path returns NULL (in lax mode) or throws
(in strict mode). 4. Mention WITH (STRICT) mode in the path: 'strict $.field' raises an error
on missing keys instead of returning NULL.
Edge cases to mention: - JSON_VALUE returns NVARCHAR(4000) by default; long strings get
truncated. Cast or use JSON_QUERY if you need the full payload. - Index a JSON path by adding a
computed column and indexing it — there's no native JSON index. - ISJSON(col) validates a string
is parseable JSON — use it as a CHECK constraint.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "SQL Server JSON is as fast as Postgres jsonb" — it's text-based
parsing, slower for path access. - Do not use JSON_VALUE to extract an object — it returns NULL
silently in lax mode and you'll debug for an hour.
Common follow-up: "How would you index a JSON path in SQL Server?" — Add ALTER TABLE t
ADD plan_path AS JSON_VALUE(preferences, '$.plan') then CREATE INDEX ON
t(plan_path).
-- SQL Server
SELECT id,
       JSON_VALUE(preferences, '$.language')      AS lang,
       JSON_QUERY(preferences, '$.notifications') AS notif_obj
FROM users
WHERE JSON_VALUE(preferences, '$.plan') = N'pro';
Q399 · SQL Server OPENJSON — Shredding to Rows
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Wells Fargo, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 416 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 417
SQL Server equivalent of JSON_TABLE — how do you turn a JSON array into rows?
The 30-second answer: OPENJSON(col, '$.path') returns a derived table. With an explicit 
WITH (col_name type 'path', ...) clause it maps JSON fields to typed columns. Cross apply
it to the parent table to get row-per-element output.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the basic form: OPENJSON(line_items) returns three
columns — key, value, type — useful for ad-hoc inspection. 2. Show the typed form: 
OPENJSON(line_items) WITH (sku NVARCHAR(64) '$.sku', qty INT '$.qty') — gives
you the column-mapped derived table. 3. Use CROSS APPLY to join with the parent — same pattern
as JSON_TABLE. 4. Mention AS JSON modifier: a column path can end with AS JSON to return
the nested fragment as JSON rather than scalar.
Edge cases to mention: - OPENJSON without WITH returns the key column as text — [0], [1]
for arrays, key names for objects. - Available since SQL Server 2016; Azure SQL fully supports it. - For
deeply nested arrays, you chain OPENJSON ... CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(value).
What NOT to say: - Do not say "this is like STRING_SPLIT" — OPENJSON is far richer. - Do not omit
the typed WITH clause for production queries — you lose type safety.
Common follow-up: "Can you use OPENJSON to feed an INSERT?" — Yes, bulk JSON ingestion is a
common pattern: INSERT INTO line_items SELECT order_id, sku, qty FROM orders
CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(...) WITH (...).
-- SQL Server
SELECT o.id AS order_id, items.sku, items.qty
FROM orders o
CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(o.line_items)
  WITH (
    sku NVARCHAR(64) '$.sku',
    qty INT          '$.qty'
  ) AS items;
Q400 · SQL Server 2022 JSON_OBJECT and JSON_ARRAY
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Wells Fargo, AmEx, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
SQL Server 2022 added new JSON constructor functions. What problem do they solve and how
do you use them?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 417 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 418
The 30-second answer: JSON_OBJECT('key': value, ...) and JSON_ARRAY(value, ...)
build JSON values inline — no more string concatenation or FOR JSON workarounds. They are part of
the SQL:2016 standard syntax and finally match what Postgres and Oracle have had for years.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the pain — before 2022, building JSON in SQL Server
meant string concatenation or FOR JSON PATH which is verbose for small documents. 2. Show 
JSON_OBJECT('id': id, 'name': name, 'email': email) — keyword-style key:value pairs.
3. Show JSON_ARRAY(sku1, sku2, sku3) for arrays. 4. Mention ABSENT ON NULL and NULL
ON NULL — controls whether NULL values produce a key or are omitted. Default is ABSENT.
Edge cases to mention: - Available only on SQL Server 2022 and Azure SQL — earlier versions still
need FOR JSON PATH. - Output type is NVARCHAR(MAX) — same as any other JSON in SQL
Server. - For aggregating into a JSON array, the standard's JSON_ARRAYAGG is not yet in SQL Server
2022; you still need FOR JSON.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "this is how SQL Server has always done JSON building" — it's a 2022
feature, candidates often miss the version. - Do not confuse JSON_OBJECT with OPENJSON —
opposite directions (build vs shred).
Common follow-up: "How would you do this in Postgres?" — json_build_object('id', id,
'name', name) or jsonb_build_object(...) — same idea, comma-separated key-value pairs.
-- SQL Server 2022
SELECT JSON_OBJECT(
  'id': id,
  'name': name,
  'email': email ABSENT ON NULL
) AS user_doc
FROM users
WHERE id = 1042;
Q401 · Generated/Computed Column from JSON + Index
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want fast equality filters on a key inside a JSON column but I don't want to expression-index
every query path. What pattern do you reach for?
The 30-second answer: Add a generated column that extracts the JSON field, then index that column
normally. Postgres calls them generated columns; MySQL calls them generated columns; SQL Server
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 418 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 419
calls them computed columns. Works in all three engines and gives you a clean, indexable, queryable
field.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the pattern: extract once at write-time, store, index, query.
2. Show Postgres: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN plan TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS
(preferences->>'plan') STORED. Stored means it's materialised on disk, so indexable. 3. Show
MySQL: same idea — ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN plan VARCHAR(32) AS
(preferences->>'$.plan') STORED. 4. Mention SQL Server: ALTER TABLE users ADD plan
AS JSON_VALUE(preferences, '$.plan') PERSISTED — PERSISTED is the keyword.
Edge cases to mention: - STORED/ PERSISTED means the value is computed once on write and re-
stored on update — eats disk space but reads are free. - Non-stored (virtual) generated columns are
computed at query time — saves disk but is slower for indexed reads. - Schema migrations on huge
tables are painful — adding a stored generated column rewrites the table in most engines.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "this is the same as an expression index" — generated columns let you
reference the field in queries by name, not just match an exact expression. - Do not skip STORED if you
plan to index — virtual columns in MySQL cannot be indexed (in Postgres, expression indexes on virtual
columns are fine).
Common follow-up: "What's the tradeoff vs an expression index?" — Generated columns are queryable
by name everywhere; expression indexes are smaller and don't change the table layout. For one or two
fields, either works; for many, prefer generated columns for readability.
-- Postgres
ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN plan TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (preferences->>'plan') STORED;
CREATE INDEX users_plan_idx ON users (plan);
SELECT id FROM users WHERE plan = 'pro';
Q402 · JSON_AGG and JSONB_AGG — Building JSON Arrays
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Return one row per user with a JSON array of all their order ids. Show me the Postgres query.
The 30-second answer: Use jsonb_agg(o.id) in a GROUP BY query: SELECT u.id,
jsonb_agg(o.id) AS order_ids FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id =
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 419 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 420
u.id GROUP BY u.id. jsonb_agg collects values into a JSONB array; json_agg is the same
for json.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the canonical use case: per-parent aggregation into JSON
for API responses. 2. Show the aggregate: jsonb_agg(o.id) produces a JSONB array. Combine
with jsonb_build_object to get arrays of objects, not just scalars. 3. Mention FILTER
(WHERE ...) — jsonb_agg(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid') aggregates only
matching rows. 4. Warn about LEFT JOIN with no matches: jsonb_agg returns [null] if there are
no rows — wrap in COALESCE(jsonb_agg(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL),
'[]'::jsonb).
Edge cases to mention: - Ordering inside the aggregate: jsonb_agg(o.id ORDER BY
o.created_at) — predictable array order. - For very wide aggregations, the resulting JSONB
document can be huge — paginate at the row level instead. - string_agg plus manual JSON
formatting is the old-school workaround for Postgres versions before 9.5; nobody should write that
today.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use the application layer to build the array" — the database does this
faster for medium-sized result sets. - Do not forget the GROUP BY — naked jsonb_agg over the
whole table returns a single mega-array.
Common follow-up: "Now return objects not just ids." — 
jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', o.id, 'total', o.total_paise)).
SELECT u.id,
       COALESCE(
         jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', o.id, 'total', o.total_paise)
                   ORDER BY o.created_at)
         FILTER (WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL),
         '[]'::jsonb
       ) AS orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id;
Q403 · json_build_object and jsonb_build_object
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Zerodha, Cred · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you build a JSON object inline from columns in Postgres?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 420 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 421
The 30-second answer: 
jsonb_build_object('id', id, 'name', name, 'email', email) — alternating key,
value, key, value. Returns a JSONB object. Use json_build_object for the text variant.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the function signature: variadic, alternating keys and
values. 2. Show how it composes with jsonb_agg for one-shot API-response construction. 3.
Contrast with row_to_json(t) — which converts an entire row into a JSON object using column
names — useful when you want every column without listing them. 4. Mention the ABSENT ON

null keys.

SELECT jsonb_build_object(

Q404 · JSON_OBJECTAGG — The SQL Standard Aggregator
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, AmEx · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does JSON_OBJECTAGG do and which engines support it?
The 30-second answer: JSON_OBJECTAGG(key VALUE value) is the SQL:2016 standard
aggregator that turns a set of key-value rows into a single JSON object. MySQL 5.7.22+, SQL Server
2022, Oracle 12c+ implement it; Postgres uses jsonb_object_agg(key, value) instead.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 421 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 422
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the use case: given a settings table with (user_id,
key, value), you want one JSON object per user with all their key-value pairs. 2. Show the standard
syntax: JSON_OBJECTAGG(setting_key VALUE setting_value) grouped by user. 3. Note
dialect differences — Postgres jsonb_object_agg(setting_key, setting_value) does the
same job with comma syntax. 4. Warn about duplicate keys — behaviour varies by engine. MySQL
keeps the last value; Postgres jsonb_object_agg keeps the last as well; SQL Server raises by
default.
Edge cases to mention: - If a key is NULL the aggregator typically raises an error — filter or coalesce
first. - For nested values you usually wrap each row's value in another JSON builder before aggregating.
- Standard syntax (KEY ... VALUE ...) is recognised by very few client tools — IDE auto-format
may mangle it.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "all engines support JSON_OBJECTAGG" — Postgres prefers its own
function name and signature. - Do not assume key order — output ordering is implementation-defined.
Common follow-up: "Write the Postgres version." — SELECT user_id,
jsonb_object_agg(setting_key, setting_value) FROM settings GROUP BY user_id.
-- MySQL / SQL Server 2022 / Oracle
SELECT user_id,
       JSON_OBJECTAGG(setting_key VALUE setting_value) AS settings
FROM user_settings
GROUP BY user_id;
Q405 · Comparing JSON Values — Semantic vs Textual Equality
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Are these two JSON documents equal? {"a":1,"b":2} vs {"b":2,"a":1}. How does
your database decide?
The 30-second answer: Semantically yes — they have the same keys with the same values. Postgres 
jsonb says yes because it stores normalised binary; json (text) says no because order differs.
MySQL JSON and SQL Server NVARCHAR also do semantic equality via JSON_EQUALS (SQL
Server 2022) or implicit comparison.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the rule: equality of JSON values is by semantic structure,
not by string form — same keys with same values, regardless of order. 2. Show the Postgres difference: 
'{"a":1,"b":2}'::jsonb = '{"b":2,"a":1}'::jsonb is true; the same comparison on 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 422 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 423
json is false because it's string compare. 3. Mention MySQL = on JSON columns is semantic;
SQL Server 2022 added JSON_EQUALS for explicit semantic compare. 4. Warn about numeric edge
cases: 1 vs 1.0 vs 1e0 — Postgres jsonb treats them as equal numbers; MySQL also
normalises numerics; some engines treat them as text-different. Always test on your engine.
Edge cases to mention: - Duplicate keys: jsonb keeps the last and dedupes, so {"a":1,"a":2}
equals {"a":2}. json keeps both, so equality is by text. - Whitespace and key order do not affect 
jsonb equality but break json/text equality. - NULL JSON values vs SQL NULL — 
'null'::jsonb is a JSON null, not SQL NULL — = on two JSON nulls is true; SQL NULLs
compare unknown.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "JSON equality is always by string" — false for the binary types. - Do not
write WHERE col::text = '{"a":1}' — fragile to whitespace and ordering.
Common follow-up: "How would you compare just one key?" — Extract the key with -> or ->> and
compare scalars: WHERE col->>'plan' = 'pro'.
SELECT '{"a":1,"b":2}'::jsonb = '{"b":2,"a":1}'::jsonb AS semantic_eq;
-- semantic_eq = true
SELECT '{"a":1,"b":2}'::json::text = '{"b":2,"a":1}'::json::text AS text_eq;
-- text_eq = false
Q406 · JSON Document Size Limits — When to Denormalize
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A team is storing user activity history as a JSON array that keeps growing. What goes wrong as
the array gets large and when do you split it out?
The 30-second answer: Once a JSON document exceeds the row-inline threshold (around 8KB in
Postgres), it gets TOASTed — stored out-of-line, so every read pays an extra fetch. Past a few hundred
KB, partial updates become slow because the entire document is rewritten on each jsonb_set. Split
into a child table once you're appending more than a few hundred rows' worth of data per parent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the practical thresholds: Postgres rows over 8KB go to
TOAST; MySQL JSON has a hard limit of max_allowed_packet (16MB typical); SQL Server 
NVARCHAR(MAX) is 2GB but performance is awful at scale. 2. Explain the write penalty: every update
of a JSONB column rewrites the full value, not just the changed bytes — even with jsonb_set. Bigger
doc = more I/O per write. 3. Explain the read penalty: TOASTed JSONB requires a separate page fetch;
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 423 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 424
for queries that only need a few fields, that's wasted I/O. 4. Give the migration rule: if you're appending
elements indefinitely (activity log, audit trail), it should be a child table from day one. JSON arrays are for
bounded, semantic groupings.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres EXTERNAL storage strategy keeps TOASTed values
uncompressed for faster access — useful if your read path is hot but writes are rare. - Compressed
(default) saves disk but adds CPU on every read; profile to decide. - For very large append-only arrays,
consider array_append semantics in a child table with proper indexes instead.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "JSON columns scale infinitely." Practical issues hit well before any
documented limit. - Do not claim TOAST is invisible — it has real read latency implications.
Common follow-up: "How would you migrate without downtime?" — Create the child table, dual-write
each new event, backfill the historical array in batches, then drop the JSON column.
-- Bad pattern: ever-growing JSON array
UPDATE users
SET activity = activity || jsonb_build_array(jsonb_build_object('ts', now(), 'event', 'login'))
WHERE id = 1042;
-- Good pattern: child table
INSERT INTO user_events (user_id, ts, event) VALUES (1042, now(), 'login');
Q407 · Schema Validation on JSON — CHECK + jsonb_path_match
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
JSON columns are schemaless by default. How do you enforce that a preferences JSONB
always has a language key with one of en, hi, ta, te?
The 30-second answer: Use a CHECK constraint with jsonb_path_match or a simpler expression:
CHECK (preferences->>'language' IN ('en','hi','ta','te')). For richer schemas use 
jsonb_path_match with SQL/JSON path predicates, or install a JSON Schema extension like 
pg_jsonschema.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the truth: SQL JSON support has no built-in schema. You
enforce shape via CHECK constraints. 2. Show the simple form: CHECK ((preferences ?
'language') AND (preferences->>'language' IN ('en','hi','ta','te'))). 3. Show
the path form: CHECK (jsonb_path_match(preferences, '$.language ? (@ == "en" || @
== "hi" || @ == "ta" || @ == "te")')). 4. Mention extensions: pg_jsonschema and 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 424 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 425
pg_jsonschema-rs validate full JSON Schema documents inside a constraint — useful for complex
shapes.
Edge cases to mention: - CHECK constraints fire on every write — heavy validation can hurt insert
throughput. - NOT VALID lets you add a constraint without checking existing rows, then VALIDATE
CONSTRAINT runs the check later in a less locking-heavy way. - For schema versioning, store a 
schema_version key inside the JSON and switch validation rules in app code or via partial check
constraints.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "validate in the application" as the only answer — that breaks under
concurrent writers or direct DB tools. - Do not invent a JSON SCHEMA keyword — it isn't standard
SQL.
Common follow-up: "How would MySQL or SQL Server do this?" — Both support CHECK constraints.
MySQL: CHECK (JSON_VALID(col) AND JSON_EXTRACT(col, '$.language') IN
('en','hi','ta','te')). SQL Server: CHECK (ISJSON(col) = 1 AND JSON_VALUE(col,
'$.language') IN ('en','hi','ta','te')).
ALTER TABLE users
  ADD CONSTRAINT preferences_language_valid
  CHECK (
    (preferences ? 'language')
    AND (preferences->>'language' IN ('en','hi','ta','te'))
  );
Q408 · Querying Nested JSON Arrays
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Each order document has items: [{sku, qty, amount_paise}, ...]. Find orders that
contain at least one item with amount_paise > 50000 AND total item count >= 3.
The 30-second answer: Combine jsonb_array_length with jsonb_path_exists (Postgres)
— WHERE jsonb_array_length(payload->'items') >= 3 AND
jsonb_path_exists(payload, '$.items[*] ? (@.amount_paise > 50000)'). Or shred
with jsonb_array_elements in a LATERAL subquery and aggregate.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Identify the two checks: array length and per-element predicate. 2.
Show the path-based form first because it's the most direct. 3. Show the LATERAL form as an alternative
when you need to project per-item values: CROSS JOIN LATERAL
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 425 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 426
jsonb_array_elements(payload->'items') AS item. 4. Mention indexing strategy: a GIN
index with jsonb_path_ops accelerates the jsonb_path_exists filter; the count check is hard
to index, accept a sequential portion.
Edge cases to mention: - jsonb_array_length on a non-array raises an error — guard with 
jsonb_typeof(col) = 'array' if you can't trust the shape. - LATERAL produces multiple
output rows per parent row — remember to DISTINCT or aggregate if you only want parents. -
MySQL: JSON_LENGTH(payload, '$.items') and JSON_CONTAINS(payload-
>'$.items', ...) are the analogues; for predicate-style queries, JSON_TABLE is the readable
form.
What NOT to say: - Do not pull every row into the app and filter there — pushdown belongs in SQL. - Do
not assume nested JSON is "free" — every query re-parses unless you have suitable indexes.
Common follow-up: "How would you find the highest-amount item across all orders?" — LATERAL
jsonb_array_elements(...) plus MAX((item->>'amount_paise')::bigint).
-- Postgres
SELECT id
FROM orders
WHERE jsonb_array_length(payload->'items') >= 3
  AND jsonb_path_exists(
    payload,
    '$.items[*] ? (@.amount_paise > 50000)'
  );
Q409 · Updating Array Elements Inside JSON
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, JP Morgan · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
An order's items JSON array has objects with sku and qty. Update only the entry where 
sku = 'SKU123' to set qty = 5. How do you do it without rewriting the whole array?
The 30-second answer: There's no native "update where" for JSON arrays. The clean pattern is: unnest
the array with jsonb_array_elements, modify the target element, re-aggregate with jsonb_agg,
and write back. Or jsonb_set by index if you know the position.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the honest truth: SQL JSON support does not have a
"update array element matching predicate" operator. You rebuild. 2. Show the unnest-modify-aggregate
pattern with jsonb_agg(CASE WHEN elem->>'sku' = 'SKU123' THEN jsonb_set(elem,
'{qty}', '5') ELSE elem END). 3. Show the index form: if you know the position, 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 426 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 427
jsonb_set(items, '{2,qty}', '5') updates the third element's qty directly — fast but
brittle to ordering. 4. Mention the concurrency risk — two simultaneous updates to different items in the
same array will conflict because the whole array is rewritten each time. Use row-level lock
( SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or push the items into a child table.
Edge cases to mention: - The unnest-aggregate pattern loses array order unless you carry an explicit
ordinality column: WITH ORDINALITY plus ORDER BY ord in jsonb_agg. - For very large arrays
this rewrites the whole document on every update — that's the underlying scalability ceiling. - MySQL
has JSON_SET, JSON_REPLACE and JSON_ARRAY_APPEND but the same "filter by predicate"
gap.
What NOT to say: - Do not pretend jsonb_set accepts a predicate — it only takes paths. - Do not
loop in application code over the array — that's slower and unsafe under concurrent writes.
Common follow-up: "If items get updated frequently, what would you recommend?" — Move items to a
child order_items table — proper row locks, indexes, partial updates without rewrites.
UPDATE orders
SET payload = jsonb_set(
  payload,
  '{items}',
  (
    SELECT jsonb_agg(
      CASE WHEN elem->>'sku' = 'SKU123'
           THEN jsonb_set(elem, '{qty}', '5'::jsonb)
           ELSE elem
      END
    )
    FROM jsonb_array_elements(payload->'items') elem
  )
)
WHERE id = 9001;
Q410 · JSON in Primary Key — Avoid
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, Goldman · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can you use a JSON column or a value extracted from JSON as a primary key? Should you?
The 30-second answer: Technically you can — Postgres lets you create a unique btree index on 
((col->>'id')) and use it as a logical PK; MySQL needs a generated column for the same. But you
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 427 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 428
almost certainly should not — JSON identity is fragile, indexes get bigger, foreign keys can't point inside
JSON, and ORMs choke.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with "can": Postgres CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON t
((payload->>'id')) plus a NOT NULL constraint via CHECK gives you a logical unique key. 2.
Move to "should not": foreign keys cannot reference an expression index — every downstream join
becomes a manual constraint. 3. Add the practical points: JSON path keys are text not numbers, so
btree comparisons are slower than bigint; replication and backups treat JSON columns as a single
value, complicating partial sync; ORM tools don't model JSON-path PKs. 4. Show the alternative —
extract the field into a real column at write time and PK that column. Cleanest design.
Edge cases to mention: - For analytical event stores where the row will never be referenced, a JSON-
derived unique index for dedup is fine. - Composite keys mixing real and JSON-derived columns are
extra messy; index size and update cost both balloon. - Some teams use a hashed JSON path as a
surrogate key for idempotency — acceptable for dedup but not as a real PK.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "primary keys cannot contain JSON" — that's an oversimplification, the
keys can exist via expression indexes. - Do not propose a JSON-derived PK in an interview — it signals
weak schema instincts.
Common follow-up: "What if I really want idempotent inserts based on a JSON field?" — Use a unique
expression index for dedup, but keep the actual PK as bigserial/ uuid.
-- Possible but discouraged
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX events_event_id_unique
  ON events ((payload->>'event_id'));
-- Better
ALTER TABLE events
  ADD COLUMN event_id TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (payload->>'event_id') STORED,
  ADD CONSTRAINT events_event_id_unique UNIQUE (event_id);
Q411 · JSON Columns and Replication
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Do JSON columns play nicely with logical replication and CDC pipelines? Any gotchas?
The 30-second answer: Mostly yes, but with two gotchas: every JSON update writes the full new
document to the WAL (no partial diff), and JSON's binary representation may not be byte-stable across
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 428 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 429
versions, so downstream consumers should compare semantically. Tools like Debezium handle JSON
columns natively but emit the entire new value on every change.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the WAL behaviour: UPDATE ... SET col =
jsonb_set(col, ...) writes the entire new value to WAL — the diff is reconstructed by the planner
but the replication payload is the full new column. 2. Explain the impact on replication bandwidth: large
JSON documents updated frequently produce large WAL volumes and long replica lag. 3. Mention CDC
tooling: Debezium, AWS DMS, Fivetran all support Postgres JSONB and MySQL JSON; they typically
deliver the after-image as a JSON object on the wire. 4. Warn about cross-version comparison: jsonb
binary format is generally stable within a major version, but ordering of object keys and whitespace
handling can shift; downstream comparisons must be semantic.
Edge cases to mention: - For row-level replication with very large JSON documents, consider 
REPLICA IDENTITY FULL carefully — it writes the old row too, doubling WAL volume. - Logical
replication slots can fall behind during JSON-heavy write storms — monitor 
pg_replication_slots.confirmed_flush_lsn. - For sub-document change feeds (only emit
changed keys), build it in app code or in the CDC consumer; the database doesn't natively diff JSON.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim JSON updates are "partial" at the storage level — they aren't. - Do not
say "Debezium can't handle JSONB" — it has had first-class support for years.
Common follow-up: "How would you reduce WAL volume from JSON-heavy writes?" — Split
frequently-updated keys into separate small columns, batch updates so each commit covers many keys
at once, or move hot fields out of JSON entirely.
-- This logs the entire new preferences blob to WAL even though one key changed
UPDATE users
SET preferences = jsonb_set(preferences, '{theme}', '"dark"')
WHERE id = 1042;
Q412 · JSON Columns and ORM Mapping
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Meesho · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do popular ORMs handle JSON columns and what's the typical bug you see in production?
The 30-second answer: Modern ORMs map JSON columns to dicts, hashes or typed objects — Django
JSONField, SQLAlchemy JSON/JSONB, Hibernate @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON), Rails 
serialize :col, JSON. The classic bug is the ORM marking the row dirty on every read because
the in-memory dict equality check differs from the database's normalised value.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 429 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 430
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the mapping landscape: every mainstream ORM has first-
class JSON support today, but the type is mapped to a mutable object. 2. The big bug — mutability: you
call user.preferences['theme'] = 'dark', and depending on the ORM, the change may not
be detected because the dict identity didn't change. SQLAlchemy needs 
MutableDict.as_mutable(JSONB) for the change to be picked up. 3. The second big bug —
equality drift: ORM reads the row, the dict has keys in one order; DB roundtrip reorders; next save thinks
the value changed. Triggers spurious updates. 4. Validation pattern: define a Pydantic / Marshmallow /
DTO schema in app code, validate before assignment, store as plain JSON.
Edge cases to mention: - Some ORMs serialise NaN/Infinity that JSON spec doesn't allow — the DB
rejects with a syntax error. - Lazy loading large JSON columns can mask N+1 problems if the column is
accessed in a loop. - For schema migrations adding fields to JSON, you don't need a DB migration —
just app-side defaulting. Tradeoff: no validation at the storage layer unless you add CHECK constraints.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "JSON columns don't work with ORMs" — they all support it. - Do not
store JSON as text-typed String columns to avoid ORM issues — you lose database-side validation
and query operators.
Common follow-up: "How do you avoid the mutability bug in SQLAlchemy?" — Wrap with 
MutableDict.as_mutable(JSONB) or always assign a new dict (user.preferences =
{**user.preferences, 'theme': 'dark'}) rather than mutating in place.
# SQLAlchemy — explicit mutable tracking
from sqlalchemy.ext.mutable import MutableDict
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import JSONB
preferences = Column(MutableDict.as_mutable(JSONB), default={})
Q413 · jsonb_set Partial Update vs Replace-Whole
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When should you use jsonb_set for a partial update versus just replacing the whole
document?
The 30-second answer: Use jsonb_set when one writer is touching a few known keys — it
preserves the other keys safely. Replace the whole document when you have a single owner and want a
clean, version-controlled write. Mixing both patterns from multiple writers is the lost-update trap.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 430 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 431
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the concurrency angle: two writers using jsonb_set on
different keys race, last-writer-wins on the whole column — neither side knows the other's change. 2.
Argue for jsonb_set when the field has multiple sub-owners with non-overlapping keys, each
updates only their slice, and the document is small enough that the rewrite cost is acceptable. 3. Argue
for replace-whole when there is a single owner (a settings page) that always loads, edits and saves the
full document — simpler, no surprise key changes. 4. Mention the optimistic-locking pattern: store a 
version integer at the row level, increment on every write, use WHERE ... AND version
= :expected so stale writes fail.
Edge cases to mention: - jsonb_set will create intermediate keys when the 
create_if_missing flag is true, which can hide schema typos — set the flag to false in strict
pipelines. - For nested updates, paths get long; the || (concat) operator is cleaner for replacing whole
subtrees: preferences || '{"notifications": {...}}'::jsonb. - Even with jsonb_set,
the storage write is the full document — there's no save in I/O, only safety against other keys.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "jsonb_set is cheaper because it's partial" — at the storage layer it
is not. - Do not advise replace-whole when you have multiple independent writers — you'll lose their
writes.
Common follow-up: "How do you make concurrent JSON updates safe?" — Either move the hot
subfields out into real columns with their own row locks, or use optimistic locking with a version column.
-- Concurrent-safe partial update with optimistic lock
UPDATE users
SET preferences = jsonb_set(preferences, '{theme}', '"dark"'),
    version     = version + 1
WHERE id = 1042
  AND version = 7;
Q414 · Reading JSON with NULL or Missing Keys
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Wells Fargo · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What happens when you read a JSON key that doesn't exist or whose value is JSON null?
Show me the SQL behaviour and how you'd handle it.
The 30-second answer: Missing keys return SQL NULL. JSON null values return SQL NULL via 
->> (text path) but return JSON null via -> (JSON path). Use COALESCE to give defaults, and
use ? (Postgres) or JSON_CONTAINS_PATH (MySQL) to distinguish "missing" from "explicitly null".
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 431 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 432
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the SQL behaviour: both missing-key access and JSON 
null typically coerce to SQL NULL — they look the same in WHERE clauses. 2. Show how to
distinguish: Postgres col ? 'key' returns true if the key exists (even if null), false if missing. MySQL 
JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(col, 'one', '$.key') is the equivalent. 3. Defaulting: 
COALESCE(preferences->>'language', 'en') — provides a fallback for both missing and null
cases. 4. Warn about the silent-bug: filters like WHERE preferences->>'plan' = 'free' miss
rows where the key is absent, even if intuitively you want to treat them as free.
Edge cases to mention: - JSON null vs SQL NULL confusion: 'null'::jsonb is a valid JSON
value (the JSON null literal); jsonb_typeof('null'::jsonb) returns 'null'. Comparisons
must use IS NULL carefully. - For "missing" semantics, prefer the explicit existence check (?) over
relying on IS NULL of an extracted value. - The ?| and ?& operators check for "any of these
keys" and "all of these keys" — handy for multi-key checks.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "missing keys throw errors" — they silently return NULL in all major
engines. - Do not assume your filter handles missing keys correctly without testing — write the test.
Common follow-up: "How do you distinguish JSON null from a missing key?" — Use the existence
operator: (col ? 'key') AND (col->>'key' IS NULL) means present-and-null; NOT (col ?
'key') means missing.
SELECT id,
       COALESCE(preferences->>'language', 'en') AS lang,
       (preferences ? 'plan')                   AS has_plan_key
FROM users;
Q415 · Store User Preferences — JSON Column or Separate Table?
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho, Flipkart · Topic: JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Classic interview prompt — you need to store user preferences (theme, language, notification
settings, feature flags). Would you use a JSON column or a separate preferences table? Defend
your choice.
The 30-second answer: JSON column for user preferences — they're per-user, sparse, schema-light,
almost never queried by content, and read together as one blob on login. A separate (user_id, key,
value) table is over-engineering for this use case; a separate column-per-preference adds migration
pain every time product adds a setting.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 432 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 433
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the access pattern: preferences are read in one go (login,
app start) and written by the user themselves, very rarely queried by other users or aggregated. JSON
column is the right tool. 2. Justify against the EAV (entity-attribute-value) table: a user_preferences
(user_id, key, value) table looks "more normalised" but adds JOIN overhead on every read,
makes "give me all preferences" a multi-row fetch, and requires app code to coerce types per key. 3.
Justify against column-per-preference: every new toggle requires a DDL migration, the table grows wide
with mostly-null columns, and SELECT * brings dead weight. JSON sidesteps the schema churn. 4.
Add the operational notes: use jsonb (Postgres) or JSON (MySQL) with a CHECK constraint for
top-level schema, a default of '{}', and a generated column for any field you actually need to filter on
(rarely needed for preferences).
Edge cases to mention: - If preferences ever become shared (team-level settings, admin overrides), the
EAV table is worth reconsidering for cross-user queries. - If a single preference becomes a hot filter
("show me all pro users"), promote that one field to a real column with an index — don't fight the JSON
column. - For very fine-grained audit ("who changed which key when"), a separate audit table records
each change with delta — keeps the JSON simple.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "JSON is the modern way, EAV is dead" — there are real cases for EAV;
the answer depends on access pattern. - Do not propose putting hot business fields (status, plan,
tier) inside the same JSON — those belong as columns.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle backward compatibility when you rename a preference?" —
Dual-write the old and new keys for a release, read both with a precedence rule, then run a background
migration to copy and drop the old key.
-- Recommended shape
CREATE TABLE users (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  preferences JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  CONSTRAINT preferences_is_object CHECK (jsonb_typeof(preferences) = 'object')
);
-- One-shot read on login
SELECT preferences FROM users WHERE id = 1042;
Chapter 10, Part B — MERGE, UPSERT, LATERAL & RETURNING
Modern SQL has finally caught up with what application developers were already doing in messy
procedural code: atomic upserts, per-row correlated lookups, capturing what just got written. These are
the DML patterns that surface heavily in product-company rounds at Razorpay, Swiggy, PhonePe, Cred
and the GCC teams at Walmart and Target — partly because they cleanly separate candidates who write
SQL daily from those who only remember it from college. MERGE went GA in Postgres 15 after years of
users asking for it, MERGE on SQL Server still has the concurrency bugs Aaron Bertrand wrote about a
decade ago, and ON CONFLICT remains the Postgres-native idiom that most senior engineers in India
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 433 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 434
actually reach for. This part of the chapter walks through every dialect's flavour, the pitfalls each one
hides, and the LATERAL / RETURNING tricks that make modern SQL feel less like a 1992 standard and
more like a real language.
Section A — MERGE and UPSERT
Q416 · MERGE Statement — The SQL:2003 Standard Syntax
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan, Oracle India · Topic: MERGE
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain the MERGE statement. What problem does it solve and what does the basic syntax look
like across dialects?
The 30-second answer: MERGE combines INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE into one atomic statement
driven by a join between a target table and a source. You specify WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE for
rows that exist and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT for new ones — useful when syncing a
staging table into a master.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the use case: nightly sync of a staging_orders feed into
the canonical orders table — some rows are updates, some are brand-new. 2. Walk through the
skeleton: MERGE INTO target t USING source s ON (t.id = s.id) WHEN MATCHED THEN
UPDATE SET ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT .... 3. Mention that MERGE landed in the
SQL:2003 standard but adoption was patchy — Oracle had it first, SQL Server added it in 2008,
Postgres only got it in version 15 (October 2022), MySQL still does not have MERGE. 4. Be ready for the
follow-up about whether MERGE is atomic — yes, the whole statement is one transaction step, which is
exactly why it's used for ETL.
Edge cases to mention: - MERGE on SQL Server has long-documented concurrency bugs — Aaron
Bertrand's "MERGE considered harmful" post is required reading. - If the source has duplicate keys for
the same target row, MERGE will error on Postgres and silently take the last row on Oracle — behaviour
differs. - DELETE inside MERGE (WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE) is supported on SQL Server and
Postgres 15+, but the semantics around multiple matches differ.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "MERGE is concurrency-safe by default" — on SQL Server it is not,
and even Postgres needs the right isolation level. - Do not say MySQL has MERGE — it does not; the
equivalent there is INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
Common follow-up: "If MERGE has bugs on SQL Server, what would you use instead?" — A serialisable
transaction wrapping a separate UPDATE and INSERT, or INSERT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS
followed by UPDATE, depending on the workload.

Q417 · MERGE in Postgres 15 — Why It Took So Long
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy GCCs · Topic: MERGE
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Postgres only got MERGE in version 15. Why so late, and how does it compare with ON
CONFLICT?
The 30-second answer: Postgres held out because INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
already covered the upsert case more safely and used the underlying unique-index machinery to handle
concurrency. MERGE finally landed in Postgres 15 for ETL workflows and SQL standard compliance, but
ON CONFLICT remains the idiom for true upserts.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the historical reason: Postgres committers were sceptical
of MERGE because the standard's semantics around concurrent modification are weak — ON
CONFLICT was deliberately designed to be race-safe using the unique index lock. 2. Note the GA
version — Postgres 15, October 2022. Anything older does not have it. 3. Distinguish the use cases:
MERGE for bulk source-to-target syncs where you want one statement; ON CONFLICT for single-row or
small-batch upserts driven by application code. 4. Mention that MERGE in Postgres 15 does not yet
support the full RETURNING clause across all branches — that came in Postgres 17.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres MERGE errors out if two source rows map to the same target row —
Oracle silently picks one. Indian product teams have been bitten by this when migrating ETL from Oracle.
- Postgres 15 MERGE cannot use WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE — that arrived later. - If you need
true atomic upsert with a returning row, ON CONFLICT is still cleaner.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres MERGE replaces ON CONFLICT" — it does not, and the
project explicitly states both have their place. - Do not assume MERGE works on Postgres 14 — it does
not. Check the version before writing it in an interview.
Common follow-up: "When would you actually pick MERGE over ON CONFLICT in Postgres?" — When
the source is itself a SELECT from another table and you want to express both insert and update in one
statement, especially for nightly ETL.

Q418 · MERGE in SQL Server and Its Known Bugs
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: MERGE
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Are you aware of any issues with MERGE on SQL Server? Have you read Aaron Bertrand's article
on it?
The 30-second answer: Yes — SQL Server's MERGE has a long list of known bugs around
concurrency, deadlocks, filtered indexes and incorrect plans. The community consensus (Aaron
Bertrand, Paul White) is to prefer separate INSERT and UPDATE inside an explicit transaction with 
HOLDLOCK.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with credibility: name the article — "MERGE Considered
Harmful" — and the author, Aaron Bertrand. This signals you actually read SQL Server material. 2. List
the categories of issues: concurrency races that can cause primary-key violations even with default
isolation, optimizer bugs that produce wrong cardinality estimates, problems with filtered unique indexes.
3. State the alternative: BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE ... WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK); IF
@@ROWCOUNT = 0 INSERT ...; COMMIT; — this is the historic safe pattern. 4. Be ready for the
follow-up about whether Microsoft has fixed any of these — some have been patched but the
community still treats MERGE with suspicion.
Edge cases to mention: - The race is real: under READ COMMITTED with default settings, two sessions
can both see "no match" and both try to INSERT — one fails on the unique constraint. - Filtered indexes
on the target can confuse MERGE into producing incorrect results — KB articles document this. - Even if
you fix concurrency with HOLDLOCK hints, MERGE can deadlock more often than separate statements.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MERGE is fine on SQL Server, the bugs are old" — many are still open
or only partially fixed. - Do not claim to use MERGE in production on SQL Server without mentioning the
locking hints.
Common follow-up: "How would you make MERGE concurrency-safe on SQL Server?" — Add WITH
(HOLDLOCK) on the target table reference; this escalates to a key-range lock that prevents the
phantom-insert race.

Q419 · MERGE in Oracle — The Original Implementation
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Oracle India, Infosys, TCS, Cognizant · Topic: MERGE
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Oracle has had MERGE for almost two decades. What does the Oracle dialect look like and what
are its quirks?
The 30-second answer: Oracle introduced MERGE in 9i (2001) and the syntax is close to the SQL
standard, with two extensions — an optional DELETE WHERE clause attached to the WHEN MATCHED
branch, and an ERROR LOGGING clause for batching error rows aside.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Note Oracle's long head start — many Indian banking and telecom
systems run ETL pipelines that have used Oracle MERGE since the early 2000s. 2. Walk through the
dialect-specific extras: DELETE WHERE inside WHEN MATCHED deletes rows that match a secondary
predicate after the UPDATE applies. 3. Mention LOG ERRORS INTO err_table REJECT LIMIT
UNLIMITED — extremely useful in batch ETL because one bad row does not abort the whole MERGE.
4. Be ready for the duplicate-source-row question: Oracle does not error on duplicates the way Postgres
does; it picks an unspecified row, which is a portability gotcha.
Edge cases to mention: - Oracle MERGE allows updating the join column itself — most other dialects
disallow this. - If both branches are written but you only need one, Oracle lets you omit either WHEN
MATCHED or WHEN NOT MATCHED — handy. - LOG ERRORS requires the error log table to be
created with DBMS_ERRLOG.CREATE_ERROR_LOG.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Oracle MERGE is identical to ANSI" — it has extensions that won't port.
- Do not assume DELETE WHERE inside MERGE works on Postgres — it does not; Postgres uses a
separate WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE branch.
Common follow-up: "How would you migrate an Oracle MERGE with LOG ERRORS to Postgres?" —
You lose the LOG ERRORS feature; the closest pattern is wrapping the MERGE in a savepoint loop or
routing failed rows through a trigger.

Q420 · ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE — The Postgres Upsert Idiom
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Postgres-heavy product teams · Topic:
UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE in Postgres. Why is it considered
safer than MERGE for upserts?
The 30-second answer: ON CONFLICT (col) DO UPDATE SET ... tells Postgres to attempt the
INSERT, and if it would violate the named unique constraint, switch to an UPDATE of the conflicting row
instead. It is concurrency-safe because it piggybacks on the unique index lock that the INSERT acquires.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the syntax: INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (1,
'x') ON CONFLICT (a) DO UPDATE SET b = EXCLUDED.b. The EXCLUDED pseudo-table
holds the row that was about to be inserted. 2. Explain the concurrency story: two concurrent sessions
inserting the same key — one wins the unique-index race, the other sees the conflict and runs the
UPDATE branch. No primary-key violation can escape. 3. Mention that the conflict target must reference
a unique constraint or unique index — you can also use ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT
constraint_name. 4. Be ready to discuss when DO NOTHING is preferable — silent dedup, like a
log-line ingest where duplicates are ignored.
Edge cases to mention: - The conflict target must match an actual unique index, including partial
indexes if applicable. - If multiple rows in the INSERT batch collide with the same target row, only one
wins — the second triggers the UPDATE on the just-updated row. - EXCLUDED.col refers to the
proposed insert value; t.col refers to the existing row.
What NOT to say: - Do not say it works for arbitrary CHECK constraints — only unique constraints /
indexes trigger ON CONFLICT. - Do not claim DO UPDATE without a target column works — you need 
ON CONFLICT (col) or ON CONSTRAINT name.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 438 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 439
Common follow-up: "How do you implement a counter increment safely?" — INSERT INTO
counters (key, n) VALUES ('foo', 1) ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET n =
counters.n + 1; — one atomic statement, no race.
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, qty)
VALUES ('SKU-1024', 50)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
  SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = NOW();
Q421 · ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — Silent Upsert
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Swiggy, Zerodha, Meesho · Topic: UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING instead of DO UPDATE?
The 30-second answer: Use DO NOTHING when duplicates should be silently dropped — typical for
idempotent event ingestion, append-only audit logs, or seed data where the row should not be
overwritten if it already exists.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the use case: payment webhook handlers receive the same
event multiple times due to retries; DO NOTHING makes the insert idempotent against a (event_id)
unique index. 2. Compare with DO UPDATE: DO UPDATE rewrites the existing row; DO NOTHING leaves
it untouched. For audit data, DO NOTHING is correct because you want the original row preserved. 3.
Mention RETURNING — INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id returns
nothing for conflict rows, which is a quirk if you need to know the existing id (see the xmax trick later in
this chapter). 4. Be ready for the follow-up about INSERT IGNORE in MySQL — semantically similar but
suppresses all errors, not just duplicates, which is a footgun.
Edge cases to mention: - ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING with no target column suppresses all unique-
constraint violations across all unique indexes on the table. - It does NOT return the id of the existing row
— for that you need either a separate SELECT or the xmax trick. - Performance-wise, DO NOTHING is
slightly cheaper than DO UPDATE because no row is rewritten.
What NOT to say: - Do not equate ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING with MySQL's INSERT IGNORE —
the latter silences all errors, including data-type errors and foreign-key violations, which is dangerous. -
Do not claim DO NOTHING returns the existing row in RETURNING — it does not.
Common follow-up: "How do you get the id of the existing row when DO NOTHING fires?" — Either run 
RETURNING then fall back to a SELECT, or use a WITH CTE that retries, or the xmax trick which we
cover separately.

VALUES ('evt_abc123', '{"amount": 4999}')

Q422 · INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE in MySQL
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Meesho, TCS · Topic: UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
MySQL doesn't have ON CONFLICT or MERGE. How do you upsert there?
The 30-second answer: MySQL has INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, which attempts
the INSERT and, if it would violate any unique key (primary or secondary), runs the UPDATE clause on
the conflicting row instead. Use VALUES(col) (older) or the AS new row alias (8.0.19+) to reference
the proposed insert values.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through the syntax: INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (1,
'x') ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE b = VALUES(b). From MySQL 8.0.19, prefer the alias form: 
INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (1, 'x') AS new ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE b =
new.b. 2. Note that ON DUPLICATE KEY fires on ANY unique-key conflict — not a specific one. That
can be a footgun on tables with multiple unique indexes. 3. Mention that the affected-rows count is 1 for
an INSERT, 2 for an UPDATE, and 0 if the existing row was unchanged. This is a classic MySQL trick
question. 4. Be ready for the follow-up about RETURNING — MySQL does not have it, so you have to
query LAST_INSERT_ID() or re-select.
Edge cases to mention: - If the UPDATE branch changes the primary key, replication and triggers can
behave oddly — avoid it. - INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE consumes an auto-increment
value even on the UPDATE path (until MySQL 8.0 with innodb_autoinc_lock_mode=0). - Multi-row
INSERT with this clause runs the UPDATE for each colliding row in order — generally what you want.
What NOT to say: - Do not equate it with MERGE — MERGE is a full standard statement; ON
DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE is MySQL-specific. - Do not claim it works on PostgreSQL or SQL Server.
Common follow-up: "What does VALUES(col) mean inside ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE?" — It
references the value from the proposed INSERT row. Deprecated in 8.0.20 in favour of the row alias.
INSERT INTO product_views (product_id, view_count) VALUES (501, 1) AS new
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE view_count = product_views.view_count + new.view_count;

Q423 · REPLACE INTO in MySQL — Why It's NOT an Upsert
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Flipkart, Walmart Labs · Topic: UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does REPLACE INTO do in MySQL, and why do senior engineers tell juniors never to use
it?
The 30-second answer: REPLACE INTO is a DELETE-then-INSERT, not an upsert. If a row with the
same unique key exists, MySQL DELETES it and then INSERTS the new one — which fires DELETE
triggers, breaks foreign-key children with ON DELETE CASCADE, and burns a new auto-increment id
every time.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the danger: REPLACE LOOKS like an upsert but
mechanically it's destructive — the old row is gone, and any audit triggers see a DELETE followed by an
INSERT. 2. The classic example: a users table with user_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY
KEY and a unique key on email. REPLACE INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('a@b.com', 'New
Name') deletes the existing row and creates a new one with a brand new user_id. All foreign keys
pointing to the old user_id are now broken (or cascade-deleted). 3. Mention that REPLACE INTO is fine
ONLY for cache-like tables with no foreign keys pointing in and no triggers — for example, a session
table or a precomputed aggregate. 4. Be ready to recommend the alternative — INSERT ... ON
DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE does the right thing.
Edge cases to mention: - Auto-increment values are consumed on every REPLACE, even when no
INSERT happens conceptually — table can run out of ids surprisingly fast. - ON DELETE CASCADE
foreign keys WILL cascade — silently deleting child rows. - Audit triggers see two events per REPLACE,
doubling audit volume.
What NOT to say: - Do not call REPLACE "the MySQL upsert" — it is not, and using it where ON
DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE was intended has caused production data loss. - Do not claim it's faster —
usually it's slower because of the extra DELETE-and-INSERT work.
Common follow-up: "Is there ANY good reason to use REPLACE INTO?" — Yes, when the semantic you
want is genuinely "throw away the old row, insert this one", such as cache rows where you don't care
about the surrogate id.
-- DANGER: deletes the existing row before inserting
REPLACE INTO sessions (session_id, user_id, expires_at)
VALUES ('sess_abc', 42, NOW() + INTERVAL 1 HOUR);
