Q424 · Detecting Whether an Upsert Inserted or Updated
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Postgres-heavy GCCs · Topic: UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
After an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, how can you tell whether the row was
newly inserted or an existing one was updated?
The 30-second answer: In Postgres, use the xmax system column in RETURNING — xmax = 0
means a fresh insert, non-zero means an update fired. It's an undocumented but widely-used trick
because there is no first-class way to ask.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the problem: you ran an upsert and you want to send a
"welcome email" only for new rows, not updates. You need a boolean per returned row. 2. Walk through
the xmax trick — every row in Postgres has hidden system columns; xmax is the deletion transaction
id. A freshly-inserted row has xmax = 0. When the row is updated through ON CONFLICT, the old
version's xmax gets set to the current xid, and the new version sees a non-zero xmax in RETURNING.
Hence (xmax = 0) AS inserted works as a flag. 3. Mention alternatives: in MySQL, use 
ROW_COUNT() — 1 means insert, 2 means update. In SQL Server with MERGE, use the OUTPUT
clause's $action pseudo-column. 4. Be ready for the follow-up about reliability — the xmax trick is
not officially documented as a contract, but it has been stable across Postgres versions and is
acknowledged in mailing-list discussions.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres, xmax is only zero for a row that has not been deleted or
updated in the current transaction. - MERGE in SQL Server provides $action in OUTPUT — values
are 'INSERT', 'UPDATE', 'DELETE'. Cleaner than xmax but only for MERGE. - In MySQL 
ROW_COUNT() returns 1 per INSERT, 2 per UPDATE, 0 if the row was unchanged — confusing
because "2" sounds like two rows.
What NOT to say: - Do not invent a column — beginners often write RETURNING xmax = 0 AS
was_inserted and miscount. - Do not claim Postgres has an official boolean for this — it does not.
Common follow-up: "What's the SQL Server equivalent?" — MERGE ... OUTPUT $action,
inserted.id — $action reports 'INSERT', 'UPDATE' or 'DELETE'.
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, amount) VALUES ('ord_42', 1999)
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET amount = EXCLUDED.amount
RETURNING order_id, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;

Q425 · Bulk Upsert Patterns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Swiggy, ETL teams · Topic: UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have 100k rows to upsert nightly. How do you do it efficiently?
The 30-second answer: Bulk-load the rows into a staging table first, then run a single 
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT from staging or a MERGE driven by staging. Avoid one-row-at-a-time
round trips at all costs.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the architecture: client-side loop calling 100k single-row
upserts is the slow path — each one is a network round trip plus an index probe. 2. Stage first: COPY
(Postgres) or LOAD DATA INFILE (MySQL) or BULK INSERT (SQL Server) into a temp/staging table
without constraints. This is at least 10x faster than INSERTs. 3. Then merge in one statement: INSERT
INTO target SELECT * FROM staging ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET .... The
optimizer can use a hash join here, batch the index updates, and do everything in one transaction. 4. Be
ready to discuss chunking — for tables with billions of rows, even one big MERGE can be too long; break
it into chunks by primary-key ranges.
Edge cases to mention: - Disable non-essential indexes and triggers on the staging table — they slow
the load without benefit. - For Postgres, INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT is the
canonical pattern. - If the source has duplicate keys, dedup in staging first with ROW_NUMBER() OVER
(PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts DESC) so only one row per key reaches the upsert.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose calling upsert in an ORM .each loop for 100k rows — that's the
anti-pattern this question is testing for. - Do not claim "one giant transaction is always best" — it can
block other writers and bloat the WAL; chunking helps.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle a 100M-row upsert without blocking online traffic?" — Chunk
by id range, throttle with pg_sleep() between batches, and consider partitioning the target.
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, qty, updated_at)
SELECT sku, qty, NOW() FROM staging_inventory
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
  SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at;
Q426 · Concurrent Upsert Race Conditions
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 443 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 444
Two sessions try to upsert the same key at the same time. Walk me through what each dialect
does.
The 30-second answer: Postgres ON CONFLICT serialises on the unique index — one wins the
INSERT, the other re-reads and runs the UPDATE branch with no race. SQL Server MERGE without
HOLDLOCK can race and produce a unique-constraint violation. MySQL 
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE is also race-safe via the unique index.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the scenario: two payment webhook handlers process the
same event_id simultaneously. Both INSERT first; one row wins. 2. Postgres path: session A
acquires the unique-index entry, session B blocks on the index lock until A commits, then session B's
INSERT sees the conflict and runs the UPDATE branch. Clean, atomic, no application retry needed. 3.
SQL Server path: with default isolation and no locking hints, MERGE can read "no match" in both
sessions, then both INSERTs run, second one violates the constraint. Fix is WITH (HOLDLOCK) on the
target. 4. MySQL path: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE is essentially safe; the storage engine's unique
index ensures serialization, similar to Postgres.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres returns the inserted-or-updated row in RETURNING regardless of
which branch fired — both sessions see correct results. - Deadlocks are possible if two upserts target
rows in opposite order — keep insert order consistent if you bulk-upsert. - SQL Server READ
COMMITTED SNAPSHOT can ameliorate but does not fully fix MERGE races.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "the application must retry on conflict" — Postgres and MySQL handle
it internally; only SQL Server MERGE without hints needs application-level retry. - Do not say "use
SERIALIZABLE for everything" — way too heavy for routine upserts.
Common follow-up: "What if two sessions update the same key with different values?" — Postgres
applies them serially — last-writer-wins on the column values, but both rows survive.
-- Race-safe in Postgres
INSERT INTO counters (key, n) VALUES ('homepage_views', 1)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET n = counters.n + 1;
Section B — LATERAL Joins and Set-Returning Functions
Q427 · LATERAL Join Basics
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy GCCs · Topic: LATERAL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 444 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 445
What does a LATERAL join do? When would I use it instead of a regular subquery?
The 30-second answer: LATERAL lets the subquery on the right side of a JOIN reference columns from
tables on the left, evaluating the subquery once per left row. It's how you say "for each row in the outer
table, run this inner query parameterised by that row".
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the syntactic restriction LATERAL removes: normally a
subquery in the FROM clause cannot reference outer columns. With LATERAL, it can. 2. Concrete
example: for each user, fetch their three most-recent orders. Without LATERAL you'd need a window
function plus a filter. With LATERAL it's a clean per-row TOP-N. 3. Mention the dialect names — Postgres
and Oracle 12c+ call it LATERAL, SQL Server calls it CROSS APPLY (and OUTER APPLY for the
LEFT JOIN variant). MySQL added it in 8.0.14. 4. Be ready for the question on what the planner does —
typically a nested loop with the LATERAL subquery on the inner side, often using an index for efficiency.
Edge cases to mention: - LATERAL with an empty subquery result drops the outer row — use LEFT
JOIN LATERAL to keep it. - LATERAL is great with set-returning functions like unnest() and 
jsonb_array_elements() — naturally per-row. - Performance depends on having a useful index on
the inner-side filter column.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim LATERAL is just a subquery rename — it has different scoping rules. -
Do not assume CROSS APPLY syntax works on Postgres — Postgres uses LATERAL only.
Common follow-up: "Can you do per-row TOP-N without LATERAL?" — Yes, with ROW_NUMBER()
OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC) and a filter — but LATERAL is often cleaner
and uses indexes better.
-- Per user, fetch the latest order
SELECT u.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1
) o ON TRUE;
Q428 · CROSS APPLY in SQL Server
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman · Topic: LATERAL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is CROSS APPLY in SQL Server and how does it differ from LATERAL?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 445 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 446
The 30-second answer: CROSS APPLY is SQL Server's name for LATERAL — same semantics,
different keyword. It evaluates the right-side table expression once per left row using values from the left
as parameters. OUTER APPLY is the LEFT JOIN equivalent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the equivalence: LATERAL (Postgres / Oracle 12c+ / MySQL
8.0.14+) and CROSS APPLY (SQL Server, Sybase) do the same thing. 2. SQL Server uses APPLY
heavily because table-valued functions (TVFs) only work in the FROM clause via CROSS APPLY — you
call a TVF per row of the outer table. 3. Walk through an example: SELECT u.id, top_orders.*
FROM users u CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 3 * FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id
ORDER BY created_at DESC) top_orders;. This is the classic per-row top-N. 4. Be ready for the
dialect comparison: when porting SQL Server CROSS APPLY to Postgres, replace with LATERAL;
replace OUTER APPLY with LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON TRUE.
Edge cases to mention: - CROSS APPLY drops outer rows with no inner match; OUTER APPLY keeps
them with NULLs. - TVFs in SQL Server are a major reason CROSS APPLY exists — they can be
parameterised by outer-row columns only via APPLY. - Older Postgres docs used the term "lateral
subquery" before SQL standard adopted LATERAL.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim CROSS APPLY is a Postgres feature — it is not; Postgres uses
LATERAL. - Do not confuse CROSS APPLY (per-row) with CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product).
Common follow-up: "Why use CROSS APPLY over a window function?" — APPLY can use a different
filter or order per outer row trivially; window functions need the same partition/order for everyone.
-- SQL Server: per user, top 3 orders by amount
SELECT u.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM users u
CROSS APPLY (
  SELECT TOP 3 order_id, amount FROM orders
  WHERE user_id = u.id ORDER BY amount DESC
) o;
Q429 · LATERAL for Per-Row Top-N
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, PhonePe, Walmart · Topic: LATERAL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
For each user, return the three most recent orders. Show me two ways — one with LATERAL and
one without.
The 30-second answer: With LATERAL: SELECT u.*, o.* FROM users u JOIN LATERAL
(SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) o
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 446 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 447
ON TRUE;. Without LATERAL: use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY
created_at DESC) and filter for rn <= 3.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with LATERAL: it reads naturally — "for each user, pull three
orders" — and uses the index on (user_id, created_at DESC) straightforwardly via nested loop.
2. Window-function alternative: a single scan of orders with ROW_NUMBER, then a filter. Good if the
orders table is small or you need a single scan. 3. Performance contrast: LATERAL is faster when there
are many users and few orders per user (index seek per user). Window function is faster when you'd
otherwise loop millions of users with sparse data per user. 4. Be ready for the follow-up: "Which would
you pick for a 10M-user table with avg 5 orders per user?" — Probably window function, one scan beats
10M seeks unless cache is hot.
Edge cases to mention: - LATERAL needs LEFT JOIN LATERAL (with ON TRUE) to keep users who
have no orders. - The ROW_NUMBER version returns ties unpredictably — use ORDER BY with a
tiebreaker. - For "top N per group with ties", use RANK() or DENSE_RANK() instead.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim LATERAL is always faster — it depends on cardinality and indexes. -
Do not omit the ORDER BY in the LIMIT subquery — the result is non-deterministic.
Common follow-up: "What if N varies per user?" — LATERAL handles this trivially with LIMIT
u.preferred_count inside the subquery. Window functions cannot do per-group variable N as
cleanly.
SELECT u.name, o.order_id, o.created_at
FROM users u
JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, created_at FROM orders
  WHERE user_id = u.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3
) o ON TRUE;
Q430 · LATERAL with Set-Returning Functions
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy teams · Topic: LATERAL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How does LATERAL interact with set-returning functions like unnest() or 
jsonb_array_elements()?
The 30-second answer: LATERAL is the standard way to expand a set-returning function once per row
of an outer table — for each row, the SRF emits N rows and you get the cartesian per-row product.
Postgres actually allows omitting the LATERAL keyword in this case as a convenience, but writing it
explicitly is clearer.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 447 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 448
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Example setup: an orders table where each row has a jsonb
column items holding an array of line-item objects. You want one row per (order, item). 2. Write the
LATERAL: 
SELECT o.id, item FROM orders o, LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(o.items)
item;. Each order produces as many rows as it has items. 3. Mention the comma shortcut: FROM
orders o, jsonb_array_elements(o.items) item works in Postgres because SRFs in FROM
are implicitly lateral. 4. Be ready for the use-case follow-up: this is how you de-normalise jsonb arrays for
analytical queries.
Edge cases to mention: - If items is NULL or empty array, the order disappears (CROSS JOIN
LATERAL semantics). Use LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON TRUE to keep it. - SRFs called in the SELECT list
(not FROM) have different semantics — they produce a single result column with set semantics, not a
join. - WITH ORDINALITY (next question) gives you an index column alongside the unnested values.
What NOT to say: - Do not omit LATERAL on non-SRF subqueries — Postgres requires it for regular
subqueries even though it tolerates omission for SRFs. - Do not assume MySQL's JSON_TABLE works
the same way — it does, but the syntax is different.
Common follow-up: "How would you do this in MySQL?" — 
JSON_TABLE(items, '$[*]' COLUMNS (...)) provides equivalent functionality from MySQL 8.0.
SELECT o.order_id, item->>'sku' AS sku, (item->>'qty')::int AS qty
FROM orders o, LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(o.items) item;
Q431 · LATERAL for Unnesting Arrays Per Row
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Meesho, Postgres-heavy teams · Topic: LATERAL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have a Postgres table where each row has an int[] column. I want one output row per (id,
array element). How?
The 30-second answer: SELECT t.id, x FROM t, LATERAL unnest(t.arr) x; — 
unnest() is a set-returning function and LATERAL gives it access to the outer row's array. One outer
row produces N output rows, one per array element.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the example: survey_responses table with a column 
selected_options int[] — each response picked some subset. 2. Write the unnest: SELECT
r.id, opt FROM survey_responses r, LATERAL unnest(r.selected_options) opt;.
Now each response contributes one row per selected option — ready for aggregation by option. 3.
Mention that unnest() returns no rows for an empty array or NULL — the parent row is dropped. Use
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 448 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 449
LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON TRUE to keep responses with no selections. 4. Be ready to discuss 
array_agg() as the inverse — collapsing rows back into an array.
Edge cases to mention: - Multi-dimensional arrays unnest by total elements unless you specify the
dimension. - unnest(arr1, arr2) unnests two arrays in parallel, padding the shorter with NULLs
— handy for paired data. - unnest() is the Postgres idiom; SQL Server uses STRING_SPLIT() for
strings, and OPENJSON() for JSON arrays.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim arrays are the same as JSON arrays — they are stored and indexed
differently in Postgres. - Do not unnest in the SELECT list when you mean to use it in FROM — the
SELECT-list usage is legacy and produces confusing results.
Common follow-up: "How do you count, per option, how many responses selected it?" — SELECT
opt, COUNT(*) FROM survey_responses, LATERAL unnest(selected_options) opt
GROUP BY opt;.
SELECT r.response_id, opt
FROM survey_responses r, LATERAL unnest(r.selected_options) opt;
Q432 · generate_series() with LATERAL
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, analytics teams · Topic: LATERAL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how to use generate_series() inside a LATERAL join to expand each row into
multiple rows.
The 30-second answer: generate_series(start, end) is a set-returning function; combined
with LATERAL it expands each outer row into one row per integer (or date) in the series. Classic use
case: filling in missing dates for a per-day report.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Use case: a subscriptions table with started_on and 
ended_on. You want one row per (subscription, day) for revenue allocation. 2. Write the lateral
generate_series: SELECT s.id, d::date FROM subscriptions s, LATERAL
generate_series(s.started_on, s.ended_on, '1 day'::interval) d;. Now each
subscription produces a row per day it was active. 3. Another use case: per-user, generate a row for each
of the last 30 days, then LEFT JOIN to orders for a presence-of-orders matrix. 4. Be ready for the date-
spine pattern: generate_series(start, end, '1 day') is the canonical Postgres way to
manufacture missing dates.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 449 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 450
Edge cases to mention: - generate_series is Postgres-specific; SQL Server uses recursive CTEs or a
numbers table; MySQL 8.0+ uses recursive CTE. - For huge ranges generate_series can blow up

SELECT s.subscription_id, d::date AS active_day

Q433 · WITH ORDINALITY — Index from Set-Returning Functions
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, analytics-heavy GCCs · Topic: LATERAL
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does WITH ORDINALITY do, and when is it useful?
The 30-second answer: WITH ORDINALITY adds an integer column to a set-returning function's
output, numbering the rows from 1 — you get the position of each element in the original set. Useful for
preserving array ordering after unnest.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Problem: you unnest() an array but lose the original index. If you
want to know "this was the third element", WITH ORDINALITY gives you that. 2. Syntax: SELECT *
FROM unnest(ARRAY['a','b','c']) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(val, idx);. You get two
columns — the value and its 1-based position. 3. Real-world example: a tags TEXT[] column where
the first tag is the primary. After unnest with ORDINALITY, filter WHERE idx = 1 to get just the
primary tag. 4. Be ready to mention this is SQL standard syntax — Postgres supports it from 9.4, Oracle
12c also supports it.
Edge cases to mention: - Ordinality starts at 1, not 0 — easy to off-by-one in code that thinks in zero-
indexed terms. - WITH ORDINALITY works with any SRF — generate_series, 
regexp_split_to_table, jsonb_array_elements, etc. - For jsonb arrays, the ordinality
column gives the array index — useful for joining back to the source structure.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 450 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 451
What NOT to say: - Do not assume ROW_NUMBER() over unnest is equivalent — it works but is more
verbose and may not preserve original array order across all dialects. - Do not claim it's a Postgres
extension — it's SQL standard.
Common follow-up: "How would you re-create the array in original order after some filtering?" — 
array_agg(val ORDER BY idx) reconstructs the array using the ordinality column.
SELECT u.id, t.tag, t.idx
FROM users u, LATERAL unnest(u.interests) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(tag, idx)
WHERE t.idx <= 3;  -- top 3 interests by original order
Section C — RETURNING, OUTPUT and DML in CTEs
Q434 · RETURNING Clause in Postgres and Oracle
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Postgres-heavy teams · Topic:
RETURNING
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does the RETURNING clause do? Why does it matter for application code?
The 30-second answer: RETURNING lets INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements return the rows
they touched, so the application doesn't need a follow-up SELECT. Crucial for capturing auto-generated
ids and audit data without an extra round trip.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the round-trip cost: without RETURNING, after an INSERT
you'd run SELECT currval() or a separate SELECT to get the id. With RETURNING, you get the id
in the same statement. 2. Show the syntax: INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...)
RETURNING id, created_at;. UPDATE and DELETE work the same — RETURNING * returns all
columns of affected rows. 3. Mention dialect support: Postgres has full RETURNING. Oracle has 
RETURNING ... INTO (slightly different syntax, populates host variables). SQL Server uses the
OUTPUT clause. MySQL does not have RETURNING. 4. Be ready for the batch-INSERT angle —
RETURNING gives you all generated ids in one shot for a multi-row INSERT.
Edge cases to mention: - RETURNING * is fine for prototyping but list explicit columns in production
— the row shape is part of the contract. - RETURNING runs after triggers fire, so trigger-modified column
values are visible. - In Oracle, RETURNING INTO only works for single-row DML unless you use BULK
COLLECT INTO.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 451 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 452
What NOT to say: - Do not claim RETURNING is universal — MySQL still lacks it (MariaDB has it). - Do
not write RETURNING * in production code without thinking about the row shape.
Common follow-up: "How do you get all 1000 generated ids in a batch INSERT?" — INSERT
INTO ... SELECT ... RETURNING id; returns one row per inserted row.
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, amount) VALUES (42, 1999)
RETURNING order_id, created_at;
Q435 · OUTPUT Clause in SQL Server
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic:
RETURNING
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
SQL Server has OUTPUT instead of RETURNING. How does it work?
The 30-second answer: OUTPUT inserted.col, deleted.col returns rows affected by INSERT,
UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE. inserted holds the new row, deleted holds the pre-update version.
You can stream OUTPUT directly to the client or OUTPUT INTO @table for further processing.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through the pseudo-tables: inserted (new values,
populated by INSERT and UPDATE) and deleted (old values, populated by UPDATE and DELETE).
MERGE populates both for updated rows plus $action. 2. Show two patterns: 
INSERT ... OUTPUT inserted.id, inserted.created_at streams the values back; 
DELETE ... OUTPUT deleted.* INTO @audit captures deleted rows into a table variable for
audit. 3. Mention that OUTPUT is older and more powerful than RETURNING in some ways — it can
capture both pre- and post-update state. For pure pre-image audit, OUTPUT is unique. 4. Be ready for
the MERGE-OUTPUT combination: MERGE ... OUTPUT $action, inserted.id, deleted.id
gives you per-row which branch fired.
Edge cases to mention: - OUTPUT INTO with a target table requires no triggers on that target (or 
INTO clause limitations). - $action is MERGE-only — 'INSERT', 'UPDATE', or 'DELETE'.
- For UPDATE without OUTPUT, you cannot get the pre-image — capture it before the UPDATE if
needed.
What NOT to say: - Do not say OUTPUT works on Postgres — it does not; Postgres uses RETURNING.
- Do not assume OUTPUT INTO a temp table works with triggers — there are documented restrictions.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 452 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 453
Common follow-up: "How do you audit which user_id changed in an UPDATE?" — UPDATE users
SET ... OUTPUT deleted.user_id AS old_id, inserted.user_id AS new_id INTO
audit_table.
DELETE FROM orders OUTPUT deleted.order_id, deleted.amount
INTO archived_orders
WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND created_at < DATEADD(year, -2, GETDATE());
Q436 · RETURNING for Capturing Generated IDs in Batch INSERT
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, ETL-heavy teams · Topic: RETURNING
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I'm batch-inserting 500 rows in Postgres. How do I get all the generated serial ids?
The 30-second answer: Use INSERT INTO t (...) VALUES (...), (...), ... RETURNING
id; — Postgres returns one row per inserted row, in insertion order. Capture them in the application or
in a CTE for follow-up DML.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the scenario: a Razorpay-style payment batch where you
INSERT 500 payment rows and need each new payment_id to send to the downstream ledger. 2. The
naive path: insert one row at a time using currval() or RETURNING id per row — 500 round trips.
3. The right path: one INSERT with 500 VALUES rows, RETURNING id returns 500 ids at once. Read
all of them in the application. 4. Be ready for the ordering question — in Postgres, INSERT order is
preserved in RETURNING output (you can rely on this in practice).
Edge cases to mention: - For very large batches, use INSERT ... SELECT ... RETURNING from
a staging table rather than 50k VALUES literals. - The Oracle equivalent uses RETURNING INTO ...
BULK COLLECT — different syntax but same idea. - MySQL does not support multi-row RETURNING;
use LAST_INSERT_ID() plus knowledge of the auto-increment increment.
What NOT to say: - Do not loop single-row INSERTs and call this "batch" — that's the slow path you're
being asked to avoid. - Do not claim RETURNING is unordered — in Postgres practice, order is
preserved.
Common follow-up: "What about for COPY-loaded data?" — COPY does not support RETURNING
directly; load into a staging table then INSERT INTO target SELECT * FROM staging
RETURNING id.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 453 / 521

WITH new_payments AS (
  INSERT INTO payments (order_id, amount, gateway)
  VALUES (1, 100, 'razorpay'), (2, 200, 'razorpay'), (3, 300, 'razorpay')
  RETURNING payment_id, order_id
)
INSERT INTO ledger (payment_id, order_id, type)
SELECT payment_id, order_id, 'credit' FROM new_payments;
Q437 · DML in CTE — Chaining Writes with RETURNING
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy product teams · Topic: RETURNING
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how to perform multiple DML statements in one query using CTEs and RETURNING.
The 30-second answer: Postgres allows INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE inside WITH clauses, each
with RETURNING — chain them so output of one DML feeds the next. Classic pattern: archive rows then
delete them, atomically.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The pattern: 
WITH archived AS (DELETE FROM orders WHERE status='cancelled' RETURNING *)
INSERT INTO archived_orders SELECT * FROM archived;. One statement, atomic — orders
cannot be deleted without being archived. 2. Note that this works only in Postgres — Oracle and SQL
Server require separate statements or different mechanisms (OUTPUT INTO for SQL Server). 3. All DML
in a single WITH happens in one snapshot — the CTEs don't "see" each other's effects on the same
rows. Be careful with overlapping row sets. 4. Be ready for the consistency follow-up — for atomic multi-
table writes that need to see each other's effects, use a regular transaction with explicit statements.
Edge cases to mention: - The CTE order in the WITH list does not determine execution order —
Postgres is free to interleave them. Use a final SELECT or INSERT to pin order. - Each CTE sees the table
state as of the statement start, not after the other CTEs' writes. - A single statement is fully atomic — if
any CTE fails, all roll back.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume DML CTEs see each other — they do not, by design. - Do not write
this in MySQL — MySQL 8.0 has CTEs but not data-modifying CTEs.
Common follow-up: "How do you move rows from one table to another atomically?" — Exactly this
pattern, with DELETE...RETURNING piped into INSERT...SELECT.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 454 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 455
WITH expired AS (
  DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < NOW() RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO session_history SELECT * FROM expired;
Q438 · UPDATE ... FROM in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy GCCs · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you update a table based on values from another table in Postgres?
The 30-second answer: Postgres extends UPDATE with a FROM clause: UPDATE t SET col =
s.col FROM source s WHERE t.id = s.id;. The FROM table provides the values; the WHERE
clause joins target to source.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set up the scenario: nightly job updates users.tier based on a
computed user_tiers_snapshot table. 2. Write the UPDATE...FROM: UPDATE users u SET
tier = s.tier FROM user_tiers_snapshot s WHERE u.id = s.user_id;. The FROM table
can be a real table, a CTE, or a subquery. 3. Watch out: if the FROM source has multiple rows matching
the same target row, the behaviour is unspecified (Postgres picks one). Dedup the source first. 4. Be
ready for the MySQL contrast — MySQL uses UPDATE t JOIN source ON ... SET t.col =
source.col syntax (next question).
Edge cases to mention: - Multiple matches on the source side produce unspecified results — Postgres
will not raise an error but may update with any one of the matching rows. - The target table cannot
appear in the FROM list (use a self-join via a subquery or CTE if you need that). - Standard SQL has 
UPDATE ... SET col = (SELECT ...) for scalar correlated updates — slower, more portable.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim UPDATE...FROM is standard SQL — it is a Postgres extension (SQL
Server also supports it with similar syntax). - Do not write it in MySQL — MySQL uses UPDATE...JOIN.
Common follow-up: "How do you ensure idempotency if the same source row appears twice?" —
Dedup in a CTE first: WITH dedup AS (SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) ... FROM source)
UPDATE users SET ... FROM dedup WHERE ....
UPDATE users u SET tier = s.tier, updated_at = NOW()
FROM user_tiers_snapshot s
WHERE u.id = s.user_id AND u.tier <> s.tier;

Q439 · UPDATE ... JOIN in MySQL
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Meesho · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Same scenario in MySQL — how do you update one table using values from another?
The 30-second answer: MySQL uses an inline JOIN in the UPDATE: UPDATE users u JOIN
user_tiers_snapshot s ON u.id = s.user_id SET u.tier = s.tier;. Multiple tables can
be joined and multiple SET targets can appear.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the syntax: target table first, JOIN second, SET third, optional
WHERE last. MySQL allows updating columns of multiple joined tables in one statement. 2. Multi-table
example: UPDATE orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id SET
o.status='paid', p.settled_at=NOW() WHERE p.confirmed=1;. Both tables are updated
atomically. 3. Note that ORDER BY and LIMIT are valid with single-table UPDATE in MySQL but not with
multi-table UPDATE — common gotcha. 4. Be ready for the porting question — MySQL UPDATE JOIN to
Postgres becomes UPDATE...FROM.
Edge cases to mention: - LIMIT does not work with multi-table UPDATE in MySQL. - If the JOIN
matches the same target row multiple times, MySQL updates it once per match — order-dependent. -
For very large UPDATE JOIN, MySQL can be slow; chunk by primary key.
What NOT to say: - Do not use the Postgres UPDATE...FROM syntax in MySQL — it will not parse. -
Do not claim multi-table UPDATE is in the SQL standard — it is a MySQL extension.
Common follow-up: "How do you simulate UPDATE...JOIN with LIMIT in MySQL?" — Use a subquery
to select ids first, then UPDATE filtered by those ids.
UPDATE orders o
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
SET o.status = 'paid', o.paid_at = NOW()
WHERE p.confirmed_at IS NOT NULL AND o.status <> 'paid';
Q440 · DELETE ... USING in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postgres-heavy teams · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 456 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 457
How do you delete rows from one table based on a join with another in Postgres?
The 30-second answer: Postgres uses 
DELETE FROM target USING source WHERE target.col = source.col — USING
introduces additional tables that the WHERE clause can reference, similar to UPDATE...FROM.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Use case: delete orders that belong to users who are flagged as
fraudulent in another table. 2. Syntax: DELETE FROM orders o USING fraud_flags f WHERE
o.user_id = f.user_id AND f.confirmed = true;. Only the FROM table is deleted; USING is
read-only. 3. Mention NOT EXISTS as an alternative — DELETE FROM orders WHERE EXISTS
(...) is portable; USING is more concise. 4. Be ready for the parallel: just as UPDATE has
UPDATE...FROM, DELETE has DELETE...USING.
Edge cases to mention: - Only the target table is deleted; USING tables stay untouched — common
confusion. - If multiple USING rows match the same target row, the target is deleted once (idempotent). -
For deleting child rows via FK, prefer ON DELETE CASCADE in the constraint definition.
What NOT to say: - Do not put the target table in USING — it deletes nothing. - Do not assume
DELETE...USING works in MySQL — MySQL has its own DELETE...JOIN syntax.
Common follow-up: "Is DELETE...USING faster than DELETE...WHERE EXISTS?" — Usually similar; the
planner often converts EXISTS to a semi-join anyway. Profile if it matters.
DELETE FROM orders o
USING fraud_flags f
WHERE o.user_id = f.user_id AND f.confirmed = true;
Q441 · DELETE ... JOIN in MySQL
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Meesho · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Same problem in MySQL — delete from one table using a join.
The 30-second answer: MySQL syntax is DELETE t1 FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON t1.id = t2.id
WHERE ... — the DELETE t1 part names which table to delete from, the FROM clause provides the
join.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 457 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 458
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Walk through the structure: DELETE followed by the table alias(es)
to delete from, FROM followed by the join, then WHERE. 2. Show example: DELETE o FROM orders
o JOIN fraud_flags f ON o.user_id = f.user_id WHERE f.confirmed = 1;. 3. Multi-
table DELETE: DELETE o, p FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE ... deletes from both atomically. 4. Be ready for the ordering follow-up — multi-table DELETE
in MySQL does not support ORDER BY or LIMIT.
Edge cases to mention: - The aliases in DELETE t1, t2 must match the FROM clause exactly —
typos here silently change behaviour. - Foreign-key cascades fire after the parent row is deleted — multi-
table DELETE can interact with cascades unexpectedly. - For huge DELETE, chunk it by id range to avoid
long-held locks.
What NOT to say: - Do not write DELETE FROM orders USING ... in MySQL — that's Postgres
syntax. - Do not assume LIMIT works with multi-table DELETE — it does not.
Common follow-up: "How do you delete rows from two tables in one statement?" — DELETE t1, t2
FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON ... WHERE .... Both tables lose matching rows in one atomic operation.
DELETE o FROM orders o
JOIN fraud_flags f ON f.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE f.confirmed = 1;
Q442 · Multi-Table DELETE
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Walmart Labs · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you actually use multi-table DELETE, and what are the risks?
The 30-second answer: Multi-table DELETE removes matching rows from multiple tables in one
statement, useful for cleaning related rows without foreign-key cascades — for example, archiving an
order and its line items together. Risks: easy to delete more than you meant if the JOIN matches
unexpectedly.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Use case: an orders table and a line_items table without ON
DELETE CASCADE — when deleting old orders, you need to delete both atomically. DELETE o, li
FROM orders o JOIN line_items li ON li.order_id = o.id WHERE o.created_at
< .... 2. Why not use cascades — cascades are great but can be surprising; explicit multi-table
DELETE makes the intent visible in the query log. 3. Risk: a typo in the JOIN (o.id = li.order_id
vs o.id = li.id) can either delete nothing or delete too much. Test with SELECT first. 4. Be ready
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 458 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 459
for the audit-trail follow-up — capture pre-image with OUTPUT INTO (SQL Server) or
DELETE...RETURNING (Postgres) into an audit table.
Edge cases to mention: - In Postgres, multi-table DELETE is not directly supported — use a CTE with
DELETE...RETURNING and a follow-up DELETE. - In MySQL, the alias list in 
DELETE a, b FROM ... controls which tables get rows removed. - If one of the multi-table
DELETEs would orphan FK children, the whole statement aborts.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume multi-table DELETE is in the SQL standard — it is not; it's a MySQL
extension. - Do not skip the test SELECT — multi-table DELETE typos have caused production data
loss.
Common follow-up: "How do you do this in Postgres?" — Two DELETEs in one transaction, or a CTE
chain: WITH d AS (DELETE FROM line_items WHERE order_id IN (SELECT id FROM
orders WHERE ...) RETURNING order_id) DELETE FROM orders WHERE id IN (SELECT
order_id FROM d);.
-- MySQL
DELETE o, li FROM orders o
JOIN line_items li ON li.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.created_at < '2024-01-01';
Q443 · INSERT ... SELECT with Column Transformation
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, ETL teams · Topic: DML
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you copy data from one table to another while transforming columns?
The 30-second answer: INSERT INTO target (col1, col2) SELECT expr1, expr2 FROM
source WHERE ... — the SELECT can include arbitrary expressions, casts, joins and CASE
statements. Standard SQL, supported everywhere.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Use case: snapshot a customers table into 
customer_archive with PII masked. INSERT INTO customer_archive (id, name_masked,
email_masked) SELECT id, LEFT(name, 1) || '***', SUBSTRING(email FROM '@.*$')
FROM customers WHERE active = false;. 2. Mention casting — 
INSERT INTO t (i) SELECT col::int FROM src (Postgres) or CAST(col AS INT)
(portable). 3. Multi-table SELECT — INSERT...SELECT can pull from joins, aggregations, CTEs. 4. Be
ready for the volume question — for very large copies, use COPY (Postgres) or 
INSERT ... SELECT in chunks to avoid bloat.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 459 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 460
Edge cases to mention: - Column order in the INSERT list and the SELECT list must match — easy to
swap by mistake. - Default values fill in for any unlisted columns. - For self-INSERT (INSERT INTO t
SELECT * FROM t WHERE ...), make sure the WHERE clause doesn't include rows already inserted
— can loop.
What NOT to say: - Do not match by name — INSERT...SELECT matches by position only. - Do not
insert without the column list in production — schema changes can silently misalign columns.
Common follow-up: "How do you do this incrementally, only new rows?" — Add WHERE NOT EXISTS
(SELECT 1 FROM target WHERE target.id = source.id) or use ON CONFLICT DO
NOTHING.
INSERT INTO customer_archive (id, name_masked, archived_at)
SELECT id, LEFT(name, 1) || '***', NOW()
FROM customers WHERE active = false AND last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '2 years';
Q444 · Atomic Increment Without Read-Then-Update Race
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: UPSERT
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I'm maintaining a counter — page views per article. Two requests increment it at the same time.
How do I avoid the race?
The 30-second answer: Never read-then-update from the application. Use a single atomic SQL
statement — UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE key = 'foo'. The database handles
concurrent increments correctly because the UPDATE acquires a row lock and reads-modifies-writes
within one statement.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the anti-pattern: app code reads 
SELECT n FROM counters WHERE key='foo', adds 1 in application memory, writes back 
UPDATE counters SET n = $new WHERE key = 'foo'. Under concurrency, two sessions can
both read N, both write N+1, losing one increment. 2. The fix is one statement: 
UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE key = 'foo'. The database serialises the row-level
updates via row locks — no lost increments. 3. Combined with upsert: INSERT INTO counters
(key, n) VALUES ('foo', 1) ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET n = counters.n +
1; — works whether the row exists or not, atomically. 4. Be ready for the high-traffic follow-up — for
very hot counters, even row locks bottleneck; use sharding (split the counter into N rows by random key
suffix and sum at read time) or write to a queue and batch-aggregate.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 460 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 461
Edge cases to mention: - In MySQL: INSERT INTO counters (key, n) VALUES ('foo', 1)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE n = n + 1; — same semantics. - For very hot rows, even row-level
locking is a bottleneck — consider sharded counters or Redis INCR with periodic DB flush. - If you need
to know the new value after the increment, add RETURNING n (Postgres) — atomic read-and-modify.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use SERIALIZABLE isolation" — way too heavy and still doesn't fix the
application-side read-then-update if you're using two separate statements. - Do not say "use SELECT
FOR UPDATE then UPDATE" — that works but is two statements where one would do.
Common follow-up: "At 10k QPS on the same counter, is n = n + 1 still good?" — No, you'll
bottleneck on the row lock. Shard: write (key, shard) -> n for 16 random shards per key, sum at
read time. Standard high-scale pattern.
-- Atomic, race-free, even with concurrent callers
INSERT INTO counters (key, n) VALUES ('article_42', 1)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET n = counters.n + 1
RETURNING n;
Chapter 10, Part C — Modern Aggregation & NULL Handling
This part picks up the modern aggregation toolkit — GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE, the 
FILTER clause, ANY_VALUE, the array/JSON aggregate family — and then walks through the NULL
idioms that interviewers love to set traps with. The aggregation side is where senior candidates show
they can collapse three UNION ALL blocks into one query that the planner only scans once. The NULL
side is where careers get derailed: NOT IN with a NULL, three-valued logic in WHERE, the IS
DISTINCT FROM operator that nobody teaches but everyone tests. Twenty-eight questions, each one
battle-tested in real Indian interview rounds — read them slowly, because every one of these has a
"gotcha" answer that the panel is hoping you'll trip over.
Q445 · GROUPING SETS — One Query, Multiple GROUP BYs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan India, Razorpay · Topic: Modern
Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want one query that returns sales totals grouped by region, separately by category, and a grand
total — all in one result set. How would you write it without using three UNION ALL blocks?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 461 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 462
The 30-second answer: Use GROUPING SETS inside the GROUP BY clause — each parenthesised
set defines one grouping level, and an empty () set produces the grand total. The optimizer scans the
base table once instead of three times.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem: three different aggregations from the same fact
table is a textbook GROUPING SETS use case. 2. Write GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((region),
(category), ()) — that gives one row per region, one per category, and one grand total. 3. The
columns that aren't in a particular grouping set come back as NULL — that's the standard SQL
behaviour and it's what GROUPING() exists to disambiguate later. 4. Mention the win: a single
sequential scan with hash aggregation, versus three full table scans for three UNION blocks.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, DB2, Snowflake, BigQuery all support
GROUPING SETS. MySQL does not — you'd fall back to UNION ALL there until MySQL adds it. - The
NULLs returned for non-grouped columns can collide with real data NULLs — that's exactly what 
GROUPING() and GROUPING_ID() solve in the next questions. - ORDER BY on a GROUPING
SETS result is tricky because of those NULLs — usually you sort with GROUPING() first to push
subtotals to the bottom.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim GROUPING SETS is just syntactic sugar for UNION ALL — the
execution plan is genuinely different and much cheaper. - Do not forget the empty () set — without it
you don't get the grand total row.
Common follow-up: "Compare GROUPING SETS to running three queries and combining them in the
application layer." — One round-trip, one scan, one consistent snapshot of the data versus three of each.
SELECT region, category, SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM orders
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((region), (category), ());
Q446 · ROLLUP — Hierarchical Subtotals
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Goldman, Target · Topic: Modern Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want sales broken down by region, then country within region, then city within country — with
subtotals at each level and a grand total. Write that in one query.
The 30-second answer: Use GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, country, city). ROLLUP generates
the hierarchical sequence (region, country, city), (region, country), (region), and () — exactly the four levels
you need.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 462 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 463
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define ROLLUP: it's a shortcut for a specific GROUPING SETS
pattern — strip rightmost columns one at a time until you reach the empty set. 2. ROLLUP(a, b, c)
expands to GROUPING SETS ((a, b, c), (a, b), (a), ()) — emphasise that it is
hierarchical, not all combinations. 3. Order matters: ROLLUP(country, region) would not make
geographic sense because country is the wider bucket — list from broadest to narrowest. 4. This is the
standard tool for a financial summary: branch → region → country → grand total.
Edge cases to mention: - ROLLUP is in the SQL standard since SQL:1999 — Postgres, Oracle, SQL
Server, MySQL 8, DB2, Snowflake all support it. - The grand-total row has NULL in every grouped
column — same disambiguation problem as GROUPING SETS, solved with GROUPING(). - ROLLUP can
be combined with regular columns: GROUP BY year, ROLLUP(region, city) rolls up only the
geography axis.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse ROLLUP with CUBE — ROLLUP is hierarchical, CUBE is every
combination. Mixing them up tags you as a beginner. - Do not write three separate SUM ... GROUP
BY queries — that's exactly what ROLLUP exists to replace.
Common follow-up: "What is the relationship between the number of columns in ROLLUP and the
number of grouping sets generated?" — N+1 grouping sets for N columns.
SELECT region, country, city, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, country, city);
Q447 · CUBE — Every Combination of Dimensions
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Modern Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does CUBE do, and when would you reach for it over ROLLUP?
The 30-second answer: CUBE(a, b, c) generates every possible grouping combination — 2^N
grouping sets for N columns. Use it for BI dashboards where the analyst slices by every dimension; use
ROLLUP when there's a natural hierarchy.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Spell out the expansion: CUBE(a, b) is GROUPING SETS ((a,
b), (a), (b), ()) — four sets for two columns, eight for three. 2. The classic use case: an OLAP-
style summary report where users want to slice sales by region, by category, by region+category, and
overall — all in one trip. 3. Compare to ROLLUP: ROLLUP gives N+1 sets, CUBE gives 2^N — CUBE is
exponentially more expensive on wide cube definitions. 4. In practice CUBE over four or more columns
gets expensive fast (16+ aggregation groups) — limit dimensionality or partition the data.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 463 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 464
Edge cases to mention: - Supported in Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, DB2, MySQL 8.0+, Snowflake —
same support matrix as ROLLUP. - A CUBE of three boolean dimensions generates 8 grouping sets,
which is fine; a CUBE of seven dimensions is 128, which the planner will hate. - Mixing GROUPING
SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE is allowed by the standard: 
GROUP BY a, ROLLUP(b, c), CUBE(d, e) — useful but always check your dialect.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume CUBE is "better" than ROLLUP — they answer different questions. -
Do not run CUBE over a dozen columns and complain about performance; the cost is in the spec.
Common follow-up: "For CUBE over four dimensions, how many grouping sets are generated?" — 2^4
= 16.
SELECT region, category, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY CUBE(region, category);
Q448 · GROUPING() — Telling Data NULL from Rollup NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, Walmart Labs, Razorpay · Topic: Modern Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When you use ROLLUP, the subtotal rows have NULL in the rolled-up columns. But your 
region column also has genuine NULLs for rows where region wasn't recorded. How do you
tell them apart?
The 30-second answer: Use the GROUPING(column) function. It returns 1 when the NULL was
injected by ROLLUP/CUBE/GROUPING SETS, and 0 when the NULL came from the underlying data.
Wrap it in a CASE to label subtotals correctly.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define the ambiguity: a row with region = NULL could mean
"data didn't have a region" or "this is the subtotal across all regions" — they collide visually. 2. Show the
disambiguation pattern: CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'All regions' ELSE
COALESCE(region, 'Unknown') END. 3. Stress that this is what makes ROLLUP and CUBE
actually usable in reports — without GROUPING(), readers can't tell totals from missing data. 4. Be ready
to chain it with COALESCE for the rare third case: actual NULL data that you want to display as
"Unknown".
Edge cases to mention: - GROUPING() takes one column argument; for multi-column checks use
GROUPING_ID (next question). - Supported in Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, DB2, MySQL 8.0+ — the
support matrix matches ROLLUP/CUBE. - It only makes sense inside a query with GROUPING SETS,
ROLLUP, or CUBE — using it elsewhere returns 0 for everything.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 464 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 465
What NOT to say: - Do not try to detect subtotal rows by checking for NULL — that's exactly the bug
GROUPING() was invented to prevent. - Do not skip GROUPING() because "my data has no NULLs" —
schemas change, and reports break silently when they do.
Common follow-up: "Order the result so subtotals appear at the bottom of each group." — ORDER BY
GROUPING(region), region puts data rows first, then subtotals.
SELECT
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'All regions' ELSE region END AS region,
  SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP(region);
Q449 · GROUPING_ID — Bitmap Across Multiple Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: JP Morgan India, Target, Snowflake-style rounds · Topic: Modern
Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If I CUBE over three columns, how do I tell which specific combination each result row represents
— without writing three separate GROUPING() calls?
The 30-second answer: GROUPING_ID(a, b, c) returns a single integer whose binary digits are
the GROUPING bits for each column. So GROUPING_ID=0 means all three columns are real data,
GROUPING_ID=7 (binary 111) is the grand total, and GROUPING_ID=4 (binary 100) means a is
aggregated but b and c are real.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the bit layout: leftmost argument is the highest bit. 
GROUPING_ID(region, country, city) returns 0 for (R, C, Ci), 1 for (R, C, total), 2 for (R, total,
Ci), and so on up to 7 for the grand total. 2. Demonstrate the typical use: filter or label subtotal rows by
integer comparison instead of chained GROUPING() calls. 3. Stress that the bit order is by argument
position — get it wrong and you'll mislabel every row in the report. 4. Mention dialect quirks: SQL Server
uses GROUPING_ID with the same semantics; Oracle pioneered it.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres added GROUPING_ID functionality through GROUPING(a, b, c)
returning the bitmap directly — slight syntax difference but identical effect. - MySQL 8.0+ supports it as
well; check your specific version. - The bitmap interpretation makes HAVING filters very clean: HAVING
GROUPING_ID(region, city) = 0 keeps only the lowest-level rows.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 465 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 466
What NOT to say: - Do not memorise specific integers in interviews — explain the bit-position
reasoning, that's what they're testing. - Do not confuse GROUPING_ID with GROUPING — the former
takes multiple columns and returns an integer, the latter takes one and returns 0 or 1.
Common follow-up: "Why is this more useful than chained GROUPING() calls?" — Single integer
comparison is cheaper to write, cheaper to index in derived tables, and unambiguous in audit reports.
SELECT region, country, city, GROUPING_ID(region, country, city) AS level, SUM(amount)
FROM orders
GROUP BY CUBE(region, country, city);
Q450 · HAVING with GROUPING SETS
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Wells Fargo, Razorpay · Topic: Modern Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want a CUBE report but only the subtotal rows, not the leaf rows. How do I filter that out?
The 30-second answer: Use HAVING GROUPING_ID(...) > 0, which keeps any row where at
least one column has been aggregated away. Filtering on grouping-set membership belongs in HAVING
because it operates on grouped output, not raw rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with where the filter belongs — WHERE runs before grouping,
HAVING after, so anything involving GROUPING/GROUPING_ID must be in HAVING. 2. Show three
useful filters: HAVING GROUPING_ID(region, city) = 0 for leaf rows only, > 0 for subtotals
only, = 3 for grand total only. 3. Combine with normal HAVING predicates: HAVING SUM(amount) >
100000 AND GROUPING(region) = 0 — keeps high-value rows only for real regions, not the rollup
row. 4. This is the standard pattern in BI dashboards where the UI wants only "rollup rows above a
threshold".
Edge cases to mention: - WHERE clause cannot reference GROUPING() because the grouping hasn't
happened yet — common syntax error. - ORDER BY with GROUPING_ID is the easiest way to put
subtotals at the bottom of each section. - In Postgres you can also use the boolean-returning
GROUPING(col) directly in HAVING.
What NOT to say: - Do not try to filter subtotals in WHERE — the engine will reject it or worse silently
drop the aggregated rows. - Do not use complex CASE expressions when GROUPING_ID does the job in
one comparison.
Common follow-up: "Show me only the rows where the grand total of amount is greater than 10 lakh."
— HAVING GROUPING_ID(...) = 3 AND SUM(amount) > 1000000.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 466 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 467
SELECT region, city, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY CUBE(region, city)
HAVING GROUPING_ID(region, city) > 0;
Q451 · FILTER Clause — Cleaner Conditional Aggregation
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Postgres-heavy shops · Topic: Modern
Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Show me how the FILTER clause replaces SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN amount END)
and tell me why it's preferred.
The 30-second answer: SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') is the SQL standard
way to write conditional aggregation. It's shorter, more readable, and on Postgres often slightly faster
because the planner can push the filter down.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the side-by-side: SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN
amount END) versus SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status='paid'). Same result, half the
noise. 2. Explain why interviewers care: it signals familiarity with modern standard SQL (added in
SQL:2003, common since 2010). 3. The big win is in pivot-style queries with five or six different per-
status totals — the FILTER version reads like a table of definitions, the CASE version reads like
obfuscated C. 4. Be ready to discuss support: Postgres has it natively, SQLite added it in 3.30, Oracle
and SQL Server still need the CASE form, MySQL 8 supports it through certain functions only.
Edge cases to mention: - FILTER works on any aggregate: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...), 
AVG(...) FILTER (WHERE ...), even STRING_AGG(...) FILTER (WHERE ...). - The
FILTER predicate sees raw rows (it runs before aggregation) — you cannot reference aggregate results
inside it. - In dialects without FILTER, the equivalent rewrite is mechanical: replace agg(x) FILTER
(WHERE p) with agg(CASE WHEN p THEN x END).
What NOT to say: - Do not say FILTER is "Postgres-specific" — it's been SQL standard for over two
decades. - Do not nest FILTER inside FILTER — it does not chain; one FILTER per aggregate.
Common follow-up: "What's the FILTER rewrite of COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) WHERE
region='South'?" — COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FILTER (WHERE region='South').
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 467 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 468
SELECT
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid_total,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refund_total,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed_count
FROM orders;
Q452 · FILTER vs CASE in SUM — Performance and Readability
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Cred · Topic: Modern Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Is there any real performance difference between SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE
status='paid') and SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN amount END)?
The 30-second answer: On most engines they produce the same plan and the same speed. The win for
FILTER is readability and standardisation — the planner treats both equivalently after parsing. Choose
FILTER when your dialect supports it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the equivalence: both forms produce identical EXPLAIN output
on Postgres 12+ for simple cases. 2. The readability argument matters in code review — six FILTER
clauses for six per-status totals reads cleanly; six CASE expressions become a wall of nested conditions.
3. The honest caveat: in some older optimizers, FILTER allowed planner shortcuts that the CASE-form
missed — modern optimizers have closed the gap. 4. Anticipate the gotcha: when the predicate is
complex (joins, subqueries), FILTER and CASE may still differ — benchmark on your real schema.
Edge cases to mention: - For COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...), the equivalent CASE is 
COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END) — note that 1, not TRUE, because COUNT ignores NULLs
and TRUE-vs-FALSE wouldn't reduce. - FILTER plays nicely with window functions: SUM(x) FILTER
(WHERE ...) OVER (...) is supported on Postgres. - Some optimizers (Snowflake, BigQuery) only
honour FILTER through partial native support — check your specific version before assuming.
What NOT to say: - Do not assert "FILTER is always faster" — measurable differences are rare on
modern engines. - Do not assert "they're identical" without the caveat — they can differ on edge cases.
Common follow-up: "When would CASE be the only option?" — On dialects without FILTER support
(Oracle, SQL Server, older MySQL).
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 468 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 469
-- FILTER form
SELECT region, SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid
FROM orders GROUP BY region;
-- Equivalent CASE form
SELECT region, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN amount END) AS paid
FROM orders GROUP BY region;
Q453 · ANY_VALUE — Picking a Representative Without MIN/MAX Hack
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Razorpay, BigQuery shops · Topic: Modern
Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want one row per user with their latest order's region, but region is not in the GROUP BY. I
don't care which region — any will do. How do I write that cleanly?
The 30-second answer: Use ANY_VALUE(region). It tells the engine "pick any value from the
group, I don't care which" — without the MIN/MAX hack and without ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY errors.
It's in MySQL 8.0+, Postgres 16, BigQuery, Snowflake, and SQL:2023.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Spell out the problem: in strict GROUP BY mode, you can't select a
non-aggregated column unless it's a group key — but sometimes you genuinely don't care which value
comes back. 2. Show the old workaround: MIN(region) or MAX(region) — which signals to
readers that you're picking a deterministic value, even though you don't care. 3. ANY_VALUE expresses
intent — "any one is fine" — which is documentation as well as semantics. 4. Mention performance:
ANY_VALUE can be slightly cheaper than MIN/MAX because the engine doesn't need to sort or
compare; it grabs the first value it sees.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres only added ANY_VALUE in 16 — before that, the idiom was MIN/
MAX or a window function with LIMIT. - BigQuery and Snowflake had it earlier than the mainstream
relational engines. - ANY_VALUE on a strict aggregation function still requires that the column actually
has values; on empty groups it returns NULL just like MIN.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use MIN, it does the same thing" — it does, but ANY_VALUE is more
expressive and may be cheaper. - Do not assume ANY_VALUE is deterministic — by definition it's not,
and that's the point.
Common follow-up: "What happens if I use ANY_VALUE on Postgres 15?" — It doesn't exist; you'd get
a function-not-found error. Use MIN/MAX as the portable fallback.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 469 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 470
SELECT user_id, ANY_VALUE(region) AS some_region, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id;
Q454 · ARRAY_AGG, JSONB_AGG, STRING_AGG — Collecting into Composites
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Flipkart, Postgres shops · Topic: Modern Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I want one row per customer with a list of all their order IDs. How would you collect them — array,
JSON or comma-separated string — and what changes?
The 30-second answer: ARRAY_AGG(order_id) returns a native array, JSONB_AGG(order_id)
returns a JSON array, STRING_AGG(order_id::text, ',') returns a CSV string. Pick array for
further SQL processing, JSON for API payloads, string for human display.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lay out the three idioms — each one solves the same shape problem
with a different output type. 2. ARRAY_AGG is the workhorse on Postgres for collecting into arrays,
which you can then unnest, slice or pass to PL/pgSQL. 3. JSONB_AGG is what you want when the next
consumer is an HTTP API — no string parsing needed downstream. 4. STRING_AGG is for reports and
CSV exports — the separator is a required argument, and you usually cast to text first.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL has GROUP_CONCAT instead of STRING_AGG with a slightly
different syntax: GROUP_CONCAT(col SEPARATOR ','). SQL Server got STRING_AGG in 2017. - All
three skip NULLs by default — to include NULLs as 'NULL' literally, COALESCE them inside the
aggregate. - STRING_AGG has a hard length limit on MySQL's GROUP_CONCAT (default 1024 bytes) —
bump group_concat_max_len or move to a different aggregate.
What NOT to say: - Do not concatenate manually with || and a subquery — that's an antipattern
when STRING_AGG exists. - Do not use STRING_AGG for data that another query will need to parse
back into rows; use ARRAY_AGG or JSON instead.
Common follow-up: "What if I want each customer's orders as an array of (id, amount) tuples?" — 
JSONB_AGG(JSONB_BUILD_OBJECT('id', id, 'amount', amount)).
SELECT
  customer_id,
  ARRAY_AGG(order_id) AS order_ids,
  STRING_AGG(order_id::text, ', ') AS order_csv
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
