Q455 · ARRAY_AGG ORDER BY — Controlling Element Order
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Postgres shops, Razorpay, Swiggy · Topic: Modern Aggregation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Your ARRAY_AGG result comes back in random order. The API contract says it must be sorted by
order date descending. How do you guarantee that?
The 30-second answer: Use ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) — the
ORDER BY clause goes inside the aggregate. Without it the order is implementation-defined and can
change between runs.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule: in SQL standard, aggregate-internal ORDER BY is the
only way to guarantee element order in ARRAY_AGG, JSONB_AGG, STRING_AGG. 2. Without ORDER
BY, the planner picks whatever order is convenient — often insertion order, but never guaranteed. 3. The
ORDER BY can use any column, not just the aggregated one: ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY
order_date DESC) orders the array elements by a different column entirely. 4. Combine with FILTER
for conditional ordered aggregation: ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY order_date DESC)
FILTER (WHERE status='paid').
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL's GROUP_CONCAT has its own ORDER BY syntax inside the
function — same idea, slightly different keyword placement. - ORDER BY inside an aggregate is allowed
by the SQL standard since SQL:2003 and supported on Postgres, SQL Server (STRING_AGG WITHIN
GROUP), Oracle (LISTAGG WITHIN GROUP), DB2. - Window aggregates with frame clauses give you
another way to order results, but inside ARRAY_AGG the internal ORDER BY is the right tool.
What NOT to say: - Do not rely on the order of rows fed into the aggregate — that's the "input order is
preserved" myth, and it's not guaranteed by the standard. - Do not sort after aggregation with 
array_sort(ARRAY_AGG(...)) when the internal ORDER BY does the job in one step.
Common follow-up: "Now sort by amount descending, breaking ties by order date." — 
ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY amount DESC, order_date).
SELECT customer_id, ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS recent_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
Q456 · ARRAY_AGG DISTINCT — Deduplicating Inside the Aggregate
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Postgres shops, Cred, Meesho · Topic: Modern Aggregation
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 471 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 472
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Each customer might order the same category multiple times. I want one row per customer with a
list of distinct categories. How?
The 30-second answer: ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT category) does it in one step — DISTINCT is a
modifier on the aggregate, not a subquery construct. Same idea works with STRING_AGG,
JSONB_AGG, COUNT, SUM.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain that DISTINCT inside an aggregate eliminates duplicate input
values before collecting — much cleaner than aggregating an already-deduped subquery. 2. Show the
side-by-side: ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT category) versus 
(SELECT ARRAY_AGG(category) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category ...) sub) — the
inline form is far shorter and the planner usually generates the same hashing. 3. Combining DISTINCT
with ORDER BY: the standard requires that the ORDER BY expression be in the DISTINCT list — 
ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT category ORDER BY category) is fine, ORDER BY
some_other_column is not. 4. Useful with COUNT too: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is the classic
distinct-count idiom.
Edge cases to mention: - DISTINCT inside the aggregate can be expensive on large groups — it needs
to maintain a hash set per group. - Some engines (BigQuery) have approximate alternatives like
APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT for billion-row distinct counts. - DISTINCT with FILTER: COUNT(DISTINCT
user_id) FILTER (WHERE region='South') — works on engines that support both.
What NOT to say: - Do not write ARRAY_AGG(category) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ...) as
your first answer — the inline DISTINCT is shorter and idiomatic. - Do not assume DISTINCT preserves
order — without ORDER BY it doesn't.
Common follow-up: "How does this perform on a customer with a million orders?" — Worst case O(n
log n) for sort-based DISTINCT, O(n) for hash-based; check EXPLAIN to see which the planner chose.
SELECT customer_id, ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT category ORDER BY category) AS categories
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
Q457 · IS DISTINCT FROM — NULL-Safe Comparison
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Postgres shops · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 472 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 473
WHERE a <> b doesn't return rows where one side is NULL. How do you write "different value
or one is NULL" in pure SQL?
The 30-second answer: Use a IS DISTINCT FROM b. It returns TRUE when values differ, and
treats two NULLs as equal (so it returns FALSE), and one NULL versus a value as different (TRUE). It's
NULL-safe by definition.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the problem: standard <> returns UNKNOWN whenever
a NULL is involved, and UNKNOWN is filtered out by WHERE. 2. So WHERE old_value <>
new_value silently misses every row where one of them is NULL — that's the change-tracking bug
that catches every junior dev. 3. IS DISTINCT FROM is the SQL standard NULL-safe inequality: 
NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 5 → TRUE, NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL → FALSE, 3 IS
DISTINCT FROM 5 → TRUE. 4. The opposite IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is NULL-safe equality —
covered in the next question.
Edge cases to mention: - Supported in Postgres, SQL Server 2022, Oracle (since 12c), DB2, SQLite
3.32+. MySQL uses the <=> operator with inverted semantics (<=> is NULL-safe equality, so NOT (a
<=> b) is the equivalent of IS DISTINCT FROM). - Inside CHECK constraints and partial indexes, IS
DISTINCT FROM is often the only correct comparison. - For trigger-based audit tables, IF OLD.x IS
DISTINCT FROM NEW.x THEN ... is the textbook pattern.
What NOT to say: - Do not pad with COALESCE to dodge the NULL problem — COALESCE(a, '')
<> COALESCE(b, '') breaks when '' is a real value in your domain. - Do not say <> "ignores
NULLs" — it returns UNKNOWN, which the WHERE clause then filters out. The distinction matters when
interviewers probe deeper.
Common follow-up: "How do you spell IS DISTINCT FROM in MySQL?" — NOT a <=> b, where 
<=> is NULL-safe equals.
-- Find rows where the new value differs from the old (including NULL transitions)
SELECT id FROM audit
WHERE old_status IS DISTINCT FROM new_status;
Q458 · IS NOT DISTINCT FROM — NULL-Safe Equality
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Postgres shops, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 473 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 474
I'm joining on a nullable column and I want NULL=NULL to be a match. How do I write that in a
join condition?
The 30-second answer: ON a.col IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.col. This is NULL-safe equality:
two NULLs match, two equal values match, mismatched values don't, NULL and non-NULL don't.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Restate the SQL default: a.col = b.col returns UNKNOWN
when either side is NULL, so the join never matches NULL-to-NULL. 2. Sometimes that's wrong: in a
"category mapping" table where NULL means "any category", you genuinely want NULL on both sides to
match. 3. IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the SQL standard way. It's a single operator, no COALESCE
tricks needed. 4. In MySQL it's spelled a.col <=> b.col — same semantics, different syntax.
Edge cases to mention: - Joining on IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is usually a hint that your schema
has too many nullable join columns — consider making them NOT NULL with a sentinel value if matching
is part of the contract. - The optimizer in Postgres can use indexes on IS NOT DISTINCT FROM
joins, but only in newer versions (PG 16+); older versions fall back to a full scan. - Partial unique indexes
often use this idiom: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL — that handles
NULL-safe uniqueness without IS DISTINCT FROM in the condition.
What NOT to say: - Do not write ON COALESCE(a.col, -1) = COALESCE(b.col, -1) as your
default — it works but breaks the moment -1 is a real value. - Do not assert that = joins NULLs — it
never does in standard SQL.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between IS NOT DISTINCT FROM and =?" — They're
identical for non-NULL values; they differ only when either side is NULL.
SELECT a.id, b.id
FROM table_a a
JOIN table_b b ON a.region IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.region;
Q459 · COALESCE — First Non-NULL, Multiple Args, Short-Circuit
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Accenture · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What does COALESCE do and how is it different from NVL or IFNULL?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 474 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 475
The 30-second answer: COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) returns the first non-NULL argument. It takes
any number of arguments (NVL and IFNULL take exactly two), is in the SQL standard, and short-circuits
— once it finds a non-NULL, it stops evaluating the rest.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Cover the basics: any number of arguments, returns the first non-
NULL, returns NULL only if all arguments are NULL. 2. Stress short-circuiting: in 
COALESCE(cheap_col, expensive_subquery()), the subquery isn't run when cheap_col is
not NULL — important for performance. 3. Compare with vendor-specific functions: NVL (Oracle) is
exactly two args, IFNULL (MySQL/SQLite) is also two, ISNULL (SQL Server) is two, COALESCE is the
portable n-ary option. 4. The "default value" use case: COALESCE(discount_pct, 0) so that
downstream math doesn't propagate NULL.
Edge cases to mention: - All arguments must be type-compatible — COALESCE('abc', 5) errors
on strict engines. - COALESCE with side-effecting functions (sequences, random) is a known footgun
because of short-circuiting; the un-evaluated ones don't fire. - For default columns in INSERT, prefer the
DEFAULT clause over COALESCE in application code — the DB enforces it consistently.
What NOT to say: - Do not say COALESCE is "the same as IFNULL but with more arguments" — that's
only mostly true; the standard guarantees apply only to COALESCE. - Do not call it "ko-uh-LESS" — it's
"co-uh-LESS" but pronunciation rarely matters; what matters is correct usage.
Common follow-up: "Write a query that gives every order a display name: order's nickname if set, else
customer's name, else 'Anonymous'." — COALESCE(order_nickname, customer_name,
'Anonymous').
SELECT id, COALESCE(discount_pct, 0) AS discount, COALESCE(notes, comments, 'N/A') AS notes
FROM orders;
Q460 · NULLIF — Opposite of COALESCE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Wipro, Walmart Labs · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you reach for NULLIF, and what does it actually do?
The 30-second answer: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a = b, otherwise returns a. Classic use
case: avoid divide-by-zero with amount / NULLIF(quantity, 0) — when quantity is zero you get
NULL instead of an error.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the divide-by-zero idiom — that's the textbook NULLIF
use. 2. The general pattern: NULLIF normalises a sentinel value to NULL. NULLIF(country, '')
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 475 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 476
turns empty strings into proper NULLs before aggregation. 3. Pair it with COALESCE for clean defaults: 
COALESCE(NULLIF(notes, ''), 'No notes') — empty string becomes NULL, then COALESCE
substitutes the default. 4. SQL standard since SQL-92, supported everywhere.
Edge cases to mention: - NULLIF requires both arguments to be type-compatible — same rule as
COALESCE. - It's an inverse of sorts to COALESCE: COALESCE turns NULL into a default, NULLIF turns
a default into NULL. - For string normalisation across data imports, NULLIF(TRIM(col), '') is a
one-liner that catches both whitespace-only and empty cells.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse NULLIF with IFNULL — IFNULL is MySQL's COALESCE shortcut,
NULLIF is the standard "return NULL if equal" function. - Do not use NULLIF for floats with NULLIF(x,
0.0) and then expect it to catch values like 0.0000001 — equality is exact.
Common follow-up: "What's the result of NULLIF(NULL, NULL)?" — NULL, because NULL = NULL
is UNKNOWN, not TRUE.
-- Avoid divide-by-zero in average price per unit
SELECT order_id, amount / NULLIF(quantity, 0) AS unit_price
FROM order_lines;
Q461 · NVL, IFNULL, ISNULL, COALESCE — Vendor Comparison
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Multi-DB shops, GCCs, panel rounds · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through the difference between NVL, IFNULL, ISNULL and COALESCE — which one
should I use in new code?
The 30-second answer: Use COALESCE — it's SQL standard, takes any number of arguments, and
works on every engine. NVL is Oracle-only (two args), IFNULL is MySQL/SQLite (two args), ISNULL is
SQL Server (two args). They all do the "first non-NULL" job for two arguments, but COALESCE wins on
portability and flexibility.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lay out the four side by side: same semantics for two args, different
syntax, different vendor support. 2. Show the portability angle: COALESCE works everywhere, vendor
functions don't survive a migration. 3. SQL Server's ISNULL is a footgun: it returns the type of the first
argument, while COALESCE returns the highest-precedence type — ISNULL('abc', 5) errors
differently than COALESCE('abc', 5). 4. NVL has a sibling NVL2 (Oracle): NVL2(expr,
val_if_not_null, val_if_null) — handy but Oracle-specific.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 476 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 477
Edge cases to mention: - IFNULL in MySQL is just COALESCE with exactly two arguments — same
result, fewer characters. - ISNULL in SQL Server is distinct from the IS NULL predicate — they share
a name but do completely different things. - For type-strict engines, COALESCE applies standard type
unification; NVL/IFNULL/ISNULL apply vendor-specific rules.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "they're identical" — type handling differs, and SQL Server's ISNULL
behaviour bites in real production code. - Do not use vendor-specific functions in new code unless you're
locked to that vendor — COALESCE is the portable default.
Common follow-up: "What does NVL2 do?" — Oracle-only three-arg variant: returns the second arg if
the first is not NULL, the third if it is.
-- Portable
SELECT COALESCE(discount, 0) FROM orders;
-- Oracle
SELECT NVL(discount, 0) FROM orders;
-- MySQL
SELECT IFNULL(discount, 0) FROM orders;
-- SQL Server
SELECT ISNULL(discount, 0) FROM orders;
Q462 · Three-Valued Logic — TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Razorpay · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
SQL has three-valued logic. What's the third value and how does it propagate through AND, OR
and NOT?
The 30-second answer: The third value is UNKNOWN, returned whenever a comparison involves NULL. 
TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE. TRUE OR UNKNOWN =
TRUE. NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. WHERE clauses keep only TRUE rows, so UNKNOWN rows are
silently dropped.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the three values: TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN — UNKNOWN is
what x = NULL returns, what 5 > NULL returns, what every comparison with NULL returns. 2. AND
truth table: TRUE and TRUE = TRUE; TRUE and FALSE = FALSE; TRUE and UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN;
FALSE dominates AND. 3. OR truth table: FALSE or FALSE = FALSE; FALSE or TRUE = TRUE; FALSE or
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 477 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 478
UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN; TRUE dominates OR. 4. NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN — that's the one
most candidates forget.
Edge cases to mention: - WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. HAVING also keeps only TRUE rows. CHECK
constraints accept TRUE and UNKNOWN — both pass the check. - IF NOT (status = 'paid')
will not include rows with NULL status, because NULL becomes UNKNOWN, NOT UNKNOWN is
UNKNOWN, which isn't TRUE. - IS NULL and IS NOT NULL always return TRUE or FALSE, never
UNKNOWN — they're the safe predicates.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "NULL is falsy" — it's not, it's UNKNOWN, and that's a meaningfully
different behaviour. - Do not write WHERE status = NULL; it's always UNKNOWN, never matches.
Use IS NULL.
Common follow-up: "Why does NOT (NULL = NULL) not return TRUE?" — Because NULL = NULL
is UNKNOWN, and NOT UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, not TRUE.
-- Returns no rows even if every order has paid status (because of one NULL)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status != 'pending';  -- misses NULL rows
-- Safer
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'pending';
Q463 · NULL in WHERE — The Silent Exclusion Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cognizant, Wipro, Wells Fargo, Cred · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If status can be NULL and I write WHERE status != 'paid', what rows do I get back?
The 30-second answer: You get rows where status is exactly any value other than 'paid' — but NOT
rows where status is NULL. The comparison NULL != 'paid' evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE
drops everything except TRUE. The fix is WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'paid' or WHERE
status != 'paid' OR status IS NULL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Name the trap: developers often think != is "any other value,
including missing", but SQL is strict — NULL is filtered out. 2. The pattern is so common that audit
reports built on WHERE state != 'closed' silently miss every NULL-state row. 3. Three fixes: IS
DISTINCT FROM (SQL standard, NULL-safe), OR col IS NULL (verbose but portable), or make the
column NOT NULL with a sentinel like 'unknown' (best long-term). 4. The general lesson: every WHERE
filter on a nullable column needs a NULL-handling decision.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 478 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 479
Edge cases to mention: - Same trap exists in HAVING, ON clauses, CASE WHEN, anywhere the engine
evaluates a boolean. - Some engines have a "strict NULL" pragma that loudly errors on these — most
don't. - Code reviewers should treat every WHERE col != value as suspect until the nullability of 
col is known.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume != "includes NULLs" — it never does in standard SQL. - Do not
solve it with COALESCE to a sentinel value unless that sentinel is impossible in the real data domain.
Common follow-up: "What about WHERE status NOT IN ('paid', 'refunded')?" — Same
trap; NULL is excluded silently.
-- Misses NULL rows
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status != 'paid';
-- Correct, NULL-safe
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'paid';
Q464 · NULL in NOT IN — The Empty Result Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I wrote WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM blocked_users) and got
zero rows back even though most users aren't blocked. What's the bug?
The 30-second answer: Your blocked_users.user_id has at least one NULL. x NOT IN (1,
2, NULL) evaluates to x != 1 AND x != 2 AND x != NULL, and x != NULL is UNKNOWN,
so the whole AND chain is UNKNOWN, which WHERE drops. Switch to NOT EXISTS or filter NULLs
out of the subquery.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. This is the most famous NULL trap in SQL — every senior interviewer
asks it at some point. 2. Walk through the logic: 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) expands to 
5 != 1 AND 5 != 2 AND 5 != NULL. The last conjunct is UNKNOWN, dragging the whole AND
down to UNKNOWN. 3. The fix: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked_users b WHERE
b.user_id = u.id). EXISTS uses correlated lookup, which handles NULLs sensibly — a NULL in 
blocked_users.user_id simply doesn't match anything, it doesn't poison the predicate. 4.
Alternative fix: WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM blocked_users WHERE
user_id IS NOT NULL). Works, but you must remember to write it every time.
Edge cases to mention: - The trap doesn't fire for IN (only NOT IN) — x IN (1, 2, NULL)
returns TRUE for 1 and 2, UNKNOWN for everything else; UNKNOWN is dropped by WHERE, but the
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 479 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 480
matches still come through. - LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.col IS NULL is the third safe anti-
join idiom — slower in some plans but always correct. - If the subquery column is declared NOT NULL, 
NOT IN is safe — but don't rely on schema you can't see.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "this is a Postgres bug" — it's the SQL standard, every conforming
engine behaves this way. - Do not paper over it with COALESCE — NOT IN (SELECT
COALESCE(user_id, -1) FROM ...) is brittle and depends on the sentinel being impossible.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this anti-join using NOT EXISTS and explain why it's safer." — NOT
EXISTS uses a per-row correlated check, so a NULL on the right just doesn't match; it doesn't propagate
UNKNOWN.
-- Trap: returns 0 rows if blocked_users has a NULL user_id
SELECT id FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM blocked_users);
-- Safe
SELECT id FROM users u WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM blocked_users b WHERE b.user_id = u.id
);
Q465 · NULL in Foreign Key — Allowed but Tricky
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Schema-design rounds, Goldman, AmEx · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can a foreign key column be NULL? If yes, what does that mean?
The 30-second answer: Yes — a FK column can be NULL unless you also declare it NOT NULL. A
NULL FK means "no parent assigned yet" and is allowed by the FK constraint (NULLs don't need to
match a parent row). Interviewers love this because juniors often think every FK needs a parent.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule: the FK constraint checks "does this value exist in the
parent table OR is it NULL". NULL gets a free pass. 2. Use a realistic example: orders.coupon_id is
FK to coupons.id. Most orders have no coupon, so coupon_id is NULL — that's intentional and
correct. 3. To force every order to have a coupon, add NOT NULL to the column itself — the FK alone
won't enforce mandatoriness. 4. Composite FKs: if any component is NULL, the entire FK check is
skipped by default in standard SQL (MATCH SIMPLE behaviour) — there are MATCH FULL and MATCH
PARTIAL options, but most engines only implement SIMPLE.
Edge cases to mention: - ON DELETE SET NULL requires the FK column to be nullable — that's a
common reason to keep it NULL-able. - Some ORMs (Hibernate, ActiveRecord) default to making FKs
nullable, which then bites you in joins where you forgot to handle the NULL case. - Designing for "always
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 480 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 481
has a parent" usually means NOT NULL + FK + DEFAULT to a system row like 'no-coupon' to keep joins
predictable.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "FKs can't be NULL" — that's wrong unless the column is also NOT
NULL. - Do not assume MATCH FULL is the default — it isn't; MATCH SIMPLE is, and it accepts any
NULL in a composite key.
Common follow-up: "Why might I make a FK NOT NULL even if ORM defaults are NULL?" — Forces
every child row to have a parent at insert time; prevents orphans by design rather than by code
discipline.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  coupon_id BIGINT REFERENCES coupons(id)  -- nullable: most orders have no coupon
);
Q466 · NULL in Unique Constraint — Multiple NULLs Usually OK
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: SQL Server shops, schema-design rounds, Walmart Labs · Topic: NULL
Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
If I have a UNIQUE constraint on a nullable column, can multiple rows be NULL?
The 30-second answer: On Postgres, Oracle, MySQL, DB2, SQLite — yes, NULL is treated as
"unknown, distinct from all other NULLs", so any number of NULLs are allowed. On SQL Server (default)
— no, two NULLs collide. The difference is a notorious portability gotcha.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the standard view: SQL standard treats two NULLs as
distinct for uniqueness purposes — that's the Postgres/Oracle/MySQL behaviour. 2. SQL Server is the
outlier: its UNIQUE constraint treats NULL as a single value, so two NULL rows violate the constraint.
Workaround: filtered index WHERE col IS NOT NULL. 3. Postgres 15 added the NULLS NOT
DISTINCT option to UNIQUE constraints — opt in if you want SQL Server's behaviour on Postgres. 4.
The implication: if you're migrating from SQL Server to Postgres (or vice versa), every UNIQUE on a
nullable column needs review.
Edge cases to mention: - Composite uniqueness has the same NULL-distinct rule per row: (a, b)
UNIQUE allows (1, NULL) twice on standard engines. - Partial indexes on WHERE col IS NOT
NULL are a portable workaround for SQL Server semantics. - ORMs sometimes generate "uniqueness
validations" in application code that don't match DB behaviour — always test at the DB level.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 481 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 482
What NOT to say: - Do not say "UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs" without the SQL Server caveat —
that's exactly the trap. - Do not assume an ORM-level uniqueness check is equivalent to a DB-level
UNIQUE — race conditions and NULL handling diverge.
Common follow-up: "How do I get SQL Server's behaviour on Postgres 15?" — UNIQUE (col)
NULLS NOT DISTINCT.
-- Standard SQL (Postgres default): multiple NULLs allowed
CREATE TABLE customers (email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (NULL), (NULL);  -- OK on Postgres, fails on SQL Server
Q467 · NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST — Controlling NULL Sort Position
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Reporting-heavy shops, Razorpay, Swiggy · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When I ORDER BY amount DESC, where do the NULL amounts end up — top or bottom?
The 30-second answer: It depends on the engine. Postgres puts NULLs last in ASC and first in DESC
by default. Oracle does the same. MySQL puts NULLs first in ASC and last in DESC — the opposite.
SQL Server puts NULLs first in ASC by default. Use the explicit NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST to
control it portably.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Acknowledge the inconsistency upfront — interviewers love this one
because the defaults differ across vendors. 2. The standard ORDER BY col [ASC|DESC] [NULLS
FIRST|NULLS LAST] lets you spell it out. 3. The most common ask in reports: "show NULL values at
the bottom regardless of sort direction" — ORDER BY amount DESC NULLS LAST does that on
Postgres, Oracle, SQLite. 4. MySQL didn't support NULLS FIRST/LAST syntax until version 8.0 — the
workaround is ORDER BY col IS NULL, col (or IS NOT NULL, col for the inverse).
Edge cases to mention: - Index ordering: if you have an index on col DESC NULLS LAST, Postgres
can use it for that exact sort but not for col DESC NULLS FIRST. - Combining sort directions: 
ORDER BY priority ASC NULLS LAST, created_at DESC — mix and match per column. - For
paginated lists with ORDER BY created_at DESC, putting NULLs last keeps the "still being
processed" rows at the bottom of every page consistently.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume NULLs sort to a specific position — different engines disagree. - Do
not rely on the default ordering for production reports — always spell it out.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 482 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 483
Common follow-up: "How would you sort by amount descending, NULLs at the bottom, on MySQL
5.7?" — ORDER BY amount IS NULL, amount DESC — the first key pushes NULLs after non-
NULL rows.
SELECT id, amount FROM orders
ORDER BY amount DESC NULLS LAST;
Q468 · NULL in JOIN — Only Matches Explicit IS NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Most product companies, Razorpay, Swiggy · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Two tables both have a region column that can be NULL. If I JOIN ON a.region =
b.region, do rows with NULL on both sides match?
The 30-second answer: No. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, and JOIN ON keeps only TRUE
rows. Two NULL regions don't match each other. If you want them to match, use IS NOT DISTINCT
FROM (Postgres/standard) or <=> (MySQL).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule clearly: standard = comparisons return UNKNOWN
whenever either side is NULL, including when both are NULL. 2. The fix depends on dialect: JOIN ON
a.region IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.region for standard SQL, JOIN ON a.region <=>
b.region for MySQL. 3. Often the right answer is "don't try to join on NULLs" — model the data so the
join column is NOT NULL, with a sentinel like 'unspecified' if needed. 4. Also relevant: LEFT JOIN
preserves the left row even when the right doesn't match, so the right-side column comes back NULL —
that's a different NULL source than the data NULLs.
Edge cases to mention: - Composite join keys: even one NULL in the composite means the row doesn't
match anything in standard SQL. - Outer joins generate NULLs in the unmatched-side columns;
downstream filters need to handle both kinds. - Index usage on IS NOT DISTINCT FROM was
historically limited — modern Postgres handles it; older versions fall back to seq scans.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim NULLs join to each other "because they're both NULL" — that intuition
is wrong in SQL. - Do not use COALESCE-to-sentinel in JOIN ON without thinking through whether the
sentinel can be a real value elsewhere.
Common follow-up: "What does a LEFT JOIN with no match produce on the right side?" — NULLs in
every right-side column for that row.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 483 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 484
-- These NULLs don't match
SELECT * FROM table_a a JOIN table_b b ON a.region = b.region;
-- These NULLs do match
SELECT * FROM table_a a JOIN table_b b ON a.region IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.region;
Q469 · DEFAULT vs NULL — When Each Is the Right Call
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Schema-design rounds, GCC platform teams, Walmart Labs · Topic:
NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When designing a schema, when should a column be NULLable and when should it have a
DEFAULT?
The 30-second answer: NULL means "this value is genuinely unknown or not applicable". DEFAULT
means "this value has a sensible starting value if none is supplied". Use NULL for optional facts (notes,
end_date), DEFAULT for mandatory facts with conventional starting values
(created_at=CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, is_active=TRUE).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The rule of thumb: if your business logic says "every row must have a
meaningful value here", use NOT NULL with DEFAULT. If the value can legitimately be missing, use
NULL. 2. Common DEFAULT patterns: created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, 
status VARCHAR DEFAULT 'pending', retry_count INT DEFAULT 0. 3. Common NULL
patterns: end_date (still ongoing), discount_pct (no discount), cancelled_reason (not
cancelled). 4. Boolean columns are the classic case study: 
is_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE is almost always better than is_active
BOOLEAN with NULL meaning "unknown" — because "unknown active state" usually doesn't have a
business meaning.
Edge cases to mention: - A column can be both NOT NULL AND have a DEFAULT — those compose:
every row gets a value either from the INSERT or from the DEFAULT. - DEFAULT expressions can call
functions: created_by INT DEFAULT current_user_id() if your DB supports session-scoped
defaults. - NULL plus DEFAULT 0 is contradictory at the schema design level — pick one. If the value can
be missing meaningfully, NULL it; if it has a default, NOT NULL DEFAULT.
What NOT to say: - Do not make every column NULL "just in case" — it makes queries harder and
indexes weaker. - Do not skip DEFAULT and rely on application code to set it — DB-level defaults are the
safety net.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 484 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 485
Common follow-up: "What about timestamps? created_at should be DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
What about updated_at?" — Same DEFAULT, plus a trigger or ON UPDATE clause to refresh on
modification.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  cancelled_reason TEXT,  -- NULL = not cancelled
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
Q470 · NULL in JSON — SQL NULL vs JSON null
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Postgres-heavy shops, Razorpay, Swiggy · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A JSON column has a field set to null. Is that the same as the field being missing, or as the
row's column itself being NULL?
The 30-second answer: Three distinct things: (1) the whole JSON column is SQL NULL — no JSON
document at all; (2) the JSON document exists but the field is missing — the key isn't present; (3) the
JSON document has the field with explicit JSON null. They behave differently in queries — extracting a
missing field returns SQL NULL, extracting an explicit null returns a JSON null.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lay out the three states with examples. Column = NULL: SELECT
data FROM t returns NULL. Field missing: data->'discount' returns SQL NULL. Field explicitly
null: data->'discount' returns JSON null, which Postgres distinguishes from SQL NULL. 2. In
Postgres, data ? 'discount' tests whether the key exists at all (catches difference between cases
2 and 3). 3. data->>'discount' IS NULL returns TRUE for both missing keys and explicit JSON
null — be deliberate about which one you want. 4. Filtering practical example: rows with data-
>>'status' = 'paid' will miss both the missing-key rows and the JSON-null rows — those need
separate handling.
Edge cases to mention: - JSONB_TYPEOF(data->'discount') returns 'null' for explicit JSON null
versus NULL (SQL NULL) for missing keys — that's how you tell them apart. - API contracts often differ:
"field absent" might mean "no opinion", "field is null" might mean "explicit no value". Treat them
differently in your queries. - Storing JSON null as a way of saying "no value" is usually inferior to omitting
the key — keeps the document smaller and the semantics cleaner.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 485 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 486
What NOT to say: - Do not treat JSON null the same as SQL NULL; modern engines distinguish them,
and so should you. - Do not assume data->'x' IS NULL covers all the missing/null cases — it
covers some but conflates others.
Common follow-up: "How do you find rows where the JSON has an explicit discount: null (not
just missing)?" — WHERE JSONB_TYPEOF(data->'discount') = 'null'.
-- Distinguishing JSON null from missing key
SELECT id,
  CASE
    WHEN data IS NULL THEN 'no document'
    WHEN NOT (data ? 'discount') THEN 'key missing'
    WHEN JSONB_TYPEOF(data->'discount') = 'null' THEN 'explicit null'
    ELSE 'has value'
  END AS state
FROM orders;
Q471 · Aggregates and NULL — COUNT(col) Ignores Them
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Accenture · Topic: NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Out of a million order rows where 100 have NULL amount, what does COUNT(*) return,
what does COUNT(amount) return, and what does SUM(amount) do with the NULLs?
The 30-second answer: COUNT(*) returns 1,000,000 (counts rows, NULL or not). COUNT(amount)
returns 999,900 (counts non-NULL values only). SUM(amount) ignores NULLs and sums the rest —
but if every value were NULL, SUM would return NULL, not 0.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the rule: aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX,
COUNT(col)) skip NULL inputs. COUNT() is the only one that counts rows including NULL. 2. AVG is the
famous one: AVG(amount) divides SUM by COUNT(amount), not by COUNT() — so 100 NULL rows
don't drag the average toward zero. 3. Empty groups: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX of zero non-NULL rows is
NULL, not 0. COUNT of zero non-NULL rows is 0. 4. For "treat NULL as zero", wrap with COALESCE
inside or outside the aggregate depending on intent: SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) versus 
COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0).
Edge cases to mention: - COUNT(DISTINCT col) also ignores NULL — distinct counts are over
non-NULL values only. - For "ratio of non-NULL to total": COUNT(amount) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) —
gives fraction of rows with values. - In window aggregates, NULL is still skipped inside the frame.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 486 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 487
What NOT to say: - Do not say SUM returns 0 on empty input — it returns NULL. - Do not confuse 
COUNT(*) and COUNT(col) — they answer different questions.
Common follow-up: "If I have 100 rows with NULL amount and want the average amount including them
as 0, how do I write it?" — SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) / COUNT(*), not 
AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)). The COALESCE inside AVG also works but the explicit form
documents intent better.
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
  COUNT(amount) AS rows_with_amount,
  SUM(amount) AS sum_amount,
  AVG(amount) AS avg_of_non_null,
  COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) AS sum_or_zero
FROM orders;
Q472 · Putting It All Together — Modern Reporting Query
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: BI rounds, GCC analytics teams, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Modern
Aggregation + NULL Handling
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Write one query that produces a region-by-category sales report with subtotals at each level and
a grand total. Use FILTER to break out paid versus refunded amounts, COALESCE to label rollup
rows cleanly, and ANY_VALUE for the most-recent currency seen per group.
The 30-second answer: Combine GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, category) for the hierarchy, 
SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status='paid') and FILTER (WHERE
status='refunded') for the conditional totals, ANY_VALUE(currency) for the representative
currency, and CASE WHEN GROUPING(region)=1 THEN 'All regions' ELSE
COALESCE(region, 'Unknown') END to label both subtotal and missing-data rows.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the GROUP BY: ROLLUP(region, category) gives
you region+category leaves, region subtotals, and a grand total. 2. Add the FILTER aggregates: one per
status you want to break out — paid, refunded, failed. 3. Add ANY_VALUE for any column where you
need a representative value (currency, primary language, primary timezone). 4. Use GROUPING() to label
subtotal versus data rows; use COALESCE for the actual NULL-in-data case. Both wrapped in a single
CASE expression. 5. Order with GROUPING() first so subtotals follow their group, and the grand total
lands at the very bottom.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 487 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 488
Edge cases to mention: - On dialects without FILTER, swap to SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid'
THEN amount END) — identical semantics. - On dialects without ANY_VALUE (Postgres <16), swap to
MIN(currency) or MAX(currency) with a comment explaining intent. - Watch out for currency
mixing: if rows have different currencies, the SUM is meaningless — usually you'd group by currency first
or convert to one currency in a subquery.
What NOT to say: - Do not write three separate queries and union them — the whole point is to do it in
one scan. - Do not skip the GROUPING-vs-NULL distinction; reports look professional when subtotals
are clearly labelled.
Common follow-up: "How would you extend this to year-over-year comparison?" — Add a CTE with
previous-year totals and join on (region, category), then compute the percentage difference.
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'All regions'
    ELSE COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')
  END AS region,
  CASE
    WHEN GROUPING(category) = 1 THEN 'All categories'
    ELSE COALESCE(category, 'Unknown')
  END AS category,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid_total,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refund_total,
  ANY_VALUE(currency) AS sample_currency,
  GROUPING_ID(region, category) AS level
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, category)
ORDER BY GROUPING(region), region, GROUPING(category), category;
Chapter 10, Part D — Generated Columns, Identity, Partitioning &
Materialized Views
This is the closer for the Modern SQL Features chapter, and it is the section that most reliably separates
a senior candidate from a mid one. The earlier parts covered expression-level features — windows,
JSON, CTEs, recursive queries. This part is about table-level declarative constructs: generated columns
that compute themselves on every insert, identity columns that issue keys without a separate sequence
call, declarative partitioning that lets the planner skip whole chunks of data, and materialized views that
pre-compute reports for dashboards. Interviewers ask these because the syntax varies wildly across
Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle, and because the right answer almost always involves a
tradeoff — STORED vs VIRTUAL, IDENTITY vs UUID, COMPLETE vs CONCURRENTLY refresh. Read
each Q twice: once for the syntax, once for the tradeoff buried in the edge cases.

Section A — Generated Columns
Q473 · GENERATED ALWAYS AS — Cross-Vendor Syntax
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo · Topic: Generated
columns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a generated column? Show me the syntax in Postgres, SQL Server and MySQL, and tell
me what the differences are.
The 30-second answer: A generated column is a column whose value is computed from an expression
over other columns in the same row — you never insert into it, the engine fills it automatically. Postgres
only supports STORED (materialised on disk), SQL Server supports both PERSISTED and non-persisted,
and MySQL supports both STORED and VIRTUAL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the one-liner: "computed from other columns, you never
write to it directly." 2. Postgres syntax: amount_paise INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS
(amount_rupees * 100) STORED. STORED is mandatory; Postgres has not implemented VIRTUAL
yet. 3. SQL Server syntax: amount_paise AS (amount_rupees * 100) PERSISTED — note SQL
Server uses AS without the GENERATED ALWAYS clause, and PERSISTED is the equivalent of
STORED. 4. MySQL syntax: amount_paise INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (amount_rupees *
100) STORED or ... VIRTUAL. MySQL is the only one of the three with a true virtual variant —
computed at SELECT time, no disk cost. 5. Be ready to explain the use case: derived totals, normalised
search keys, JSON field extraction. Anything you would otherwise do in every SELECT.
Edge cases to mention: - The expression must be deterministic — no NOW(), no RANDOM(), no
calls to non-deterministic functions. Postgres rejects these at table creation time. - You cannot reference
another generated column in the same table in Postgres; SQL Server allows chained computed columns
if the dependency is acyclic. - INSERTs that try to write a value into a generated column either error (with 
GENERATED ALWAYS) or are silently ignored — vendor-specific.
What NOT to say: - Do not call it a "computed column" in Postgres or a "generated column" in SQL
Server — get the vendor terminology right. - Do not claim Postgres supports VIRTUAL — it does not, as
of the current major version, and that is the single most common interview gotcha.
Common follow-up: "If the expression changes, what happens to existing rows?" — In Postgres and
SQL Server you have to drop and re-add the column; the engine does not retroactively recompute
STORED columns when you ALTER the expression.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 489 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 490
-- Postgres
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  amount_rupees NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  amount_paise BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (amount_rupees * 100) STORED
);
Q474 · STORED vs VIRTUAL Generated Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Walmart Labs · Topic: Generated columns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
In MySQL you can mark a generated column as STORED or VIRTUAL. When would you pick each
one, and what does Postgres force you into?
The 30-second answer: STORED writes the computed value to disk on every INSERT or UPDATE —
costs space and write time, but reads are free and the column is indexable like any other. VIRTUAL
computes on every SELECT — saves disk but pays CPU on every read, and indexing rules are more
restrictive. Postgres supported STORED only for generated columns through version 17; VIRTUAL
generated columns were added in Postgres 18 (September 2025).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame it as a classic space-vs-time tradeoff: STORED pays at write
time, VIRTUAL pays at read time. 2. Pick STORED when the expression is expensive (string
normalisation, JSON extraction, hashing) or when you need to index the column. SQL Server requires
PERSISTED before you can index a non-deterministic computed column. 3. Pick VIRTUAL when the
expression is cheap (simple arithmetic on existing columns), when storage is constrained, or when you
need to add the column to a huge existing table without rewriting the heap. 4. Mention that VIRTUAL
columns in MySQL can still be indexed — the index itself stores the computed value, so you are paying
the storage cost in the index rather than the row.
Edge cases to mention: - Adding a STORED column to a billion-row table is a full table rewrite —
schedule the migration carefully, or use a pt-online-schema-change style tool. - A VIRTUAL column that
gets read in every query may end up costing more CPU than just storing it — measure before you
assume VIRTUAL is cheaper. - Some replication setups (older MySQL row-based replication) ship the
computed value over the wire for STORED columns but recompute for VIRTUAL — bandwidth
implications.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "VIRTUAL is always cheaper" — it is cheaper on disk, not in CPU. - Do
not say "you cannot index VIRTUAL columns in MySQL" — you can, since MySQL 5.7.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 490 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 491
Common follow-up: "If you index a VIRTUAL column, where does the computed value actually live?" —
In the index B-tree leaf entries. The row itself does not store it, but the index does, so the storage cost
moves to the index pages.
-- MySQL: VIRTUAL with an index
CREATE TABLE products (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  name_lower VARCHAR(200) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (LOWER(name)) VIRTUAL,
  INDEX idx_name_lower (name_lower)
);
Q475 · Generated Column from JSON Field
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Meesho · Topic: Generated columns + JSON
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
I have an events table with a JSONB payload column and I keep filtering on payload-
>>'event_type'. The query is slow. What is the idiomatic fix?
The 30-second answer: Add a generated column that extracts the JSON field, then put a B-tree index
on the generated column. The engine maintains the extracted value automatically, the index works like
any normal index, and your query stays readable.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Diagnose: filtering on payload->>'event_type' without an
index forces a full scan plus JSON parsing per row. 2. The blunt fix is a functional index — CREATE
INDEX ON events ((payload->>'event_type')) — which works but the column does not exist
as a real attribute, so you cannot select on it cheaply or add a foreign key. 3. The senior answer is a
STORED generated column: event_type TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (payload-
>>'event_type') STORED. Now you have a real column, you can index it, you can constrain it, you
can join on it. 4. Mention that this is the standard pattern for shredding hot JSON keys out of a JSONB
blob — a hybrid model where the blob holds the long tail and generated columns expose the hot fields.
Edge cases to mention: - If payload is NULL or the key is missing, the generated column is NULL —
make sure your downstream queries handle that. - The expression must be marked IMMUTABLE in
Postgres for the column to be valid; ->> is immutable, but a custom JSON parser function may not be.
- Backfilling a generated column on an existing huge table rewrites every row — do it during a
maintenance window or use a partitioned table where you migrate one partition at a time.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 491 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 492
What NOT to say: - Do not suggest moving the field out of JSON entirely as the only option —
generated columns let you keep schema flexibility while getting query speed. - Do not forget the index —
the generated column by itself does not speed up the filter, it just makes the data structurally visible.
Common follow-up: "What if you also need a GIN index on the whole JSONB?" — Keep both. The
generated column with a B-tree handles equality on the hot key; the GIN index on the JSONB handles
ad-hoc containment queries on everything else.
-- Postgres
ALTER TABLE events
  ADD COLUMN event_type TEXT
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (payload->>'event_type') STORED;
CREATE INDEX idx_events_type ON events (event_type);
Q476 · Generated Column for Case-Insensitive Search
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Generated columns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Users search for customer names case-insensitively, but WHERE LOWER(name) = ? is slow.
Solve it without changing the application.
The 30-second answer: Add a generated column name_lower computed as LOWER(name), index
it, and rewrite the query — or let the application keep calling LOWER(name) = ? and add a functional
index on LOWER(name). Generated column is cleaner because the lowercased value is a first-class
attribute.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Acknowledge the symptom: the function call on the left side of =
prevents the planner from using a normal index on name. 2. Two fixes — functional index or generated
column. Both work; the generated column gives you a real attribute you can also SELECT, ORDER BY
and use in joins. 3. The generated column should be STORED (or PERSISTED in SQL Server) so the
engine can index it and the read path does no extra work. 4. For Postgres, you could alternatively use a
case-insensitive collation (ICU) or the citext extension — mention these as the more modern
alternative, especially if name search is pervasive.
Edge cases to mention: - LOWER on Unicode strings is locale-dependent — Turkish dotless i is the
canonical example. Use a deterministic ICU collation if you care about correctness across locales. - The
generated column doubles your storage for the name field — fine for one column, painful if you do it for
ten. - If you also need accent-insensitive search, layer unaccent(LOWER(name)) — both functions
must be IMMUTABLE for Postgres to accept the expression.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 492 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 493
What NOT to say: - Do not suggest a trigger that maintains a parallel column — generated columns
exist precisely to avoid that anti-pattern. - Do not say "just store everything lowercased" — you lose the
original casing for display, which is a UX regression.
Common follow-up: "What if the search is partial — WHERE name_lower LIKE 'rahul%'?" — B-
tree on name_lower still works for prefix matches because the leading anchor is a constant. For
arbitrary substring matches you need a trigram index (pg_trgm in Postgres).
ALTER TABLE customers
  ADD COLUMN name_lower TEXT
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (LOWER(name)) STORED;
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_name_lower ON customers (name_lower);
Q477 · Generated Column for Derived Totals
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Accenture, Walmart Labs · Topic: Generated columns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
An order_items table has quantity and unit_price. Every report computes 
line_total = quantity * unit_price. Is there a better way?
The 30-second answer: Yes — add line_total as a generated column GENERATED ALWAYS AS
(quantity * unit_price) STORED. Reports now read the column directly, you cannot drift
between application and database calculations, and you can index line_total if you need to filter
on it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem: when the same arithmetic happens in many
places, you eventually get a bug where one report uses pre-tax and another uses post-tax. A generated
column is the single source of truth. 2. STORED is the right pick here because the multiplication is cheap
but you might index line_total for queries like "all line items above ₹10,000". 3. Mention that this
composes — you can have line_total = quantity * unit_price and then taxed_total =
line_total * (1 + tax_rate) if the engine allows chained generated columns (SQL Server does,
Postgres does not). 4. Be ready for the question about updates: if quantity or unit_price is
updated, the engine recomputes line_total automatically on UPDATE.
Edge cases to mention: - If quantity is INT and unit_price is NUMERIC, the result type is
NUMERIC — set the generated column type explicitly to avoid implicit-cast surprises in downstream
queries. - A generated column cannot be the target of a foreign key in some engines — usually not a
concern for derived totals, but worth knowing. - Discount logic that depends on customer tier cannot live
in a generated column because it needs another table — use a view for that, not a generated column.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 493 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 494
What NOT to say: - Do not say "just compute it in the application" — that loses the constraint that the
database enforces consistency for every read path, including ad-hoc analyst queries. - Do not over-
engineer with triggers — triggers are the pre-generated-column workaround and they are strictly worse.
Common follow-up: "What if quantity can be NULL?" — NULL * anything = NULL, so 
line_total will be NULL. Either constrain quantity to NOT NULL, or wrap the expression in 
COALESCE(quantity, 0) * unit_price.
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  quantity INT NOT NULL,
  unit_price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  line_total NUMERIC(12,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (quantity * unit_price) STORED
);
Q478 · Indexing Generated Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, PhonePe, Cred · Topic: Generated columns + indexing
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can you index a generated column? Does it matter whether it is STORED or VIRTUAL?
The 30-second answer: Yes — STORED generated columns are indexable everywhere. VIRTUAL
columns are indexable in MySQL (the computed value lives in the index), not directly in SQL Server
unless persisted, and not at all in Postgres because Postgres does not support VIRTUAL. The index
works exactly like any other B-tree, hash or GIN index.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Open with the rule: STORED is always indexable; VIRTUAL depends
on the engine. 2. In MySQL, indexing a VIRTUAL column writes the computed value into the index leaves
— the row stays slim, but the index pays the storage cost. The optimizer can use that index for queries
that reference the original expression too. 3. In SQL Server, a non-persisted computed column is
indexable only if the expression is deterministic and precise — otherwise you need PERSISTED. The
engine refuses to create the index if these checks fail. 4. In Postgres, since only STORED exists, indexing
is straightforward. The functional-index alternative (CREATE INDEX ON tbl ((expr))) does the
same thing without a column — pick generated column when you also want the value accessible as an
attribute.
Edge cases to mention: - Multi-column indexes can mix generated and regular columns — useful when
you want a composite key like (status, line_total) for fast filtering plus ordering. - A unique
constraint on a generated column enforces uniqueness on the computed value — handy for normalised
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 494 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 495
forms (e.g. lowercase email). - Index maintenance overhead applies to UPDATEs that change any input
to the generated expression — measure the write penalty if you index aggressively.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim you can index a VIRTUAL column in Postgres — Postgres has no
VIRTUAL. - Do not assume an index on a generated column will speed up the original expression query
— in Postgres, only WHERE generated_col = ? uses it; the planner does not automatically rewrite 
WHERE LOWER(name) = ? to use an index on a name_lower column.
Common follow-up: "How do you make Postgres use the generated-column index when the application
keeps querying the raw expression?" — Either change the application to query the generated column
directly, or add a functional index on the expression too. The generated column is for structure, the
functional index is for query rewriting.
-- Postgres: composite index on generated + regular columns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_total
  ON orders (status, line_total);
Q479 · Constraints on Generated Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo · Topic: Generated
columns + constraints
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Can you put CHECK or NOT NULL or UNIQUE constraints on a generated column? Are there
gotchas?
The 30-second answer: Yes to all three, with caveats. CHECK and NOT NULL work the same as on
regular columns. UNIQUE works on STORED generated columns. Foreign keys are partially supported —
Postgres allows them on STORED generated columns since version 12; SQL Server has more limits. The
main gotcha is that constraint violations surface on the INSERT, not on the expression definition.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with NOT NULL — straightforward, but if the underlying
expression can produce NULL, your INSERT fails. This is actually a feature: it forces you to think about
NULL inputs. 2. CHECK constraints work and are useful for narrowing the domain — e.g. CHECK
(line_total >= 0) ensures the multiplication did not overflow into a negative. 3. UNIQUE on a
generated column enforces uniqueness on the computed form — perfect for normalised email columns,
slug columns, or canonicalised phone numbers. 4. Foreign keys: Postgres 12+ allows a FK on a STORED
generated column. SQL Server requires PERSISTED and a few additional rules. Mention this only if asked
— it is a niche but slick pattern.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 495 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 496
Edge cases to mention: - A CHECK on a generated column is evaluated after the expression is
computed — so if the expression itself errors (division by zero), you get the expression error, not the
CHECK error. - UNIQUE plus a NULL-producing expression behaves per standard: multiple NULLs are
allowed in most engines, which may or may not be what you want. - If you DROP the column that the
generated column depends on, the generated column goes too — there is no auto-fix.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim generated columns cannot be the parent side of a foreign key in any
engine — that was true historically, but Postgres relaxed it. - Do not use CHECK constraints to validate
cross-table invariants — they are row-local; cross-table needs triggers or assertions.
Common follow-up: "If a CHECK constraint on a generated column suddenly starts failing, what is the
most likely cause?" — A change in the input data distribution. The expression is deterministic, so the only
way it newly violates a CHECK is because the inputs now produce values that did not exist before.
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL,
  email_lower TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (LOWER(email)) STORED,
  UNIQUE (email_lower),
  CHECK (LENGTH(email_lower) > 3)
);
Section B — Identity, Sequences and Auto-Increment
Q480 · GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Wells Fargo · Topic: Identity columns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is the standard SQL way to declare an auto-incrementing primary key, and how does it
differ from the older SERIAL syntax?
The 30-second answer: The standard form is id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY
PRIMARY KEY. It is the SQL standard syntax adopted by Postgres in version 10 and by Oracle in 12c.
SQL Server does not support GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY — it uses its proprietary 
IDENTITY(seed, increment) syntax. It replaces vendor-specific things like SERIAL (Postgres), 
AUTO_INCREMENT (MySQL) and IDENTITY(1,1) (older SQL Server).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with the canonical form: GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS
IDENTITY lets you omit the column on INSERT and the engine assigns the next value, but also lets you
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 496 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 497
override with an explicit value if you need to. 2. Contrast with SERIAL in Postgres — SERIAL is just
shorthand for "create a sequence and set the default to nextval(...)". It works but it is not the standard,
and you lose some metadata (the sequence is owned by but not bound to the column). 3. Mention 
GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY as the stricter variant — it disallows manual inserts unless you
use OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE. 4. Be ready to explain why GENERATED BY DEFAULT is the
more practical default for application tables: you can still seed data, replay logs and import dumps
without fighting the engine.
Edge cases to mention: - Identity columns in Postgres are backed by a sequence under the hood —
you can still query pg_sequences and manipulate it directly. - After a COPY or bulk insert with
explicit IDs, you must ALTER SEQUENCE ... RESTART WITH to avoid duplicate-key errors on the
next auto-generated value. - BIGINT is the right type — INT runs out in a few years on a busy production
system, and the schema migration to widen the key is painful.
What NOT to say: - Do not use SERIAL in new Postgres schemas — it is the legacy spelling and the
docs themselves recommend GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY. - Do not say "identity columns are
slower than sequences" — they use the same mechanism.
Common follow-up: "What is the practical difference between BY DEFAULT and ALWAYS?" — BY
DEFAULT lets you write INSERT ... VALUES (5, ...) and the engine accepts the 5. ALWAYS
rejects it unless you say OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE. ALWAYS is safer for systems where IDs must
come from the database.
-- Postgres / SQL Server / Oracle
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
Q481 · GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY — Preventing Manual Inserts
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic: Identity columns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
When would you use GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY instead of GENERATED BY
DEFAULT? What happens if someone tries to insert an explicit value?
The 30-second answer: Use ALWAYS when the ID must come from the database and never from the
application — typically for surrogate keys in tables where consistency depends on monotonic, gap-
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 497 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 498
tolerant generation. An attempt to insert an explicit value raises an error, unless the inserting session
uses the OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE escape hatch.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Explain the contract: ALWAYS means the engine is the authority on
the value. The application cannot accidentally collide with an existing ID by passing one in. 2. The most
common scenario where this matters: tables that are being replicated or where the ID is used in business
contracts. If an application accidentally inserts id = 999999999, the next auto-generated value
clashes and inserts start failing. 3. The escape hatch — INSERT INTO t (id, ...) OVERRIDING
SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (...) — is intentionally verbose so that bulk loads, restores and migrations
can override but accidental inserts cannot. 4. Mention that ALWAYS does NOT prevent you from
updating the column after insert — it only governs insertion. If you also want to lock the value, add a
separate trigger or use a constraint.
Edge cases to mention: - Restoring a logical dump into a table with ALWAYS often needs 
OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE plus a sequence restart — pg_dump handles this, but custom dump
scripts may not. - Some ORMs do not know how to issue OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE — test your
migration tooling before flipping to ALWAYS. - In SQL Server the equivalent is SET IDENTITY_INSERT
t ON — the spirit is the same but the syntax is procedural rather than per-statement.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim ALWAYS is "more secure" in a vague hand-wavy way — be specific
about the consistency guarantee. - Do not blanket-recommend ALWAYS for every table — for staging or
replay tables where bulk-loading with explicit IDs is routine, BY DEFAULT is friendlier.
Common follow-up: "What error do you get on an explicit insert into an ALWAYS column?" — Postgres: 
ERROR: cannot insert into column "id" with a hint to use OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE.
Knowing the exact wording shows the interviewer you have actually hit it.
CREATE TABLE payments (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
);
-- This errors out:
INSERT INTO payments (id, order_id, amount) VALUES (1, 100, 500);
-- This is the escape hatch:
INSERT INTO payments (id, order_id, amount)
  OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (1, 100, 500);
Q482 · Explicit SEQUENCEs vs IDENTITY
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Flipkart · Topic: Sequences
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 498 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 499
When would you create a standalone SEQUENCE instead of using an IDENTITY column?
The 30-second answer: Create a standalone sequence when the generated number is used outside a
single column — shared across multiple tables, used as an order number visible to the user, or pre-
fetched in batches by the application. IDENTITY is the right default; standalone sequences are the
escape hatch for these specific scenarios.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the default: IDENTITY first. Standalone sequences are not
"more advanced"; they are a different tool with different ergonomics. 2. Use case one — shared
sequence across tables. If invoice_number must be globally unique across invoices_2025 and 
invoices_2026, a shared sequence is the cleanest way. 3. Use case two — pre-fetch. The
application calls nextval('order_seq') once per batch and uses the values internally before
inserting. Identity columns do not let you pre-fetch easily. 4. Use case three — business-visible IDs.
Order numbers shown to customers often want gaps avoided, monotonic, maybe even with a prefix; a
sequence with custom CACHE and CYCLE settings gives you full control.
Edge cases to mention: - Sequences are not transactional — nextval advances even if the
transaction rolls back. You will see gaps. Document this for stakeholders who expect contiguous order
numbers. - CACHE n on a sequence pre-allocates n values per session — improves throughput,
increases gap size on crash. - Sequences are session-aware: currval returns the last value
generated in the current session, useful for getting the just-assigned ID without a round-trip.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim sequences are gap-free — they explicitly are not. - Do not use a
sequence where IDENTITY would do the same job — you are inviting future maintainers to wonder why.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle the gap problem when stakeholders demand contiguous
invoice numbers?" — Either accept the gaps and explain that gap-free is incompatible with concurrent
inserts, or use a separate gap-fill process that allocates numbers in a single-writer service. Trying to
solve it with SELECT MAX(...) + 1 is a race-condition trap.
CREATE SEQUENCE invoice_number_seq START 100001 INCREMENT 1 CACHE 50;
INSERT INTO invoices (invoice_number, customer_id, amount)
VALUES (nextval('invoice_number_seq'), 42, 1500.00);
Q483 · AUTO_INCREMENT (MySQL) vs IDENTITY
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant · Topic: Identity columns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 499 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 500
In MySQL the syntax is AUTO_INCREMENT. How is it different from the standard 
GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY you would use in Postgres or SQL Server?
The 30-second answer: Functionally similar — both assign a monotonic integer to a column on insert.
AUTO_INCREMENT is MySQL-specific, lives in the column definition, and lets you read and reset it via 
LAST_INSERT_ID() and ALTER TABLE ... AUTO_INCREMENT = n. Standard IDENTITY is
portable across most modern engines and has finer-grained control over BY DEFAULT vs ALWAYS.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the syntactic difference: id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT
PRIMARY KEY in MySQL vs id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
in Postgres or SQL Server. 2. MySQL has only one mode — it is equivalent to BY DEFAULT in the
standard. You cannot configure it to reject explicit inserts the way GENERATED ALWAYS does. 3.
Resetting the next value differs: ALTER TABLE t AUTO_INCREMENT = 1000 in MySQL versus 
ALTER SEQUENCE seq_name RESTART WITH 1000 in Postgres. 4. Cross-engine portability: if you
write generic SQL, prefer the standard form. AUTO_INCREMENT is a deal-breaker for anyone migrating
to Postgres or SQL Server.
Edge cases to mention: - MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT counter is in memory in older InnoDB versions
and can reset to MAX(id)+1 after a server restart — leading to ID reuse after a delete. MySQL 8 fixed this
by persisting the counter. - LAST_INSERT_ID() returns the first ID of a multi-row insert, not the last
— a sharp-edge that bites people. - AUTO_INCREMENT works only with integer types; the standard
IDENTITY also requires integer in most engines but the spelling is more forgiving.
What NOT to say: - Do not say AUTO_INCREMENT is "older" or "worse" — it is just MySQL's idiom.
Worse and better depends on context. - Do not assume the counter is persisted across restarts in old
MySQL versions — that bug bit a lot of production systems.
Common follow-up: "What does LAST_INSERT_ID() return after a 10-row INSERT?" — The auto-
generated ID of the first row. To find the last, you do LAST_INSERT_ID() + ROW_COUNT() - 1.
This is exactly the kind of trivia that catches mid candidates off-guard.
-- MySQL
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
);
-- Reset the counter
ALTER TABLE orders AUTO_INCREMENT = 100001;
