Q484 · IDENTITY Columns vs UUID — Distributed Systems
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Identity vs UUID
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
For a new payments microservice running on three database shards, would you use IDENTITY
columns or UUIDs for the primary key? Defend your choice.
The 30-second answer: UUIDs (specifically UUIDv7 or ULIDs, which are time-ordered) are the better
default for distributed systems because they let any node generate keys without coordination. IDENTITY
columns require either a single sequence service, shard-offset schemes, or interleaved ranges — all of
which are operationally fragile compared to a 128-bit time-ordered identifier.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. State the constraint that drives the decision: with multiple writers
(shards, regions, edge nodes), a monotonic integer requires global coordination — and global
coordination defeats the point of sharding. 2. Three options for sharded integer IDs: a central sequence
service (single point of failure), shard offsets (shard1: 1, 4, 7..., shard2: 2, 5, 8... —
clever but ugly), or per-shard sequences with a shard prefix (works but the application has to assemble
the key). 3. UUIDv7 / ULID give you time-ordered, locally-generated 128-bit identifiers — no
coordination, sortable by creation time, and index-friendly because new rows cluster together. 4. The
classic objection — "UUIDs are 16 bytes, BIGINT is 8" — matters in tight inner loops but is rarely the
bottleneck. Storage is cheap; coordination overhead is expensive.
Edge cases to mention: - Random UUIDv4 fragments B-tree indexes because every insert lands in a
random place — UUIDv7 fixes this by encoding the timestamp in the leading bytes. - Some clients still
serialize UUIDs as strings — switch to binary representation (16 bytes vs 36) for the storage savings. - If
the table is small and single-master, the UUID overhead may not pay for itself — IDENTITY is simpler.
Pick based on the actual architecture, not future plans.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "UUIDs are always better" — they have real costs, especially in inner-
loop joins and on cache-bound workloads. - Do not propose UUIDv4 for a primary key without
acknowledging the B-tree fragmentation — that is the senior-vs-mid signal.
Common follow-up: "How does UUIDv7 fix the B-tree problem?" — The first 48 bits are a Unix
timestamp, so consecutive inserts land in nearby pages of the B-tree, behaving much more like an
IDENTITY column for cache efficiency. This is why UUIDv7 has become the recommended UUID variant
for primary keys.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 501 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 502
-- Postgres with UUIDv7 (extension or generated client-side)
CREATE TABLE payments (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
  order_id UUID NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
Q485 · Resetting and Restarting Identity Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Wipro, Accenture, Wells Fargo · Topic: Identity management
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
After truncating a table or migrating data, how do you reset the identity column so the next insert
starts from 1?
The 30-second answer: Postgres: ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id RESTART WITH 1 or 
ALTER SEQUENCE seq_name RESTART WITH 1. SQL Server: 
DBCC CHECKIDENT('t', RESEED, 0). MySQL: ALTER TABLE t AUTO_INCREMENT = 1.
TRUNCATE by itself resets the counter in Postgres and SQL Server but not always in MySQL.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Lead with TRUNCATE behaviour because it surprises people: 
TRUNCATE TABLE t RESTART IDENTITY in Postgres explicitly resets the sequence. Plain 
TRUNCATE does not, and MySQL's TRUNCATE resets AUTO_INCREMENT to 1 only sometimes
(storage-engine-dependent). 2. For Postgres identity columns, the per-column syntax is ALTER TABLE
t ALTER COLUMN id RESTART WITH 1. If you used SERIAL instead of IDENTITY, you need 
ALTER SEQUENCE t_id_seq RESTART WITH 1. 3. For SQL Server, DBCC CHECKIDENT('t',
RESEED, 0) sets the seed so the next inserted value is 1. Note the documented quirk: if you reseed
below MAX(id), you will get duplicate-key errors on the next insert. 4. Always reset to MAX(id) + 1 after a
bulk load with explicit IDs — otherwise the next normal insert collides. This is the single most common
production incident around identity columns.
Edge cases to mention: - Restarting an identity sequence does not delete existing rows — you can end
up with duplicate keys if existing IDs are >= the new restart value. - In replication setups, restarting a
sequence on the primary does not replicate to replicas in some configurations — verify your setup. - For
Postgres, setval(seq_name, n) is the function-level equivalent and is what most migration tools
use under the hood.
What NOT to say: - Do not just use DELETE FROM t expecting the identity to reset — DELETE never
resets, only TRUNCATE does (and only with the right options). - Do not reset to 1 on a production table
without checking MAX(id) first — that is a fast path to a duplicate-key outage.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 502 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 503
Common follow-up: "After a logical restore from pg_dump, the next insert fails with a duplicate-key
error. Why?" — The dump restored rows with explicit IDs, but the sequence still points to its old position.
Run SELECT setval('seq_name', (SELECT MAX(id) FROM t)) to fix it.
-- Postgres
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN id RESTART WITH 1;
-- or
TRUNCATE TABLE orders RESTART IDENTITY;
-- SQL Server
DBCC CHECKIDENT('orders', RESEED, 0);
-- MySQL
ALTER TABLE orders AUTO_INCREMENT = 1;
Section C — Declarative Table Partitioning
Q486 · Postgres Declarative Partitioning — RANGE, LIST, HASH
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic: Partitioning
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through declarative partitioning in Postgres. What are the three strategies and when do
you pick each?
The 30-second answer: Postgres 10 introduced declarative RANGE and LIST partitioning; HASH
partitioning was added in Postgres 11. RANGE for time-series (one partition per month), LIST for discrete
categories (one partition per country code), HASH for even distribution when the access pattern does not
have a natural key — typically used for sharding without natural shard keys.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. RANGE: PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at), then CREATE
TABLE orders_2026_01 PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO
('2026-02-01'). This is the workhorse — almost every "we have a huge events table" answer ends
in monthly RANGE partitions. 2. LIST: PARTITION BY LIST (region) with one partition per known
region. Good when partition boundaries are categorical and stable (state codes, payment status). 3.
HASH: PARTITION BY HASH (user_id) ... WITH (MODULUS 8, REMAINDER 0). Distributes
load evenly when there is no natural range or list key — typically used when you want parallelism within a
single server. 4. Mention that declarative partitioning (Postgres 10+) replaced the old inheritance + trigger
approach — much faster, much less code, and the planner is partition-aware.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 503 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 504
Edge cases to mention: - The partition key must be part of every primary key and unique constraint —
you cannot have a globally unique constraint that ignores the partition key. - Foreign keys to a partitioned
table are supported in modern Postgres but each partition must accept the FK — there are some still-
evolving constraints. - Cross-partition updates that change the partition key are slow because they
delete from one partition and insert into another — design to avoid them.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse declarative partitioning with the old inheritance approach — they
look similar but the new one is what every Postgres tutorial today shows. - Do not partition unless you
have a real reason — partitioning a 10-million row table adds complexity without benefit.
Common follow-up: "At what table size does partitioning start to pay off?" — Rule of thumb: when a
single index no longer fits in memory and queries naturally scope to a sub-range. Often hundreds of
millions of rows for time-series. Small tables are slower with partitioning, not faster.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_05 PARTITION OF orders
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01');
Q487 · Partition Pruning
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Goldman, PhonePe · Topic: Partitioning + planner
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is partition pruning and when does the planner actually use it?
The 30-second answer: Partition pruning is the planner's ability to skip partitions whose key range
cannot possibly satisfy the WHERE clause. It works when the WHERE clause references the partition key
with a constant or a value the planner can evaluate at plan time — and modern Postgres also supports
execution-time pruning for parameterised queries.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the example: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE
created_at >= '2026-05-01' on a table partitioned by month. The planner reads only the May
2026 partition. 2. Two flavours of pruning — plan-time (the planner knows the partition at plan time) and
run-time (the value is a parameter, but the executor still skips at execution time). Run-time pruning was
added in Postgres 11 and is essential for prepared statements. 3. Pruning fails when the WHERE clause
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 504 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 505
uses a function the planner cannot reason about — 
WHERE date_trunc('month', created_at) = '2026-05-01' may not prune because 
date_trunc is not a simple comparison. 4. Always verify with EXPLAIN — look for "Subplans
Removed" or "Partitions Removed" in the plan output. If you do not see it, the query is hitting every
partition.
Edge cases to mention: - Pruning happens after the planner sees the WHERE clause — if you wrap the
partition key in a function or apply implicit casts that the planner cannot push through, pruning silently
fails. - JOINs across partitioned tables can prune partitions on both sides if the join condition uses the
partition key — but only with enable_partitionwise_join on (it is off by default). - Default
partition (the catch-all) is always scanned unless the planner can prove no value in the WHERE clause
maps to it.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume pruning happens automatically for every query — write the EXPLAIN
and read the plan. - Do not partition a table just to get parallelism — without WHERE clauses that prune,
you get full scans of every partition.
Common follow-up: "Why does 
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days' sometimes not prune?" — In
older Postgres versions, this could be evaluated at runtime rather than plan time, defeating plan-time
pruning. Modern Postgres handles it via run-time pruning, but if you see surprising plans, check the
version and consider rewriting to use a literal constant.
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND created_at < '2026-06-01';
-- Look for: "Subplans Removed: N" indicating pruning is active
Q488 · Partition-Wise Joins
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic: Partitioning + joins
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a partition-wise join and when is it actually worth turning on?
The 30-second answer: A partition-wise join is when the planner joins two partitioned tables partition-
by-partition — for each pair of matching partitions on each side, it does a smaller join and unions the
results. It is worth turning on when both tables are partitioned by the same key with matching bounds,
the partitions are large enough that the per-partition join is non-trivial, and you have parallelism available.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 505 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 506
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Set the stage: you have orders and order_items both
partitioned by created_at with monthly ranges. Without partition-wise join, the planner joins the
whole orders table to the whole order_items table. 2. With enable_partitionwise_join =
on, the planner generates plans like "join orders_2026_05 to order_items_2026_05, then union with the
next month, and so on". Each sub-join is smaller and can run in parallel. 3. Wins are biggest when the
per-partition data fits in memory and the join keys have selective indexes. Losses appear when partitions
are tiny and the per-partition planning overhead dominates. 4. Mention partition-wise aggregation as the
sibling feature — enable_partitionwise_aggregate = on lets the planner aggregate per
partition and combine results, which is huge for time-series analytics.
Edge cases to mention: - Partitions must be bound-compatible — same key, same boundaries. If 
orders is monthly and order_items is weekly, partition-wise join does not work. - The planner
has to consider many more plans, so query planning time goes up — for short OLTP queries this can
hurt, for analytical queries it is worth it. - Memory pressure: each per-partition join needs work_mem, so
eight parallel partition joins can use eight times the memory of a single join.
What NOT to say: - Do not turn it on globally without measuring — it adds planner overhead even when
it does not produce a better plan. - Do not assume it works on heterogeneous partition layouts — it really
does require matching bounds.
Common follow-up: "What if the two tables are partitioned by the same key but with slightly different
boundaries — say monthly vs every 28 days?" — Partition-wise join does not apply. You either re-
partition one side to match, or accept the non-partition-wise plan.
SET enable_partitionwise_join = on;
SET enable_partitionwise_aggregate = on;
EXPLAIN
SELECT o.user_id, SUM(oi.line_total)
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi
  ON oi.order_id = o.id AND oi.created_at = o.created_at
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY o.user_id;
Q489 · Adding Partitions for New Time Ranges — Automation
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Meesho · Topic: Partition automation
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You have a table partitioned by month. How do you make sure next month's partition exists
before the first insert hits it?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 506 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 507
The 30-second answer: Automate it. Either schedule a job that runs on the 25th of every month to
create next month's partition, use an extension like pg_partman that manages the lifecycle for you, or set
up a default partition as a safety net so unexpected dates do not error out.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the failure mode: if 2026-06-01 arrives and there is no 
orders_2026_06 partition, every INSERT for June fails. This is a 3 AM page nobody wants. 2. The
classic fix is a cron job that runs CREATE TABLE orders_YYYY_MM PARTITION OF orders FOR
VALUES FROM (...) TO (...) for the upcoming month. Run it well in advance — at least a week.
3. pg_partman is the Postgres extension that does this declaratively — you tell it the partition interval and
retention period, it handles create-new-partition and drop-old-partition. 4. Always have a default partition
as the safety net — CREATE TABLE orders_default PARTITION OF orders DEFAULT. New
rows that do not match any explicit partition land there, you get alerted on a monitoring metric, and you
fix it before the volume becomes huge.
Edge cases to mention: - Creating a partition takes a brief lock on the parent table — fast on idle
systems, can wait behind long transactions on busy ones. - pg_partman also handles partition retention
— old partitions can be dropped or detached and archived to cold storage. - Default partition should be
small in normal operation; if it grows, your automation has failed and you have a backlog of misplaced
data to redistribute.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "we will just create them manually when needed" — that is fine until the
on-call person is on vacation. - Do not skip the default partition because "it should never happen" —
defensive design is exactly the kind of thing senior interviewers test for.
Common follow-up: "What happens to rows in the default partition when you later add the missing
explicit partition?" — They do not move automatically. You have to detach the default, redistribute the
rows, and reattach. Plan a clean-up window if the default partition has accumulated meaningful data.
-- Default partition as safety net
CREATE TABLE orders_default PARTITION OF orders DEFAULT;
-- Automate next month's creation
DO $$
DECLARE
  next_month DATE := date_trunc('month', NOW() + INTERVAL '1 month')::DATE;
  next_next  DATE := date_trunc('month', NOW() + INTERVAL '2 months')::DATE;
BEGIN
  EXECUTE format(
    'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders_%s PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM (%L) TO (%L)',
    to_char(next_month, 'YYYY_MM'), next_month, next_next);
END $$;
Q490 · Default Partition — The Catch-All
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Partitioning
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 507 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 508
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a default partition in Postgres and why would you use one?
The 30-second answer: A default partition is the catch-all that receives any row whose partition key
does not match any explicit partition. It prevents insert failures when an out-of-range value arrives —
useful as a safety net during automation gaps, but never as the primary storage strategy.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Define it crisply: CREATE TABLE orders_default PARTITION
OF orders DEFAULT. Any row that does not match an explicit partition goes here. 2. The primary use
case is operational safety — your monthly partition automation missed a month, the next morning's
inserts still succeed, and your monitoring alerts you that the default partition has data. 3. The secondary
use case is LIST partitioning with a long tail — you partition by region for India, US, UK, and put
everything else in default. Cleaner than enumerating fifty more regions. 4. Mention the cost: the planner
always has to consider the default partition during pruning, because it cannot prove that no satisfying
row is in there. This is small in practice but it does prevent some partition pruning optimizations.
Edge cases to mention: - You can add an explicit partition later that covers some of the default
partition's range, but Postgres requires the default to be empty for that range — you must move the rows
out first. - Default partitions inherit the same indexes as the parent — they are not a place to dump
unindexed data. - For HASH partitioning, you cannot create a default partition because hash partitions
always cover the full space.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "you can just dump everything in default" — defeats the purpose of
partitioning. - Do not omit the default partition from your design out of misplaced strictness — it is the
safety net that buys you debugging time.
Common follow-up: "Can you add a new explicit partition that overlaps with rows currently in the
default?" — Not directly. You have to detach the default, move the conflicting rows, attach the new
explicit partition, and reattach the default. Plan a maintenance window.
-- LIST partition with default for long-tail regions
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id BIGINT,
  region TEXT NOT NULL,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY LIST (region);
CREATE TABLE customers_in PARTITION OF customers FOR VALUES IN ('IN');
CREATE TABLE customers_us PARTITION OF customers FOR VALUES IN ('US');
CREATE TABLE customers_other PARTITION OF customers DEFAULT;

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Q491 · Sub-Partitioning
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, JP Morgan India, Goldman · Topic: Partitioning
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is sub-partitioning and when does it actually help?
The 30-second answer: Sub-partitioning is partitioning a partition — for example, partition orders by
month at the top level, then sub-partition each month by region. It helps when both dimensions
independently scope your queries and each individual sub-partition is still big enough to justify the per-
partition overhead.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem: you have orders and your queries always
filter by month and by region. Partitioning only by month means scanning all regions within the month;
partitioning only by region means scanning all months within the region. 2. Sub-partition: top-level
RANGE by month, second-level LIST by region. Each leaf partition is orders_2026_05_in, holding
May 2026 Indian orders only. 3. The win is double pruning — the planner can drop entire months and
entire regions independently. Combined with partition-wise joins, this gets very fast for analytical queries.
4. Acknowledge the cost: you now have N×M partitions instead of N+M. If you had 36 months and 5
regions, you go from 36 partitions to 180. Operational overhead climbs.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres declarative partitioning supports sub-partitioning since version 10 —
every partition can itself be PARTITION BY .... - Default partitions at the sub-level are allowed,
giving you a per-month catch-all. Useful for new regions. - Index management becomes harder — each
leaf has its own index, which means more files on disk and more vacuum work.
What NOT to say: - Do not sub-partition speculatively — the operational overhead is real and you
should have measured the access pattern first. - Do not sub-partition by HASH inside RANGE just for
parallelism — single-server parallelism within a partition is usually a better lever.
Common follow-up: "What is the simplest signal that you are about to over-partition?" — When a typical
query touches dozens of partitions and the per-partition fixed cost (open file, look at index root) starts to
dominate the actual scan time. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and look at the planning time — if it grows
linearly with partition count, you are over-partitioning.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 509 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 510
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  region TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_05 PARTITION OF orders
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01')
  PARTITION BY LIST (region);
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_05_in PARTITION OF orders_2026_05 FOR VALUES IN ('IN');
CREATE TABLE orders_2026_05_us PARTITION OF orders_2026_05 FOR VALUES IN ('US');
Q492 · MySQL Partitioning (Legacy Approach)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant · Topic: MySQL partitioning
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How does MySQL partitioning differ from Postgres declarative partitioning?
The 30-second answer: MySQL has had partitioning since version 5.1 with its own syntax — 
PARTITION BY RANGE/LIST/HASH/KEY defined inside the CREATE TABLE statement. It is
functional but less flexible than Postgres declarative partitioning — no default partition, the partition key
must be part of every unique key, sub-partitioning is limited to HASH or KEY at the second level, and
partition-wise joins are not supported.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Show the syntax: 
CREATE TABLE orders (...) PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created_at)) (PARTITION
p2025 VALUES LESS THAN (2026), PARTITION p2026 VALUES LESS THAN (2027),
PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE). 2. The MAXVALUE partition is MySQL's
equivalent of a default partition — anything beyond explicit ranges lands there. You can split it later but it
is not as ergonomic as Postgres default. 3. MySQL supports RANGE, LIST, HASH, KEY (hash on the
primary key), and RANGE COLUMNS / LIST COLUMNS (multi-column partition keys). Sub-partitioning is
allowed only as RANGE→HASH or LIST→HASH — not the freeform composition Postgres allows. 4.
Crucial constraint: every unique key (including the primary key) must contain the partition key. This forces
a lot of schemas to add the partition key column to keys that semantically did not need it.
Edge cases to mention: - Foreign keys are not supported on partitioned tables in MySQL — a hard
limitation that often disqualifies partitioning for transactional schemas. - Partition pruning works for
simple expressions on the partition key — the optimizer is less aggressive than Postgres in pushing
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 510 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 511
through function calls. - ALTER TABLE to add or drop partitions takes a metadata lock — generally fast,
but can stall during heavy concurrent writes.
What NOT to say: - Do not treat MySQL and Postgres partitioning as syntactic variants of the same
thing — the feature sets differ meaningfully. - Do not suggest MySQL partitioning for a schema that uses
foreign keys — the lack of FK support kills the design.
Common follow-up: "If you cannot use foreign keys, how do you maintain referential integrity in a
partitioned MySQL table?" — Application-level checks plus careful transaction discipline. Or you keep
small reference tables unpartitioned and only partition the high-volume fact tables that did not need FKs
to begin with.
-- MySQL
CREATE TABLE events (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT,
  user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  payload JSON,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created_at)) (
  PARTITION p2025 VALUES LESS THAN (2026),
  PARTITION p2026 VALUES LESS THAN (2027),
  PARTITION pmax  VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);
Q493 · SQL Server Partitioning — Functions and Schemes
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: SQL Server partitioning
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Explain SQL Server's partition function and partition scheme model.
The 30-second answer: SQL Server splits partitioning into two objects: a partition function that defines
the boundary values, and a partition scheme that maps partitions to filegroups. You then create the table
or index ON scheme_name(partition_column). The model is more verbose than Postgres but it
gives you fine control over which storage goes to which partition — useful for moving cold partitions to
slow disks.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the two-object split: CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION
pf_monthly (DATETIME2) AS RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES ('2026-01-01',
'2026-02-01', ...). 2. Then the scheme: CREATE PARTITION SCHEME ps_monthly AS
PARTITION pf_monthly TO (fg_2025, fg_2026_01, fg_2026_02, ...). The scheme binds
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 511 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 512
each partition to a filegroup. 3. The table: CREATE TABLE events (...) ON
ps_monthly(created_at). SQL Server now stores each row in the partition (and the filegroup) that
the function maps it to. 4. The killer feature is partition exchange via ALTER TABLE ... SWITCH
PARTITION, which is a metadata-only operation — practically instant — used to load and unload data
in bulk.
Edge cases to mention: - RANGE RIGHT vs RANGE LEFT determines whether the boundary value
belongs to the right or left partition — confusing but matters at the boundary. - Splitting an existing
partition can be expensive — it physically moves rows. Plan splits during maintenance windows. -
Alignment: indexes should be "aligned" (partitioned the same way as the table) to benefit from SWITCH
operations.
What NOT to say: - Do not confuse partition functions with table-valued functions — completely
different objects. - Do not skip the filegroup design — the partition scheme is most of why people pick
SQL Server partitioning in the first place.
Common follow-up: "How would you move data from a staging table into a specific partition of a
production table?" — Load into a staging table with the same structure and filegroup as the target
partition, then ALTER TABLE staging SWITCH TO production PARTITION n. Metadata-only,
takes milliseconds.
-- SQL Server
CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION pf_monthly (DATETIME2)
  AS RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES
  ('2026-01-01', '2026-02-01', '2026-03-01');
CREATE PARTITION SCHEME ps_monthly
  AS PARTITION pf_monthly
  TO (fg_old, fg_2026_01, fg_2026_02, fg_2026_03);
CREATE TABLE events (
  id BIGINT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at DATETIME2 NOT NULL,
  payload NVARCHAR(MAX)
) ON ps_monthly(created_at);
Q494 · Partition Exchange — Fast Bulk Load Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic: Partition operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
You need to load 200 million rows into a partitioned table every night. The straight INSERT is too
slow. What is the idiomatic pattern?
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 512 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 513
The 30-second answer: Load the data into a staging table that has the same structure as one partition,
build all the indexes on the staging table, then attach the staging table as a partition (Postgres: ATTACH
PARTITION; SQL Server: SWITCH PARTITION). The exchange is metadata-only, so the production
table sees the new data instantaneously.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Frame the problem: straight INSERT updates indexes row-by-row,
blows out the buffer cache, and competes with read traffic. For huge nightly loads this is a dealbreaker.
2. The pattern — build a standalone table with identical schema, bulk-load it (COPY in Postgres, BULK
INSERT in SQL Server), create indexes on it in parallel, validate it, then attach. 3. In Postgres: ALTER
TABLE parent ATTACH PARTITION staging FOR VALUES FROM (...) TO (...). The
planner checks that the data in staging matches the bounds — if it does, attachment is metadata-only. 4.
In SQL Server: ALTER TABLE staging SWITCH TO production PARTITION n — even faster,
because SQL Server has explicit partition exchange semantics.
Edge cases to mention: - For Postgres attach to be fast, the staging table must already have all the
same indexes as the parent, and a CHECK constraint matching the partition bounds (CHECK
(created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND created_at < '2026-06-01') — Postgres uses the
CHECK to skip the scan. - For SQL Server SWITCH, both tables must be on the same filegroup and have
identical schema, including all indexes. - The reverse — DETACH PARTITION in Postgres or SWITCH
PARTITION OUT in SQL Server — is how you cleanly archive a cold partition to a separate table that
you can then dump or drop.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose plain INSERT for the nightly load — interviewers test specifically
whether you know this pattern exists. - Do not skip the index build on the staging table — if you attach
without indexes, the parent's queries will be slow for that partition.
Common follow-up: "What goes wrong if the staging table contains a row whose partition key falls
outside the declared bounds?" — Postgres rejects the ATTACH outright. SQL Server's SWITCH also
validates and rejects. Always run a sanity query (SELECT MIN/MAX of the partition key)
before attaching.
-- Postgres bulk-load pattern
CREATE TABLE events_2026_05_staging (LIKE events INCLUDING ALL);
COPY events_2026_05_staging FROM '/data/may_2026.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv);
ALTER TABLE events_2026_05_staging
  ADD CONSTRAINT chk_may
  CHECK (created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND created_at < '2026-06-01');
ALTER TABLE events ATTACH PARTITION events_2026_05_staging
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01');

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Section D — Materialized Views
Q495 · Materialized View Basics — Postgres and Oracle
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Goldman · Topic: Materialized views
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
What is a materialized view and how does it differ from a regular view?
The 30-second answer: A regular view is a saved query — every SELECT against it executes the
underlying query. A materialized view physically stores the query result on disk, so reads are as fast as
reads from a table. The cost is that the stored data is a snapshot — it goes stale until you refresh it.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Start with the dichotomy: regular view = virtual, materialized view =
physical. The application queries both the same way; the difference is where the work happens. 2. Use
case: a sales-by-month dashboard runs a 30-second aggregation query. Wrap it in a materialized view,
refresh nightly, and the dashboard reads in 50 ms. 3. Mention that Postgres added materialized views in
version 9.3 — the syntax is CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW name AS SELECT .... Oracle has had
them forever and has more advanced refresh modes. 4. Be ready for the refresh-strategy question — that
is where the depth lies.
Edge cases to mention: - A materialized view in Postgres can have indexes, just like a table — and
those indexes are maintained during refresh. - Refresh is a full re-execute of the query in vanilla Postgres
— there is no incremental refresh built in (Oracle has FAST refresh; Postgres relies on extensions). - The
view is empty immediately after creation if you use WITH NO DATA — you have to refresh once before
queries return anything.
What NOT to say: - Do not call a materialized view "a cached query" — that minimises the operational
implications. It is a real table that needs space, indexing and refresh strategy. - Do not assume
materialized view data is automatically up-to-date — that is the single biggest source of bugs in
dashboards built on them.
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between a materialized view and a summary table?" — A
materialized view has a declarative query attached, so the engine knows how to refresh it. A summary
table is whatever you populated it with — usually maintained by your own ETL code. Materialized views
are summary tables with batteries included.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 514 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 515
-- Postgres
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW sales_by_month AS
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       region,
       SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1, 2;
CREATE INDEX idx_sales_by_month_region ON sales_by_month (region, month);
Q496 · Refresh Strategies — COMPLETE vs CONCURRENTLY vs FAST
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Materialized view refresh
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Walk me through the refresh options for materialized views in Postgres and Oracle.
The 30-second answer: Postgres has two modes: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (rebuilds and
takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — blocks reads) and REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
CONCURRENTLY (rebuilds into a new copy and swaps — reads keep working but the view needs a
unique index). Oracle has COMPLETE (rebuild) and FAST (incremental, requires materialized view logs on
the base tables).
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres COMPLETE (the default): the engine truncates the view, re-
runs the defining query, and rebuilds the indexes. Fast for small views, terrible for big ones because the
table is locked for the duration. 2. Postgres CONCURRENTLY (added in 9.4): the engine computes the
diff using the unique index and applies INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to bring the view in sync. Reads see
consistent state throughout. Mandatory prerequisite: at least one unique index on the view. 3. Oracle
COMPLETE: same as Postgres — full rebuild. 4. Oracle FAST: incremental refresh using materialized view
logs (essentially triggers on the base tables that record changes). The view applies only the deltas — fast
for big views with small change rates, but the logs add write overhead on the base tables.
Edge cases to mention: - Postgres CONCURRENTLY is slower than the non-concurrent version
because it has to compute the diff — pick concurrent only when read availability matters more than
refresh speed. - Oracle FAST refresh has many restrictions on the defining query — joins, aggregates and
subqueries must all be in the supported subset. Read the Oracle docs carefully. - pg_ivm and similar
Postgres extensions are starting to bring incremental refresh to Postgres — worth mentioning if asked
about the future direction.
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 515 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 516
What NOT to say: - Do not call REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW "non-blocking" — without
CONCURRENTLY it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks every reader. - Do not promise
Oracle-style FAST refresh in vanilla Postgres — it does not exist yet in the core product.
Common follow-up: "Why does CONCURRENTLY need a unique index?" — Because the diff algorithm
joins old and new rows on the unique key to figure out which rows are insertions, deletions, and updates.
Without a unique key it cannot identify rows.
-- Postgres
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_sales_by_month_pk ON sales_by_month (month, region);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY sales_by_month;
Q497 · Indexed Views in SQL Server (Equivalent)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Topic: Indexed views
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
SQL Server does not call them materialized views — it calls them indexed views. How do you
create one and what are the restrictions?
The 30-second answer: You create a view with WITH SCHEMABINDING, then create a unique
clustered index on the view. SQL Server then physically materialises the view and keeps it up to date
automatically as the base tables change. The restrictions are extensive — deterministic SELECT, two-
part names, no outer joins, no subqueries in many positions, and the right SET options on the session.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. The recipe: CREATE VIEW v WITH SCHEMABINDING AS
SELECT ..., then CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX idx ON v(...). SCHEMABINDING
prevents the underlying tables from being altered in ways that break the view. 2. Once the clustered
index exists, SQL Server automatically maintains the view on every base-table change — no manual
refresh. This is the key difference from Postgres materialized views. 3. The cost: every INSERT, UPDATE,
DELETE on the base tables now also writes to the indexed view. For heavy-write tables this can double
or triple write cost. 4. The restrictions are real: deterministic, schema-bound, certain aggregates only
(COUNT_BIG, SUM, but not COUNT directly), referenced tables must be in the same database. Read the
official list before designing.
Edge cases to mention: - Required session SET options for the connection that creates the index
include ANSI_NULLS, ANSI_PADDING, ANSI_WARNINGS, ARITHABORT,
CONCAT_NULL_YIELDS_NULL, QUOTED_IDENTIFIER all ON. Forgetting one breaks the index creation.
- The clustered index on the view must be unique — same constraint as Postgres CONCURRENTLY. -
The Enterprise edition optimizer can use indexed views automatically even when the query references
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 516 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 517
the base tables directly (query rewrite). Standard edition does not — you must reference the view by
name with WITH (NOEXPAND).
What NOT to say: - Do not claim SQL Server indexed views are "just like Postgres materialized views"
— the auto-maintenance changes the entire operational model. - Do not forget SCHEMABINDING —
without it, the index creation fails.
Common follow-up: "Why do you need SCHEMABINDING?" — Because the indexed view
materialisation depends on the schema of the base tables. SCHEMABINDING prevents ALTER or 
DROP of those tables in ways that would invalidate the view.
-- SQL Server
CREATE VIEW sales_by_month_v
  WITH SCHEMABINDING AS
SELECT region,
       CAST(YEAR(created_at) AS INT) AS yr,
       CAST(MONTH(created_at) AS INT) AS mo,
       SUM(amount) AS total,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS row_count
FROM dbo.orders
GROUP BY region, YEAR(created_at), MONTH(created_at);
CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX idx_sbm
  ON sales_by_month_v (region, yr, mo);
Q498 · Materialized View vs Denormalization vs Cache
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Cred · Topic: Architecture tradeoffs
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
A dashboard needs aggregated metrics that take 30 seconds to compute. You could materialize
the result, denormalize the underlying schema, or cache the response in Redis. How do you
choose?
The 30-second answer: Materialize when the underlying query is complex but stable and the data can
be slightly stale. Denormalize when you need real-time accuracy and you control all the writers. Cache
when freshness windows are very short, the data is identical to what you return to the user, and you want
minimal database changes. They are not exclusive — many production systems use all three at different
layers.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Materialized view sits in the database, refreshed on a schedule. Pros:
declarative, queryable with SQL, indexable. Cons: stale until refresh, refresh load on the database, no
incremental refresh in vanilla Postgres. 2. Denormalization moves aggregates into the base tables — 
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 517 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 518
users.total_orders updated on every order insert. Pros: always fresh. Cons: every writer has to
maintain the column, race conditions if multiple writers, schema couples reads to writes. 3. Cache
(Redis, Memcached) sits outside the database. Pros: very low read latency, no database load, easy to
invalidate. Cons: another piece of infrastructure, stale-after-update window, harder to query slices of. 4.
Pick by access pattern: dashboards with daily refresh → materialized view. Per-user counters →
denormalized. Hot per-page response data → cache. Often you layer: materialized view feeds the cache
feeds the dashboard.
Edge cases to mention: - Materialized view refresh becomes a load spike — schedule it carefully.
CONCURRENTLY helps but does not eliminate the spike. - Denormalized counters are race-prone — use
atomic UPDATE (SET count = count + 1), not read-modify-write. - Cache invalidation is the
second hardest problem in computer science — pick TTL-based or write-through deliberately.
What NOT to say: - Do not declare one approach universally best — interviewers want the multi-axis
reasoning. - Do not skip the operational story (refresh load, cache eviction, schema migrations) — that is
what separates an architecture answer from an implementation answer.
Common follow-up: "Walk me through a layered architecture for the dashboard." — Base tables →
materialized view refreshed every 15 minutes → cache layer with 60-second TTL → API. Each layer
absorbs a different latency budget, and a failure of one layer degrades gracefully.
-- Hybrid: materialized view as the truth, app caches reads
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW dashboard_metrics AS
SELECT region, date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1, 2;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_dm ON dashboard_metrics (region, day);
Q499 · Stale Materialized View Detection
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic: Materialized view
operations
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
How do you know whether a materialized view is up to date, and how do you alert when it has
become stale?
The 30-second answer: Track the last refresh time as metadata — either in a small audit table you write
to after every refresh, or by reading from system catalogs (pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 518 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 519
is a rough proxy; better is a custom audit table). Alert when NOW() - last_refresh exceeds your
SLO. Some teams also compare row counts between base tables and the view to detect refresh lag.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Postgres does not store the last refresh time on the materialized view
itself — the catalog has no last_refreshed_at column. You have to record it yourself. 2. The
simple pattern: a mv_refresh_log table with mv_name, refreshed_at, duration_ms, 
rows_after. Insert a row at the end of every refresh job. Your monitoring queries this. 3. Detect lag
with SELECT NOW() - MAX(refreshed_at) AS lag FROM mv_refresh_log WHERE mv_name
= 'sales_by_month'. Alert if lag exceeds the SLO — e.g. 90 minutes for a 60-minute refresh
schedule. 4. Mention freshness queries — comparing the latest event timestamp in the base table to the
latest in the view tells you the data lag, not just the wall-clock lag.
Edge cases to mention: - Wall-clock lag and data lag are different — the view might refresh on time but
the source data ETL is backed up. Track both. - Refresh failures should alert separately — a refresh that
errored out leaves the view at the last successful state, which silently goes stale. - For very large views,
the refresh duration itself can exceed the refresh interval — instrument to catch this.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume the database has a built-in "is this view stale" function — Postgres
does not. - Do not poll the materialized view itself to check freshness — query a metadata table, the view
is what you are trying to test.
Common follow-up: "What if the refresh job runs but the data inside the view is somehow wrong?" —
That is a data quality problem, not a freshness problem. Add a separate validation step — e.g. compare
aggregate sums between the view and a sample re-aggregation of the base table.
-- Audit table + refresh wrapper
CREATE TABLE mv_refresh_log (
  mv_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  refreshed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
  duration_ms INT,
  rows_after BIGINT
);
-- Alert query
SELECT mv_name, NOW() - MAX(refreshed_at) AS lag
FROM mv_refresh_log
GROUP BY mv_name
HAVING NOW() - MAX(refreshed_at) > INTERVAL '90 minutes';
Q500 · Materialized Views for Reporting — Common Patterns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart · Topic: Reporting patterns
The question (interviewer's verbatim phrasing):
Learn & Excel · Core SQL Library — 500 Questions 519 / 521
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 520
Give me three concrete patterns where materialized views are the right tool for reporting.
The 30-second answer: First, daily aggregates — sales_by_day refreshed nightly powers every
revenue dashboard. Second, expensive joins denormalized once — enriched_orders that joins
orders, customers, products and payments. Third, rolling windows — 
last_30_days_active_users recomputed hourly. All three replace a slow query with a fast table
read, accepting controlled staleness in exchange.
Step-by-step thought process: 1. Pattern one — pre-aggregated time series. Base table orders
with millions of rows, materialized view sales_by_day with hundreds. Dashboard queries are sub-
second. Refresh nightly with CONCURRENTLY so dashboards stay available. 2. Pattern two — flattened
wide table for BI tools. Joins five reference tables to produce a fact table that Tableau or Metabase can
query directly without complex SQL. Refresh hourly or whenever upstream tables change. 3. Pattern
three — rolling-window metrics. WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days' is
expensive to compute on every dashboard load; materialize it and refresh hourly. Acceptable lag for
cohort analytics. 4. Mention what is NOT a good fit — anything that needs real-time accuracy
(transaction confirmations, current account balance), anything where the underlying data changes too
fast to make any refresh window viable.
Edge cases to mention: - For dashboards with multiple users, the staleness perception is per-user —
show a "last updated at" timestamp so users know they are not looking at live data. - If two materialized
views feed the same dashboard and refresh independently, they can briefly disagree — schedule their
refreshes together or document the inconsistency window. - Some materialized views naturally evolve in
size — sales_by_day adds one row per day per region. Plan for retention and archiving.
What NOT to say: - Do not propose materialized views for ledger or balance queries — staleness is
unacceptable there. - Do not use materialized views as a substitute for proper schema design — if your
base tables are unfit, no view can save them.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle a materialized view whose source data backfills retroactively —
e.g. someone corrects a record from three weeks ago?" — Schedule a deeper refresh window that goes
back further than the natural change horizon. Or use a partition-aware refresh that rebuilds only the
affected time slices. This is exactly the sort of operational nuance that signals senior experience to the
interviewer.

-- Pattern: rolling 30-day active users
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW active_users_30d AS
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS event_count, MAX(created_at) AS last_seen
FROM events
WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY user_id;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_au30_user ON active_users_30d (user_id);
-- Refresh hourly via cron
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY active_users_30d;
